en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
A New Commentary on the Sīlakkhandha Chapter of the Dīghanikāya.
(Second Part) 2.
Commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta: Commentary on the Discourse concerning the King and His Ministers.
150. Now, in order to show that the sequence for the commentary on the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* has arrived, he said: “Thus... [the] Sutta,” and so forth.

Therein, “explanation of the words in successive order” (*anupubbapadavaṇṇanā*) means an explanation of the words according to their sequence; what is meant is an explanation word by word in succession.
For it was stated previously that even an explanation of a word that is already clear, when given elsewhere, is called an “explanation of the words in successive order.”
Thus it is said. And having done so, they also read it as “Apubbapadavaṇṇanā,” meaning “the commentary on words not previously commented upon.

It is called by that name because it was taken up by kings as being preeminent due to its possession of excellence in difficult countries, locations, and distinctions, and not merely by way of its name;
thus he says, “For that...,” and so forth. [Objection: But is it not in the Mahāvagga, in the Mahāgovinda Sutta?
"This priest has arrived; it is not the king. Why was he taken as one who should be addressed by the title 'king'? [The answer is:
Although this [territory] was already possessed by the priest Mahāgovinda, it was likewise possessed by the Magadhan king named Reṇu;

thus it was said because of the possibility of such a situation, but he was not taken as one who should be addressed by the title "king" because he was not actually the king. For the description of his being possessed by Mahāgovinda...
At that time, this was the sign that Reṇu had been taken into the king’s service;

for he was the chaplain who performed all the king’s duties, and it is a common practice in the world to say, "Even what is done by one occupied with royal business is done by the king. This is what is meant:
after King Mandhātu had appointed the Bodhisatta Mahāgovinda as his chaplain, and King Reṇu [had likewise taken him into his service].
It is called Rājagaha because it was surrounded by other kings. Some, however, say that Mahāgovinda was a certain ancient king of great power.
"Because it was surrounded" means because it was surrounded by being made the royal capital. For "gaha" means that which is seized;
it is "Rājagaha" because it is the seizure (gaha) of kings, or by kings. The neuter designation is used in view of the word "nagara" (city).
Furthermore, it is called Rājagaha because it was caused to be built by a king who had entered the city;
it is also called Rājagaha because it resembles a house surrounded by kings, being encircled by the five mountains beginning with Gijjhakūṭa;
it is also called Rājagaha because it is a royal residence due to its magnificent palaces; and it is so called because, due to its well-arranged protection, one who desires to cause harm—

It is called Rājagaha because it was the "seizing place" (gaha) for rival kings who came against it; it is called Rājagaha because it became the "home" (geha) for those kings, having been properly established by them after they saw it;
it is called Rājagaha because it "shines" (rājati) with the beauty of its parks and groves;

and it is called Rājagaha because beings grasp it and take possession of it through their sense of ownership due to the comfort of living there. Such are the ways [it is explained]. It is merely a name.
The meaning is "in the manner previously stated. Furthermore, because that region is a distinguished place and thus a domain for exalted beings, he says, "But this," and so forth.

Therein, the phrase "at the time of a Buddha and at the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch" is stated by way of general prevalence, since it can occasionally occur at other times as well; and the phrase "there is a city" is merely an illustration of a human habitation.
Because it is impossible. For it has been said: “At other times it is empty,” and so forth. “Of them” means of the *yakkhas*.

“Residential grove” (*vasanavana*) means a nearby park that serves as a place of recreation. “Without distinction” means by way of the commonality of being a monastery (*vihāra*), without reference to a specific qualification established by the proximity of another word.
The meaning is as follows: It is established by the proximity of other words in such passages as, “He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; he dwells having attained the first jhāna;
he dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;
he dwells having attained the signless concentration of mind through non-attention to all signs. Thus it is said.
By means of a specific qualification (*visesa-parāmasana*), there is, in due order, an indication of one who possesses a particular mode of abiding such as the postures (*iriyāpatha*) and so forth;
this [present case] is not like that, for it indicates one who possesses a certain mode of abiding without such a specific qualification.

And even though, according to the method already stated, it indicates one who possesses a certain mode of abiding, here it is specifically the indication of one who possesses a particular mode of abiding consisting of the postures.
He shows that it is possible by means of the passage beginning with “But here,” and so forth.
But why is it that, even in the absence of a specific reference established by the proximity of another word, a description of one who possesses a particular state of dwelling is possible here?

It is precisely because there is no specific term—counted as another word—that describes one who possesses a particular state of dwelling. For when a specific term is absent, one who desires a specific [meaning]...
"A distinction must be applied. Furthermore, since it is established by implication through the demonstration of the association with postures (*iriyāpatha*), only such a demonstration is possible.
Why is this meaning established? Because it is common even to the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*) and so forth;
for never does that exist without the dwelling in a posture, as there would be no maintenance of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) in its absence.

Iriyā is the movement of postures; it is bodily activity. Because it is the means for the occurrence of that activity, it is called *iriyāpatha* (mode of deportment), such as standing, sitting, and so forth.
Indeed, it is not possible to carry out any bodily activity without the states of standing, sitting, and so on;
therefore, these are said to be the means for its occurrence. One dwells or proceeds by means of this; thus, it is mere dwelling (*viharaṇamatta*).

Or, "vihāra" means a state; that very state is "tathā. In terms of its meaning, however, it is simply a continuity of the fourfold stream of material form proceeding in the manner of standing, sitting, and so forth.
"Dibba" (divine) means existing in the heavens (*divi*); the meaning is that it exists there in the world of the gods, such as the Brahmā-pārisajja, because it occurs frequently there.
Alternatively, it is "dibba" because it conduces to divine power (*dibbānubhāva*) therein, by way of the exercise of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and so forth.
Or, because it is of great range (*mahāgati*), it is divine; that itself is the abiding (*vihāra*). Or, an abiding that brings about a divine state is a "divine abiding" (*dibbavihāra*);

these are the sublime jhānas (*mahaggatajjhānāni*). However, in the *Netti* [Netti 86], the four formless attainments (*āruppasamāpatti*) are mentioned separately as "imperturbable abidings" (*āneñjavihāra*).
This, however, indicates their status as a specific type of cultivation, just as the jhānas of loving-kindness and so forth have the status of "divine abidings" (*brahmavihāra*).
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṇḍhāya*). However, in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), because they bring about a divine state, they too are called "divine abidings" (*dibbavihāra*).

They are "divine abidings" (*brahmavihāra*) because they are the most excellent (*seṭṭha*) abidings due to their proceeding by way of bringing about welfare for Brahmas or those who have become Brahmas.

They are the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) that proceed by way of the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettā-jjhāna*) and so forth. They are "noble" (*ariya*) because they are supreme and not shared by others.
Or, "abodes of the Noble Ones" (*ariyavihārā*) refers to the four attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

Here, however, the divine, brahma, and noble abodes of the Blessed One consist of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) that proceed by means of it, and the attainment of the supreme fruit belonging to the fourth jhāna.
Regarding the phrase "indicating possession of one or another abode": because those [abodes] do not occur simultaneously, it indicates the state of being possessed of one or two of them.
This is a description [of the Blessed One] either by the omission of the state (*bhāva*) or by emphasizing the state itself.
For the Blessed One, when the world is overwhelmed by greed, hatred, and delusion, enters and dwells in various abodes for the purpose of training those to be trained through his own practice.

Thus, it is said that whenever beings act wrongly regarding sense-pleasures, at that time the Blessed One dwells in the divine abode (*dibba-vihāra*) for the purpose of generating the wholesome root of non-greed in them.
“Perhaps, having seen this practice and developed a liking for it, they might become dispassionate toward sensual pleasures.

But when beings act wrongly toward one another for the sake of power, he then dwells in the divine abode of loving-kindness (*mettā*) in order to arouse the root of non-hatred (*adosa-kusalamūla*) in them, thinking:
“Perhaps, having seen this practice and developed a liking for it, they might pacify their hatred through non-hatred.”
But when those who have gone forth dispute over matters pertaining to the Dhamma, he dwells in the noble abode for the sake of generating the wholesome root of non-delusion in them, thinking:

"Perhaps, by seeing this practice and conceiving a liking for it, they might pacify their delusion through non-delusion. And having acted thus, through these divine, brahma, and noble abodes, for the sake of beings...

It carries away various kinds of welfare and happiness; and by means of the maintenance of the postures (*iriyāpatha-vihāra*), it carries the personal existence (*attabhāva*) along without it falling, having interrupted one posture that is causing distress with another posture. Thus it is said: "The indication of one who possesses a particular state of abiding.
The passage beginning with "By that" is a demonstration of the excellence of the aforementioned commentary; the meaning is "therefore," which serves as a corroboration of the meaning already stated.
Or: "He dwells by means of that mode of conduct (*iriyāpatha*)," such is the connection. Furthermore, in the phrase "he dwells speaking thus," the word *vi-* indicates the sense of separation;

it makes known that the root *harati* has the meaning "leads" or "carries out," because it is stated in the manner of a separation and a leading away in the passage beginning with "even while standing.
For this being the case, what [is separated] there, and by what?
"Cutting off" and "how does he lead whom?"—this is said with reference to the urging of one who is hidden within. The connection beginning with "For he...

and so forth is also thus established. Even though the Blessed One is able to maintain himself for a very long time in a single posture, nevertheless, in order to show that this is the nature of a body subject to grasping (*upādinnaka*), he says: "The obstruction of one posture," and so forth.
It is said. "Not falling" (*apari-patanta*) is a neuter present participle; the meaning is "having made it so that it does not fall.

Furthermore, because the Blessed One dwells wherever he may be, teaching the Dhamma to those capable of being trained and spending his time in various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), he brings manifold happiness to sentient beings and to himself; therefore, [the phrase] means "he brings manifold [happiness]."
"Viharati" (dwells)—in this context, the meaning should be understood in this way.

Having stated "at Rājagaha" for the purpose of indicating the village that serves as his resort, he said "in the Mango Grove" again for the purpose of showing the dwelling place appropriate for Buddhas; thus he said, "This is his," and so forth. "His" means the Blessed One's. "That" refers to...

Of the alms-resort village known as Rājagaha. By means of this phrase, "in the mango grove near Rājagaha," he shows that the word for the location, "at Rājagaha" (*rājagahe*), occurs by virtue of its proximity to that [grove], and thus it too must be spoken of in terms of its proximity to it.
"In the sense of proximity" (*samīpatthe*) means in the sense of the vicinity of the mango grove. "This" refers to the expression "at Rājagaha. "The locative case" (*bhummavacanaṃ*).
This refers to the locative case. For it is called "locative" (*bhummavacana*) because it denotes a location (*bhūmi*), that is, a locus (*ādhāra*);

or alternatively, it is the grammatical inflection (*vibhatti*) occurring in the locative, and what is connected with that is likewise so called. The meaning is: a word joined with the seventh (locative) inflection.
This is what is intended: although the Blessed One dwells right in the mango grove itself, yet because [the person] has come into its vicinity...

The locative expression "in Rājagaha" is also stated for the purpose of indicating the village within its range, just as one says, "the cows graze in the Gaṅgā," or "the Gaggas' family lives at the well. By this very principle, if the Blessed One dwells in Rājagaha, then it should not be said that he is "in the Mango Grove";
and if he is in the Mango Grove, likewise it should not be said that he is "in Rājagaha. It is not [a contradiction].

It should be understood that the objection—that because there is no locus within a locus here (as there is in expressions such as “he dwells in the palace at Pāṭaliputta”), a dual designation of the locus would be appropriate—is rendered groundless.

[The term] *komārabhacca* is simply *kumārabhata*, with the suffix added for its own sake (*sakatthavuttipaccaya*), or according to etymological method (*niruttinaya*), just as “medicine” (*bhesajja*) is simply “the best of roots” (*bhisagga*). This is shown by the phrase beginning with “As it has been said.”
He establishes that meaning by means of the Khandhakapāḷi. And as to why the mango grove is mentioned in connection with Jīvaka, in response to this inquiry, he says “But this...
and so forth, showing that matter from its very beginning.
“Overwhelmed by humors” (dosābhisanna) means having humors aggravated by wind, bile, and so forth. “Having purged” (virecetvā) means having separated [the body] from the provocation of the humors.
"A pair of Siveyyaka cloths" means a pair of highly valuable cloths produced in the kingdom of Sivi.
"Two or three times a day" means two or three times during the course of a single day; this genitive case is used in the sense of the locative, meaning "twice or thrice on one and the same day.
"With the color of a copper plate" means with the color of a plate of red copper.

“With robes and almsfood” means with robes and with food. By the phrase “referring to that,” it is shown that the Blessed One did not dwell merely in the mango grove itself, but rather in the monastery constructed in that manner.

Furthermore, this indicates the meaning of what was spoken with reference to that, as it is not mentioned separately as a distinct legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) because it is subsumed under that [monastery].
For when there is a general category, there is a specific determination (*niddhāraṇa*) made with reference to it.
"Half-thirteen" means twelve and a half. [The phrase] "by such hundreds of monks" refers here specifically to the hundred.

Since the word *addha* (half) is used in connection with that which possesses a portion of it—and that portion being fifty—it is stated as "by a hundred less half" (*addhasatena*) and so forth, in order to convey the meaning: "thirteen hundred monks less fifty. Thus, it is simply "a hundred less half."
Or half of a hundred, likewise.
It "shines" (rājati) because it glitters and is beautiful through its own perfection of sovereignty.

It "delights" (rañjeti) by means of giving and so forth, and by the four bases of sympathy such as agriculture and prosperity; or the meaning is that it causes passion for itself. Here, the word "and" (ca) [indicates]...
The meaning is "determination. Because the word *puthu* (many) refers to the inhabitants of the country, it is stated as "of the Magadhans";

or else, because by mentioning the country its inhabitants are included. "Of the king" means of his father, King Bimbisāra. He "seeks to injure" (*sasati*) or "harms" (*hiṃsati*), thus he is a *sattu* (enemy);
one who is an enemy from birth is *Ajātasattu*. And by the statement "pointed out by those who read omens," [it is shown] that for him while yet unborn...
The state of being an enemy does not yet exist; however, he shows that it is spoken of in this way precisely because the state of being an enemy has been designated in such a manner.
Furthermore, they say that even though he is not yet born, he is called the king’s enemy because the queen’s pregnancy craving (*dohaḷa*) arose with the thought, "May I drink the blood of the king."
With the words beginning “In that,” he explains and establishes that meaning. *Dohaḷo* means longing or desire.
*Bhāriye* means heavy, or that which is impossible for others to accomplish. *Asakkontī* means being unable; *akathentī* means while not speaking.
*Nibandhitvā* means having bound with words. *Suvaṇṇasatthakena* means with a golden knife, made of solid gold.
The meaning is as follows: they say it is improper to bring the king’s body near an iron [implement].

Or, even if the phrase "with an iron knife encased in gold" is taken in this sense, the intended meaning remains the same. "Having had his arm slit open" means having had the arm slit by means of piercing the blood-carrying vessels (*lohita-sirā*).
Because pure blood is difficult for a pregnant woman to digest, he mixed it with water.
He made [her] drink. "He will be killed" (*haññissati*) means "he will be killed," the sense being that he will be slain in the future.
With the intention that the words of the fortune-tellers might either be true or false, it was said: "It is not known whether [it will be] a son or a daughter.
By the words "of himself" (*attano*), etc., he showed another reason and prevented [the killing]. The state of a king is *rajja*; near to the kingdom...
It functions as *oparajja*, meaning a position or office. *Mahā* means great;
for the substitution of *mahā* for the word *mahanta* occurs both in compounds and in sentences. *Dhurā* means those who have become the leaders of the group;

the sense is that they are "bearers" (*dhorayha*) or elders. "I take up the burden" (*dhuraṃ nīharāmi*) means I carry the responsibility of the group; I shall bring about the cohesion of the community.
This has been said. With the words “He was not able,” etc., he shows again the manner of reflection.

“By a miracle of psychic power” means by the transformation of his appearance into that of a youth wearing a girdle of snakes. “By that” means by the state of having a short lifespan. “Hi” is a mere particle.
Or, “tena hi” is a particle used in the sense of encouragement. Therefore it is said: “He dismissed the youth... [and so forth]... saying, ‘I shall become a Buddha.’”

Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "this"; the meaning is: "according to the method that has come down in this Khandhaka. By the words "previously indeed" (*pubbe kho*) and so forth, it is also the Khandhaka-pāḷi itself.
*Potthaniya* means a knife; it is also called a "claw" (*nakhara*). "Day by day" (*divā divase*) means even during the day.

This locative case is used in the sense of comparison, as seen elsewhere in the expression "day by day" (*divā divasassa*). It may also be understood as "during the day of the day" (*divassa divase*).
It is permissible [to use the word *diva*] even for that which does not end in *-a*, because the word *diva* exists [in this sense].
Grammarians also accept the word *diva* as a *nepātika* (irregular) form; the meaning is "at the time of midday. For that [time] is a specific part of the day, yet it is called "the day" (*diva*).

The phrase beginning with "frightened" (*bhīto*) is a synonym; or rather, he is "frightened" by the stiffening of the body. He is "agitated" (*ubbiggo*) by the throbbing of the heart-flesh. This is due to the suspicion: "They might find out, or they might not."
*Ussaṅkī*: being terrified because of the fear that was arising within himself once he had become aware [of the danger].
*Vuttappakāraṃ*: the manner spoken by Devadatta; *vippakāraṃ* means harm, lack of benefit, or contrary action. *Sabbe bhikkhū*: this refers to the assembly of Devadatta. *Acchinditvā*:

having plundered by way of removal. *Rajjena*: by means of the conquered territory. For it is said that the place where the command of a single king prevails is called "kingdom" (*rajja*), or it may mean by way of the state of being a king.
The etymologists explain that *manoratha* is derived from *manasa-attha* (the aim of the mind) by adding the letter *r* and dropping the letter *t*;

or, because it causes the mind to wander among various objects, it is like a chariot for the mind, thus called *manoratha*; or alternatively, it is called *manoratha* because the mind itself is like a chariot.
"I am one who performs good deeds" means: I am a doer of good deeds. "Disrespect" means: contemptuous disregard.
"Root-annihilation" (*mūlaghacca*) is said with reference to the taking of life; this is a neuter noun in the locative case.
It is said that the execution of royal families by means of the sword was not the custom of kings; therefore, he spoke the words beginning with "But surely, venerable sir.
A "house of heating" (*tāpanageha*) is a house for being subjected to heat, but that [execution] was carried out by means of smoke alone. Hence it is called a "smoke-house" (*dhūmaghara*).
“For the purpose of performing work” means specifically for the purpose of performing labor such as heating [the body].
“With a high limb” (*uccaṅga*) refers to one whose limb is elevated because it is covered by something; here, it is intended in the sense of a concealed, protruding limb.

Therefore it was said: “Do not let them enter having made [it] a high limb. There is also a reading, “having placed in the lap” (*ucchaṅge katvā*); if that were the case, it would refer only to the middle limb.
The meaning is: "having placed something to be taken in the lap. *Moḷi* refers to the topknot, as in such passages as "having cut off the topknot scented with choice perfumes," and so forth.
Therefore he said, "having bound the topknot. Regarding *catumadhura*:
they say it is a specific kind of drink prepared from the four sweets—namely, ghee, sugar, honey, and coconut oil; this [explanation] is according to the text of the *Mahādhammasamādāna-sutta*.
It does not agree. For it is said there: "Curd, honey, ghee, and molasses mixed together in one place," and in its commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) it is said:
"Curd and honey means very pure curd and very sweet honey.
'Mixed together in one place' means having been made into one, blended, and stirred. Of that..."

“While he was drinking that medicine of the four sweets,” the King, reflecting that “death by one’s own hand is not fitting,” sustained himself by licking her body; for the Noble Ones do not bring about their own downfall.
“By the bliss of the path and fruit” means possessing the bliss of the path and fruit, and by means of walking meditation associated with the bliss of the fruit of stream-entry.

The meaning is "he maintains himself. "I shall take away" means "I shall remove. "With charcoal that has been stripped of its glow" means with pure embers from which the glowing heat has departed and the cinders have vanished.
"By someone being made known" means by someone being properly informed; it is said, "by being exhorted. "For the purpose of grooming the beard" means for the purpose of cleaning the beard.
"Act according to his mind" means act in such a way that it is pleasing to the king. "Formerly..."
In a previous existence. On the terrace of the cetiya (*cetiyaṅgaṇe*): on the ground of the cetiya, which serves as a place for worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
For the purpose of sitting (*nisajjanatthāya*): for the sake of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha’s sitting down. A prepared mat of reeds (*paññattakaṭasārakaṃ*): a superior mat of reeds that ought to be prepared.
For such a mat is called a "mat of reeds" (*kaṭasāraka*). Of that (*tassa*): of the two kinds of deeds mentioned above.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this was done by him solely through the corruption of the mind. As it is said:
"States have mind as their forerunner, mind is their chief, they are all mind-made.
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind..."
“Then suffering follows him, like the wheel follows the hoof of the draught-ox.
Here, *paricāraka* means a companion. Although there is no actual division, the expression of division is well-known in the world; thus it is said, “he was reborn as a *yakkha*.
For here, even though it is a single act of arising, the expression of division is used because he exists by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Alternatively, the phrase "arising by way of occurrence" (*pavattivasena nibbatti*) should be applied to each [term] individually;

or rather, the single term "arising" (*nibbatti*) is stated with two words in order to indicate a preeminent arising known as "occurrence" (*pavattanasaṅkhāta*) by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhivasena*).
For such a statement is seen only in the context of arising by way of rebirth-linking: "The divine son named Makkaṭaka arose, and the one named Kaṇṭaka... [and so forth]."
It is as in such passages as, "He was reborn, [a being] named Maṇḍūka... he was reborn," and so forth.

Alternatively, with respect to the sense of the abstract state (bhāva) of two words, the nominative case is used in the sense of a genitive (sāmī-attha) in terms like "of a yakkha" (*yakkhassa*), because the latter qualifies the former;

thus the meaning is "rebirth by way of the state of a yakkha who is a servant," or else the suffix *-tvā* here has the sense of a causal condition (*hetvattha*), [meaning] "from the state of a yakkha."

"Causes for its continued existence. Furthermore, although this king possessed great merit, it should be understood that he was reborn in that very place due to his long-accumulated inclination (*nikanti*) from having been born there frequently in the past.
"On that very day" means on the very day of the king's death. "Having shaken" [it]—this is because of the powerful nature of his affection for his son.
Because of the force of that co-nascent joy and its expansive nature, it churned the entire body by means of pervading it with the material phenomena (rūpadhamma) originated by that [joy].
Therefore he said: "It remained in contact even with the marrow of the bones. "The quality of affection" refers to the quality of the father’s attachment toward himself.
Hence it was said: "Even when I was born," and so forth. "Release! Release!"—this was due to his urgency.
And it was spoken on account of grief.
"Without having made [him] dance" means without having abandoned him.

Regarding the phrase "having caused the elephant Nālāgiri to be released," here the word *iti* has the sense of "manner"; by this, it is meant: "by such a manner as the dispatching of murderous men, and so forth."
He refers back to the three types previously mentioned; however, that [specific type] has not been seen anywhere.
"The five grounds" refers to the five grounds stated in the Vinaya, beginning with: "It would be good, Bhante, if the bhikkhus were forest-dwellers for as long as life lasts.

Regarding the word "having requested," the meaning is "having acted as if he were requesting"; for it is not the case that one who intends to practice actually requests—it is in this sense that the term is used.
This is indeed stated in the Vinaya. The connection is: "Having thought, 'I shall persuade him,' he caused a schism in the Saṅgha.
And this was said by way of showing that his duty had not yet been relinquished; for even if a schism in the Saṅgha had not been caused, he would have been persuaded by them nonetheless.
"Warm blood" means blood that has become warm, produced by intense grief. "In the Great Niraya" means in the Avīci Niraya.
"Vitthārakathānayo" means the mere method of the detailed discourse that ought to be told by way of pleasing Ajātasattu and so forth.
To the objection—"Why is this not stated here? Is it not true that, like the Saṅgīti-kathā, it should be told even though it appears in the Khandhaka?"—he says:
"But because it has already been included [elsewhere], everything has not been stated. This means: because it has already appeared in the Khandhaka, only a small portion [is mentioned here].

The intention is that because the sequence of the words has been stated, there is no contradiction here whatsoever. The phrase beginning with “Thus” (*evaṃ*) is the conclusion according to the logical connection (*anusandhi*).
Regarding “of King Kosala,” this refers to Mahākosala, the father of Pasenadi Kosala.
To dispel the objection that the meaning “Videhī is the daughter of King Videha” could possibly arise, he says “not of King Videha. Now, in what sense?
He said: "This is a designation for the wise (*paṇḍita*)," meaning it is a synonym for the wise, or its sense is "the name of the wise.
As for the word-meaning, he asks "By what derivation? and says "In this regard... and so forth. "They know" (*vidanti*) means they understand.

"By knowledge" (*vedanā*) means by means of knowledge acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Regarding the word "it occurs" (*īhati*), the commentary states that its meaning is also "it proceeds. He says "of Vedehī" because here [the suffix] belongs to the *nadādi* group.
It is indeed that very day; however, by means of the seventh case ending, the word *tadahū* (on that day) is established. "Therein" (*ettha*) means on this very day.

To show that the word *vasa*, when distinguished by the prefix *upa*, refers specifically to fasting (*upavāsana*) and not merely to dwelling (*vasanamatta*), and that fasting is indeed the undertaking of the precepts (*samādāna*), the phrase beginning with "by virtue of the moral habit" (*sīlena*) was stated.
And here, "by virtue of the moral habit" (*sīlena*) is said with reference to the Noble Uposatha within the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
"By fasting" (*anasanena*) refers to the external *uposatha* consisting of mere abstention from food. Here, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of non-restriction;
by it, certain types of mental misconduct as well as immorality (*dussīlya*) and so forth are included.

For instance, the cowherds’ *uposatha* was described in terms of a mind accompanied by covetousness, while the Jains’ (*nigaṇṭha*) *uposatha* was described in terms of lying and other such faults. As it is said in the Visākhā *uposatha*: [text follows].
“Thus he passes the day with that mind accompanied by covetousness,” and “At whatever time one should be exhorted to truthfulness,
at that very time one exhorts one to false speech,” and so forth.

Having thus shown the etymological derivation (nibbacana) in accordance with the intended meaning, now, by way of extracting the meanings, [the derivation] in accordance with the etymology is as follows:
He said "But this [expression], however," and so forth, in order to show the intended meaning. "Therein" refers to the word *uposatha*.
An "extraction of meanings" (*atthuddhāra*) is the extraction of various distinct meanings of words that share a common verbal root;

alternatively, it is also acceptable to define it as the extraction of the very meaning intended from among those meanings expressed by the common word. For the demonstration of multiple meanings serves to clarify the intended meaning.

It is for the purpose of extraction (*uddharaṇattha*) alone. But has it not already been stated below that the objection and the resolution regarding the extraction of the meaning—in the passage beginning with "Do words adhere to the mere thing (*atthamatta*)?"—have indeed been explained?

Furthermore, since a specific term (*visesa-sadda*) lacks denotative power, the word *uposatha* even when referring to the recitation of the Pātimokkha and so forth is merely a common noun (*sāmañña-rūpa*);
why then is it stated here as having the specific scope of the recitation of the Pātimokkha and so forth?
This is true; however, this meaning was stated by way of showing the various possible meanings that occur in each respective context, without taking into account such a commonality of sound.

This applies everywhere. It is called *uposatha* because it is observed (*vasīyati*)—that is, one does not depart from it—by those who are endowed with and harmonious in virtue and view (or purity of virtue), [namely] the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*. [It is also so called] by way of undertaking and by way of resolution.
The *uposatha* is the virtue (*sīla*) that is to be approached and dwelt in for the sake of the noble abodes (*ariyavāsa*) and so forth; it is that which is to be entered and inhabited.
The *uposatha* is the fast (*upavāsa*), consisting of the undertaking of vows (*vatasamādāna*), which is to be approached and observed through fasting and other such practices.

Furthermore, the term *uposatha* is used by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi-vasena*) with reference merely to the fact of being born into that family, as in the case of a noble elephant belonging to the "Nine Great Families," regardless of any specific action performed.

This is a conventional designation; therefore, it should be understood there as a conceptual description (*nāmapaññatti*). Regarding *uposatha*: it is so called because it burns away (*dāheti*) those who have approached their enemies;

for those skilled in phonology state that the word *usa* also means "to burn. As for the application of the term *uposatha* to the day, this has already been explained in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
In such passages as "For the pure one, indeed, [there is] always the *Phaggu*," the word *suddhassa* means "by virtue of being entirely free from the stains of the defilements."
"Of one who is completely pure. *Vā* is merely a particle, or its meaning is "or. *Sādā* means "at all times.
*Phaggu* refers specifically to the *phagguṇī* lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), for that is appropriate; and its derivation is established according to the rules of etymology (*nirukti*).
For when the brahmin named Sundarika Bhāradvāja was performing his ritual bathing at a ford on a day joined with the *uttaraphagguṇī* mansion during the month of Phagguṇa, even for a whole year...

The view is that there is the removal of committed evil. To refute that, the Blessed One stated this in the *Vatthasutta* of the *Mūlapaññāsa* within the *Majjhima Āgama*: "For one who is pure, the Uposatha is truly auspicious.

This means that for one who is completely purified by the cleansing of the stains of the aforementioned defilements, the dwelling in the Uposatha at all times—even if one does not undertake the Uposatha factors or the observances—is [the true Uposatha].
The meaning is: "it becomes thus. In passages such as "Monks, [you] should not," the connection is established by extracting the phrase: "A residence without monks should not be gone to.

"The day for the observance" (*upavasitabbadivasa*) means the day on which the observance is to be performed; or, the suffix *-tabba* should be understood in the sense of the locus (the day being the site of the observance).

For it is in this way that it accords with the etymological explanation given in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). This is achieved through an inclusionary restriction (*antogadhāvadhāraṇa*) and through the exclusion of other possibilities (*aññatthāpohana*).
And with reference to the exclusion [of other meanings], it was stated: "for the purpose of excluding the remaining two.
Beginning with the word *pannarase*, he said "therefore it was stated," etc., showing that the etymological derivation as previously mentioned is made by way of the day.
For the day is called *pannaraso* in the sense of completing fifteen lunar days (*tithi*).
If only "they exist here" were stated, there might be the objection that these [terms] also exist elsewhere;
therefore, in order to preclude that, the words beginning with "it is said that at that time" (*tadā kira*) are spoken.

By this, he shows that the scope of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix is applied here many times or in an eminent sense. Furthermore, *cātumāsī* and *cātumāsinī* are synonymous terms in the feminine gender due to specific grammatical suffixes.
The term *pariyosānabhūtā* is said with reference to the state of being complete, because the four months are fulfilled together with that [full moon]. The word *idha* refers to the Pāḷi text.
By the phrase beginning with “by the fullness of the month,” it shows the meaning of *puṇṇā* as “filling by way of three modes.
Therein, the “fullness of the month” (*māsapuṇṇatā*) is the fullness of the Kattika month at that time; for from the previous full moon until—

The other full moon (puṇṇamī) marks the end of that month; such is the conventional usage there. It is called "fulfillment of the season" (utupuṇṇatā) because of the fulfillment of the rainy season (vassāna-utu).
It is called "fulfillment of the year" (saṃvaccharapuṇṇatā) because of the fulfillment of the year characterized by the month of Kattika.
From the preceding month of Kattika until the subsequent month of Kattika, it is one "Kattika-year"; thus it is by way of the fulfillment of the year.
This has been stated. However, according to the opinion of worldly people, the designation "year" is characterized by means of months.
And likewise, that characteristic is based on the transition of the heavy [seasonal] periods. For it is said in the *Jotisattha*:
"The sun goes to its setting with the same constellation with which it rose."
"Regarding that, it should be stated there: 'the month by means of the māsaka.
It is called *mā* because the day is measured (*minīyati*) by it; for by its movement, the day is measured as 'the first day' (*pāṭipada*), 'the second,' 'the third,' and so forth.
Here, 'full' (*puṇṇa*) means full through the completion of all its phases during this night; for it is the sixteenth part of the moon."
It is called a "digit" (*kalā*); and at that time, the moon is seen as being complete by way of all sixteen digits.
Herein, the phrases "on that very day, on the Uposatha, the fifteenth" are stated by way of the day, while "Komudī," etc., are stated by way of a portion of that night.

However, in order to show a portion of the justification for the objection—"Why was the king sitting surrounded by his ministers and not alone?"—he speaks the words beginning with "evarūpāya" (of such a kind) without merely explaining the literal meaning of the text. By these [words], this justification is shown:
"He sat surrounded in that manner because at that time it was night as he desired. Regarding the phrase "dhoviyamānadisābhāgāya":
The word *viya* (like/as) should also be applied here. “Emerging from silver palaces” means either having issued forth from silver palaces or being radiated by the splendor of silver palaces.
The term “*visara*” (diffusion) is also an adjective qualifying the pearl necklaces and so forth.
According to the method of the Pāḷi, these four are the defilements: cloud, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. “By kings and ministers” means by those originating from royal families.
"By ministers. Alternatively, the meaning is "by both kings devoted [to him] and by ministers. "On a golden throne" means on a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*).
For it is said: "The throne of kings is indeed made of gold; furthermore, there is the lion-throne, the whisk-bearer, and the female yak-tail fan (*cāmara*).
"Why is he seated? is a challenge regarding the mere act of sitting. "This" refers to the wailing or the awakening. "Thus" (iti) means for this reason.
“Nakkhatta” means the festival of the Kattika constellation. “Proclaimed correctly as ‘the festival is now at hand’” means it was announced by the community.
That city whose house doors were adorned with five-colored flowers, parched grain, and full water-jars—this is the city with its five...
[etc. ...doors. A *dhaja* is a banner. The Sinhalese say a *paṭāka* is a cloth strip. At that time, it is said:
The lunar mansion was determined by means of lighting lamps. For it is stated in the same way even in the *Ummādanti-jātaka* and others that this was done in the month of Kattika.
Therefore, he said: "all the quarters of the directions were adorned with rows of brightly burning lamps.
A *vīthi* is a carriage road, a major highway; a *racchā* is a narrow path that has not been cut through [the surrounding area]. By virtue of sitting here and there, they shared a common portion.
The meaning is that it is said to be "interspersed" by one who is experiencing the festival of the constellations individually.
Although this was stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, the sense is that a definitive conclusion (*sanniṭṭhāna*) was made right there.
"Udāna" and "udāhāra" are one in meaning. "Māna" refers to the vessel for pride as the agent; "avaseka" is [so called] by way of pouring out.
The flood is by way of hearing. "A word of rapture" means a word originating from rapture, acting as the object (kamma). "The heart" means the mind, acting as the agent (kattā).
"To grasp" means to grasp by way of not letting it escape outward; the intention is that one is unable to keep it within the heart alone.
Therefore it was said: "Having become excessive," and so forth. This is what is meant: whatever word...
Independent of a recipient, it issues forth suddenly from the mouth by its own essence through the power of sublime rapture (*pīti*) alone;
that is what is intended here by the term "udāna.

As for *dosiṇā*, it means those things which have gone (*itā*), moved, or departed due to faults (*dosehi*); the letter *ta* is changed to *na*, just as in the expression "one who has conquered the defilements is a conqueror" (*vijitāvī*).
The Victor said, "Free from hatred. Although it is stated in the Sutta:
"Bhikkhus, there are these four defilements of the moon and sun, by which defilements the moon and sun are defiled so that they do not glow, do not shine, and do not radiate.
What are the four? Clouds, bhikkhus... mist... smoke, dust, and Rāhu, bhikkhus..."

Although it was said, “the defilement of the moon and sun,” nevertheless, in order to show the classification of the third defilement according to the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated, “by five defilements. And this meaning is understood from the connection with words such as *ramaṇīya*;
thus he says, “therefore,” and so forth. Furthermore, the suffix *-anīya* also frequently expresses the sense of the gerundive (*kattabbattha*), as in the word *niyyānika*.

He shows this by the word "dhammā" (the moon) and by the phrase "it delights. By the expression "vuttadosavimuttāya" (freed from the stated defects), he speaks of the night's beauty by way of its brightness;
for here, the "stated defects" refer to clouds and the like. This reason should also be connected with the phrase "fit to be seen.
For that reason, as well as due to the excellence of the season, its loveliness is to be understood. A day joined with such a night—
"A month, a season, a year"—in this way, it is appropriate for [these terms] to serve as the means for observing the characteristics (*lakkhaṇā*) of days, months, and so forth;

therefore, they are "to be characterized" (*lakkhitabbā*), hence "characterizable" (*lakkhaṇiyā*). That very same thing is "that which is to be characterized" (*lakkhaññā*), by virtue of the substitution of the letter *ña* for the letter *ṇa* according to the rule *ya-vato ṇa-kārassa ña-kārādeso*. Thus he says: "of days, months, and so forth."

Because of the statement, “One whose mind might become serene by attending upon him,” it is here the ultimate ascetic (*paramattha-samaṇa*) and the ultimate brahmin (*paramattha-brāhmaṇa*) that are intended, not merely one who has gone forth as an ascetic, nor one who is a brahmin by birth alone;
this is stated in the passage beginning with “by the state of having stilled evil” (*samitapāpatāya*). He is called a brahmin because he carries away (*bahati*) evils, that is, he casts them out.
According to the method of *nirutti* (etymological interpretation): when the plural should be used, the singular is employed;

or when the singular should be used, the plural is employed—this is the meaning of "transposition of number" (*vacanabyatti*) or "inversion of number" (*vacanavipallāsa*). Here, however, although "payirupāsataṃ" (plural) should have been said, "payirupāsato" (singular) is stated;
thus, a transposition of number is shown by using the singular where the plural ought to be used. [This refers to] oneself, one who stands in the position of a teacher.

For indeed, the use of the plural number even for a single entity is well-established. Furthermore, *payirupāsato* is an expression where there is a substitution of phonemes (*vaṇṇavipariyāya*), just as in the case of *payirudāhāsī*.
This is a usage frequently observed: namely, that when the sound *pa* is followed by *ya*, there is a substitution of phonemes.
Thus, the grammarians say: "In the case of *pari* and others, the phoneme *ra* and so forth [is replaced] by *ya* and so forth..."
"Reversal" means: "that" refers to the ascetic or the brahmin. "By this entire statement" refers to the statement beginning with "Truly delightful.
"The act of making a sign that is an illumination" means an act of making a sign that has become an illumination;
the meaning is the clear production of a sign. "Because of great offense" means because of great fault.
“*Tena hi*,” and so forth, is the explanation of that meaning. Regarding the phrase “and Devadatta,” the word *ca* (and) functions here as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) to introduce a further point;

by this it is meant that just as King Ajātasattu committed a great offense by killing his own father—an Ariyan disciple and attendant of the Teacher—so too did he commit a great offense by providing support to Devadatta, who caused such great harm to the Blessed One.
He brings [him] near. "In his shadow" is a mere conventional expression; it means by leaning against Jīvaka’s back, that is, making him the front support—this is what is meant.
"For the purpose of cutting off distraction" means for the purpose of severing the distraction arising in relation to his own discourse which is about to be spoken;
the intention is "for the purpose of its non-arising. Therefore he said:
“*Tassaṃ hi*,” and so forth. “Of those who are untrained” means those who have lost their training in the restraint of body and speech.

“In the case of family-visiting teachers” (*kulūpaka*) refers to teachers who have entered among families. “Because of having grasped what is worthless” means because of being devoid of the essential quality that ought to be grasped. “Without casting aside” means free from the removal of others.
“Auspicious” (*bhadda*) means beautiful due to being endowed with a refuge.
151. This meaning is established by this shadow of the text (*pāḷicchāyā*);

or, showing that it is stated thus in the text itself by being included within this very meaning, he says "therefore he said," and so forth. One who, though not actually a teacher, is recognized as a teacher—that is, one recognized as a teacher (*satthupaṭiññāto*)—even while being a non-Buddha yet recognized as a Buddha, [claims]:
"I alone am the instructor in the world regarding the welfare and the Dhamma."
This was said with reference to the fact that he had been acknowledged as a teacher.

The phrase beginning with “So kira” is stated using the particle *kira* according to the method of the ancient commentaries (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*) to indicate mere hearsay. This same principle applies to the subsequent etymological analysis of the word *Makkhali*.
“Fulfilling ninety-nine [slaves]” means having made himself the hundredth, thereby completing a full hundred slaves minus one.
Fulfilling [his purpose], thus was this Maṅgaladāsa born. "As if with gold" means as if with the very mode of being born from the mother’s womb;
or rather, just as beings are born unclothed and uncovered, so too [he was born] "as if with gold. "Approaching" means having come near and becoming devoted.
"He took up that very renunciation" means that he took up that very noble form, thinking, "This indeed is what is called renunciation."
Thinking, "May it be so," he went forth and received the ordination. "They went forth" means they followed him after he had gone forth.

By the phrase "reckoned as a multitude of those who have gone forth," he shows that it is called a *saṅgha* merely because it is a multitude of those who have gone forth, and not because of being united by the commonality of views leading to liberation, purity of view, or virtue.
"It belongs to this" means it exists as an attendant retinue belonging to this one who has declared himself a Teacher.
“*Saṅghī* and *gaṇī*” are synonymous terms; they differ only by way of convention. Therefore, he said “[it is] that very same person,” and so forth.

And “that very same person” means precisely one who is designated as a member of the community of those gone forth (*pabbajita*). Some, however, say: “He is a *saṅghī* by virtue of being a member of the community of those gone forth, and a *gaṇī* by virtue of being a member of the community of householders (*gahaṭṭha*);

but that is merely their own opinion, because in the world the word *saṅgha* is established [only] in reference to a group of those gone forth. [The passage continues with] the practice of the ascetic vow of nakedness (*acelaka-vata-cariyā*), etc.
Conduct (*ācāra*) is merely that which is conceived by oneself. It is "renowned" (*paññāta*) because it is well-known through its association with the Saṅgha and so forth.

"Having few desires" (*appiccha*) and "being content" (*santuṭṭha*) are one in meaning. In this context, to show the state of having few desires as it actually occurs, it is said: "Out of fewness of desires, he does not even wear a robe.
For in that [state], the kind of fewness of desires characterized by concealing one's existing virtues—as found among those belonging to the Dispensation (*sāsanika*)—is not what is meant here.
“Yaso” means fame or reputation. “Tittha” is so called because it is recognized as that by which one crosses the flood of *saṃsāra*;
it is approved as “good,” yet it is not approved by the good. This meaning is expressed by the words beginning with “ayaṃ.
For its being approved by the good is not found [in such a person]. “Sundaro sappuriso” has a twofold meaning. “Assutavato” refers to one who has not heard the Dhamma of the Noble Ones.
And this is a genitive case-ending used in the sense of the agent (*sāmivacana*).

He knows many nights [thinking], “These vows of mine have been well-practiced for such a length of time. However, because those nights have become long in duration, it is said, “He has gone forth for a long time,” and so on;
this is a compound with the final member having the sense of another word (*antattha-aññapadattha-samāsa*), just as in the expression “born for a month” (*māsajāta*). Now, of those two words...

If it is asked, "What is the distinction?"—by the mention of one who has long been ordained, his wisdom and virtue are shown; by the mention of one who is of long standing (*rattaññū*), his clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) therein is demonstrated;
this is his distinction. But with what purpose did that minister speak thus? It was said: "Of one who has not long been ordained," and so forth.
"Worthy of conviction" means worthy of being believed. "For a long time" means for a long duration. And how much is that? He said: "Two or three..."
“*Rājaparivaṭṭe*”: the meaning is the succession of the governance of two or three kings.

Although it was already said “*addhagato*,” the repetition of the term “age” (*vaya*) indicates that this pair of words refers to the final stage of life, as there is a specific distinction in the meaning of these two terms;
this is shown by the phrase “the last stage of life” (*pacchimavaya*). “Both” (*ubhaya*) refers to the pair of words: “*addhagato, vayoanuppatto*.”
*Kājara* is a specific kind of tree, which is also called a "leaf-tree. The connection is: "as if having seen [it], he was displeased. He says, "Jhāna... [etc.
...kāma," with reference to having previously gone with his father into the presence of the Teacher and having heard the teaching.
*Tilakkhaṇabbhāhataṃ* means struck by the three characteristics. *Dassanena* means...
This is merely an illustration. For he, having seen him and engaged in conversation with him, and having subsequently heard his doctrine of non-action, became displeased.
Regarding the phrase "in the talk of virtues," it refers to talk of non-existent virtues; hence he said, "he became even more displeased.
To clear away the objection—"If he was displeased, why did he remain silent?"—he says, "Even though he was displeased," and so forth.

152. "In the village named Gosālā": this is what is stated. However, its name becomes especially appropriate based on the meaning "the shed where cattle are settled during the rainy season," because it is common and not shared by others.

Nevertheless, since that [meaning] was not heard from the ancients, it is designated as the "partial view" (*ekaccavāda*). Based on that statement, [it is said]: "The owner said, 'Do not stumble! (*mā khalīti sāmiko āhā*).
This shows that its designation is by means of a verb. For when there is a desire to express a name, even a verb becomes a noun, as in the case of "Aññāsikoṇḍañño.
The word "the rest" refers to the statement beginning with "He [wrapped it] with a leaf," and so forth.
153. Just as Sirivaḍḍhaka and other names are applied to slaves and others, "Ajita" is merely his name. A blanket woven from hair.
The word *yassā* is also appropriate [as a feminine form]. *Paṭikiṭṭhataraṃ* means more inferior.

With the words beginning “As it is said,” he cites the Makkhali-sutta from the Tika-nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya. *Tantāvūtāni* means woven on a loom. By the words beginning “Cold in the cold,” he demonstrates its greater inferiority through six modes.
154. He is called *pakudha* because he fumes (*pakujjhati*) and becomes resentful (*byāpajjati*) toward those of right view.
Regarding the phrase "even after defecating," the word "even" (*pi*) here includes the sense that this applies even after eating food or being smeared with some kind of impurity.
"Having made a mound of sand" means having made a heap of sand under the pretext of undertaking a vow; furthermore, in such a place that ought not to be approached...
It means that one goes having taken up a vow.

Regarding the phrase "the defilement of binding" (*gaṇṭhanakilesa*), its synonym is "the defilement of entanglement" (*palibundhanakilesa*); the meaning is: a defilement such as lust and so forth, which functions to bind one within *saṃsāra* and has as its object fields, lands, children, wives, and so on.
By the phrase "for one who speaks thus," it refers to this [defilement] by way of its acquisition (*laddhi*).
This shows that it is a name, but not something that exists [in reality]. For as long as it has not been eradicated by the Path, it indeed still exists.
However, this is the etymological meaning: one who "grasps" (gaṇhāti) the thought "I have no knot" (natthi mayhaṃ gaṇṭho) is a "Nigaṇṭha. "Of Nāṭa" means of the one with that name.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion concerning Jīvaka Komārabhacca.
157. However, with reference to the state of being entirely silent, it was said: "This nāga... [and so on]... is like [that].
*Supaṇṇa* means *garuḷa*, or according to the Greek (Sanskrit) system, *garuḍa*; for they say therein that there is no distinction between *ḍa* and *ḷa*.
Because he did not act according to his intention, it was said: "Alas, this is a misfortune for me. *Upasantassa* means having attained tranquility through restraint in every respect.
“Of one who has gone. Jīvaka’s silence was like crushing my intention;

therefore, by asking about that very silence and making him speak, my intention must be fulfilled. Showing that this was the King’s intention here, he said, “But as for the elephant...,” and so forth.
He shows that *kiṃ* is a particle used in a question regarding a reason by saying, “For what reason? (*kena kāraṇena*).

By this [phrase], he shows the meaning: "For what reason are you silent? In that context, having set forth the possible reasons, the words beginning with "of these" (*imesaṃ*) are spoken to reveal the underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
The phrase *yathā etesaṃ* means "just as there is one who frequents their families (*kulūpaka*). Thus, it asks: "Is it for one of these three reasons that you remain silent?"
The intended meaning is "he asks.
"He causes to speak" means he desires to cause [the other] to speak. Regarding the phrase "with the fivefold prostration," the meaning here is "standing facing [the teacher] with five limbs";
that is, having brought together the five limbs known as the feet, knees, elbows, hands, and head.
It is said that "having bowed down and standing facing [the elder], one first pays homage.

Furthermore, they cite the Vinaya Piṭaka passage beginning, "O Upāli, when a junior monk is paying homage at the feet of a senior monk, he should pay homage to the feet after having established these five qualities within himself," and so forth;
this refers to the acts of placing one shoulder [in a respectful posture], joining the palms in añjali, massaging the feet, and establishing affection and reverence.
Regarding the phrase "the five-limbed prostration," that is not intended here, because in a prostration performed from a distance, the aforementioned five limbs are not complete.
Here, "prostration" (*vandanā*) means bowing down, the joining of the hands in the *añjali* gesture, and the bringing together of the palms.

By the words "having prostrated with the five-limbed [posture]," physical bowing is expressed; by the words "of my Teacher" and so forth, verbal bowing is expressed; and these two are preceded and followed by mental devotion.

Regarding the phrase "mental aspiration": although every aspect of the Tathāgata’s practice is indeed unique, wondrous, and marvelous, nevertheless, his descent into the womb, birth, great renunciation, full enlightenment, turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and the twin miracles followed by his descent from the deva realm are exceedingly well-known throughout the world with its devas;
they cannot be denied by anyone, and thus it is these alone that are highlighted here.

"Thus become" (*itthambhūta*) means one who has attained such a state; the "description of that which is thus become" (*itthambhūtākhyāna*) is the statement regarding that [state], and its meaning is the "meaning of the description of that which is thus become.
Alternatively, "thus become" (*itthambhūta*) means one who has become or arisen in such a manner;

the "description of that which is thus become" is the statement that [the person] is of such a kind, and its meaning is the "meaning of the description of that which is thus become"; in that [sense], there is the accusative case.
The meaning [of the compound] is as follows. In the word *abbhuggato*, the prefix *abhi-* indicates the sense of "specifying a state" (*itthambhūtakhyāna*) by way of prominence;
it is a karmapravacanīya because it illuminates the function of emerging after having overcome [something].

Therefore, by virtue of that usage, although the accusative case in the phrase "that Blessed One" (*taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ*) is identical in its governing sense (*sāmivattha*), it is employed here to indicate the sense of specifying a state by way of non-prominence.
It is stated: “in the sense of describing a state of being thus. For this very reason, he says: “The meaning is ‘of that Blessed One.
But is it not the case that, as in the example “Devadatta went towards his mother,” the word *abhi* is not employed here in the phrase “that Blessed One”?
How then can there be the accusative case due to the employment of *tam*? [The answer is: Because it is employed by way of its meaning.
For among the various applications of the word *abhi*, the application as "meaning" (*attha*) alone is primary. This is what is meant:

just as in the expression "Devadatta is kind toward his mother," where the accusative case is used to express a state of being (an *itthambhūtākhyāna*) due to the application of the word *abhi*, so too here: "Regarding that Blessed One, such a beautiful report has arisen."
Regarding the statement "the locative case is employed in the sense of 'thus having become' (itthambhūtākhyāna) due to the usage of *abhi*":

for instance, in the example "Sādhu devadatto mātaramabhi" ("Devadatta is kind toward his mother"), there arises the possibility of using either the locative case or the genitive case—meaning either in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) as in "Devadatta is kind toward his mother" (*mātaramabhi* = *mātuvisaye*), or in the sense of possession (*sāmi*) as in "he is kind to the mother" (*mātari*).
It is by means of the indicator of "thus having become" that [the specific relation is determined].
By means of the verbal suffix *ppavacanīya*, which expresses an action, the instrumental case is employed due to the nature of the usage;

likewise here, when the genitive case is applicable in the sense of "belonging to" (*sāmi*), just as in that instance the meaning is understood to be "Devadatta, in relation to his mother, or one connected to his mother, has attained a state of excellence," so too here the meaning is:
"The fame belonging to the Blessed One has arisen, having overcome [all others]."
The meaning to be understood here is: "having reached the state of rising. For in this context, the mention of "fame" (kittisadda) is like the mention of Devadatta;
the mention of "the Blessed One" (bhagavantam) is like the word "mother"; and the word "risen" (uggata) should be understood as being like the word "good" (sādhu).
“Kalyāṇa” means auspicious (*bhaddaka*). Its state of being auspicious consists in its having excellent qualities as its object; thus he says, “endowed with excellent qualities. The meaning is:
endowed with excellent qualities, it is joined with them by virtue of having them as its object. Here, “being endowed with” (*samannāgama*) refers to having that as its object;
the intention is that it is dependent upon those [qualities] by virtue of having excellent qualities as its object. This same method applies even when “excellent” (*seṭṭha*) is used as a synonym.

For the excellence of the sound of praise (*kittisadda*) consists precisely in its having excellent qualities as its object, as in such passages as: "The word ‘Bhagavā’ is excellent; the word ‘Bhagavā’ is supreme.
Because it enumerates qualities through phrases such as "Worthy, Perfectly Enlightened One," and because it is to be praised, the sound of praise is indeed a *vaṇṇa* (eulogy);
thus he said, "It is simply a *kitti* (praise). For it is a *vaṇṇa* precisely because it is to be praised.
“Kitti” (renown) is called “sadda” (sound) because it is worthy of being sounded (*saddanīya*). For the word *sadda* is a synonym for *kitti*, as in the passage:

“The sages, possessed of virtues and asceticism, have a sublime sound (*uḷārasaddā*) [of renown]. The term “kittisadda” indicates a difference in grammatical substratum (*bhinnādhikaraṇatā*), showing that it is a sound proceeding by way of renown;
this is made clear by the phrase “the sound of praise (*thutighosa*). Here, “kittisadda” is a synonym for praise (*thuti*), meaning the act of praising (*kittana*) or extolling (*abhitthavana*).
*Kittī* means sound proceeding by way of praise; the meaning is "the sound of praise," that is, an utterance of eulogy.
The prefix *abhi-* signifies overcoming (*abhibhavana*), and here "overcoming" is explained as "pervading" (*ajjhottharaṇa*); thus it is said "having pervaded.

Because it proceeds by taking hold of qualities that are not shared by others, the meaning is "having encompassed" (*abhibyāpetvā*). Regarding the question "What [is it]? (*kiṃ*) in the inquiry "It has arisen," [the answer is] "Thus indeed... (*itipi*).
In order to show the connection [of the text], it is said: "What then?

*Padasambandha* (the connection of words) refers to the linking together of the words. "That Blessed One" (*so bhagavā*) refers to him who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections (*pāramī*), shattered all defilements (*kilesa*), and awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara sammāsambodhi*), is the god beyond gods (*devātideva*), the Sakka beyond Sakkas.
The Lord of the World, who is more exalted than even Brahmā, has his fame and reputation spread throughout the world including the devas for reasons such as his possession of good fortune;
he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavā*). For the word "that" (*yaṃ taṃ*) is always connected [to what follows].
And this first phrase, "the Blessed One," is the naming of the Teacher's title. Thus the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said: "This name 'Blessed One' was not given by his mother..."
"Not by his father," and so forth. However, the word "Bhagavā" (the Blessed One) is a praise of his qualities.

Just as one who practices meditation on a subject (*kammatthāna*) recollects the Buddha’s qualities by joining the particle *iti pi* to each of the nine epithets beginning with "Arahan," so too does one who praises the Buddha’s qualities here;
thus he said, "Thus indeed the Arahan... [and so on] ...thus indeed the Bhagavā. For when this is the case, by means of these nine [epithets] beginning with "Arahan"...

The qualities of the Buddha that are exceedingly well-known and renowned in the world with its devas are analyzed in their various aspects by the two words "itipi," since these two words indicate their manifold nature.
For here, as in such passages as "Thus this is real, thus this is true," the word *iti* has the sense of making something proximate and evident, while the word *pi* has the sense of inclusion.
And by this, their state of being manifold is illuminated; furthermore, those grounds for discerning qualities are directly evident to wise persons endowed with faith.
Therefore, showing that one who recites them must do so having brought them directly before the mind, he said: "It is meant: 'by this and this reason.'"
When one praises [the Buddha] after investigating in this way, the listener develops an exceeding degree of serene confidence (*pasāda*) toward the Blessed One.

"Because of being far removed" means because of being very distant from the defilements (*kilesa*). "Of enemies" refers to the enemies that are the defilements. "Of spokes" refers to the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra.
"Because of being destroyed" means because of having been shattered. "Of requisites, etc. refers both to the requisites such as robes and to specific forms of honor.
"Absence of seclusion" (*rahābhāva*) is due to the absence of secluded places such as those for the eye and so forth.
For it is said that "absence of seclusion" means not transgressing the path where there is no opportunity for committing evil deeds. In this way too, the intended meaning is obtained.
"From that" (*tato*) means from the *Visuddhimagga*. And just as [it is explained] in the *Visuddhimagga*, their detailed exposition should be understood from its commentary, the *Paramatthamañjūsā*.

Because Jīvaka had stood for a long time in the presence of the Teacher having heard the qualities of the Buddha, and because he was free from doubt regarding the Teacher’s dispensation due to his realization of the Truth (sacca), and had attained confidence (vesārajjappatto) in speaking of the Teacher’s qualities, he spoke thus in detail;
hence it is said, "But Jīvaka," and so forth. With the words "And here," etc., he states the sense of implication (sāmatthiyattha). Strength (thāma)...

The knowledge of teaching (*desanāñāṇa*) is indeed [the same], but the power (*bala*) is the knowledge of the Ten Powers (*dasabalañāṇa*). "Confidently" (*vissattha*) is a neuter noun in the locative case; the meaning is "without apprehension.

"In five colors" (*pañcavaṇṇāya*) means in five modes, such as the *khuddika* (small) and so forth. It was "continuously pervaded" (*nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ*) because of the state of having performed the requisite task (*katādhikārabhāvato*).
For by way of an obstacle to karma (*kammantarāya*), the king’s body of virtues (*guṇasarīra*) becomes damaged and impaired. But why did he [speak] only to Jīvaka?
He said "imāya" (by this) and so forth because he was instructing her as she was ready to depart.
Having stated "the best," it is shown that the reason for this is not only its excellence, but also its quietness;
thus, "horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and so forth" was said. And among elephant-vehicles, he took only those that were without trappings.

He had the female elephants also caparisoned. "Following step by step" (*padānupadaṃ*) means following the footprints; that is, making their own steps follow the footprints of the elephant vehicle as it goes ahead.
Here, the word *pada* refers to the tracks left by the feet. "Of one who has attained peace" (*nibbutassa*) means of one for whom the distress of all defilements has been stilled.
"Only when they have attained peace" (*nibbuteheva*) means only when the agitation caused by noise has been stilled through the absence of sound.
*Kareṇū* is a synonym for a female elephant (*hatthinī*). It is called *kareṇu* because it makes a sound (*kaṇati*), or because its trunk (*kara*) is not long—that is, its tusks are not long.
There is also the reading *kareṇukā*; the derivation of the word is established according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*).
"Mounting" refers specifically to the fastening of the saddle-cloth and other trappings. *Opavayha* means fit to carry the king. There is also the reading *opaguyha*.

They recite [the word *gopetum*], meaning they are capable of embracing and protecting the king. The passage beginning with “*evaṃ kirassā*” (*thus indeed she*) and so forth serves to illustrate her wisdom.
“The discourse proceeds” means that, having found the opportunity, a discussion on the Dhamma takes place.
“In order to dispel the King’s apprehension, women were seated upon the female elephants because of their status as those who move close by,” so it was said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the reason for this has already been stated: "There is no fear for men when relying on women; one may go happily surrounded by women.
It may have been said thus by the Teacher because this [other] reason must also apply.
In order to show that the king was difficult for others to approach, he had those women take the guise of men.
They were made with weapons in their hands. Regarding the phrase "hundreds of female elephants" (*hatthinikāsatāni*): here, *hatthinikā* refers simply to female elephants (*hatthinī*).

Although there is a reading in some places as "five hundred female elephants" (*pañca hatthiniyā satāni*), that is indeed incorrect, because in such instances—as in the expression "with about five hundred monks" (*pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi*)—one observes that the compound consists solely of the latter member.
Regarding the phrase "of someone or other": [it refers to] when a great multitude has assembled.

"Of whomever it may be"—this implies that for others as well, it will serve as a strong support (*upanissaya*) for the future attainment of the paths and fruits; thus he said, "It will be of benefit to the great multitude.
"He made known" means he informed them. "A term of courtesy" means a mere conventional expression, intended only for that specific purpose.
“Because there is no finality. Therefore he said, “Do that very thing according to your own preference. For by this alone is the conclusion of that matter reached.
“You think” means you already know by nature. “That very thing” refers to going and coming itself.
The meaning is: if you wish to go, then go; if you do not wish to go, then do not go; your own preference is the authority in this matter.
159. They are *pacceka* (separate) by way of their individual connection (*sandhi*). Regarding the word *mahañca*, it is said that the nominative case ending is used in the sense of the instrumental;

thus he says "by means of greatness" (*mahatā*). The state of being great is *mahañcaṃ*. It is not only the reading with the nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*), but also the reading with the long vowel *ā*;
thus he says, "there is also the canonical text reading *mahaccā*. Just as when one should say "khattiyā" [in the plural],...

“Khatyā”: thus, where one should say *mahatiyā*, it is *mahatyā*. Furthermore, by repeating the particle *ca* and through the rules of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), the word is established as *mahaccā*.

What should have been stated in the masculine gender is here changed to the feminine gender; this is a reversal of gender (*liṅgavipariyāya*). For an adjective (*visesana*) takes on the gender and other attributes of the noun it qualifies (*visesya*).
“*Tiyojanasatānan*” means of those [mountains] each measuring three hundred yojanas in circumference.
The phrase "the sovereignty and glory of two great realms" refers to the lordship over the realms of Aṅga and Magadha.
He explains its meaning with the words beginning with "of that," and so forth. "Bound turbans" means turbans tied around the head.
"Swords fastened on" means swords girded upon the shoulder by way of hanging down. "Javelins with jeweled shafts" means goads with jeweled handles.
With the words beginning “Aparāpi,” those who attend on foot are mentioned. Hunchbacks and dwarfs are shown by way of their appearance;
Kirātas, Savaras, Andhakas, and others are shown by way of their birth as their attendants. “Trustworthy men” is said with reference to the chief ministers (*vassavare*).

Those for whom greatness (*mattā*)—that is, measure (*pamāṇa*)—in terms of family, wealth, power, and so forth, is great, are “high officials” (*mahāmattā*), that is, royal ministers of great influence.
"Like young *vijjādhara*s" means like young *vijjādhara* boys endowed with the supernormal powers (*iddhi*) consisting of knowledge through the power of mantras.
"Sons of *raṭṭhiya*" means sons of hunters (*bhojaputta*). For hunters are called *raṭṭhiya* because they roam about in the forest;

the meaning is that their sons, due to their familiarity with various weapons, have become royal retainers. Alternatively, "sons of *raṭṭhiya*" are the sons of those who rule over intermediate districts; they are *khattiya*s.
The word *bhoja* as used in the commentary should be understood as denoting a "ruler" (*bhojaka*), as in such passages as "let them be devoted" (*anuyuttā bhavantu te*).
"Having raised up" (*ussāpetvā*) means having extended upwards. "The sound of victory" (*jayasadda*) refers to sounds connected with victory, such as "Victory to the Great King! (*jayatu mahārājā*).
"The enclosure of the bow-string" (*dhanupantiparikkhepa*) means the surrounding line of bow-strings; in all instances, it should be understood according to what encompasses that [enclosure].
*Hatthighaṭā* means a herd of elephants. *Paharamānā* means striking against one another. *Aññamaññasaṅghaṭṭanā* means being joined together through continuous movement.

*Seṇī* refers to guilds such as perfumers’ guilds, cloth-dealers’ guilds, and so forth—as in passages such as, “without having obtained permission from the king, the Saṅgha, the *gaṇa*, the *pūga*, or the *seṇī*, one should not ordain anyone except for those who are already ordained. [The eighteen...]
Some write, "the armies were unshakeable," but this is not seen in many manuscripts.

Furthermore, it would be entirely inappropriate for numerous armies to have been counted previously. At that time, considering that even an arrow from all the weapons travels a great distance, he arranges the king’s retinue according to the measure of the arrow's range of flight.
To the question "For what purpose? he says, "If... and so forth.
Fear is the terror of the mind in the sense of being itself afraid; it is so called because one fears in whatever way one fears.
Knowledge is fear because it discerns fear as fear—that is, because it investigates in the manner of fearing that "this is to be feared" when the object to be feared has appeared as fear.
For this very reason, it is said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "But as for the knowledge of the appearance as fear..."

"Does it fear, or does it not fear? "It does not fear. For that is merely an investigation [to the effect]: 'Past formations have ceased; present ones are ceasing; future ones will cease. It is called "fear" in the sense of being an object of fear, because one fears from it.
It is called "moral dread" (ottappa) in the sense of being the cause of fear, because one fears evil by means of it.
"Having made [it so]. "Terrifying" means the state of being fearful. "They too" refers even to the long-lived deities.
"The teaching of the Dhamma" refers to the teaching of the Dhamma adorned with the fifteen characteristics within the five aggregates.

"For the most part" means by way of the majority, setting aside those deities whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), because of the abundance of others. For, due to their having exhausted the taints, not even fear of mental terror arises in them.
Granted that in the commentary on the *Sīhopamasutta* (The Simile of the Lion), even the fear of mental terror is stated to be for the sake of that [same] purpose;

however, here, in accordance with the context of the treatise, only the fear of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*) is taken. "A sense of urgency" (*saṃvega*) means knowledge accompanied by moral dread (*sahottappa*).

"Terror" (*santāsa*) means being utterly terrified. Because it is something to be feared, it is "fear" (*bhaya*); because it possesses a terrifying nature, it is "dreadful" (*bherava*). Thus, "fear-and-dread" (*bhayabherava*) refers to the object of what is to be feared.
Therefore he said, "He comes"; the meaning is that this terror and dread surely come upon that man.
"They praise the timid" means that the wise praise the timid person because of their fear of evil and their being struck with alarm.
