"For they do not praise the brave therein" means that they do not praise the brave person—the one who destroys shame—in the commission of such evil. Therefore he said:
“Indeed, the virtuous do not commit evil out of fear. In this context, “out of fear” (*bhayā*) means from the dread of evil; the meaning is: due to moral shame (*ottappa*).

“Of one who is trembling” (*chambhitassa*) means of one who is paralyzed with fear; there is a substitution of the letter *cha* for the letter *tha*. He explains its meaning as “the shaking of the entire body,” which means the quivering of the whole body due to fear. “Uyyodhanaṃ” means a clash or a battle.

"Some" refers to those residing in the Uttaravihāra. The passage beginning with "In Rājagaha" is an explanation of their intention. There were sixty-four small gates, two being placed at each of the four main gates. With the words "At that time," etc., he shows the reason for its not being a cause.

Now, in order to present the opponent's position (*sakavāda*), the passage beginning with "But this" was stated. The passage beginning with "It is said that Jīvaka... is a demonstration of the manner of suspicion. "His" refers to King Ajātasattu.
"Distressed" means dissatisfied. The connection is: "He thought he wished to raise the royal parasol."
"Bhāyitvā" means "because of fear. "Tassa" refers to Jīvaka. The word *samma* has the same meaning as *sāmāna*;
since it denotes a state of equality in age, he says, "an expression for [one of] the same age. One who is equal in age is a *vayassa*, just as one says, "the king of the same color as Hari.
Grammarians desire the substitution of *sa* for *sama*; therefore, the expression (*abhilāpa*) is an address (*ālapana*), and this is a conventional designation (*ruḷhī-niddesa*).

This is like the address “Mārisa. For just as the term *mārisa*—an expression denoting freedom from suffering—is used even for those in hell who are subject to suffering, as in such passages as, “When, O Mārisa, stake meets stake in your heart,” and so forth;
likewise, anyone who is a companion, even if not of equal age, is called “Samma. Therefore, the meaning is simply an expression of friendship. *Kacci*...

The connection is with the phrase "do not deceive" (*na vañcesi*) in the Pāḷi. Although it is stated as "do not entice" (*na palambhesi*), here the sense of "supposition" (*parikappa*) is what is possible;

thus it is said, "you should not mislead" (*na vippalambheyyāsi*), which means "you should not allure" (*na palobheyyāsi*). "Conversation" (*kathā*) is the dialogue; that itself is the sound, and thus [it is called] "thereby.

"He would perish" (*vinasseyya*) means he would be afflicted by mental distress. This is said with reference to the words beginning with "Not that, O gods" (*na taṃ devā*); [the word] "firmly" (*daḷhaṃ*)...
The word "having done" (*katvā*) is stated. By the phrase "or hurrying" (*taramāno vā*), he shows that this is a reduplication used in the sense of urgency.
Having said, "Come forward, Great King," the words beginning with "these" (*ete*) were spoken to show the reason for that;
thus, showing the connected meaning, he said, "Great King, what is called a band of thieves," and so forth.
Commentary on the Question on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life (Sāmaññaphala-pucchā-vaṇṇanā) 160.
This space outside the gatehouse is called the "ground of the Nāga. Therefore he said, "of the monastery," and so forth. "The splendor of the Blessed One" means the majesty of a Buddha.
It pervaded the king’s body, just as it did that of the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa when [he was in the presence] of the Blessed One.
As he was approaching the vicinity of the forest grove, "remembering his own transgression, a great fear arose"—this is the explanation for the breaking out of sweat.
For the breaking out of sweat does not occur through the power of the Buddha alone; rather, it arises because [the Buddha] is the cause of tranquility for both body and mind.
"Eketi" refers specifically to those residing in the Uttaravihāra monastery. He shows that this is indeed appropriate by means of the words "by this," and so forth. "Abhimāre" means archers.
"Dhanapāla" refers to Nāḷāgiri; for at that time, because he received heaps of wealth offered by the citizens, he was commonly known as "Dhanapāla.
Not only had he been seen before, but the Blessed One was [well-known] by nature as well.
He said “the Blessed One indeed,” and so forth, in order to show that he was well-known. “One possessed of excellent marks” refers to the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
“Adorned with secondary characteristics” refers to the eighty secondary characteristics (a detailed explanation is found in the *Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā*, in the commentary on the *Vijāta-maṅgala*).
“With six-colored rays” refers to the rays existing at that time. “With the grace of sovereignty” means by way of the splendor of his lordship.
To the objection that a question posed to the Blessed One with a display of lordliness would indeed constitute a lack of respect, he said, "For this is the nature," and so forth;
the intention is that because he asked out of his natural disposition, it was not a lack of respect.
Although the Saṅgha of monks was seated surrounding him, from the perspective of the actual meaning, he was as if seated directly in front of him. Therefore, he said, "surrounding," and so forth.
161. By the phrase “yena tena,” he shows that the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative, as indicated by the words “yattha tattha.
Since it was stated that he approached “by way of the gate of the circle,” it is appropriate here to say “he approached” (upagato), because the act of arriving has already been expressed.
“In a suitable place” means in a spot where people of discerning nature stood.
In that [place]. But what is this so-called "suitable location"?

It is a location free from the defects of sitting too far away and so forth, or free from the eight defects of sitting such as behind one's back and so on. As the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā have said:
"Neither behind nor in front, nor too near or too far;..."
“Neither in a marsh nor in a headwind, nor where it is unevenly sloped;
having avoided these faults, they stood to one side.
At that time, in order to show that the silence of the Saṅgha of monks was pervasive without exception, [the text says] “silent...”.
The phrase "become silent" is stated as a term of reproach; thus he says, "From which... indeed," meaning "from whichever [instance], O monk.

*Hatthakukkucca* refers to the state of fidgeting with the hand, or lack of restraint, and the performance of an act lacking clear comprehension. The same applies to *pādakukkucca* (fidgeting with the feet).
The word "or" (*vā*) is used here to include unmentioned alternatives; by it, other forms of lack of restraint, such as regarding the eyes, ears, and so forth, are included.

It has been analyzed that [this] does not exist. However, since among those [restraints] the restraint of the eye is the very first and is difficult to ward off, the passage beginning with "adorned with all ornaments" was spoken in order to demonstrate its absence.
"Like a perfectly clear lake" means like a pond of undisturbed water. The connection is: "by which [I am now]... pe... by this for me... pe... let it be."
He said, “By which,” and so forth, because the sequence of meaning is one thing and the sequence of words is another.
Therein, since mental tranquility is obtained by inference from the tranquility of body and speech that has been attained, it is stated as “and by mental [tranquility].
“By tranquility of virtue” means by the restraint of virtue. To corroborate the stated point through worldly custom, he said, “For it is difficult,” and so forth. “Attained” means having obtained.
They attain restraint, which is defined as the perfection of conduct. By the words "In this way" (*evaṃ*) and so forth, he shows the reason for such a desire.
"He" refers to the grandfather, or Udayabhadda. "Even though" (*kiñcāpi*) and so forth is a corroboration of that point.

"He will surely cause him to be killed" is said with reference to that specific time; therefore he says, "he caused him to be killed. For this is a statement referring to the present moment. "Five turnings" (*pañcaparivaṭṭo*) means five royal turnings.

Why did he say this? The intention is: "Does the king not say anything directed toward the Blessed One? Regarding "a distinction of speech" (*vacībhedo*), it refers to the aforementioned distinction of *udāna* speech.
"Silent and pure" (*tuṇhī niravo*) is a figurative expression (*pariyāyavacana*). "This," and so forth, is a demonstration of the manner in which the mind is known.
The connection is: "Having known that 'this... will not be able to [speak]'... "Immediately after the speech" means immediately after the *udāna* speech.
“By which” (*yena*) means either by whichever place or by whichever range of hearing. The same principle applies here as appropriate to the phrase “by which affection” (*yena pemaṃ*).
It is said that “the mouth does not suffice” with reference to the fact that addressing one who has committed an offense is difficult.
Or else, it refers to the statement “You have come, Great King, according to our affection,” which occurs in the manner of illustrating that meaning at that time.
It should be understood that this was said with reference even to the Blessed One’s sweet speech, which is variegated by various methods (*naya*).
For the Blessed One teaches even a single point in such a way that the wisdom of his listeners is brought forth. It is with reference to this that it is stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*):
"There is no passage in the scriptures left unexplained by the Blessed One; the meaning of all [passages] has indeed been spoken."
“By five ways” means by the five reasons consisting of equanimity toward the desirable and the undesirable, and so forth.

For this has been said in the *Mahāniddesa*: “One who is such (tādī) is such in five ways: he is such because he has transcended the desirable and the undesirable; he is such because he has crossed over; he is such because he has gone beyond; he is such because he is liberated;
he is such because of that designation. How is the Arahant such toward the desirable and the undesirable? The Arahant is such in gain and in loss, in fame and in disrepute, in praise...”

He is the same in blame as he is in praise, in pleasure as he is in pain. If they were to smear one arm with perfume and carve the other arm with an axe, there would be no lust for the one and no aversion for the other;

having abandoned both attraction and repulsion, having transcended both exaltation and depression, and having surmounted both compliance and hostility—thus is the Arahant the same toward the desirable and the undesirable.

How is it that the Arahant is one who has cast off and is thus "such" (tādī)? For the Arahant... [as before] ...there is no stiffness, no hostility, no conceit, no arrogance, no intoxication, no negligence;

all defilements, all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, and all wholesome volitional formations have been cast off, vomited out, released, abandoned, and relinquished. In this way, the Arahant is one who has cast off and is thus "such."

How is it that the Arahant is one who has crossed over and is such (tādī)? The Arahant has crossed over the flood of sensual desire, crossed over the flood of existence, crossed over the flood of views, and crossed over the flood of ignorance.
He has crossed over, has emerged from, has gone beyond, has transcended, and has passed beyond the entire path of saṃsāra.
He has completed his dwelling, practiced the conduct, and reached the destruction of birth and death; for him, there is no more wandering in the cycle of birth and death.
For him there is no further becoming; thus the Arahant is "one who has crossed over" (tinnavī) and is such-like (tādī).

How is the Arahant "one who is liberated" (muttavī) and such-like? The mind of the Arahant is liberated, fully liberated, and well-liberated from lust, from hatred, from delusion, from anger, from resentment, from contempt, from insolence, from envy, from avarice, from deceit, from guile, and from obstinacy.
From exertions, conceits, overweening pride, intoxications, and negligences— from all defilements,
all misconducts, all distresses, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome volitional formations— the mind is freed, liberated, and well-liberated.
Thus the Arahant is "one who is freed" (muttāvī) and "such-like" (tādī).
How is the Arahant “such” (tādī) by way of that designation? The Arahant is “such” by way of that designation: when there is virtue, he is “virtuous”; when there is faith, he is “faithful”;
when there is energy, he is “energetic”; when there is mindfulness, he is “mindful”;

when there is concentration, he is “concentrated”; when there is wisdom, he is “wise”; when there is true knowledge, he is “possessor of the three knowledges” (tevijjo); when there is direct knowledge...
"One who possesses the six direct knowledges is a *tādī* by virtue of that description; likewise, an Arahant is a *tādī* by virtue of that description.
But the Blessed One is a *tādī* who surpasses all such *tādīs*. Therefore he said, "Well-established.
And this was also said by the Blessed One in the Kāḷakārāma Sutta: "Thus, monks, the Tathāgata, regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized..."
“Among all things, he alone is the ‘such-like one’ (tādī); and I say that there is no other such-like one superior or more excellent than him.
Alternatively, the meaning is that he is well-established in the characteristic of “such-likeness” through five modes by means of the fivefold accomplishment of noble psychic power.
For this was said by the Venerable Dhammasenāpati in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:
“What is noble supernormal power (*ariyā iddhi*)? Here, a monk, if he should wish:

‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive; if he should wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ dwells there perceiving the repulsive;
if he should wish: ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive’...”

‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive; if he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive;
if he wishes, ‘Avoiding both the repulsive and the unrepulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,’ he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
“He dwells therein equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
*Bahiddhā* means outside of the Dispensation, that is, in a non-Buddhist system (*asamaya*).

*Esa* refers to the manner of paying homage to the Saṅgha of monks. To establish this matter by means of a worldly simile, the passage beginning with “the king” was stated. *Okāsa* means the place where one should inquire.

"There is no burden for me in answering questions"—this is a statement made in substance by the Teacher, who possesses unimpeded range of knowledge in all respects; for this meaning is already implied when he says, "If you so desire.
The same principle applies here to the words, "I shall answer everything for you. Indeed, it is implied by the very words, "Ask whatever you desire."
This meaning is established. The connection is: "The invitation of omniscience is unique.

If they do not say, "Whenever you wish," then how do they speak? To this he says, "Having heard," and so forth. It should be understood that they speak thus because they abide only in partial knowledge (*padesañāṇa*).
However, the connection is: "But the Buddhas extend the invitation of omniscience."

Regarding the scriptural passages beginning with "Ask, friend, whenever you wish," it is said "of the yakkhas, lords of men, devas, recluses, brahmins, and wanderers" in order to show the types of persons for whose sake these were spoken.
For therein, "Ask, friend, whenever you wish" was an invitation granted to the yakkha Āḷavaka, while "Ask, Great King" [was addressed to a lord of men].
It should be understood that this constitutes the granting of an opportunity to the lords of men with the words, “Ask, Vāsava”; to the lord of the gods with the words, “Then indeed...”;
to the recluses with the words, “And to Bāvari...”; and to the wanderers with the words, “Ask me, Sabhiya.
“Vāsava” is an address to the lord of the gods; for this occurs in the *Sakkapañha Sutta*. “Manasicchasi” means you desire with the mind.
"Since you have been granted leave by me, therefore ask whatever doubt you desire in your minds—whether it concerns Bāvari, yourself, Ajita, or all the others;
ask, ask! This is the construction. And here, "ask in your minds" refers to the doubt of Bāvari, whereas "all of you" refers to the doubt of everyone else.
The intention is: "Ask whatever you wish, both mentally and otherwise.
For Bāvarī had commanded his pupils, "Ask your own doubts mentally alone. For it is said:
"If the Buddha will be one who sees without obstruction..."
“A question asked by mind, he will answer with speech. This occurs in the *Pārāyana-vagga*.
Likewise, there is the passage beginning, “Ask me, Sabhiya,” and so forth.

“The stage of a Buddha” (*buddhabhūmi*) refers to the state of a Buddha, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*), and omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*). The “stage of a bodhisatta” (*bodhisattabhūmi*)...
The term *nāma* refers to the state of a Bodhisatta, which is the knowledge of the accumulation of the perfections (*pāramī*). Alternatively, the word *bhūmi* denotes a stage;

thus, the meaning is "the stage of a Buddha" and "the stage of a Bodhisatta. For, according to the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*), it is indeed the stage itself within the aggregates (*khandha*) that occurs as they evolve, based upon their respective modes.
Of that Blessed One, who, while established in partial knowledge on the stage of a Bodhisatta, made the proclamation of omniscience—his...
The connection is: "That very thing is wonderful. To ask how, he says: "O Koṇḍañña, the questions," and so forth.
Therein, "Koṇḍañña" is an address to Sarabhaṅga by way of his clan. "Viyākarohi" means "explain. "Sādhurūpā" means "of a virtuous nature.
"Dhamma" refers to the eternal, traditional lineage-dhamma. "Yaṃ" is a reference to the act of coming, or else it refers to the reason.
The connection is: "He comes; answer him with that. "Vuddha" means one who has attained growth through virtue, wisdom, and so forth;
the sense is "venerable. "Esa bhāro" means this burden, namely the severing of doubt; the intention is that this burden which has arrived must necessarily be carried by you.
"May the venerable ones, having been granted leave by me, ask. Why is that? Because, having known for myself this world and the world beyond, I shall answer each of your questions.
The word "sayam" means "by oneself," that is, without the instruction of another.
Thus, the connection is that at the time of Sarabhaṅga, he made this invitation of omniscience.

“Questions” means questions regarding the sacrifice of the Dhamma. “Ending-maker” means one who brings about the final conclusion. “By Sucirata” means by the brahmin named thus. “Having asked” means having inquired.
“By birth” means by rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*); some also say it means “by different birth. It should be connected as follows:
while playing in the dust, Prince Sambhava, even while sitting down, made his request.
*Taggha* is a particle used in the sense of emphasis (*ekamsatthe*). The phrase *yathāpi kusalo tathā* means:

"Just as the Buddha—who is skilled in all phenomena and knows all phenomena—knows and speaks, so shall I declare to you"; this is the meaning. For the word *jānāti* (he knows) here enters into a connection [with what follows].
As it has been said: "Whatever is connected with something, even if it stands far away, that belongs to it. And in this context, "knowing" is synonymous with "speaking."
This meaning has been stated by the Teacher as: "By means of this, one knows that.

And as for whether the King will do it or not—whether the Kaurava king who sent you here to ask about that matter which was asked by you, or the matter explained by me when questioned by you, actually carries it out or does not carry it out—I, however, [shall speak] according to the Dhamma.
“I shall tell you” means “I will explain. In the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, however, it says:
“And as for ‘the king,’ I shall tell you that question in such a way that the king knows it—that he is able to know it.
Beyond that, whether the king acts according to what he knows or does not act, [it is up to him].”
"It will belong to him alone, whether he does it or does not do it; there is no fault on my part"—thus the word *jānāti* (he knows) is stated in a sense common to both sentences.
163. *Sippāyatana* means "the sphere of craft," because the word *āyatana* expresses the state of being that [craft]. Furthermore, because it is something to be learned...
That craft is a "craft-sphere" (*sippāyatana*) because it is either the cause for the livelihood of beings or their support.
Regarding the phrase *seyyathidaṃ*, it is either a single particle or a collection of particles.

To the question "Which of those are they?"—meaning "Which among them are these here?"—he says, "But which are they? This meaning also applies individually to the phrase *ime katame pi*. Thus it is in all instances.
And this is stated by way of reference to those who ought to be spoken of; therefore, the meaning is: "Which of these are they that subsist by the various crafts?

For, having first pointed out the crafts in general as "the various fields of craft," those who actually live by each respective craft are subsequently specified in a discourse that takes individuals as its subject.
Why is this? Because [the author] wishes to avoid prolixity. Otherwise, indeed, [he would have had to list] exactly those intended...
Having shown the fields of craft (*sippāyatana*), one might further have to show those who subsist by those various crafts, since they too are intended here primarily.
But if that were the case, there would be an excessive proliferation of discourse (*kathāpapañca*).

Therefore, in order to avoid that proliferation, he spoke thus by including the various fields of craft within those who subsist by craft; to show this meaning, [he says] "elephant-riders," and so forth.
"It shows those who live by depending on various crafts," it is said. To the question "Why?", he says "For this... and so forth.
Those who live depending on a craft are "craft-livelihooders" (*sippūpajīvino*).
Those who mount elephants are "elephant-riders" (*hatthārohā*), meaning warriors mounted on elephants. Those who cause others to mount the elephant are also "elephant-riders" (*hatthārohā*).
"Elephant trainers, elephant physicians, elephant tamers, and so forth.
For this includes all those who provide the training by which a person becomes fit to mount an elephant; thus he said, "all of them as well," and so on.
In that context, "elephant trainers" refers to those who instruct elephants and elephant riders. "Elephant physicians" refers to...
*Hatthibhisakkā*. *Hatthimaṇḍā* refers to the elephant-keepers. They are called *hatthimaṇḍā* because they adorn (*maṇḍayanti*) and protect (*rakkhanti*) the elephants;
thus they are *hatthimaṇḍā*. Alternatively, they are *hatthimaṇḍā* because they measure (*minenti*) the elephants or injure them (*hiṃsanti*) by means of proper training.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), those who provide barley and other provisions for the elephants are included. Regarding *assārohā* (horsemen), here too [the agent] is expressed in its pure causal sense.
The meaning is exactly as stated. *Rathikā* are those engaged with the chariot. *Ratharakkhā* are those who protect the axle-pins (*āṇi*) of the chariot.
*Dhanuggahā* are those who take up the bow; they are archers. Or, *dhanuggahā* are those who cause others to take up the bow; they are the masters of the art of archery (*dhanvācariyā*).
*Celakā* are those who go to battle with a cloth banner (*celapaṭākā*); he says, "those who seize the victory-banner."
“In battle,” and so forth. *Jayadhaja* means a banner raised for the purpose of victory, or one held aloft at the time of victory. *Purato* means in front of the army.
They are called *calaka* because they cause those soldiers stationed here and there to move and shift from side to side by means of maneuvering the battle formations (*byūha*).
Thus it is said, “In this case, of the king,” and so forth. Like a hawk and other birds toward a lump of meat, [they attack] the mass of the enemy army.
They are called *piṇḍadāyakā* because, having cut off the *piṇḍa* (the cluster of fruits) again and again with violence, they fly up and fly up and depart.
Therefore he said, “It is said that they...,” and so forth. They are *sāhasikā* because they act with violence; they are indeed great warriors.
Regarding the phrase “like a *piṇḍa*,” some say it means “like a cluster of palm fruits,” while the Teacher stated, “like a lump of flesh. In all instances, [the reference is] “by the Teacher.”
When this has been said, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla alone is to be understood [as the author]. Regarding the second alternative:

they are "givers of alms" (*piṇḍadāyakā*) because they go as if leaping toward the "alms," which is to say, toward the crowd consisting of a multitude of people; the word *daya* means "going," or it is derived from the root *aya* with the addition of the letter *da*.
*Uggatuggatā* means having risen exceedingly high upon reaching the battle by way of speed, prowess, and so forth.
*Tadeva* refers to that very same head or weapon mentioned by the opponents. *Pakkhandanti* means they enter the enemy army without hesitation due to their heroic and courageous nature.
Their resemblance to great elephants is due to their possession of firmness, speed, strength, prowess, and so on. Therefore he said: "Even among elephants, etc."
*Ekantasūrā* means "solitary heroes," because the word *anta* here functions in the sense of "being alone";

the meaning is that they fight while remaining solitary by virtue of their heroism. *Sajālikā* means "with armor. *Sannāha*, *kaṅkaṭa*, *vammo*, *kavaca*, *uracchada*, and *jālikā* are one and the same in meaning.
*Sacammikā* means "with skin," as in being provided with skin for the protection of the body, just like the *jālikā*.
*Camma-kañcukaṃ* means a leather armor (*cammamaya-kañcukaṃ*). *Pavisitvā* means having entered within it; "having put it on" is what is meant.
*Sarapaṭṭhāna-cammaṃ* is a cloth fastened with leather, or a shield made of leather.
*Balava-sinehā* means those who have excessive affection for their mistress. *Gharadāsa-yodhā* means warriors belonging to the category of slaves born within the household.
“*Gharadāsikaputtā*” is also a reading, meaning the sons of female slaves born within the household.
*Āḷāraṃ* refers to the kitchen; those appointed there are *āḷārikā*. *Pūvikā* means makers of cakes—those who live by preparing various kinds of cakes and selling them.
[They also live] by grooming people’s hair and nails, and so forth.

They fashion the rules for adornment and arrange them, thus they are *kappakas* (barbers). They bathe and perform ablutions by means of powders, ointments, and so forth, through the method of removing dirt and perfecting the complexion, thus they are *nhāpikas* (bathers).
A recitation of the *Gaṇa-gaṇṭhi* that proceeds according to the sequence beginning with "Navanta" is called *acchiddaka* because it lacks any gaps in between;
those who recite that very [text] are *acchiddakapāṭhakā* (reciters of the *acchiddaka*). By hand...
It is the making known of one’s intention, or counting by means of hand-gestures (*muddā*).
For the contraction of the fingers is called *muddā*, and by means of that, there is either communication or counting.

And here the word "hand" (*hattha*) should be understood as referring to the fingers, which are parts of it—as in such expressions as "while eating, I will not put my whole hand into the mouth"—for they live depending upon it.
A seal-ring. Therefore he said, "By means of hand-signs," and so forth.

A metal-worker is a smith. An ivory-worker is a turner. A painter is a wall-painter. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is an inclusion of the carver, the engraver, the wax-modeler, the bricklayer, the carpenter, and others.
"In this very life" (diṭṭheva dhamme) means in this very [existence].
Regarding "in one's own person" (*attabhāve*): having shown it by way of accomplishing the instrument, [the text says] "precisely visible in this very life" (*sanditṭhikam eva*).

This means it is to be seen by oneself because it pertains to the present life, and it is to be experienced by oneself; that is, it is within the range of one's own direct perception (*attapaccakkha*). "They subsist upon" (*upajīvanti*) means they live depending on it. "Happy" (*sukhitaṃ*) means one who has attained happiness.
Since being endowed with fortitude and strength itself is nourishment, he said: "nourished, endowed with fortitude and strength."

"Upari" means in the world of the devas; likewise, it is also "uddham. For that [world] is above the human world. It is called "agga" because it is like the tip; it is the fruit. The Teacher has said:
"Because the fruit is produced from the performance of karma, that [fruit] is like the crest of a flame of fire.
Furthermore, "sagga" means the supreme fruit. "Sagga" means the excellent tip, consisting of the tenfold [realm] beginning with visible forms and sounds.

The meaning is that it is worthy to produce its own fruit. *Sovaggikā* is derived from *su-aggi* according to the rules of etymology (*nirutti*), and the feminine gender is used throughout in view of the word *dakkhiṇā*. *Sukha* means a means to happiness—desirable and lovely. *Agge* means sublime.
External form to be enjoyed by oneself is "beauty" (*rūpa*), while one's own complexion and physical excellence is "complexion" (*vaṇṇa*); this is the distinction between them.
It is called *dakkhiṇā* because people perceive and increase [merit] by means of it; thus he says, "The *dakkhiṇā* is giving (*dāna*)," meaning merit consisting of relinquishment.

Considering that the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*) is the path of one who is a recluse (*samaṇa*), defined as one who has stilled evil, the noble fruit is the fruit of recluseship because it is its result.
He establishes this meaning by way of the Pāḷi of the Mahāvagga-saṃyutta with the words, "As it was said," and so forth. That...
This king does not know because of his lack of skill in the noble Dhamma.

For he thought, "For those who have gone forth, having become like slaves or farmers, the receiving of salutations and so forth from the world is indeed called a visible fruit of the ascetic life (sandiṭṭhikaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ)," and thus,
while investigating whether there might be some ascetic or brahmin who knows such a thing, he [approached] Pūraṇa and the others.
Having asked them and not having gained understanding from their discourse, he asked the Blessed One about this same matter. Therefore it is said:
"He asks with reference to the simile of the slave and the farmer.
"Royal ministers" (*rājāmaccā*) means ministers born into the royal family; the meaning is also those who are both devoted to the king and are his ministers.
"The dark side" (*kaṇhapakkha*) refers to the faction of defilement associated with the speculative views available regarding the matter as asked.
"The bright side" (*sukkapakkha*) refers to the faction of purification found in the subsequent sutta, which is the opposite of that [dark side].

"The clamor of recluses" (*samaṇakolāhala*) means the clamor of recluses—the mutual contradictions among the various doctrines of recluses. "The quarreling of recluses" (*samaṇabhaṇḍana*) means, due to that very contradiction, [the dispute] of those who hold such views...
“This is the fault of those ascetics and brahmins; this is the fault of those who hold such views”—this is the censure of their respective doctrines.
By demonstrating the nature of things—that the world follows a Supreme Lord—he establishes that meaning.
He does so through his own skill in teaching, taking up the burden for the King, and not for any other reason such as disparaging others.
164. Just as the word *nu* is a particle used in a question, so too is the word *no*; thus he said, "Do you recollect? (*abhijānāsi nū*).
Regarding the phrase "and this," the word *ca* here has a conjunctive sense, meaning: "not only by the word 'do you recollect,' but also by the word 'having been asked.
To remove the objection as to how it should be construed, he says "for this" (*idañhi*), and so forth. "Having been asked" (*pucchitā*) refers to one who previously performed the act of questioning.
"Do you recall that state of being questioned? means: do you remember having been asked such a question? "Has it not been forgotten by you? means:
has this matter not been lost to your memory? "The state of discomfort" means: the condition of unhappiness resulting from speaking in such a manner.

"Of those who merely resemble wise men" (as if they were wise themselves, though their speech is like that of fools): [this refers to] the speech of those who appear to be wise, yet whose words are like raw grain instead of cooked.

"In the Pāli words, meanings, and phonemes" means: in the words comprised by the term "Pāli," in their meanings, and in the syllables included therein; or else, the word *byañjana* has the sense of "sentence," as in such expressions as "syllable (*akkhara*), word (*pada*), and sentence (*byañjana*).
One who possesses a form (*rūpa*) like that of the Blessed One—that is, whose nature (*sabhāva*) is like his—is "one having the form of the Blessed One" (*bhagavantarūpa*);
the meaning is that he is exclusively wise, just like the Blessed One.
Commentary on the Teaching of Pūraṇa Kassapa:
165. Regarding the phrase *ekam-idāhaṃ*: here, *idaṃ* is merely a particle; the meaning is simply "at one time.

It is called *sammodanīyaṃ* because it causes mutual greeting (*sammodeti*) or brings about friendly exchange (*sammodanaṃ karoti*). For the suffix *-anīya* frequently expresses the sense of the agentive or active function, as in [the following examples].
“Leading out” (*niyyānika*) means it produces gladness; thus, by way of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), it is “gladdening” (*sammodaniya*).
It is “to be remembered” (*sāritabba*), hence “rememberable” (*sāraṇīya*); or alternatively, it is “suitable for remembering,” hence “recollection-inducing” (*sāraṇiya*).
To show this meaning, it is said: “producing gladness and suitable for being remembered. And “suitable for being remembered” means “fit for recollection.”
166. *Sahatthā* means "with one's own hand"; by this, he indicates the agent acting directly. By the word *āṇatti* ("command"), however, he indicates the agent acting through another.
Here, even the offenses involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) and those concerning fixed penalties (*thāvara*) are included under the category of acting with one's own hand.
*Hatthādīni* refers to the hands, feet, ears, nose, and so forth. Regarding "cooking, burning, and harming," he says: "of one who presses down with a stick. [End of] the *Papañcasūdani*.
In the *Madhyamāgama-aṭṭhakathā*, however, a second meaning for the word "pacato" is stated as "of one who threatens";
here, the Master has stated that since threatening and reviling are included within punishment, it is simply said, "of one who oppresses with punishment.
Yet, the reading "of one who threatens (*tajjentassa vā*)" also appears in current manuscripts.
It is frequently seen. "Sorrow" (*soka*) means the cause of sorrow; it is also appropriate to take it as "the act of grieving," since by bringing about the cause, the result must also be performed.
"By others" means by those who carry out one's own words, acting as the instruments. Regarding "trembling":
here, a purely active sense based on another’s trembling is not obtained; rather, it is based on one’s own trembling. Thus he said: "another trembling."
"Even while trembling at the time of another's trembling"—the meaning is that one trembles oneself through the application of causing harm to another by means of one's own action.

He shows that the term "of one who causes to kill" applies both to the simple agent (*suddhakattari*) and to the causal agent (*hetukattari*) by means of the phrase "of one who kills and of one who causes to kill.
"In all instances" refers to [the phrases] beginning with "of one who takes up" (*ādiyato*). "By way of doing and causing to do" (*karaṇakāraṇavasena*).
By way of acting oneself or causing another to act.

The junction both inside and outside the wall of a house is the "house-junction" (*gharasandhi*). Because it is a plundering that leaves nothing remaining—without exception—it is called "plundering" (*nillopa*);
thus he said "great plunder" (*mahāvilopa*). Plundering pertaining to a single house is "single-house plunder" (*ekāgārika*). Therefore he said:

“‘Ekameva’ and so forth. Regarding the phrase “standing in the path,” he shows by means of the words “of those who have come and gone” and so on that the meaning established by the context here is that one stands specifically for the purpose of seizing.

The teacher has also stated the meaning: “Obstruction (paripantha) is the act of killing (hanana) completely (parito) on the path (panthe). By the phrase “with the perception ‘I am doing it,’” he expresses the state of being intentional (sañcetanika).
By this he shows: "Even for one who acts intentionally, it is said that [the evil] is not done, how much more so for one who acts unintentionally.
"Evil is not done" means that because it is impossible to produce what was previously non-existent, evil is indeed uncreated. Therefore he says, "There is no evil.
If this is so, how is it that beings engage in evil? [The author], wishing to remove the fault imputed by others to his own doctrine, says:
Pūraṇa says "But as for beings... and so forth in order to demonstrate this point as well.
What is meant is that the expression "they commit evil" is a mere designation (*saññāmatta*); in reality, evil does not exist at all. For he thinks thus:
"The actions of these beings, such as violence and the like, do not reach the self because of its permanence and immutability; the body, however, is insentient, comparable to a wooden log."
Even when that [rim] is damaged, no evil arises. "Pariyanta" means the rim (*nemi*), because it stands at the end (*pariyosāna*).
Therefore, the Teacher said: "by one with a rim made of whetted iron. In the second interpretation, the end of the wheel itself is the *pariyanta*;
that which has a rim similar to a razor is "razor-edged" (*khurapariyanta*). And here, by the mention of the "razor," the edge of the razor is intended.
“Seized” is said because of being captured by that [weapon]. In the Pāḷi, “by a discus” (*cakkena*) means by a specific weapon fashioned in the shape of a discus.
“*Tatonidānaṃ*” means that for which the cause or reason is the act of making a mark on the flesh; thus it is “on account of that. Regarding this, it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathās:

“In the case of the ablative suffix *to*, it is a substitute for the nominative case, and there is no elision of the *ca* in the compound. Master Sāriputtatthera says: “The ablative case is also appropriate in the sense of the nominative.”
The grammarians also state that [the word] is a collection of particles used in the sense of causality.

The phrase "if on the south" (*dakkhiṇañce*) and so forth was spoken with the intention that the southern direction of the Ganges is an unsuitable location, whereas the northern direction is a suitable location;
and in order to show that this refers to the inhabitants of those places by means of the designation of the region and direction, he said "on the southern bank" (*dakkhiṇatīre*) and so forth.

For the performance of giving is dependent upon that [self-restraint]. "Great sacrifice" (*mahāyāga*) refers to a great sacrifice similar to the sacrifice of a great world-conquering king (*vijitarāja*).
The word *dama* (taming) is a synonym for both the restraint of the sense faculties and the Uposatha precepts; thus he said, "by the taming of the faculties and by the Uposatha rite.
However, some maintain that the phrase "by the Uposatha rite" is a qualification of the taming of the faculties; therefore, [it means] "by that which consists of the Uposatha rite."
Regarding the phrase "by the restraint of the faculties" (*indriyadamena*), they say it refers to "the goal" (*attha*);

however, that is indeed incorrect, because the word *dama* denotes both meanings, and those two meanings are used with specific distinctions. For now, in some manuscripts, the word *vā* is seen, and the word *ca* is also seen.
"By the restraint of virtue" (*sīlasaṃyamena*) means by the other types of bodily and verbal restraint. "By truthful speech" (*saccavacanena*) means by that which is free from falsehood.
It is mentioned separately because it is considered the gravest among merits in the world.
For just as false speech is the gravest among unwholesome qualities, so too is non-falsehood the foremost among meritorious qualities. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the *Itivuttaka*:
“For a person who has transgressed this one thing, the speaker of falsehood...”
“For one who has disregarded the next world, there is no evil that should not be done.
“Occurrence” (*pavatti*) means the arising [of an action] within the continuum of the one who performs it, by way of being a condition for the production of its fruit.

For it is in this way that the doctrine of non-action—“there is no karma, there is no fruit of karma”—is fulfilled. Indeed, if there were a fruit of karma, there could be no state of non-performance of karmas.
"How will it be? "In every way" means in every manner stated [in the passage] beginning with "one who acts. "Labuja" refers to the *likuca* fruit.
He rejects only the performance of evil and merit; the intention is that he does not explain the visible fruit of recluseship asked about by the King.
For this restriction is for the purpose of excluding the rejection of the ripening [of karma].
For whoever rejects action, by that very fact, its result is also effectively rejected. Thus he will say:
"By one who would also obstruct action," and so forth.
It is called a *vijita* because it is specifically conquered (*jita*) by being such that it cannot be overcome by rival kings; it is the domain where the command of a single king prevails.
“Do not dwell within my realm”—this dismissal of one who has gone forth is indeed a form of harassment known as expulsion;
thus it is said, “one should be harassed. The confirmation, observation, and grasping of the meaning stated by that [harassment] as being “just so” is what is meant here;
he rejects it by means of this [statement], saying, “not grasping it as essential. Of that meaning, however—
"Uprighting" (*nikkujjana*) means supporting with the mind by way of bringing about a state of endurance;
he shows that this is rejected by the phrase "by way of the core... not setting it down. "By way of the core alone" (*sāravaseneva*) means by way of the supreme alone;

or else, because it is not otherwise, the firm meaning which cannot be moved by others is called the "core" (*sāra*) due to its lack of pithlessness (*apheggubhāva*); "by way of that alone" means by way of that very thing.

The meaning (*attha*) is the escape from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). The ultimate meaning (*paramattha*) is the unerring meaning, or the meaning that serves as the object for supreme knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
As for the phrasing (*byañjana*), however, it is both as it was grasped and as it was set down, precisely because it was spoken in the presence of the Blessed One.
Commentary on the Discourse of Makkhali Gosāla.

168. "By both" means by the statement negating the causal condition (*hetupaccaya*). By the phrase "only that which exists," he shows that when one rejects even that which exists by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), ignorance alone is the cause.

"Condition for defilement" (*saṃkilesapaccaya*) is the cause of being defiled or stained. "Condition for purification" (*visuddhipaccaya*) is the condition for purification or cleansing from defilement.
The word *attakāreti* is formed from the singular nominative case ending *-e*; for example, as in “*vanappagumbe yathā phusitagge*” (just as in a forest thicket with its tops in bloom).
Alternatively, it is a locative case used in the sense of the nominative, as in “*idampissa hoti sīlasmiṃ*” (this too is his virtue).

The phrase “*attakāro*” demonstrates this same meaning. Furthermore, it refers to the action that must be performed by each respective being through themselves, or the effort to be accomplished by themselves.
Or rather: therefore he says “by which,” and so forth. “Omniscience” means perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). “That” refers to the deed performed by oneself.
“By the second phrase” means by the phrase “there is no success through the agency of another. Now, what is called “the agency of another” is an effort that succeeds through the exertion of another.
Therefore it is said: “whatever [is done] through the agency of another,” and so forth. “Instruction and admonition” means an admonition that consists of instruction; or else, first...
This is the exhortation and the subsequent instruction. Furthermore, this demonstration of the meaning is by way of illustrating the term "assistance from others" (*parakāra*);
for there is no dependence on assistance from others regarding supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*), thus he says, "excepting the Great Being.

However, such assistance does indeed exist in regard to mundane states (*lokiya-dhamma*), as was the case when our Bodhisatta, relying on Āḷāra Kālāma, attained the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhiññā*) and mundane meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
And that was said with reference to the Great Being in his final existence; for even the Pacceka-bodhisattvas are included right here, as they too lack those [other types of karma].
"Human good fortune" (*manussa-sobhagya*) means the state of being fortunate among humans.

"In this way" means by rejecting the doctrine of non-action (*akiriyavāda*) and the doctrine of non-causality (*akammavāda*). Regarding the "Wheel of the Conqueror" (*jinacakkra*): "There is, monks, karma..."

In the Buddha’s teaching, when the existence of kamma and the fruits of kamma is demonstrated through such methods as “black [kamma] with black result,” etc., to speak in opposition [to this] is like dealing a blow; thus it is said, “he deals a blow.
Precisely because there is no such thing as acting for one's own sake or for the sake of another, there is no such thing as individual personal effort (paccatta-purisakāra) for sentient beings.
Having in mind the statement “there is no human agency,” the passage beginning with “by whom” was spoken in order to show the rejection of that [agency].
The phrases beginning with “even godhood” and “human prosperity” refer to the types of states already mentioned.

Having said “established in strength,” the phrase “having exerted energy” was spoken to show that in this context, energy is what constitutes strength; for it is energy that brings about for beings success in matters pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the attainment of Nibbāna.

"He rejects it, thinking 'there is no power of energy' (vīriyabalaṃ); and this rejection of the power of purification (vodāniyabala) is merely by way of illustration, because by that [rejection] the defiling power is also rejected.
If energy and the rest are synonyms for human effort (purisakāra), then why are they mentioned separately? To this he says: "This is through our energy," and so forth. "This is through our energy."
"This fruit has arisen through our own energy. By way of refuting the conventional expression "arisen" [used by others]:
that is, by way of refuting the conventional linguistic usage of others.

By way of refuting the doctrine of those who assert that [things] arise through the power of energy, strength, and exertion—just like the phrase "there is no strength"—all these [terms] likewise [function].
The intended meaning is that [the faculties] are taken up by it. This is stated from the perspective of the meaning of the term (*vacanīyattha*);

however, from the perspective of the meaning of the word (*vacanattha*), it is "power" (*bala*) in the sense of being predominant (*ussanna*) in respect of each respective activity. It is "energy" (*vīriya*) in the sense of bringing about the state of being brave and heroic.
That same [quality], by virtue of its firmness and because it must be exercised by one bearing the human yoke, is "human effort" (*purisathāma*). By way of ascending to ever higher stages...
It should be understood that "manly exertion" refers to the process of active engagement.

[Regarding the terms *satta* and *pāṇa*: they are called *satta* because of being bound and fettered by form and so forth; they are called *pāṇa* because of breathing through inhalation and exhalation.

Although these two terms are identical in this sense, one distinguishes them from the category of *satta* by classifying *pāṇa* according to the number of faculties, such as those with only one faculty, and so on.
Having considered this, he said, "He speaks thus: 'A single-facultied one,' and so forth. He shows by the passage, "An egg...

he speaks thus," that although the terms *bhūta*, *satta*, and *pāṇa* are synonyms for a living being, these [terms] are stated to be distinct from them in the sense of "coming into existence" (*sambhavana*) within the eggshell and so on.
The "womb-envelope" (*vatthikosa*) is the interior of the womb. Because they grow as if supporting their life-breath (*pāṇa*), they are "living beings" (*jīvā*). Therefore, he said:
“*Sāli-yavā*,” etc. By the word “etc.,” grasses and trees that have grown are included. They are called *avasā* because they lack mastery (*vaso*) or capability regarding defilement and purification.
Likewise, they are weak and devoid of effort. Thus he said, “of these,” and so forth. “Fixed” (*niyatā*) means being determined;
because their occurrence is fixed—like an indestructible gem strung on an unbreakable thread—in terms of destiny, birth, bondage, and liberation.
The meaning is "it leads to" (*niyāmeti*). In that context, "in each of those" means in each of those various births.

"Going" (*gamana*) refers to the coming together or meeting by way of combination with those things that have become related to the six classes of beings (*abhijāti*). Although the word *bhāva* (nature/being) does not depend on a correlate, it expresses its own essential meaning as if accompanied by a correlate;
thus he says, "only the nature itself," just as in the case of the sharpness of a thorn or the [astringency] of wood-apple fruits and so forth.

The meaning is this: the circularity [of the earth], the diverse forms of animals and birds, and likewise the transformation of the entire world in such and such ways, occurs without the intervention of a cause or condition;
it is simply its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Therefore, it was said: "By which," and so forth. "Transformation" (*pariṇamana*) means the attainment of various states.
"By which" refers to beings, living creatures, and so on. The connection is: "just as it ought to be, so indeed it is."
The six classes of beings will be explained in detail later.
By saying, "They experience both pleasure and pain," it is stated that Makkhali does not know the plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure in its entirety;
thus, it is said, "he shows that there is no other plane of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. This statement, "they experience both pleasure and pain," functions as an instrument [of proof].

This is the opinion stated by the Teacher after having taken [the text]. However, in the manuscripts, only this reading is seen: “He shows that there is no other ground for pleasure and pain,” and not “the ground of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

This being so, taking the phrase “in the six classes of birth” (*chasvevābhijātīsū*) as the locus (adhikaraṇa), it means the experience of pleasure and pain occurs only within those six classes of birth.

It should be understood that it is stated [in the commentary] to show that [the feeling] is not elsewhere than by those [bases], but is precisely that plane of pleasure and pain, and nothing other than that.
And this alone is the more logical [interpretation], because the meaning to be negated is stated by way of its plane (*bhūmi*).
For if there were a demonstration of what is to be negated by the statement, "they experience both pleasure and pain," then [the text would have said], "other... [than that].

If one were to show [it] as "there is no neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling]," it would not be shown as "the plane of neither-painful-nor-pleasant," because the word *bhūmi* (plane) lacks the sense of a cause for the vision.
And this [statement] shows precisely the absence of such a plane; therefore, it is understood that this reading and this meaning are more appropriate.

"Of noble births" (*pamukhayoni*) means, among humans, by way of the *khattiya*, *brāhmaṇa*, and so forth; and among animals, by way of the lion, tiger, and so forth—referring to those whose birth is preeminent (*padhāna*).
Here, "preeminence" (*padhānatā*) means excellence (*uttamatā*). Therefore, he said, "of supreme births" (*uttamayoni*).
"Sixty hundreds" means six thousand. The explanation of the phrase "and five hundred actions" (*pañca ca kammuno satāni*) is "five hundred actions."
And [the phrase] “It is the same method” refers by way of extension to this very meaning: that “he demonstrates a view that is entirely useless through mere reasoning alone.

And here, when he says “by mere reasoning,” it is because logicians—lacking the goad-like method of grasping the true state of things which serves as a support—due to their unrestrained nature, imagine whatever they have imagined to be essential, and thus [regard it] exactly so.
Having adhered [to these views], they grasp at them as dogmatic opinions; therefore, he clarifies this intention:
that wise persons should not engage in critical investigation regarding the basis for those views. "Some" refers to the residents of the Uttaravihāra monastery.
"By way of the five faculties" means by way of the five faculties beginning with the eye. For they [assert]: "These five faculties, consisting of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body..."
“They say, ‘The non-Buddhist sectarians (titthiyā) prescribe five types of action (kamma),’ and they also say, ‘Bodily, vocal, and mental actions are the three types of action.

The doctrine is that both of these [the five and the three] constitute complete action because of their grossness; the doctrine is that mental action is half-action because of its subtlety—this is the construction.
When it should have been said, ‘sixty-two paths,’ [they use] the conventional terminology of their own school.”
Not knowing [the correct form], he says "two sixty-three ways" (*dvaṭṭhipaṭipadā*); therefore, it is said "sixty-two ways" (*dvāsaṭṭhi paṭipadā*).

However, the *Saddaracakā* states, "In *dvāsaṭṭhi*, there is elision of *sa*, and it is *attamā*"; that is indeed incorrect, because it is not established through the application of grammatical rules (*yoga*) within the natural language (*sabhāvanirutti*).
For if it were established by rule, it would be nothing other than the natural language; and if that were the case, [it would contradict] the teachers...
They say that [this] contradicts their own opinion. However, such expressions as “eighty-four thousand” and so forth are simply the natural language (sabhāvanirutti) used elsewhere.
For it is seen in the *Visuddhimagga* and other works:
“Eighty-four thousand aeons do those gods remain.”
"But they do not remain even for that long, being confounded by two thoughts.
Regarding "in one eon" (*ekasmiṃ kappe*): this refers to one among the four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*).
Even there, it is said "sixteen intermediate eons" (*dvaṭṭhantarakappā*) with reference specifically to only one [eonic period] known as the "standing of the evolution" (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).
For he, being one who has not heard the Dhamma of the Teaching, does not know the others because they are outside the scope [of his knowledge]; the meaning is that, not knowing, he speaks thus.
They kill urabbhas (rams), or having killed them, they make a living from them, thus they are *orabbhikā* (shepherds). This same method applies to the fowlers (*sākuṇika*) and the rest.

*Luddā* refers to those remaining who are hunters (*nesāda*) making their living by means of four-footed animals; for in the word *māgavika* (deer-hunters), only the species of deer such as the *rohitā* and others are intended.
"Seized. Those who cause one to be led to a prison are "prisoners" (*bandhanāgārika*). "Of cruel deeds" means those whose actions are harsh.

This entire group is called "of dark birth" (*kaṇhābhijāti*) because they are devoted to dark kamma; this is said by taking it to mean that for whom there is the birth—that is, the arising—of a dark state.
"Bhikkhus" refers to bhikkhus within the Buddha’s dispensation. "Thorns" refers to desire and lust (*chandarāga*).

Their insertion [of the requisites] is by way of binding them together. It is said, "having inserted them into thorns," with the intention that they eat while bound by desire and lust, which are like thorns. Why? Because his misconception is that "they enjoy extremely refined requisites";
therefore, even when enjoying requisites obtained through right means, they [follow] the doctrine of the Ājīvakas.

Regarding the term *kaṇṭakavutti*: it means they live together with the "thorn" as previously described; he says that for those who have adopted a contrary course, they are said to "eat by throwing [conditions] into thorns.
"This is his own scripture" (*pāḷi*) means that this exposition of Makkhali’s doctrine, composed by himself, supports the aforementioned meaning. Some indeed are called *kaṇṭakavuttika*.
The meaning is: "There are other outsiders who have gone forth; they say [he is] 'of blue birth'.
For they are especially devoted to the practice of self-mortification. Indeed, because they live as if on thorns, they are called "thorn-livers" (*kaṇṭakavuttika*).
He whose "birth" (*abhijāti*)—that is, origin—is from the "blue" (*nīla*) dhamma is "of blue birth. The same applies to the others as well.
The Nigaṇṭhas are those who have gone forth among outsiders who claim, "We have no fetter or bond. They are called "Ekasāṭakas" because they wear only a single garment.

The phrase "It is said that these... and so forth was spoken in order to show their doctrine of progressive purification—how it is completely pure from black, then blue, and then red, and so on in sequence. They are called "paṇḍaratarā" (whiter) because of their adherence to vows such as the prohibition against eating and bathing.
They are more purified than the black-blue because they can be described as having a state of purity even compared to the red.
"Clad in white" means wearing white garments. "Disciples of the naked ones" refers to those who were disciples of the Ājīvakas.

It is said that because their minds were purified by the Ājīvaka doctrine, they were even whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas, having attained a state of purity even in comparison to the former, who were the color of turmeric.
With the words “Thus,” etc., he shows his arrival out of desire. The Ājīvakas were those who had gone forth as disciples of Nanda and others;
likewise there were Ājīvakinīs. It is said that Nanda and the others remained having brought such a practice of the Ājīvakas to its highest excellence;
therefore, they are described as being whiter than the Nigaṇṭhas who had gone forth as Ājīvaka disciples, as being of the most supreme white birth—this is his (the teacher's) tenet.
"Purisabhūmiyo" (stages of manhood) is a description of the exertion. These stages are desired even by women. "For seven days" is an expression of extreme confinement;
[it is said] because they are so dull and deluded for even that long. "From the cramped place" refers to the mother's womb.
They weep and wail, recollecting that [former state]. "Khedana" (toil) and "kīḷana" (play) are both included by the single term "khiḍḍā" (sport).
The "ground of play" (*khiḍḍābhūmi*) has been explained. "Placing of the foot" (*padanikkhipana*) means the act of setting down the foot.

When one is capable of placing the foot in such a manner, that is the state known as the "ground of testing the step" (*padavīmaṃsabhūmi*). This refers to the time of knowing what is proper and improper (*vatāvatassa*).

The phrases "a monk who has entered" (*pannaka*) and so forth are also found in the scriptures (*pāḷi*) of those outsiders. In that context, "one who has entered" (*pannaka*) means one who wanders for alms (*bhikkhāya vicaraṇaka*).
Or he is one who has practiced their way. *Jina* means "worn out" (*jiṇṇa*) by virtue of old age, having his constituent elements (*dhātu*) diminished;
or, having conquered the adversary to his own practice, he stands firm. It is said that being such, he did not speak even the Dhamma to anyone.
Therefore it is said: "He said nothing. Even when distortions were made regarding his lips, face, and so forth, he said nothing because of his forbearance.

They say: "He is one who does not receive from the mouth of a jar," and so forth; thus, by way of being endowed with the causes for non-gain as stated in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, he is "one who has no gains.
Precisely because of that, being overcome by the weakness of hunger, he is called a "pannabhūmi ascetic" in the sense of being intent on lying down.
“Hundreds of means of livelihood” (ājīvavuttisatāni) refers to hundreds of ways of life that constitute the livelihoods of beings.
Although it is said “hundreds of wanderers” (paribbājakasatāni), he, not knowing their natural gender, says “hundreds of wanderers” (paribbājakasate). The same applies to other cases as well.

Therefore, he says “hundreds of wanderer-ordainings” (paribbājakapabbajjāsatāni). “The abode of the nāgas” (nāgabhavana) is a circle of nāgas, just as in the expression “the circle of Mahīsakas” (mahiṃsakamaṇḍala).
"Particles such as atoms" (*paramāṇu-ādi rajo*). By the mention of "cattle," the species of sheep is included;
by the mention of "wild animals," the species of wild animals such as the *ruru* deer and the *gavaya* are included. "In a knot" means in a joint; the meaning is "in a node.

There are many gods, categorized by way of the Four Great Kings, the Brahmakāyika gods, and so forth, as well as by way of their internal subdivisions. Among those, the internal subdivisions of some of the Four Great Kings are [explained] by the *Mahāsamaya Sutta*.

It should be illustrated. By the words beginning with "But he," it is shown that since he does not know, he speaks of even many devas as merely *sattas* (beings), and thus demonstrates his lack of measure.
Humans are also infinite by way of the distinctions of continent, country, clan, lineage, livelihood, and so forth. *Pesācā* means just *pisācas*;
they are "very great" by way of being *aparapetas* and so on—the meaning is that they are more numerous. In the non-Buddhist systems...
However, the Teacher stated: "The Chaddanta Lake and the Mandākinī are designated by the names Kuvāḷiya and Mucalinda.
*Gaṇṭhikā* refers to mountain joints (*pabbagaṇṭhikā*). For the word *pavuṭa* is used for a mountain joint. *Mahāpapātā* means great precipices.

By way of elimination (*pārisesanayena*), there are hundreds of small precipices. It is the same regarding dreams. As for the term "Mahākappino," it is synonymous with "Mahākappānaṃ" (of the great aeons).
This must be understood. Furthermore, it is not subject to critical examination to say that he speaks thus because he does not know the word;
for he says this because he was unable to say "eighty-four hundred thousand" (*caturāsīti satasahassāni*).
However, the *Saddanīti* states: "In the case of *caturāsīti*, there is a substitution of *tu* for *ca*, *lu* for *ra*, and doubling of the consonant."
“Such great lakes” means great lakes of such a magnitude; that is, seven great lakes. “It is said” (*kirā*) is a particle used when recalling someone’s statement.
Even a wise person... [omission] ...does not go. Why? Because the time for the wandering of beings is fixed.
By the phrase “by the practice of nakedness or by any other [practice whatsoever],” he refers back to what was previously stated by the words “of a similar kind.”
“By the work of asceticism” means by the performance of ascetic practices. Here too, the governing term is “in such a way. The construction is: he who...
purifies himself “ripens karma that is not yet ripe. “In between” means within the interval of eight million four hundred thousand great aeons (*mahākappa*).
“Time after time” means having reached [the opportunity] again and again. “The stated measure of time” refers to the duration measuring eight million four hundred thousand great aeons.
"At the right time. This is what is meant: one causes unripened karma—which is the cause for wandering in saṃsāra—to ripen quickly through the attainment of purity by means of virtue and so forth;
and one brings about the exhaustion or disappearance of ripened karma by bringing it to its state of full maturation at the appropriate time.
"By a doṇa-measure" means by a doṇa or a tumba used as a measure. The meaning is according to the form of the word.

"It is obtained" is stated as "just like a measured [quantity]. By the words "not the cycle of existence," etc., he shows that there is no decrease or increase based on whether one is wise or foolish.
Increase is the upper limit (*ukkaṃsa*); decrease is the lower limit (*avakaṃsa*). "In a ball of spun thread" means in a coil of spun thread.
"It rolls away" (*paleti*)—it rolls away (*pareti*)—just as in the term "the future life" (*abhisamparāyo*), where the letter *ra-* [is elided].

However, it was stated thus by adding the letter *la*, just as in the word “*palibuddho*” (obstructed). And because it belongs to the *cur-ādi* group [of roots], it is stated that it means “he goes” (*gacchati*).
By this simile, he clarifies the meaning that this saṃsāra of beings is exhausted only gradually and does not increase, because its form is limited;
thus he said, “when the thread is exhausted,” and so forth. “Right there” means precisely at the place of exhaustion.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Ajita Kesakambalin (171):

“Given” refers specifically to the volition of giving under the heading of the object to be given. By means of that [volition], he shows the result [of the gift] with the phrase, “the absence of fruit for what has been given.
For, in the primary sense, “what has been given” is the material basis such as food; how could he possibly reject that?
This same method applies here as well to the terms *yiṭṭhaṃ* and *hutaṃ*. A "great sacrifice" (*mahāyāga*) is a great gift common to all.

"Hospitality" (*pāhunakasakkāra*) is the honor that ought to be performed toward a guest. "Fruit" (*phala*) refers to both the fruit of benefit (*ānisamsaphala*) and the outflow fruit (*nissandaphala*). "Resultant ripening" (*vipāka*) is the fruit of similarity.
For just as the attainment of a high station and so forth is the benefit in a gift endowed with the four factors, so too was it for the Brahmin Saṅkha.
In the case of giving, the outflow (*nissanda*) is merely the acquisition of protection, while the result (*vipāka*) is the similar fruit known as rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
This world and the other world are said to be obtainable through karma; this is stated because [the opponent] rejects them with reference specifically to the absence of such a fruit.
For how could the world, which is directly perceived, be rejected by him? [The opponent claims: "All things are cut off right there, in each respective place."
By this he states the reason: wherever these beings abide—whether in the various realms of existence (*bhava*), modes of birth (*yoni*), and so forth—they are cut off right there;

the meaning is that they perish by way of non-arising and non-destruction. "In them" means in the mother and father. He speaks solely by way of the absence of fruit, not because of the mother and father themselves, nor because of the absence of honor or dishonor currently being performed toward them in the world.
Because it is directly perceived. He said, "There are no spontaneously born beings," in order to show that the arising of these beings is merely like that of a bubble;
there is no prior process of passing away and coming into existence. [He further said:
"A true ascetic, knowing things as they really are, should not speak to anyone without being restrained."
It must be so; otherwise, it would be a mere "oh-my-man" (ahopurisa) boast. For what can one person do for another?
Likewise, there would be no basis whatsoever for the accomplishment of one's own goal, as everything would simply perish right where it stands.
It is with reference to this meaning that he said: "Those who... [etc. ...proclaim. This is the meaning according to the remainder of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathāvasesaka*).

“Consisting of the four great elements” (*cātumahābhūtamaya*) is said in order to show its nature as a mere thing, whereas it is “composed of the four great elements” (*cātumahābhūtiko*) because it is connected with the four great elements.
For just as a vessel produced from clay is called “made of clay,” so too this [body], being produced from the four great elements, is called “consisting of the four great elements.
“Internal earth element” (*ajjhattika-pathavīdhātu*) refers to the earth element existing within the continuum of a sentient being.
"External earth element" means the great external earth; by this, he shows that the body is indeed earth.
"Follows" means it accompanies. "By both [phrases]" refers to the two words [“follows” and “approaches”].
"Approaches" and "goes toward" mean that from the external body of earth, a portion of that very earth comes and, having attained the state of being internal, becomes established as a sentient being.

And that great earth returns to, or approaches, that very same external mass of earth which has now become a composite whole—just as the earth contained within a jar [returns to] the earth [outside it];
the meaning is that it attains a state of non-distinction and oneness with that entire external mass of earth.
This same method applies to water and the other elements as well; herein, the water taken from the great ocean by Pajjunna...
The intention of the proponent of that wrong view is merely a conceptualization: that [the soul] enters again into the great ocean as rainwater does;
it enters again into the sun’s rays as the heat known as fire is taken up by the sun’s rays; and it enters again into the mass of great winds as a great wind has issued from the mass of great winds.
It approaches, it goes back to—such is his intent through mere imagination.
"Mind as the sixth among the faculties" means those faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—for which the mind is the sixth;
they say that space enters into them by way of being their objective domain (*visaya*). For by mentioning the possessor of the object, the objects themselves are indeed included.
How is it that "the bed is the fifth" is calculated? He says: "The bed itself... [etc. ...is the meaning. The cremation ground.
“Cemetery” (*susāna*) and “charnel ground” (*sivathika*) are synonymous in meaning. “Terms for qualities and defects” (*guṇāguṇapadāni*) refers to categories of virtues and faults;

alternatively, the body itself is the “terms,” because it is reached through various actions. “The color of a pigeon’s wings” (*pārāvatapakkhivaṇṇāni*) means the colors of the bird named the pigeon (*pārāvata*).
The reading is “*pārāvatapakkhavaṇṇāni*,” which means having the color of the feathers of the pigeon-bird. “With ashes” (*bhasmantā*).

"It ends with the ashes. Therefore he said, "only ending with the ashes. By the word *āhuti* here, he shows that all kinds of giving—namely, what is described as "given, sacrificed, and offered"—are included; this is indicated by the phrase "the gift given, consisting of hospitality and so forth.

Alternatively, this is an instance of a grammatical elision (*virūpekasesa-niddesa*). "Meaning" (*attha*) refers to the meaning from the perspective of intention (*adhippāya*), while [the literal] meaning is from the perspective of the word (*sadda*).
Because it has not been attained by him. It is the same in such cases as these. "Dabbā" means those who are deluded; they are foolish persons (bālapuggalā), [and thus] "by the dabbās.
What is meant? He says: "The fools give," and so forth. In the Pāḷi, "those who have the view that 'the world exists' are the *atthikā*";
"exists" (*atthi*) here is a *neppatika* (indeclinable) word. The doctrine of those who hold this view is the *atthikavāda*; that is the *atthikavāda*.
*Therein*: among those three types of wrong-claimants mentioned above. He denies *kamma* because of his state as a proponent of non-action (*akiriyavāda*).
He denies *vipāka* (result) by completely rejecting rebirth in the future in every respect. And "result" (*vipāka*) refers to all three kinds of results:
benefit (*ānisamsa*), outflow (*nissanda*), and similar fruit (*sadisaphala*). He denies both entirely.
Because by the very negation of the cause, the fruit is also negated. "Both" refers to both karma and its result.

For he who says, "Beings become defiled and purified without cause and without condition," indeed rejects both of these, since he demonstrates the absence of any causal status for either defilement or purification in the case of the result, just as in the case of karma.
Resultant [kamma] is warded off because, in the absence of [prior] kamma, there is an absence of result. Kamma is warded off because, in the absence of a result, it would fall into meaninglessness.
"Thus" (*iti*) indicates the aforementioned sense. "In meaning" (*atthato*) means according to their specific nature;
although they appear individually in the Canon as indicators of their respective views, the sense is that both of them ward off [the other].

Each of these three types of views is indeed a "repeller of both," because they repel both [kamma and its result]. For the phrase "repellers of both" is a statement of reason (*hetuvacana*), since that qualification contains the reason.
The phrase "those who maintain the doctrine of causelessness" (*ahetukavādā*) and so forth is a statement of thesis (*paṭiññāvacana*), because it is determined as the fruit of that [reason].
Therefore, they are "deniers of the result" (*natthikavādā*) because they repel the ripening (*vipāka*), and they are "deniers of action" (*akiriyavādā*) because they repel kamma.

Because they reject both [kamma and its fruit], these are called "theories of causelessness" (*ahetukavāda*); thus, the connection between cause and fruit should be understood according to what is applicable.

For one who holds the nihilistic view (*natthikadiṭṭhi*) and is an annihilationist (*ucchedavādī*) by rejecting the result of maturation (*vipāka*), is in fact a proponent of non-action (*akiriyadiṭṭhi*) by rejecting kamma in substance, and is a proponent of causelessness (*ahetukadiṭṭhi*) by rejecting both; the same principle applies to the other two as well.
With the words “Or those who,” etc., the determination of the entry into the fixed course (niyāma) for those who hold such views is stated. Therein, “of them” refers to Pūraṇa and the others.
“Recite” means they learn and recite that text which elucidates their view, having mastered it however they have composed it.
“Investigate” means they deliberate upon its meaning. The phrase beginning with “Of them” is an illustration of the manner of investigation.
The connection is with those who investigate thus: “For one who acts... [etc. ...it is cut off. Regarding that object:

in the object of the view termed wrong view—which proceeds by way of such passages as “no evil is done by one who acts,” and so forth—concerning the non-existence of the fruit of action and other such matters as they have imagined;
there, wrong mindfulness comes to rest. That which is termed wrong mindfulness...
Craving accompanied by dogmatic conviction becomes established.

For when an object acquired through hearsay—such as the idea that "no evil is done by one who acts"—is presented to the mind in its own form through reflections on its specific aspects, as if it were something directly perceived, and then, through long-term familiarity, comes to be accepted as something capable of withstanding investigation with the thought "it is indeed so," and is grasped in various ways through such acceptance (nijjhānakkhanti): [craving becomes established].
For one who repeatedly practices and cultivates [it] in that very same way, craving— accompanied by wrong resolve,
brought about by wrong thought, supported by wrong effort, and seizing even what lacks that nature as having that nature—
is called "wrong mindfulness" because it proceeds from taking what is false and unreal as a refuge. This meaning has indeed been stated in the *Caturaṅguttara-ṭīkā* as well.
For there is no such separate dhamma as "wrong mindfulness" (micchāsati) in the way that there are wrong intention and so forth;
rather, this is a designation for all four unwholesome aggregates when they are grasped under the heading of craving.
This is stated in the *Sallekha Sutta* commentary of the *Madhyamāgama-ṭīkā*.

"Citta becomes one-pointed" means that, by obtaining its respective conditions such as applied thought (*vitakka*), it abandons distraction through its stability upon that object and becomes one-pointed, as if fixed.
Here, under the heading of "citta," it is actually wrong concentration (*micchā-samādhi*) that is spoken of;
for when strengthened by specific conditions, it performs a function that merely resembles true concentration in such a state.
It should be understood as being like [the piercing of hair] and so forth.
"The impulsions impel" means that when several such preliminary series of impulsions have occurred in that manner, seven impulsions impel in the final, decisive series of impulsions.
The statement, "In the first impulsion they are curable with difficulty, and likewise in the second and so on," is merely a demonstration of the intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*) of phenomena.
However, it cannot be seen that at that moment their treatment can be performed by anyone;

for once they have reached that state, because the seventh impulsion—which necessarily arises—cannot be turned back, and because in such a rapid revolution of the mental process, treatment is impossible through instruction or admonition. Therefore he said: "Even for Buddhas, they are incurable."
"Those who do not turn back. "Like Ariṭṭha and Kaṇṭaka" means like the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇṭaka;
