it is said that, like them, they were born as those of wrong destination, incurable and not turning back.
"Therein" refers to among those three types of wrong views. "Someone enters upon one view" means for whom [it occurs] in only one.
When both insistence (*abhinivesa*) and repetition (*āsevanā*) have occurred, one enters into a single [wrong] view.
Some enter into two, some even into three; thus, for one in whom both insistence and repetition have occurred regarding two or three [views], they enter into two or even three.
By this statement, however, which previously [stated] by way of their being obstructors of both: "Thus all these, in meaning, are obstructors of both," etc., [the point is established].
The state of being possessed by all [wrong] views has been explained in meaning and established; that [state] belongs to the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāgiyā*).

However, as for that which constitutes the entry into the fixed course of falsehood (*micchattaniyāmokkantibhūtā*), it shows that because they are established through the convergence of their respective conditions, these specific attainments—like various objects of focus—do not arise together as one, but rather follow one another in immediate succession.
This is shown by the passage beginning with "Even when one has entered," and so forth, regarding all three.
This explains their equal capacity and their identical fruit. By way of being an obstruction to heaven and so forth, these [three] are both of equal capacity and of identical fruit;
therefore, even when all three arise in a single person, they are indeed uninterrupted.
It should be understood that when one has bestowed its result, the others act as its supporting forces. "He has reached the obstruction to the path to heaven," and so forth.
Having said this, he clarifies that very point with the words beginning “incapable.
“An obstruction to the path of liberation” means an impediment to the Noble Path, which is the way to Nibbāna. “Even before” (*pageva*) is a particle used in the sense of negation; the meaning is:

what need is there even to mention going to Nibbāna, which is termed “liberation”? Furthermore, “even before” (*pageva*) means *pā* + *eva*; it signifies that one is incapable of going to liberation even earlier.
It is thus stated that [this being] is even further away from the attainment of liberation. This should be applied similarly to other instances as appropriate.
The statement, “This being is indeed a stump in the cycle of existence,” has only a meaning to be interpreted (*neyyattha*), not a direct meaning (*nītattha*).
For it is said in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya*: “But is this [stump] in only one single existence (*attabhāva*)...?”
"Is one fixed [in that view] only, or also in another? "One is fixed in only one [existence], but by way of habituation, one will simply find pleasure in this or that view even in another becoming.
For this unwholesome [state] is weak and feeble, not strong or very powerful like the wholesome;
therefore, it is stated therein that "one is fixed in only one individual existence (attabhāva). Otherwise...

Just as the determination toward rightness (*sammattaniyāma*) is absolute, so too might the determination toward wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*) be absolute; yet it is not absolute. To the question, "If this is so, how can the illustration of the stump of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakhāṇu*) be appropriate?
he says, "By way of repetition," and so forth. Therefore, just as it is stated in the *Sattanga Sutta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*:
"Even one who has submerged but once is indeed submerged, a fool" [AN 7.15; identical in meaning], so too is the illustration of the stump of the cycle of existence.

It has been stated. For it cannot be said that once this person has entered upon such-and-such a view in dependence upon certain conditions, he will never again, in dependence upon conditions opposed to them, abandon that [view].

Therefore, both there and here in the Aṭṭhakathā, the inclusion of the word "generally" (*yebhuyyena*)—in the phrase, "for one of such a kind, generally there is no emergence from existence"—is intended to exclude such cases.
It is said that because one delights in various views through the power of habituation even in other existences, there is generally no emergence from such a state of existence;
thus, this person has become what is called a "stump in the round" (*vaṭṭakhāṇuka*).

However, this should be understood as being of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*)—because it must be drawn out and its significance understood—and not of direct meaning (*nītattha*), for it is not due to the absolute finality of the fixed course of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*). With reference to this, [it was said]: *...*

In the Abhidhamma as well, it is stated: “The arahant, and those worldlings who will not attain the path, do not fully understand the aggregate of form and will not fully understand the aggregate of feeling,” and so forth.
“Guardian of the earth” means a protector of the earth for the reasons already mentioned. To establish that meaning, the phrase “for the most part” and so on was stated.
Thus, in order to arouse mindfulness in his listeners by following upon the supreme blameworthiness of wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*), he said, "Therefore," and so forth.

Therein, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means: because such a state has become an unfailing condition even for the nature of the "stump of cyclic existence" (*saṃsārakhāṇu*); therefore, the connection is that one "should avoid" it.

"Unwholesome persons" (*akalyāṇajana*) refers to people devoid of wholesome qualities (*kalyāṇadhamma*), that is, wicked people. "A venomous snake" (*āsīvisa*) refers to one whose poison is immediate and lethal.
"Desirous of welfare" means desiring one's own increase through virtues by way of the benefits pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal.
"Discerning" means one who perceives various meanings with the eye of wisdom; the sense is "wise.
*Commentary on the Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana*
174. Regarding the word “akaṭā,” it is said that the letter *ta* has been replaced by the letter *ṭa*, thus [it becomes] “akatā.
This means they were not made, nor produced, by any cause whatsoever, whether equal or unequal. The same applies to the phrase “akaṭavidhā.

They are called “akaṭavidhā” because they possess no *katavidhā*—that is, no process of making (*karaṇavidhi*). By both these phrases, the fact that they are not produced by any cause or condition in the world is expressed.

[The text] shows this. Therefore he said, “Do it thus,” and so forth. “Not even created by psychic power (iddhi)” means not created by the psychic power of anyone—whether a person who has attained mastery over the mind, a deity, or a lord (issara), etc. “Not fashioned” (animmāpitā) means not fashioned by anyone.

Although [the term] is appropriate from the perspective of the sound (*sadda*), and its meaning (*attha*) is the same as the preceding [term], nevertheless, in the Canon (*pāḷi*) and in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*)...
This shows that the future itself is the reason for its being ungraspable, by means of the passage beginning with “That is not even in the Pāḷi.
This has the same meaning as what was stated in the *Brahmajāla-sutta-vaṇṇanā*. Here is the mere application [of the logic]:

for "barren" means fruitless and non-productive of anything, like barren cattle or barren palm trees; therefore, it negates the state of the earth-element and so forth being producers of form and the rest.
He rejects [this]. For his tenet is that visible forms, sounds, and so forth have an existence independent of the earth-element and the other elements.

They are called "peak-like" (kūṭaṭṭhā) because they stand like the peak of a mountain; the intention is that just as a mountain peak is not produced by anyone and does not produce anything else, so too are these six classes of beings (sattakāya).
As for this statement, "the sprout and so forth are born from the seed," [it is rejected].
It is said that what exists there emerges from that, not what does not exist; otherwise, one thing might be perceived from something else entirely.
In this same way, these seven bodies are established like a pillar. "Because they are established" means because they are well-established in a state free from modification (*nibbikārabhāvena*).
"They do not move" means they do not undergo change. For, due to the absence of change in those seven...
The bodies stand like pillars, characterized by immovability and remaining fixed in their own nature. Therefore, he said, "they do not undergo transformation.
"Nature" (pakati) means intrinsic essence (sabhāva). Precisely because they possess the quality of being non-transformable, they do not harm one another.
For if there were a state in which a modification could be induced, there might be harmfulness; likewise, if there were a state in which assistance could be rendered, there might also be helpfulness.

To demonstrate the absence of that [self], the text states "it is not fit" (*nālam*) and so forth. Because it is a portion of the body, "earth" itself is called the "earth-body," just as one says "the ocean is seen.
Alternatively, it is a collection of earth, because the word *kāya* denotes a collection, just as one says "a herd of elephants" (*hatthikāya*).
Because the bodies, including the living being as the seventh, are eternal and thus devoid of modification, they are not to be slain, nor are they to be caused to be slain.
And therefore, in order to show that there is neither any killer nor any instigator of killing, it is said in the Pāḷi: "Of seven bodies indeed," and so forth.
To the objection, "If there is no killer, how is there the striking with a weapon for them?", he says "Just as," and so on.
Therein, "of seven indeed" means of exactly seven. Here, the word *iti* is merely a particle. "Struck" (*pahataṃ*) means struck.
A weapon such as a single-edged blade enters only between [the joints], not into them. This is what is meant:

there is merely the perception on their part that "I am depriving this one of life," but in the ultimate sense (paramattha), there is no actual killing or slaying at all, because the bodies cannot be dismembered.
Commentary on the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta:
177. *Catuyāma* means four watches (*yāma*) or parts; *cātuyāma* is simply the same as *catuyāma*.
Here, the word *yāma* has the sense of a "part," as in the expression "the first watch of the night. Since that part here is characterized by restraint, he said: "by way of four divisions..."

“Restrained by restraint”: the word *yāma* has the sense of restraining; for, taking it as “restraint” (*yama*) means “the act of restraining” (*saññamana*), even though it lacks a prefix, it expresses the sense of restraining just like those [terms] such as “self-restrained” (*yatatta*) where it does have a prefix.
However, since that [restraint] occurs in four modes, he said, “by restraint consisting of four divisions.
For in meaning, “mode” (*ākāra*) and “division” (*koṭṭhāsa*) are one and the same. All that is to be avoided has been warded off.
"He by whom all water is forbidden," as in the phrase "one who has kindled the fire. Therefore, it says "one who has forbidden all water.
Here, by the word *vāri*, the enjoyment of water is meant, just as in the expression "one who refrains at night" (*rattūparato*).
Thus, it refers to one for whom the use of all cold water is prohibited. "That" refers to cold water. "Engaged in forbidding all water" expresses merely the characteristic of restraint (*saṃvara*).
"Sabbavāridhuta" (shaken off by all restraints) has the characteristic of the wearing away of evil; "sabbavāriphuṭa" (cleansed by all restraints) has the characteristic of the destruction of karma.
Demonstrating this meaning, he said "by all," etc.; for one who is "yoked with the restraint of all evil" is endowed with the restraint of evil in every way, characterized by total self-restraint.
"Dhutapāpa" (one whose evil is shaken off) is one whose evil has been shaken off by the restraint of evil characterized by the wearing away of all [defilements].

“Touched” (*phuṭṭho*) means touched by the complete warding off of all evil, which is characterized by the destruction of karma through the exhaustion of even the eight types of kamma and the attainment of liberation;
the meaning is that he stands having reached that state. As in such passages as “There are only two destinations, no other,” the root *gam* has the sense of a final destination;
thus it is said, “one whose mind has reached the pinnacle,” meaning one whose mind has attained the supreme noble state through the realization of liberation.
The meaning is as follows: He is one whose mind is restrained because there is nothing further to be restrained among the faculties such as the body.
Here, the word *ta-* refers back to what has preceded. He is one whose mind is well-established because there is no remainder of anything further to be restrained.

The phrase "anything in accordance with the Teaching" is said with reference to the warding off of evil. "Because of impure acquisitions" means: "There is a soul, and it may be eternal, or it may be impermanent."
"For the sake of benefit from such defilements as these. "All" refers to all forms of reflective acceptance regarding objects such as the analysis of the nature of kamma.
"Only views" means that they have arisen as merely wrong views.
*Commentary on the Teaching of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta*

179–181. “The method stated for *amarāvikkhepa*”: this means the very method stated in the commentary on the doctrine of *amarāvikkhepa* in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. Why? Because it is a form of evasive answering (*vikkhepabyākaraṇa*), and because the doctrine of evasion is presented there in that same way.
Commentary on the First Fruit of the Homeless Life (*Paṭhamasandiṭṭhikasāmaññaphala-vannanā*) 182.
“Having squeezed (*pīḷetvā*)”: having pressed with an oil-press; by this, he expresses the King’s intention (*ābhoga*). For it is by virtue of his intention that he speaks.

In all cases, the determination of the meaning [is as follows]. The masters of the commentaries (Aṭṭhakathācariyā) are those who understand the intended application [of the words] and do not contradict the meaning handed down through tradition;

therefore, it should be understood that the meaning has not been stated in every instance merely because it was obtainable from the context of the phrasing, but rather according to what they wished to express.
And having done so, in various places, by way of extracting the meaning and so forth—
"The analysis of the meaning has been performed.
(183) "In whatever way it may please you": the meaning is that the matter now being asked by me should please your mind;
it should be pleasing to your mind. This verb is used in the sense of the object (*kamma*). Or rather, the matter now being asked by me—
It is also permissible [to say] "it would please you," provided that you are the one who has bestowed [the gift]. One born from the womb of a house-slave is *antojāta* (born within).
One purchased for wealth is *dhanakkīta* (bought with wealth). One seized by force is *karamarānīta* (brought as a captive).

One who has himself, for some reason or other, entered into the state of slavery is *sāmaṃdāsabyopagata* (one who has personally entered into servitude). For *sāmaṃ* means "by oneself"; *dāsabyaṃ* means "the state of being a slave."

Even someone who is a slave, if he is lazy and does not perform his work, is not called a "laborer"; however, since this person is not like that, the word "analaso" (diligent) and so forth is used as a qualification.
"From afar" means having come from a distant place. "Right at the outset" means even before approaching his own nearby location, that is, earlier than that.
"He rises up" means rising up out of a sense of reverence.
"Stands by" means "rises up to meet [him]. "Afterwards" means after the master has lain down.

"While he has not risen from his bed" means while he has not risen from his sleeping place at the time of dawn. "From the time of the early morning" means from the time of the early morning of the night that has passed.
"Until the master falls asleep during the night" means until the falling asleep of the next, future night at the time of dusk.
The meaning is that having performed all duties during the interval between the time when the night has passed and the time when evening approaches, one lies down afterwards.
Regarding the phrase "only what is to be done" (*kiṃ kārameva*): since it must be performed as a response to the question "What is to be done?

(*kiṃ karaṇīyaṃ eva kinti*), the sense is that one performs the services [of the teacher] after having asked. Because attending closely is expressed by the very act of assent, he said: "assenting... (*paṭisuṇanto*).
"He wanders about" means that he is unable even to look at a face that is repulsive; this is shown by the phrase "smiling and exultant.
"Like a god" refers to one endowed with sovereignty, a retinue, and so forth, like a preeminent deity;
by this, it is made known that the word *maññe* here has the sense of a simile, just as in the passage: "The inner apartments of King Mahāsudassana stood, as it were, struck by lightning."
“Adorning [it]. Regarding the phrase *so vatassāham*: here the word division is *so vata assaṃ ahaṃ*, meaning “May I indeed become like that.
If one asks, “In what way? the meaning is: “If I were to perform meritorious deeds, by means of those. Thus he said, “So vata ahaṃ,” and so forth.
The word *vata* is used in the sense of a comparison. Therefore he said, “of such a kind. He uses the term *puññāni* (meritorious deeds) with reference to a most exalted merit.
It was stated [previously] because of the intention for a sublime going-forth (pabbajjā) based on merit performed at another time. Regarding the reading “*so vatassāyan*,” the meaning is:
“May I also be like that king. How so? Because the sense is possible—“if one were to perform meritorious deeds”—it is said, “this very meaning [is intended].
For when used in conjunction with a term denoting a superior person (*uttamapurisa*), the word *ahaṃ* (I), even if not explicitly employed, is understood through the word *ayaṃ* (this).

It is as if it were connected through the act of referring back (*parāmasanato*). Some maintain that the meaning of the first reading is: "May I indeed be such a one, if only I were to perform meritorious deeds.

If this were the case, then in the second reading one could not say, "This very same meaning," because the word "this" (*ayaṃ*) would be referring back to the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), and there would be nothing else for the word "that" (*so*) to refer back to.
"According to possibility. "The gift": even a hundredth part; that is to say, even if the king's gift were divided into a hundred parts, it would be not even one such part—this is what is meant.
"I shall not be able to give for as long as I live":
even if I were to exert myself for the sake of giving for the rest of my life, I would not be able to give even a mere hundredth part; therefore, I shall go forth.
The meaning is: "having made an effort toward going forth. Regarding the phrase "yaṃnūna" (what if now), it is stated that this particle has the sense of reflection;
thus, it means "the state of thinking in this way.
"Guarded by body" means by way of restraining the unwholesome states that arise through the door of the body and which ought to be restrained by the body.

It is shut. However, because the meaning [of the phrase] is expressed through the term *ussukka* (diligence), it must be connected with the word *vihareyya* (should dwell); thus he said, "having closed the door for the entry of unwholesome states.

For the word *hutvā* (having been) is the ellipsis. And "the door for the entry of unwholesome states" refers to the door known as bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*), which serves as the gateway for the entry of unwholesome states consisting of bodily actions. The same applies to the other two phrases: "restrained in speech" and "with the mind..."

In both instances of the phrase "restrained" (*saṃvuto*), it refers to being established in the state of excellence (*paramatā*) regarding the pursuit of food and clothing by way of effacement (*sallekha*),
or in the sense of being at the highest level. One for whom food and clothing alone are the supreme limit and boundary—
seeking no other kind of material thing beyond that and not even desiring it— is called "one for whom food and clothing are supreme" (*ghāsacchādanaparamo*).

The state of that [body] is also called "having food and clothing as its highest aim"; this is a method found even outside the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). It is called *ghāsa* because it is to be eaten and consumed;
it is called *acchādana* because one thoroughly covers and wraps oneself with it—namely, a garment. Furthermore, it is appropriate to explain it as:
*ghasanaṃ* (the act of eating) is *ghāsa*, and that which is thoroughly covered (*ābhuso chādīyate*) is *acchādana*. *Etadatthampi* means "also for the sake of food and clothing."
"Searching" (*eṣaṇā*) refers to the twenty-one kinds of inappropriate searching.

"With bodies withdrawn from seclusion" (*vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ*) means those whose bodies are situated in solitude, away from the company of crowds; the connection is that this is the bodily seclusion belonging to them.
"Delighting in renunciation" (*nekkhammābhiratānaṃ*) means delighting in the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). "Having attained supreme purity" (*paramavodānappattānaṃ*)—by that very [means]...
This refers to those who have attained the supreme, most excellent purification of mind, which is the cleansing resulting from delight in *jhāna*.

"Those without substrate" (*nirupadhīnaṃ*) means those who are utterly free from the substrates of defilements, kamma-formations, and the five aggregates. "The unconditioned" (*visaṅkhāraṃ*) is said to be Nibbāna; those who have reached its attainment are "those gone to the unconditioned" (*visaṅkhāragatā*), namely the Arahants.
By the phrase "When this was said," he shows that this passage has been handed down in the *Mahāniddesa*. And here, the first [type of] seclusion—
It should be stated that [the third seclusion] exists together with the other two seclusions as well, because when the others are accomplished, this one is also accomplished;
and even when this one is accomplished, the others are accomplished simultaneously. Likewise for the second.

However, the third should be stated only together with the others, and not separately, because it is to be understood that it is accomplished only when the others have been accomplished. [The text continues: "Association with a crowd..."
The passage beginning with “having abandoned” (*pahāya*) is an exposition of that intended meaning. In this context, *gaṇasaṅgaṇikā* is the gathering together in a group or a social assembly;
having abandoned that. He dwells and moves about alone in body because he is without a companion in terms of persons.
*Cittakilesasaṅgaṇikā* is the gathering together of defilements in the mind; having abandoned that. He dwells alone because he is without a companion in terms of defilements.

Because the Path lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, and because the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and other states merely take that as their object, there is no extraordinary contact with the bliss of Nibbāna by way of them;
rather, it is extraordinary by way of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Therefore, he said: "either the attainment of fruition or the attainment of cessation. For cessation is the conclusion of the fruit. "Having entered" means...

"Having included [it] by way of attainment. "Having reached Nibbāna": this is an expression of exertion (*ussukka*), because what is intended here is the attainment of peace (*nibbuti*) through making it the object of focus and through the cessation of mind and mental factors. "In the sense of inciting": in the sense of making an effort to make [someone] know.
184. "Having brought forward": having led [them] into a state of presence. "Him": him who dwells thus having gone forth. "Bringing forward" (*abhihāra*):...
“Bringing by invitation” means by way of being invited. The connection is made through the elliptical sense of the words, “I shall fulfill the need for robes and so forth.
Likewise, [it refers to] the phrase, “Speak whatever you require. “Deficiency in robes and so forth” means the state of being incomplete due to the worn-out condition of robes and other requisites.
“Both of these” refers to those very two types of bringing. “Suitable” means bringing benefit by way of removing all ailments.
Protection (*rakkhāgutti*) is preservation by way of not allowing a future misfortune to arise; guarding (*āvaraṇagutti*), however, is preservation by way of preventing a present misfortune.
To the question, "For what purpose is the qualification 'righteous' (*dhammika*) used?", he says, "But this," and so forth.
"Within the monastery boundary" (*vihārasīmāya*) means within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*) or the distribution boundary (*lābhasīmā*).
185. If the word *evaṃ* (thus) were alone, it would depend on a meaning previously stated; thus it is said, “If [he] were your slave,” and so forth.
“*Evaṃ santē* (this being so)” means when it is obtained in this way. The state of being first (*paṭhama*) is in relation to a second;
therefore, by saying “first,” he indicates the existence of something else as well. And making that very reason the basis, in order to show that the king also spoke thus, [it is said...]
“Saying ‘the first’,” and so forth, was stated. “By that very [word]” means by the word *paṭhama* (first) itself, which indicates that there is also another [result]. 186. *Kasati* means he plows;
he performs cultivation (*kasiṃ karoti*). Regarding the term *gahapatiko*, it is stated here that the syllable *ka-* is devoid of meaning (*appattho*).
“*Ekagehamatte jeṭṭhako*”: this is what is meant. A *gahapati* is the master of a house (*gaha*);
a minor *gahapati* is a *gahapatika*. He is called the senior (*jeṭṭhaka*) in respect of that very single house alone;

and since his status as minor is determined by way of the house itself, it is said “in respect of a single house alone. By this, he excludes the status of being the senior of many families. The house—
And they grasp [the meaning] as being identical in substance. Regarding the word *kara*, it is stated that it refers to a "bali" (offering), thus it is called "designated as a bali.
"He makes" (*karoti*) means he brings about or accomplishes. "He increases" (*vaḍḍheti*) means he creates a great accumulation by producing [wealth] further and further.
To the question "Why are both of these mentioned?", he says "For just as... and so forth. It is difficult to renounce even a small amount in order to go forth.
And this is for the purpose of making known that his vision was indeed great; for it is the nature of storytellers to make known some further point by whatever means possible.

Furthermore, the difficulty of going forth even after abandoning very little is illustrated by the *Laṭukikopama-sutta* in the *Majjhima Nikāya*, the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsa*. For it is said there: "Just as..."

"Udāyi, suppose there were a man who was poor, destitute, and without means, whose single little hut was dilapidated and ruined, unfit for even a crow to alight upon, and who had a single ragged blanket that was worn out and unsightly"—this is the full account.
If it is difficult to go forth having abandoned even a small amount of wealth, why was the mention of "wealth" not included even in the section on the slave? To this he said:
“Even in the case of a slave,” and so forth. “Not even master of himself” means that he is not himself master even of his own self.
Just as a slave’s possessions are effectively no possessions at all because they are dependent on another, so too are his kinsmen;

thus it should be understood that even the mention of a circle of kinsmen was not made in the context of a slave. It is called a *parivaṭṭa* because it revolves (*parivaṭṭati*) all around by way of succession.
It is simply relatives. Therefore he said: "The circle of relatives is indeed relatives.
189. Regarding the commentary on the more excellent fruits of recluseship:
*taṃ* (that) is as it was stated in the section on the slave with "just so" (*evameva*); it is not so here in the section on the farmer, for that [phrase] was not spoken.

The meaning is: "Why should one apply oneself [to this]? "In this very way" means when it is said, "Is it possible to explain in exactly the same manner as the first and second fruits of recluseship were set forth?
"By such similes" means by similes similar to those already mentioned, such as the analogies of the slave and the farmer.
He is able to illuminate the fruit of recluseship because of his infinite eloquence and because of his state of teaching through diverse methods.
*“Tattha”* means in this manner of explaining. There is no limit because it exists as a teaching through infinite methods;
or, because hearing it generates an ever-increasing desire to hear due to a lack of satiety, there is no limit to that desire to hear—this is the meaning.
*“Even so”* (*tathāpi*) was stated by the Teacher [Ācariya Buddhaghosa] to mean: “even though the teaching possesses a state of variety through increasingly superior and diverse methods,” even so...

Thus, it is also appropriate [to understand] it as having an "unlimited" nature. Having reflected by means of inferential knowledge (*anumāna-ñāṇa*), he asks about the "further distinction" above that, inquiring specifically about the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) that stands superior to it. He asks "Why? and says "In hearing," etc.
By this, he illuminates this point: although words have multiple meanings, they indicate their respective meanings only according to the speaker's intention and the sequence [of usage].
"Sādhukaṃ" and "sādhu" have the same meaning, because the word *sādhu* itself has been extended by the addition of the letter *ka*.
For this very reason, when explaining the meaning of the word *sādhuka*, the word *sādhu* was cited as a way of extracting its meaning.
By this, any objection that "only the meaning of the word *sādhuka* should be stated, not that of the word *sādhu*" is refuted. [The term] "in entreaty" (*āyācanāya*)...
*Abhimukhaṃ yācane*: the meaning is "in requesting with direct intent" or "in longing for. *Sampaṭicchaneti*: in receiving. *Sampahaṃsaneti*:
in gladdening or satisfying by way of existing virtues; the meaning is "in causing upliftment.
The verse beginning with *sādhu dhammarucī* is from the Ummādantī Jātaka. Regarding this, the following is the tradition of the commentary’s exposition: in the Dhamma of good conduct...

“Delighting in the Dhamma” (*dhammaruci*) means one who finds joy in the Dhamma; the sense is “one who delights in the Dhamma. For such a person, even when giving up his life, does not do what should not be done.
“Possessed of wisdom” (*paññāṇavā*) means wise and endowed with knowledge. “Not treacherous toward friends” (*mittānamaddubbho*) refers to the state of not being treacherous toward friends.
The Teacher has stated: “One who is non-treacherous and non-injurious. There is also a reading *adrubbho*, formed by changing the letter *da* to *dra*.
“Daḷhīkamma” means the act of persistence. “Āṇattiyaṃ” means in the sense of commanding. “Idhāpi” means even here in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*. “Assa” refers to the word “sādhuka.
For by the word “sādhuka” in the phrase “Listen thoroughly, attend carefully,” both the persistence in hearing and attending, as well as the command for that [persistence], are illuminated.
And because commanding is common to [the act of] exhorting through entreaty, it is [called] a command.

“Included” means it was not stated separately in the enumeration of meanings. For there is a distinction: the command (*āṇatti*) belongs to one who is entitled to command, while the entreaty (*āyācana*) belongs to one who is not so entitled.

“Even in the beautiful” means even in the sense of beauty. Now, in order to show the specific distinction manifested by the three meanings of the word *sādhuka* as previously stated, or rather, to clarify the suitability of those three meanings in this context, [the text says]: “In the sense of strengthening... (*daḷhīkammatthena*).
"‘Hī’ and so forth was said. ‘Grasping what is well-grasped’ means grasping after having made it well-grasped.

‘Sundaraṃ’ (beautiful) is a neuter noun. ‘Bhaddakaṃ’ (auspicious) means praised; it is connected with the word ‘dhammaṃ’. Alternatively, ‘sundaraṃ bhaddakaṃ’ are synonymous terms for that which assists hearing.

Regarding ‘manasi karohi’ (attend to it): here, the attention (*manasikāra*) does not have the characteristic of directing toward an object (*ārammaṇa*), but rather it is preceded by the attention that directs [the mind] through the cognitive process (*vīthi*) and the impulsion (*javana*)."
Showing that its characteristic is fixing in the mind, he said: "Be attentive, apply your mind.

"With an undistracted mind" means having a mind that is not agitated, by way of fixing it upon a single object through the sequence of mental engagement (manasikāra) preceded by the two aforementioned types of attention. "Listen" means hear;
or alternatively, it means place this rare jewel of the Dhamma, difficult to find, within the casket of the heart like a priceless gem.

This is the meaning. Therefore it was said: “Make [it] in the mind. Having thus shown the meaning of each of the two words by way of their individual application, he now says “Moreover,” etc., in order to show it by way of their counterparts.
Therein, the warding off of distraction of the ear-faculty is shown to mean “lend an ear,” because it precludes other activities by way of directing one toward listening.
The warding off of distraction of the mind-faculty is achieved by means of attention through its application in strengthening [the mind] and by the prohibition of other thoughts.

The warding off of grasping at a distorted literal sense is due to the fact that it is stated with the qualification "thoroughly" (*sādhuka*). This same method applies to the warding off of grasping at a distorted meaning as well.
Regarding the phrase "in retention, investigation, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes weighing, scrutinizing, and the like, as well as the thorough penetration of view.

And it encompasses [the meaning]. It manifests or reveals the intended meaning; or, it is called *byañjana* because one expresses [it] by means of this itself—namely, the conventional linguistic expression (*sabhāvanirutti*).
"With *byañjana*" (*sabyañjana*) means "endowed with *byañjana*"; the sense is that it is complete in its *byañjana*.
For "being endowed" (*sampannatā*) is of many kinds, such as "co-occurrence," "conjunction," or "existence," but here it refers specifically to completeness (*sampannatā*).

Because nothing else is possible [in that context], it should be understood that although the etymological derivation is made as "together with the letter" (*saha byañjanena*), the Master has stated the meaning as "endowed with the letter" (*byañjanasampanno*).
Just as in the case of "not wholesome, unwholesome," which means "the opposite of the wholesome" because it is to be sought after, approached, and pursued;
so too, [it refers to] the fourfold purification of virtue and so forth, together with its meaning (*saha atthena*).

“Meaningful” means that it is endowed with meaning in the manner already described. The single word *sādhukaṃ* (well) is common to both [the teaching and the penetration] and should be applied to both senses by way of repetition and so forth.
To explain how this is so, he says “because,” etc. “Dhamma” refers to the textual tradition (*tanti*).

“Teaching” (*desanā*) refers to the teaching of that textual tradition as it has been determined by the mind. “Meaning” (*attha*) refers to the meaning of the textual tradition. “Penetration” (*paṭivedha*) refers to...
[It is profound] because of the penetration of the scriptures and the meaning of the scriptures as they truly are.

And since these penetrations—the teaching of the Dhamma and the realization of its meaning—are difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom and provide no foothold, like the great ocean for fish and other aquatic creatures, they are therefore "profound.
Thus it was said: "Because... attend closely. And herein, [it is profound] because penetration is difficult to achieve.

The profundity of the Dhamma’s standing point should be understood as being due to the difficulty of the teaching— because of the difficulty of the knowledge of the teaching, because of its inability to be produced [by others],
and because of the difficulty of the arising of the knowledge that has it as its object— and also due to the profundity of penetration.
Whatever needs to be said on this matter has already been stated in the commentary on the Introduction (Nidāna).

By saying, “Listen attentively” and “Pay careful attention,” he shows that this construction is not only according to the sequence of meaning (*atthakkama*), but also according to the sequence of words (*saddakkama*), as it connects both parts.
Here too, the phrase “It is possible, Great King” carries forward from the previous context:
“There is another fruit of recluseship visible here and now... which is even more sublime.”

He said: "Thus was the teaching on the fruits of recluseship promised. By the phrase "speaking in detail," he strengthens the very meaning [of the promise] with the words "I shall teach" and so forth, which indicate the brief summary.

Here, the word *hi* (for/indeed) is indicated as being elided. This is what is meant: "teaching" (*desanā*) means pointing out; "speaking" (*bhāsana*) means explaining in detail, that is, speaking clearly.

Thinking that this meaning is possible, the passage beginning with “Therefore he said” was stated in order to establish the aforementioned point by means of a verse-line from the Vaṅgīsa-sutta in the Sagāthāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
“Like the cry of a myna bird” (sāḷikāyiva nigghoso) means like the cry of a myna bird; just as the call of a myna bird is sweet and pleasing to the ear.

"Delightful" (*pemanīyo*) means "thus" (*evam*); this is the sense. "Eloquence" (*paṭibhāna*) is an adjective for this [mind], since adjectives are seen even when there is a difference in gender, as in "the quality is the measure" (*guṇo pamāṇam*).
And the word "eloquence" (*paṭibhāna*) is called "speech," because it manifests—that is, it appears—in various forms.
"He uttered" (*udīrayī*) means he pronounced; or it is said that [he was] spoken to. This is a verb containing an object. By this—

This illustrates the following: wishing to praise the Venerable Dhammasenāpati and demonstrating the distinction between the teaching and the exposition, the Venerable Elder Vaṅgīsa—who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)—applied the qualifiers "in brief" and "in detail.
By this, the following meaning is understood.
“Thus spoken” means when [the Buddha] said, “I shall speak.

Having heard that phrase, thinking, “It seems the Blessed One will not teach merely in brief, but will indeed speak in detail as well,” he became filled with enthusiasm; the meaning is that he was joyful and elated.
This is the intention of the Master (Ācariya). Furthermore: “Therefore, Great King, listen and pay close attention...”
The entire passage beginning with "I shall speak" is intended as a form of encouragement and a promise to proceed, since enthusiasm arises from every single part of it;
therefore, when it is said, "Listen, pay close attention, I shall speak," the meaning should be understood as follows:
enthusiasm was generated by all three phrases together. *Paccassosi* means he listened back [in response].
The meaning is that immediately after the Blessed One’s speech, he heard [the answer] afterwards; or, having asked with the words beginning “But is it possible, Bhante?
and so forth, he again heard it with the words “So it is, Bhante. Furthermore, since that act of acknowledging is in substance nothing other than acceptance, he said, “He accepted, he received.
For this very reason, instead of saying “this is the meaning,” it was stated as “this is what is meant.”

190. Having shown the mere connection between the words with the phrase, “Then the Blessed One said this to him,” and having analyzed the word “said this,” he spoke the passage beginning with “Now” in order to demonstrate the meaning.

By the word “here” (*idha*), he shows that the locus being spoken of is intended to be the very world which is the place of the Tathāgata’s appearance; thus he says, “it is a particle used in the sense of a specific location.”

By this [word]. "Instruction regarding a location" (*desopadeso*) means pointing out a location; [the phrase refers to] in that [context]. If [the rule applied] everywhere in the instruction regarding a location, then one might raise the objection:

"This meaning should not be stated, because it is already obtained even without being stated. To this, he says "this very... and so forth. The word *svāyaṃ* was spoken by taking the word *idha* in its general sense, and not as something to be qualified [by a specific term]. For he will say later: "In some cases..."
“It is merely for the purpose of completing the meter. It is spoken of with reference to the world (*loka*) because it stands in grammatical apposition with the word *loka*.
Here, "the world" refers to the field of birth; even within that, it is this particular world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) that is intended.

It is spoken of as a "recluse" (*samaṇa*) with reference to the teaching (*sāsana*), due to the proximity of other words. For this is a passage from the *Catukka-aṅguttara-nikāya*. Therein, the first recluse is...
The stream-enterer. The second ascetic is the once-returner. For this has been said in that very same place:
“And who, monks, is the first ascetic? Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, is a stream-enterer.
And: “And who, monks, is the second ascetic? Here, monks, a bhikkhu, through the complete destruction of the three...”
“With the complete destruction of the fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner,” and so forth.
The word “standing” (*tiṭṭhamānassa*) is said with reference to a certain location due to the proximity of other words.
“Standing right here” means standing established in this very Indasāla Cave, having become a deity.
"Me" (*me satoti*) means "by my state of being a god," or "having become a god, while existing as such. "Me" (*meti*) is a genitive case used in the sense of disregard (*anādarayoge*).
Again, "me" (*puna meti*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kattutthe*). For this has been cited from the *Sakkapañha Sutta*.

It is merely for the purpose of completing the meter (*padapūraṇamattam*), because there is no possibility of indicating a location (*okāsāpadisanassa*), and thus no other meaning is understood. Previously...
The word "world" (*loka*) is stated with reference specifically to that which has become the place of the Tathāgata’s arising.

He addresses him again as "Great King," referring to the previous address used in the context of making a promise to depart. The words beginning with "worthy one" (*araha*) are to be understood as being explained in detail.
For in terms of meaning, the detailed exposition occurs precisely through the medium of the words; thus, the term "word" (*sadda*) is employed in both instances. Since...

Furthermore, the term *tathāgata* has been explained by the Master in other ways in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā* and other works, beginning with "the Blessed One is a *tathāgata* for eight reasons," and terms such as *arahant* have been explained in other ways in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*.
Therefore, their meaning should also be understood according to the methods stated therein. Because the *Tathāgata* is included within the category of sentient beings...
Having stated, "In this context, however, the world of beings (sattaloka) is intended," he said,
"And even when arising in the world of beings," and so forth, in order to show the particular class of beings and the specific location where one arises.
As for what should be said regarding [the fact that it is] not in the world of devas nor in the world of Brahmas, that will be explained further on.
"Beyond that" means beyond that town; "outside of it" is what is meant. "From there" means from the great sal tree.
"Within the middle" refers to the interior central region. "Thus delimited" means as if a boundary were fixed by five signs—delimited by the five aforementioned signs.
"Two hundred and fifty leagues" means [two hundred and fifty] by way of fifty leagues.
It is less than eight hundred yojanas. For this Middle Country is shaped like a drum (mudiṅga), being neither perfectly circular nor perfectly square;
it is eighty yojanas long in some places and one hundred yojanas in others.
Nevertheless, when measured by its curved boundaries, its total circumference is nine hundred yojanas.
Therefore it was said: “in nine hundred yojanas. Regarding the phrase “eighty great elders,” this is stated by way of the majority;
for even the Elder Puṇṇa of Sunāparanta is included among the great disciples. Indeed, the country of Sunāparanta was a frontier region.
Thus, in the Majjhima Āgama, concerning the acceptance of the sandalwood pavilion, it is said that the Blessed One did not let the dawn rise there.

This is stated in the *Saṃyutta-Āgama-aṭṭhakathā*. "Attained to the essence" means being essential by way of lineage, wealth, sovereignty, and so forth, as well as by way of the essence of virtue (*sīla-sāra*) and so on.
"Brahmins and householders" refers to brahmins such as Brahmayu and Pokkharasāti, and householders such as Anāthapiṇḍika and others.
"Therein" means in the Middle Country, or in that very statement, "he arises. "By Sujātā" means by one who has this name.
First, [the commentary] on the Elder Yasa’s mother’s going for refuge. Among these four alternatives, the first is stated by way of showing a practice that is closer to the state of Buddhahood.
For even one established in a practice that is closer [to Buddhahood] is said to "arise," because arising is certain;
how much more so one established at the very pinnacle of such practice. The second [alternative] is from the point of view of the renunciation that brings about the state of Buddhahood.

The second [period] is shown by way of demonstrating the practice that is merely proximate; the third is shown by way of demonstrating the practice for the state of Buddhahood, beginning from the time when the qualities that produce a Buddha are fully perfected.

For there is no such thing as the "accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment" for Great Beings starting from their final birth, because they establish themselves therein while simply awaiting the proper time for Buddhahood.
The fourth [section] is by way of showing the state of certainty regarding enlightenment (*bodhi*), starting from the undertaking of the qualities that produce Buddhahood.
For from the moment one attains the state of certainty regarding enlightenment, it is possible for the wise to say, "A Buddha arises," because the arising is certain.
Just as one says, "The rivers flow," based on the uninterruptedness of the action of flowing;

This is the usage for the present tense (*vattamāna-payoga*). Thus, in all four alternatives, it is said "it is arising" (*uppajjati nāmā*) with reference to the non-interruption of the activity of proceeding toward origination; furthermore, this is a term for the present that expresses the state of being currently occurring (*pavatta-aparata-vattamāna-vacana*). For indeed, a fourfold characteristic of the present is elucidated in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*): [1] that which has already begun but not yet finished; [2] that which is beginning now; [3] that which is expected to begin soon; and [4] that which is included within the duration of a single action. It is with reference to these four characteristics of the present that it was stated, "it is arising. This is because the word "arising" (*uppajjati*) denotes the present state of occurrence. Thus, the meaning of the present tense is established. Furthermore, the word "present" (*vattamāna*) is used here in its primary sense (*mukhyattha*), as it refers to the actual process of arising. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the statement, "The past and future are not real existents (*na atthi*). This is because the words "past" and "future" denote the two states of existence prior to and subsequent to the present moment. Therefore, the meaning of the present tense is established. Moreover, the word "arising" (*uppajjati*) is a synonym for "becoming" (*bhava*). It is a term for the present because it signifies the state of being currently occurring. Thus, the meaning of the present tense is established. Furthermore, the word "arising" (*uppajjati*) is a synonym for "origination" (*samudaya*). It is a term for the present because it signifies the state of being currently occurring. Thus, the meaning of the present tense is established. Moreover, the word "arising" (*uppajjati*) is a synonym for "manifestation" (*pātubhāva*). It is a term for the present because it signifies the state of being currently occurring. “Near to the occurrence of the pleasant, likewise far from the occurrence [of the pleasant];
and far from the occurrence [of the unpleasant]—thus the occurring [consciousness] is fourfold.
For, unlike the disciples of the Buddhas, the supernormal powers, the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, and so forth, do not arise for them in a fixed sequence.
However, along with the path to Arahatship itself, the entire mass of qualities such as omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is said to have arrived;
therefore, because all their functions have been accomplished, it is stated in the commentary on the *Ekaka-nipāta* that they are "arisen" at the moment of the fruit of Arahatship.
For if all their functions were not accomplished, they could not properly be called "arisen" merely by that much. First and foremost—

"Uppannabhāvaṃ" (the state of having arisen) refers to the existence of the Tathāgata, characterized as his having arisen, which was stated in the very first of the four alternatives: "The Tathāgata... has indeed arisen for Sujātā...

It is with reference to this very fact that it is said "he arises," because what is intended is one who stands precisely in the practice that is closest to the state of Buddhahood. This indeed is the meaning.
It should be said that it arises primarily. Therefore he said: “The Tathāgata… [the meaning].
And here, when “arisen” (*uppanna*) is stated, someone might understand it in the sense of the past tense;
to preclude that, “has arisen” (*uppanno hoti*) is said. For in this context, as in the case of “arisen phenomena” (*uppannā dhammā*) and so forth, the word “arisen” refers to the present time.
But surely it is the Tathāgata, defined as one possessing the fruit of Arahantship, who has already arisen and who accomplishes such things as making known and teaching;
why then is the Tathāgata intended here as that which is "arising," namely the culmination of the path to Arahantship as previously described?

For it is not he [the one possessing the fruit] who accomplishes the making known and teaching, but rather [it is the path] from the consumption of the honey-milk-rice until the attainment of the path of Arahantship.
Is it because those duties have not been accomplished? No, it should not be viewed in that way;

for by the very inclusion of what arises while one is established in the practice closest to Buddhahood, there is also the inclusion of what has already arisen, namely, the possession of the fruit of Arhatship.
Indeed, by the inclusion of the cause, the fruit is also included, because of their inseparability. Thus, [this applies] to one who accomplishes the proclamation, the teaching, and so forth.

Since this must also be accepted even for the Tathāgata who possesses the fruit of Arahatship, this statement "arises" (uppajjati) should be understood as having a meaning that requires further interpretation (neyyattha).
For thus, in the Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā, in the analysis of the meaning according to the three times—namely, "arising," "arises," and "has arisen"—it is said:
"From the time he received the prophecy at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, until [the attainment of] the fruit of Non-returning, he was 'arising'..."
It is said: "At the moment of the path of Arahatship, it is called 'arising'; at the moment of the fruit of Arahatship, it is called 'having arisen'.

This is the opinion of the teacher, the Venerable Dhammapāla Thera. However, in the commentary on the *Ekaka-Nipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the explanation of the sutta passage, "Bhikkhus, one person, when arising in the world, arises," it is stated [as follows]: "In this case too..."
In the Sutta, it is stated that [the knowledge] "arises" with reference specifically to the moment of the fruit of arahantship, and it is recorded as: "The meaning here is 'it has arisen'.
Therefore, he shows that here too, it is stated that it "arises" with reference specifically to the moment of the fruit of arahantship by means of the phrase:
"with reference to the state of having arisen for the very first time. Thus he said: "'It has arisen'—this is the meaning here."

The meaning is: "the state of having arisen first of all. And the phrase "the state of having arisen first" means the state of having arisen prior to all those to be trained (veneyya) by way of the fruit of arhatship (arahattaphala).

By the expression "has arisen," he indicates the past time by way of the moment of the fruit of arhatship. And this very method is intended by the author of the Aṅguttara-ṭīkā, the Venerable Ācariya Sāriputta Thera.
“Thus, the Blessed One”: he who is the Tathāgata whose qualities have been extolled by such terms as “Arahant” and so forth—he is the Blessed One.
Now, the word *idaṃ* (this) indicates that which is to be spoken, because it refers back to the meaning currently being expressed. This is what is meant:

this expression “this world” is not said merely with reference to the presence of the common crowd; rather, it refers to that which will be described by the words “together with its devas,” and so forth.

"With reference to exhaustive inclusion" means: the analysis of the words according to the sentence was stated as "together with the devas, including the world of devas" (*saha devehi sadevakam*), etc.;

however, according to the individual word, it should be stated as "including the devas" (*sadevako*), etc. And these are compounds whose external referent is understood through their qualities (*tagguṇasaṃviññāṇabāhiratthasamāsa*).
For here, while the analysis is made by way of a part, the meaning of the compound is the whole, just as in the case of a world-part analyzed to express the whole world.
Because it is obtained as appropriate. For when the word *saha* is used in the sense of indicating a gathering (*samavāya*), this very compound is understood.

And by "deities" (*devehi*) is meant the deities of the five sensual-sphere realms (*pañcakāmāvacara*) or the deities of the formless-sphere realm (*arūpāvacara*). By "Brahmā" (*brahmunā*) is meant a Brahmā of the form-sphere or formless-sphere, or indeed a Brahmā of the form-sphere alone;
for their establishment [is possible] like that of many agents and so forth. "Because they have been born" (*pajātattā*) means according to their respective [realms].
Because they cause rebirth in various ways through kamma and defilements.

Having thus shown the meaning from the perspective of the etymology (*vacanatthato*), the passage beginning with “*tatthā*” is stated to show the meaning from the perspective of what is to be expressed (*vacanīyatthato*).

The mention of the five classes of sense-sphere devas is by way of elimination (*pārisesañāyena*), since the others have been separately mentioned by other terms. The mention of the sixth class of sense-sphere devas...

By way of proximity. For Māra was born there and is a resident there; and because he is well-known for dwelling there—like the son of a murderous king—he is mentioned as distinguished by that very name, even though other Great Kings such as Vasavatti exist, since he is more prominent.
This method has indeed been explained in the *Madhyamāgama-aṭṭhakathā*. By the mention of "Māra"...
And here, the deities associated with that [world] are also included, because the world of beings (*sattaloka*) is taken together with the world of space (*okāsaloka*).

For in this way, there is a complete and exhaustive inclusion of the world of beings who exercise mastery (*vasavatti*). The inclusion of the Brahmakāyika and other brahmās is also by way of the principle of proximity (*paccāsatti-nāya*).
Regarding the inclusion of "adversaries, enemies, recluses, and brahmins": adversaries are indeed enemies; they are the very same.
Regarding "ascetics and brahmins," the inclusion of those [terms] is intended in that way; thus, it is stated as an inclusion of outside ascetics and brahmins.

Furthermore, this is merely an illustration, since even those who are neither adversaries nor enemies are included by this term. However, the inclusion of "ascetics and brahmins who have stilled evil and cast out evil" should be understood as an inclusion of the ascetics and brahmins belonging to the Dispensation (the Sāsana).
Granted, regarding the specific qualifications such as "together with the devas," etc., [the following applies...]
Because they share the same grammatical connection (*tulyayoga*), the word *loka* is understood to have the sense of "beings" (*satta*) through its sense of "collection" (*samavāya*);

however, in cases such as "having hair" (*salomako*) or "having wings" (*sapakkhako*), this compound is found even where the connection is not equal, because it occurs there in the sense of "existence" (*vijjamāna*).
Since this demonstrates an exception (*vyabhicāra*), he stated the inclusion of the term *pajā* (people/beings) as a rule that indicates the meaning without such exceptions.
“The term ‘beings’ (pajā) includes the world of beings,” it is said; however, this was stated because the world of beings had not yet been included by the word “world” (loka).
Therefore he said: “By the three phrases, the world of beings together with the physical world [is indicated].

Since the phrase beginning with “together with devas” (sadevaka) includes the devas born of rebirth, and the phrase “together with recluses and brahmins” includes the purified devas, it is said: “Together with devas... [etc.]”
“...the inclusion of humans. In this context, “conventional gods” (sammutideva) refers to kings.

“The inclusion of the remaining humans” means the inclusion of those humans remaining after the conventional gods, as well as the recluses and brahmins. “In these” means in these locations. “By three phrases” means by the phrases *sadevaka*, *samāraka*, and *sabrahmaka*.
“By two” means by the phrases *sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī* and *sadevamanussa*. Regarding the meanings of the compound words:
Because the world of beings has already been included according to the method previously stated, it is said: "the world of beings together with the world of space.
With the words "Another way," etc., he states another meaning that ought to be expressed.

He says: "By the inclusion of 'together with the gods' (sadevaka)," because even formless beings, while dwelling in their own imperturbable state (*āneñjavihāra*), deserve this etymological derivation: "they shine, therefore they are gods" (*devā*).
"The formless-world sphere (arūpāvacaraloka) is included. For this very reason, the Blessed One said in the Brahmajāla Sutta and others:

"To the companionship of the gods who have reached the base of infinite space," and so forth; the meaning is that both the world-sphere of space (okāsaloka) and the world of sentient beings (sattaloka) belonging to the formless realm are included.
This is likewise the case here for the six sense-sphere deva worlds and the fine-material Brahma worlds. Regarding the six sense-sphere deva worlds specifically:
Because it proceeds under the control of Māra, it is said: "By the inclusion of 'together with Māra,' the six sense-sphere heavens (chakāmāvacaradevaloka) are meant.

For that is the place where his sovereignty is exercised, just as in the case of a bandit. The world of the fine-material Brahmās (rūpī brahmaloka) is included by way of elimination (pārisesañāya), since the immaterial Brahmā-world (arūpībrahmaloka) has been taken separately.
"By way of the four assemblies" refers to those counted as: Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, householders, recluses, the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa gods, Māras, and Brahmās.
Among the eight assemblies, the four assemblies beginning with the khattiyas are included by the mention of "together with the devas" and so forth, which encompasses those other than them.
But how, in this context, is the human world included by way of the four assemblies?
By the phrase "with recluses and brahmins," the assembly of recluses and the assembly of brahmins are included; by the phrase "with devas and humans," the assembly of khattiyas is included.
And the assembly of householders. By the word "people" (*pajā*), however, these very four assemblies are meant; for here the meaning is "the people consisting of the four assemblies.
Otherwise, he states how it should be understood: "or the world of humans together with the conventional deities. But how is it so understood?
By the phrase “with recluses and brahmins,” recluses and brahmins are included;
by the phrase “with devas and humans,” those called conventional devas—namely, khattiyas—and the remaining humans, namely householders and suddas, are included.

Since there are no other human beings besides these, by the word “generation” (pajā), it is these very human beings existing in these four ways who are spoken of. This refers to the division into four classes.

For here, the meaning is "they understand. Thus, since in both of these two alternatives the term *pajā* (people) refers specifically to humans by way of the four assemblies, it is now said, "or the entire world of remaining beings," in order to show that all other sentient beings are also included.
Here too, the entire world of remaining beings is taken together with the human world already included by way of the four assemblies.
Or, it should be construed as "the rest of the world of all beings together with conventional deities. And by way of nāgas, garuḷas, and so forth, there is the rest of the world of all beings.
This is what is meant: either the rest of the world of beings—such as the pure nāgas, supaṇṇas, and denizens of hell—along with the four assemblies;
or the rest of the world of beings—such as nāgas, supaṇṇas, and denizens of hell—along with humans distinguished into the four castes.

Having thus far shown the *yojana* by taking the world according to its divisions, he now says “But here too,” etc., in order to show the *yojana* by taking the world according to its specific distinctions rather than its divisions. Therein, “by way of the limit of the highest” means by way of the limit of the supreme destination;
it is said that this is known through that [distinction]. For, according to the first method, among the five destinations (*gati*), [the *yojana* is measured]...
They are superior by way of such distinctions as being included within the celestial realm (*devagati*), possessing the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), and having long life.

According to the second method, however, they are exceedingly exalted by such distinctions as being formless (*arūpin*), having defilements and suffering utterly eradicated, possessing peaceful, sublime, and imperturbable abidings (*vihāra*), and having an extremely long lifespan. But the Teachers [prefer] only the second method.

This was said with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*). Thus, although the state of having realized [the truth] for the entire world is established by the first phrase alone through the method of striving (*padhāna*), he shows that the remaining phrases were spoken for this specific reason by means of the passage beginning with "Then, of those...
The connection is: "He spoke after the first phrase. When it is simply stated, "The Lord of the six sense-sphere deities," [it might be thought to refer to] Sakka and others as well.
The term "vasavattī" (one who wields power) is stated in order to dispel the suspicion that his sovereignty might be subject to another;
by this, it shows that his sovereignty consists precisely in his being brought under the control of [the higher deities] through the performance of such daring deeds.

For he is not even the master in the sixth divine world, because the King of the Vasavatti gods alone is the master there. Thus the Blessed One said in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the excellent *Aṭṭhanipāta*, in the *Dānānisaṃsa Sutta*:
“In this regard, monks, the deity Vasavatti, having performed an abundance of the basis for meritorious action consisting of giving... [etc.
...surpasses the gods who Wield Power over the Creations of Others in ten respects,” so it is said in detail.
It is also stated in the *Madhyamāgama-ṭīkā*: “For there King Vasavatti rules his kingdom, whereas Māra [rules] over only one region with his own retinue.”

“Exercising sovereignty, he dwells like a rebellious prince in a border region of a kingdom”—this and the passage beginning “Brahmā of great majesty” are spoken with reference to Mahābrahmā of the ten-thousandfold world system.
For it has already been stated below that this is the highest possible limit.
The phrase beginning “With a single finger” is a partial demonstration of his great majesty. “Unsurpassed” (anuttara) means the supreme, namely the nine supramundane states (lokuttara).
*Puthu* means many or separate. *Ukkaṭṭhaṭṭhānānaṃ* means of those who have reached the highest state.
*Bhāvānukkamo* refers to the sequence of the phrases beginning with "together with the world of devas" according to the disposition of others in accordance with their own inclinations;
or, *bhāvānukkamo* is the sequence of the thematic development, meaning the order of the connection between both the meanings and the words.
Alternatively, this very reading is correct because it is seen in the *Samantapāsādikā* and was praised by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta.
The reading “vibhāvanānukkamo” is also seen, but since that is not found in those [sources], it is not good.
Now, in order to show the method of commentary used by the ancients, the words beginning with “the ancients, however, said” (*porāṇā panāhu*) were spoken. Therein, by means of another word...
Because the entire world of beings has been grasped without remainder, the phrase "the remaining world everywhere" is stated as a complete and exhaustive inclusion.

Therefore he said, "beings who have entered the three states of existence" (*tibhavūpage satte*); the meaning is: beings who have entered the three existences (*bhave*) comprised within the triple realm (*tedhātuka*).

"In three ways" means by the three modes consisting of being accompanied by gods, Māras, and Brahmas. "In three locations" refers to [the phrases] beginning with "together with the world of gods" (*sadevaka*).
"In the three sections. "Having included" means having grouped them according to their purpose.

The word "again" (punā) is stated in order to indicate that those very beings who have entered the three realms of existence are included in the two phrases "together with recluses and brahmins" and "together with devas and humans," by way of those respective modes—that is, by way of being "together with devas" and so forth, and by way of being "together with recluses and brahmins" and so forth—as "beings who have entered the three realms of existence."
Having said this, those who state "only the three realms" (tedhātukam eva) show that the world of beings (sattaloka) is included along with the world of space (okāsaloka).
The ancient masters, however, say: "The three realms alone are exhausted"—this is the construction [of the sentence].

By the word "himself" (sāmaṃ), meaning by oneself, he expresses the negation of others through the exclusion of anything else (aññatthāpohana) or through a restrictive inclusion (antogadhāvadhāraṇa): "not led by another" (aparaneyyo).
"Having sacrificed" means that one should not cause others to sacrifice on one's behalf.

"Abhiññā" is a designation formed by the elision of the letter *ya*, as in the expression "having understood through wise reflection" (*paṭisaṅkhā yoniso*), which is stated as "by higher knowledge" (*abhiññāya*).

By the prefix *abhi*, it is shown that it is not merely a qualifier, but rather indicates the instrument (*karaṇa*) by way of its qualification, as expressed by the phrase "by superior knowledge. This implies the exclusion of inference (*anumāna*) and other such means.

Here, by the word "etc. (ādi), it includes the act of making known through mere slight causes such as analogy, implication, the proximity of another word, conjunction, disjunction, association, and so forth, because they share the same means of cognition.

For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have direct perception of all phenomena due to the unobstructed range of their knowledge in all respects. "It awakens" and "it makes known"—this is the explanation of the meaning from the perspective of the word (*sadda*).
"He proclaims" is said from the perspective of his intention. In this manner, it should be analyzed in all instances.
"The unsurpassed bliss of seclusion" refers to the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

Regarding the inclusion of the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even having abandoned," this was done with the understanding that the Blessed One’s teaching sometimes occurs even during the intervals between the attainment of fruition. For when the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma...

At whatever moment the assembly gives a cry of approval or reviews the Dhamma as it was heard, at that very moment he delimits it by means of prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*) and enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

Then, emerging from that attainment according to his own delimitation, he teaches the Dhamma starting from the point where he had previously stood; this is the meaning stated in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

"Teaching little or much" means teaching little for one who understands through a condensed summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*), or teaching much for one who understands through detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*) and for one who is guided by instruction (*neyya*).
To the question "How does he teach?", he says: "Even at the beginning," and so forth.

The excellence of the Dhamma consists in its being conducive to liberation (*niyyānikatā*), and its being conducive to liberation is due solely to its being entirely blameless; thus it is said: "Having made it entirely blameless."

"By way of teaching" (*desanāya*): Teaching is the act of bestowing and awakening [others] through the method of command and so forth, by means of the Teacher of the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*).

Although, in the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "collection" apart from its constituent parts, yet when those parts are viewed as a collective form, they receive the designation of "verse" (*gāthā*) and so on; therefore, it is that [collection] which is meant.
Having treated it as if divided and having applied the conventional designation of "beginning, middle, and end," he said: "There is a beginning, middle, and end to the teaching.

Regarding the phrase "of the Dispensation" (sāsanassa): this refers to the Dhamma of practice. For the Dhamma of practice is called the "Dispensation" (sāsana) because it instructs according to the degree of fault and so forth in those persons to be instructed, and because it disciplines them by means of the removal of defilements through the various methods of discipline (*tadaṅgavinaya*, etc.).
The connection is: "There is the beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation. Regarding the phrase "even in a four-line [verse]," the word *pi* (even) here expresses a possibility;
by it, one acknowledges that such excellence of the beginning, middle, and end exists even in what is so small, let alone in what is more extensive.
And here, a "line" (*pada*) is a fourth part of a verse, which is also called a "foot" (*pāda*); by this very term, [the definition applies] to three-line and six-line verses as well.

He shows the division according to what is possible. Having thus shown the three excellences (*kalyāṇattaya*) in the components of a discourse (*suttāvayava*), he says, "of that which has a single connection" (*ekānusandhikassa*), and so forth, in order to show them in the entire discourse as well.

Therein, he says "of that which has a single connection" with reference to a discourse having a single connection by way of its sequence (*anusandhi*), provided it does not have too many divisions. However, in the case of the other [discourses], by that very same division of the Dhamma...
Because the beginning, middle, and end are obtained, the phrase "of that which has many connections" and so forth was stated.
"Nidāna" refers to the introductory section (nidānagrantha) established by the Elder Ānanda, characterized by the indication of the time, place, teacher, assembly, and so on.
"Idamavoca" (Thus he spoke) is merely an illustration of the conclusion (*nigamana*), since the conclusion must also be included, as in: "Thus it was said; this was said with reference to that."

For it should be understood that even the introductory narratives (*nidāna*) and conclusions (*nigamana*) established by the compilers of the Council are included within the Teacher’s own teaching, as they conform to it.
Regarding the phrase "at the end, the connection" (*ante anusandhi*): this refers to the very last connection.

By the words "Virtue, Concentration, and Insight" (*sīla-samādhi-vipassanā*), etc., he clarifies here that the Dispensation (*sāsana*) consists of the Dhamma of practice (*paṭipatti-dhamma*). However, because it is stated as "the Dhamma of the Dispensation" (*sāsanadhamma*) in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*—
“Refraining from all evil, undertaking of what is wholesome,
and the purification of one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas. Thus,

it is the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) that elucidates this instruction of the Teacher as spoken above, by way of its meaning such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth, in order to reveal the Three Excellences (*kalyāṇattaya*).
[The term] has been explained [elsewhere]. Here, however, it refers specifically to practice (*paṭipatti*). Therefore, he will say: "Here, the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching are intended.

Morality (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and insight (*vipassanā*) are called the "beginning" because they constitute the root of the superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) that comprise the excellence of the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
"Wholesome states" (*kusalā dhammā*) means blameless states (*anavajja-dhammā*). "View" (*diṭṭhi*) here refers to insight (*vipassanā*), due to its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*).
In this context, there is the mention of concentration (*samādhi*). This is a passage from the Bāhiya Sutta in the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta.
Granted, it is stated in the Sutta that the Noble Path is the "middle way" by virtue of its departure from the two extremes;

however, because of the commonality of being "middle," it is appropriate to say that it also establishes the middle state of both the undertaking and the accomplishment of right practice. Thus he said.
“When it is said, ‘Monks, there is a middle way realized by the Tathāgata,’ the noble path is what is meant by ‘the middle.

The intention is that the noble path is called ‘the middle’ because it occupies the intermediate position between the undertakings—consisting of virtue, concentration, and insight—and the accomplishments—consisting of the fruits and Nibbāna. This is with reference to the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining.”

The fruit is called the "conclusion" by way of the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining (*sopādisesa-nibbānadhātu*), whereas Nibbāna [itself] is so called by way of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*). For the Nibbāna-element is the conclusion of the Dispensation (*sāsana*). The accomplishment of the Path occurs by way of the fruit and through the realization of Nibbāna;
it is stated thus because there is nothing further to be done beyond that. Now, regarding the fact that both of these are the conclusion of the Dispensation:
In order to establish this through scripture (*āgama*), he says, "For this purpose, this," and so forth. "For this purpose" (*etadatthaṃ*) means that which has this very fruit as its purpose.
"O Brahmin!"—the Blessed One addresses the Brahmin Piṅgalakoccha. For this is a passage from the *Cūḷasāropama-sutta* in the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa* of the *Majjhima Āgama*.
"This essence" (*etaṃsāraṃ*) means that which has this very fruit as its essence, by means of the elision of the nasal stop (*niggahita*).
"Thus it has this conclusion. "Nibbānogadhaṃ" means "plunged into Nibbāna. "Friend Visākhā" is the elder nun Dhammadinnā’s address to the householder Visākhā.

For in the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, because of the proximity of other words such as "with meaning and with phrasing," it is stated that "here, the beginning, middle, and conclusion of the teaching are intended."

Having thus shown the analysis of the threefold excellence (*kalyāṇattaya*) of the teaching by way of the sequence of words, he says “The Blessed One (*bhagavā*), etc.”, showing it also by way of its meaning.
For by means of the word *hi*, he establishes that this [meaning] is indeed intended by him.
And by way of this establishment, he shows the analysis of the threefold excellence by way of the meaning. As for the meaning, however, this...

The "teaching" (desanā) spoken of here is precisely the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma), which consists of a sequence of words established by way of verses (gāthā) and discourses (sutta) that have been composed for various specific purposes;
its meaning is specifically virtue (sīla) and so forth, hence he says, "Virtue in the beginning," and so on. For this is a statement of distinctions.
However, by the mention of "virtue" in a general sense, virtue along with its constituent factors (sasambhāra-sīla) is included.

Likewise, by the inclusion of the "path" (magga), the term encompasses the entire meaning of the scripture (pariyatti) in its entirety through three aspects—namely, the path together with its requisites—thereby exhausting the subject matter without remainder.
