For otherwise, the distinction between the three excellences would not be universally applicable.

And here, because the Dispensation (sāsana) has virtue as its root, its excellence in the beginning is stated by means of virtue; this is because the attainment of the Dispensation occupies a middle position.
The state of being good in the middle is due to the Path. The state of being good in the end is due to Nibbāna, because there is nothing further to be done beyond the attainment of Nibbāna.

"By that" refers to the demonstration of virtue and the other factors; for it is by way of their purpose (*atthavasena*) that the teaching's quality of being good in the beginning and so forth is stated here.
The passage beginning with "Therefore" is a demonstration of the instruction for listeners, following the sequence as previously described.
*Esā* means "in the manner already stated. *Kathikasaṇṭhiti* refers to the established mode of a Dhamma-preacher, that is, his steady engagement in preaching.
*Vaṇṇanā* is the exposition of the meaning, or else it is praise. *Na so sātthaṃ deseti*:

he does not teach with a purposeful aim, because that teaching is devoid of the aim of deliverance (*niyyānattha*). *Tasmā*: because of the teaching of the aim of deliverance, such as the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and so forth. *Ekabyañjanādiyuttā*: joined with single consonants and so on, among the various types such as the soft and the hard consonants.
Like the Tamil language, it is joined with consonants in only one way or two ways among the ten consonants.

Like the Kirāta language, its consonants are entirely "without lip-contact" (*sabbaniroṭṭhabyañjana*), because they must be articulated without touching the lips due to the openness of the vocal organs, and thus all its consonants are entirely devoid of lip-contact. All [its consonants] are "fully released" (*sabbavissaṭṭhabyañjana*). All...
“Having consonants that are entirely subject to release” means having consonants entirely released [from vowel-inherent sounds], like the Savara language.

“All its consonants are suppressed” means all its consonants are entirely accompanied by the *bindu* (anusvāra) due to the presence of the *sānusāra* (the nasalizing quality), like the Mleccha languages such as Persian and so forth.
Thus, the phrase “like the languages of the Damilas, Kirātas, Savaras, and Mlecchas” should be applied to each [of these four] respectively. “Mleccha” means...
And [this includes] the Persians and others. All of these are called "non-syllables" (abyañjana) because they lack the fullness of syllables, as they occur only by way of a portion of a syllable.
The letter to be articulated by making the places of articulation and the efforts relaxed is the first and third [consonants] in each of the five groups.
"Relaxed. Having made those [consonants] non-relaxed, one should pronounce the second or fourth [consonant] of those very [vowels] as aspirated.
A syllable of two measures is long; one of one measure is short.
"The measure is that of one measure, from the closing and opening of the eyes," so they say.
They say that [the duration] is even by the measure of a finger-snap.
That which ends in a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*) is long and heavy; that which does not end in a consonant cluster is short and light.

The *niggahīta* (anusvāra) is to be pronounced with the mouth unopened, having suppressed the points of articulation and the vocal organs. That which is to be pronounced in connection with a following word is a "conjunction" (*sambandha*).
Likewise, it is "determined" (vavatthita) when it is not confused. It is "released" (vimutta) when it is to be uttered with the mouth open and the points of articulation (ṭhāna-karaṇa) relaxed.

Regarding the phrase "in ten ways" and so forth, the meaning is that there is a tenfold classification of the phonemes (byañjana) by way of the slackness and other qualities of the consciousness termed "phoneme-intelligence" (byañjanabuddhi), which produces the syllables (akkhara). For all syllables...
They are "produced by mind" (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*), and they are called "phonemes" (*byañjana*) because they manifest and clarify the intended meaning through their expression;
or alternatively, it is also appropriate to say that there is a tenfold classification of phonemes by means of the instrumentality of the cognition of phonemes.
"Without smearing" (*amakkhetvā*) means without defiling or without destroying; the sense is "without losing. To explain that point, he said: "only with complete phonemes."

"Having made [this known]" means that whatever meaning the Blessed One teaches—even if he teaches it by means of a single verse or a single sentence—he teaches that very meaning through a teaching consisting of perfectly rounded words and phrases;
this is what is meant. Therefore, "tasmā" (therefore) refers to the teaching of the Dhamma with complete phrasing. The word *kevala* here signifies "without remainder";
it does not signify "unmixed" and so forth, as he states: "it is a synonym for 'entire'. *Paripuṇṇaṃ* (complete).

It is entirely complete (*sabbaso puṇṇaṃ*). In its actual meaning, however, it is said to be "the statement that is neither deficient nor excessive" (*anūnādhikavacana*) because it precludes both deficiency and excess.

In this context, "non-deficiency" (*anūnatā*) should be understood as the fact that it establishes the purpose for which it was taught; "non-excess" (*anadhikatā*) is due to the fact that what is contrary to that purpose does not establish it.

Alternatively, non-deficiency is due to the absence of anything further to be added for the sake of purification that has not already been stated, and [non-excess] is due to the absence of anything to be removed...
There is no deficiency because there is an absence of anything stated that has the sense of defilement (*saṃkilesa*). "Entire" means possessing all parts.
"Complete" means full in every respect. Therefore he said: "There is nothing incomplete even in a single part. The teaching is impure because it is defiled by craving (*taṇhā*).
Worldly baits (*lokāmisa*) are the requisites such as robes and so forth, because they are to be grasped by craving in the world.

Among these, he is "indifferent to worldly gain" because his mind is unattached. "By pervading with welfare" means by the pervasion of welfare—that is, by the bestowal of welfare—acting as a qualification.
He is "soft-hearted" through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) acting as the instrument.

"Established in the nature of rescuing" means established in the mode of lifting [beings] out from all defilements and from the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*); what is meant is "by an intention of compassion."
“Giving” (*dāna*) is a “vow” (*vata*) in the sense of being undertaken with the thought, “From now on I shall give, and I shall give in this manner.

It is “divine” (*brahma*) in the sense of being excellent because it is prescribed by the wise; alternatively, it is the conduct (*cariya*) of the divine ones (*brahmā*), the excellent ones, and thus giving itself is “the divine life” (*brahmacariya*).

Because it is practiced through the suppression of stinginess, greed, and so forth, giving itself is “well-practiced” (*suciṇṇa*). “Success” (*iddhi*) means “divine success” (*deviddhi*). “Splendor” (*juti*) means radiance or majesty. “The attainment of power and energy” (*balavīriyūpapatti*)...
"Endowed with great strength and energy. "O Naga! is an address by the wise Vidhura to Varuṇa, the king of the nāgas.
"Generous lords" means masters of giving. "Become like a well" means like a watering place for water.
"O steadfast one!"—with this he addresses the wise Vidhura.

*Madhussavaṃ* means the flowing of sweet juice. *Puññaṃ* refers to the fruit of merit, spoken of by way of the cause. *Brahmaṃ* or *brahmānaṃ cāriyaṃ* is "the conduct of the noble ones" (*brahmacariya*), meaning service. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
*Tittiriyaṃ* means that which was spoken by Tittira, the king of birds.
*Aññatra tāhi* means excluding those who have become the wives of others. *Amhaṃ* means our.
"Ascetic, austere, loathsome, secluded"—because of having performed these four kinds of difficult practices, it is "endowed with four factors.
*Sudam* is merely a particle. The *Lomahaṃsana Sutta* is found in the *Mūlapaṇṇāsaka* of the *Majjhima Āgama*; they also call it the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*.
*Iddham* means successful. *Phītam* means blossomed. *Vitthārikam* means become extensive. *Bāhujaññam*...
It was known by many people as something leading to liberation (*niyyānika*). "Puthubhūtaṃ" means "become manifold" (*bahubhūtaṃ*).

Regarding the phrase "as far as gods and humans": in the *Pāsādika-sutta-aṭṭhakathā*, this is stated with the intended meaning that it is well-expounded from the world of the gods down to the world of humans;
thus, the sense is "as far as both gods and humans. "Tasmā" (therefore) means because the entire teaching (*sakala-sāsana*) comprises the three trainings (*sikkhattaya*).
Here, it is intended as "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*);
therefore, showing the meaning by connecting all the terms in grammatical apposition with this word "holy life," he says, "He teaches the Dhamma," and so forth.
For by the phrase "teaching thus," he shows that the word "Dhamma" and the others have the same meaning as the word "holy life" (*brahmacariya*), [as in] "he teaches the Dhamma."
Having stated this, he further clarifies that the statement “he proclaims the holy life” (brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti) is intended to reveal its meaning through its specific form.
“Endowment with the aforementioned qualities” means the endowment with the various virtues such as being excellent in the beginning (ādikalyāṇa), and so forth, as already described.

Proper practice in the Teaching is possible only for one who has cast pride far away, not for one of a proud nature; thus it is said, “because of having humbled pride. “Because of its abundance” means...
Because they occur frequently. Intoxications based on wealth, physical beauty, and so forth, are easy to abandon because their signs do not persist;
intoxications based on lineage, learning, and so forth, are not so, because their signs do persist.

Therefore, even for those born into noble Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa families who have gone forth, the indulgence in conceit supported by birth and learning is difficult to abandon; thus he said: "For the most part... [conceit]..."
"...they do. "Because of being born into a different [status]" (*vijātitāya*) means because of being born into a contrary status; the meaning is "because of being born into a low status.

It is said thus because, for the most part, those endowed with the necessary support (*upanissaya*) are indeed of good birth, not of bad birth. "They are unable to establish themselves" means they do not strive to establish themselves in virtue (*sīla*);
it is meant that they are unable to guard virtue having made it thoroughly pure. Virtue alone...
For it is indeed a foundation in the Dispensation; or rather, it is to "be established" by means of the penetration of truth, that is, to be established upon the supramundane foundation.
For that, in the ultimate sense, is what is called "establishment in the Dispensation.

Having thus explained the meaning through the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*), he speaks also by way of inclusion (*anvaya*) with the words, "But as for the sons of householders," and so forth. From their armpits...

"By those emitting sweat": this is an instrumental expression used to denote a characteristic state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*). Likewise, "with the back blooming with salt" means having a back that is blooming with salt because the armpits are emitting sweat;
or the meaning is that they are characterized by those particular conditions.
"Having ploughed the earth" means from the act of ploughing the earth; what is meant is, "from subsisting on a field. "Of such a kind... [and so forth].
[This refers to] the support for one who possesses birth. Weakness is conceit (*māna*); strength is arrogance (*dappa*). "Kamma" means preliminary work (*parikamma*).

By the phrase beginning with "by the others," he explains the causal term "because of being excessive. Having said "thus" (*iti*), he shows what is not to be referred back by the phrase beginning with "because of having humbled conceit" (*nihatamānattā*);
or else, the word *iti* is used in the sense of illustration, meaning "in this way, according to the method already stated. This same method applies to such cases.
Regarding the term *paccājāto*, it is said to be "reborn" (*patijāto*) because here the prefix *ā* is merely an intensifier.
"Pure" (*parisuddha*) means completely purified in every respect due to the absence of defilements, as it illustrates the absolute abandonment of lust and the other taints.

He is the "Lord of Dhamma" (*dhammassāmī*) in the sense of being the master of the Dhamma by virtue of its production, or else he is the Lord of the world including the devas by means of the Dhamma. "Faith" (*saddha*) refers to faith that transcends the level of ordinary persons.

Faith. For those of a discerning nature, the accomplishment of faith is preceded by the apprehension of the excellence of the Dhamma, because among the four types of persons there is the person who takes the Dhamma as the measure and has confidence in the Dhamma.
One acquires faith [thinking]: "The Blessed One is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One, for his Dhamma is thus well-expounded. Or even in a place a hundred yojanas away. "Husband and wife" means...

“Husband and wife. Although by saying simply “husband and wife” (*jāyampatikā*) one understands that only two people—the master of the house and the mistress of the house—are meant, there is no need to speak further regarding a man who has many wives.
Even with just one, cohabitation is indeed a confinement; it is for the purpose of showing this that “two” is stated. [The term refers to] the possession (*kiñcana*) consisting of lust and so forth.
That which is accompanied by the obstacles (*palibodha*) of fields, land, and so forth, and which exists together with both of these, is "possessing obstacles" (*sakiñcana-palibodhana*);

that very meaning is expressed in that way. Passion (*rāga*) itself is "dust" (*raja*); the dust of hatred, delusion, and so forth begins with that. For it has been said: "Passion is dust, but it is not called 'grit' (*reṇu*)," and so on.
Since the sense of "path of arrival" (*āgamanapatha*) is identical to the sense of "place of arising" (*uṭṭhānaṭṭhāna*), both commentaries have the same meaning; only the phrasing differs.
"Knowledge. "In the sense of non-adherence" means in the sense of not clinging, having the nature of being unobstructed.
The inclusion of the word *viya* (as if) is used to show that it is like an open space (*abbhokāsa*), either by way of its physical form or by way of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*).

Having thus shown that household life and the life of renunciation are respectively cramped and spacious by virtue of being the proper and improper spheres for the occurrence of unwholesome and wholesome states, [the author now proceeds] by way of the improper and proper spheres for the occurrence of wholesome states alone.
To demonstrate their state as such, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) was stated. The connection is: “like a place where kings assemble.

A concise explanation (*saṅkhepakathā*) is a commentary on the meaning that does not provide the extraction of individual words separately. “Even for a single day” means even for the duration of one day.
“Having made it unbroken” means having made it free from gaps by not committing even a mere *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing).
"The final consciousness" means the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*). "By the stain of defilements" means by the stain of craving (*taṇhā*) and so forth. "Undefiled" means not defiled.
"Scrubbed like a conch shell" means it is washed, being stainless in the sense of being purified; thus it is "scrubbed like a conch shell" (*saṅkhalikhita*).
To show merely the meaning, it is said to be "like a scrubbed conch shell. "Resembling a washed conch shell" has that same meaning.

The commentary (*vivaraṇa*). Furthermore, it shows that *saṅkhalikhita* is like *saṅkhā* (writing) and *likhita* (written)—just as in the expression "one who has established the fire" (*aggi-āhito*)—and because it resembles that, it is also called *saṅkhalikhita*. This is a neuter noun in the abstract sense (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*).

Regarding the word *ajjhāvasati*, because of its connection with the prefix *adhi* used as a karmapravacanīya, the word *agāra* functions in the accusative case to express the locative sense; thus he says, "in the midst of the home" (*agāramajjhe*).
The connection is: "If indeed I were to go forth, it would be well. By the phrase "because of being yellowed by an astringent taste," he shows that *kāsāyāni* means "dyed with an astringent.
And as to why these [robes] were taken, he says: "They are suitable for those leading the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
"Having clothed oneself" is a mere conventional expression; the meaning is "having put them on."
And that is by way of wearing the lower garment and the upper robe. "House" (*agāra*) is [derived from] *agāravāsa* (house-dwelling) through the elision of the latter member;

"belonging to that" (*tassa*) refers to work such as farming or trade that brings about welfare and growth. "The homeless state" (*anagāriya*) means in that state of homelessness. 192. "From a thousand" means from a thousand *kahāpaṇa* coins.
"Mass of wealth" (*bhogakkhandha*) means a heap of wealth. "In the sense of binding" means [binding] the son...
By means of the passage beginning with “nattā pana nattā,” a limit is established by way of affection; by this, it is shown that the word *parivaṭṭa* has the sense of binding (*ābandhana*).
Alternatively, it is also appropriate to understand *parivaṭṭa* in the sense of revolving (*parivattana*) by way of [the succession of] grandfather, father’s son, and so forth.
They are called *ñātayo* (relatives) because they are known as “these are ours.”

193. Being one whose doors of body and speech are closed by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, and being considered "endowed" with that very restraint, it is said: "possessed of the Pātimokkha restraint.

The detailed exposition of conduct (*ācāra*) and resort (*gocara*) should be taken from the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* and other such works. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "endowed with conduct and resort" refers to that very state of being restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint.
This is the demonstration of conditions. Because it is minute due to its similarity to an atom (*aṇu*), it is called "minute" (*aṇu*); thus he says, "in regard to what is minute.
Its minuteness is due to the nature of minor offenses committed unintentionally, and due to the arising of unwholesome states of mind that occur impulsively.
"One who sees danger" means one whose nature is to see danger. "Properly" (*sammā*) means without error, or beautifully; its state [is "propriety"].
And [he trains] respectfully throughout his life by way of non-transgression.

When it is said simply "in the training rules" (*sikkhāpadesu*), because the meaning "having undertaken that constituent part of the training rule, he trains" is already understood, the object-case word was not stated; therefore he says "that particular training rule," meaning each individual portion of the training, or the means for attaining that training.
Or they depend [on it]; this is the meaning.
"Therein" means in this statement beginning with "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "By the mention of conduct and resort alone" means by the expression "endowed with conduct and resort.
Therefore he said: "Even though wholesome bodily and verbal actions have been included," for it is not [established] by the mere words "conduct and resort" alone.
The inclusion of wholesome bodily and verbal action is possible; by this, he shows a trace of the objection regarding tautology.

"Of that" refers to the virtue of purity of livelihood. "For the purpose of showing the door of its arising" means for the purpose of showing, by way of the term "action," the door consisting of bodily and verbal intimation through which it arises; by this, he shows the resolution of the aforementioned objection. This...
It is said: even when something is already established, a restatement is made either for the sake of restriction or to bring out another meaning;
here, however, it brings out another meaning, and therefore it is stated for the purpose of showing the door of its arising.

Regarding the phrase "by what is wholesome," this means by that which is blameless because of the complete abandonment of improper search. To the question, "How does that show the door of its arising? he says: "Because..."
“...and so forth. The intended meaning is that he is one whose livelihood is purified because he is endowed with blameless bodily and verbal actions arising through the doors of body and speech.
For it is precisely those two [types of action] rooted in livelihood that constitute the virtue of purification of livelihood.
Now, in order to correlate this with another sutta, he said: “Or rather, it was stated thus by way of the Muṇḍikaputtasutta.”
And here the word *vā* has the sense of an alternative option (*vikappana*) for another meaning, namely, the correlation with another sutta.
The *Muṇḍikaputtasuttanta* is found in the *Majjhima Nikāya*, in the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsa*; it is also called the *Samaṇamuṇḍikaputtasutta*.
Therein, "Master carpenter" (*thapati*) is the Blessed One addressing the carpenter named Pañcakaṅga; for the word *thapati* is a synonym for a carpenter (*vaḍḍhaki*).
This is what is meant: because, after showing that virtue consists of wholesome bodily and verbal action by asking, "And what, carpenter, are wholesome virtues?

Wholesome bodily action and wholesome verbal action," [the Buddha] delivered the teaching in the Muṇḍikaputtasutta beginning with, "I say, carpenter, that purity of livelihood is also included in virtue. Thus, by means of bodily and verbal action...
Having shown that virtue consists in wholesome bodily and verbal action by saying, "endowed with what is wholesome," this teaching in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*—
which proceeds with the words "pure livelihood"— is entirely unified, converges,
and harmonizes as the waters of the Yamunā do with the waters of the Gaṅgā; therefore, such a majesty of the Blessed One’s teaching truly exists.
"In regard to virtue" (*sīlasmiṃ*) means "I speak of virtue" (*sīlaṃ vadāmi*); or, it is that which is included and contained within virtue as its support;
or, from the collective whole consisting of the various types of virtue, I speak of one specific virtue.

"In three ways" means in three ways by way of the minor virtue, the intermediate virtue, and the major virtue. By the phrase "with the mind as the sixth," he refers specifically to the group beginning with the body as the fifth.
It excludes the grasping [of the term]. Regarding the seven places that will be explained in the subsequent exposition:

"in three ways" means that for each of the four [bases], there are three modes according to what is obtained, according to one's strength, and according to what is appropriate. This concludes the commentary on the Minor, Middling, and Great Virtues (*sīla*).
194–211. Thus, by way of the method beginning with, “Having thus gone forth, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,” and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “In virtue” (*sīlasmiṃ*), this is the locative case used for selection (*niddhāraṇe*); since one thing is to be selected from that [group], he says, “one virtue” (*ekaṃ sīlaṃ*).
Furthermore, by this he shows the locative case used for the substratum (*ādhāre*), because a whole is designated by means of its parts, just as...

“‘A branch on a tree’: by means of the word ‘this’ (*idaṃ*), it is shown to be in grammatical apposition through the sense of the locative case functioning as the sense of the accusative, because the locative case occurs in the sense of the accusative—as in ‘just as in a forest thicket with its tips touched.

Or rather, this locative is in the sense of the nominative,” by this [statement] he shows that “this very meaning” is precisely the meaning of the nominative case. In the *Brahmajāla* commentary, that is, in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
Or, it means "in the words of the Brahmajāla Sutta," according to the method stated by way of commentary. Regarding the phrase "this is his virtue" (*idamassa hoti sīlam*):
since there is no [separate] entity being singled out here by means of the culmination of great virtue, only the meaning of the singular case-ending is possible;
thus he says, "the meaning is 'this is his virtue'. For that very reason, it should be understood that the particle *api* was not included in the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
212. Fears such as self-reproach, reproach by others, and the fear of punishment are rooted in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
The Teacher has stated: “‘From non-restraint of virtue’ means from the absence of restraint in virtue; that is, from the lack of the restraint of virtue.

However, regarding the phrase “that which [is the fear] from the restraint of virtue,” the explanation of its meaning is: “That fear which might arise from the restraint of virtue”; thus, it is because of the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara-hetu*)...

And because the meaning [of the phrase] “he does not perceive fear” is established through the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) and by reason of that restraint of virtue, this very meaning is what arises.
For even the reading “whatever fear might arise from the restraint of virtue” is seen.
Having stated the cause as “from restraint,” it is also [explained] by way of the purpose attained thereby: “due to the absence of fear rooted in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).”
He states the reason. "By that which was performed according to the prescribed rule" means by that which was accomplished in accordance with the rule.
"By the consecration of a khattiya" means by the consecration that brings about the status of a khattiya. "Poured upon the head" means sprinkled right upon the crown of the head.
And here, by the phrase "by that which was performed according to the prescribed rule," one factor is indicated, namely, being endowed with the procedure practiced by the ancients.

By the phrase "with the consecration of a khattiya," it shows the quality of bringing about the status of a khattiya; by the phrase "sprinkled upon the head," it shows the state of being sprinkled specifically upon the head.

Thus, the consecration of a khattiya, endowed with these three factors, has been described—by means of which the royal majesty of consecrated kings is accomplished. But by what is this meaning understood?
According to the method of the ancient teachers, for it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Aggañña Sutta*, in the section explaining the consecration of Mahā Sammata:
"And those lords of the fields performed his consecration with three sprinklings (*saṅkha*).
And it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* on the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta* of the *Majjhima Āgama*: "'Anointed on the head' means by the kṣatriya-consecration with three sprinklings."
In the *Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā* as well, in the commentary on the *Cūḷasīhanādasutta*,
it is stated: "First, for kings receiving consecration, three types of conchs— made of gold and so forth—
as well as water from the Gaṅgā and a noble maiden, must be obtained," and so on.
Now, according to the method of the Arahants, this is the determination of the procedure for the consecration: for the sake of the auspiciousness of the consecration,

having seated the noble-born Kṣatriya worthy of consecration upon a well-established auspicious Udumbara throne in the center of a decorated pavilion prepared inside a pavilion made of Udumbara branches, first, those adorned with auspicious ornaments...
A noble maiden of perfect birth, having carefully grasped with both hands a golden conch shell from the great ocean filled with water from the Ganges and raised it above his head,
pours the consecration water over his crown and speaks thus: "O King, all the hosts of kshatriyas [protect themselves] by means of this..."
“By means of consecration, they make the Great King one who is consecrated. You, standing firm in the duties of a king, should rule the kingdom with righteousness and impartiality.
Toward these groups of kṣatriyas, be of a mind accompanied by affection for them as sons and compassion;

be of a mind characterized by benevolence, equality, and loving-kindness; and be their protector, guardian, and defender through your protection, shelter, and security. Then, furthermore, the domestic priest—
Adorned and prepared with ornaments appropriate for the station of a chaplain,
he respectfully takes a silver conch filled with water from the Ganges in both hands, raises it above his head,
and pours the consecration water over his crown, while saying: "Your Majesty, all the hosts of brahmins, for the sake of protecting themselves by means of this..."
"By means of consecration, they make the great king one who is consecrated; you, standing firm in the duties of a king, should rule the kingdom with righteousness and impartiality.
Toward these groups of brahmins, may you be of a mind accompanied by affection for them as a son and a mind of equal benevolence and loving-kindness;
and for their protection, defense, and security, may you be their guardian. Then, once again, the merchant, adorned with the ornaments that grace the station of a merchant—
Having carefully taken with both hands a conch shell made of jewels and filled with water from the Ganges,
and having raised it above his head, he sprinkles the water of consecration upon his head and speaks thus: "Your Majesty, all the assemblies of householders,
for the sake of protecting themselves, make you a consecrated Great King by means of this consecration."
“Established in the duties of a king, rule your kingdom with righteousness and impartiality;

toward these groups of householders, be of a mind accompanied by affection for your children and compassion, and possess a mind of equal benevolence and loving-kindness; and for their protection, defense, and security, be their protector.
As they were speaking thus to him, [they said], “If you act in accordance with our words...”
"It is well if you shall rule; if you do not, may your head split into seven pieces!"—this should be understood as being like a curse uttered against the king.
This matter should also be clarified by means of the *Vaḍḍhakīsūkara-jātaka* and others, and the requisites for the consecration should be taken from the *Samantapāsādikā* and other such texts.
The connection is: "Because he has destroyed his enemies, therefore he does not perceive [them].

He says, "Wholesomeness by way of being wholesome," and so on: "wholesome virtue as its proximate cause. This is what is meant: the states of non-remorse, gladness, rapture, and tranquility have wholesome virtue as their proximate cause;
and one experiences the mental pleasure that has arisen with non-remorse and the rest as its sign, [a pleasure] produced by the origination of mental pleasure.
And it is the bodily pleasure that arises for one whose body is touched by exquisite forms.

213. Since the state of being a recluse (*sāmañña*) requires a specific qualification, even though the specific [quality] intended here has not been explicitly excluded by that [general term], it is nonetheless implied.
He said: "The word 'eye' (cakkhu) in some instances refers to the Buddha-eye," and so forth.

For it is only that which exists as the referent (*abhidheyya*) that a particular term (*visesa-sadda*) clarifies by means of its specific meaning through the exclusion of other [possible] meanings; it does not clarify that which does not exist.

This same principle applies to the remaining terms as well. The "Buddha-eye" (*buddha-cakkhu*) is the vision belonging exclusively to the Buddhas, not shared with others; it is the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya-ñāṇa*).

And the knowledge of the degrees of others' faculties (*indriyaparopariyattañāṇa*). In the sense of seeing completely and in every way, it is "the universal eye" (*samantacakkhu*), which is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
"Like that" means like the summit of a mountain; the connection is with the phrase "the palace made of Dhamma. The meaning is:
"O Sumedha, you who possess the universal eye, look upon the people. "The wisdom of the three lower noble paths" refers to the wisdom of the three lower noble paths.
“The ‘Dhamma-eye’ (dhammacakkhu) refers to the three lower paths and the three fruits,” as stated in the *Saḷāyatanavagga-aṭṭhakathā*.
However, here [the author] shows it by including the fruits within the paths themselves. For the Dhamma-eye is the eye regarding the Dhamma consisting of the Four Truths.
The wisdom-eye (paññācakkhu) is wisdom itself in the sense of seeing; it is the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa).
“In the divine eye” refers to the second clear knowledge (*vijjā*). “Here” refers to this passage: “Having seen a form with the eye.

This word “eye” (*cakkhu*)—by the phrase “by way of the conventional expression ‘eye of sensitivity’”—indicates that here the word “eye” applies directly (*nippariyāyato*) only to the sensitivity of the eye;
however, by way of indirect usage (*pariyāyato*), because that which depends may be designated by the name of its support, it also applies to eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*).
"‘The beds are making a loud clamor’—this shows [the meaning]. Here too, because the discussion including the constituent parts remains, the word ‘also’ (pi) is included in the remaining phrases;
the meaning is that it applies even to phrases such as ‘one who does not grasp at signs. ‘Various eating and distressing is affliction’ (byāseko);
affliction itself is the affliction. One who is devoid of that is ‘thus’ (tathā). And being devoid of it is non-mixture; the state of non-mixture is [non-entanglement]."
And because it is pure due to the absence of association, he says, "unmixed and pure"; the meaning is that it is not mixed with the suffering of the defilements and is therefore perfectly purified.

When mindfulness and the restraint of the faculties are well-purified, the practice of higher consciousness (adhicittānuyoga) comes into one's very hands through the disappearance of the evil states that are the primary factors among the hindrances; therefore, it is indeed the bliss of higher consciousness.
By the phrase "the bliss of higher consciousness" (*adhicittasukha*), he shows that it is called "the bliss of non-distraction" (*abyāsekasukha*).
Commentary on the Discussion of Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension (214):
One who knows thoroughly, in all ways, or who knows in an eminent or distinguished manner, is "clearly comprehending" (*sampajāna*); the state of being so is "clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*).
Thus, there is knowledge regarding what has occurred; the analysis of that is the "Exposition on Clear Comprehension" (*sampajaññabhājanīya*).
Within that Exposition on Clear Comprehension, by the word "going," he expresses "approaching" (*abhikkanta*) as a noun denoting the state of action (*bhāvasādhana*).
Likewise, "returning" (*paṭikkanta*) is stated as "turning back. And here, "going" refers to both going after having turned back and going without turning back.
Turning back, however, is merely a turning back; these two are simply the reciprocal acts of taking up [the body].
To the question "How is this obtained?", he says "In walking," and so forth. "Bringing forward" means moving the body by way of walking. "Turning back" means returning from that again.
"Shifting away" means redirecting it by way of stepping aside. "Of the seat" refers to a seat such as a bench and the like.
“Facing the front part of the body” means facing the front parts such as the chest and so forth. “Moving forward” means crawling forward.
“The region of the back part of the body” means the region of the back parts such as the buttocks and so forth. “Moving backward” means crawling backward.

By the phrase “the same method applies,” he shows that for one who is lying down, there is likewise crawling forward and crawling backward toward the front. For in the cases of standing, sitting, and reclining—
That which is the forward movement of the body, devoid of going, is "approaching" (*abhikkama*). That which is the backward movement is "receding" (*paṭikkama*);

this is the defining characteristic. "Full awareness" (*sampajañña*) means being fully aware; one who has the habit of performing the duties to be done by oneself through that [awareness] is "one who acts with full awareness.
Thus it is said: "one who performs all duties with full awareness. Alternatively, by the phrase "one who acts with full awareness," [it refers to] one who is fully aware.

This shows that he is one whose nature is to act and who acts with clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). The passage beginning with “For he” (*so hi*) and so forth is an explanation of the second alternative.

Furthermore, by the word “clear comprehension” (*sampajañña*), it is stated that the term *sampajāna* is a synonym for clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). For thus it was said by the Venerable Ācariya Ānanda:
“Clear comprehension (*sampajāna*) is knowing thoroughly, correctly, or equally; that very thing is clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). This is [the meaning].

Another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Sampajañña-kāra" is the act (*kāra*) or performance (*karaṇa*) of one who possesses clear comprehension (*sampajāna*), such that it produces non-delusion regarding the "gone beyond" (*abhikkanta*) and so forth. One who has this is a "possessor of clear comprehension" (*sampajānakārī*).
It is "meaningful" (*sātthaka*) because it functions together with the goal (*attha*) known as progress (*vaḍḍhi*), namely the "gone beyond" and so forth; [it is] of one who is meaningful...

Clear comprehension of purpose is clear comprehension of what is beneficial (*sātthaka-sampajañña*). Clear comprehension of suitability is clear comprehension of what is appropriate for oneself and fitting.

Clear comprehension of resort (*gocara-sampajañña*) is clear comprehension regarding the resort of the alms-round—consisting of walking and so forth—and regarding other resorts consisting of the meditation subject that is never abandoned.
For the word "resort" is used [here] either by way of a general description or by the method of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*).

It occurs in both of those two meanings. Regarding "non-delusion" (*asammoha*)—which is defined as non-confusion with respect to crossing over and so forth—it is precisely this non-delusion that constitutes clear comprehension;
thus it is "clear comprehension as non-delusion. "By means of the mind alone" means by means of the mind itself; the sense is that it follows the mastery of the mind.
"Having encompassed" means having weighed and investigated; the sense is "having reflected upon. By the very act of seeing the Saṅgha, for the purpose of the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, and so forth...
Going is included [in the definition]. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the preliminary work for the kasiṇas and so forth is intended.
To explain the meaning of what was stated in brief, it is said, "or at a cetiya," and so on. "He attains arahantship" is a description of the highest limit (ukkaṭṭha-niddesa).

For even the arising of serenity and insight is indeed progress for a bhikkhu. "Therein" means in the object of foulness (asubha). "Some" refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. "From material things" (āmisato):
[This is] because of material requisites such as robes and so forth. To the question "Why?", he says:
"Depending on that," and so on. "In that" refers to the purpose grasped by means of purposeful clear comprehension (*sātthaka-sampajañña*).
Since, from the perspective of the Dhamma, growth alone is what is called "purpose," therefore whatever going is intended as "purposeful" is entirely suitable.
In order to preclude the suspicion that this might apply indiscriminately to anyone, he began with the words, "First, the visiting of the cetiya," and so forth.
"With a great offering" (*mahāpūjāya*) means with a grand offering; it is said to refer to the day of offering for many people.
"Like painted figures" (*cittakammarūpakāni viya*) means like images fashioned by painting, or like images performing various kinds of diverse actions through the application of machinery.
"Among them" means among those assemblies. "His" refers to the bhikkhu. What is called "non-regard" is the improper apprehension of an object by way of household-based ignorance and equanimity;

with reference to this, it was said: "Upon seeing a form with the eye, equanimity arises in the fool, the deluded worldling," and so forth. By way of contact with women, there is the offense of bodily contact.
There is a threat to life due to being trampled by elephants and the like;

there is an obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*) due to seeing unsuitable forms and so forth, in the manner described in the passage beginning, “An assembly gathers within a distance of ten or twelve *yojanas*.
The phrase “having a great retinue of followers” is said with reference to a retinue consisting of a mixture of men and women for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma and other such occasions.
"‘For the purpose of illustrating that meaning’ means for the purpose of illustrating the meaning consisting in the fact that the contemplation of foulness is purposeful.
It is the custom for monks, from the day they go forth, to engage in conversation by way of giving a reply;
therefore, conversing without following that custom by way of not giving a reply is called his ‘second [fault],” thus he said: “Two...”
“What discourse indeed has not been spoken before? For there are two kinds of discourse: discourse concerning what is to be done and what is not to be done.

Of these, only the discourse concerning what is to be done has been spoken before; the second has not been spoken before. Therefore, the meaning is that because she was easy to speak with, she gave a reply.
By the word “thus,” he refers back to everything of the aforementioned kind, beginning with, “But if [there is] a great festival for the Cetiya.”

It is not merely [the meditation on] the foulness of a woman for a man, and so forth. One who has grasped what is purposeful and suitable is "one who has grasped what is purposeful and suitable" (*pariggahitasātthakasappāyo*);
by this term, he shows the grasping of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) in its proper sequence.
A meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is the object of development because it is the basis for the occurrence of the practice of yoga being described.
Because that very [object] becomes the range of meditation through its state as an object of cultivation, it is called "the range known as the meditation subject" (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Having mastered" means having performed the mastery of learning in such a way that the sign of learning (*uggahanimitta*) arises.
"In the range of the alms-round" means in the range consisting of the alms-round; by this, both the meditation subject and the alms-round are indicated.
He shows that "gocara" means sound.
"Here" means in the Dispensation. "Carries away" means he leads the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) by way of its continued practice;

the meaning is that he applies himself to it until his return from the alms round. "Does not bring back" means [he does not bring back] the meditation subject from the time of engaging with food until his arrival at the daytime resting place.
"He does not go back. "Therein" means among those four monks. "By obstructive states" means by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). "Even earlier" means at the very break of dawn.
"Body-care" refers to the grooming of the body, such as washing the face and so forth. "Two or three cross-legged postures" means two or three sessions of sitting.
Here, a "cross-legged posture" (*pallaṅka*) is the *ūrubaddhāsana* (the squatting position with the thighs bound). "Heat" refers to two or three periods of warming oneself.

It has been said: "Having devoted himself to the meditation subject" means having devoted himself to the meditation subject that serves as the root on that very day. "By way of the meditation subject alone" means by way of the meditation subject itself;

what is meant is that he does not abandon the meditation subject. By this, it is shown that he does not abandon the meditation subject that will be explained in the passage beginning with "Even a stone is insentient," or rather, that which is being cultivated according to his practice.
“Having gone” means having reached. If the meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), that itself is the means of performing service.
The words beginning with “If,” however, were spoken to show that if it is something else, it is as if no service has been performed.

Having set that aside because it is not within one’s scope, the passage beginning with “If there is a great shrine” demonstrates the absence of elaboration (*papañca*) in the meditator’s attention to the primary meditation subject.
But by another [method], it should indeed be worshipped either in that way or otherwise. "In that very same way" means exactly three times.

Because a bodily relic shrine (*sārīrikacetiya*) is more venerable than a shrine of use (*paribhogacetiya*), the phrase "having worshipped the shrine" is stated according to the sequence of prior actions.
As it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "The branches of the Bodhi tree should be removed even if they obstruct the shrine. This is the teacher’s [view].

Regarding the statement, "even by one who has reached the Bodhi-maṇḍapa," if the Bodhi-maṇḍapa were located on the alms-round path after leaving the Cetiya-maṇḍapa, that too would have to be venerated.
Thus, the phrase "having venerated the Cetiya" refers to an action occurring at a prior time according to the sequence of the path, rather than according to the sequence of relative importance.
For if it were otherwise, then even one who reaches the Bodhi-maṇḍapa first [would have to venerate it before the Cetiya].

The meaning is clearly understood as follows: after having paid homage to a shrine, one should pay homage [again] when it has been reached; even with only a bowl, that same [shrine] should be paid homage to when reached;

and neither of these two should be paid homage to when not reached. For this is an illustration of the intermediate duty (*antarāvatta*) to be performed at the place where the bowl is kept while on the path during alms-round;
it is not an illustration of the regular daily duty (*dhuvavatta*), for that duty has already been performed previously.
Therefore he said, “Having first performed the duties pertaining to the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard,” and so forth.

By the phrase, “having shown reverence as if in the very presence of the Blessed Buddha,” he demonstrates that it is appropriate to perform acts of homage even toward shrines containing the utilization of the Bodhi-tree and other relics, by means of recollecting the qualities of the Buddha.
The term “the place where [the items] were brought back” refers to the commonality of being at the base of the steps.

It is said that [they do so] after reaching an outdoor area from the courtyard of the shrine (cetiyāṅgaṇa) or the courtyard of the Bodhi tree (bodhiyaṅgaṇa), which have become the objects of joy focused on the Buddha; that is what is meant.
"Near a village" means in the vicinity of a village. The connection is: "At that time, they either ask questions or desire to hear the Dhamma.
"For the purpose of gathering people" means for the sake of supporting the great multitude with the Dhamma, thinking: "If I do not speak, who else will speak to them?"

For the purpose of inclusion. To support the statement of the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariya*), it is said: "Indeed, there is no talk on the Dhamma that is devoid of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Therefore—because the commentators say that "talk on the Dhamma must indeed be given," or because there is no talk on the Dhamma that is devoid of a meditation subject—therefore, [one should give] talk on the Dhamma.

The connection is with the word "having spoken. However, the Elder Ācariya Ānanda has stated that the connection for the word "therefore" (*tasmā*) is with the phrase "they say it must indeed be spoken.
"By way of the meditation subject itself" means by not abandoning the meditation subject one is personally maintaining;
the meaning is: having spoken a discourse on the Dhamma that is concordant with that [subject]. The same applies to the second phrase as well.
This is the method. Regarding the phrase "having expressed appreciation," here too the governing principle is "by means of the meditation subject as the primary focus.

"There" refers to the very place where he departed from the village. By the passage beginning with "the ancient bhikkhus," he strengthens the aforementioned point by showing that it was the practice of the ancients.
“By the mere act of attaining” means without making a distinction such as “familiar” or “unfamiliar,” but by the very limit of attainment;
the meaning is: by the mere coming together. “By power” means by the force of assistance. “In fear” means in fear of foreign armies and the like.
“In famine” means in a time of scarcity.
“Having spent even the last watch of the night in sitting and walking meditation,” and so forth, as described.
“While doing” means while actually performing; this use of the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is in the sense of disregard. “Kamma-born heat” is said with reference to the digestive fire (*gahaṇi*).

“Flares up” means it generates a state of warmth. For that very reason, it takes hold of the clung-to (the physical body), and sweat is released. [The practitioner] brings the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) to the path.
It does not ascend because the body is exhausted by hunger and fatigue, resulting in a lack of concentration (*samādhāna*). The rice and so forth are non-clung-to (*anupādinna*);

the lining of the stomach is clung-to (*upādinna*). For if the substance of rice and so forth were absent within the belly, the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*) would arise and seize the lining of the stomach, making it cry out, "I am hungry, give me food!
At the time of eating, however, [the fire takes] the lining of the stomach...

Having released the physical basis (*vatthu*), it takes hold [of a new one]; thus the being becomes solitary, which is why it is stated in the Commentaries that "the heat born of karma is like a shadow-demon" (*chāyārakkhaso*).
In the phrase "even before," the word "therefore" (*tasmā*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Of the cattle-herds" (*gorūpānaṃ*) means of cows, or of herds of cows;
the meaning is: "at the very moment of departing for the sake of grazing. By a method contrary to what was stated, the clung-to (*upādinnaka*)...
Having let go of what is not clung-to, he takes up [what is]. "In the midst of the meal" means in the middle of the meal;
the meaning is: as long as he has not yet eaten the meal. Therefore he said: "Having consumed food under the heading of the meditation subject.

"In the remaining places" means in those instances not included by the rice gruel. "From there" means from the eating. "Succession of arrows" refers to the non-interruption of the presence of the meditation subject.
This is a demonstration of non-interruption; the meaning is "one after another.
Just as there is no interruption in a succession of arrows proceeding one after another (poṅkhānupoṅkha), so too there is none in this establishment of the meditation subject—this is what is meant.
By the words "And such as this," etc., he shows that the attention given to the meditation subject likewise possesses purpose. "Seat" means a seat for sitting.
"One who has laid down the burden" means one who has not taken up the burden regarding the application of meditation, being one whose energy is unaroused.
"Having broken all the observances" refers to the failure to fulfill the duties of conduct.
"One whose mind is bound by the fivefold mental stakes" means a mind associated with the fivefold mental stakes and their binding. For it is said in the *Cetokhila Sutta* of the *Majjhima Āgama*:

“Of which person, monks, are the five heart-fetters not abandoned? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is doubtful of the Teacher, doubtful of the Dhamma, doubtful of the Saṅgha, doubtful of the training, and is angry toward his fellow celibates.
“Of which person, monks, are the five mental shackles not severed?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from lust for the body, not free from lust for forms, and eats until his belly is full...”
“Having eaten, he dwells devoted to the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of lying down, and the pleasure of drowsiness;
he leads the holy life aspiring for some order of gods.
This is the detailed explanation. However, the Teacher, by way of indicating a portion of the phrase, [refers] specifically to the state of mind characterized by the fivefold mental bond.
It has been explained. The state of the mind being like refuse or chaff is a "mental thorn" (*cetokhila*);
the state of binding the mind and holding it as if in a fist is a "mental fetter" (*cetaso vinibandha*). Herein, the first is by way of the fault of doubt, while the second is by way of greed;
this is the distinction between them. "Having wandered" means having roamed about. It is "empty" by way of being devoid of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Gatapaccāgatika" refers to the practice consisting of going for alms accompanied by meditation and returning [from the almsround] likewise;
it is by means of that practice. "Attakāmā" means those desiring their own welfare and happiness; the meaning is that they possess a desire for the Dhamma.
For the Dhamma is indeed welfare and happiness, as well as the cause thereof. Alternatively, because it is indistinguishable from the self (*ātman*) for the wise, [it is so called].
Because it is included within one’s own being (*attabhāva*), the Dhamma is called "self" (*atta*); those who desire or wish for that are "those who desire self" (*attakāmā*).

Now, however, the reading *atthakāmā* is seen, using the word *attha* as a synonym for welfare; its meaning is: those who desire welfare connected with the Dhamma, or those who desire the Dhamma which constitutes welfare.
"Those oppressed by debt" (*iṇaṭṭā*) means those afflicted by debt. The same applies to the other two phrases as well. "In this" (*ettha*) means in the Dispensation (*sāsana*).
A *usabha* is twenty *yaṭṭhis*; a *gāvuta* is eighty *usabhas*. "By that perception" means by such a perception of the rock;
the intention is that they go knowing, through attention to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), "We have come this far.
"It" refers to the defilement (*kilesa*). Because he did not wish to lift up his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject.
"He stands" means that the one who follows behind wishes not to overstep the standing position. "He" refers to the monk in whom defilements have arisen.
"This one" refers to the follower behind. "That" refers to the other person's knowledge. "Right there" means in the very place where he was established.
"The same method" means that the same method which was stated for standing—beginning with "this monk"—applies to sitting as well. [This applies] to those coming from behind.
"One should cultivate appropriate attention even out of fear of being deprived of one's food"—this too should be understood as included within "knowing another" itself.
"In the very first step" means in the footprint left by the foot when it was lifted with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject at the outset.
"He goes" means he proceeds. This was stated by way of an illustration, such as "like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, the resident of the Ālindaka," and so forth.
“Where has he practiced in this way before?”—this [phrase] removes such doubt.
“Crushing” means crushing rice-heads and the like in a place for threshing grain. “His” refers to the Elder; this is a term requiring two referents.
And on the day he attained Arahantship, at the end of his walking path. Having created a distraction through a lack of desire for further attainment...
Having bound [the vow] and having made his formal declaration, he announced it.

First of all, the phrase "first of all" (*paṭhamaṃ tāva*) is a figurative expression used for the sake of poetic beauty. "The Great Struggle" (*mahāpadhāna*) refers to the Blessed One’s practice of austerities;
thinking, "I shall honor in accordance with my ability this practice of austerities performed by the Lord of the World for our sake over six years," [he proceeded].
This is the meaning. For worship through practice alone is more highly praised as worship of the Teacher than is material worship.
The phrase "only while standing or walking" is stated with reference to the postures (iriyāpatha) that one must resolve upon;
it is not intended as a prohibition against sitting, which must necessarily be done at times such as eating. Indeed, by the word "only" (eva), he excludes other forms of sitting and lying down.
Regarding the phrase "turning back what has been lifted by one who is dissociated," this is said with reference to placing back exactly that foot which was lifted by one who is associated.
Having stated, "having gone near the village," he explains the meaning of that with the words beginning "the cow... and so forth. "From between the armpits" means from within the armpit;
it is said to be the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) held in the armpit. "A mouthful of water" means that which forms a water-bubble in the mouth.
"Of which lunar days (*tithi*) is it the completion? Which one?"—the meaning is that he asks about the day, such as "Is it the fifth of the fortnight, or the eighth?
and so forth. He reports [the date] because it is not to be done otherwise. For it has been said:
"I allow you, monks, for all of you to learn the counting of the fortnight," and so on.
“Having swallowed water, he announces it,” according to the method stated. *Tattha* means at the village gate. *Niṭṭhubhanaṃ* means the place for spitting out water. *Tesu* refers to those people.
He is called *cakkhumā* (possessed of vision) because he is endowed with the eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*). *Īdiso* means such as one who has well-swept the courtyard of a cetiya and so forth.
*Visuddhipavāraṇaṃ* means an invitation [to a meal] by virtue of being one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
"Having observed the streets" means that after entering the street, one should first observe the streets themselves without looking here and there.
This refers to what was said: "With graceful deportment in going forward and returning," and so forth.
To demonstrate that manner of walking, he said "And therein," etc. For indeed, it is not by speed that the ascetic practice of alms-gathering (piṇḍapātika-dhutanga) is defined.
By the phrase "Is there anything? he shows the unsuitability [of such behavior], which is like the conduct of one who is greedy for gain while traveling with speed.
"Water-cart" means a water-drawing cart; for when it reaches uneven ground, it must be kept perfectly still. "Suitable thereto" means suitable for the giving of alms.
Whatever needs to be said regarding the passages beginning with "Having established the perception of repulsiveness in food," etc., is as follows:

It will come from another. That bringing [of food] is like three similes: the lubrication of a chariot’s axle with oil, the application of ointment to a wound, and the eating of one’s own son’s flesh.
"Endowed with the eight factors" means having made it endowed with the eight factors stated in the passage beginning, "only for the maintenance of this body, for its sustenance," and so forth.
“Neither for sport,” and so forth, is a mere demonstration of prohibitions. “Fatigue from food” means fatigue arising on account of food.
“Before the meal,” etc., is stated by way of day; “the first watch,” etc., is by way of night.
Showing the meaning as the carrying away and returning of the meditation subject during going and returning, he says: “consisting of carrying away and bringing back.”

He said: "If one is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*)," this [phrase] should be connected everywhere, including in the passages beginning with "having become a son of the gods.

In that regard, the perfection of the supporting conditions for *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) consists of two incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) and a hundred thousand [aeons], along with the accumulation of the corresponding requisites of merit and knowledge;
for the chief disciples (*aggasāvaka*) of *sāvakabodhi* (disciple-enlightenment), it is one incalculable aeon.
For one hundred thousand aeons [the attainment of the Great Disciples], and for exactly one hundred thousand aeons [that of the others];

however, for the rest, there is wholesome merit conducive to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya-kusala*) produced through the support of the process of turning away (*vivaṭṭupanissaya*) in past births, without any restriction as to time.
With the words "Just as if," etc., there is the presentation of witnesses—the Elders—who were established as "foremost" (*etadagga*) in their respective positions. Therein, the Elder...

"Bāhiya of the Tattered Robe" refers to the Elder known as Bāhiya because he was born and raised in the territory of Bāhiya, and as Dārucīriya because he wore robes made of bark. That venerable one said:
"Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: 'In the seen, there shall be merely the seen; in the heard, in the sensed, in the cognized...'"
‘In what is cognized, there will be only the cognized’—thus, Bāhiya, should you train yourself.

When, Bāhiya, in what is seen there will be only the seen, in what is heard, in what is sensed, and in what is cognized there will be only the cognized, then, Bāhiya, you will not be [defined] by that.
When, Bāhiya, you are not [defined] by that, then, Bāhiya, you will not be there. When, Bāhiya...
"There is no more for you there; therefore, Bāhiya, neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two—this is the end of suffering.
By this much of a teaching, he realized arhatship. In this same way, the sūtra passages illustrating the great wisdom and other qualities of the Elder Sāriputta and others should be stated in detail.
Specifically, however, these are the *etadagga* (foremost) sūtra passages found in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
“Reached the peak” (*sikhāppatta*) means reached the summit, having attained the ultimate end because it is complete in every respect.
“That” refers to non-delusion. “In this way” means it should be understood in the manner now being described.
By the phrase “the self advances,” there is the grasping of a view; by the phrase “I advance,” there is the grasping of conceit. However, of both of these...

Because it does not proceed without craving, the phrase "by way of grasping through craving" shows the confusion of the blind, foolish worldling during his forward movement due to all three types of conceiving (*maññanā*).
Having stated, "not being thus confused," he spoke the words beginning with "I am moving forward" in order to show that very non-confusion which arises through the resolution of the compact mass.
[This refers to] the wind element originated by mind (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-vāyodhātu*).
It arises originating from that very mind of advancing, or it is the air element originated by that mind.
"Intimation" refers to bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). It arises while producing [that intimation] because it is the state of its modification. "Thus" means therefore, because of its arising.
"By way of the diffusion of the air element produced by the functional mind" means by way of the bodily intimation, which is the mode of movement of the air element originated by the functional mind.
"Of that" means of the skeletal frame. "As he steps forward" means as he is stepping forward. "Inferior" means lowly or of poor quality.
By way of the air element and the fire element, the other two elements [are implied].
This is what is meant: because here the fire element, which is accompanied by the air element, is the condition for lifting up.
For the fire element has the function of lifting up; therefore, when there is lifting up by it, the air element possesses the state of being concomitant with it.
Thus, between these two, there is intensity here by virtue of their functional capacity, while the others are weak due to the absence of such [capacity].
Furthermore, because the air element, which is concomitant with the fire element, is the condition for drawing back and pushing forward.
For the air element, which is characterized by functional activity, possesses an especially prominent function in the acts of drawing in and sending forth;
therefore, the fire element follows along with it in those instances.

Thus, by the phrase "likewise in drawing in and sending forth," he shows that these two [air and fire] are predominant here due to their capacity, while the others are subordinate because they lack such capacity.

Furthermore, although there is a distinction here between the pursuer and the pursued, the term "thus" (*tathā*) is employed with reference merely to the state of being the fire element and the air element.
For in the first method, the fire element is the pursuer and the air element is the pursued;
in the second, however, the air element is the pursuer and the fire element is the pursued. In that regard, from the place where it has stepped...
Lifting up the foot is *uddharaṇa*; carrying it forward after passing the place where it was standing is *atiharaṇa*.
Carrying it sideways for the purpose of avoiding stumps and the like, or for the purpose of avoiding contact with the foot already placed on the ground, is *vītiharaṇa*.
Carrying it as far as the foot is placed down is *atiharaṇa*; carrying it beyond that point is *vītiharaṇa*.
Or this is the distinction between them:
because the water element, which follows upon the earth element, is the condition for discharging. For the water element has the nature of being heavier;
therefore, in its discharge, there is a state of following upon the earth element. Thus, of these two here—
Showing that there is intensity due to its functional capacity (*sāmatthiya*), and that there is meagerness in the others because they lack that capacity, he says: "In the act of releasing...

[they are] powerful. Furthermore, since the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) accompanying the water element (*āpodhātu*) is the condition for depositing [the body], and because its function is preeminent not only in providing a foundation but also in establishing [the body] upon it, the earth element is said to be "accompanied" by the water element.
Likewise, because the completion of the cessation through the action of striking occurs by way of the earth element, the water element also persists during that cessation;

therefore it is said, "likewise in the placing and the cessation. Although there is a distinction between the persisting agent and the object to be persisted upon, the word "likewise" (tathā) is employed with reference merely to the status of being the earth element and the water element respectively.
It is said. For in the first method, it is the earth element that follows and the water element that is followed;
but in the second, it is the water element that follows and the earth element that is followed.
Herein, "releasing" refers to the lowering of the foot, while "placing down" refers to setting it down upon the ground or other surfaces after having lowered it. Having set it down...
The cessation and stopping of the movement by way of its suppression is "stopping" (*sannirujjhanam*).
"Therein" means in that act of crossing over, or in those six factors already mentioned, namely: lifting up, carrying across, shifting across, letting go, placing down, and stopping.
"In lifting up" means at the moment of lifting up. "Material and immaterial phenomena" refers to those occurring in the mode of lifting up.
Material phenomena and the immaterial phenomena that originate them do not reach across [to another place], because they exist for only a moment.
This principle applies everywhere. "Right there, right there" means wherever they arise—whether in lifting or any other such action—it is precisely there.
For there is no movement of phenomena from one location to another, due to their extremely rapid transformation. "Joint by joint."
"Each section, each section. "The joints, the joints," [meaning] "the knots, the knots. "The divisions, the divisions," [meaning] "each part.
All of this should be understood as stated with reference to the homogeneous continuity (*sabhāga-santati*) regarding sections such as the extraction (*uddharaṇa*).

For it is precisely for other material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) as well that the moment of occurrence (*pavatti-khaṇa*) is the "going" (*gamana*), the "yoking to going" (*gamana-yoga*), and the "delight in going" (*gamana-ssāda*) of the sons of the gods.
Even faster than the meeting of the hooves of horses galloping head-on from above and below, as their heads and feet collide;

and just as the breaking of sesame seeds is characterized by the crackling sound they make when being crushed, so too is the arising of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) indicated for the sake of demonstration—
thus it is said, "crackling" (*paṭapaṭāyantā*), even though they do not actually produce a crackling sound by way of their arising.

The meaning is "while acting. For just as the characteristic of breaking sesame seeds is the sound *paṭapaṭāyana*, so too is arising the characteristic of breaking conditioned things (*saṅkhata*), because that which has arisen is entirely distinct [from its cause]. "Therein" means in the act of advancing. Who is it that alone advances? None at all advances.

Or for whom would there be the act of advancing for one who is alone? It would not exist at all. Why? Because, in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), [there is no self, but only] the elements (*dhātu*).
“Lying down”; this is the meaning. For this statement is intended for the blind, foolish worldling who is deluded, to show his own advancing and retreating.
Alternatively, in response to the challenge, “Who is it alone... advancing?,” the justification beginning with “In the ultimate sense, however... was stated.
“In each respective part” means in each of the sixfold parts as previously described, because walking and so forth are not found therein.
The phrase “it arises and ceases together with form” (*saddhiṃ rūpena uppajjate, nirujjhatī*) is connected with this verse-line.
Regarding that, in connection with the first clause, “with form” (*rūpena*) means with whatever form arises simultaneously [with the consciousness].

In connection with the second clause, however, the term “with form” refers to that which has arisen at the moment of arising of the seventeenth consciousness subsequent to the consciousness that is then ceasing.

This was said with reference to that materiality (*rūpa*) which ceases together with the cessation of that very consciousness as it is ceasing, and which has a lifespan of seventeen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*). Otherwise, material and immaterial phenomena would have to be of equal lifespan.
And if they were so, then [it would contradict] such statements from the Commentaries as, "Materiality is heavy in its transformation and slow in its cessation," and, "O monks, I do not see..."
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as: "I see even a single dhamma that changes so rapidly as this: the mind.

For the mind and mental factors, having the nature of possessing an object (*sārammaṇa-sabhāva*), arise only while manifesting their respective objects—which serve as their object-condition—according to their capacity;
therefore, their cessation occurs immediately after the accomplishment of that manifestation of their own nature, unlike material phenomena (*rūpa-dhammā*).
However, they must be manifested as being without an object; thus, the accomplishment of their state of being manifested occurs through sixteen moments of consciousness.
Therefore, it is intended that material phenomena have a lifespan of seventeen consciousness-moments, including the one moment of consciousness that has already passed.

Because the specific types of consciousness, which revolve rapidly, serve merely as a condition for the conjunction [of the aggregates], and because the three aggregates possess merely the conjunction with their respective objects—
Furthermore, consciousness has a rapid transformation, whereas matter has a slow transformation due to its dependence on the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
Now, the knowledge of the various elements as they truly are belongs only to the Tathāgata;

moreover, he has stated that only material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are antecedent conditions (*purejātapaccaya*), and likewise for post-nascence conditions (*pacchājātapaccaya*). Thus, it is simply not tenable that material and immaterial phenomena could exist at the same moment.
"Therefore, the meaning here should be understood according to the method already stated"—this is what the Teacher said;
and this was said because it is easy to understand that there is a simultaneous cessation with the intimation (viññatti) that follows upon consciousness.
Thus, together with the material form that has arisen at the moment of arising of the seventeenth consciousness, preceded by the intimation, another consciousness ceases.
The meaning should be understood as follows: one consciousness ceases and another consciousness arises—thus it should be construed.

For the sequence of words is one thing, while the sequence of meanings is another. Indeed, that preceding consciousness which has arisen ceases precisely by serving as a condition—such as the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and so forth—for another consciousness arising subsequently;
it is only by having thus obtained such a condition [that it ceases].
Another consciousness also arises, and here it is different due to the distinction of its specific state.
To refute the objection that "if this were so, an interval between those two [moments] would be found," he says: "The succession of mind is continuous like the Avīci hell.
Just as no interval (vīci) is found there, so too the wise consider this to be without distinction; thus, the continuum of consciousness is a continuous succession (anu-anu-sambandho).
The meaning is that the continuum of form proceeds like the flow of water in a river, just as the current of a stream flows within a river.
The term *avīci* is a neuter noun used in the sense of "uninterruptedness.
Regarding *ālokita*, he says it is "looking forward" because it is looking (*lokita*) directly in front (*abhimukham*). It is that direction toward which one goes.
It means looking toward that [object] while standing, sitting, or lying down.
And because such looking is called *ālokita*, he says "looking at the intermediate directions" (*vilokita*) to refer to the gazing toward the directions following upon that;
it means various kinds of looking toward the left and right sides as they extend in accordance with the direction one is facing. For [the definition of] looking downward, upward, or behind is...
The terms *olokita*, *ullokita*, and *apalokita* are included [here]. "By way of suitability" means by way of what is appropriate for a recluse (*samaṇa*);
by this very phrase, it is established that the others are excluded by way of unsuitability. *Olokita* refers to looking [ahead] when performing sweeping, plastering, and so forth;
*ullokita* refers to looking upwards when removing ceiling-beams and the like; and *apalokita* refers to looking behind to avoid dangers approaching from behind and so forth.
And since there might be the possibility [of another way], he said, “Or by this,” etc., thereby showing that this is merely an illustration (*upalakkhaṇamatta*).
“One who has realized with the body” (*kāyasakkhin*) means one who has made it manifest through direct experience; the meaning is “one who has accomplished it.

For that venerable one, at the time of insight (*vipassanā*), [reflected]: “Whatever adverse state, such as lack of delight in the Teaching, I have experienced due to not guarding the doors of the sense faculties—”
Having attained this, and being filled with enthusiasm, thinking, "I shall thoroughly restrain that very [mind]," he possessed powerful moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*).

Because he had performed his duties therein, he reached the highest perfection (*ukkaṃsapāramippatto*) in the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*). For that very reason, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position, saying:
"Bhikkhus, among my disciples, the bhikkhus who guard the doors of their sense faculties, Nanda is the foremost. Regarding Nanda:
The word "kattum" (to do) is in the genitive case. By the word "iti" (thus), it means "by this looking.

The connection is made by supplying the words "ālokitavilokitassa" (of looking forward and looking around), which should be understood as "the purposefulness and suitability of looking forward and looking around. Therefore, [the mindfulness] is present even while looking forward and looking around, precisely because one does not abandon the meditation subject;

this is due to the state of clear comprehension regarding the range of movement (*gocara-sampajañña*). Thus it is said: "Because of the state of clear comprehension regarding the range of movement here..."

Regarding looking ahead and looking aside: "By means of one's own meditation subject alone" means that looking ahead and looking aside should be done by means of the meditation subjects such as the aggregates;
the intention is that no other method should be sought. "By way of the meditation subject itself" means precisely by way of the meditation subject that will be explained below.
Since looking ahead and so forth are merely specific modes of occurrence of a mere phenomenon (*dhammamatta*), therefore, knowing them as they truly are—
In order to show "clear comprehension of non-delusion," the words beginning with "within" are stated.
"Looking forward" means looking ahead; likewise for "looking around. "Intimation" refers to bodily intimation. "Thus" means because it arises from that [intention].

"By way of the diffusion of the air-element produced by functional consciousness" means by way of bodily intimation, which is defined as the mode of movement of the air-element originated by functional consciousness. "The eyelid" [is mentioned].
