The eye-lid. "Sinks down" means it goes downward as if sinking. "Leaps upward" means it goes upward as if leaping.
"By means of a mechanism" refers to the rotating wheel that holds the ropes attached to the eye-lids.
"Thence" means from the sinking and leaping of the eye-lids in that manner. This is the thorough understanding of the primary cause of the impulsion consciousness associated with the mind-door.

Fundamental full understanding (*mūlapariññā*). "The state of being adventitious and temporary" (*āgantukatāvakālikabhāva*) refers to the condition of that which has arrived as a guest and exists for only a brief moment; it is by way of these two.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means among those seven types of consciousness shown in the verse. "Accomplishing the function of its factors" (*aṅgakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ*) refers to accomplishing the primary function of its constituent factors.
"Producing" means "becoming the body"; this is what is intended. For the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is the primary factor because it resembles the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi*);
and that which is primary is called the "body. Alternatively, the meaning is that it accomplishes the function of the cause by being the basis for uninterrupted occurrence.
"Having turned back that" is stated by way of the general nature of the life-continuum; however, by way of the specific mode of its occurrence—
It is threefold by way of the past and so forth; and therein, there is only the turning back toward the cutting off of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).

"Because of its cessation" means because of its ceasing; this is a statement of cause by way of the condition of immediate proximity (*anantara-paccaya*). The passage beginning with "In the first impulsion... up to...
in the seventh impulsion" refers to the absence of lust, hatred, and delusion—such as "this is a woman" or "this is a man"—within the cognitive process of the five doors.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For in that context, because [the process] proceeds by way of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) occurring prior to the adverting (*āvajjana*) and determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) moments—functioning through the mode of improper adverting and determining—a mere impulsion (*javana*) accompanied by greed arises toward a desirable object such as a woman’s form, and a mere impulsion accompanied by hatred arises toward an undesirable object;
however, there is no intermittent arising of joy or displeasure, etc., at the mind-door (*manodvāra*).

In this way, there is lust, hatred, and so forth, occurring at intervals; however, for that lust, hatred, and so forth belonging to the mind-door, the root is the five-door javana, or rather, all [states] such as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as previously described.
Thus, "root-full-understanding" (mūlapariññā) is stated with reference to the root cause of mind-door javana;
whereas "guest-nature" (āgantukatā) and "temporary nature" (tāvakālikatā), however, belong specifically to five-door javana by virtue of its not having existed previously.
And by way of brevity. "In the arena of battle" means in the place of combat.
"By way of upper and lower" means by way of revolving above and below; the meaning is, by way of the successive arising of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
For their breaking and falling occurs by way of the production of the life-continuum; however, by this [phrase], it refers to the successive arising of the lower and upper life-continuums.
This shows the arising of the mind-door javana, which is distinct from the five-door javanas, because it is precisely by means of that [mind-door javana] that passion and so forth proceed.
For this very reason, it is said: "Looking ahead and looking around occur by way of passion and so forth.
"Come into range" (*āpātha*) means the state of being an object. "By way of accomplishing its own function" means by way of accomplishing functions such as adverting (*āvajjana*).

That is the impulsion (javana). Because adverting and the other [mental states] proceed due to the coming into the range of the visible form at the eye-door, it is said to be "become a house" by way of being the cause for their occurrence, not by way of being their support (nissaya). "Like a guest" means like a person who has newly arrived.
For there are two kinds of guests: by way of a regular visitor (atithi) and a person who has newly arrived (abbhāgata). Among these, one who is already familiar is called a "regular visitor."
"One who has not yet cultivated familiarity" means "one who has newly arrived"; this is what is intended here. Therefore he said, "Just as in another's house," and so forth.

The connection is that for that [consciousness], namely the impulsion (*javana*), it is improper to be stained by passion, hatred, or delusion. "While they are seated" means while they are sitting. "Issuing commands" means exercising one's own authority.
"Together with" means together with the associated states such as contact (*phassa*) and the rest. "Right there, right there" means in the very place where its own function is to be accomplished.
They break up. "Thus" (*iti*) means therefore, because they break up starting from the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) and ending with the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*).
"Momentary" (*ittarāni*) means having a short duration. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that statement; the sense is: "this is the simile.
"Of such brief duration" (*tāvakālikāni*) means those whose time is delimited by arising and passing away; the state of being so is "momentariness," and it is by way of that [state].
This is non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*). "In this" means in this aforementioned collection of phenomena. "Seeing" refers to eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*);

because it is by means of that alone that there is looking forward, looking around, and cognizing, advertence (*āvajjana*) and the other [mental factors] are not included. "In the assembly" means in the harmony [of the factors]. "Therein" means while looking forward, looking around, and cognizing by way of the five aggregates.
This locative case is used in the sense of a cause; for who else, apart from that [consciousness], could look? None at all looks. And who...
“Eko viloketi natveva viloketī” means that he does not look about.
The phrase beginning with “tathā” refers to the seeing [of objects] by way of the sense bases (āyatana) and by way of the elements (dhātu).

Just as the eye and visible forms are respectively the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) and the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for seeing, so too is adverting (āvajjanā) the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya), and light is the decisive-support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

The conditionality for seeing (*dassana*) has been stated according to the method of the Suttas by way of a figurative exposition (*pariyāya*). The co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) also belongs to seeing alone;
and this is merely an illustration, since other conditions such as mutuality (*aññamañña*), association (*sampayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*) are also applicable.
Furthermore, the reading "co-nascent and other conditions" (*sahajātādipaccayā*) is now seen in the text. The words "In this way," etc., constitute the conclusion.
Now, in order to clarify full awareness regarding the bending and stretching of limbs according to the text, he says: "In bending and stretching," and so forth.

Therein, "of the joints" (*pabbānam*) means of those things that have become joints. For it is by the very bending and stretching of those [joints] that the bending and stretching of all the hands and feet occurs.

Alternatively, they are "joints" (*pabbā*) because they possess joints (*pabbavante*), just as one is called "faithful" (*saddho*) because one possesses faith (*saddhā*); thus, it means "of those possessing joints."
"Meaning. "By means of the mind alone" means either by the inclination of the mind or by the capacity of the mind.
Whatever thought arises—whether for a purpose or for no purpose—to bend or to stretch, it is said that one performs that bending or stretching only in accordance with that very thought.
The connection here is that within those acts of bending and stretching, the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful should be understood.
“Moment by moment” is a statement regarding the desire for analysis of the moment of presence (*ṭhitakkhaṇa*).

“Feeling” (*vedanā*) refers to the state of being afflicted by stiffness and so forth. By the passage beginning “feeling arises,” he shows the successive causal sequence; likewise by the passage beginning “those feelings do not arise.
For each preceding term is a statement of the cause for each succeeding one. “In time” means in order to contract or to extend.
Or at the appropriate time. "Phāti" means growth. However, the specific distinctions are the jhānas and so forth.
In this context, the "method" (naya) refers to the method consisting in the demonstration of the basis for discerning what is suitable and what is unsuitable.
Since the benefit in discerning those [qualities] is clarified by seeing the disadvantage in not discerning them, these [examples] should be understood as illustrations here.
"In the courtyard of the Mahācetiya" means in the courtyard of the Great Shrine named Hemamālī, which was built by King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī. For it is said:
"The Elder who inspires confidence in the Island, to my royal grandfather, [said]:
'Thus indeed, O grandson, will King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī speak.'"
"In the future, one of great merit will cause to be built the Great Thūpa, beautiful with golden garlands, delightful to the mind, and two hundred cubits high.

Here, the term *bhūmippadeso* (a portion of ground) refers to the courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*), as in such passages as "he found mud there in the courtyard" (*udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avindum*); therefore, it refers to the area surrounding [the stupa].
The meaning is: "in a well-prepared location on the earth. For that very reason, he became a householder;
having become disenchanted due to the cause of engaging in physical contact, he returned to the lower life. "A meditator" means he attained the state of burning away [defilements] through meditation.
It is said, "on the pegs of the robe-hut," because they had built a robe-hut in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya and were reciting there. Regarding the robe-hut...
The meaning is: "a handle made for the purpose of covering a robe. Regarding this, the Elder Ācariya Ānanda and the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla have stated:
"They say that what is called a 'jewel-serpent' is a certain species of snake found on the island of Siṃhala.
Furthermore, by not saying "some," "others," or "another [group]," but simply using the word "they say" (*vadanti*), it is intended to indicate that one should grasp the statement as being essential.
Because it does not speak of what should be understood otherwise, therefore "blue snake" and so forth should not be understood here as "jewel-snake.
"By means of the story of the Great Elder" means by means of the story of the elder of that name.
"By the pupils" means by one pupil among the many pupils sitting there; thus he said, "The pupils questioned him. "Meditation subject" (kammaṭṭhāna).
The meditation subject on the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*), which will be explained in the manner beginning with “the self within,” etc., is understood from the context as well.
In that regard, the plural form “by you” (*tumhehi*) is used again for the purpose of including those who are standing there and asking the question.
Thus, “one whose nature is such” (*evarūpo*) refers to one whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is form (*rūpa*), by way of the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra).

The meaning is: "by way of the nature of attention to the meditation subject. "In this case too" (*evametthāpi*)—by means of the word *api* (also)—he includes the looking ahead and looking around mentioned below.
This method applies further on as well.
"By way of pulling a thread" (*suttākaḍḍhanavasena*) means by way of drawing in the threads attached to a machine. "Of a wooden machine" (*dāruyantassa*) means of [a machine] made of wood.
Of a mechanical form (*yantarūpa*). It goes to, that is, reaches, various actions;

or, assuming various shapes with its hands, feet, and so forth, it goes—that is, moves—thus it is a "machine" (*yantra*), such as the puppet-forms of actors and the like, or likewise a machine made of wood.
And this is merely an illustration. For indeed, because it is to be adorned with cloth and raiment, it is a "cloth-puppet" (*potthalikā*); [the word] *pañca*...
Because its limbs possess life as it were, they call it a "pañcālika" (puppet).
"Waving of hands and feet" means the trembling of the hands and feet, or the making of graceful gestures with the hands and feet.
Regarding "the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes," here there is a single mention because the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and the robes (*cīvara*) are worn together.

The meaning is as follows, according to the context: for the purpose of removing heaviness due to knots, by way of wearing the *antaravāsaka* as an undergarment, and by way of wearing the remaining robes as upper garments.
"Therein" refers to the wearing of the *saṅghāṭi* robe and the carrying of the bowl. "Of the kind described" means the various classifications stated in the Sutta by way of the method of reflection.
“For one accustomed to heat” means for one whose body has much feverish burning. “For one accustomed to cold” means for one whose body has much coldness.
“Thick” means tightly woven. “Double-layered” is mentioned merely as an illustration;
for it is said: “The outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) should be fourfold, the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) double, the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) double, and for rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*), as much as required.”
"Contrary" (*viparīta*) means contrary to both of those; it is unsuitable for all three of them. To the question "Why?", he says: "By the gift of door-bolts and so forth," and so on.
A *aggaḷa* is a piece of cloth used for fastening after being removed [from the loom]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he includes tailoring work and other such tasks.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) has the sense of drawing in [the previous point], meaning that it is indeed unsuitable. *Paṭṭuṇṇa* is cloth produced by insects in the region of *paṭṭuṇṇa*.
“Made of fine cloth” (*vākaviśeṣamaya*) refers to white-colored *dukūla* fabric. By the word “etc. (*ādi*), one includes other suitable, allowable robes such as silk (*koseyya*) and wool (*kambala*).
Why [is this said]? It is stated: “For such [a robe],” and so forth. It is said that it creates an obstacle to dwelling alone in the forest;
this refers to a portion of the obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacariya*). And it is likewise stated because it is common to thieves and others. In the primary sense, that...

The connection is with the term *asappāya* (unwholesome). By this very [statement], it is shown that what has been described as unwholesome is not absolute, because for someone at some time, wholesomeness may arise through such-and-such a condition.
However, these two [types of livelihood] are exclusively unwholesome, because there is no occasion when they are wholesome for anyone.
That by which one lives wrongly is "wrong livelihood" (*micchājīva*); it is the application of effort in seeking the requisites of life by means of improper search.
Wrong livelihood proceeds by means of hinting (*nimitta*), and so forth; by this, he refers to the twenty-onefold practice of improper search (*anesanāpayoga*).
For it is said in the commentary on the *Suttanipāta* and in the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*, in the explanation of the *Mettasutta*:
"He who, having gone forth in this Dispensation, does not apply himself rightly, is one of broken virtue (*khaṇḍasīla*), [practicing] the twenty-onefold..."
He makes his living by means of seeking [gifts]. That is to say:
the giving of bamboo, the giving of leaves, flowers, fruits, tooth-sticks, water for rinsing the mouth, bathing, bath-powder, and clay;
flattery, bean-soupery, servility, running errands on foot, medical practice, acting as a messenger, going on errands, and the collection of alms from house to house.
“Giving and further giving, the science of sites, the science of astrology, and the science of bodily marks.
However, the Elder Ācariya Ānanda, the commentator on the Abhidhamma, stated as follows:
“The twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood are: practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, and acting as a go-between.”
One lances an abscess; one applies ointment to a wound; one administers an emetic; one administers a purgative;
one cooks nasal oil; one cooks wound oil; one gives a gift of bamboo;

one gives a gift of leaves, flowers, fruits, bathing requisites, tooth-sticks, water for rinsing the mouth, powder, or clay; one performs flattery; one serves bean soup; one acts as a personal attendant.
"The twenty-second, the 'sending on an errand to the shanks' (jaṅghapesanika), is similar to the 'messenger's work' (dūtakamma); therefore, there are twenty-one.

Here, the statement from the *Aṭṭhakathā* is given according to the method of the Suttanta, such as the *Brahmajāla-sutta*, while the statement from the *Ṭīkā* follows the method of the Abhidhamma, such as the *Khuddakavatthu-vibhaṅga*.
Therefore, some say that there is a discrepancy here; this should be investigated and understood accordingly. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "sign-making and so forth" (*nimittakammādī*):
By this, the discourses on the appearance of signs (*nimittobhāsa*) have been stated. "Wrong livelihood" (*micchājīva*), however, refers to the aforementioned practice;
therefore, both the act of sign-making and wrong livelihood are included. The meaning is that what arises by way of these is unsuitable because it brings about harm through the destruction of virtue.
For even in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvanda*), the masculine gender usage is occasionally seen, as in the expression "arising of consciousness" (*cittuppāda*).
"In one who has excessive delight, lust and the like increase; and in one who has excessive aversion, hatred and the like increase. Thus he said, "unwholesome states increase.
"That" refers to both of those. "By way of not abandoning the meditation subject" means by way of not abandoning the meditation subject that will be explained.
Having shown, in brief, non-delusive clear comprehension with the words, "There is no so-called 'self' within," etc., [he says] "therein, even the robe..."
By the passage beginning with "insentient," he elucidates that point by demonstrating the body’s emptiness of self—just as he did for the robe—with the words "the body too is insentient.

It should be understood that he thereby clarifies the reason for the contentment with whatever one has, which was stated in the passage beginning with "Therefore, having obtained neither a fine robe...
For in this way, the connection should be explained as follows: while demonstrating clear comprehension through non-delusion...

He said, “‘Within’ (abbhantare),” and so forth. However, in order to illuminate that meaning by means of the manifestation of the emptiness of self (attasuññatā), he stated, “Therein, the robe,” and so forth.

Now, demonstrating the quality acquired—namely, contentment with whatever is obtained—which serves as the purpose for the manifestation of the emptiness of self, he said, “Therefore, neither beautiful,” and so forth.

Therein, "within" means within one's own continuum (*santāna*). "Therein" means in that act of donning the robe; or, it refers to those two—the robe that is the agent of donning and the robe that is to be donned.
"The body too" means even the body, which is a mere designation (*paññatti*) for the self. The word "therefore" (*tasmā*) must be supplied; the meaning is "because of its lack of volition.
"I" refers to the body as the object of the action. "Elements" (*dhātu*) refers to the external elements designated as the robe. "An aggregate of elements" refers to what is designated as the body.
The internal collection of elements (*dhātusamūha*). The connection is that, just as when a cloth-image (*potthakarūpa*) is covered, the elements cover the collection of elements.
*Pottha* means nourishing, which is the pouring of moisture, or filling; it refers to the actions of plastering and digging.
That which is made by these is a *potthaka*. Such is the form itself; here, what is intended is the form consisting of wood, clay, and so forth, produced by the work of digging.

Therefore, because they are insentient or because they are empty of a self, an anthill is a "nāgavammika" (serpent-ant-hill), being the dwelling place of serpents (*nāga*). A tree that serves as a site for veneration is a "cetiyarukkha" (shrine-tree).
These are mentioned here because they are suitable as similes for the body, which may be honored by some and yet not honored by others.

"By that" means by means of garlands, perfumes, excrement, urine, and so forth. Because of the emptiness of a self, it is said that one should not produce either joy or dejection through what is called "the body," which is like a self in the case of the Nāgavammika Cetiya tree and others.

One should accept [what is offered] only after reflecting, "Shall I receive it or not?", and by seeing the purpose in receiving it with the thought, "I shall receive it. For it is in this way that there is clear comprehension of what is purposeful; thus he says, "without taking it hastily," and so forth.
*Garupatta* means a bowl that has become excessively heavy. *Catupañcagaṇṭhika* refers to four or five knots;
for here, as in the expressions “two or three bowls” (*dvattipattā*) or “six or five words” (*chappañcavācā*), the meaning of the particle *vā* (or) acting as a separate word is predominant.
Thus, the sense is conveyed by way of an alternative: a bowl struck with four knots or struck with five knots is difficult to clean.

Because it is being grasped. One who has been struck by four or five knots is called "struck by four or five knots" (*catupañcagaṇṭhikāhato*), just as one is called "one who has kindled the fire" (*agyāhito*);
or alternatively, he is struck by four or five knots. This is a statement containing the cause for its state of being difficult to clean.
And although, according to the training rule regarding less than five repairs (*ūnapañcabandhana-sikkhāpada*), even a bowl struck by five knots may be used for consumption...
It has been stated; however, it should be understood that because it creates an obstacle merely by being difficult to clean, it is unsuitable here.
"A bowl that is difficult to wash" refers to a bowl that is naturally difficult to clean, even when scrubbed with a pumice stone.
The passage beginning with "While he is washing it... provides the reason for why both of those are unsuitable. "But a jewel-colored bowl is enticing."
By this, he shows that although it is permissible according to the method of the Vinaya, it is nevertheless unsuitable because it creates an obstacle according to the method of the Suttanta.
For in the commentaries on the Vinaya (*Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*), it is stated: "They put the bowl on a turn-stick, polish it, and cook it, thinking, 'We shall make it jewel-colored';
this is not allowed. Thus, they say that only the act of cooking itself is prohibited. So they speak.
“However, it is permissible to use a bowl of gem-like color that has been made by another and obtained.
This is because, as stated in the section on robes, “such a thing creates an obstacle for one living alone in the forest,” and also according to our own explanation:
“But what is obtained through acts such as *nimittakamma* (hinting) is entirely unallowable, as it brings about harm through the destruction of virtue.”
It should be applied as appropriate. “For one who cultivates” (*sevamānassa*) is a causal expression for the non-increase and non-decrease [of defilements].
“Within” (*abbhantare*), etc., is the brief statement. “Therein,” etc., is the detailed explanation by means of the manifestation of self-emptiness (*attasuññatā*).

“With a pair of tongs” (*saṇḍāsena*) refers to a specific kind of iron tongs used by smiths. “In the grasping of a leaf that has the color of fire” (*aggivaṇṇapattaggahaṇe*) refers to a leaf that has become the color of fire because it was burnt by fire.
Regarding "in the bowl": it is said that such a simile is appropriate for a bowl that has become a source of the feverish burning of lust and other defilements.

With the words "Moreover," etc., he demonstrates the clear comprehension of non-confusion regarding both the wearing of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭicīvara*) and the carrying of the bowl. The connection is with "a helpless person whose hands and feet have been cut off.
As for "blue flies," they are the *āsāṭika* insects; for indeed, blue flies [infest] the wounds of oxen and other animals.
The eggs produced as a cause for ruin and disaster are called *āsāṭikā*. "In the hall of the destitute" means in the hall where the destitute dwell.
"Compassionate" means full of pity. "Bandages the size of a wound" means pieces of cloth cut to the size of a wound for the purpose of covering it.
"Of some" refers to some among the many destitute people. "Thick" means stiff.

*Tattha* means "in that [attainment]"; this locative case is used in the sense of a characteristic (*bhāvalakkhaṇa*) or a cause (*nimitta*). Why was it said, "merely by covering the wound," and so forth?

In the phrases *coḷakena* (with a rag) and *kapālena* (with a bowl), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the object (*kamma*) because of its connection with the meaning, or in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Furthermore, the phrases "merely by covering the wound" and "merely by applying medicine" are qualifications.

But there is no purpose [in them] by way of adorning, experiencing, and so forth. Since the body is perpetually afflicted by the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) and the like, it is appropriate that the bowl and robe—which serve as its requisites—should be compared in this very way; thus the statement should be understood.

Because of his habit of performing the highest form of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) through subtle observation, and because he was one who practiced clear comprehension even more than those mentioned previously...
"Supreme" means one who acts with supreme clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).

Because of the connection with specific types of action regarding activities such as eating, a specific type of activity accompanied by those specific actions is understood through the very words "eating" and so forth;
thus it is said: "‘Eating’ refers to the consumption of alms-food," and so on. "The eightfold meaning" refers to the eightfold variety of specific purposes (*payojana*).

In this context, regarding the eating of alms-food and so forth, "purpose" (attha) demonstrates the eightfold motive as stated in the Sutta beginning with, "for the maintenance of this body," according to the teaching of the Elder Mahāsiva. For the Elder Mahāsiva said:
"The four factors mentioned below are indeed prohibitions, whereas the eight factors above are to be combined by way of their purpose."
He speaks thus. Therein, “only for the maintenance of this body” is one factor;
“for its sustenance” is one; “for the allaying of affliction” is one; “for the support of the holy life” is one; “so that I may ward off old feeling” is one;
“and I shall not give rise to new feeling” is one; and “and there will be for me sustenance” is one.
One [factor] is “blamelessness,” another is “easeful living,” while “the benefit of food” is merely the purpose; thus, the eight factors should be combined according to their purposes.
Otherwise, however, “not for sport” is one factor, “not for intoxication” is one, “not for beautification” is one, “not for adornment” is one, and “only as far as for this... [is the remainder].
“for the maintenance and preservation of this body” is one [benefit]; “for the cessation of affliction and for the support of the holy life” is one;
“thus I shall terminate old feelings and not give rise to new feelings” is one; “and there will be sustenance for me” is one;
but “blamelessness and a comfortable dwelling” is merely the benefit of the food itself.

The eight factors mentioned here are not intended [in this context]. Why? Because there is an absence of any purpose for them, and because they alone are expressed here by the word *attha* (meaning/purpose).

But is it not the case that, by the phrase "stated in the manner beginning with ‘not for sport’ (*nevadavāya*) etc.," the fact that the second method alone is intended here is understood through that delimiting statement?
No; for [the statement] "not for sport" and so forth is presented by way of showing the factor of prohibition (*paṭikkhepaṅga*).
Because it is taught in the text of the review (paccavekkhaṇa), it is shown as having the nature of a boundary precisely according to the sequence of the discourse as it was taught.
For it is said, "in the manner beginning with 'not for sport,'" according to the sequence of the recitation (pāṭhakkama) and not according to the sequence of the meaning (atthakkama);
however, by that [meaning-sequence], it ought to be stated as "for the maintenance of this body," and so forth.
With reference to the twofold grasping occurring when giving in three ways, it is said: "receiving is indeed [the act].

The successive processes of eating and so forth—such as the lowering of the hand for the purpose of taking food and the like, and the forming of mouthfuls for the purpose of eating—are explained by way of the air element (*vāyodhātu*) alone.
Regarding the phrase "by the expansion of the air element alone," the word "alone" (*eva*) serves to exclude other factors.
He shows this with the words beginning, “No one at all. A *kuñcikā* is a bolt or latch; it is also called a *tāḷa*. By a *yantaka* means by a wheel-mechanism.
It is called a *yantaka* because one exerts effort (*yatati*) by means of it in such actions as opening, closing, lifting up, or setting down.
The function of a pestle is to pound into fine powder. The function of a mortar is to provide a place for things to be placed inside.
The function of the hand consists in turning [the food] over by means of stirring and churning. "Iti" means "thus.

"Tattha" (in that regard) is the locative case used in the sense of the accomplishment of the hand's function, as a characteristic of a state, or as a causal sign. "Thin saliva" refers to clear saliva; "thick saliva" refers to turbid saliva.
"Turning with the tongue-hand" means turning it here and there by means of the tongue, which is designated as a "hand," through the process of stirring and churning.
*Kaṭacchu* and *dabbī* are sometimes used as synonyms; for it is said: "The word *kaṭacchu* is masculine, while *dabbī* is feminine.

However, in this context, it should be understood that the instrument by which one takes up food and so forth after having enclosed it inside is a *kaṭacchu*, whereas that by which one performs the lifting out and other such actions of those things is a *dabbī*.
A "bed of straw" (*palālasanthāra*) is a bed made of straw and the like that serves as a foundation.
This is merely an illustration. "Bearing" means receiving [the food] by way of providing a foundation.

By the phrase "it remains by means of the air element alone," it is shown that the food consumed remains in the stomach just as water supported by the earth is supported by the wind that sustains it, or as the air element itself sustains it.
For the air element pushes the food thus consumed downward.
And having formed a solid enclosure all around, both vertically and horizontally, it establishes [the food] within the stomach by means of its confinement until it is digested.
"Uddhana" refers to that place where one sets up pots and the like to cook; it is also called a "cully. "Rassadaṇḍa" means a staff.
"Patoda" means a goad-stick. The word "iti" indicates the aforementioned manner. Of that very manner already described...
For there is a manifestation according to the elements (*dhātu*). Regarding this, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla says: "It brings [food] across (*atiharati*) means it carries it up as far as the mouth;
it brings it forth (*vītiharati*) means it carries it from there, making it mixed within the stomach.
However, the Elder Ācariya Ānanda said: "It carries it from there as far as the stomach. Both of these are identical in meaning; in both cases, [the sense is the same].
This is because what is intended here is merely the act of taking [the food] into the womb.

Furthermore, "he brings it over" (*atiharati*) means he brings it while passing through the gateway of the mouth. "He brings it across" (*vītiharati*) means he brings it once it has entered the belly.
"He sustains it" (*dhāreti*) means he establishes it within the stomach (*āmāsaya*). "He turns it over" (*parivatteti*) means the turning from one side to another.
It acts [upon the food]. "Grinds" means it performs a grinding as if with a pestle. "Dries up" means it makes it not too dry.
"Extracts" means it expels what is vile from within. Regarding the functions of the earth element as well, the meaning is exactly as stated.
However, those functions—maintaining, transforming, grinding, and drying up—the food occur only when accompanied by the earth element.
The air element is able to perform its function, but not alone; therefore, those functions are also described as belonging to the earth element by way of their functional state.

"Moistens" means it makes wet. "And maintains moisture" means that it maintains the moist state so that there is no excessive drying out caused by the air element and the others, by way of preventing it from becoming too dry. "Straightway" refers to the entry, transformation, and exit of the food.
The path. "Consciousness-element" refers to the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), because it is intended here as the consciousness that knows searching, swallowing, and so forth.

"In this and that" means in each respective function such as searching, swallowing, and so on. The application (*payoga*) which serves as the condition for each respective knowing and which actually produces it is called "right application" (*sammāpayoga*).
For it is by means of that application that searching and the rest are accomplished.
Thus, even the act of knowing is said to "accomplish" [the object], because it is inseparable from it; the meaning is:

"having approached and relied upon that. "He adverts" means: by way of seeking, and by way of experiencing the swallowing, digestion, and so forth, he adverts to and cognizes those things—namely, the seeking, the swallowing, the digestion, and so on. This is because cognition is preceded by adverting.
It should be understood that "discerning" (vijānana) is also included here. Alternatively, "right application" (sammāpayoga) means right practice (sammāpaṭipatti).
Having come to that, one "turns toward" (ābhujati)—that is, attends to or discerns—by way of such [reflections] as, "There is no such thing as an 'inner self' (attā) that is an eater," and so forth.
For all the activity of consciousness is preceded by mental turning (ābhoga); thus it is said simply, "one turns toward."

"By way of going" means by way of going toward the village for almsround (*gocaragāma*) on account of the practice of begging for alms (*bhikkhācāra*). The returning is also included by this very term, because it possesses the same nature as going.

"By way of seeking" means wandering about for alms in the village for almsround. Because it possesses the same nature as seeking, approaching the refectory (*paṭikkamanasālā*) and so forth is also included by this very term.
"By way of consumption" [means] by means of the teeth and the mortar...
Because, having crushed it, at the very moment it is being turned over by the tongue, one consumes food that is utterly loathsome—
its specific qualities of color, smell, and consistency having vanished, like the vomit of a dog in a dog’s trough.
"From its receptacle" means because the food thus consumed becomes a receptacle for bile, phlegm, pus, and blood, thereby becoming a cause of supreme disgust.
It is so called because it is the fourfold seat consisting of bile and the rest, which is situated above the seat of the stomach (*āmāsayo*).

It is a "seat" (*āsaya*) because, although they occur together in one place, they remain and function without mutual confusion due to their being established by the power of karma and by way of boundaries;
for that wherein they stay and function is a "seat. Thus, it refers to the fourfold seat of bile and the rest, which is situated above the seat of the stomach. Its meaning is that of a boundary.
For this is the mode (ākāra). "As a receptacle" means as a place of storage. For that which is called the "stomach" (āmāsayo) is so termed because whatever food has been eaten remains stored there.
"Unripened" means not yet ripened by the fire born of karma, known as the digestive organ (gahaṇī), which ripens the food that has been eaten.
"Ripened" means ripened by that very same fire born of karma as previously described. "As a fruit" means...

Alternatively, the meaning is: "by way of production," that is, by way of the successive production of effects such as the corpse-like matter of head-hair and so forth, or the disease of the *daddu* (boils) and so forth, from food that is being properly digested and from food that is not being properly digested, respectively.
For it has been said: "This is its fruit. "By way of exudation" means by way of trickling out from many openings, such as the eyes and ears, hither and thither. For it has been said:
“Food, drink, hard food, and costly soft food, having entered through a single door, flow out through nine doors.
Regarding “smearing”: at the time of consumption and after consumption, [it smears] upon the hands, lips, and other parts—that is, upon the nine doors.

And it is [to be understood] as "from smearing" in every respect, according to what is appropriate. The construction is to be joined with the elliptical remainder of the text: "In all cases, the repulsiveness of food is to be reflected upon.
Furthermore, this sequence beginning with "from going" and so forth is established according to the order of the production of their respective functions.
As for "thorough smearing," although it occurs in the context of consumption and so on, it is mentioned specifically by way of its secondary consequence (nissanda).
"Repulsive" (paṭikkūla) should be understood as that which is placed last of all.
"At the proper time" means at the appropriate time; or, because it is fully cooked by the aforementioned heat, it is at the time when it has reached the state of feces and urine.
Due to the fever produced by the suppression of the natural urge, sweat is released from the entire body. For that very reason, the eyes...
They wander about and the mind is not one-pointed. Furthermore, other diseases such as sores and fistulas arise.
"All this" refers to the sweating and so forth.
"In an improper place" means in an unsuitable location, such as a field or a shrine dedicated to humans or non-humans; for in such a place...
Angry humans or non-humans may even bring about the end of one’s life for doing so.
As for "an offense," it refers to a *dukkaṭa* or *pācittiya* as appropriate for monks and nuns. "In an unsuitable place" means in a location contrary to what was stated.
To dispel the foolish notion that there is some "self" who causes the exit out of its own desire, [the text says] "the one who causes the exit. All this refers to the offense and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “without desire”: it means that by his own lack of wish or through non-application, [the excrement] emerges solely by the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*).
“Accumulated” (*sannicitā*) means existing in a state of mass. “Compressed by the force of the wind” (*vāyuvegasamuppīḷitā*) means being pressed from all sides by the force of the air-element;
this is a statement of the cause for its emergence. “Accumulated feces and urine” (*sannicitā uccārapassāvā*).

Having said this, the repetition of the words “this excrement and urine” is for the purpose of showing that the use of the masculine gender is possible even in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). For its defining characteristic is fixed as being singular.
Because it is relinquished without regard for oneself, it does not belong to oneself; nor is it given away to anyone, because it has not been formally assigned as a gift.
And because it is loathsome, it does not bring joy to another—this is the meaning. "A mere outflow from the body" means simply the trickling forth or the mere emission from the body.
Some say it is merely a benefit of the body, in the sense that it occurs when the body exists and not when it does not;
however, this is indeed improper because of the inconsistency with the illustration. For in that context, it is stated: "It is merely a matter of grooming."
The meaning is simply "merely for the purpose of cleansing. A water vessel made of bamboo tubes and so forth is a *udakatumba*.

Regarding the word "gone" (*gate*), the Elder Ācariya Ānanda stated: "Since 'going' (*gate*) means 'in going,' and since the previous mention of 'coming forward and returning' already described the shifting of the body both forward and backward while walking, here only the act of walking itself is intended. This is the view of some.

This was composed by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla. Why is this? Because the act of walking, which is restricted to the lifting of the feet, already includes the carrying of the body forward and backward that occurs during that movement, since they are inseparable;

and because [otherwise] it would contradict the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā* and other texts. For therein, the inclusion of both aspects and their distinction regarding walking are stated: [The text continues: "In both cases, walking is included... and there is a distinction..."
“And here, one posture is mentioned in two places.
It should be understood that in the passage ‘in going forward and in returning,’ it is spoken of in terms of traveling on a journey when going to and coming from the village for alms;
whereas in the passage ‘in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down,’ it is spoken of in terms of the minor postures such as shifting the feet while staying in the monastery.”

In the passage beginning with “Gates,” it is stated “while going” and so forth in order to show that there is a difference in activity according to the difference in state, but no difference in meaning.
Therefore, he says “Therefore,” etc. Therein, “in the Sutta” refers to the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta recited in both the Dīgha Nikāya and the Majjhima Nikāya;
“postures pertaining to the journey” (addhānairiyāpathā) means postures that have been maintained for a long time and have persisted over a long duration.

Because the word *addhāna* signifies a long period of time—as in such expressions as “it would be lasting for a long time (*addhaniya*)”—the postures that set in motion travel over a journey are those pertaining to a long-distance traveler.
Indeed, the word *addhāna* is a synonym for a long path, as seen in phrases like “the time for traveling a long distance.
The term “moderate” refers to those occurring by way of walking for alms and so forth, which are neither of excessive duration nor pertaining to excessively long distances.

Modes of deportment (*iriyāpathā*). "Fragmentary modes of deportment" (*cuṇṇiyairiyāpathā*) refers to those modes of deportment occurring in a monastery or elsewhere by way of turning here and there, which—due to their minor nature—have become fragmented and scattered. For in the world, even something very slight is called "fragmented and scattered" (*cuṇṇavicuṇṇa*).
There is also the reading "minor fragmentary modes of deportment" (*khuddakacuṇṇikairiyāpathā*); having become minor, they are fragmentary in the manner already described.
The meaning is "postures" (*iriyāpatha*). "Therefore" means because of thus describing the mere differentiation of postures according to the distinction of states.
"In these too" refers even to [the phrases] "when walking, when standing," and so forth. "By the method stated" means by the method stated in the passage beginning with "in advancing" (*abhikkante*).

"At a later time" means at a time subsequent to the posture of walking. "Standing" means endowed with the posture of standing. "Right there" means right there on the walking-path (*caṅkamana*). Thus it is in all cases as appropriate.

Just as with the terms for going, standing, and sitting, the sequential mention of lying down and reclining is inappropriate because, for the most part, there is no such sequence; thus, it is simply stated as "having arisen.

Furthermore, by the proximity of the word *jāgarita* ("awakened"), it is shown that here "reclining" refers specifically to falling asleep by crossing over the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), and not merely to stretching out one's back, as expressed in the phrase "of those whose activity consists of occurrence," and so forth. This is according to the rule regarding the daytime rest (*divāseyya-sikkhāpada*).
Because stretching out the back also shares the same characteristic as lying down in terms of being a posture (*iriyāpatha*), it should be understood as being included here.

*Karaṇa* means action; it refers to the functions of the body and so forth. They are called "consisting of action" (*kiriyāmayāni*) because they produce that [action], since derivative words (*taddhita*) have multiple meanings.
Alternatively, "action" refers to the function of the two types of adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*); those produced by or fashioned through that are "consisting of action. By way of adverting...
For when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is interrupted, the process-thoughts (vīthicitta) arise.
They are called "occurrent" (pavattāni) because they proceed and revolve through various modes by way of successive arising.

However, the reading "of thoughts" (cittānaṃ) found in some places should be understood as not being the ancient reading, since it contradicts the Abhidhamma commentaries and their sub-commentaries. Thus, only those consisting of functional (kiriya) states are "occurrent."
The impulsion (javana), or indeed all six-door cognitive process consciousnesses. Therefore, it is said in the *Abhidhammatīkā*:

"Because it consists of functional activity such as bodily action, and because it arises from functional adverting, it is called 'impulsion'; or rather, everything that proceeds through the six doors is termed 'proceeding by way of functional activity.
"Non-proceeding" (appavatta) should be understood to mean that which does not arise at the time of falling asleep; this is the meaning of "sutta."

For this is a statement of explicit meaning (*neyyattha*); otherwise, the occurrence of all door-freed consciousnesses (*dvāravimutta-citta*)—which arise by way of being preceded or followed by the six-door consciousnesses—would also have to be called "sustained" (*sutta*).
And if that were the case, one should understand that the occurrence of door-freed consciousnesses arising at times other than when falling asleep would also be included under "awake" (*jāgarita*).
He says, "In dependence on the lips, etc.," because sound arises in its respective location depending on the lips and so forth, which serve as the instrumental causes for the application of the mind.

Although sound arises in its appropriate place, the intention is that it arises only through such an application as the movement of the lips and so forth, and not without that application. However, some say that the phrase "in dependence on the lips, etc. is a demonstration of the locations where sound originates.

That is indeed incorrect because it is not stated as such. For a statement regarding location cannot logically occur through a grammatical construction involving a conjunction, such as "depending on the lips," and so forth. "Appropriate to that" means suitable for that word.
Because speaking is incompatible with reflection, in the case of remaining silent, it is not said that "one reflects, 'It was spoken later,'" and by this it is understood.
“The meaning is that he reflects while remaining silent.
This distinction would be appropriate if there were a difference in the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) between speaking and silence; it would not be so if there were none.
To address this inquiry, he says: “For in the occurrence of derived matter (*upādārūpa),” and so forth. Thus occurs the occurrence of the sound-base (*saddāyatana*), which is derived matter.
"Proceeding" means speaking; "non-proceeding," however, is said to mean silence.

But since, according to the doctrine of the Elder Mahāsiva, full awareness in action is understood as the seeing of the cessation right there and then of the material and immaterial phenomena that proceed in each successive posture, therefore, in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta—

This should be understood by way of the section on insight (vipassanā) characterized by non-delusion and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*), and not by way of the fourfold classification of clear comprehension;
therefore, showing that this is intended there [in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta] and not here, he says "Now this... and so forth.
"Non-delusion" (*asammoha*) is the burden, the primary factor, of which statement; thus it is "the burden of non-delusion," [referring] to that very Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

This statement contains the reason for the intended meaning of the word. However, since all four kinds of clear comprehension (sampajañña) are found here—because this teaching has as its primary purpose the demonstration of the specific fruits of recluseship—that [specific kind] is what is intended here;
thus, it was said, "In this [context], however," and so forth. "In the manner already stated" means:
[This is] in the same manner as explained regarding the "abhikkanta" [passages]. One might raise the objection:

"Is this not the detailed exposition (*niddesa*) for the summary (*uddesa*) 'endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension' (*satisampajaññena samannāgato*)? Then why is the elaboration made solely by way of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*)?

Clearing away this objection, he says: "And as one who acts with clear comprehension," and so forth. This is because the meaning must be understood precisely through the clear comprehension that is associated with mindfulness; thus...

The meaning is that "the detailed exposition has been made. By the phrase "only for one associated with mindfulness," he shows the sense that just as the predominance of clear comprehension is grasped by way of its function, so too is that of mindfulness;
it is not, however, a mere demonstration of the coexistence of mindfulness and clear comprehension. For there is never any occurrence of knowledge devoid of mindfulness.
But surely this detailed exposition is by way of clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) alone;
so why does he also resolve the objection that the meaning should be understood by way of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness? He does so by means of the statement:
"For this is the detailed exposition of the phrase 'endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension'. This is what is meant: "'Endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension'..."

Thus, because the meaning stated briefly is expanded upon, both [mindfulness and clear comprehension] are taken as being of equal weight in the exposition (niddesa) just as they were in the brief statement (uddesa).

For by this too, he demonstrates their very equality of weight through the showing of the expansion of the meaning stated briefly, since that meaning is thereby established. Now, by way of the Vibhaṅga method as well, that same meaning...

The passage beginning with "In the Vibhaṅga-pakaraṇa, however... was stated in order to establish [the point]. For by this too, he clarifies that mindfulness (*sati*) alone is predominant here, just as clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) is [predominant] elsewhere.
Therein, "these words" refers to the enumerative phrases such as "he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning.
They are "already analyzed" because, without being joined with clear comprehension, they apply to all instances through mindfulness alone.
They are indeed distinguished separately.
However, the Majjhimabhāṇakas and the Ābhidhammikas say this: one bhikkhu goes along thinking of one thing and reflecting on another;
another goes along without having relinquished his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Likewise...
One stands thinking of one thing and reflecting on another; the other stands without relinquishing his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
One sits thinking of one thing and reflecting on another; the other sits without relinquishing his meditation subject.
One lies down thinking of one thing and reflecting on another; the other...

One lies down without relinquishing the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). However, since clear comprehension of the range of activity (*gocara-sampajañña*) is not made manifest by this much alone, they illustrate it by means of walking meditation (*caṅkamana*).
For when a bhikkhu has descended to the walking path and stands at one end, he discerns:
"The material and immaterial phenomena occurring at the eastern end of the walking path do not reach the western end; right here..."
Ceased: even those mental states occurring at the western end of the walking path cease right there without reaching the eastern end;
those occurring in the middle of the walking path cease right there without reaching either end;

and the material and immaterial phenomena occurring during the walking cease right there without reaching the standing position; those occurring while standing cease when one sits; [those occurring while] sitting...
"Having occurred, it ceases right here without reaching the bed"—as he thus examines [the process], while still examining, he sinks into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga);
when rising, he rises having grasped the meditation subject. This bhikkhu is called one who acts with clear comprehension regarding going and so forth.
In this way, however, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) remains unclear in the discourse; and a meditation subject that is unclear should not be practiced.
Therefore, a bhikkhu who is able should, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, grasp the situation thus:
"The body is insentient; the bed is insentient. The body does not know, 'I am lying on the bed,' nor does the bed [know this]."
He does not know, “The body is lying on me”; the insentient body lies on the insentient bed.
While examining in this way, as soon as he is examining, he lets his mind sink into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); waking up, he wakes up having grasped the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
This one is called “one who acts with clear comprehension while asleep.”

“A monk who discerns that ‘Because it consists of that [consciousness] due to its being produced by the activities of the body and so forth, and because it arises from the activity of adverting, the impulsion (javana) is called ‘active’;

or rather, all that proceeds through the six doors is called an active process, and when that exists, there is what is called wakefulness,’ is one who acts with clear comprehension regarding wakefulness. Furthermore, [he discerns] the six divisions of the day and night...”
Even while keeping watch over the five portions [of the body] he is called one who acts with full awareness in wakefulness.

Even while teaching the Dhamma under the heading of the bases of liberation, or even while delivering appropriate discourse based on the ten topics of talk after abandoning the thirty-two kinds of frivolous conversation, he is called one who acts with full awareness in speech.

Even while directing his attention toward whichever among the thirty-eight objects of meditation suits his inclination, or even while having attained the second jhāna, he is called one who acts with full awareness in thought.
"One who acts with full awareness in silence" means this: for the second jhāna is specifically called "silence" because it is devoid of verbal formations.
This method, too, should be brought forward and explained here because it is a method of distinction from the previous one;
for in the *Abhidhamma-ṭṭhakathā* and other works, having begun with the words, "But here is another method," this very method has been elucidated exactly as stated.

“‘In this way, Great King,’ and so forth, is the conclusion of the meaning as it has been explained; therefore, demonstrating the meaning in accordance with that explanation, he says ‘In this way’ and so on.
For ‘of the clear comprehension associated with mindfulness’ is the statement of the meaning in accordance with the explanation.
The analysis of that has already been stated. By the word ‘in this way,’ [it refers to] in the manner described regarding going forward, returning, and so forth.”
The meaning is that in each of the seven instances, it is fourfold.
[In the commentary on the Discourse on Contentment:
Since the meaning is understood even from the word "seeing the benefit" (*atthadassana*), one should consider contentment within oneself without depending on the specific word.
In order to show the mere meaning—that a bhikkhu is called "content" because of [such] existence—it is said: "endowed with contentment regarding various requisites.
For the etymological derivation (*padanibbacana*) of the word is: "he is contented, he does not become greedy.

Furthermore, when the meaning has been stated by way of etymological derivation, that specific kind of contentment by whose presence within oneself one is called "contented" is not yet manifest; therefore, that...
For the sake of making it clear, he states the mere meaning as "endowed with contentment regarding this or that requisite" (*itarītarapaccayasantosa*);
the meaning is: one who has become possessed of contentment regarding any suitable requisite (*kappiyapaccaya*) such as robes and so forth.
For the word *itara* signifies indefiniteness; when stated twice, it becomes synonymous with the word "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*). Therefore it is said: "regarding whatever... [and so on].

“...regarding allowable requisites. Alternatively, one thing is called “other” because it is different from the superior; likewise, the superior is also [called other] because it is different from the inferior.

For the state of being “other” is established through mutual dependence. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: one who has become endowed with contentment regarding allowable requisites such as robes, whether they be inferior or superior.
Or, it means he is contented by that, or the mere state of being contented.
Contentment (*santoṣo*) is non-greed (*alobha*) as it occurs in that manner, or the four aggregates (*khandhā*) dominated by non-greed. Gain (*lābho*) is the act of obtaining;
contentment with gain according to what one has obtained is "contentment with whatever is gained" (*yathālābhasantoṣo*). Strength (*balaṃ*) is physical strength;

contentment with strength according to what one possesses is "contentment with whatever strength one has" (*yathābalasantoṣo*). Suitability (*sāruppaṃ*) means what is appropriate, fitting, and becoming for a monk.
Contentment appropriate to one’s own suitability is "contentment according to suitability" (*yathāsāruppasantosa*).

According to another method: that which is obtained is "gain" (*lābha*); whatever gain there is is "according to gain" (*yathālābha*), meaning the requisite of this or that; contentment by means of such gain is "contentment according to gain" (*yathālābhasantosa*).
That which occurs in accordance with one's strength is "according to strength" (*yathābala*); it refers to a requisite suitable to one's own strength.

And here, the word *yathā* expresses an appropriate action together with its instrument (*sasādhana*), just as in the term *adhicitta*, the prefix *adhi* expresses a locative action together with its instrument. Contentment according to one's strength is *yathābalasantoso*.
It is *sāruppa* because it is suitable (*sāruppati*) or because it brings about beauty (*sobhanaṃ āropeti*); whatever is suitable is *yathāsāruppa*.
"Suitable conditions for a bhikkhu" means contentment according to what is appropriate, i.e., *yathāsāruppa-santosa*.
"Exposition of the classification" (*pabhedavaṇṇanā*) is the commentary that follows the aforementioned classification.

"Here" (*idha*) means in the Dispensation (*sāsana*). "He does not long for anything else" expresses the state of not longing for what has not been attained; "even when obtaining [it], he does not take hold of it" means...

It is the absence of aspiring for what has been attained. Since the first [phrase] expresses only the absence of aspiring for what has not yet been attained, one might think that this mode of conduct—namely, not aspiring for anything other than what has already been obtained—could also be a manifestation of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*).

Therefore, because there is the possibility of such a confusion with fewness of wishes, it should be understood that the second [phrase] expresses the absence of aspiring even for what has been attained, in order to show the specific nature of contentment (*santosa*).

The same applies to what follows. "Naturally weak" (*pakatidubbalā*) means naturally frail even in the absence of illness and the like. "One who has a common portion" (*sabhāga*) refers to one whose portion consists of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth;
or, one who exists together with the portions of qualities such as virtue is "one who has a common portion. This refers to a modest and amiable monk.
"Having exchanged that" means that for those who are naturally weak and so forth, heavy robes do not bring about comfort but rather cause physical exhaustion.
The phrase "it happens" refers to the exchange [of robes] by way of purpose, not by way of excessive desire and so forth.
For if one exchanges [robes] through such modes as excessive desire, the use of light robes becomes opposed to contentment;
however, because that [excessive desire] is absent in him, even the use of light robes after exchanging them for the aforementioned purpose is not opposed to contentment.
He said: "Even one who subsists with light [robes] is indeed content. The inclusion of the word *api* (even/also) here is for the purpose of showing the intended meaning:
that even the use of light robes after having exchanged them for a specific purpose does not yet contradict contentment, let alone their use without such exchange.
This is also stated in the *Cīvaraniddesa*: "Any one of the alms-bowl, robes, etc."
The statement "according to the literal meaning" (*yathārutaṃ*) is for the purpose of showing that contentment with robes is included within contentment with all remaining requisites.

The phrase "of the elders who have long been ordained" is used here to indicate that the term "elders" (*thera*), which occurs even as a mere designation in such expressions as "this venerable Mallaka is an elder," applies here specifically to those who have been ordained for many years, starting from ten years of seniority onwards.
It is said; or, by "elders," he refers to the senior of the Saṅgha. By "those long gone forth," he means the remaining senior bhikkhus.
"From heaps of rubbish, etc. means from piles of refuse and so forth. "Rags" (*anantakāni*) means pieces of cloth or rags (*pilotikā*).
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā*: "The syllable 'a' here is merely a particle. And thus they say: "A rag (*nantaka*) is a tattered garment, a worn-out cloth."
Regarding the term *paṭaccara*: those things which have no inner border (*anta*) reckoned as a fringe (*dasā*) are called *nantaka*.

However, if the negative particle *na-* is not substituted [by *an-*], the form *anantakāni* is also appropriate. Yet, since it was not stated thus by the teachers who are experts in linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), this should be accepted after careful consideration.
There is also the reading *sanantakāni*, meaning rag-robes (*paṃsukūla*) that are stitched together with scraps (*nantaka*).
"Robes" (cīvarāni) is the meaning. "Saṅghāṭī" refers to any one of the three robes. For all three robes are called "saṅghāṭī" because they are stitched together.

Having obtained a robe of great value, or having obtained many robes and then discarding them to take others, if one does not abide by the principle of non-greed (*mahicchatā*) but instead abides by the principle of suitability (*yathāsāruppa*), [this is not a fault].
Because it is established in this way, it does not contradict contentment; thus he said: “Even while keeping them... one remains truly content.

Even the taking up of something else after setting aside what was obtained according to the method appropriate to one’s station does not yet contradict contentment, let alone the non-taking of anything else and the consumption of only what was obtained according to the method appropriate to one’s station.
This is stated here for the purpose of demonstrating the intended meaning as it is conceived.

The inclusion of the word "api" (also/even) should be understood as having the same intended meaning when it occurs in the descriptions of the remaining conditions according to their respective strength and suitability.
"Contrary to one's nature" means that which is inherently unsuitable. The search for suitable conditions is undertaken under the heading of performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
Since consuming [the food] is particularly more appropriate [for the practice], in order to indicate a different meaning,

it is said "even while performing the duty of a recluse" rather than "even while maintaining oneself. "Mixed food" refers to food prepared by mixing various kinds of staple and non-staple grains, such as rice, mung beans, and so forth.

Showing contentment with whatever lodging is appropriate, he said, "For whoever," and so forth. For in the first method, contentment with what is appropriate is stated by means of relinquishing what has been obtained;
in the second, however, it is stated by means of not accepting what has been received.
This is the distinction between them. Here, the word *hi* indicates an alternative position. [This is] from the *Madhyamāgama-ṭīkā*.

Furthermore, the word *pi* (also/even) is seen [in the text]. Having stated, "An excellent lodging is a place for negligence," the phrase beginning with "for one sitting there" was spoken in order to demonstrate that very state.

"Overcome by sleep" means: because of the state of illness in the mind and mental factors due to the onset of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), one is overcome by "sleep," which is defined as the continuity of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-santati*); that is, for one who is actually sleeping.
This is the meaning. "Awakening" means that for one awakening by means of such an object, sensual thoughts arise as the cause of that awakening;
this is what is stated. For the reading "paṭibujjhanato" (from awakening) is also seen in some places.
"This too" is said with reference to the first method.

"By what was brought by them" means by those elders and others who brought it; alternatively, the connection is made by supplying the word "belonging to" (*santaka*), as in "by whatever belonged to them.
"Muttaharītaka" refers to myrobalan fruit (*harītaka*) that has been infused with cow urine, or myrobalan that has been released—that is, discarded—due to its state of decay.
However, the reading "gomuttaharītaka" now found in manuscripts is not the ancient reading, as evidenced by its commentary.

Because of their contradiction. "The four sweets" (*catumadhura*) refers to the four sweets consisting of curd, honey, ghee, and molasses, as stated in the *Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta* of the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
The meaning is: "Having placed the four sweets in a single vessel, take whichever among them you wish, O Bhante. With the words "If it [should]...
and so forth, he demonstrates that both of those things have the quality of pacifying disease. By the Buddhas and others...
"Praised" means commended by the Perfectly Enlightened One and others through such statements as, "The going forth is dependent upon medicine consisting of fermented urine.
He is "supremely contented" because he is satisfied with the highest degree of excellence in contentment, owing to his being directed toward contentment distinguished by fewness of desires.
And although there are indeed more than the aforementioned twenty kinds of contentment regarding robes and twenty regarding almsfood—[which are] divisions of contentment—...
There are fifteen [types] regarding robes, fifteen regarding lodgings, and twenty regarding medicinal requisites for the sick; however, here only twelve kinds of contentment are stated in brief.
But the further subdivisions beyond that should be understood from the commentary on the *Mahāariyavaṃsa-sutta* in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
Therefore he said, "By this, however," and so forth. Thus: "In this case, O Great King, a bhikkhu is content."

Here, having shown the various types of contentment by means of the term "contented" itself as explained with reference to the individual (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), [the author] now shows, in accordance with the teaching,

the various types of requisites suitable for one who is contented through that contentment— namely, the robes that suffice for the body and the alms-food that suffices for the belly— as well as their state of being sufficient for the body and the belly.

"Explaining [this], he says thus"—this is the connection here. Granted, his contentment with robes and alms-food respectively, which serve to maintain the body and the belly, has been stated in the text;

nevertheless, it is improper to wander about without the other four requisites, and since the state of maintaining the body and the belly is to be found in all of them, [the commentary] explains it in the Aṭṭhakathā.

It should be understood that this explanation has been stated. "One who uses a tooth-stick chopper" is merely a characteristic description, since other duties are also to be accomplished by means of it;
therefore, he will say: "and at the time of arranging the parts and legs of beds and chairs, robes, huts, and staffs," and so forth.
And this has also been stated in the ancient commentaries: "For this does not appear anywhere in the Canon (Pāḷi)."

"Bandhana" means a waist-band. "With a water-strainer" (*parissāvanena*) means with a water-strainer, or alternatively, it means "together with that. "Yuttayoga" refers to one for whom there is application (*yoga*)—consisting of the cultivation of the meditation subject—or to whom application is appropriate;
[the text says] "of him. "Kāyaparihāriyā" means those which maintain and nourish the body, or those whose purpose is the maintenance and mere nourishment of the body;
here, the letter *ka* is changed to *ya*. In this context, "nourishment" (*posana*) means growth or sustenance. The same applies to "kucchiparihāriyā" (those that maintain the belly).

"In this manner, it is 'beneficial to the body' (kāyaparihāriya) according to the method already stated"—this indicates the reason; therefore, "it is beneficial to the body because it nourishes [the body].

"At the time of plastering the perimeter of the hut" means at the time of smearing and smoothing the ground all around the hut.
*Aṅga* refers to a specific accessory for the bed or chair placed upon its legs, where one constructs a foot-rest, a backrest, and so forth; it is also called *aṭanī*.

It is taken up by the passage beginning with "So hi" (for he...).

By means of that very [passage], through the suitability of the Pāḷi text beginning with "With robes sufficient for the body," it is understood that his state of desiring [them] is established on account of his having departed in such a manner. For by showing the causal status of that which is to be expressed, the causal status of the expressive word itself is also shown.
And having done so, the phrase beginning with "Thus, of this one" is also an expression of the qualities already obtained.
It is appropriate. "One whose livelihood is light" means *sallahukavutti*; the state of being such is *sallahukavuttitā*, which [is what is meant].
By the phrase "by means of merely maintaining the body," he shows that this is an expression emphasizing the state (*bhāva*) or an expression omitting the state;
the meaning is "by the measure required for the nourishment of the body. Likewise, [it applies] by "maintaining the belly."

In this case as well. Here, the meaning of the word is twofold according to the method already stated; however, since the first meaning was explained previously in the *Ṭīkā*, it should be understood that only the second is presented here.
"Attachment" (*āsango*) refers to the craving for "mine-making" (*mamāyanatā*). "Bondage" (*bandho*) refers to the craving for "possessiveness" (*pariggaha*).

"Released from the bowstring" means released from the bowstring of a war-chariot. "From the herd" means from a troop of elephants. "An elephant in rut with threefold-flowing ichor" refers to a rutting elephant whose temporal secretions flow in three ways.
"Vanapabbhāraṃ" means a mountain slope in the forest.
It is "four-faced" (catuddiso) because it has four directions which serve as places for dwelling in happiness due to the pleasantness of the four quarters,
or because they serve as the bases for the pervasion of the development of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) according to the method beginning with "having pervaded one direction."

"Cātuddiso" means one who is the same toward the four directions (*catasso vā disā catuddisaṃ*); it is "cātuddiso" because he is thus according to the method already stated, just as [one is called] "faithful" (*saddho*).
He is "non-reactive" (*appaṭigho*) because he does not resist any beings or conditioned phenomena in those very directions with fear, nor is he himself resisted by them.
"Being content" means being content with what is one's own, or with what is peaceful, or being simply equanimous.
Or "one who is content. "By this or that" means by whatever condition, whether high or low.
They lie around or move about, and body and mind; or they surround and overcome them—thus they are "dangers" (*parissaya*).

These include external ones such as lions and tigers, and internal afflictions of body and mind such as sensual desire and the like. And here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
"Sahita" means one who is patient through the patience of acceptance (*adhivāsanakhanti*) and, as appropriate, through the qualities such as energy (*vīriya*), and who is a grasper;

this is the meaning. "Fearless" (*achambhī*) means being without the fear that causes rigidity. "One should wander alone" (*eko care*) means that one should be able to wander or dwell as a companionless solitary.
For the suffix *-eyya* is used in the sense of capability, as in the *Khaggavisāṇasutta*: "Who could unravel this tangle? [implying one capable of doing so].
By the phrase "like the horn of a rhinoceros," he shows that he dwells alone.

A *khagga* is that which has a single horn rising from its head, resembling a rhinoceros in shape—since the word *khagga* refers to a horn similar to that [of a rhinoceros]—referring to a specific type of wild animal the size of a buffalo, which is called "palāsāda" or "gaṇṭhaka" in the world; [the term refers to him] by way of its horn.
The meaning is "similar by way of being one. Furthermore, it is stated thus also to show that he is "like the rhinoceros horn" because of his solitary dwelling.
The detailed meaning of this, however, should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta* and in the *Cūḷaniddesa*.
"Thus praised" means that it was revealed through such a teaching, or extolled, by the Blessed One in the *Khaggavisāṇa-sutta*.
The phrase "like the horn of a rhinoceros" means it is similar to the horn of a rhinoceros-like deer.
Here, the word *kappa* functions in the sense of a resemblance (*paṭibhāga*), as in such passages as, "Indeed, sir, they were deliberating with a disciple who was like the Teacher.
Its state is "rhinoceros-horn-likeness" (*khaggavisāṇakappatā*). The connection [of the sentence] is: "he attains that."
A bird might have its wings broken by the impact of wind or other causes, or its wings might not yet have grown; however, here it is one possessing wings who is capable of flying that is intended.

To show this distinction, the text says "a winged bird," rather than for the sake of showing a mere synonym, as in such passages as "he walks in the sky, in the atmosphere. Thus he said: "possessing wings."

“A bird. “Flies up” means it flies upward, goes up; the sense is that it leaps forth. “Shaking” means rending asunder or causing to waver. “For today” means for the sake of the present day. The same applies here to “for tomorrow.
One whose own acquisitions (*patta*) are his burden is “one who has the burden of acquisitions” (*sapattabhāra*).
He is “unattached” by way of the craving of self-identification (*mamāyana-taṇhā*); [he is] by way of the craving of possessiveness (*pariggaha-taṇhā*).
"Without expectation. "Wherever one’s desire" means wherever one’s own preference lies; or this is a gerundive (bhāvanapuṃsaka).
For "yena kāma" means that by which desire proceeds, and thus "yathākāma" is the meaning.

216. Having raised the inquiry with the intention of asking, "What is the purpose of stating again, in summary, the fourfold set of meanings already explained previously?
he clarifies it with the words, "He... pe ... what does this show? and so forth. "Perfection of conditions" means the fulfillment of the necessary requisites.
"These four" refers to the four previously mentioned: restraint of virtue, restraint of the sense faculties, clear comprehension, and contentment.
The requisites for one living in the forest. "It does not succeed" means it does not come to pass, it does not bear fruit.
He shows that it is not merely a failure to succeed, but rather that this too is a fault, by saying "by animals," and so forth. "One incurs censure" means:
"The dwelling of such-and-such a bhikkhu in the forest is merely like that of animals or forest-rangers."
However, one might fall into the position of speaking by way of censure, thinking, "There is no right practice whatsoever suitable for dwelling in the forest";
yet, because this would contradict the intended meaning [of the text], it should be understood that the word *saddhiṃ* (together with) is not archaic [in this context].
Alternatively, it may refer to practicing wrongly together with wild animals living in the forest, or with people of a different class who roam the woods.
