It attains the state of being something that should be inhabited. For in such passages as, "Monks, one should not dwell in the forest with a formal resolve; whoever should so dwell, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," the word *vatthabba* is a synonym for "should be lived in.
Thus it is also stated in the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*: "For the dwelling in such a forest is similar to the dwelling in a wilderness inhabited by black monkeys, bears, leopards, and wild deer."
"Are they present? means "they are dwelling there. It has been stated by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta that they first cause a terrifying sound to be heard;
at that point, for one who does not flee, they even strike him on the head with their hands and make gestures to drive him away.

Having thus demonstrated how the perfection of conditions is shown through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he now demonstrates it through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
The passage beginning with “yassa panete” has been stated. To explain how this succeeds, he says “so hi,” and so forth.
“Kāḷaka-tilaka” is a synonymous term used elsewhere for a disease that causes a change in complexion. For it is said: “Dunnāmaka, arisa, chaddika, and vamathu.”
“Davathu, paritāpo, and also tilaka and tilakāḷaka. It is called *tilaka* because it arises shaped like a sesame seed;

it is called *kāḷaka* because it arises having become black. Here, however, the grave offense (*thullavajja*)—which consists of the transgression of the rules of discipline—is called *kāḷaka* because it resembles something black;
the minor offense (*aṇumattavajja*)—which consists of the transgression of wrong conduct—is [called *tilaka*] because it resembles a sesame seed.

This is the distinction: "tilakanti" (they mark). "Taṃ" refers to that joy (*pīti*) thus produced. "Comprehension by way of dissolution" (*khayavaya-sammasana*) is so called because it appears through the state of disappearance;
for "dissolution" (*khaya*) itself is "vanished" (*vigata*) in the sense of passing away, or it is called "falling away" (*vaya*) in the sense of going (*ayana*) in a contrary manner.
"The noble plane" (*ariyabhūmi*) is the supramundane plane (*lokuttarabhūmi*). "Iti" (thus) is used because of the ascending to the noble plane and because of the praising of the deities.
Alternatively, it means that having heard the words of deities here and there, his fame has spread;
and by taking it thus, the "spreading of ill-repute" mentioned below should also be understood as being due to the reporting of matters to deities.
Regarding the word *vivitta*, he says "empty" (*suñña*) in the sense of seclusion from people; that, moreover, should be understood by the absence of the sound of people's voices.
To show that [the place] is "a thorn to jhāna" because of noise, it is said: "the meaning is 'little sound, little noise.
For here, by the mention of the "producer" (janaka), the "produced" (jañña) is also included. Thus it is stated in the Vibhaṅga:
"That which is 'little noise' is itself 'free from the breath of people'. And "little sound" refers to the absence of ordinary sounds; "little noise" refers to...

The absence of sounds such as the clamor of a city. For regarding such cases, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathās* that while the phrasing (*byañjana*) appears to be incomplete, the meaning (*attha*) is exhaustive.
However, in his commentary on the *Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla said this:
"It was stated that 'the phrasing might be incomplete' with reference to the sense of 'limited' (*paritta*) applied to 'little sound' (*appasadda*)."

Therefore he said, "For not of that," and so forth. Furthermore, it can be understood here that the word *appa* (little) has the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*), as in such passages as, "I perceive freedom from illness" (*appābādhataṃ*).
Correlating this meaning with the text of the *Vibhaṅga*, he said, "This very same," and so forth.
And the phrase "this very same" means precisely the soundlessness (*nissaddataṃ*) being described by me. "Even nearby" refers to villages and the like.
"Even nearby, such a place is called secluded," let alone far away—this is the meaning. "Unfrequented" (*anākiṇṇa*) means not crowded, not congested.

When there is a mountain thicket, a forest thicket, or a river thicket extending for a *gāvuta* or even half a *yojana* all around a lodging, such that no one is able to approach it at an improper time, this is called "unfrequented" even though it is near. "He lies down" (*seti*)...

*Sayati* means "he sits" (*āsati*). By the word *ettha*, he shows that the words *sena* and *āsana* have the sense of a locus (the locative case), and by the particle *ca*, he shows that these two words form a compound in the sense of the fourth case (the dative). With the words "Therefore it was said," etc., he cites the text of the *Vibhaṅga* itself.
Now, in order to clarify the meaning of that very passage by way of showing the different types of lodgings (*senāsana*), the words beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) were spoken.
This classification refers specifically to the types of dwellings (*senāsana*) as they are shown in their actual form by way of illustration in the *Vibhaṅga-pāḷi*.
Among them, a *vihāra* is an entire residence enclosed by a wall. An *aḍḍhayoga* is a long palace;
some also call it a "palace shaped like a garuḷa. A *pāsāda* is a square palace. A *hammiya* is a palace with a flat roof. An *aṭṭa* is suitable for repelling rival kings.
A *catupañcabhūmaka* is a specific type of dwelling with four or five stories. A *māḷa* is a specific type of dwelling consisting of a single upper story (*kūṭa*) and possessing many corners.
According to another method: a *vihāra* is a long-faced palace (*pāsāda*). An *aḍḍhayoga* is a house with a roof covering only one side.
It is said that its wall on one side is higher while the wall on the other side is lower; therefore, it has a single roof. A *pāsāda*...
A long rectangular palace (*pāsāda*). A watchtower (*hammiya*) with a flat roof and provided with a courtyard (*caṇḍika-aṅgaṇa*). A cave (*guhā*) refers exclusively to a mountain cave.
A grotto (*leṇa*) is a mountain slope with a closed entrance. The rest is exactly as previously stated.

Regarding the term "pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*), it is described as a "branch-pavilion" (*sākhā-maṇḍapa*) by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla and by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta, the author of the *Aṅguttara-ṭīkā*.

In the *Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is explained that "vihāra" refers to a dwelling-place constructed after showing the surrounding path for circumambulation, as well as the night-quarters and day-quarters within;
"aḍḍhayoga" is a house with a curved roof like that of a garuḷa; "pāsāda" is a long palace built using two corner-brackets;
and "aṭṭa" is a structure with thick walls made of bricks for the purpose of repelling rival kings and others.
A dwelling consisting of four or five stories. A *māḷa* is a circular pavilion similar to a dining hall.
However, in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated as "a square palace comprised of a single roof.

A *leṇa* is a lodging constructed by carving into a mountain or by erecting walls in a space that cannot accommodate [a structure] on a mountain slope. A *guhā* is a natural cave in the earth where one dwells day and night.
It is said that one must obtain a lamp, or else a mountain cave or a ground cave.

That which serves as a dwelling, being a place of rest and a lodging in the sense of a place to dwell in, is called a "vihāra-senāsana" (monastery-lodging). There are four kinds of beds, beginning with the *masāraka* (wooden-framed bed).
Likewise for the stool (*pīṭha*). There are five kinds of cushions (*bhisi*), beginning with the woolen cushion (*uṇṇabhisi*). [The pillow] should be the size of the head.
A bolster: in width it is four fingerbreadths [or] a span; in length, its measure is the same as the width of the bed, and here the measure is that of the head.

The *masāraka* and so forth are "beds and chairs" (*mañcapīṭha*) by virtue of being beds and chairs themselves; the mattress (*bisi*) and pillow (*upadhāna*) are "beds and chairs" because they are connected to the beds and chairs.
For a dwelling-place that is itself a bed or chair, or one connected to a bed or chair, is designated by the common term "bed and chair."
Alternatively, by way of the *ekasesa* (single-remainder) method, it is called "bed, chair, and lodging. The Elder Ācariya Sāriputta also speaks in this very way.
However, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has stated: "Bed, chair, and lodging means both the bed and chair themselves, as well as the lodging associated with the bed and chair.
What is called a *cimilika* is [a covering] made of pieces of cloth and so forth for the purpose of preserving the color of the ground that has been treated with plaster (*sudhā*).
It is made by sewing. "A piece of hide" (*cammakhaṇḍa*) refers to any kind of hide, such as those of lions, tigers, leopards, hyenas, and so forth;
for in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), no hide is seen that is prohibited for the use of lodgings (*senāsana*).

"A layer of grass" (*tiṇasanthāra*) is a layering of any kind of grass. The same method applies to a layer of leaves (*paṇṇasanthāra*) as well. A mat of cloth (*cimilikā*) and the like may be spread upon the ground.

“Santhata-senāsana” (prepared bedding and seats): excluding these couches and so forth, whatever place the monks gather at—whether they retreat there or not—all this is called “senāsana. Thus it is said;

the remaining places such as the foot of a tree, which are to be retreated to, are “okāsa-senāsana” (open-air lodging) because they lack any artificial preparation and serve merely as a space for lying down and for relinquishment (*nissajjā*).

"By the taking up of lodgings" means: either by the taking up—that is, the physical acquisition—of a secluded lodging by means of this word "lodging" (*senāsana*), or by the verbal expression [of it];
for that which is grasped by a general designation is already established as a particular, and a particular must be employed by one who seeks a particular.
To the inquiry, "Since this is so, why is 'forest' (*arañña*) and so forth stated again?", he says, "But here, moreover... and so on.

The intention is that although the types of lodgings have been mentioned in this way, it is stated again thus because he wishes to show a lodging that is truly suitable for the bhikkhu described above.
The phrase "it has come down by way of the bhikkhunīs" means that it is indeed found in the Vinaya.

This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*), not in the Abhidhamma. For in the Vinaya, under the training rule concerning leaving the group, because the forest-dweller’s ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is prohibited for bhikkhunīs, this [distance] is what constitutes "forest" for them;
it is not the case that only a dwelling five hundred bow-lengths (*dhanus*) from the boundary is considered forest.
Furthermore, for them, even this [distance] constitutes an offense for leaving the group, but it is not only the area within five hundred bow-lengths that does so.
The forest (*arañña*). For it is said therein:

"If she should be left behind from a group, or if she should leave the range of sight or the range of hearing of her companion nun in a forest that is devoid of villages, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*; once [the range] has been left, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
Indeed, the same meaning is stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*s as well. But in the Abhidhamma, "forest" is defined as follows: "Having gone out..."

"Everything outside the threshold post is forest," so it is said. For both the Vinaya and the Suttanta are indeed teachings by way of a figurative method (pariyāya-desanā), whereas the Abhidhamma is a teaching not by way of a figurative method (nippariyāya-desanā). Therefore, that which is not included within the precincts of the village is "forest";
this was stated in that manner to show [the definition] according to the non-figurative method. Having gone outside the threshold post, whatever place exists—
The meaning here is that all this is called "forest" (*arañña*). As for the terms "belonging to the forest" (*āraññaka*)...

[etc] ...and "western," these are stated according to the method of the Suttas with reference to a monk who dwells in the forest (*āraññika*) in the training rule on forest-dwelling; they are appropriate for this monk.
Therefore, the definition given for it in the *Visuddhimagga* in the description of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) is indeed correct.
The intention is that it should be understood there according to the method stated therein.
"Shaded" (*sandacchāya*) means cool shade. Therefore he said, "For there," and so forth. "At the foot of a tree" (*rukkhamūla*) means near a tree.
For this has been said: "As far as the shadow spreads all around at midday, and where leaves fall in a windless place..."

"To this extent is it 'the foot of a tree. Regarding "a mountain" (*pabbata*): all three types of mountains—those consisting of pure rock, pure earth, or a mixture of both—are intended here, not only those made of stone.
However, because the word *sela* (rock) is used as a general synonym for mountain, it is stated thus.
With the words "For there," etc., he demonstrates the suitability of both [types of mountains]. "While the quarters are visible" means:

"Appearing by way of being directed toward the ten directions. Some say that this was stated to show that one-pointedness of mind might arise even through such a cause as being fanned by wind coming from all directions;
others say it is for the purpose of showing the state of being fanned by wind arriving from every quarter.
"Kaṃ" is said to mean water, because it is the producer of the removal of thirst. "Whatever is called a river-mouth (*nadītumba*) or a river-grove (*nadīkuñja*)."
“The teachers say that even a place that is not a mountain range, such as a difficult-to-access region where a river turns back, is called a ‘kandara’;
thus it is understood that the terms *nadītumba* and *nadīkuñja* denote a place where a river turns back.
And a ‘place where a river turns back’ is a difficult-to-access region where the water exiting from the river flows back again.”

But by saying "even in a mountain region," the commentator indicates that while it was first called a "mountain region" merely as an illustration in the commentary, the aforementioned river region is likewise a "cleft.
By the words "for there," etc., he shows its suitability [as an example] through that very illustration. "Having raised up" means having made into a heap.
Having said this, the teachers state: "For those situated near two mountains, there is an opening like a small chamber or the like;

however, on a single mountain alone, it is like a tunnel (umaṅga). Indeed, there is an inner cave like a tunnel on a single mountain because it is covered above, whereas there is not such [an opening] on two [mountains] because they are not so covered; therefore, it is said to be "like a tunnel."
This [phrase] is to be connected with the words “in that very one. However, the term “great chasm” (*mahāvivara*) applies to both.
And as for “resembling a *umaṅga*,” the Teacher stated it is “resembling a *suduṅgā*.

For *suduṅgā* is a designation for an underground dwelling (*bhūmigṛha*), as seen in such passages as, “Having seized him, the ogress threw him into the *suduṅgā*, where he was screaming,” and so forth. Of men...
“A place not frequented” means a place that should not be traversed by people according to their ordinary course of movement.
For here, what is intended is the prohibition of ordinary movement by way of plowing, sowing, and so forth. Therefore he said: “where they do not plow or sow.
By the word “and so forth” (ādi), however, it is meant: “A forest retreat (vanapattha)—this is a designation for lodgings; ‘forest retreat’ [means]...”
This remainder of the *vibhaṅga* text includes: "‘Bhīsanaka’ is a designation for this; ‘vanapattha’ is a designation for that which causes the hair to stand on end;
‘vanapattha’ is a designation for the outskirts; ‘vanapattha’ is a designation for lodgings that are not within the reach of human habitation.
For *pattha* is the level ground of a mountain, which is also called *sānu*; it is so called because of its similarity to that.

However, a forest that is not a place where people frequent is a *vanapattha*; therefore, it should be understood that the term *vanapattha* is a descriptive compound with the latter member placed first (*visesanaparanipāta*).
An open space facing all directions for everyone is called *abbhokāsa*;
thus he says "uncovered" (*acchanna*), meaning it is not covered by any covering whatsoever, even by the branches of a tree. [The robe] over the *daṇḍaka*...
A robe-shed (*cīvarakuṭi*) is one that has been constructed by covering [a space]. "Having driven out" means having expelled.
What is intended here is simply a heap of straw resembling a mountain cleft or a cave; otherwise, there might be the inclusion of a spread of grass or leaves.

Thus it is said, "in a dwelling resembling a mountain cleft or a cave," meaning in something like a mountain cleft or like a cave. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "even trees, thickets, and so forth," the previous method is included.
“Seeking almsfood” (*piṇḍapāta-pariyeṣaṇa*) [is used] by eliding the final member of the compound;
one who has returned from that is “one who has returned from seeking almsfood,” thus he said, “returned from the seeking of almsfood. Regarding *pallaṅka*:
here the prefix *pari-* has the sense of “all around”; therefore, an “all-around marking seat” is a *pallaṅka*, where the letter *r* becomes *l* and there is a doubling of the syllable.
Having done so, as in the expression "obstructed," the state of being "all-around" (samantabhāva) consists in placing both thighs evenly and joining the two feet together.
Therefore, it is said: "the cross-legged posture bound all around the thighs.
Sitting by way of binding the thighs is what is meant here by *pallaṅka*; it is not stated that it must be made with imported tiger skins.
"...is. Regarding "having folded" (ābhujitvā): it means having both feet folded and drawn in so that the sitting posture is achieved by way of the cross-legged position (pallaṅka).
Furthermore, since this refers specifically to the act of binding those two feet in such a manner, he says "having bound" (bandhitvā). Regarding "the body straight":
here the word *kāya* refers to the upper body, because the placing of the lower body in a non-straight position is already implied by the term "sitting."
Regarding the statement "because it has been made known," it is said: "having placed the upper body straight.
That placing of the upper body straight is shown in its specific form by the passage beginning with "eighteen," etc.;
the intended meaning is that such placing consists precisely in joining the tip to the tip of the eighteen vertebrae of the spine.
Now, demonstrating the purpose of placing [the bowl] in such a manner, he said, "For thus," and so forth. Therein, "thus" (*evaṃ*) means when it is placed in that way, or by reason of that placement.
"Do not incline" (*na paṇamanti*) means they do not bend down. "Then for him" (*athassā*) and so forth, however, is a demonstration of the successive purpose.
"Then" (*atha*) refers to the state of not bending down in this way. "Pain" (*vedanā*) refers to pain from back ailments and the like.
"It does not fall away" means it does not disappear; it does not overstep its course.
For that very reason, through the attainment of successive distinctions, the meditation subject reaches growth, expansion, and abundance.
Here, the word *pari* is a synonym for *abhi*, meaning "facing toward"; thus it is said to be "facing toward the meditation subject," having turned back from external, manifold objects.

The meaning is: "having placed the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) right before [the mind]. By the phrase "or having placed it near the mouth," he shows that the word *pari* has the sense of proximity;
what is meant is that it is established in the mind as if fixed in close proximity to the mouth.
To establish that the word *pari* has the sense of proximity by means of the text of the Vibhaṅga, the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*teneva*) was stated.
"At the tip of the nose" means at the tip of the nostrils. "The sign of the mouth" refers to the middle portion of the upper lip where the nasal breath strikes.
And here, just as by such statements as "he resorts to a secluded lodging," a lodging suitable for meditation has been shown, [so too is the object of meditation shown].

Thus, by the phrase "sits down," a mode of conduct that belongs neither to the side of depression nor to the side of agitation is shown; by the phrase "having folded his legs crosswise," the firmness of the sitting posture is shown;
and by the phrase "having established mindfulness before him," the means of grasping the object is shown.
In the word *pari*, the sense is that of grasping (*pariggaha*), as in such terms as *pariṇāyikā* ("guide"). The word *mukha*—
The sense of "departure" (*niyyāna*) is as in such passages as "the door to the void liberation" (*suññatavimokkhamukha*). For departure is indeed the act of emerging from what is opposed.
The sense of "establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the state of non-forgetfulness. "Therein" refers to the method of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidānaya*).
"Grasped departure" means that mindfulness is grasped by way of being entirely free from forgetfulness, and it is "departure" by way of having abandoned its opposite, which is forgetfulness.
"Having done so, one should establish supreme mindfulness and circumspection"—this is what is meant.

This is the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla and the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta. Alternatively, it means "grasped by way of its excellent occurrence regarding the body and so forth, and for that very reason, conjoined with the state of leading to liberation;
or else, grasped by virtue of being associated with the knowledge that discerns the body and so forth."
"And for that very reason, it means 'having established mindfulness as the means of escape'"; this is the opinion of the Elder Ācariya Ānanda. 217.

It is called *abhijjhā* because one is covetous, greedy, and longs for by means of it; it is the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*). "In the sense of breaking" means in the sense of disintegrating;
the meaning is "in the sense of disintegrating moment by moment," according to the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla, the commentator on the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*.
And it was said by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta. It is also seen in the Suttas: "It is 'shaken off' (*lujjati*), O Bhikkhu, that it is called the world (*loka*).
And what is shaken off? The eye, O Bhikkhu, is shaken off; forms are shaken off; eye-consciousness is shaken off," and so forth.
However, in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā and here in the current manuscript, it says: "in the sense of shaking off and being shaken off."
It has been written. Therein, the word *lucana* itself is stated by way of the synonym *palucana* as a specific distinction.
For the word *luca* also carries the sense of "looking" and so forth—as in the expression "he looks"—but here the meaning is in the sense of breaking up and falling apart.

However, it is stated in the *Vaṃsatthappakāsinī*: "Because its nature is to peel away (*lucana*) by way of momentary dissolution, and because its nature is to peel away (*palucana*) by way of death-dissolution."

Regarding the phrase "the world" (*loko nāma*)—in the commentary on the fifth verse of the first chapter of the *Mahāvaṃsa-ṭīkā* known as the *Vaṃsatthappakāsinī*—some, however, state that the meaning is "in the sense of breaking up and arising.
This is indeed incorrect, because it contradicts the meaning of the words spoken by [the Buddha] himself, and because the root *luc* denotes non-arising. Furthermore, even by the teachers...
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of plucking and pulling out," one might have stated the meaning by merely citing that very reading;
however, it should be understood that because it was transmitted through successive tradition, it is not seen here and there due to scribal negligence.

Or else, "the world" (loka) refers to that which, even when grasped, does not remain as it was—neither being plucked nor pulled out—or it is so called because it is plucked away by the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā).
The world must indeed be understood as that which breaks up and perishes; therefore, for those supramundane states (lokuttara) which are devoid of such grasping, there is no "world-ness.
Or, it is stated that the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) is the world, as in: "The five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) are the world.
Thus, even on account of these various statements, the meaning previously mentioned by some is not tenable.
Therefore, because the five aggregates of clinging alone constitute the world:
regarding the phrase "by way of suppression," here "suppression" means non-arising and non-occurrence by way of abandonment through substitution (tadaṅgappahāna);

it does not mean that the opposites are thoroughly abandoned by way of abandonment through suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna). For the expression "because they are abandoned" is stated with reference to a state similar to what is abandoned in that manner.

Why is that? Because jhāna has not yet been attained. However, it is by virtue of such abandonment through prior-stage cultivation (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) that this consciousness is called "free from covetousness" (vigatābhijjha), and not because it is devoid of covetousness by its very nature (sabhāva) like eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa).
To show this, it is said: "not similar to eye-consciousness. Regarding the phrase *yathā taṃ*, here *taṃ* is merely a particle.
Or that mind itself. What is meant is that the purification consists in the act of relinquishing it now and, furthermore, not taking it up again in the future.

And just as this mind is free from covetousness because it has been purified by development in its prior stages, so too should its freedom from ill will, freedom from sloth and torpor, lack of restlessness, and freedom from doubt be understood.
Showing that "the same method applies to 'having abandoned ill-will and hatred,' etc.," he said this. "Rotten sour gruel, etc. refers to last night's barley gruel and the like.
"Its former nature" means its state of being pure and white; by this, he shows the meaning as "it undergoes a transformation.
"By undergoing a transformation" means by undergoing a change characterized by the abandonment of its former nature. By the words "both," etc., [he explains].

He states that they share the same meaning in their compound form. For it is taught in the Abhidhamma that "stiffness" (*thina*) is defined by the passage beginning, "that at that time there is unfitness of mind," while "torpor" (*middha*) is defined by the passage beginning, "that at that time there is unfitness of body.
Therefore, it is said: "Stiffness is the sickness of the mind; torpor is the sickness of the mental factors. This is so even though stiffness and torpor are mutually related.

In the case of non-separation, just as with the lightness of mind and body, one should see that the specific conditionality of those [factors]—such as their lack of sluggishness (*akallatā*) and so forth—which constitutes their respective particularities for the mind and mental concomitants in their proper order, is their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"Seen light" (*diṭṭhāloka*) refers to the light of the moon, lamps, torches, and so forth seen at night, and the light of the sun and so forth during the day; both by night and by day.
The perception capable of cognizing that [light] is "perception of light" (*ālokasaññā*). And its existence here is intended as being purified and free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
For the vowel *ī* indicates the understanding of the meaning of "existence" (*atthi*) as distinguished by the sense of intensity;

thus he said, "even during the night," and so forth. This was stated because it is the cause for the state of being free from sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). This meaning is well-known in the Suttas.
"He is mindful" means he possesses mindfulness (*sati*); "he is clearly comprehending" means he possesses clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
By the phrase "endowed with mindfulness and knowledge," [the author] shows that this is a description of the person (*puggala-niddesa*). To dispel the following inquiry:

why is only this pair mentioned, even though other qualities such as energy (*viriya*) and concentration (*samādhi*) also exist; or, why is this pair stated here specifically, rather than being stated elsewhere among those who are free from covetousness and so forth?
"This both" and so forth was said; the meaning is that "this both" refers to mindfulness and clear comprehension as defined by way of the person.

He states that the word *ta-* has a past sense in the phrase "standing having transcended," and transcending is indeed the abandoning [of defilements] through prior-stage cultivation (*pubbabhāga-bhāvanā*).
"How this, how this" occurs—thus it is called *kaṅkhā* (doubt).
Doubt (*vicikicchā*); one who has this is a "doubter" (*kathaṃkathī*). One who is not a doubter is "non-doubting" (*akathaṃkathī*);
such is the literal meaning of the word. However, to show the essential sense, it is said: "He is 'non-doubting' because [his mind] does not proceed in the manner of 'How is this?
How is this?'". The phrase "regarding wholesome states" (*kusalesu dhammesu*) should be connected with the term "non-doubting."
He said: “The meaning is ‘he does not doubt, he does not hesitate.

Regarding the phrase “by way of the analysis of the meaning, characteristic, and so forth,” here the word “and so forth” (ādi) should be understood as including the condition, that which is abandoned, the abandoner, and so on; for these too must be explained according to their distinctions. 218.
It is stated that “wealth taken for interest is called debt,” as in the expression “having taken wealth for interest. [The prefix] *vi-* signifies...
That which has an end (*byanta*) is *byanta*; that which has such an end is *byantī*. Therefore he said, "with its end removed" (*vigatanta*);

the meaning is that one should make it free from the limit of debt to be repaid. "Of those" refers to the debts and wealth taken up for the sake of increase. A "limit" (*pariyanta*) is the remainder of the debt to be repaid beyond that point.
One who has no debt is *aṇaṇo*. The state of being such is *āṇaṇya*. That very source is the "source of debtlessness" (*āṇaṇyanidāna*).
The meaning is: "having the state of being free from debt as its cause" (*āṇaṇya-hetu*) and "having the state of being free from debt as its reason" (*āṇaṇya-kāraṇa*).

Or alternatively, it is called "having the state of being free from debt as its source" (*āṇaṇya-nidāna*) because freedom from debt itself is its source or reason; this connects with the words "gladness" (*pāmojja*) and "mental joy" (*somanassa*).
One attains powerful gladness thinking, "I am released from the obstacle of debt. One achieves mental joy thinking, "I still have what remains for the sake of my livelihood."

219. "Dissimilar feeling" (visabhāgavedanā) refers to painful feeling (dukkhavedanā). For it is dissimilar to pleasant feeling because it stands in opposition to the continuum of wholesome karmic fruition (kusalavipākasantāna), being the cause for its arising. "As if with a saw" means as if with a saw.
"The four postures" (catuiriyāpatha) refers to the fourfold posture. For one who is afflicted by disease is unable to stand or walk as they normally would.

The same applies to sitting and other postures. "Afflicts" means it oppresses. Only the disequilibrium that has become a disorder of the wind (*vāta*) and other elements is called "affliction" (*ābādha*).
Therefore he said: "Suffering from the pain arising therefrom. The meaning is:

suffering from, or possessed of, the pain consisting of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*) which arises from that affliction. Regarding the state of being an affliction in the case of painful feeling, at the beginning...
"Because it afflicts (*bādhati*), it is called an affliction (*ābādha*); thus, one who has an affliction is 'one afflicted' (*ābādhika*) by means of the primary disease designated as 'affliction.
The meaning should be understood as being 'pained' by means of the secondary disease designated as 'suffering,' which arises repeatedly.

For if this is the case, the way in which the word "pained" (*dukkhita*), spoken by way of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*), is to be qualified by the word "one afflicted" (*ābādhika*) becomes clear; such is the view here according to the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla.
The method has been stated. "Excessive" (*adhimatta*) means a measure that is beyond the limit; it is intense.

One who is "excessively ill" (*adhimattagilāna*) is one whose body is utterly exhausted by the dissolution of the physical elements due to being severely ill. "Because of being overcome by excessive illness" means because of being oppressed by excessive illness.

"It would not be pleasing" (*na rucceyya*) means it would not be agreeable; this is a word expressing the object of the action, as seen in the phrase "and her food" (*bhattañcassā*), where "her" (*assā*) indicates the agent.
The word *matta* means "measure" (or "extent"), as it is said: "Strength-measure (*balamattā*) means simply strength. Alternatively, a small amount of strength is "strength-measure.

"Both of those" refers to gladness (*pāmojja*) and joy (*somanassa*). The meaning of the canonical text is: "One would obtain gladness [thinking], 'I am freed from disease,' and one would attain joy [thinking], 'I have bodily strength.'"
220. Regarding the term *kākaṇikamatta*, they say it means "the size of a single *guñja* seed. However, in the *Vinaya-ṭīkā*, it is stated as "the size of one and a half grains of rice.

Furthermore, the word *kaṇa* (husk) is used in the sense of chaff, as in the passage: "Having cooked the pure, fragrant grain of rice, free from husks and without powder, in a *tuṇḍikīra* [frying pan], they eat that food," and so forth.
For it is said in the Abhidhāna, in the section on the Bhakaṇḍa, in the fourth varga of four hundred and fifty-four verses: “*Kaṇo tu kuṇḍako bhave*.
However, a small *kaṇa* is called a *kākaṇa*, just as [the color] is called “black-colored” (*kālavaṇa*). Therefore, that which has a *kākaṇa* as its measure is *kākaṇika*;
*kākaṇika-mattaṃ* means simply *kākaṇika*, the sense being that it is merely the size of a small *kuṇḍaka*. This is how the meaning should be understood.
For this being so, it does not contradict the statement in the Umaṅga Jātaka: “A royal gift as small as a single *kākaṇika* coin is not permitted; he gives meat worth half a *māsa*.
“Decline” (*vaya*) means exhaustion and dissolution; for one who reflects, “I am released from bondage,” both of these occur.
Therefore it was said: “One may obtain gladness, one may attain...”
Regarding the phrase "somanassan" (mental joy), the statement "the remainder is to be understood according to the method already stated" and so forth was made with reference to the remaining words.
"According to the method already stated" means according to the method stated in the first and second sections. "In all sections" refers to the three divisions beginning with the third.
For each individual simile-side is called a "section."
221–222. *Adhīna* means dependent; it does not mean being joined with the state of a master (*seribhāva*). Therefore he said: “He does not obtain to do anything according to his own wish.

The same applies to the other case as well. In order to show the construction with an elided portion of the text (*sapāṭhasesayojana*)—namely, that there is no going at will to where one desires to go—he stated “by which,” and so forth.
Furthermore, this word *kāmaṃ* is a neuter gerundive (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*), or it may be used in the sense of “at will” (*kāmena*) or “according to desire” (*icchāya*).

The word *kāmaṅgamo* is formed by the elision (*niggahītāgama*) [of the final vowel] of *kāmaṃ*. By the phrase "from the state of being a slave" (*dāsabhāvā*), he shows that the word *bya* here has the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvattha*).
One who is to be sought and directed in one's own duty as if it were one's own arm because of freedom from dependence is called *bhujisso*;
this is the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) meaning "one who is self-dependent. "Arm" (*bhuja*) means the employment of oneself according to one's pleasure; that is the *issa*.
"It is called *bhujissa* because it is desired (*icchitabba*) here; [it means] one who is not a slave (*assāmika*)," so it is stated in the *Mūlapaṇṇāsaka-ṭīkā*.
However, showing merely the meaning, he said "belonging to oneself" (*attano santaka*); what is meant is that it belongs to oneself alone, not to another.
It is a *kantāra* because they cross (*tārenti*) water (*kaṃ*) there due to the lack of water (*anudakatā*); furthermore, the word *addhāna* is a synonym for "long."
It is said: "A long journey without water. 223. "The rest" refers to ill will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth.

"Therein" means in the act of seeing. "This" refers to the similarity now being described, by which the status of debt and so forth becomes that of the simile (*upamā*), and the status of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth becomes that of the thing compared (*upameyya*); this is their relationship as simile and thing compared.
“Similarity” (sadisatā) is how it should be understood. “By them” means by others, the creditors.

“To ward off anything” means that he is unable to prevent even a harsh word or the like, because he is incapable of paying the debt. Why? It is said: “Because of the cause for enduring,” and so forth;

the meaning is: because of being the cause for enduring the debt. “Whoever is stained with sensual desire for whom” refers to whichever person is stained with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) toward whichever [object].
One is lustful toward a person who has become the object of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) by means of that very sensual desire. One grasps that object with craving-accompanied [desire];
thus, by means of sensual desire which consists of craving, one grasps that person who is the object of sensual desire as "this is mine.
Here, the word *sahagata* (accompanied) signifies mere coexistence, as in such passages as: "This craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and lust... and so forth.
"By him" means by the person who has become the basis for sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). Why? He says "the cause for endurance," etc.;
the meaning is that it is the cause for enduring sensual desire. Here, a defiled mental state dominated by lust, which resembles endurance, is called "endurance" (*titikkhā*);
it is not, however, the kind of endurance characterized by non-hatred (*adosa*) found in such passages as "Endurance is the supreme austerity" (*khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā*).
The arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*). "By the masters of the house" means by those who have become the masters of the house, namely the fathers-in-law and mothers-in-law.
The connection is: "Just as lust for women is a cause for endurance.

By the phrase beginning with "But just as," the similarity of the remaining [afflictions] to diseases and so forth is stated. Therein, one afflicted by a bile disease is so due to the provocation of a disorder of the *pitta* humor.
Because his bile was provoked, even all things such as honey and sugar became non-sweet for him; thus it is said:

“He vomits, thinking ‘it is bitter, it is bitter. In the *Ṭīkā*, the reading extracted is “*tumhe upaddaveyyāthā*” (you should afflict), where the meaning is derived from the verbal root according to the form “*upaddavaṃ karothā*” (you should cause affliction);
however, the reading now seen is “*tumhehi upaddutā*” (afflicted by you).
"Vibbhamati" means he wanders here and there, or he turns back toward the inferior state.

The connection is as follows: "He does not find, does not experience, does not know, and does not obtain the taste of honey, sugar, and so forth. "Sāsanarasaṃ" means the taste of the Dispensation, or the Dispensation itself as the taste.

A *nakkhattachaṇa* is a festival for a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*). Thus he said: "Oh, what dancing! Oh, what singing! *Mutta* means released from bondage. *Dhammassavanassa* means of the Dhamma that is to be heard. *Accāyika* is a task that must be performed quickly.
For the prefix *ati-* has the sense of "quickly," as in such terms as *pāṇātipāta* (taking life) and so forth.
*Vinaye apakataññū* means one who is unskilled in the sequence of the Vinaya. One who knows the established conclusion and the legal decision is called *pakataññū*.
One who knows what has been done, and likewise one who does not know what has been done; for he does not know, as it truly is, what is allowable and what is unallowable.

Therefore he said, "In regard to anything at all," and so forth. "Even in the case of allowable meat" means even in the case of pork and the like. "By the perception that it is unallowable meat" means by the perception that it is bear-meat and the like.
"Even by the sound of a staff" means even by the sound of a branch-staff. "Suspected and apprehended" means both suspected and apprehended.
"Apprehensive on all sides" means he is exceedingly apprehensive. The demonstration of that state is given by the words "he even goes," and so forth.
For he indeed goes a little way; yet, while going, because of that state of being suspicious and fearful, he stops here and there.
In such a wilderness, thinking, "Who knows? What might happen? he even turns back. Therefore...
The place not yet traversed is far more extensive than the place already traversed;
for that very reason, he reaches the land of safety only with difficulty and toil, or perhaps does not reach it at all.

"With difficulty and toil" is a synonymous expression: exhaustion through bodily suffering is "difficulty," while oppression through mental suffering is "toil. "The land of safety" means that which has become secure.
Because the word *anta* (end) has the sense of "absence" (*tabbhāva*), or because it is the destruction of fear (*khaya*), it is *khema*;

that which has such an end or boundary (*pariccheda*) is likewise [called] *khema*. That very ground is the "ground of safety" (*khemantabhūmi*); the meaning is "that region free from fear. Regarding the phrase "in eight places":
"In this regard, what is doubt (*vicikicchā*)? One is hesitant and doubtful regarding the Teacher; regarding the Dhamma; regarding the Saṅgha..."

"In the eight points mentioned in the *Vibhaṅga*—namely, in regard to training (*sikkhā*), the past (*pubbanta*), the future (*aparanta*), both the past and the future (*pubbantāparanta*), and the phenomena that are dependently originated through specific conditionality (*idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppanna*)—one wavers and doubts.
Having resolved (*adhimuccitvā*) means having determined or having gained conviction. "To grasp by means of faith" means by way of believing that the object worthy of faith is "just this."

The meaning is that one is unable to grasp it or believe it. "Iti" (thus) means: because of being unable [to grasp or believe] in the manner described, there is a connection to the fact that it creates an obstacle.
For one who has entered the forest, the initial slithering of doubt—thinking, "Is it there?
Is it not there?"—is *āsappana*. Following that, the slithering all around or upwards is *parisappana*.
By both [terms], he shows wandering right there due to doubt. Therefore he said "non-penetration" (*apariyogāhana*);

the meaning is non-penetration on all sides as to "this is thus. "Trembling" (*chambhitatta*) refers to the state of being terrified that has arisen from the perception of the forest—the quivering of the heart-flesh;
"fright" (*utrāsa*) is what is meant. On the side of the illustration (*upameyya*), the meaning is the same as appropriate.
224. Herein, this "similarity" should be understood according to the method stated regarding the side of what has not been abandoned.
For to the same extent that sensual desire and the rest are like debt and so forth, to that same extent their abandonment is like freedom from debt and so forth.
This, however, is merely the meaning of the words not [yet] explained: "prosperity" (*samiddhatā*) means wealth (*aḍḍhatā*). Previously, when a leaf had been placed [on the scale],...
"Accompanied by interest" (*savaḍḍhika*) means it exists together with interest. "A document" (*paṇṇa*) refers to a written document characterized by the recording of a loan's giving or receiving.

Again, "a document" (*paṇṇa*) refers to a written message composed for the purpose of requesting a loan. "By way of being unstained" (*nillepatāya*) means by way of not being smeared due to the absence of a connection with wealth;
likewise, it means by way of not being attached. These two are indeed synonymous terms. Alternatively, "by way of being unstained" (*nillepatāya*)...
The meaning is "by way of non-adherence," which is a qualification characterized by the state of not being smeared according to the method already stated. "Six things" refers to these six qualities:

the apprehension of the sign of foulness (*asubhanimitta*), application to the development of foulness (*asubhabhāvanā*), guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamittatā*), and appropriate talk (*sappāyakathā*).

"Having developed" means having increased, or having produced within oneself, by way of the manifestation of the non-arising of what has not yet arisen and the abandoning of what has already arisen, and so forth.
Because it has come down in the Pāḷi with particular detail in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, it was said: "We shall comment upon the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna.
And by "Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna," he refers to that which is chanted in this Dīgha Āgama, not to that in the Majjhima Āgama, because that belongs to a different collection (nikāya).
For they say that even a meaning found in another collection is generally stated by the teachers elsewhere [in this work]. This is the method.

"Also in the stage of abandoning ill-will and so forth. "In another's person" means: in another person who has become the object. Because of the absence of the sense of "mine," there is no attachment;
because of the absence of grasping, he is not bound. The word "api" (also/even) is used for emphasis, meaning: even when seeing divine forms, defilement does not manifest, let alone human ones.
"One who does what is harmful" means one who acts for the detriment of both oneself and others. "Six things" refers to these six qualities:

grasping the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, the sense of being the owner of one's own kamma, frequent reflection, having virtuous friends, and talk that is conducive to progress.
"Right there" means in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta itself. A training precept is formulated specifically with reference to conduct and virtue (*cārittasīla*).
It is said, “the formulation of conduct. By the word “etcetera,” it includes the training rules (sikkhāpada) that formulate prohibitions.

“Admitted” means caused to be admitted. For a man who has not obtained the enjoyment of a festival night because he was caused to be admitted to prison on that very festival day is called “the man who was admitted to prison on the festival day,” or [he is so called] because of being admitted specifically on the festival day.
It is also appropriate to say that a person who has acted in such a way for the purpose of not experiencing [the result] is described thus.
"In another" means in a subsequent one, or on another lunar day (nakkhattadivasa). "Opportunity" means the occasion for inflicting punishment, or the moment of inflicting punishment.
"Causing great harm" means causing great misfortune by way of the loss of benefits pertaining to this life and so forth. Six.

"Dhamma" refers to these six things: grasping the sign in overeating, changing one's posture, attending to the perception of light, dwelling in the open air, having virtuous friends, and appropriate talk.
"Of the festival of Dhamma" means of the festival consisting of the aforementioned Dhamma that is to be heard; for even Dhamma, in the sense of producing joy for the virtuous, is like a festival.
"Star" is what is said.
Regarding restlessness and worry (*uddhacca-kukkucca*): by means of bringing about dependence on others, it is described according to the method already stated as a creator of great harm.
"Six qualities" refers to: being well-versed in the scriptures, being one who asks questions, being knowledgeable in the Vinaya, and associating with the elders.
These are the six things: having virtuous friends and appropriate talk. "By force" means by means of one's own strength;

"coercion" (*balakkāra*) refers to the doing of what one desires by means of that strength. "The practice of renunciation" (*nekkhammapaṭipadā*) is the practice of emerging from the hindrances, which is precisely access concentration (*upacārabhāvanā*), not the first jhāna. For this is the section concerning access concentration.

"Powerful" (*balavā*) means possessing power through the strength capable of crushing adversaries; this is because it makes known the sense of "having" (*vatthu*), which is distinguished by the sense of "overpowering" (*abhibhava*).

"The essence of wealth in his hand" (*hatthasāraṃ*) means the essential wealth that has come into his hand. "With weapons ready" (*sajjāvudho*) means having equipped himself with weapons such as a bow;
the meaning is "having donned the fivefold armor. "Accompanied by a retinue" refers to being accompanied by brave and heroic attendants. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to what was previously described.
A man. Because of his strength, his being armed, and his having a retinue, thieves would flee upon seeing him even from afar.
"Causing harm" means causing disadvantage in the manner already described, by creating an obstacle to right practice (*sammāpaṭipatti*). "Six qualities" refers to:

great learning (*bahussutatā*), inquisitiveness (*paripucchakatā*), knowledge of what is established in the Vinaya (*vinaye pakataññutā*), abundance of resolute confidence (*adhimokkhabahulatā*), and friendship with the virtuous (*kalyāṇamittatā*).
"Suitable talk" refers to these six things. Just as great learning and the other [five] qualities lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse, so too do they lead to the abandoning of doubt;
thus, in this context, the three qualities beginning with great learning are included.
However, both having a virtuous friend and suitable talk lead to the abandoning of all five hindrances; therefore, regarding each of those hindrances, [the respective factors are applied].
It should be understood as the practice of what is appropriate. "As if it were grass" means that, out of fear, one does not even count [the offense] as grass.
"Having crossed the wilderness of misconduct" means having crossed the wilderness known as misconduct by way of overcoming doubt, which serves as the means for engaging in misconduct.
For doubt, by way of being the cause for not proceeding toward right practice, [acts as an obstacle].
"Only wrong practice is nourished" means that its non-abandonment is the means for engaging in misconduct, while its abandonment is the means for shaking off misconduct. 225.
By the phrase "an appearance of contentment," he shows what is called *pāmojja* (gladness), which is a form of nascent joy (*taruṇapīti*). For, because of its nascent nature, it is in some way...

The state of being satisfied (*tuṭṭhāvatthā*) is merely the outward manifestation of satisfaction. The phrase “of one who is satisfied” (*tuṭṭhassa*) is a synonym for “of one who is gladdened” (*pamuditassa*).
Its meaning is stated in the *Ṭīkā* as “of one who is satisfied by means of rapture (*pīti*) that has reached the stage of ‘descending’ (*okkantika*)”;
if this were the case, then by the term “gladness” (*pāmojja*), only descending rapture would be included. [Rapture] is the rapture that agitates the entire body.

Regarding the meaning of the phrase “it arises,” it is stated that “joy (pīti) arises with the characteristic of pervading, shaking the entire body through its own expansive nature and by the arising of sublime matter originating from itself. This being the case, only the joy of pervasion would be included by the term “joy” (pīti);
however, the reason for this must be investigated here. But in this context, as opposed to elsewhere—
Furthermore, because the meaning of the two terms is illustrated by their commonality with "fresh" and "strong" respectively: any fresh joy is *pāmojja*, while strong joy is *pīti*;

or, because the fivefold types of joy arise in successive order as fresh and strong, some say that each preceding one is *pāmojja* and each succeeding one is *pīti*. This is the meaning appropriate to this context.
“Of one who is content” means of one who is content by way of the fresh joy known as *pāmojja*. For the word *ta-* has the sense of the past;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of an absence of the relationship between cause and fruit, and such a relationship between cause and fruit has indeed been stated.
By the phrase “shaking the entire body,” he shows that here “joy” (*pīti*) refers to powerful joy (*balavapīti*). For that [powerful joy]...
Due to its own expansive nature and because it gives rise to sublime material forms originating from itself, it arises agitating the entire body.
Here, "agitation" (*saṅkhobhana*) refers to the production of the force of joy and the expansion of joy throughout the whole body.
"Joy-accompanied" (*pītisahita*) is a compound formed by the elision of the final member; that [accompanied] thing is the mind (*mano*), thus the compound means "that which has joy as its mind."
The phrase "the mind associated with joy" (pītiyā sampayuttaṃ mano) is also acceptable; however, to show the mere meaning, it is stated as "of the person whose consciousness is associated with joy.

Here, "body" (kāya) refers to the entire immaterial aggregate (arūpakalāpa), and not merely the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling—as in the case of bodily lightness (kāyalahutā) and so on—nor does it include the material body—as in the case of the body-base (kāyāyatana) and so on. This is shown by the term "mental body" (nāmakāyo).
By this [term]. Here, "tranquility" (passambhana) is intended specifically in the sense of the two kinds of tranquility;

and since tranquility is the state of being free from the distress of the defilements, he says, "he is free from distress" (vigatadaratha), meaning that the distress of the defilements such as restlessness has been abandoned.

By means of the aforementioned preliminary development (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā), while experiencing mental happiness, because his body is permeated by the sublime matter (rūpa) originated by that [happiness],...
It is said, "he experiences even bodily pleasure," meaning "he experiences both bodily and mental pleasure.

By this "pleasure of renunciation"— which is described as "experiencing pleasure" because it has emerged from the side of defilements and hindrances and belongs to the side of the first jhāna— he [experiences] the appropriate access-pleasure known as renunciation.
And by means of absorption-happiness. It is said here that "concentration is achieved through both of these," namely, "by way of access and by way of absorption.

However, the intended meaning here is as follows: from the abandonment of sensual desire up until the experience of happiness by one whose body is tranquil, it is the preliminary development (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) that is described, just as before, and not absorption. For it is in the abandonment of sensual desire...
The Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated: "Regarding the phrase 'by way of suppression' (*vikkhambhanavasena*):
here, suppression means non-arising and non-occurrence; it does not mean the complete abandonment of opposites.

And the term 'abandoned' (*pahīna*) is said with reference to a state resembling what has been abandoned, because the jhāna has not yet been attained. [This applies] also to the experience of pleasure by one whose body is tranquil, as previously described.

Through the development of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāgabhāvanā*), while experiencing mental pleasure, one also experiences bodily pleasure because the body is touched by the refined matter (*paṇītarūpa*) originated by that [mental pleasure].

Furthermore, what need is there to mention what others might say, since it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself in various places that "having developed six things" refers to the development of the preliminary stage? For one who is happy, there is the concentration of the mind (*cittasamādhāna*).

However, because it is a cause for absorption just as the access development of happiness is, and because it connects with the absorption to be described by the words "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," etc.,
in terms of cause and fruit, it is called both preliminary concentration and absorption concentration; or alternatively, just like preliminary happiness,
absorption happiness too is indeed a cause for absorption concentration, and thus that too [is included].
Failing to observe this fact— that the pleasure of absorption (*appanāsukha*) was taken by the Elder Dhammapāla as the cause for absorption concentration—
some people, not grasping the meaning of "renunciation" (*nekkhamma*) as it truly is, have made the text and even the commentary confused and muddled.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the first jhāna.

226. Since it might be argued that by the statement, "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," the concentration of the mind has already been described both in terms of access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā), then what is the purpose of the teaching beginning with, "He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures..."?
To answer this objection, it is said: "It should be understood that [the teaching] beginning with 'He, quite secluded... was spoken. In that context, the word "concentrated" (samāhite) refers to...
The two phrases, "stated for the purpose of seeing," should be understood as being connected with these [preceding words];
the intended meaning is that they were stated for the purpose of seeing in that way because of the state of being concentrated (*samāhita*).

"For the purpose of showing the higher distinction" means for the purpose of showing the distinctions—the first, second jhāna, and so forth—that are to be attained beyond access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and the concentrations of the first jhāna and so forth. By the very attainment of access concentration...
For it is possible to attain the distinctions of the first jhāna and so forth, but not without that [purity].

It should be understood that even in the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, a succession of causes beginning with the arising of gladness must be desired, just as the purification by knowledge and vision of the way is required for the attainment of the second path and so forth.
"By means of absorption concentration" means by means of the absorption concentration of the first jhāna and so forth. "Of that concentration" means...
The concentration characterized by absorption (*appanālakkhaṇa*), which is described in a general sense as "the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," belongs to that concentration.

"For the purpose of showing its divisions" means for the purpose of showing the subdivisions of the second jhāna and so forth, as well as the subdivisions of the first direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and so forth.

"The body born of karma" (*karajakāya*) refers to the body composed of the four great elements, which consists of a collection of material phenomena belonging to the four continuities (*catusantatirūpa*).
For it is called "born from the womb" (*karaja*) because it is produced from what is reckoned as a "womb" (*kara*), since it arises from the production of a flower;

for it produces the name "flower," which is the mother's blood, and "production," which is the father's semen, and that which is born from these is specifically the body dwelling in the womb by way of the egg-born and the moisture-born. Granted, this also applies to the spontaneously born (*opapātika*) and others.

Although the attainment of the aforementioned concentration is possible for those endowed with the necessary causes, nevertheless, because it is prevalent and because it is manifest, it is said to occur in that very body.
It is called "the maker" (*kara*) because it produces or generates sons; semen and blood are the "maker," and they say one is "born from the maker" (*karaja*).
But surely the mental body (*nāmakāya*) as well would receive such assistance through the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; so why is it stated [only] as above?

Is it the form-body (*rūpakāya*) alone that is intended here? Because it is understood through its connection with other words. For, by virtue of its connection with other words such as "he moistens" (*abhisandeti*), it is understood that the form-body alone is spoken of here by the Blessed One; thus, it is established that this [body] alone is fit for the activities of moistening and so forth.
"He moistens" means he performs the act of moistening; for, according to the distinction [of the commentary], it says: "He moistens this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion."
Here, causal activity is found only as a conceptual construct based on the relationship between a whole and its parts;
however, "moistening" (*abhisandana*) refers to the bringing about of a state of saturation in the physical body through the joy and bliss consisting of jhāna, which entirely removes its dryness.
Thus he said, "it moistens, it makes unctuous," meaning the state of being parched and the state of being dry.

The meaning is "it makes. In terms of its actual function (*atthato*), however, "cohesion" (*abhisandana*) should be understood as the suffusion of the body by the refined material qualities (*rūpa*) produced by the aforementioned joy and pleasure.
For this very reason it is said: "It produces joy and pleasure occurring everywhere.

Indeed, the state of joy and pleasure occurring everywhere exists precisely through the suffusion of the material qualities produced by that [joy]. This also applies to the terms "it moistens" (*parisandeti*) and so forth.
The same method applies here. *Bhasta* means a leather bag. *Parippharati* is a pure verb of action.
Therefore it is said: “It touches on all sides”; the meaning is that this very body becomes touched on all sides by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
Here, only the action of touching is intended, not the action of pervading, because the monk alone is the pure agent.
“Possessing all” (*sabbavā*) means that all things exist in this; it is like the term “virtuous” (*guṇavā*). Regarding that which possesses all (*sabbavato*), according to the grammatical rule:

“In a relationship between part and whole, the case ending for possession (*sāmivacana*) applies to the whole,” one should consider that this word “all” (*sabba*) has as its referent only the whole, because it is connected here with the part “something” (*kiñci*).
Thus, by way of the part known as the constituent elements such as skin and flesh...
Showing the state of being a composite whole (*avayavībhāva*), he says: “of the body possessing all its parts. For the term “anything whatsoever,” the explanatory gloss is:

“the place where [it] rests... [etc. up to ... the place. The connection is as follows: in the place where the continuity of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*) proceeds—that is, in the place where the continuity of matter born of karma (*kammajarūpa*) proceeds—there is nothing that is not pervaded.
“Followed by skin, flesh, and blood” means followed by the matter born of karma such as skin, flesh, blood, and so forth.
Wherever there is matter born of kamma, there also matter born of mind pervades it;
therefore, with reference to the fact that the body is touched by that [matter], it is said: "There is nothing that is not touched.
(227) "Cheko" means skillful. That skillfulness, however, is understood from the proximity of other words such as "having poured washing powder into a bronze bowl," and so forth.

By the words beginning with "capable" (*paṭibalo*), he shows that [the term] is to be understood by way of its capacity for the preparation, the application, and the mixing of bathing powders according to the manual.
Furthermore, the word *kaṃsa* occurs in reference to gold in such passages as "in a large bronze bowl" (*mahatiyā kaṃsapātiyā*);

it occurs in reference to brass in such passages as "just as a bronze vessel is struck" (*kaṃso upahato yathā*); and [it refers to King Mahākaṃsa] in the passage "King Upakaṃsa [was the son] of Mahākaṃsa."
In passages such as "born here" (*atrāja*), it refers to mere designation (*paṇṇattimatta*).
But here, regarding the phrase "by whatever metal," he says: "in a vessel made by any metal whatsoever. To ward off the objection—"Is this not merely for the sake of providing a simile?
Then why was the bronze bowl specifically mentioned?"—he provides the answer with the words "earthenware vessel," and so forth.
“While it is being pressed” means that it breaks even as one is kneading it into a lump; it is not, however, capable of withstanding being pressed.
This genitive case (*sāmivacana*) expresses the characteristic of disregard. For the occurrence of another action at the very moment another action occurs is the characteristic of disregard.
“Repeatedly moistening” is a neuter present participle (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*).
This is shown by the phrase "having sprinkled again and again. Here, the word *phusa* refers to sprinkling, as in the expression during a rainstorm:
"the rain falls in small drops (*thokaṃ thokaṃ phusāyati*). Therefore, the meaning is:
having repeatedly sprinkled with water over the bathing powder from here and there, so as to cause it to spread. For even a word that is without a prefix may function as if it were with a prefix.

It is like an illustration of the meaning obtained from the treatise (*pakaraṇa*). However, the expression “having sprinkled again and again” is for the purpose of making known its status as a qualifier for the word “paripphosakaṃ paripphosakan” in the phrase “he should sprinkle. It is the same in such cases.
Regarding the word “sandeyyā,” it is stated that the term *sanda* means “making into a mass,” as in “he should make a mass. [The word] *anugatā*...
“Approached” (*upagatā*) means gone by way of entering. “Encompassed” (*pariggahitā*) means grasped all around, touched on every side.

“With the inside and the outside” (*santarabāhirā*) refers to that which occurs together with the internal and external parts; it is a bath-powder ball (*nhāniyapiṇḍi*). There is also the reading “*samantarabāhirā*”;
the letter *m* has been added by way of euphonic conjunction (*padasaṃdhi*). It is “with the inside and the outside” precisely because of the aforementioned state of being encompassed.
Regarding the phrase "the soap-ball was soaked with water-moisture," he said, "it was soaked with water-moisture everywhere.
*Sabbatthaka* means occurring everywhere; this is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*), meaning it was soaked while existing in every part.
And by the phrase "soaked inside and out," he expresses the state of the soap-ball being completely saturated with water.
Furthermore, by the phrase “and not leaking,” its dense and solid state even when soaked is indicated.
Therefore he said, “not drop by drop,” and so forth. The meaning is: it does not leak or drip drop by drop of water.
In some places the reading is “bindum udakan,” which means a drop consisting of water. As for the word *bindu*:
For it is used here in the sense of a constituent part of a stream, as in the phrase “*byālambambudharabindu*” (drops falling from a cloud) and so forth.
Furthermore, because it trickles down, it is possible to grasp it with one hand, or with two or three fingers, or to rub it between the palms.
For if it were merely flowing away, it would become dry due to the loss of its moisture and, becoming stiff, could not be grasped or rubbed in such a manner.
"Capable" (sakkā) is what is meant. "By way of a ball" (ovaṭṭikāya) means by way of being rounded or by way of a globule; the meaning is that it is possible to form that lump.
Commentary on the Second Jhāna (229):
It breaks forth, emerging upwards through various water-veins, thus it is called "breaking forth" (ubbhida); such is the water.
Regarding the word *yassa*: it is *ubbhidodako*. However, when the letter *da* is changed to *ta*, it becomes *ubbhitodako*;
this is stated as "ubbhinnaudako" (one whose water has overflowed) in order to show this meaning. The sense is that it is like a well dug on a riverbank, where the water breaks through [the surface].
Even water that breaks through may, in some cases, rise up from below in the form of a stream and go outwards; no one [can stop it].
One is able to make it established within [the water] itself because it rises in the form of a stream;
however, here it is understood that—like [water rising] on a sandy bank—it breaks forth from within the pool and remains right there, rather than rising as a stream and flowing outward.
This is the meaning intended by "unshakeable" and "settled" water.
Having intended this, he said, “Not below,” and so forth. “Below” refers to the great water-vein beneath the lake;
just as a blood-vessel is permeated by blood, the portion of earth permeated by water is called a “water-vein.
“Water rising up” means water that wells up in the form of a stream. “Only within” means precisely on the level ground inside the lake.
*Ubbhijjanakaudakaṃ* means water that, having welled up, remains right there. *Āgamanamaggo* means the path of approach leading from the outside toward a body of water.
Regarding *kālena kālaṃ*, this is a conventional expression (ruḷhīpada) similar to "one by one" (*eko ekāya*) and so forth;
thus it is said as *kāle kāle*. Regarding *anvaddhamāsaṃ*, here the prefix *anu* signifies pervasion; [it means] half a month of the rainy season.
The meaning is "half a month. It is the same in the case of "anudasāhaṃ" (day after day). "Vutthiṃ" means raining. "Anuppavaccheyya" means he would not wait for.
By the phrase "na vasseyya" (it would not rain), he shows that the derivation [of the word] comes from the root *vas* (to rain).
Regarding the feminine noun "sītā vāridhārā" (a cold stream of water), the explanation of its meaning as "sītaṃ dhāraṃ" is given in the neuter gender.

This is for the purpose of indicating that the word *dhāra* possesses both genders. "Cool" (*sīta*) means cool due to the absence of agitation, or white and pure due to the absence of being strewn with old leaves, grass, wood, and so forth;
for "white" (*seta*) and "cool" (*sīta*) are synonyms.

As to why only a pond of water that has overflowed is taken here and not the others, he removes this objection with the words "for the water rising up from below," and so on. Having risen up again and again...
"Breaking apart" means breaking open by repeatedly rising up in the manner of spraying droplets, or else being destroyed.

"Agitates" means churns. "Rainfall" means the act of raining. "By the falling of streams and by bubbles" means by the falling of streams of water and by the layers of foam consisting of bubbles of water that arise from right there.
Thus, for all three [elements], in their respective order—
Having stated that water from a lake should not be taken, he says that only water from a spring (*ubbhidodaka*) should be taken with the words “only when it is still,” and so forth.
In this context, “only when it is still” (*sannisinnameva*) means sitting properly or evenly; the intention is that it is perfectly motionless due to its lack of agitation.
“As if created by psychic power” (*iddhinimmitamiva*) means as if it were produced in that manner by one possessing psychic power (*iddhimat*).
*Therein*: in those words concerning the simile and the subject of the simile. *The rest*: [the passage] beginning with “it moistens,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Third Jhāna (231):
“A lotus pond,” etc., is a designation for both a grove and a forest; however, here [it refers to] “as far as the top, as far as...”
By way of the statement "and roots," because [the phrase] beginning with "some" must be understood as referring specifically to lotus thickets and so forth, it is the forest itself that is intended.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "‘Lotuses’ means lotus thickets; ‘therein’ means in the lotus forest," and so on.
For an analysis of a whole is made by means of its parts. Indeed, a single lotus thicket and so forth is simply a "lotus" and so forth, even if it consists of only four or five [plants].

However, it is conventionally designated as a "grove of blue lotuses" (*uppalavana*) and so forth; in the *Sāratthadīpanī*, even a body of water is described by way of its being a "place of blue lotuses" (*uppalinī*) and so on.
Regarding the phrase "herein" (*ettha ca*): this refers either to these three words or to the three meanings comprised by the terms *uppalaka*, *paduma*, and *puṇḍarīka*.
In the expression "white, red, and blue," only the blue lotus is mentioned; [the full list] is: white lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses.
This is the meaning. Whatever lotus it may be, it is indeed a *uppala*, because the word *uppala* applies to all of them by way of being a common name (*sāmaññanāma*).

Regarding the term *satapatta*, here the word *sata* is a synonym for "many," as in expressions such as "the sun has a hundred [rays], a hundred [spokes]," because it denotes a plurality rather than the specific number one hundred.
By taking it in this sense, the inclusion of even those with many petals within the category of *paduma* is established.
There it is. By "bowl" (patta), the petal of a flower is intended. According to the terminology of the Teaching (sāsana), the white lotus is the *paduma* and the red one is the *puṇḍarīka*;
however, in common worldly usage, they say "the red lotus (*paduma*) and the white *puṇḍarīka*. For it is said: "The *puṇḍarīka* is white;
the red is the *kokanada* and the *kokāsaka*. This is because [the term] causes dogs named *koka*, due to their red color, to howl.
Because it is summoned by those [names] and because they must be eaten by them, the lotus is called "Kokanada" and "Kokāsaka. As it is said:
"Just as the fragrant Kokanada lotus. However, the etymological meaning here is as follows: it guards the water (*udaka-pāti*), or it floats upon the water (*udake plavati*), thus it is an *uppala*.
It sports or moves in the mud (*paṅke davati gacchati*), or it sports or grows in a particular manner (*pakārena davati viruhati*), thus it is a *paduma*.
Its color is white (*paṇḍara*); or, because of its greatness, it is to be crushed or broken—thus it is *puṇḍarīka*, by changing the letter *m* to *p* and so forth.
For etymologists maintain that the word *muḍi* or *muḍari* has the sense of "breaking. And here, the derivation of the word is from the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
This is for the purpose of showing the state of being thoroughly moistened by water from the tip down to the root.
In the Pāli text, the expression “not emerged from the water” means simply that they have not come out of the water; it does not mean that they have gone into the water accordingly.

Thus he said, “from the water... gone. Here, however, the physical body (karajakāya) should be regarded as being like the blue lotuses and so forth, while the bliss of the third jhāna is like the water.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Fourth Jhāna: 233.

Since it is precisely the consciousness of the fourth jhāna that is called "by the mind" (*cetasā*), and since that [consciousness] is free from defilement and stainless due to the departure of the stains of the secondary defilements such as lust, therefore the very removal of those secondary defilements constitutes its state of complete purity; thus he said: "In the sense of being free from secondary defilements..."

"Completely pure. And because it is only for one who is already completely pure that there is a specific manifestation through specific conditions—a state of extreme clarity similar to the brilliance of refined gold resulting from polishing—it is said, "It is 'completely pure' in the sense of being luminous," meaning that extreme clarity itself is what constitutes complete purity.
Like lightning, its radiance flashes forth here and there.
“Radiant” (*pabhassara*) is like [the term] “radiant-beings” (*ābhassara*). Regarding the phrase “with a white cloth,” here the word “white” (*odāta*) is used as a quality-term;
thus it is said: “with a white... [etc. ...this. “For the purpose of pervading the temperature” means for the purpose of showing the pervasion of the hot temperature.
As to why, he says: “with a soiled cloth,” and so forth. “The temperature is not pervaded” means that, unlike with a white cloth, it is not specifically pervaded.
The intention is that there is no pervasion by temperature; it is merely slight. Therefore he said: "At that moment... it becomes powerful.

And by the phrase "by what is washed and purified at that very moment," the word *odāta* here signifies "purified" alone—just as in such expressions as "a householder dressed in white garments"—and not "white," since it refers to whatever is washed and purified at that very moment.
He shows [this] by means of the phrase "due to the pervasion of temperature.
But surely, in the Pāḷi it is said: "There was no part of his entire body that was not covered by the white cloth";
this describes the pervasion of the body by the white cloth, and not the pervasion of the cloth by temperature. So why, then, is it [said to be] the pervasion of temperature?

Regarding the phrase "stated here," he says by way of explanation, "Of this [body]," and so forth. Since the body made of primary elements (karaja-kāya) is like a cloth and the bliss of the fourth jhāna is like the pervasion of weather, it should be understood that the meaning is as follows;
for by this [comparison], since it is impossible for a white cloth to pervade the entire body, and because it would be inconsistent with the object of the comparison, [the word] "body" is used.
The cloth supported by that [body] should be understood; and by the mention of the cloth, he shows the pervasion of temperature conditioned by it.
For this simile was spoken in its indirect (neyya) sense. Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, employ diverse methods of teaching.
