For the yogi, the body born of kamma should be regarded as being like the cloth, because it is to be suffused with the bliss of the fourth jhāna, which is similar to the pervasion of temperature.
The bliss of the fourth jhāna is like the pervasion of heat, because it pervades the physical body (karajakāya) just as that heat pervades a cloth;
and the fourth jhāna is like a man’s body, because it serves as the basis for the bliss that stands in the place of the pervading heat.
Therefore he said, “Therefore,” and so forth. This indeed is a demonstration of the excellence of the statement just mentioned. And here in the Pāḷi, “by the purified... [the text continues].
By the inclusion of the word "with the mind" (*cetasā*), it should be understood that the Blessed One stated this to indicate the bliss of the fourth jhāna;

thus, it should be seen as having been said: "the bliss of the fourth jhāna, by means of the bliss of the fourth jhāna. But is it not the case that what is called the bliss of the fourth jhāna lacks the characteristic of gratification (*sātālakkhaṇa*)?
True; however, because its intrinsic nature is peaceful, it is equanimity itself that is intended here by the term "bliss."
Therefore it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*: “But equanimity, because of its peacefulness, is described as ‘happiness.
By this much means: from the point of illustrating the attainment of the first jhāna up to the illustration of the attainment of the fourth jhāna, according to the sequence of the words.
*Lābha* is obtaining; one who has that is a *lābhī*. One who is a possessor of the fine-material-sphere jhānas is a “possessor of fine-material-sphere jhānas.”
As in the expression, “one who obtains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,” *lābhī* means one whose nature is to obtain;
or, what is it that he is disposed to obtain? It is also appropriate to say “the fine-material jhānas. The same applies to the other [phrases].

“One who does not obtain the immaterial jhānas” should not be understood in that way; this is how it should be construed. Why? Because it says “for indeed,” and so forth, regarding all eight attainments.
It is said that [this is known] because of the inseparable connection with the attainment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) above. "In fourteen ways" means:

by way of the direct order of the kasiṇas, by way of the reverse order of the kasiṇas, by way of the direct and reverse order of the kasiṇas; by way of the direct order of the jhānas, by way of the reverse order of the jhānas, by way of the direct and reverse order of the jhānas;
by way of skipping jhānas, by way of skipping kasiṇas, by way of skipping both jhānas and kasiṇas; by way of shifting the factors (*aṅga*), by way of shifting the objects (*ārammaṇa*), and...

"By means of these fourteen modes mentioned in the *Visuddhimagga*—namely, by the transition of the factors as objects and by the determination of the factors and the determination of the objects"—this shows that although there are five kinds of mastery (vasībhāva) such as adverting and so forth regarding the jhānas, this fourteenfold mastery alone must absolutely be attained for the production of the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Thus it is said: "having practiced mastery in fourteen ways."

It has been stated; and by this it should be understood that he shows the inseparable connection between these [formless attainments] and the acquisition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), because without mastery over the formless attainments, attainment does not succeed even through mastery over the fine-material attainments alone.
He clears away the objection—“Should the analysis not be stated exactly according to the text?”—with the words beginning, “But in the Pāḷi...”.
What is meant is that this determination should be stated after extracting [the details] from the remaining portion of the text.
If this is so, then the immaterial jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*) should also have been included in the Canon; why, then, did the Blessed One leave them out, making the text incomplete?

Because all the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), especially those of the form realm, are based upon the fourth jhāna of the form realm. For even though they are invariably concomitant with it, [they are distinguished] specifically...
These [formless attainments] have the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere as their basis;
therefore, the teaching was given right there in order to make known their state of having that as a basis, and not because the immaterial-sphere jhānas have no application here. Thus he said:
"The immaterial jhānas must be brought forward and explained."
Commentary on the Discussion of Insight-Knowledge (Vipassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 234.
Regarding the objection—"Even though it was said, 'Furthermore, O Great King, monks,' why was the word 'he' spoken again to show what purpose?"—the author replies:
"He... [etc.]... shows," both according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*) and according to the implicit meaning (*neyyattha*).
The intention is that this was said in order to show a bhikkhu who has attained distinction through mastery (*vasitā*) in the eight attainments (*samāpatti*) already mentioned.
"The rest" refers to the remaining matter to be stated in the passage beginning with "When he is thus concentrated," along with its underlying intention (*sādhippāya*).
It is called "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) because it knows what is to be known; it is called "vision" (*dassana*) because it sees by making that very knowledge direct experience. Knowledge itself is vision.
"Knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*) does not refer merely to the eye and so forth; rather, it refers to all five kinds of knowledge.

Furthermore, showing by way of an enumeration of its meanings all those specific types of knowledge for which this term "knowledge and vision" is conventionally established within the Teaching, he said:
"Knowledge and vision is also called path-knowledge," and so on. "For the purpose of purification of knowledge and vision" means for the sake of the purification of knowledge and vision.
“Comfortable dwelling” means a pleasant dwelling that constitutes an Ariyan dwelling. “Of the Blessed One too” means that it was not only the deities who perceived this;
rather, at that time, knowledge and vision also arose in the Blessed One—this is the meaning. “One who has been dead for seven days” means one whose death occurred seven days prior.
“Kālāma” is stated by way of his clan. [The] liberation of mind. [In the commentary, it is *cetovimutti*].
This is the attainment of the fruit of arahantship. Because insight-knowledge knows the conditioned phenomena of the three planes— termed "the knowable"— as impermanent and so forth, and because,
starting from the contemplation of dissolution, it sees them directly, it shows that in the sense described above,
what is called "knowledge and vision" has arisen, by means of the passage beginning with “But here...”.
"Abhinīharati" means that he leads the mind, having drawn it away from other duties, toward insight;
this is the meaning according to the word (*saddato*). However, to show the intended meaning (*adhippāyato*), it is said: "Of insight-knowledge," and so forth.

For being directed toward that [insight] is precisely what constitutes its leaning toward it and so on; and that occurs when the mind is endowed with the eight factors in the manner already described.
It should be understood that this is simply the directing of the mind toward insight (vipassanā) as it arises through the sequence of insight meditation.

"Inclined toward that" (*tanninna*) means inclined toward that very insight. The other two terms are synonyms for that same state; their meaning is "sloping toward it," "bending toward it," "leaning toward it," or "lowing toward it.

This is stated precisely in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. It is "accumulated" (*upacīyati*), meaning it is built up and increased by means of boiled rice and sour gruel; thus, it is called "accumulation" (*upacaya*).
The phrase beginning with “with rice” was spoken with reference to the meaning of “it increases.

Regarding the expression “subject to the nature of being impermanent, to being covered, to being rubbed, to breaking, and to disintegrating,” the word *dhamma* (nature/phenomenon) should be applied individually to each term, such as “of an impermanent nature” and so forth.

In that context, “of an impermanent nature” means having a transient character due to its perishability. “For the purpose of counteracting bad odors” means for the removal of foul smells from the body.

"Anointing as its nature" (*ucchādanadhammo*) means having the essential quality of being something to be anointed; the sense is that it consists of rubbing with scented water and so forth because of the foul-smelling state of this putrid body.

For through anointing, there occurs the removal of the heaviness and foul odors caused by sweat, wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth, within the putrid body. It is like the great massaging performed by wrestlers and others for the purpose of increasing the strength of their arms and so on.
However, for the purpose of dispelling afflictions of the limbs and members, only minor massage is appropriate;
thus he said, "by means of minor massage," which means by means of gentle massage. "Of a nature to be rubbed" (*parimaddanadhammo*) means having the essential quality of being something to be rubbed.
Having thus explained the meaning by way of an unspecified time, he now explains the meaning by way of a specified time, beginning with the words "in early life."
And here, the word *vā* is not employed because the alternative sense is already understood through the demonstration of meaning; or it is indicated as being elided (*lutta*).
"At the time of infancy" means at the time shortly after birth. The connection is: "having laid [the child] down, it has the nature of being rubbed by means of stroking, pressing, and so forth.
"Moderate" (*mita*) is a neuter noun in the abstract sense; by that, it means "according to its measure."
Or it shows [the body] as slowly being stretched, pressed, and so forth. Here, "stretching" (*añchana*) means pulling; "pressing" (*pīḷana*) means massaging.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes bending, rising, and other such actions. "Even when thus maintained" means even when nourished with comforts such as ointments and the like.
"It breaks up" means it perishes by way of impermanence and so on. "And it is scattered" means that while breaking up in this manner, it [scatters] something...

One who does not accomplish the purpose becomes merely distracted. Thus, by means of these nine terms, the contemplation of the body as subject to the nature of arising and passing away is shown according to what is appropriate;
explaining this point, he said, "In that regard," and so forth. Therein, "by six terms" refers to these:
"possessing form, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, a mass of boiled rice and sour gruel, subject to anointing, subject to rubbing."
[The opponent asks: "It may be appropriate that the origin of the body is explained by the middle three terms, since they illuminate that meaning;
but how can it be appropriate to explain it as such by means of the [first] three terms—'possessing form,' 'subject to rubbing,' and 'subject to pressing'—since they do not illuminate that meaning?
[The response: It is indeed appropriate even for those [three].

Because it illustrates that meaning. For the term "rūpī" (possessing form) is an illustration of the meaning "one who possesses form" by means of the form consisting of temperature and nutriment which serves as its own condition. Indeed, this suffix *i* is used in the sense of "having the nature of" (*atthiattha*) when distinguished by connection with a condition.
And these two phrases, "of a nature to be rubbed" and "of a nature to be massaged," [are used] through the production of such form.
It is a "lamp" for the purpose of establishing the [correct] configuration.

"By two" means by the two phrases: "subject to breaking" and "subject to dissolution. And it is "dependent" because the insight-consciousness depends upon the heart-base (hadayavatthu), which is included within the body.
For it is precisely the insight-consciousness occurring at that time which is spoken of as "this is my consciousness" by way of immediate direct experience.
And because it does not function without being bound to the body, and because it takes as its object those material phenomena designated as "body," [it is so called].
235. It shines intensely, thus it is *subha*; it is a gem endowed with radiance.

To show merely the sense that the gem is "excellent" (*bhadrata*) by virtue of that very possession of radiance, it is said: "*Subho* means beautiful. It is precisely that which originates from a perfectly pure mine.
Regarding the phrase "the gem’s state of being of very pure birth," it says: "Of pure birth, arisen from a perfectly pure mine.

The meaning is: "arisen from a source of gems that is perfectly pure. For the specific distinctions in the birth of a gem, such as its being of the *kuruvinda* type and so forth, are rooted precisely in the purity of its mine.
However, the beryl gem intended here [was found] not far from Mount Viḷūra and the village of Viḷūra.
It is of a pure nature, for it has arisen for the most part from that [source]. Indeed, because it arose not far from a mountain named Veliūra and a village, it was known as "Veliūra";

and even though it occurs in the world of the gods, it received that same name because its color resembles that [stone], just as things in the human world receive names based on what they are called there.

In the world of the gods, among the deities, it is said by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla in the *Paramatthadīpanī* that its color is either like the neck of a peacock, or like the wing of a crow, or like the luster of a smooth bamboo leaf.
However, in the commentaries on the Vinaya, they say it is "the color of raw bamboo.
For this reason, it has also acquired the name "bamboo-colored" (*vaṃsavaṇṇa*). It is also described as "the color of a circle of kittens' eyes" (*mañjārakkhimaṇḍalavaṇṇa*).

And because it has been described thus, it is well known in this region as the "Mañjūsaka Jewel. However, its mention in the actual text (*pāḷi*) should be understood as referring to its state of being an exquisite gem worthy of being enjoyed by a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*).
As it is said: "Furthermore, Ānanda, the jewel-treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana;
it was a beryl gem, beautiful, of pure origin, and eight-faceted," and so forth. It is precisely by way of removing defects such as stones and grit that [it is called a gem].
By the phrase "with stones and pebbles removed," he shows the perfection of the preparatory work (*parikamma-nipphatti*).
It is the clarity due to the smoothness of the surface alone, not of the entire mass; thus he says, "clear" means "having a smooth surface.
To show that it is exceptionally bright because of that very quality, it is said, "well-purified. This is the excellence of the form of a gem used for enjoyment (*paribhoga-maṇiratana*).
“Possession of all excellent qualities. Therefore he said, “By washing, piercing, and so forth,” and so on. Washing is the state of being washed upon stones and the like;
piercing is the state of being pierced for the purpose of removing black spots and the like, and for the purpose of threading with string.
By the word “and so forth” (ādi), heating, smoothing, and other such processes are included. “Perfection of color” refers to the perfection of the color of the threaded string. Why?
It is said, “of such a kind,” and so forth; what is meant is that it is precisely for one who is thus clothed [in the body] that [the truth] becomes manifest.
The physical body made of kamma should be contemplated as being like a gem. Consciousness should be contemplated as being like the thread woven through it, because it remains having entered into it.
A bhikkhu who has attained insight is like a man with sight, because he sees it correctly; as for that man...
Just as the time when a gem becomes manifest is due to the manifestation of its physical basis, so too is the time when that bhikkhu’s body becomes manifest due to the manifestation of its basis.

Just as the time when a thread becomes manifest is due to the manifestation of what is dependent upon it, so too is the time when those phenomena become manifest due to the manifestation of their basis.
This is the explanation of the reason for establishing the simile here; for in some places it is said: "Insight-knowledge is like a thread woven through [a gem]."
Regarding the reading: because of the statement “and this consciousness,” the reading “consciousness” (*viññāṇa*) alone is more excellent;
or it should be “insight-consciousness” (*vipassanā-viññāṇa*). “Having directed the mind toward insight-knowledge” means having brought the mind forward facing insight-knowledge.

“Therein” refers to the beryl gem. “Of those having that as their object” means of those having the material phenomena designated as the body as their object. This refers to the three phrases beginning with “of those consisting of contact as the fifth.”
Since it is a qualifying term, and because the gender, case, and number are subject to modification according to the sense— as in the case of the subsequent term—

it should be understood that by the inclusion of "contact as the fifth" and by the inclusion of "all consciousness and mental factors," the phenomena grasped are indeed comprised within the conscious arising of insight (*vipassanā*).
For, because they fall under the category of insight-consciousness, they are designated as "insight-consciousness," just as a thread threaded through [jewels] is called "the string."
The statement spoken previously is not contradicted. But why is only the consciousness of insight (vipassanā-viññāṇa) mentioned?
Because of that very statement: “And this consciousness of mine is dependent here, bound here.

For, having contemplated with the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) by means of [the formula] “This indeed is my body,” and so forth, [one understands] “that very [consciousness] associated with the knowledge of insight...”
One attends to it by way of its support, object, and so forth, thinking, "Consciousness is attached here, bound here.

Therefore, it should be understood that only this [consciousness] can be grasped here, and not any other. Hence he said: "Or rather, it is the time when the insight-consciousness itself becomes manifest.
And because they are evident according to the method taught in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* and other texts, the [factors] beginning with contact as the fifth...

It should be understood that this is a "comprehension" because it encompasses everything without exception—namely, all consciousness and mental factors—and because, according to the literal sense, it constitutes the primary state of insight-consciousness as it has been taught.
Now, do these [characteristics] become manifest to the knowledge of reviewing, or to the person?
They become manifest to the knowledge of reviewing itself; however, because that [knowledge] has become manifest, they also become manifest to the person.
Therefore, it is said that "it is the time when [insight] has become manifest for the bhikkhu.

However, since this knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) occurs immediately after the knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa), it ought to be mentioned after the mundane superknowledges (lokīyābhiññā) and before the sixth superknowledge;
so why, then, is it mentioned before all the superknowledges?
Having shown a mere trace of the objection and setting it aside, he said, "And this is insight-knowledge," and so forth.
By the words "And this is immediately after path-knowledge," he shows the aforementioned trace of the objection.

Therein, "immediately after path-knowledge" is said with reference to the change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*), which constitutes the culmination of insight. For that very [knowledge] is immediately prior to the path of Arahatship, or indeed to all paths and fruits.
However, by the term "exertion" (*padhāna*), the inclusion of all insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) should be understood without distinction, because it is taught here in its general sense.

And by the word "path" (*magga*), only the path of Arahantship is meant, because that alone is included within the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), and because the objection arises in connection with those higher knowledges.
The insight-knowledge mentioned prior to the mundane higher knowledges—

It is not because these [mundane abhiññās] lack immediate succession that they are unhelpful; rather, it is because they are helpful by way of immediate succession to the supramundane direct knowledge (lokuttara-abhiññā) known as the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), which was mentioned previously.
Therefore, this should be stated after the mundane abhiññās and before the sixth abhiññā.
But why did the Blessed One not place them in that position where they would be helpful, but instead in a position where they are unhelpful?
For the word "said" implies a challenge. The passage beginning with "Even though this is so" shows the resolution. Therein, "even though this is so" means:
even if it is helpful because it immediately precedes the knowledge of the path in the sequence of knowledges, even so—this is the meaning.
"In the section on direct knowledge" refers to the section of the teaching spoken by way of the six direct knowledges. "There is no other section for this" [refers] to the five [knowledges].

When the mundane superknowledges (*lokiyābhiññā*) have been discussed—as in the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta* and other such texts—the sixth superknowledge must necessarily also be mentioned, because it is included therein by virtue of possessing the characteristic of a superknowledge (*abhiññālakkhaṇa*). Furthermore, insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*) is not a mundane superknowledge;

therefore, it should not be mentioned by inserting it between [the first five] and the sixth superknowledge, as it lacks the characteristic of a superknowledge and is not included therein. Thus, of this...
There is no opportunity for insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) between those supernormal knowledges (abhiññā);
therefore, because there is no occasion for it there, the intention is that insight-knowledge is explained here specifically after the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
With the words "And because," he states another point. Therein, the word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction; by it, it is indicated that not only is there no opportunity for insight-knowledge...
Regarding this, the Teacher has stated that the very same reason applies to "seeing," but furthermore, he uses the word *iti* here to collect this additional meaning.
However, those learned in grammar say that in such a context the particle *ca* has the sense of *vā* (or), and that it signifies an alternative (*vikappa*);
this too is indeed appropriate, because it is employed to indicate another meaning. For [the particle *ca*] is used for a meaning that exists and is intended to be applied by oneself.
Particles (*upasagga*) and indeclinables (*nipāta*) are like branches broken off when showing the path, and like lamps that do not appear when illuminating;
such is the case with these [particles]. And there is this verse:
“If the word *ca* is seen in the sense of indicating another meaning, [it functions as a particle].”
"In a compound, it should be understood as either a conjunction or an alternative by one who discerns.

The phrase "of one who has not performed synthesis" contains an implied causal reason; the same applies to "of one who has performed synthesis. Regarding the statement, "With the divine eye, he sees even a terrifying form":
here, having fashioned a terrifying form by means of the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*), [he sees it] with the fleshly eye (*maṃsa-cakkhu*).

"It should also be said that [the fear] is past. For even in this case, fear and terror arise in one who has attained the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) but has not fully understood the basis [of phenomena], just as it did for the Elder Mahānāga who lived at Uccavālika," so the Teacher said.

And just as it is here, so too in the passage "hearing a terrifying sound with the divine ear-element" (*dibbāya sotadhātuyā*), [it refers to hearing] a terrifying sound by means of the knowledge of the supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*).
It must indeed be said that even one who hears sound by means of the fleshly ear after having fashioned it [through supernormal power] experiences fear and terror;

for even in the case of one who has attained higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), if the basis [of the perception] is not fully understood, fear and terror arise, as in the case of the Elder Mahānāga, who lived at Uccavālika.

For according to the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), the elder, having conjured up and seen a completely white elephant-nāga accompanied by the cry of a crane, and having heard it, was seized by fear and terror.
It has been said. The connection is: for one who has performed comprehension by way of impermanence and so forth, fear and terror do not arise through the divine eye...
[and so on]. "The cause for the dispelling of fear" means the state of having performed comprehension by means of insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*);

the meaning is: for the purpose of accomplishing that, or by means of that. "Right here" means immediately after the fourth jhāna. Regarding the passage beginning with "Moreover," it follows the sequence of the text.
This demonstrates a more appropriate method. The happiness that has come through the succession of joy, rapture, and tranquility occurring during insight (vipassanā) is "the happiness of insight.
"Distinct" means separate from and unmixed with the jhānas, higher knowledges (abhiññā), and so forth; it is the fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) that is visible here and now.
Therefore, the Blessed One said in the *Dhammapada*:
“From whatever [aspect] one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for one who knows it,” and so forth. Here too it is said:

“This, Great King, is a fruit of recluseship visible here and now... and it is even more sublime. Therefore, by way of correlating this with the Pāli text, they say that this very method is more appropriate. “At the very beginning” means at the very start of the direct knowledges (abhiññā).

Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Mind-made Power (Manomayiddhiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 236–7. Regarding the term *manomaya*, here the word *maya* occurs in many senses, such as "another designation," "transformation," "completion of a phrase," and "arising.
However, in this context, it is stated that it means "produced by the mind" (*manena nibbattita*) in order to show that its sense is "arising."
The Master stated that the meaning is "produced by means of the mind of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*)"; however, in the *Visuddhimagga*, it is said:

"It is 'mind-made' (*manomaya*) because it is fashioned by means of the mind of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). Since it is produced by both the mind of direct knowledge and the mind of resolution, both of these explanations are indeed appropriate.
An "extremity" (*aṅga*) refers to a collection of specific parts such as hands, feet, and so forth; a "minor limb" (*paccanga*)...

The term *kappa-rajaṇṇu-ādi* refers to a constituent part within its respective aggregate. Regarding the phrase "with unimpaired faculties" (*ahīnindriya*), here "unimpairedness" (*ahīnatā*) means completeness alone, not the absence of deficiency;
and this state of completeness pertains specifically to the configuration (*saṇṭhāna*) of the eye, ear, and so forth.

Indeed, it is stated that "the faculties are unimpaired by way of configuration" in order to show that in a created form (*nimmitarūpa*), there is no such thing as sensitivity (*pasāda*). By this very [statement],...

It should be understood that the absence of his life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and the other faculties has also been stated. "By way of shape" means by way of a mere shape resembling a lotus petal and so forth, not by way of the faculties such as the sensitive matter (*pasāda-rūpa*) derived from the primary elements (*bhūta*) that are capable of receiving physical impact.

In order to support the meaning already stated—that he was "possessed of all limbs and minor parts with unimpaired faculties"—the author says, "by one possessing psychic power," and so on. "With unpierced ears" refers to the custom of his family.
One whose ears have not been pierced [is meant] for the purpose of adorning and ornamenting the ears; this is merely an illustration.
Therefore he said, “in every way,” meaning in all ways such as color, shape, specific parts, and so forth. “By him” means by the possessor of psychic power (iddhimatā).
This very meaning has also been clarified in the Pāḷi, which is why he said: “For even in the triad of similes beginning with ‘the reed from the sheath,’ ... it is stated.”
In some places, however, the reading is found as: “The passage beginning ‘From the muñja grass, the īsika reed,’ etc., is merely a simile;
for even that which is stated is only for the purpose of showing a state of similarity. Therein, by the phrase “merely a simile,” he excludes the indication of a different meaning;
but by the phrase “for even that which...,” he establishes its status as a simile. Furthermore, by the use of the pronoun *yaṃ* (which), without regard for a fixed referent—
He refers back precisely to the statement beginning with “from muñja grass, a reed,” etc.
“For the purpose of showing similarity” means solely for the purpose of showing similarity in shape, color, and specific parts. As to how there is similarity, it is said:
“for they are indeed similar to muñja grass,” and so forth. Muñja is a particular kind of grass with which one makes mats and other such items. “One should sweep away,” etc.
By the phrase "it is inside the sheath," he shows that it is precisely the sheath situated within that is intended. "Sheath" (*īsikā*) means a bamboo shoot (*kaḷīra*);
however, in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*, it is stated as "cane" (*kaṇḍa*). "Of a rounded sheath" means of a rounded sword-sheath. "Spread out" means a strip of cloth.
It is called a "box" (*karaṇḍa*) because it can be carried (*karaḍitabba*) or divided; it is a casket (*peḷā*). It can be carried...
"It should be loathed" refers to the *karaṇḍa*, that is, the slough. Here too, it is specifically the slough that is meant; thus he says, "‘The *karaṇḍa*—this also’," and so forth.

A "wicker basket" (*vilīvakaraṇḍa*) is a box. He clears away the objection—"Why is it called by the name of the snake's slough alone, and not by the name of the wicker basket?"—with the words, "For the snake's slough...
and so on. It is similar to the snake itself; therefore, it is said to bear that very name.
...it exists. However, in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā*, it is stated: “Regarding ‘from the *karaṇḍa*’: they say it means from a basket (*peḷā*) or from its skin (*nimmoka*).
In that context, the mention of the basket (*peḷā*) should be examined for its dissimilarity with the snake.
For if this were so, [the Buddha would have said]: “Great King, just as a man might pull a snake out from a basket (*karaṇḍa*). [But he did not say that. From the basket of a man...
This meaning would be contradicted by the simile of the snake-extraction. For he is not able to extract it from there with his hand;

thus, in response to this objection, he says “therein,” and so forth. Although the word “should extract” is an indefinite statement, because extraction by means of the hand is what is commonly understood, it has become like a demonstration of that. Therefore he says: “as if extracting with the hand. “For this,” and so forth.
This is the demonstration of the cause for being drawn out by the mind. Regarding snakes, it is said that they do not transcend their own species in five instances:
at birth, at death, when shedding their slough and waking from sleep, when engaging in sexual intercourse with one of their own kind, and when casting off their worn-out skin.

Thus it is said, "standing in his own species. He abandons [the fetters] while remaining only within the snake-species; he does not do so by means of the *nāga*-power (*iddhi*) as one who has assumed the form of another species.
The meaning is as follows. For this was said with reference to a Nāga of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*).

"As if devouring its own body" means as if devouring its own skin and its own body. "Loathing the old skin" means loathing the old skin that, due to decrepitude, is in some places detached and in some places hanging down.
"By four" refers to [the factors] such as "standing in one's own class," "relying on," and so forth.
"By one's strength, feeling disgust"—this refers to the four reasons already mentioned. "From that" means from the slough.
"By another" means by something other than oneself. "With the mind" means with the man’s mind alone, not with his hand.
It is just as if a man, having seen a snake, were to think, "Oh, would that I could extract this snake from its slough," and [then] [extract it] from the basket with his mind.
He might pull it out, and he would think: "This is the snake, this is the basket; the snake is one thing, the basket is another;
indeed, the snake has been pulled out from the basket. In the same way... [as before]... he creates from this body another body... [as before]...
"with unimpaired faculties"—this is the intended meaning here.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of the Modes of Supernormal Power (Iddhividhañāṇa), etc. 239. Just as well-prepared clay and other materials serve as the basis for the act of fashioning vessels and so forth, the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividhañāṇa) should be understood as the basis for the act of transformation (vikubbanakiriyā). 241.
As in the previous section on the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇappahāna), the mention of a "desert" is omitted; instead, there is only the mention of a "road journey" (addhānamagga).
It is for the purpose of showing the path of safety. But why is there a showing of only the path of safety and not the path through the wilderness?

Anticipating the objection, "Is this not merely a presentation of a simile? he says, "Because," and so forth. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "For it is free from fear" shows the reason for taking up only the path of safety.
[The phrase] "having made a cloth covering for his head" means for the purpose of warding off wind, heat, and so on.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the language is made complete in such a way for the purpose of applying the illustration to the object of the illustration through the perfection of the simile;

for the purpose of making the intended meaning of the object of the illustration easily understood; and for the purpose of pleasing the minds of those of discerning nature through speech endowed with reasons, examples, things to be analyzed, and means of analysis. This applies everywhere. "He defines it easily" means:
One perceives and delimits [the meaning] without difficulty and without effort. 243.
Considering that even a dull infant lying on its back is called "young" (*dahara*), the word "youthful" (*yuvā*) was stated for the sake of distinction;
thus, thinking that the meaning of the word *dahara* must indeed be specified by the word *yuva*, he explains it as "tender" (*taruṇo*).

It has been stated. Likewise, since there might be some youth who is not desirous [of adornment], and because he is by nature one who does not desire adornment, the phrase "by nature fond of adornment" (*maṇḍanajātiko*) and so forth was stated for the purpose of distinguishing him from such a person.

Considering this, the expression "endowed with youthfulness" (*yobbannena samannāgato*) was used to show the specific meaning of the word "youth" (*yuvā*) as it is qualified by the terms "fond of adornment" and the rest. For in the Pāḷi, the three terms follow their respective order.
The commentary was composed in that manner by way of expressing the relationship between the qualifier (*visesana*) and the qualified (*visesitabba*);
otherwise, a commentary accompanied by its full retinue would have had to be made for each individual word alone so as to convey the intended meaning.
He said "of the day," and so forth, in order to explain what was already stated as "having the nature of adorning. The word *kaṇika* is a synonym for *dosa* (fault), and *dosa* indeed...
The phrase "black moles, etc. is indicated by the words beginning with "black moles" (*kāḷatilaka*).

Black moles (*kāḷatilaka*) are spots the size of black sesame seeds, or they are dark and discolored, and are also called "mustard-seed-sized" (*sāsapabījika*). Moles (*tilaka*) are spots the size of sesame seeds.
A "deformity" (*vaṅga*) is a misshapen limb or a deformed member. "Youthful pimples" and so forth are facial blemishes, which are also called "rough pimples" (*kharapīḷaka*).
"Tipi" means "also. "Mukhanimittaṃ" means the reflection of the face. "Mukhadoṣo" (mouth-fault) refers to a fault that has gone into the mouth;
this is merely a term of definition (*lakkhaṇavacana*), because what is intended is the manifestation of even a non-fault in the mouth.

Alternatively, just as there is a fault in the mouth, so too a non-fault in the mouth is called "mouth-fault" by the elision of the middle syllable (*saralopa*), since it can be understood to have multiple meanings through a general designation (*sāmaññaniddesa*) and by the elision of the particle *pi*.
Or this meaning should be understood as follows: for even a meaning not explicitly stated is understood as if it were stated by way of summary.
Furthermore, the meaning here should be seen according to the method of *ekadesasarūpa-ekasesa* (retaining one part of similar forms), namely: *mukha-doso* and *mukha-adoso* together as *mukha-doso*.
For it is through the completeness of the meaning in this way that the statement, "the sixteenfold consciousness of others becomes manifest," is justified.
It is thus established. Therefore, this is said:
“The apprehension of what remains to be stated is done by means of an illustration and so forth, by the elision of words such as ‘api,’ or by the method of ‘single remainder’ (ekasesa).”
"In the case of dissimilar sounds, [the classification] is threefold; in the case of similar sounds, it is fourfold;
and it should also be understood by the discerning person through the description of common characteristics.
Thus, the sixteenfold consciousness described in the Canon beginning with "a mind with lust" and so forth [is explained].
245. "By means of the simile for the knowledge of past lives" (*pubbenivāsañāṇūpamāyā*) means by means of the simile shown for the knowledge of past lives, or for the knowledge of past lives itself.
To resolve the objection as to why only the triad of villages is taken as the simile in the Pāḷi, it is said:
"On that day," and so forth. Deeds performed on that very day are generally evident even to an ordinary person; therefore...
The intention is that on that day, the Blessed One accepted only three villages as being able to be reached, and nothing beyond them.

Although the mention of "that day" does not appear in the Pāḷi, it should be understood that the mention of "that day" was made in the Aṭṭhakathā because, by the acceptance of the three villages, the performance of the formal act (kamma) on that very day was intended. It is precisely by the acceptance of the three villages reached on that day...

And it should be understood that by means of the great resolves (*mahābhinīhāra*), the deeds performed by others who have attained the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsañāṇa*) in all three states of existence (*bhava*) are for the most part made manifest;
for it is for this purpose that the mention of the "triad of villages" is included. Regarding the phrase "deeds performed in the three states of existence":

this refers to actions performed in future lives (*abhisamparāya*), whereas in the present life (*diṭṭhadhamma*), one sees what was done previously, and [the phrase] "of one who has performed the task in the past" refers to the present.
247. In the Pāḷi, "crossing from one carriage-road (*rathikā*) to another carriage-road" means crossing from one road to another;
by this, the act of moving back and forth is shown, which is why it says "moving from one to another.

This is stated as "moving here and there according to their respective duties," for this is precisely the meaning since the words *rathikā* and *vīthi* have the same referent. "In a crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*)"—so it is said.

In the fourfold sequence of the cognitive process (*vīthi*), the bhikkhu’s body born of karma (*karajakāya*) should be regarded as a palace, because for one established therein, the vision of what is to be seen is accomplished.
For it is through the possession of the physical eye that the attainment of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) occurs. As it is said: "The arising of the physical eye is the path to the divine eye.
This very bhikkhu, having attained the divine eye, stands like a man possessed of sight.

Because of the seeing of that which is to be seen. Just as one entering a house and then leaving it, so too, entering the mother’s womb by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and leaving it by way of birth, the mother’s womb is similar to a house. For thus it is said:
“You call the mother a hut; you call the wife a nest. This is the *Aṭṭhakathāmuttaka*.

The method is as follows: because the personal existence (*attabhāva*) is like a house, one who enters it by way of rebirth is like one entering a house, and one who departs from it by way of death is like one leaving a house. For it is said:
"O builder of the house, you have been seen; you shall not build the house again."
"A being wandering from one state to another" means a being who repeatedly wanders through *saṃsāra*.
"In an open space" means in a location that is an open-air area. "In the center" means at a crossroads situated in the middle of the city.
"There and there" means in each respective portion of those various births. "Beings reborn" means beings who are arising. For by this [phrase], in each respective birth...
He speaks of beings who have been born and raised as "beings who migrate from one state to another"; however, by this, he refers to common beings whose timing is not thus restricted.
For in this way, their respective similes of "migrating" and "seated" persons become appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "the time when beings born in the three realms of existence have manifested," it refers to all those of the aforementioned types.
The inclusion of beings should be understood as being unrestricted.
Now, is this not a discourse on the divine eye? Then why is the inclusion of the fourfold existence (*catuvokārabhava*) made by saying "in the three realms of existence" (*tīsu bhavesu*)?
Anticipating the objection that "it does not have immaterial phenomena as its object," he says "And this... and so forth. Therein:
“This refers to the beings born within the three realms of existence”—this is the Master’s opinion here;
for if this were so, the objection raised by the authors of the *Aṭṭhakathās* in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself would be resolved.
However, this is our own preference: Is this not a discourse on the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and why then [does it say] “with the divine eye”?

By the passage beginning, "With the purified [vision] that transcends the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn," the inclusion of those who have entered the fourfold existence (*catuvokārabhava*) without distinction is established.
Indeed, in order to resolve the objection that this [knowledge] does not have immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) as its object, he says, "And this," and so forth.
In that context, "this" refers to the statement: "He sees beings passing away and being reborn," and so on.
For this being the case, the aforementioned inquiry was already addressed by the authors of the commentaries within the *pāḷi* itself.
To the same extent that it was addressed in the *pāḷi*, it is likewise absent from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) because there is no explanation of its meaning there.

"Merely for the sake of ease of teaching" means it was stated without distinction solely for the sake of ease of teaching; however, it does not apply to those who have entered the fourfold existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*) regarding the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

Because of the manifestation and existence [of beings]. Or, by saying "excluding the formless existence" (*ārūpabhava*) or "in two existences," one sees beings passing away from the sense-sphere existence (*kāmāvacarabhava*) and the fine-material-sphere existence (*rūpāvacarabhava*), or being reborn in the sense-sphere existence and the fine-material-sphere existence.

For a teaching stated in this way is easy to understand—both easily and with difficulty—through the manifestation of the distinctions between what is to be divided and the means of division, as appropriate.
And it does not exist; however, when stated in this general way, it is easy to understand both its pleasure and its lack of pleasure.
For the purpose of making it easy to teach and easy to understand is what is meant by the phrase "for the sake of ease in teaching. Why? He says: "In the formless [realms]...
there is none," meaning that because of the absence of material phenomena (rūpadhamma) which are the objective domain of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).

Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints (Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā) 248. Here, the fourth jhāna consciousness that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā) is to be understood;

it is not, as in the case of the mundane higher knowledges (abhiññā), the basis for those higher knowledges themselves. And "basis for insight" means that which has become the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for insight; and insight...
This insight is threefold, according to the distinction between types of persons who possess it:

the insight of great bodhisattvas, the insight of paccekabodhisattvas, and the insight of disciples (sāvakas). Among these, the insight of great bodhisattvas and paccekabodhisattvas is connected with knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*) and constitutes self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhu-ñāṇa*);
however, that of disciples is connected with knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).

It arises from the instruction of others. It is described in many ways in the *Visuddhimagga*— in various ways such as "having emerged from any one of the remaining fine-material or immaterial jhānas, except for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," and so forth—
and in many ways by means of any one of the methods for discerning the elements that were taught under the heading of the "definition of the four elements" by way of the formless [meditations].

It is analyzed according to various methods; moreover, because it proceeds through twenty-four hundred thousand million gates for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas, it causes one to grasp the embryo of preliminary knowledge—which serves as the foundation for the noble path-knowledge that is the support of omniscience—and brings it to maturity;
it is supremely profound, exceedingly subtle, and not shared by others.
There is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), which is called "the great diamond-knowledge" (*mahāvajira-ñāṇa*) in the commentaries;

and by way of its functional manifestation, there are the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) through which the Teacher daily moves about, numbering twenty-four hundred thousand times ten million, which serve as the basis for that [insight] that is divided into twenty-four hundred thousand times ten million varieties.
This practice of insight of the Buddhas is described in the *Paramatthamañjūsā*.
In the *Visuddhimagga-vaṇṇanā*, this was shown by the teacher by way of enumeration; therefore, it should be taken from there by those who desire it.
Here, however, only the insight (*vipassanā*) of the disciples is intended.
Regarding the phrase “for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints” (*āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya*), this is the dative case used in the sense of the purpose of the action; therefore—

Even when there is no word explicitly stating the purpose, the meaning should be understood by way of the purpose itself; thus he said, "for the sake of producing the knowledge of destruction" (*khayañāṇa*).
This applies to similar cases. Here, by way of a supreme description, Nibbāna and the path of Arahantship are called "destruction" (*khaya*);
the knowledge regarding that is "knowledge of destruction" (*khayañāṇa*). Its purpose or function is the production thereof; "for the sake of that" is the meaning. It destroys (*khepeti*).
"Destroying evil states" is *khaya* (destruction); this refers to the Path. However, that destruction of evil does not exist without the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).

Therefore, by the term "destruction" (*khaya*) in the phrase "knowledge of destruction," he shows that it is specifically the destruction of the taints that is intended, as indicated by the words "the destruction of the taints.
"Knowledge of non-arising" is knowledge regarding the Noble Fruit, which is the state of the non-arising of the taints. They have been destroyed.

"Khaya" (destruction) means the fruit [of the path], because the taints (*āsava*) are destroyed therein. One is a "samaṇa" (ascetic) by virtue of having stilled evil; and this state of having stilled evil occurs, in the primary sense, only through the fruit of Arahantship.
Therefore, it is said: "In the phrase 'one becomes a samaṇa through the destruction of the taints,' the fruit is meant here.

Furthermore, "khaya" means the state of being destroyed. It is "khaya" because the taints are destroyed therein; thus, it refers to Nibbāna. However, in the compound "āsavakkhayā," [the word is used] by way of a collective compound (*samāsa*).
Because it is stated as having two aspects, the term *āsavakkhaya* (destruction of the taints) is included in the extraction of the meaning for the phrase “the destruction of the taints.
The verses beginning with “One who observes the faults of others” are from the *Dhammapada*. In that context, *ujjhānasaññino* means those who have a perception of reproach.
*Ārā* means far away. For this particle has the sense of distance, as in such expressions as “I smell the water-born [lotus] from afar” (*ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ*). The reading *ārā* is also found.

The word *ārā* should be understood as a single indeclinable particle used in the sense of distance, just like the word *ārā*. Indeed, that very term is cited in the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*).

Although it is stated in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* that "one has gone far away (*ārā*) by means of what is reckoned as the path of Arahatship," nevertheless, one who increases formations through the increase of the taints (*āsava*) is very, very far from the state of non-formation (*visaṅkhāra*).

Therefore, since the term "destruction of the taints" (*āsavakkhaya*) can also be a designation for the "dissolution of formations" (*visaṅkhāra*) in the passage "far from that is the destruction of the taints," he says "Nibbāna.
"Destruction" (*khaya*) means the act of destroying; it is the momentary cessation of the taints. The rest are its synonyms. The construction is:
"the breaking up of the taints is called destruction. Here, however, both Nibbāna and the Path [are included] because they are inseparable.
For the destruction of the taints does not occur by means of the path alone without taking Nibbāna as its object.
"Inclined toward that" means inclined toward that knowledge of the destruction of the taints. The remainder is a synonym for that very thing.
In the text, "This is suffering" refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering having been delimited and without exception at that time for that bhikkhu.
In order to show that this is a demonstration of the state of having been apprehended through direct experience (*paccakkha*), the words "to such an extent" (*ettakaṃ*) and so forth were spoken.

For therein, "this much is suffering" is a demonstration of its state of being apprehended by way of delimitation; "not more than this" is a demonstration of its state of being apprehended without remainder.

Therefore he said, "the entire truth of suffering," and so forth. Understanding precisely as it is (*yathābhūtaṃ*) occurs solely by way of penetration into the specific characteristic (*sarasalakkhaṇa*).
By the phrase "through the penetration of the specific characteristic" (*sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena*), he shows what is meant by "understanding.

"Specific characteristic" (*rasa*) is so called because it is one's own nature (*sabhāva*), which is to be tasted—that is, to be known. Its own nature is its "specific characteristic" (*sarasa-lakkhaṇa*);

the meaning is: "by penetrating that through non-delusion. And what is called "penetration through non-delusion" is such that, when that knowledge has proceeded, subsequently [there is the realization] of the truth of suffering.
There is no delusion regarding the discernment of identity and so forth; it is simply the occurrence of that [discernment]. Therefore it is said: "He understands it as it really is.
By the term "productive" (*nibbattika*), the etymological derivation is shown: "That from which suffering arises is the origin of suffering" (*dukkhasamudaya*).
"Both of those" refers to suffering and the origin of suffering. "Having reached that state" refers to Nibbāna.

"Having come to that which has become the cause by way of being the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya) for the Path. For "basis" (ṭhāna) is said to mean "cause," in the sense that the fruit stands therein because it is dependent upon it.
"Having reached both of those" is stated as if there were an attainment of both by the person who possesses them.
Indeed, the attainment of Nibbāna belongs to the person alone, by virtue of the person's act of making it its object.

It does not belong to both. Furthermore, *patvā* means "by way of reaching" (*pāpuṇana-hetu*), that is to say, by way of entering [meditation] through the person’s taking [an object] as a mental object (*ārammaṇa-karaṇa-vasena*).

For it is well known in the grammatical treatises (*sadda-sattha*) that the suffix *-tvā* occurs in the sense of a cause (*hetvattha*) even when the agents are identical, just as when they are different.
*Appavatti* means the cause for non-occurrence; it is so called because "both of those do not occur by means of this," and it refers to the state of non-occurrence.

Or, having established that "neither of these two occurs here," this [term] demonstrates the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) as "that in which suffering ceases" (*dukkhaṃ nirujjhati ettha*) or "by means of which [it ceases]" (*etenāti vā dukkhanirodho*).
Furthermore, the inclusion of the origin of suffering (*dukkhasamudaya*) should be understood as being for the purpose of showing its cessation as well, since that which produces it also ceases.
The word *ta-* [in *tappahānāya*] refers specifically to Nibbāna.
The word *ayaṃ* is stated again [in the compound] as "returns. For a pronominal term (*sabbanāmika*) takes on the gender of either what has already been stated or what is about to be stated.
*Tassa* means "of the cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodhassa*). *Sampāpakaṃ* means "truly excellent" (*sammadeva pāpakaṃ*) by way of realization.
And by this [explanation], it is called "leading to the cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodhagāminī*) because it leads to the cessation of suffering, or because one goes by means of it.
"This very same practice is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"—this shows the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*).
"By way of defilements" means by way of the defilements known as the *āsava*s. He spoke again showing that very same thing by way of the *āsava* terminology;
therefore, the intention is that there is no fault of redundancy here. For the quality of teaching by way of synonyms (*pariyāya*) is indeed a unique attribute of the Buddha’s teaching.

This meaning has already been stated below. Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that the taints (*āsava*) have a designation as the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) alone, and not as the other truths?

Then why is it said that [the Blessed One] spoke thus, showing again by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*) those very truths already shown in their own form, now by way of the defilements (*kilesa*)?
True. However, because the remaining truths are connected with them, the designation of their origin (*samudaya*) and so forth is also applicable to them.
It should be understood that this was said [in this way].

For since the origin of the taints (*āsava-samudaya*) and so forth are connected to the taints as they occur in the exposition of the truth of suffering (*dukkha-sacca*), it should also be construed as: "while showing the truths.

Furthermore, because the passage begins with "for the sake of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (*āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāya*), it should be seen that only the taints are mentioned here, and not the remaining defilements (*kilesa*), as they were not introduced in that manner. Thus, [the text says]: "The mind from the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*)..."
By the passage beginning with “is liberated,” the liberation from all defilements is stated by means of the very pinnacle of liberation from the taints (*āsava*).
By the passage beginning with “one understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’” the mixed path itself is taught here, because the mundane insight is mixed with the supramundane path;
thus it is said, “he spoke of the path that has reached its culmination together with insight. [The phrase] “for one who knows and sees”:

By this, all three—full understanding (*pariññā*), realization (*sacchikiriyā*), and development (*bhāvanā*)—are stated, because the accomplishment of these four functions occurs precisely through the comprehension of the Four Noble Truths.

However, the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) is stated by the phrase "is liberated" (*vimuccati*) through the method of elimination (*pārisesato*). Thus he said, "it shows the moment of the Path.
For indeed, the four functions are accomplished only through the comprehension of the Four Noble Truths. As it is said: "Now, this suffering..."
“Bhikkhus, regarding these states unheard of before, the eye arose in me that ‘the noble truth has been fully understood’,” and so forth.
This is the method independent of the commentaries: “For one who knows and sees” is a description of the cause; the construction is as follows:

“By reason of knowing, by reason of seeing, the mind is liberated even from the taint of sensual desire,” and so on. And here, [it should be noted] that between the actions of knowing and seeing and the action of being liberated—

And although there is simultaneity [of the cause and effect], nevertheless, even for phenomena that are simultaneous, the state of being a condition and the state of having arisen from a condition is obtained through the category of "conascent" (sahajāta) and so forth;
thus, they say this is intended to show a specific distinction within the category of causes.

Furthermore, by the inclusion of the "taint of existence" (bhavāsava), just as with the lust for existence (bhavarāga), the view of existence (bhavaditthi) is also fully encompassed; therefore, the "taint of views" (diṭṭhāsava) is also included.

The inclusion [of this reading] should be noted; however, the reading "the mind is liberated even from the taints of views" (*diṭṭhāsavehi pi cittaṃ vimuccati*) is seen in some places, but it is not ancient and should be understood as having been written down later through negligence.

This is because it has been commented upon in exactly that way in many works, such as the *Bhayabherava-sutta-vaṇṇanā*. And here, although in the Pāḷi the penetration of the Truths refers to an unspecified person...
Although it is stated by way of indefinite time, nevertheless, with reference to its presence at the moment of clear realization (*abhisamaya*),
the designation of the present tense is made in the phrase "knowing thus, seeing thus. And while that [knowledge] may indeed, for some,
be of the past time from the moment of the path onwards until the present, its very first occurrence as past time is by virtue of the moment of the fruit (*phalakkhaṇa*).

"It should be understood" means that by the phrase "when it is liberated," the moment of the fruit (phalakkhaṇa) is indicated. "Reviewing knowledge" refers to the reviewing knowledge of the fruit, because it has been stated as such.
By mentioning that [specific type], however, the remaining types should be understood without exception due to their inseparability from it;
or alternatively, they may be taken partially, since review can occur even when incomplete. This is indicated by the phrases beginning with "Birth is exhausted."
“With the words ‘there is no more of this state of being’ at the conclusion. “Of that” refers to the knowledge of reviewing.

“Ground” means the sphere of occurrence. Now, one might raise the objection: “Since it was stated, ‘When liberated, [one knows] “I am liberated,”’ the fruit itself is its ground in the sense of being its object;
so how can its ground be shown by such statements as ‘birth is exhausted’? To resolve this, [the text says] “Therefore, etc.”

It has been said. However, because through the reviewing of abandoned defilements one understands "birth is exhausted" since even existing karma will not lead to rebirth in the future, and because through the reviewing of the path and so forth one understands "the holy life has been lived" and so on, it is therefore said that "birth is exhausted" and so forth demonstrate his plane. "By that knowledge..."
The meaning is: by means of the fivefold reviewing knowledge grasped according to the literal expression and through its inseparable connection.
Regarding the phrase "Birth is exhausted," he raises an objection as if in the presence of others—using the words "But which...
and so forth—in order to make it easily understood for those who hear. Having revealed the intention with which that objection was raised, he provides the answer.
Wishing to speak, he said, "Not yet for him," and so forth. Indeed, this objection was raised with the very meaning about to be stated—namely, "not yet...

because it still exists"—in mind. In that regard, "his past birth has not yet been exhausted" means that for this bhikkhu, his past birth has not yet been exhausted by the cultivation of the Path. He states the reason for this: "because it was already exhausted previously."
The intention is that [birth] is "exhausted" by virtue of ceasing even earlier than the cultivation of the path. The construction is:
"Birth for him is not exhausted by the cultivation of the path in its future state. Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because there is no effort toward the future.
And this is said by taking the commonality of the "future state" itself, in order to clarify the underlying purpose of the objection through a figurative expression.
The meaning is that there is no application of effort for the purpose of discarding a future distinction, because there is no such application in the cultivation of the path regarding the future.
For it is said that application is possible only with respect to what exists, not with respect to what does not exist. However, a "future distinction" is intended here;

and indeed, even with respect to its discarding, effort is certainly obtainable. Therefore he says, "But as for that which belongs to the path," and so forth. This is what is meant by "a future distinction."
And the distinction of the immediately preceding birth is said to be that which is liable to arise when the path has not yet been developed.
The construction is: "His present birth has not been exhausted by the development of the path. Regarding this, he states the reason:

"Because it exists," meaning because it exists as being comprised within a single existence (*ekabhava*). For birth is characterized by the first manifestation in each respective existence. "That which... [the text continues].

However, it should be understood that by the passage beginning with "panā," the exhaustion of future birth itself is demonstrated by way of the destruction of the cause of defilements through the cultivation of the path.

The mention of the three types of existence—namely, "in one-, four-, and five-aggregate existences"—is for the purpose of showing the complete exhaustion of birth according to the method already stated;
here, too, there is an elision of the latter member of the compound in the first two preceding terms. [The phrase] "distinguished as one, four, and five aggregates" [is explained as follows]:
The same method applies here as well. The passage beginning with “That he [knows]” is the statement of the resolution to the challenge, “And how does he understand it?
Therein, “that” (*taṃ*) refers to birth as previously described. “He” (*so*) refers to the bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted.
“Having reflected upon” (*paccavekkhitvā*) shows the reflection on the defilements abandoned prior to the act of understanding. And by doing so, through a succession of reflections—

It should be understood that full understanding (*pajānanā*) is established in this way. Indeed, the two present-tense verbs "knowing he fully understands" (*jānanto pajānāti*) are stated solely for the purpose of further clarifying the subsequent reflection;
the meaning is that having become one who knows, or by means of knowing, he is said to fully understand.
As for "dwelling in the holy life" (*brahmacariyavāsa*), from the perspective of the exalted description, it is simply the production of the holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*); thus he said.
“Parivutthaṃ” means dwelt upon completely and without remainder; that is the meaning. But why does he understand this by way of the past time?
To answer this inquiry, he says: “For together with the puthujjana-kalyāṇaka,” and so forth.
For even the puthujjana-kalyāṇaka, whose characteristics were described below, is one who has set out for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.

Because it has been stated exactly so in such discourses as the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga-sutta*. "They are called those who dwell" means they are indeed dwelling, not those who have already completed their residence.
"Therefore" means because of having completed their residence. But is it not the case that in the Pāli text, by the passage beginning "He understands as it really is:
'This is suffering,'" only right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is mentioned, and not right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*) and the rest? Why then [is this said]?

Is it not stated in a general sense regarding the Eightfold Path that "the sixteenfold task—consisting of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing—is brought to completion by means of the four paths with respect to the four truths"? [The answer is:

Because right intention and the others also function by way of accomplishing these four tasks. For, in the case of right view, it functions by way of accomplishing the tasks of full understanding and so forth with respect to the four truths.
When [the path] is occurring, the occurrence of right intention and the other remaining factors is indeed in accordance with the full understanding (*pariññā*) of the truth of suffering;
furthermore, their occurrence in relation to the other truths by way of the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*) and so forth is quite evident.

Considering that in the cases of the cessation of suffering and the path, the full understanding, realization, and cultivation occur respectively only for the sake of abandoning the origin (*samudaya*), they serve that very purpose.
In order to clarify the intended meaning of the phrase “what was to be done has been done” by means of their inclusion, the words beginning with “therefore” (tenā) were stated.
By the phrase “the root of suffering has been cut off,” he clarifies that very same point through another mode of expression.
As for the question, “Why, however, is there a past designation here in ‘what was to be done has been done’? he says: “The virtuous worldlings and so forth,” etc.
By the phrase "for the sake of this state" (*itthabhāvāya*), he shows that "thisness" (*itthatta*) refers to these modes;

the word *āya* has the sense of a recipient (dative), meaning "for the purpose of that. Furthermore, those modes intended here are thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) and the rest, which constitute the activity of the Noble Path.
Thus it is said: "for the sake of becoming thus possessed of the sixteen functions. For, when one reviews the Path, by the power of the Path—
They become manifest when the path is reviewed, because even the reviewing of that function is easily accomplished.

Thus, having explained how there are sixteen functions in the four paths collectively by way of four functions each, [it is said] that among those functions, abandonment alone is primary because the others—full understanding and so forth—exist for its sake; therefore, that alone is distinguished.
He said, "Or for the sake of the destruction of the defilements," in order to make this clear.

Furthermore, it should be understood that after demonstrating the method of reviewing through a succession of reviews according to the previous method, he spoke thus now in order to demonstrate specifically the method of reviewing the defilements abandoned because of their importance. In the second alternative:

This "pakāra" means "thus" (itthaṃ); its state is "itthattaṃ. Here, the word *āya* indicates that it functions as an ablative sense (*nissakkattha*) belonging to a term expressing the recipient of an action, as shown by the phrase "from this state of being" (*itthabhāvato*).

However, when one says "from this very manner," there is no actual difference in meaning between the manner and that which possesses the manner. For if there were such a difference, [the manner] would belong to that very [possessor].
The suffix *-pakāra* would not [otherwise] be [used]; therefore, the word *itthaṃ* denotes that which possesses a mode (*pakāravantavācaka*).

Furthermore, although there is no difference in terms of the actual referent (*atthato*), there may be some sense of differentiation by way of the conceptualization of distinctions such as part and whole;

thus, he shows that the word *itthatta* denotes a mode (*pakāravācaka*). This is the method found here in this commentary (*ṭīkā*), as well as in the commentaries on the Majjhima Nikāya, the Vinaya, and so forth.

Those skilled in grammar, however, desire this according to the following characteristic of occurrence (*pavatti-nimitta*): "That which has this mode (*pakāra*) is *itthaṃ*; [thus] it possesses a mode.
For the application of secondary derivatives (*taddhita-vutti*) is manifold. Its state is *itthattaṃ*, meaning "the mode. Demonstrating this meaning, he said:

"Because of this state of being thus, from this very such mode. This same method applies as appropriate even in the first alternative. Now, regarding "the present continuity of aggregates" (*vattamāna-khandha-santāna*):
This is the explanation of the words as they appear. "The others" refers to the future. The reading currently found is: "But these five aggregates, having been fully understood, remain.
However, the reading cited in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*, the *Vinaya-ṭīkā*, and other works, as well as the reading indicated here in this *ṭīkā*, is:
"But these five aggregates, designated as the final existence (*carimakattabhāva*), having been fully understood, remain. In that context, "designated as the final existence" means...
They are said to be the final existence by virtue of being included within a single continuum. "Thoroughly understood" means known by way of cutting them off through the Path.
"They remain" means they remain without a foundation or without a place to stand. By this, he shows that those aggregates lack a foundation because they lack a root of non-understanding (*apariññā*).
For a foundation is rooted in non-understanding; but due to the absence of that, there is the state of being without a foundation.
As it is said: "Bhikkhus, if there is lust for edible food, if there is delight, if there is craving, consciousness becomes established and grows there," and so forth.

He illustrates this with the simile, "like trees whose roots have been cut," meaning that just as trees whose roots have been cut remain without support or place to stand due to the absence of roots, so too do these [defilements].

"Because of the absence of a root in the form of non-comprehension. This is the application of the simile here. "By the cessation of the final consciousness" means by the cessation of the consciousness at the moment of Parinibbāna.

"Without fuel" means without a substrate (anindhana). "The state of being beyond designation" means that while certain aggregates exist, there is a designation established through various conceptual constructions;
because those [aggregates] are absent, there is the state of being beyond designation due to the absence even of that currently existing designation.
They will go. For *paṇṇatti* and *paññatti* are one in meaning, just as "fifty" (*paññāsa*) and "fifty" (*paṇṇāsā*).
Grammarians say that *paññāsa* is a substitution for *paṇṇa*.
(249) It is called a "concordance" (*saṅkhepa*) because it is mostly abbreviated or contracted; it refers to the summit of a mountain, for that—

Gradually, from the foot of the mountain, it becomes extensive, then contracted, and finally diminished. Therefore he said, "on the summit of the mountain" (*pabbatamatthake*), which means on the peak of the mountain.
This is the method not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāmuttako nayo*):

that which is summarized and reckoned by way of being a mountain is a "summarized region" (*saṅkhepo*); it is a location included within the mountain. [The phrase] "in that location included within the mountain" refers to this.
“*Attha*” means: *anāvilo* (unclouded) means not turbid; and since that lack of turbidity in him is due to the absence of mud, he says “*nikkaddamo*” (free from mud).
That which moves even while sleeping or lying down is *sippi*; small *sippi* are *sippiyo*, formed by changing the letter *ka* to *ya*;
it is also called “*muttiko*” (the pearl-oyster). That which flows or spreads is *sambuko*; it is what is called “*jalasutti*” (water-cord) or “*saṅkhalikā*” (a chain).
And they so designate [it]. Because a collective compound (samāhāra) is predominantly used in the neuter gender, it is stated as "the shells and the oysters" (*sippiyasambuka*).
It is the same in such cases. "Gravel" (*sakkharā*) refers to stones the size of a fist. "Potsherds" (*kathalāni*) refers to fragments of broken pottery.
Since the word *ghaṭā*, which denotes a collection, is seen to have a feminine gender as well, the author shows the meaning of the term "cluster" (*gumba*) by means of this word "mass" (*ghaṭā*).
And although in the passage, “The oyster, the shellfish, the pebbles and gravel, and the schools of fish—
whether stationary or moving,” the pebbles and gravel are indeed stationary while the oysters, shellfish, and schools of fish move as well as stay, nevertheless, by way of their association,
all are said to be “moving” as if they were all moving together; thus, showing this meaning, [the text says] “even while staying...”
He said, “Even while walking,” and so forth. Therein, by the words “the pebbles and gravel remain just as they were,” he shows the meaning according to what is possible;
but by the words “but just as,” he shows the method of concomitance (*sahacaraṇa*). The word *pana* indicates a lack of approval; the sense is “nevertheless.
“From time to time” (*antarantara*) means even when there are cows standing among many other cows that are present. “Cows” (*gāvo*)—
"Cows. "The others too" means both those standing and those sitting. They are called "moving" by way of their tendency to move together.

Regarding the phrases "standing still" and so forth, the intended meaning is this: because even for oysters, shells, and schools of fish, there is no absolute certainty regarding the act of standing due to their connection with the activity of moving, one must take as the object something that stands absolutely and never moves at all, such as a pebble or a stone.
It is said that "the oyster, the shellfish, and the shoals of fish are standing," but this is not said with reference to the act of standing on their part.
Rather, with reference to the act of moving on their part, the word "pi" (also/even) should be understood as being elided here in the phrase "carantampi" (even while moving).

The other pair is mentioned thus by way of the individual terms: the oyster, the shellfish, and the shoals of fish. And the other two are likewise just the oyster, the shellfish, and the shoals of fish.
Regarding the statement "while walking," here too, with reference to their state of action, there is an elision of the word *pi* (also) as in "even while standing";

thus, in this instance, the method of "concomitance" (*sahacaraṇanaya*) has been shown by the masters of the Aṭṭhakathā. However, the Elder Dhammapāla has also presented the method of "taking according to what is available" (*yathālābhanaya*).
For it is said: "What is the use of this concomitance? [One should take] according to what is available."

In this context, it should be understood as follows: the construction should be made thus—"standing by way of pebbles and gravel," and "both standing and moving by way of oysters, shells, and schools of fish.

This is the method of concomitance (*sahacaraṇanaya*) regarding the mere teaching of a meaning even when it is not explicitly obtained, by way of its association; and [it applies] to a meaning taught by way of commonality.
The method "according to what is available" (*yathālābhanaya*) applies in both ways: with respect to analysis by way of possibility, and with respect to analysis according to what is available.

Thus they say here: in the Commentary, by the statement, "The pebbles and gravel remain fixed, while the others both move and remain fixed," the method according to what is available is shown, because the meaning has been analyzed according to what is possible.

Regarding the phrase “But as for ‘yathā panā’,” etc., it should be understood that although the method of association (*sahacaraṇanaya*) is not found [in the primary text], it is revealed merely as a teaching by way of the companionship of the meaning;
thus, this too is entirely faultless because the meaning is appropriate, and because such a presentation is possible in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
