The passage beginning with “Tatthā” is the correlation of the simile. [The word] “tīreti” means...
"On the bank of a water-lake" (*udakarahada*). Now, the term "water-lake" (*rahada*) is sometimes used for the ocean, as in such passages as:
"There is a deep lake there; the ocean has flowing waters. In other instances, it refers to any reservoir of water, as in:
"There is a lake there called Dharaṇī, from which the clouds rain down, and from which the rains spread forth. Here, too, it refers specifically to a reservoir of water. That—
It is called an *udakarahada* (lake) because it gives a secluded place (*raha*) by means of water; here, the vowel *o* is changed to *a*.
However, those learned in grammar say: "It is an *udakarahada* because it carries water (*udakaṃ harati*)," according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*).

By the words "To this extent," etc., [the text] shows that starting from the knowledge of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*) demonstrated immediately after the fourth jhāna, the aforementioned meaning [is established].
The summary. Therein, "by this much" means by this extent of the sequence of words beginning with, "Furthermore, O King, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated...
he directs his mind toward the knowledge and vision [of the way to cessation]," or by that which is of such measure.
"Insight-knowledge" refers to the insight-knowledge shown under the name "knowledge and vision," and by showing it as a separate enumeration.
It should be understood that among the three methods to be discussed following the fourth jhāna below, the suitability of the third method alone has also been demonstrated.

Although the inclusion of mind-made knowledge (*manomaya-ñāṇa*) within the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) was stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, it is treated separately here because it is taught as a distinct item in the Canon;
and such a separate teaching is for the sake of a specific, visible fruit of recluseship (*sandiṭṭhika-sāmaññaphala*).

It should be seen. Because the two types of knowledge—the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) and the knowledge of how beings fare according to their deeds (yathākammūpagañāṇa)—are not explicitly mentioned in the text, it is stated that they are "accomplished by means of the divine eye. This means that since those two knowledges are accomplished by means of that [divine eye], they are included by the mention of it.
For the divine eye indeed possesses both the knowledge of the future and the knowledge of how beings fare according to their deeds.
"Paribhaṇḍāni hontīti" means: "The divine eye-knowledge" refers to the divine eye-knowledge shown by the name "knowledge of passing away and rebirth.

However, since the classification of the objects of all ten knowledges has not been presented in the *Visuddhimagga*, the passage beginning with "Of these" (*tesaṃ*) was stated in order to show the classification of the objects of those knowledges that have not yet been mentioned there. "Of these" (*tesaṃ*) refers to the ten knowledges. "Therein" (*tattha*)...
Regarding that classification of objects, or those ten knowledges: from the distinction of plane, it is limited (*paritta*) or sublime (*mahaggata*);
from the distinction of time, it is past, future, or present; and from the distinction of continuity, it is internal or external. Thus, insight-knowledge has seven kinds of objects.

Its classification of objects is indeed by way of the triad beginning with "limited object" (*parittārammaṇa*), and not by way of the tetrad beginning with "path-object" (*maggārammaṇa*). It consists merely of the created base of visible form (*nimmita-rūpāyatana*).

It is also appropriate to say that it is simply the visible-object base (rūpārammaṇa) created by oneself, or simply the visible-object sphere (rūpāyatana) existing within the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya) created by oneself.
For this is stated because that knowledge proceeds by taking only the visible-object sphere as its object while the mind-made body is being conjured up;
it is not because of the absence of the odor-sphere (gandhāyatana) and so forth therein. Indeed, a mass of material form is never devoid of the odor-sphere and the rest.
"It exists" refers to a created form (*nimmitarūpa*) that is entirely and completely perfected. Therefore, he said "having a limited, present, external object";
the meaning is that it has a threefold object according to the distinctions of plane, time, and continuity, respectively.

Although the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) likewise has a single dharma as its object by way of Nibbāna, it is shown to have a threefold object—limited, etc.—by way of the triad of limited, immeasurable, and indeterminate objects; thus he said "having an immeasurable, external, and indeterminate object."
It has been stated. For that [object] is immeasurable in its aspect as a protective charm (*paritta*), external in its aspect as internal, and of unspecified range in its aspect as past.
By the term "superior" (*seṭṭhatara*), he shows that the words "more excellent" (*uttaritarasadda*) and "more refined" (*paṇītatarasadda*) are synonyms. The Peak of Jewels (*Ratanakūṭa*).
Just as the peak (*kūṭa*) is the highest part of a gabled house (*kūṭāgāra*), so too, because the Blessed One’s teaching culminates in Arahantship,

he said, “by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship. He brought the teaching to its conclusion— that is, [a teaching] which exposes the doctrines of the heretics, which destroys various kinds of hypocrisy, flattery, and other forms of wrong livelihood,

which illuminates the supreme practice of extreme effacement adorned with the threefold morality, and which is beautified by superhuman states such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).

He brought to completion the teaching on the fruits of recluseship—which is not shared by others and is adorned with the fourteen kinds of great fruits—like a jeweled house with a pinnacle of jewels, namely the pinnacle of Arahantship, by means of the words "I am liberated"; for the meaning is that the fruit of Arahantship was taught thereby.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse concerning Prince Ajātasattu’s declaration of his status as a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

250. Having thus provided a commentary on the meaning of the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* as taught by the Blessed One, [the author] now provides a commentary on the meaning of the passage beginning with "When this was said," which was compiled by the Dhamma-recorders.
In order to first demonstrate the connection, he says "The king," and so forth. Therein, "therein" (*tattha*) means in each respective fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphale*).
Or in the sections of the suttas. *Karaṇa* means making; thus, one who makes [the Buddha] say "well" (*sādhu*) in such ways as, "Excellent, Blessed One!
Excellent, Sugata! and so forth. "Beginning, middle, and end" refers to the beginning, the middle, and the end of the teaching.
Having heard with care, with respect, and with reverence—here, the word "having reflected" (*cintetvā*) expresses an action occurring at a prior time. These are the questions.
The construction is as follows: "Alas, for a long time I have been asking many ascetics and brahmins;
even though I asked in this way, like one threshing chaff, I did not obtain any essence. Likewise, "Oh, how great is the perfection of the qualities of that Blessed One who... [and] answered!
Alas, for a very long time I have been deceived, not knowing the power of the qualities of the One Possessing the Ten Powers."
“I am deceived. This means that one is deceived by ignorance—that is, ensnared—and covered over by delusion; this is what is meant.
Therefore he said, “not knowing the power of the qualities of the One Possessing the Ten Powers. For a general statement stands in relation to a specific instance.
The connection is: “having reflected, he makes it known. Even for one capable of leaping, there may be no leaping despite the presence of the rapture of uplift (*ubbega-pīti*).
He said, “It may be,” meaning, “his body was suffused with the fivefold joy (*pīti*). “Suffused body” (*phuṭasarīra*) means a body touched (*phusita*);

it does not mean a body pervaded (*byāpita*), because [the Buddha] was not pervaded by every kind of joy. “That” is a manifestation of his own confidence and a proclamation of his status as a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
This was undertaken by the compilers of the Dhamma.
“Abhikkanta” means transcended or departed; and since the state of having departed is itself destruction (khaya), he said, “it is seen in the sense of destruction.
For it has been stated thus: “The first watch has passed away. “Abhikkantatara” means exceedingly desirable or delightful;
and such a thing is called beautiful or auspicious (bhaddaka), hence he said, “in the sense of beauty.”
The verse beginning with “Who am I to me? and so forth is found in the *Vimānavatthu*. Therein, “who” (*ko*) means which one among the gods, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so on;

“me” (*me*) means to me; “feet” (*pādāni*) refers to the feet—this is a change of grammatical gender; “by power” (*iddhiyā*) means by such divine power; “by glory” (*yasasā*) means by such a retinue and attendants;
“shining” (*jalanti*) means blazing and radiating light; “by its excellence” (*abhikkantena*) means exceedingly.
"With lovely" means with what is desirable; "with beautiful" is what is meant. "With complexion" refers to the color of the skin, the radiance of the body's appearance.
"Illuminating all directions" means illuminating all ten directions. The connection is: "Who pays homage, making a single radiance and a single light like the moon and like the sun?"
*Abhirūpa* means having an exceeding form, endowed with a magnificent complexion. *Abbhānumodanā* means in the act of expressing approval, in the state of being greatly delighted.

To the question, "For what purpose is the expression 'in the act of expressing approval' used?", he says "Therefore," and so forth. This determines the scope of the repetition (*āmeḍita*) by way of resolving the objection:
"Granted that it is appropriate in the context of expressing approval, why is this stated twice?"

“By means of this grammatical characteristic (*saddalakkhaṇa*) ‘in fear, in anger,’ etc., which serves as the cause, it is stated thus; that is to say, ‘by this and that object’—this is what is meant.

Alternatively, they explain the connection by saying: having shown the meaning through the repetition (of the word) “Excellent, excellent, venerable sir,” he spoke thus while determining its specific scope.
In that context, regarding examples such as “thief, thief! or “snake, snake!”—
Reduplication occurs in cases of fear, as in “pierce, pierce! and “strike, strike!”; in anger, as in “well done, well done!”;
in praise, as in “go, go! and “reap, reap!”; in haste, as in “come, come!”;
in wonder, as in “thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha’”; and in cases such as “Come, venerable sirs! Come, venerable sirs! [in which it expresses urgency].

In laughter, such as "Where is my only son? Where is my only son? and the like; in sorrow, such as "Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness! and the like; and in confidence, such as "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!

The particle *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*samuccaya*) for what is not explicitly stated; by it, the inclusion of censure (*garahā*), disrespect (*asammāna*), and so forth should be understood.
For instance, in "A sinner, a sinner! and the like, there is censure; in "Handsome, handsome! and the like, there is disrespect. Thus, among these...
In the nine [instances] and in other objects as well, a wise person should employ repetition (*āmeḍitavacana*); the meaning is that he should apply it.
Repetition (*āmeḍana*) is uttering again and again; or, that which is repeated—that is, uttered again and again—is called *āmeḍita*.
It is the speaking of the same meaning two or three times. For the root *meḍ* signifies madness, but with the prefix *ā-*, it refers to uttering two or three times.
Just as in the phrase, "This very thing when Vāsava repeats my words.
Having thus shown that it was spoken twice by way of repetition (*āmeḍita*), he now says "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth,
demonstrating that this was not spoken twice solely by way of repetition, but rather also by way of two distinct meanings.
Some say that after showing the meaning by way of repetition (*āmeḍita*), he spoke thus also by way of distributive iteration (*vicchā*);
however, that is indeed incorrect, because that which is to be distributed has not been stated twice [in this case].

For *vicchā* is the desire for distribution, wherein that which is to be distributed is expressed two or three times by means of the distributor—whether it be a quality, an action, or a substance—as in "Village after village is delightful" (*gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo*). In that instance...

“Exceedingly wonderful” (*abhikkanta*) means “to be approached with delight”; its state [of being so] is due to its extreme desirability, hence it is said “exceedingly desirable” (*atīṭṭha*), and so forth.
These three terms are synonyms. “In this” refers to the two occurrences of the word *abhikkanta*.
It is expressed in the neuter gender in reference to the word “exceedingly wonderful,” yet that speech of the Blessed One is indeed the teaching of the Dhamma.

Having said this, he spoke [the words] “This, namely, the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma. The meaning is: that which has been heard by me as the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma—this speech, designated as the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, is excellent (*abhikkanta*).

For even such a restatement is indeed appropriate because there is no difference in its actual meaning, as in the case of [passages] such as “where a gift is said to be of great fruit. “Excellent” (*abhikkanta*)...

Or rather, this is merely a demonstration of the meaning of what was said; therefore, a change of gender and case-ending should be understood by way of the meaning, and here the change of case-ending occurs by way of a change in grammatical function (*kāriya*). For "word" (*vacana*) is the remainder [of the implied sense]:
"Excellent is the Blessed One’s word! That teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One which has been heard by me is excellent, truly excellent."

The meaning [is as follows]. Regarding the second phrase as well, this method should be applied accordingly, starting with: "It is expressed in the neuter gender with reference to 'loveliness' (*abhikkanta*) as a state of serene confidence (*pasādana*).

By the words "the word of the Blessed One" and so forth, he demonstrates the nature of the two meanings. Therein, "from the destruction of faults" means from the eradication of the defilements such as lust (*rāga*), which are faults.
"By way of attaining qualities" means by way of bringing about the attainment of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
Regarding those qualities that the teaching brings about, since it was stated "by way of attaining qualities," one must show the qualities that constitute the primary ones among those very qualities;

therefore, in order to first show those primary qualities, it is said: "by way of generating faith (*saddhā*) and by way of generating wisdom (*paññā*). For mundane [qualities] have faith as their primary factor.

The qualities (guṇa) are supramundane, with wisdom as their preeminent feature; this is a description of their preeminence, since it is possible to apply this teaching also to the pairs of virtue and concentration, and so forth, which are to be realized through attainment.

Furthermore, he shows another two meanings by means of the phrase beginning with "sātthato" (possessing meaning). It is "possessing meaning" (sāttha) because of the perfection of its purpose, namely virtue and the rest.

It is "possessing phrasing" (sabyañjana) because of the perfection of its essential nature and its etymological expression. It is "of clear words" (uttānapada) because of the employment of sounds that are easy to understand.
It is profound in meaning because its sense is difficult to discern due to its subtle and delicate nature.
It is pleasant to the ear because it employs sounds that are smooth, soft, and sweet. It is heart-stirring because its meaning is vast, pure, and lovely.
It does not exalt oneself by dispelling pride and arrogance. It does not disparage others by crushing stubbornness and contentiousness. It proceeds with the intention of promoting welfare.

It is cool with compassion because it pacifies the fever of passion and other defilements in others. It is bright with wisdom because it dispels the darkness of the afflictions (*kilesa*). "Bright" (*avadāta*) and "white" (*odāta*) are identical in meaning.

It is charming to the senses through its sweetness like the song of the *karavīka* bird. It is capable of withstanding scrutiny due to its extreme purity and consistency between what precedes and what follows.
It is pleasant to hear precisely because of its charm to the senses. It is capable of withstanding scrutiny because it proceeds from an intention directed toward the welfare [of others].
And because it is beneficial when being investigated—thus the meaning should be understood here. Furthermore, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the following are included]:

because it turns back the wheel of saṃsāra; because it sets in motion the wheel of the True Dhamma; because it destroys false doctrines; because it establishes right doctrine; because it uproots the roots of unwholesomeness; because it plants the roots of wholesomeness;
because it closes the doors to the states of misery; because it opens the doors on the path to heaven; and because it pacifies the obsessions.
The inclusion of such phrases as "the eradication of underlying tendencies" (anusaya-samugghāṭanato) should be understood.
The word *pi* (also) has the sense of a conjunction, indicating that it is not merely by these two phrases, but also by the four similes that follow.
The phrase "Those with eyes see forms" is a mere indication of the manner of the fourth simile, "one should carry an oil lamp."
But it is not by seeing another example that he says, “by four similes.
“Placed face down” means placed face down by someone. “Born facing downward” means born with its face downward by its very nature.
“He would open it” means he would make it wide open. The phrase “taking it by the hand” is stated for the purpose of illustrating the act of pointing it out; [he points it out] “facing eastward,”...
It means that rather than merely saying words such as, "Go facing north," he should take [the person] by the hand and show the way without doubt, saying, "This is the path;
go thus. "Kāḷapakkhacātuddasī" refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
A "ghanavanasaṇḍa" is a dense forest thicket characterized by a continuous growth of trees. A "meghapaṭala" is a mass of clouds.

"Covered by clouds" is what is meant. "One would turn upside-down what was turned upside-down" means that one would turn upward—that is, place facing upwards—a certain vessel that had no support for anything to be placed within it, by way of providing it with a support. Because it was produced facing downwards, it is "turned away" (*vimukha*);
because it was set down with its mouth downward, it is "fallen into what is not the True Dhamma" (*asaddhamme patita*). Thus, these two phrases [explain] the phrase "turned upside-down."
The two points as they have been shown should be applied appropriately, not according to their numerical order.
For this king was indeed averse to the True Dhamma by his very nature, but he fell into unwholesome states because he was incited by the evil friend Devadatta to commit patricide and other such acts.
The connection is with the phrase "by the Blessed One causing him to emerge [from that state]."
The phrase beginning with “of the Blessed One Kassapa” is intended merely to show the implication of a meaning that was not explicitly stated by the king at that time.

Granted, sensual desire and the other hindrances are also concealers because they function as obstacles; however, wrong view is especially a concealer because it causes beings to adhere to what is false.
Therefore, he said, “concealed by the thicket of wrong view. Thus the Blessed One said:
“Monks, I say that wrong view is the supreme fault,” [AN 1.310; identical in meaning]. This means it is concealed by the thicket known as wrong view.

By saying, “He reveals the teaching concealed by the thicket of wrong view,” he establishes that for all Buddhas there is but one connection and one teaching, and thus [he speaks] regarding Kassapa’s...

It should be understood that the teaching of the Blessed One also constitutes a single teaching together with this [text]. For it is stated exactly so in the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries;
and by taking it thus, the statement regarding the opening of the teaching—which had been concealed by the thicket of wrong views—becomes appropriate.
The entire path leading to the states of misery, comprised of unwholesome states, is called a "bad path" (*kummagga*) because it is a contemptible path. Of right view and the rest...

Because they are the direct opposites [of the right path], the eight factors of wrongness—wrong view and so forth—are called the "wrong path" (micchāmaggā), considering them to be a false and erroneous path in contrast to the path to liberation (mokkhamagga).
For this very reason, with reference to their being the opposites of both [the mundane and supramundane paths], it is said: "by one who reveals the path to heaven and liberation.
Indeed, every wholesome state (kusaladhamma) is a path to heaven. [The eight factors] beginning with right view...
The qualities of rightness (*sammattadhammā*) are the path to liberation. A lamp dependent on ghee and such substances is not as bright as one dependent on oil;
thus, there is the mention of an "oil-light. "Dhāreyya" means he should bear [it]; the meaning is that he should collect it or kindle it.

"The forms of the Jewels beginning with the Buddha" refers to the sense-spheres of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) belonging to the three Jewels beginning with the Buddha. Of those forms of the Jewels beginning with the Buddha, [of that which conceals...]
The dispeller of the darkness of delusion is likewise the lamp known as the Teaching.

Having analyzed these two by way of their common substratum, it is said, "by the bearer of the lamp of the Teaching that dispels the darkness of delusion which conceals that [Truth]," in the sense of being its sustainer and kindler.
"By these synonyms" refers to the aforementioned acts of turning up what was overturned, uncovering what was concealed, pointing out the path, and bearing the oil-lamp.

It is "summarized" by way of the fourfold similes and their respective objects of comparison, or by the various modes of exposition that reveal the destruction of the manifold wrong livelihoods such as hypocrisy and flattery already mentioned.
Therefore he said: "The Dhamma has been proclaimed in many ways.

By the words "Thus," etc., he shows the connection with the reading beginning with "This I... [referring to the *Saccavibhaṅga Sutta*]. Through the state of a clear mind, he displays the aspect of clarity.

He performs [this]. And the phrase beginning with “by this teaching” was spoken in order to make known the meaning that the state of having a confident mind arises precisely from hearing this teaching.
“By this teaching” means by that which has become the cause. “The manner of confidence” refers to the honor that should be performed for those who are confident by virtuous people.
“Refuge” means a resort; therefore he said “the ultimate resort” (*parāyaṇa*). Furthermore, the quality of being an ultimate resort consists in the prevention of what is harmful.
And it is said, "by the accomplishment of welfare," as in: "O protector from evil (agha), and ordainer of welfare (hita). *Agghassa*: This is the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative;
the meaning is "from evil" (*pāpato*). Some also say it means "from suffering" (*dukkhato*). *Tātā*: He protects (*tāyati*) by providing refuge, thus he is a "protector" (*tātā*).

*Hitassa*: This is the genitive case used in the sense of the accusative. *Vidhātā*: He ordains (*vidahati*), that is, he makes arrangements, thus he is an "ordainer" (*vidhātā*). "Thus... [and so forth].
By saying "with this intention," he shows that "the word *iti* is indicated here as elided (*lutta*), and it has the sense of 'manner' (*ākāra*).
"Going for refuge" (*saraṇa*) means going. It is either associating with [the Buddha] with the aim of welfare, or knowing [him].
And having done so, in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā and other texts, the meaning is stated together with the word *iti*, as in "I go for refuge. For here, this is not the verb-root *gami*.
Like the verb *nī* (to lead) and others, it takes two objects; therefore, just as one says, "He leads the goat to the village," it is not possible to say, "We go to the Blessed One for refuge.
Rather, it should be said, "We go [to him], [thinking of him] as 'refuge'.
Thus, it should be understood that here the word *iti* is indicated by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭha*). And having done so, [the meaning of] "he who goes to the Buddha for refuge" [is established].
Therefore, the objection raised in the *Khuddakanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*—“He would go to the Buddha or take refuge”—is without foundation.
For the grammarians do not treat the word *gami* as belonging to the class of roots beginning with *duh*. Let it be that the word *gami* has a single object;
nevertheless, in such passages as “he goes indeed to the eastern direction, he goes to the western direction,” and so forth...
Is it appropriate for the two words "the Blessed One" and "refuge" to have a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) as if they were identical?
No, because it is impossible for those two words to possess a state of common substratum.

For if that state of common substratum were intended, even one who approaches the Blessed One with a hostile mind would be said to have "gone to the Buddha for refuge. This is because [the word] specified as "the Buddha" is...

"He has gone to that very refuge"—here there is no need for an impossible meaning; therefore, "Bhagavant" is an illustration of the sense of the act of going, while "refuge" (saraṇa) illustrates the mode of going.
Thus, according to the method already stated, the meaning should be understood through the elision of the suffix "-ti.
This same principle applies here to the phrase "the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. And in this regard, there are these verses:
“Because of its being a single action with ‘going,’ one should understand that there is an elision of the suffix -ti;
because of the possibility of opposition [to the sense], there would not be identity of meaning.
Therefore, the preceding word alone is the indicator of the meaning ‘to be gone to.’”
"Regarding the mode of going to another, it is said [in the context] of the three refuges.
However, one who says, "With this intention, I go to the Blessed One," thereby determines that going for refuge (saraṇagamana) is indeed resorting to or knowing [the Buddha] with this very intention.
In that regard, among the phrases beginning with "I go," for each preceding term...
Each subsequent phrase of meaning—“I go,” “I resort to,” and so forth—is a distinct expression of meaning intended to show that this [act] is not shared with others.
For "resorting" (*bhajana*) is approaching with the intention of seeking refuge;
"serving" (*sevana*) is remaining in his presence; and "waiting upon" (*payirupāsana*) is attending by performing duties and services.

Thus, in every respect, he demonstrates that this is unique and not shared with others. Having thus shown the meaning of "going" (*gati*) for the word "I go" (*gacchāmi*), he says "or thus" (*evaṃ vā*) and so forth in order to show its meaning as "awakening" (*buddhi*). Therein, "thus" refers to the intention expressed by "The Blessed One is my refuge," and so on.
Now, one might raise the objection: why is the meaning "I awaken" obtained for the word "I go"?

He clarifies this with the passage beginning, “For those...,” and by this he demonstrates that, apart from the method of etymological derivation (*nirutti*), the meaning of the verbal root *gam* is simply "understanding" (*buddhi*) by its very nature.
The term "of roots" (*dhātūnam*) refers to those designated as primary words (*mūlasadda*), such as *i*, *yā*, *kamu*, *gamu*, and so forth.
By the two phrases, “having reached the path” and “having realized cessation,” only those at the stage of the fruit (*phalavastha*) are shown, not those at the stage of the path (*mārgavastha*).

Showing this, he said: "And for those who practice according to the instruction. Now, is it not the case that even a "good worldling" (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) is said to "practice according to the instruction"?

Although he is so called, only those established on the path (*maggaṭṭha*) should be described in that way in the primary sense (*nippariyāyena*), and not the other, because of the latter's lack of entry into the fixed course of rightness (*niyāmokkama*).
For it is they alone who [are said to be] "not falling into the states of misery" (*apāyesu apatamāne*).

"...maintains [the precepts]," it is said. For by entering the fixed course of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*), the possibility of liberation from the states of misery (*apāya*) arises. Thus it has been stated by many commentators on the Vinaya and Suttantas.
This is said in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*) with reference to those who are liberated from the states of misery by way of entering the fixed course of rightness;
however, in a secondary sense (*pariyāyato*), one is liberated from the states of misery by virtue of the non-occurrence of such states.
It should be understood that even a "virtuous worldling" (kalyāṇaputhujjana) is indicated by the phrase "practicing according to the instruction.
For he is described in such suttas as the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga* as one who has entered upon the practice for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry;
in this regard, the young brahmin Chatta in the *Chattavimāna* serves as an illustration. [This applies to one] who has attained the path and realized cessation.

And by the phrase "having ensured that the person who practices according to the instruction does not fall into the states of misery," the construction is to be understood with the remainder of the text.
For, by the first two words in the past tense, only the stage of fruition (*phalaṭṭhāna*) is grasped;

and together with the last word in the present tense, only the stage of the path (*maggaṭṭhāna*) along with the noble worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) is grasped. Furthermore, by the word "not falling" (*apatamāne*),...
The demonstration of the mode of retention shows that it retains by means of preventing falling; or rather, it is a demonstration of the essential nature of retention.

Retention indeed consists solely in the prevention of falling, and this prevention of falling is itself an emergence from the round of existence (*saṃsāra*) by way of destroying the defilements that produce rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*) and so forth.
For the phrase "in the states of misery" is stated with emphasis because those places abound in suffering.
The meaning should be understood as follows: it maintains [the mind] by preventing it from falling into any of the sufferings of saṃsāra (*vaṭṭadukkha*).

For it is said in the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā*: "In this context, the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) emerges from the state of the woeful realms (*apāyabhava*); the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmimagga*) [emerges] from one portion of the happy states of the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*);

the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) [emerges] from the sense-sphere existence; and the path of arhatship (*arahattamagga*) [emerges] from the fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpārūpabhava*)."

"Thus it is said that one emerges from all states of existence. Having established this, in order to show by way of its own nature that both the Noble Path and Nibbāna are, in the ultimate sense, what is called "Dhamma"—the former because it leads to deliverance, and the latter because it is the cause for the accomplishment of that goal—it is stated:
"In terms of its actual meaning, it is both the Noble Path and Nibbāna. For it is when the Noble Path obtains Nibbāna as its object...
The accomplishment of that purpose and this specific meaning are established by the Pāḷi itself; thus he says, "And this has been stated," and so forth. *Yāvatā* means as many as there are.

*Tesaṃ* refers to those same number of phenomena (*dhammā*). In the phrase "it is declared as the foremost" (*aggo akkhāyati*), the vowel *o* is changed to *a*, and the letter *m* is inserted, resulting in the expression "it is declared as the best" (*aggamakkhāyati*).
Furthermore, in the word "it is declared" (*akkhāyati*), the particle *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*).

Or it has the sense of "kind," by which it includes such Sutta passages as, “Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is declared to be the foremost among them.
Alternatively, by the word “in detail,” the inclusion of the remainder is intended.
For, since the noble fruits have been severed by the Path—as indicated by such statements as “by that faith which is not yet stilled”—[they are no longer subject to arising].

The state of being the Dhamma is obtained through this method: because the [path] has the function of pacifying and abandoning the defilements, it is conducive to deliverance and culminates in deliverance;
whereas the scripture (pariyatti) is conducive to deliverance because it is the cause for the attainment of the Dhamma that leads to deliverance.
Therefore, including both of these, he said, "And not only... and so forth.
By the words beginning with "For it is said," he shows that this very meaning is established by the text itself. Therein, regarding the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna*:
it is said that there was a brahmin youth named Chatta in Setavyā;
having learned his craft from the brahmin Pokkharasāti at Ukkaṭṭhā, he was traveling toward Ukkaṭṭhā thinking, "I shall give a heavy teacher’s fee. Then, for him—
The Blessed One, seeing him on the way beset by robbers and reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, taught the procedure for going for refuge by means of verses.
For that one who had reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, his thirty-yojana palace was the Chatta-māṇavaka palace.
Indeed, even in the world of the gods, he retained his name from the time of his human existence, just as [one speaks of] "Maṇḍūka the deva-son" or "Kuvera the king of the gods."

Furthermore, because this discourse has the *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna* as its subject matter and cause—using the term "Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna" by eliding the latter member of the compound—it is called the "Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna" teaching, beginning with the words:
"The sun does not shine so brightly in the sky, nor does the moon or Phussa shine, as...
This verse is included therein; therefore, it should be understood that the meaning is "in the teaching on the subject matter of the Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna."

Because by means of this, all lust—comprising such divisions as sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and lust for existence (*bhavarāga*), which has manifested since beginningless time—is dispassioned (*virajjati*) and abandoned, it is "the fading away of lust" (*rāgavirāga*);

that is, the Path. Because craving, reckoned as "agitation" (*ejā*), and sorrow characterized by inward brooding have been entirely exhausted at its arising, there is no agitation and no sorrow in this; thus it is "undisturbed" (*aneja*) and "sorrowless" (*asoka*).

The fruit. In the commentary on that [passage], however, it is said: "It is 'without sorrow' (asoka) because of the subsiding of the defilements which are the causes of sorrow remaining due to craving.

Having fully understood Nibbāna as the unconditioned (asaṅkhata)—meaning it is unconditioned because it is not produced by conditions coming together, and it is the ultimate reality (paramattha-dhamma) because it maintains its own intrinsic nature—the commentary on that [passage] states: *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.*

However, it is said: “‘Dhamma’ means a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*). For this is a phenomenon to be grasped by way of its intrinsic nature—namely, the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna—and not the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*) by way of conventional designation (*paññattidhamma*).
This being so, the word *dhamma* should be applied to all three instances. And by the term “non-repulsive,” only Nibbāna is taken there, [as it is said]: “There is nothing here...”
Having taken [something] as "even slightly repulsive," and because it demonstrates non-opposition, "not repulsive" means that which is not opposed, or rather, that which is desirable and sublime.
It is "familiar" (*paguṇa*) because it occurs in a familiar form, or because it manifests distinguished qualities;
as it is said: "O Brahmā, perceiving harm, I did not speak the familiar, sublime Dhamma among men."
The construction is: "the aggregates of Dhamma have been spoken. Thus, here by all four terms, only the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) is taken;

however, in its commentary, it is said: "It is 'sweet' because it is desirable at all times—at the time of hearing, at the time of investigation, and at the time of practice—and because it has proceeded from the perfection of inspired eloquence which is supported by omniscient knowledge."

"It is said: 'By the three terms—*paguṇaṃ*, *suvibhattaṃ*, and [the context of] *pariyattidhamma*—one refers specifically to the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*). It is *paguṇaṃ* because it is well-practiced due to its continuous recitation and its subtle nature;

it is *suvibhattaṃ* because it is well-analyzed by means of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth, by way of the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth, and by way of the summaries (*uddesa*) and so forth.
Just as at the time of first entering [the stream], even at the time of bathing, for one who is speaking..."

Even for one who hears [the teaching] as if it were before them, the word "this very" (*idheva*) is used in the sense of immediate proximity to express the state of being directly perceived by both parties.
Furthermore, the term "Dhamma" is a general designation for all four kinds of Dhamma mentioned above.

For even the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*), by merely establishing one in the refuges and the precepts, protects one from falling into the states of misery through practice that accords with reality.
And it should be understood that this very *Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna* is the proof for this meaning.
Having made the aforementioned Dhamma manifest by way of its commonality, he spoke again, saying "this.

And because this *dodhaka* verse is adorned with three instances of the letter *bha*, therefore, in the third line, the letter *ma* is even more abundant in the word *madhurasadda* [and] in the words *ariyacariyā* and so forth.
It should be understood that it is "without fault" because it is composed of many syllables and words. Regarding the phrase "by means of what is comprised of view and virtue":
this refers both to the view described as, "That noble view which is leading, which leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering;
he dwells having attained conformity in view with such a view," and to [the virtue]... [which are]... *yāni*...
"Those virtues are unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration;

he dwells having attained conformity with such virtues"—this refers to the state of being "united" (*saṃhata*) with respect to the virtues thus described, meaning through conformity in both view and virtue. "United" (*saṃhata*) means joined together (*saṅghaṭita*).
"United" is what is meant. For noble persons (ariyapuggala), even when standing anywhere far apart, are indeed united by the harmony of their own virtues.
With the words "For it has been said," etc., he supports [the argument] with a direct scriptural citation (āhaccapāṭha).
"In which" means in which Saṅgha. "Given" refers to the gift of food and other things to be given that have been relinquished; and here, because of the constraints of the verse meter—
There is the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsikalopa*). This is a *Dodhaka* verse. “They say it is of great fruit” means that the Buddhas and others have declared it to be “of great fruit.
Furthermore, the word “and” (*ca*) in the phrase “in the four” (*catūsu*) is stated as an addition, yet it is not a fault according to the method already explained.

[The term refers to] those who are pure because they are utterly purified from the impurity of the defilements (*kilesa*). It refers to those mentioned in such passages as: “The stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry,” and so forth.

Regarding the four pairs of persons: they are "seers of the Dhamma" because of their direct vision of the Dhamma of the Four Truths and the Dhamma of Nibbāna, or because of their direct perception of the Noble Dhamma.

These individuals, without counting the pairs of those established on the path and those established in the fruit, become eight when counted as separate persons. For the purpose of taking refuge in this Saṅgha...
For refuge, for the ultimate resort, for protection from the suffering of the states of woe and the suffering of the cycle of existence—approach, go to, resort to, and serve [this Sangha];
or rather, know this thus and awaken to it—such is the meaning when construed with the preceding words.
"In whomsoever, among those four pairs of pure persons, a gift is said to yield great fruit; those eight individuals are the seers of the Dhamma—to this Sangha, approach for the sake of refuge."
Or [it is] a connection. Thus, it should be understood that this restatement is indeed appropriate because there is no difference in meaning.
Furthermore, for the sake of metrical ease in the verse, the vowel *ī* has been added to the word *purisa*, and the vowel has been shortened in the word *puggala*.

"To this extent" means by way of the sequence of words beginning with "I am he. The three bases (*vatthu*) are the "goings for refuge" (*saraṇa-gamana*), or alternatively, they are the goings for refuge performed three times; thus, they are "refuge-goings. "He declared" means he made known what was in his own heart by means of speech.
Commentary on the Discourse on Going for Refuge:
Just as there is a need for the clarification of the object, the classification, the fruit, and the defilement of going for refuge, so too is there a need for the clarification of the agent;
therefore, in order to demonstrate proficiency in that regard, the method is shown together with the agent: "Now, regarding those goings for refuge..."

It is said: “...for the sake of proficiency... it should be understood. For by the phrase “he who goes for refuge,” the agent is made manifest, since going for refuge is impossible without him; and by the phrase “going for refuge,” the act of going for refuge itself is indicated.
By the terms “refuge” and so forth, however, the objects and other factors are indicated respectively. Why, then, is purification (*vodāna*) not included here?
Is it not the case that the analysis of purification (*vodāna*) also serves for proficiency in that regard? True, this is so;
however, since that [purification] is already implied by the inclusion of defilement (*saṃkilesa*), it was not mentioned separately.

For purification occurs through the absolute non-arising of those causes of defilement—such as ignorance and the rest—when they have not yet arisen, and through the abandoning of them when they have already arisen.
*Atthato* means "from the meaning of the word *saraṇa*"; there is also a reading as *saraṇatthato*, which has the same meaning.
Showing that this is established by way of the verbal root *sara*, which has the sense of "to destroy," he states, "It destroys, thus it is a refuge (*saraṇa*).
Then, by the words "of those who have gone for refuge" and so forth, he clears away the objection: "Of whom does it destroy? How? And what [is destroyed]?"
"Who indeed [protects] those who have gone for refuge? "By what? "By that very act of going for refuge. "Of whom? "Of fear and so forth"—this is the clarification according to the respective order.

Therein, "those who have gone for refuge" means those who have gone to what is called "refuge. "By the going for refuge" means by the wholesome state (*kusala-dhamma*) consisting of going to what is called "refuge.
"Fear" refers to the fear of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa-bhaya*). "Terror" refers to mental agitation; by that [term], the suffering of the mind (*cetasika-dukkha*) is indicated.
Because it is included [within suffering]. "Suffering" (dukkha) here refers to physical suffering.

"Affliction in a miserable destination" (duggatiparikilesa) refers to all suffering comprised within miserable destinations, taking it as "afflicting, oppressing, or tormenting within a miserable destination.
All of this will be clarified later in the discussion on the fruit. And here, "harming" (hiṃsana) means simply destruction.
But he shows that it is not like the harming of beings by means of the words "he kills" and "he destroys.
"This" refers to the word *saraṇa* (refuge). "Designation" (*adhivacana*) means a name, or a well-known term, or a term applied with reference to a quality as it truly is.
Therefore he said, "of the Triple Gem alone."

Having thus shown, without distinction, the meaning of the word *saraṇa* (refuge) by way of its sense of "protecting" (*hiṃsana*), the phrase beginning with "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) is now stated to show that same meaning specifically.
For this specific explanation differs from the previous method only in that it demonstrates the cause for protecting each member of the Triple Gem individually.
In that context, "by causing [beings] to engage in what is beneficial" refers to: "O monks, those who are perfected in virtue... [and so forth].
By enjoining beings toward what is beneficial through such statements as "Dwell [thus]," etc.;

and by turning them away from what is harmful through the demonstration of danger, etc., by means of passages such as "The ripening of the taking of life is evil, and the future state is evil," etc., thus turning beings away from what is disadvantageous.
For "fear" (bhaya) destroys; that is, it destroys the calamity caused by the non-engagement in or engagement with what is beneficial or harmful.
He destroys [suffering] by bringing about its non-occurrence. The Dhamma designated as the Path brings beings across the wilderness of existence;
furthermore, the Dhamma designated as the Fruit and Nibbāna harms the fear of beings by bestowing consolation—this is the construction.
"Of honors" means of those services brought forth by way of giving and by way of worship. For even a word that is not a prefix can, like one with a prefix, express a specific meaning.
As in such passages as, “Even a small deed performed becomes merit of great fruit,” it should be connected thus:
“For he protects (*hiṃsati*) beings from fear by causing them to obtain abundant fruit, owing to his being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
By this method also—that is, by explaining it through showing the reasons for each member of the Triple Gem being a source of harm (*hiṃsaka*).

For this reason: since this word *saraṇa*—like the word *nātha*—expresses both its conventional meaning and its etymological meaning because it is a pure nominal stem (*suddhanāmapada*), one should understand that the meaning "refuge" (*saraṇa*) and "resort" (*parāyaṇa*) was stated previously.
Having thus shown the meaning of "refuge," he now states "through confidence in Him" (*tappasādā*) and so forth, in order to show the meaning of "going for refuge."

In this context, "confidence in that Triple Gem" (*tappasāda*) refers to the confidence in that Triple Gem expressed by such statements as, "The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha has practiced well.
"One for whom that very Triple Gem is venerable" (*taggaru*) means one who holds that Triple Gem in high esteem.

The state of being such is "veneration of it" (*taggarutā*). "Confidence in it and veneration of it" (*tappasādataggarutā*) refers to both of these together. By means of these two, one whose defilements have been destroyed...

Because he has shaken off the evil states such as doubt, delusion, and lack of faith, that very Triple Gem is his supreme resort (*parāyaṇa*), his ultimate goal, his protection, and his refuge; thus, he is "one who has that as his supreme resort" (*tapparāyaṇa*).

The state of being so is "the quality of having that as one's supreme resort" (*tapparāyaṇatā*); the mode [of consciousness] characterized by that is "the mode of having that as one's supreme resort" (*tapparāyaṇatākāra*);

and that which proceeds by means of this is "proceeding with the mode of having that as one's supreme resort" (*tapparāyaṇatākārappavatta*). And here, by the mention of "serene confidence" (*pasāda*), mundane going for refuge is indicated.
For that is an exertion of faith, not an exertion of knowledge; yet it is supramundane because of its grasping at weightiness.

For the Noble Ones regard the Triple Gem as weighty—due to their direct knowledge of its qualities—just as one regards a stone parasol. Therefore, one should construe the passage thus: by means of confidence in that [Triple Gem], defilements are dispelled through the abandoning of factors associated with them;
and by means of that weightiness, they are abandoned through the total eradication of the causes for showing disrespect.

In this context, "having that as one's final resort" (*tapparāyaṇatā*) means "having that as one's ultimate goal" (*taggatikatā*); it should be understood that by this term, all four kinds of going for refuge (*saraṇagamana*) which will be explained are included.

Alternatively, since "veneration through serene confidence" (*pasādagarutā*) is expressed without distinction, the mention of "serene confidence" (*pasāda*) includes both mundane confidence that does not rely on [the Dhamma] (*anaveccappasāda*) and supramundane confidence that does rely on it (*aveccappasāda*);
likewise, the mention of "veneration" (*garutā*) includes the mundane [veneration].
By both terms—“veneration” (*garukaraṇa*) and “supramundane” (*lokuttara*)—both types of going for refuge, mundane and supramundane, should be connected.

It is called "arising" (*uppāda*) because consciousness arises by means of it; it is the collection of associated states. And that which is consciousness and that which is arising is "consciousness-arising" (*cittuppāda*).
For grammarians maintain that even in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), the masculine gender may sometimes be used.
The consciousness that arises with that aspect, accompanied by states associated with faith, wisdom, and so forth, is called "going for refuge" (*saraṇagamana*), because it is said:
"it goes [to the refuges] by means of this. The phrase "one who possesses that" (*taṃsamaṅgī*) and so on is an analysis of the agent.
One who possesses that aforementioned arising of consciousness is "one who possesses that" (*taṃsamaṅgī*). Therefore, he says: "by the arising of consciousness of the kind described."
"Approaches" (upeti) means he frequents, serves, and attends upon; or it means he knows or awakens—this is the sense.
To the question "Who seeks the supramundane going for refuge? he says "those who have seen the Truths," meaning the eight types of noble persons (ariyapuggala).
To the question "When does that succeed? he says "at the moment of the Path" (maggakkhaṇe), and this connects with the word "succeeds" (ijjhati).

For when the Path is being realized through the attainment of the Four Truths, the state of being a fruit-attainer is also established as one who has gone for refuge, because there is no distinction in the supramundane going for refuge and because those [refuges] belong to a single mental continuum.

To the question, "How is that established? he says: "By the complete eradication of the defilements of going for refuge," and so forth; [this is established] by the eradication of the secondary defilements and by way of the object.
It is said that it succeeds in all three Jewels by way of its function (*kicca*).

Here, the phrase "by the eradication of the defilements of going for refuge" refers to the realization of abandonment (*pahānābhisamaya*), while "by way of the object" (*ārammaṇato*) refers to the realization of verification (*sacchikiriyābhisamaya*).

For one should construe it thus: "having become an object consisting of Nibbāna, it succeeds by way of the object. Furthermore, the particle *tvā* expresses a causal sense, as in the example: "Sakka..."
“Having become [thus], it arises. Furthermore, by the phrase “having Nibbāna as its object,” he specifies in concrete terms the very meaning already stated as “from the perspective of the object.

The phrase “from the perspective of function” is said with reference to the remaining types of realization, namely, the realization through development (*bhāvanābhisamaya*) and the realization through full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*).
Alternatively, by the phrase “having Nibbāna as its object from the perspective of the object,” he indicates that at the moment of the Path, there is a single object corresponding to that occasion.
Having shown this, it should be understood that by the phrase "by way of function" (*kiccato*), the remaining three functions—other than abandoning—are demonstrated.

Furthermore, because it is stated, "at the moment of the Path, having Nibbāna as its object," it is understood from the sense of the meaning that the attainment of the Four Truths, which is termed "knowledge of the Path," is itself the supramundane going for refuge. For in that attainment of the Four Truths, [the defilement of] the going for refuge...

The severance occurs by way of the clear realization of abandoning; however, the phenomenon of Nibbāna is realized by way of the clear realization of verification, and the phenomenon of the Path is realized by way of the clear realization of cultivation. It is precisely while being penetrated that these fulfill the purpose of going for refuge.

Furthermore, the qualities of the Buddha, which fall within the range of disciples, fulfill the purpose of going for refuge when they are penetrated by way of the clear realization of full understanding.
The qualities of the Noble Saṅgha are accomplished in the same way. Therefore he said, "It succeeds even in the entire Triple Gem.

Here, it should be understood that the inclusion of the fruits and the teachings (pariyatti) occurs because they function in accordance with the Path according to the method already stated, and because the qualities of the Buddha and the Saṅgha—which are not themselves to be fully understood—are included due to their commonality with those [Path] qualities. For in this way, the expression "the entire state" is distinguished.

"It is appropriate" means that it succeeds simultaneously with [the path], and it should be understood that it does not succeed sequentially like a mundane state, because it has been penetrated through penetration characterized by non-delusion.
For, like a lamp, the four functions of the path are accomplished in a single moment.
However, those who say, "The going for refuge does not occur having Nibbāna as its object, because the path has already been attained... [should be corrected].
"But for some, such as those possessing the threefold knowledge (tevijja) and so forth, that [refuge] is indeed already attained, just like worldly sciences (vijjā) and the like.
According to their statement, the going for refuge would be merely mundane (lokiya) and not supramundane (lokuttara); and that is indeed incorrect, because both types [of refuge] must be admitted.

By means of abandonment through substitution of opposites (tadaṅgappahāna), there is the suppression of the defilements (upakkilesa) of the going for refuge. From the perspective of the object (ārammaṇato)...
“Having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object” (buddhādiguṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā): here too, the meaning is according to the method already stated;
that is to say, because it suppresses the defilements of going for refuge and because it has [the Triple Gem] as its object, it is said to be accomplished with respect to the entire Triple Gem.

“That” (taṃ) refers to mundane going for refuge. The acquisition of faith by means of the formula beginning “The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One,” etc., is called “rooted in faith” (saddhāmūlikā).

It is preceded by faith as previously described. For it is precisely through its state of being preceded [by faith]—in the sense of being co-nascent—that it is rooted in that [faith], since right vision regarding the Buddha and so forth is impossible for one devoid of faith.

Right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is so called because it sees the Buddha’s perfect Buddhahood, the Dhamma’s perfect Dhamma-nature, and the Saṅgha’s perfect practice, by means of correct knowledge through mundane awakening. “The acquisition of faith” (*saddhā-paṭilābha*).
By this, it is shown that even faith devoid of right view constitutes mundane taking of refuge;

however, by the statement “right view is rooted in faith,” it is indicated that wisdom, as previously described, has faith as its decisive support (*upanissaya*). For mundane taking of refuge is also twofold:
associated with knowledge and dissociated from knowledge. Therein, by the first phrase, [the refuge of] children and others who are urged on by their mothers and so forth is indicated.
By the first [statement], going for refuge dissociated from knowledge is included; by the second, however, that associated with knowledge is included.
To show both of these as a specific basis for meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*), he said: "Among the ten bases of meritorious action, it is called the straightening of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*).
For, in the sense that view itself is made straight by its own conditions, it refers to right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
It is the state of straightening views; furthermore, it is also faith in the sense that "by this, view is made straight.
Here, by the mention of "faith" and "right view," there is the inclusion of the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) in which these are predominant.

And by the term "straightening of views" being used as an instrument (karaṇasādhana) as previously stated, the statement made below—"the arising of consciousness proceeding in the mode of having that as its ultimate resort"—is thus justified.

It is established that the separate mention of faith (*saddhā*) and right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) should be understood as being because the arising of consciousness associated with them has those two as its primary factors.
The phrase "this, moreover" refers specifically to mundane going for refuge, because there is no such differentiation in the supramundane case. Of that...
For, since such an undertaking does not exist—because [the undertaking] succeeds only at the very moment of the Path in the manner already described—this distinction is not possible.
"Surrendering oneself" (*attasanniyyātana*) means that by means of this, one surrenders, alienates, and relinquishes oneself;
it refers to the rectification of view (*diṭṭhijukamma*) consisting of going for refuge as previously described. This is because the Three Jewels are his ultimate resort and refuge.

The state of having that as one’s supreme resort—whether it be a person or an arising of consciousness—is "having that as one's supreme resort" (*tapparāyaṇatā*); that itself is the straightening of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*).

By the intention of "taking refuge," one approaches the state of being a student (*sissabhāva*), which is reckoned as the status of a pupil (*antevāsikabhāva*) through the performance of duties such as service and attendance;
thus, it is "approaching the state of being a student. It is by means of this very intention of going for refuge that one prostrates oneself; thus, it is [the act] by which one bows down.

Prostration (*paṇipāta*) and bowing down (*paṇipatana*) here refer specifically to acts of salutation, rising from one's seat, joining the palms in reverential salutation (*añjalikamma*), and respectful service (*sāmīcikamma*).
In all these cases, it should be understood that, in actual meaning, they are simply the rectification of views as previously described.

The relinquishing of one’s own personal existence for the sake of escaping the suffering of *saṃsāra* is the relinquishing of self (*attapariccajana*). This also applies to taking [the Buddha] as one’s supreme resort and so forth.

The same method applies here. By way of the discourse on instruction for one's welfare (*hitopadesakathā*), the status of being a teacher (*ācariya*) is also attributed to the Dhamma, as in such passages as:
"The mango tree with fruit and the one without fruit—both these teachers are mine. Thus he said, "a pupil of the Dhamma" (*dhammassa antevāsiko*).

The phrase beginning with "reverence" (*abhivādana*) is an explanation of the meaning of prostration (*paṇipāta*). The restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "of the Buddha and so forth only" (*buddhādīnaṃyeva*) applies even to the acts of self-surrender (*attasanniyyātanā*) and the rest.
The application should be understood by way of the lion’s gait; for in this way, the exclusion of anything else is accomplished.
The passage beginning with “For of these” (*imesañhi*) is an exposition of the capacity for fourfold occurrence, or rather, a demonstration of the cause.
Having thus shown the surrendering of oneself and so forth by one method, [the author] now proceeds to show them by other methods as well.
The passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apica*) is commenced;

by this, he shows that the four factors—self-surrender, dedication, reliance, and so forth—are indeed identical to self-surrender, dedication, reliance, and so forth through other synonyms (*pariyāyantarena*), because there is no difference in their meaning, just as in the case of the expression “renunciation of training and false reporting.
The term *jīvitapariyanti* is a neuter noun in the accusative case; the meaning is “I go [into homelessness] for as long as life lasts” (*yāvajīvaṃ gacchāmi*).
It is said that Mahākassapa himself, having taken the robes of one gone forth,
departed from the brahmin village of Mahātittha and was traveling along; having covered three *gāvuta* of the road as he went out to meet him,
he saw the Blessed One sitting all alone at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree, between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, and [thought], "This is the Blessed One..."
"Even though he did not know that [Mahākassapa] was an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, he went for refuge, saying, 'If only I could see the Teacher, I would see the Blessed One,' and so forth.
Therefore it is said, 'Just like Mahākassapa’s going for refuge.
The detailed account should be taken from the *Kassapasaṃyutta-ṭīkā*. In that passage, 'If only I could see the Teacher...'"
"I would see the Blessed One himself; if I were to see the Teacher, I would see this very Blessed One.

For it is not possible for me to have a teacher other than him. And if I were to see the Sugata, I would see the Blessed One himself"—if I were to see one called the Sugata because he has gone well through right practice, I would see this very one.
"I would see only the Blessed One. For it is not possible for there to be another Sugata other than him.

And if I were to see a 'Perfectly Enlightened One' (Sammāsambuddha)—meaning, if I were to see one who has awakened to the truths rightly and by himself—I would see only this Blessed One; for there can be no other for me besides him."
"It is possible to become a perfectly enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha)"—this is the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on this point.
In all instances, the word *ca* and the word *vata* are merely for the purpose of completing the meter; or rather, it should be understood as *ce*, because the commentary states "if" (*sace*).
Furthermore, it is also appropriate to consider that the word *vata* indicates a sense of certainty regarding the desire to see.

"So I have," and so forth, is found in the Āḷavaka Sutta of the *Suttanipāta*. Therein, although his going for refuge had already occurred by way of the Path itself, it is stated in the commentary on that passage that he uttered these words in this manner for the purpose of demonstrating his status as a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and for the purpose of showing his state of serene confidence (*pasāda*).
"From village to village" means from one divine abode to another divine abode; [this refers to] the deities.
"Or small, and large" means even a village. "Purā" and "puranti"—here too the method is the same. Regarding "the well-established nature of the Dhamma" (*dhammassa sudhammatan*):
this refers to praising the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment (*subuddhatā*), the Dhamma’s well-established nature (*sudhammatā*), and the Saṅgha’s correct practice (*suppaṭipannatā*).
The meaning is expressed through both conjunction (*saha samuccayena*) and ellipsis (*pāṭhasesena*). Thus, while paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One, the Proclaimer of the Dhamma [spoke].
"Having sacrificed, I shall wander"—this is what is meant.
Regarding the phrase "Āḷavaka and the others," the word "and others" includes Sātāgira, Hemavata, and so forth. Now, one might ask:
since these individuals such as Āḷavaka have already attained the Path and thus went for refuge by means of the Path itself, why is it said that they went for refuge with him as their supreme resort?
Is it stated [in this way]? Yes, because even by those who have gone for refuge through the path, the aspect of having that as their ultimate resort (*tapparāyaṇatā*) has been made known.
For by these [verses]—“I shall wander... [and so on]... according to the excellence of the Dhamma; we shall wander from village to village, from mountain to mountain... [and so on]...
according to the excellence of the Dhamma”—the aspect of having that as one's ultimate resort is made known. Therefore, without regard for the specific distinctions of going for refuge...
It should be understood that this was said merely by way of indicating the mode of expression.

"Then" refers to the time at the conclusion of the answer—beginning with "He who knows his former abodes"—to the eightfold question asked [by the Brahmin] with the words, "How, indeed, does one become a Brahmin?
For in the *Brahmāyu Sutta* of the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsaka*, "he kisses" means he touches closely; "he embraces closely" means...

He rubs [them] all over. "In this way too, prostration is to be understood"—thus, in this manner as well, prostration is to be understood by means of the highest form of submission (*paramanipaccakāra*).

"And that" refers to prostration. Regarding the phrase "by way of relatives... etc.": here, because it is heard following a series of dual compounds, it should be applied to each term individually—namely, by way of relatives, by way of fear, by way of teachers, and by way of those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*). In that context, "by way of relatives" means:
By way of their state of being relatives. For this is an exposition emphasizing the state (*bhāva*), or rather an exposition omitting the state, since it is precisely that state which is intended.
Likewise, in the remaining cases as well, these are connected with the term "prostration" (*paṇipāta*), because prostration is fourfold according to those [bases].
Therefore he said: “by means of prostration toward those worthy of offerings,” meaning by means of prostration itself, which has the state of being worthy of offerings as its cause.

The meaning is as follows. "By the others" refers to prostrations caused by factors such as kinship. The phrase beginning with "Precisely by way of being the best" is a corroboration of that same point.
Now, in order to show in detail, in their proper sequence, the three meanings already stated in the passage beginning with "Not by the others," the words beginning with "Therefore" were spoken.
"A Sākiya" indicates a family of kinsmen from the father’s side; "a Koliya" [indicates one from the mother’s side].

The word “or” (*vā*) refers to the maternal side. “Pays homage” (*vandati*) is a term that characterizes prostration. “Honored by kings” (*rājapūjita*) means honored by kings or for kings, just as in the expression “honored by the village” (*gāmapūjita*).
For those learned in grammar maintain that when a word for honor is employed, the genitive case is used for the agent.
“Of the Blessed One” (*bhagavato*) refers to the Blessed One while he was a bodhisatta or after he had become a Buddha. “Learned” (*uggahita*) means a craft that has been studied.
“Fourfold,” and so forth: in the *Siṅgālovāda Sutta*, the phrase “dwelling at home” (*gharamāvasanti*) means dwelling in the house;

here, because it is joined with a term denoting an action (*kammappavacanīya*), the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. “He should employ work” means he should engage in such work as agriculture, trade, and so on.
For the affairs of families do not proceed identically at all times; sometimes misfortunes arise due to kings and other causes.
Therefore, it was said, "One should store [it] with the thought: 'It will be for when misfortunes arise,'" meaning "for misfortunes that may occur.

Furthermore, from among these four portions, one should take only the portion stated as "one may enjoy wealth with one portion" and give gifts to the bhikkhus, to the poor, to travelers, and so forth, as well as to weavers, barbers, and others.
"‘Wages must be paid’—this is an instruction regarding the acquisition of wealth; the meaning is: ‘having received such an instruction.
For this is said with reference only to matters pertaining to the present life (diṭṭhadhammika).

However, it should be understood that even one who desires an instruction pertaining to the future life (samparāyika) or leading to liberation (niyyānika) performs, at the very least, a prostration toward those worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya). [The passage continues: “He who...”
The passage beginning with “panā” and so forth is an elaboration of the meaning stated in the phrase “he takes [it] precisely by way of the best,” and so on.
The passage beginning with “eva” and so forth, however, demonstrates the contrast (byatireka) to what was stated in the phrase “and it is divided by way of the best.

Since one may effect a change in gender and case according to the sense (atthavasā), this should also be construed as “or for a female lay follower who has taken refuge. This applies to similar cases.

Regarding the phrase "even though he has gone forth," the word *pi* (even) is said to have the sense of emphasis (*sambhāvana*), as indicated by the expression "how much more so one who has not gone forth.

The taking of refuge does not break because [the Buddha] was not saluted in his capacity as the Supreme One (*seṭṭha*). The particle *tathā* is used here in the sense of a connective (*anukaḍḍhana*), meaning "the taking of refuge does not break.
It is "honored in the kingdom" (*raṭṭhapūjitatta*) because he is honored in the kingdom, or because he is honored by the inhabitants of the kingdom. This, moreover, is due to fear.
This is merely an establishment of the state of being worthy of homage, and not a demonstration of the reason for its non-differentiation;

however, the reason for that [non-differentiation] should be understood as the fact that [the Buddha] is not worshipped by way of being "pre-eminent" (*seṭṭha*). For it is said: "And it is differentiated by way of being pre-eminent.

"By way of being pre-eminent" means by way of the state of being pre-eminent due to being the foremost object of offerings (*aggadakkhiṇeyya*) in the world. Therefore he said: "He is the foremost object of offerings in the world."
"Even one who pays homage to a member of another sect (titthiya) does not break [the refuge], let alone anyone else.

Thus, "the classification of going for refuge" refers to the analysis of going for refuge; and since the non-distinction can also be easily shown here through its connection with that analysis, the demonstration of non-distinction has been made.
The Noble Path itself is the supramundane going for refuge; thus, the four fruits of recluseship are spoken of as results of fruition (*vipākaphala*).
"The destruction of all suffering" refers to Nibbāna, which is the non-arising cessation of the entire round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
In this context, it should be understood that the result of fruition is similar to the kamma, while the result of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*) is its opposite. For example:
The fruits of rice seeds and the like, when fully matured, are said to be "ripened" and receive the designation "resultant" (vipāka),
but not so their roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, or stems; likewise, the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome states,

being similar in their nature as non-material phenomena (arūpadhamma) and in their possession of an object (sārammaṇa), are said to be "ripened" and receive the designation "resultant," but not [their causes].
Other [results] produced by karma are also similar to the karma; however, they are called "benefits" (*ānisamsa*), and they receive only the designation of "benefit.
By the words "For it has been said," etc., he introduces and demonstrates the canonical text (*pāḷi*) concerning the story of the Brahmin Aggidatta from the *Dhammapada*.
In the phrase "And whoever," the word "and" (*ca*) indicates contrast (*byatireka*); the meaning is "but whoever. Herein, this is the intended sense for illustrating the meaning of contrast:

If the security that was spoken of in such passages as, “Many indeed go for refuge to mountains and forests,” were not the secure refuge, nor the supreme refuge, and if by resorting to this refuge one were not liberated from all suffering—then, what thing indeed would be the secure refuge? What thing would be the supreme refuge? And by resorting to what thing as a refuge...
"Is one liberated from all suffering? "Yes.
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha...
[as above] ...This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge."
"By coming to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.

In such cases as these, because the mundane going for refuge can be disturbed and shaken by acts such as paying homage to those of other sects, it is the supramundane going for refuge alone—which is unshakable and immovable—that is being elucidated by [the statement]: "The Four Noble Truths, with right wisdom..."
"...sees," it is said. Here, the shortening of the vowel in the word *sammā* is for the sake of the euphony (*vācāsiliṭṭhattha*) of the speech.
"Suffering" and so forth is a demonstration of the actual nature of what was stated as "the four noble truths. "And they transcend suffering" refers to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodha*).
"Leading to the subsiding of suffering" means leading to the cessation of suffering (*dukkhanirodhagāmi*). "'This'": this refers to what was stated thus: "He sees the four... and so on.

The vision of the Noble Truths is what is termed the supramundane going for refuge. The particle *kho* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and should be applied to all three words [in the phrase].
Regarding the phrase "by way of not approaching as permanent," etc., scholars of grammar maintain that the particle *to* is used to indicate things to be pointed out by means of the particle *iti*.
With the words "For this has been said," etc., he cites the canonical text (Pāḷi) found in the *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* and other suttas as supporting evidence.
"Impossible" (*aṭṭhāna*) is a negation of the producing cause (*janaka-hetu*). "No opportunity" (*anavakāsa*) is a negation of the conditional cause (*paccaya-hetu*).

By both terms, he negates the very existence of a cause. "That" (*yaṃ*) refers to the reason by which. "One possessed of right view" (*diṭṭhisampanno*) is a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) endowed with the vision of the Path.

"Any conditioned thing" (*kañci saṅkhāraṃ*) refers to even a single conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*) among the conditioned formations belonging to the four planes of existence. "He might approach it as permanent" (*niccato upagaccheyyā*) means...

One might grasp [it] as "permanent. One might approach it as "pleasurable" means that one might grasp it as "pleasurable" by way of a self-view (*attadiṭṭhi*), thinking: "The self is exclusively happy and free from disease after death";

however, with a mind dissociated from such views, the noble disciple—like a clean Brahmin who has narrowly escaped a rutting elephant and seeks the allaying of his fever—[approaches] even a dung-hill [as something pleasant].

One regards volitional formations as pleasant. In the section on the self, instead of saying "volitional formations" (*saṅkhāra*), it is said "phenomena" (*dhamma*) for the purpose of including the designations such as the kasiṇas.
As it is said in the Parivāra:
"All volitional formations are impermanent; conditioned things are suffering and non-self."
“Nibbāna itself and conceptual designation are non-self; such is the certain conclusion.
Now, in these three sections, the delimitation for the noble disciple should be understood either by way of the four planes or by way of the three planes alone.
For whatever an ordinary person grasps as “permanent, pleasant, and self,” [the noble disciple understands it otherwise].
Grasping at each of those [objects] as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," the noble disciple unties his grip. Regarding the terms "mother" and so forth:
the mother is the biological mother; the father is the biological father; and the "Arahant" refers to one who has become a human being and has destroyed the taints (*khīṇāsava*).
But would the noble disciple take the life of any other living being for the sake of those [three]? That too is impossible. Even for the sake of universal sovereignty or his own life...

Indeed, he would not deprive him of life; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was said for the purpose of showing the great blameworthiness of the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and for the purpose of powerfully revealing the state of an Noble One (*ariya*).
"With a corrupt mind" means having a mind corrupted by a murderous intent, or a defiled mind. "He should shed blood" [means] from a living body.
One might cause even as much blood as could be drunk by a small fly to flow.
