"He would split the Saṅgha" means he would split the Saṅgha—those who share the same communion and reside within the same boundary—by means of five causes. For it has been said: "Ānanda, the Saṅgha is split by five ways:
by formal act (kamma), by recitation (uddesa), by speaking (voharanta), by proclamation (anussāvana), and by the drawing of lots (salākaggāha)."
“To take another teacher”: this means that it is impossible for one to adopt another founder of a sect outside of this [teaching], thinking, “This is my teacher.

“Perfection of existence” (*bhavasampadā*) refers to perfection through existence in a happy destination; this is the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*). “Perfection of wealth” (*bhogasampadā*) refers to perfection through human and divine enjoyments;
this, however, is the fruit of benefit (*ānisaṃsaphala*). With the words “For it has been said,” etc., [the author] cites the Pāḷi from the *Devatāsaṃyutta* and other sources.
He shows it by way of being a practitioner (*sādhaka*).
In the phrase "gone there" (*gatā seti*), *se* is merely a particle. "They will not go to the plane of misery":

those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha will, because of that, not go to the state of misery (*apāya*). And in the word "human" (*mānusa*), the description is by way of a change in grammatical number (*visaṃyoga*) for the sake of metrical composition (*gāthābandha*).
"Born among humans" is the meaning. "The host of devas" (*devakāya*) refers to the assembly of devas or the city of devas, taking it to mean "wherein there is a body or multitude of devas.
With the words "And another [result]," etc., he states another result mentioned in the Saḷāyatanavagga of the Moggallānasaṃyutta;
the meaning is that another result was spoken by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. "Other devas" refers to those devas who have not gone for refuge. By ten...
“By means of ten grounds” means by ten reasons. “With the divine,” etc., is the demonstration of its specific nature. “They surpass” means they overcome and remain having transcended [them].
By the phrase “this is the method,” he refers by extension to the Sutta passage: “It is indeed good, O Lord of Devas, to go for refuge to the Dhamma.
In the *Velāmasutta* of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, in the ninth chapter (*Navanipāta*), [the Buddha speaks] regarding birth, lineage, physical form, wealth, faith, wisdom, and so forth.
Because he was endowed with sublime qualities that transcended all boundaries and limits,
there is a discourse concerning the eighty-four thousand kings who were his teachers and brahmins during his time as the Bodhisatta named Velāma;
for therein [it is told] of eighty-four thousand gold plates, silver plates, and bronze plates, each measuring a quarter of a *karīsa* in size.
In due order, [he gave] eighty-four thousand vessels filled with silver, gold, and bullion;
eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with all ornaments; eighty-four thousand horses; eighty-four thousand chariots;
eighty-four thousand milch cows; eighty-four thousand maidens; eighty-four thousand couches; and eighty-four thousand...

Compared to the great *velāma* almsgiving that proceeded continuously for seven years and seven months by the relinquishing of thousands of millions of garments and immeasurable varieties of food such as hard and soft edibles,
the gift given to a single stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) bears much more abundant fruit; and compared to the gift given to a hundred stream-enterers,
the gift given to a single once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*) bears even greater fruit.

Then, the gift given to one non-returner is more fruitful than that; the gift given to one arahant is more fruitful than that; the gift given to one paccekabuddha is more fruitful than that; the gift given to the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha is more fruitful than that; the gift given to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha is more fruitful than that;

the construction of a monastery dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters is more fruitful than that; and going for refuge is even more fruitful than that—this is the meaning revealed. For it has been said:
“Householder, compared to the gift that the brahmin Velāma gave as a great offering, it is more fruitful for one to feed a single person accomplished in view;
and compared to feeding a hundred persons accomplished in view, it is more fruitful still for one to feed a single once-returner,” and so forth.
It should be understood that by this, the fruit of going for refuge has been shown from the perspective of the highest limit—that is, of the supramundane refuge alone.
For it is said in the commentary on the Velāma Sutta: "Regarding the phrase 'should go for refuge,' what is intended here is the refuge that does not turn back, which is attained through the Path;
however, others say that because one has surrendered oneself [to the Triple Gem], the act of going for refuge yields even greater fruit than that."

In the *Kūṭadantasutta-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it will be said: "And because what is called 'going for refuge' is a meritorious deed consisting of the sacrifice of life for the sake of the Three Jewels, which bestows the attainment of heaven, it should be understood as being more fruitful and more beneficial.
By this method, even for mundane going for refuge—
It should be understood that the result has indeed been shown here.

For it is known that this very meaning was intended by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla as well, because it is stated without distinction both here and in other works such as the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*;
and this meaning would also be favored by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta, as seen in the *Sāratthadīpanī* and the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*.

“Because it is stated in terms common to both. However, others say, “In the *Kūṭadanta Sutta-aṭṭhakathā* as well, the fruit of going for refuge is described as belonging only to the supramundane (lokuttara)”;

that is indeed incorrect, because it was not stated in that way. For in the passage beginning, “Since... he gives,” the fruit of both types [of refuge] is stated there by way of causes common to both. As for the *Velāma Sutta* and so forth...
Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of such texts as the *Aggappasāda Sutta*, the *Chattamāṇavaka Sutta*, and the *Vimānavatthu* should be understood.
Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is the non-knowing of the qualities of the Triple Gem; it is delusion (*sammoha*) regarding them.

Doubt (*saṃsayo*) is perplexity (*vicikicchā*) such as, "Is the Buddha [truly] so, or is he not? Wrong knowledge (*micchāñāṇa*) is the conceptualization of the qualities of the Triple Gem as being non-qualities.
"Grasping in a perverted way. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those who are disrespectful and lack reverence are included.
"Becomes defiled" (*saṃkilissati*) means it becomes soiled or stained. Phrases such as "not of great radiance" are also merely synonyms for defilement.
In this context, "not of great radiance" means not greatly brilliant; the sense is that it is unpurified and unclean. "Not of great expansion" means not of great power.
"Unrefined" (apaṇīta) means "not sublime" (anuḷāra). "Blameworthy" (sāvajja) means it is tainted by craving, views, and so forth.
To clarify that very point by way of its result, it is said to be "of undesirable fruit" (aniṭṭhaphala); the meaning is that because it is blameworthy, its fruit is disagreeable.
Worldly going for refuge, like the undertaking of the training rules, has no fixed limit of time and lasts only as long as one's life; therefore, of that...
The breach [of the Saṅgha] occurs through the breaking up of the aggregates; and because that [act] is devoid of craving, wrong view, and so forth, it is not a fault.
Thus he said, "It is blameless at the time of death. This refers to the breach of taking refuge as being blameless.

Even though it is blameless, it does not even have a desirable fruit, let alone an undesirable one, because it lacks karmic ripening. For that is not unwholesome; rather, it is merely the act of breaking.
This is the intended meaning. "Even in another existence" means in any other birth.
Because the word *dhara* takes two objects, "lay follower" (*upāsaka*) is also an object;
and in order to show the mere sense—that it is in the place of the suffix—it is said: "May he hold [this] thus: 'He is a lay follower'. And "may he hold" means "may he reflect upon."
The meaning [of the verb] is this: by the words "let him know," he shows that "sustaining" here is indeed knowing.

"For the sake of skill in the method of the lay follower" means for the sake of skill in establishing the state of being a lay follower (*upāsaka*). "Who is a lay follower? is a question concerning the essential nature; what is meant is:
"What are the characteristics of one called a lay follower? "Why? is a question concerning the cause; [it asks] by what causal basis the word "lay follower" applies to that person.
The intended meaning is that [the term] is established with reference to a person. Therefore he asked: "Why is one called an *upāsaka*?

For the very cause for the application of a word to its referent is the reason for the existence of that object [in that way]. The question "What is his virtue? is a question regarding the undertaking of vows; it means:
what kind of virtue does this *upāsaka* possess, and by the undertaking of how many vows does he come to be known as "one perfected in virtue"?
"Meaning" (*attha*): "What is livelihood? (*ko ājīvo*) is a question concerning the undertaking of kamma;

he asks, "What is his right livelihood? By what undertaking of kamma does his livelihood come to be? Since that [livelihood] occurs through the avoidance of wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*), wrong livelihood is also analyzed.
"What is failure? (*kā vipatti*) is a question concerning the misconduct of both [the precepts and livelihood]; it asks, "What is the failure of this lay follower’s virtue (*sīla*)?"

"And the failure of livelihood" (ājīvassa ca vipatti) means this. For when there is a reference to "asceticism" (sāmañña), the mention of what follows immediately is because a rule or prohibition applies to that which is immediately subsequent.
"What is success? is a question regarding the correct practice of both those [asceticism and livelihood]—that is to say, according to the stated method, it means:
"What is the success of this lay follower's virtue and livelihood? This is by way of explaining the meaning of the words as they appear, and so forth.
It is scattered in various ways, thus it is *pakiṇṇa*; that itself is *pakiṇṇaka*, meaning a determination of meaning that occurs in manifold modes.
"Whoever" (*yo koci*) refers to anyone among the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and so forth; by this phrase, he shows that distinctions such as birth and so on are not the cause here.
But by the words "gone for refuge" (*saraṇagato*), he shows that going for refuge alone is the criterion here. And [the word] "householder" (*gahaṭṭho*)...
By this it is shown that the term *upāsaka* (lay follower) is established only for householders, not for those who have gone forth into homelessness.

Demonstrating this point by means of the Mahānāma Sutta in the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta, he said, "For it has been said," and so forth. Therein, "yatā" means from the act of going for refuge to the Buddha and the others.
"Mahānāma" refers to the Sakyan king named Mahānāma, the son of the Blessed One’s own paternal uncle, Sukkodana.

He addresses [the Buddha]. The intention is this: by this much—namely, by going for refuge to the Buddha and the others—one becomes known as an *upāsaka*, and not on account of birth or other such factors.
Granted that there is also a two-fold verbal status of an *upāsaka* as in the case of Tapussa and Bhallika, yet because of the absence of the Three Jewels at that time, that occurs only occasionally;
therefore, [the text speaks of] the three-fold verbal status of an *upāsaka* which occurs at all times.
It is said "one who has gone for refuge" in order to show this. For even they [the others] later go for refuge to the Three;

and it should be understood that it was stated thus also to make known this meaning: that it is not possible here for one who has rejected another [refuge] and gone for refuge to only one or two to be called a lay follower (upāsaka).

"By means of attendance" (*upāsanato*) means by means of attending upon [the precepts] through that very act of going for refuge, and through the application of reverence, esteem, and so forth, by performing them with thoroughness; by this, he shows the meaning of the gerundive suffix (*katvā*). Therefore he says, "For he," and so forth. Regarding the term "abstentions" (*veramaṇiyo*):
here, "enmity" (*vera*) refers to misconduct such as killing living beings; because of the abstaining from—that is, the slaying and destruction of—that enmity, they are called "abstentions.
These are the five abstinences (*virati*), because abstention is the primary element of that virtue (*sīla*). For it has been stated thus:

In the Mahānāma Sutta, the passage beginning with “He abstains from taking life” and so forth is presented as proof by the phrase “as it has been said,” and it demonstrates the actual form [of the practice],
just as a single application of water to a watering place by a park-keeper results in the watering of both small and large trees.
As it is said in the Ambavimāna:
“Both the child has been bathed and the ascetic has been washed;
I too have performed no small amount of merit.
Thus, with joy, he suffuses his entire body.”
“Both have been sprinkled with water, and the ascetic has been bathed;
much merit has been produced—oh, what a fruitful life! [This is the root text here according to the commentary.
Thus it is in such cases. “By this much” means by merely abstaining from the five precepts.
*Micchāvaṇijjā* means improper trade; it is not right trade, but rather unseemly commercial activities—this is the meaning.
*Pahāya* means having abandoned by simply not performing them. *Dhammena* means in accordance with the Dhamma, not departing from the Dhamma;
by this, he rejects other unrighteous modes of livelihood besides the wrong trade. *Samena* means fairly, without unevenness; by this, he rejects misconduct such as bodily unevenness and so forth.

Having avoided [the aforementioned], he demonstrates livelihood through bodily good conduct. By the words "For it has been said," etc., he brings forward the *Pañcakaṅguttara* scripture as proof and shows its specific form.
"Trade" (*vaṇijjā*) means that which belongs to traders; it is the selling of anything whatsoever. This is a feminine noun.
"Sword-trade" (*satthavaṇijjā*) refers to making weapons, having them made, or obtaining them as they have already been made, and then [selling] them.
Trade: "Dealing in living beings" refers to the trade of human beings. "Dealing in meat" refers to the trade of meat after having raised deer, pigs, and so forth, like butchers and others.
"Dealing in liquor" refers to the trade of whatever intoxicant one has prepared.
"Dealing in poison" refers to the trade of poison after having prepared it or collected it. Among these, "dealing in weapons" [is as follows].
They are called "not to be done" because they are the cause of obstructing others: trading in living beings because it renders them unfree; trading in meat because it is a cause for slaughter;
trading in intoxicants because it is a basis for negligence; and trading in poisons because it is a cause for harming others.
"Of that very same" refers both to the virtue characterized by the five abstentions as previously described, and to that characterized by the abandonment of the five wrong trades and so forth.
And it is a description of livelihood. "Failure" means breach and provocation. Having thus shown the failure of a lay follower by way of failure in virtue and livelihood, he says "Moreover...
and so forth, showing it also by way of lack of faith and the like. "By which" refers to the misconduct consisting of lack of faith and so on.
"Outcaste" means a lay outcaste in the sense of being born into a base nature. "Stain" means...
In the sense of being defiled, it is the "stain of a lay follower" (*upāsakamala*). In the sense of being base, it is the "lowest of lay followers" (*upāsakanīhīna*).

That too—namely, the misconduct consisting of lack of faith and so forth—should be understood as the failure (*vipatti*) of that lay follower. As for the question "What, however, is this?", it is said: "And those," and so forth.
These are found in the *Upāsakacaṇḍālasutta* and the *Upāsakaratanasutta* in the *Pañcakaṅguttara*. Therein, regarding the Buddha and the others...
Regarding karma and its fruits, the opposite of faith is wrong liberation (*micchāvimokkha*), which is lack of faith (*assaddhiya*); one who possesses that is "faithless" (*assaddho*).
One is "immoral" (*dussīlo*) by way of the aforementioned failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*) and failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*).

[One is so called] by means of the auspicious sights, sounds, smells, and tastes—termed "superstition" (*kotūhala*)—which are imagined by foolish people as "this very thing is an auspicious sign because of this view, etc. (*iminā diṭṭhādinā idaṃ nāma maṅgalaṃ hoti*).
"One who is possessed of [the belief in] omens and auspicious signs" means that he believes only in omens—such as those classified as "seen omens" (*diṭṭha-maṅgala*) and so forth—and not in karma;

thus, he does not believe in the doctrine of the ownership of action (*kammassakatā*). "And outside of this" means outside of this teaching of the Omniscient Buddha, namely, in the systems of the outsiders (*bāhiraka*).
The word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of impossibility (*aṭṭhāna-payutta*), and should be applied in all instances such as "one who lacks faith" (*assaddho*) and so on.
"He seeks out one worthy of offerings" means that, perceiving someone of wrong practice as being worthy of offerings, he searches for them. "Therein" means in the external, non-Buddhist systems.
"He performs a prior service" means that he first performs wholesome deeds such as giving and honoring;
it is said that having first performed wholesome deeds in the non-Buddhist systems, he does so later within the Dispensation.

"Among them" (tattha) means, according to some, "among those external sectarians" (tithiyānaṃ). And here, by treating the preliminary practice of seeking those worthy of offerings as one, five factors are to be understood.
"His" (assa) refers to the lay follower (upāsaka). "Perfection of virtue" (sīlasampadā) is the perfection through the virtue characterized by the five abstinences as previously described.
“Perfection of livelihood” (*ājīvasampadā*) means perfection by means of a livelihood characterized by the abandonment of the five kinds of wrong trade and so forth.

Having thus shown the excellence of the lay follower (*upāsaka*) by way of perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) and perfection of livelihood, he says “And those which... and so forth, showing it also by way of faith and the other qualities.
The construction is: “And those five qualities—these too are his perfections. By “qualities” (*dhammehi*) is meant virtues. Of the four assemblies...

In the sense of producing delight, a lay follower (*upāsaka*) is itself a jewel; thus, he is a "lay-follower-jewel" (*upāsakaratana*). Because of the fragrance of his virtues, beauty, fame, and reputation, a lay follower is himself a lotus;

thus, he is a "lay-follower-lotus" (*upāsakapaduma*). Likewise, he is a "lay-follower-white-lotus" (*upāsakapuṇḍarīka*). The remainder should be understood by reversing the descriptions given for failure.

"Of the Nigaṇṭhīs" means of the female ascetics of the Nigaṇṭha sect. "At the beginning" means in the first place. "A cluster of sugarcane" (*ucchaggam*) means the top of the sugarcane, the finest part of the sugarcane.
The same applies here to the phrase "the tip of a bamboo" (*veḷagga*). "At the end" (*koṭiyaṃ*) means at the terminal limit; the meaning is "at the boundary.
"Sour-tip" (*ambilagga*) refers to a portion that is sour. Likewise, the same applies here to "bitter-tip" (*tittakagga*).

"By the corner of the dwelling" (*vihāraggena*) means by the portion consisting of a room—by way of the specific section of the place of residence such as, "for those living in this chamber, this particular fruit is attained," and so forth.
The meaning [is as follows]. Regarding the phrase "starting from the courtyard" (*pariveṇaggena*), the same method applies here as well.

In the word *agge*, there is either the substitution of the vowel *e* for the accusative case ending, or it is a change of number; furthermore, the word *katvā* is a remainder [of the compound], which is why it is said, "starting from the beginning" (*ādiṃ katvā*).

By the phrase "the state of today" (*ajjabhāvaṃ*), he shows that the word *tā* has the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvattha*); and "the state of today" (*ajjabhāvo*) refers to the quality of being present at that time of hearing the Dhamma.

For at that time, taking as its sign the state of existing by way of dependence upon that [day], the word *ajja* (today) occurs within the interval starting from sunrise on that very day until the next sunrise;

therefore, the meaning should be understood as "beginning with the state of being today (*ajjabhāva*), which is defined as the state of existing at that moment. Alternatively, *ajjataṃ* means simply *ajja*.
The meaning of the word *tā* is used in its own sense (*sakatthavuttito*), as in the term "deity" (*devatā*); this is the opinion of the teachers.

Having thus shown the meaning in accordance with the reading seen with the first syllable, he now says, "Or rather, the reading is *ajjadagge*," etc., in order to show the meaning in accordance with the reading seen with the third syllable.
Because it is merely a traditional transmission (*āgamamattattā*), the letter *da* serves to join the words (*padasandhikaro*).
For the word *ajja* (today) here is a relative term (*nepātika*). Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'today as the limit'.

To make it known that the word *pāṇo* refers in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) only to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and that the compound *pāṇupetaṃ* is formed with the sense of an instrumental, he said:
"As long as my life proceeds, for so long [be] approached. For one who approaches or goes near is called *upeta*.
The meaning intended by the teachers is that "endowed with life" (*pāṇupeta*) means "endowed for as long as life lasts. By this, it clarifies the following point:
"The phrase 'endowed with life' (*pāṇupeta*) demonstrates that this going for refuge extends until the end of one's life.
For by the term "endowed with life," it is shown that one goes for refuge for as long as one's life-breaths persist; and in going [for refuge], it is not merely by words, nor...
And it is not merely by a single arising of the thought; rather, by way of relinquishing living beings for as long as life lasts, the state of "until the end of life" (āpāṇakoṭika) is demonstrated.
The phrase "gone for refuge... gone" is a synonym for the expression "gone for refuge.
However, the phrase "having no other teacher" shows the meaning that must be excluded by means of an internal restriction and by the setting aside of other possibilities.
It is said that for a certain person, the meaning of the word *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes allowable) is also expressible by the word *upāsaka* (lay follower);

thus it is stated, "a lay follower who is a *kappiyakāraka*. Alternatively, this should be understood as being said with reference to the going for refuge through self-dedication (*attasanniyyātana*).
In this way, by the term "for as long as life lasts" (*pāṇupeta*), the lifelong nature of that going for refuge is shown according to its definitive meaning (*nītattha*).
Having shown this and speaking thus, the King reveals his intention by saying, "I preserve my going for refuge while honoring the Triple Gem with my very life.
Thus, explaining the King's intention as it was revealed through its interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*), he said, "For I," and so forth.
In that context, the word *hi* (for) signifies either a condition (*samatthana*) or a reason (*kāraṇattha*); by means of it—
By this reasoning, or by this cause, the meaning "May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower" is clarified.
*Accaya* is the act of proceeding by transgressing and crushing a good boundary; it is a fault consisting of bodily misconduct and so forth—thus he says "an offense" (*aparādho*).
Alternatively, *accaya* is that by which one proceeds having surpassed or overcome [the norm]; it refers to the transgression of the body and so forth.
The fault (dosa), which consists of unwholesome states (akusaladhamma) that cause [the mind] to proceed [toward evil], is called an "offense" (aparādha) because one offends by means of it.
For it proceeds by overcoming a person who is committing an offense. Therefore, he said: "proceeding by transgressing and overcoming.
"Dhamma" refers to the ten qualities of a king (dasarājadhamma). Its detailed exposition, however, should be clarified through such works as the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka.

“Carati” means he practices or performs. “By the Dhamma alone” means by that which does not deviate from the Dhamma; the meaning is, by that which is not devoid of wholesome qualities (kusala-dhamma).
Therefore, he said: “not by unrighteousness such as patricide and so forth. Regarding the phrase “May he accept,” the literal meaning is “may he endure” or “may he receive”;
however, to show the intended sense, it is stated as “may he forgive.”
Furthermore, by the words "again, of such a kind," etc., he shows that non-doing in this context is restraint (*saṃvara*).
"Offense" (*aparādha*), etc., are synonyms for one another.

By the phrase "just as the Dhamma stands, so [it is]," he also states the meaning of the word *yathā* as "conformity" (*anurūpa*), namely, in conformity with wholesome qualities well-practiced by the virtuous.
This is the meaning. By the word "karosi" (you do), he shows that the prefix *pati-* signifies "making it purposeless.

Some also say it means "you perform a counter-action. He says, "it is said that 'he asked for forgiveness,'" because making amends according to the Dhamma is simply the act of asking for forgiveness from one who has committed an offense.
By the phrase "paṭiggaṇhāma" (we accept), he shows the meaning to be "we endure" or "we consent."

By the word “*khamāmā*” (I forgive). In the phrase “for this is growth,” the letter *ha* is an augment (*āgama*) for the sake of the euphony of the sentence, or the word *hi* is a mere particle (*nipātamatta*).

“This” refers to the act of rejecting [the offense] according to the Dhamma and the undertaking of restraint for the future. Therefore he said: “He who... [acknowledges] his transgression... attains [growth].
By the world including the devas, the Tathāgata is called a “refuge” (*saraṇa*) because he is to be approached as one who is free from affliction (*araṇīya*).

Regarding the phrase "the Noble One," it is said: "of the Buddha, the Blessed One. It is called *vinaya* because by means of it one disciplines (*vineti*) sentient beings; thus, it is the Teaching (*sāsana*).
It is called *vuddhi* because by means of it one increases (*vaddhati*) in the attainment of heaven and liberation.

To remove the objection—"But what is this increase (*vuddhi*) that has been pointed out as 'this'?"—the author shows the connection by stating "that which is [the confession] beginning with 'whatever transgression... and so forth, using the words "what is it" and so on.
This undertaking of restraint is indicated by the word "this" (*esā*); the meaning is that it is called "growth.

Regarding the phrase "he makes amends according to the Dhamma," this is stated as "having made amends according to the Dhamma, he undertakes restraint for the future" in order to demonstrate that this is the preliminary action for the undertaking of restraint in the future.
For this is the custom of the teachers: namely, [to state the result] by whatever means possible.

This indicates another underlying intention (*adhippāya*). However, with this phrase, a further specification (*paṭiniddesa*) of that [intention] is also possible, because one sees that there is something to be specified, namely:

"he makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma" (*yathādhammaṃ paṭikaroti*). Some, however, maintain that "he makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma" is merely a demonstration of the prior action itself, not a specification of something further to be specified.
[They argue that] "and he undertakes restraint for the future" (*āyatiñca saṃvaraṃ āpajjati*)...
However, some say that this was stated for the purpose of making it known that [the offense] must be specifically demonstrated;
but that is indeed incorrect, because even the act of seeking forgiveness is stated [as a remedy] for slandering the Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) by virtue of its being a cause for growth.

For otherwise, even in the absence of seeking forgiveness, the removal of the slander of the Noble Ones would have been stated as occurring solely through the undertaking of restraint for the future; yet it was not so stated.
Therefore, the meaning should be understood exactly according to the method already stated.

However, to resolve the objection—namely, "Why is the description of the phenomenon (*dhamma*) shown by means of 'by which' and so forth, when in the Canon the description of the person (*puggala*) is made by means of 'whoever' and so forth?"—the passage beginning with "But as for the teaching... is commenced. [This refers to] the person-based designation (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).
"Making" means making a teaching of the Dhamma by way of a person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). For a teaching of the Dhamma by way of a person is twofold:
that which is a teaching of the Dhamma by way of a person, and that which is a teaching of a person by way of a person.
This is the intended meaning here: although a teaching by way of the Dhamma was commenced with the words "For this is growth," etc., nevertheless, by again making it a teaching by way of a person—
The teaching beginning with “He who [admits] a transgression,” etc., is commenced by way of the elegance of the teaching and by way of the disposition of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
Indeed, it is precisely by way of these two that the fourfold teaching—distinguished as that which has the Dhamma as its basis (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), and so forth—is established.
252. *Vacasāyatte* means "dependent upon speech. Some say it means "bound by speech"; however, that is refuted by the passage beginning with “For he...”.

It appears as if contradictory. However, the meaning "the purpose of the conclusion of speech" (*vācāpariyosānattha*) is appropriate for the term *sāya*, because the word *sāya* is derived from the root *sā-* (to conclude) with the suffix *-ya*, just as in the case of the word "dāyo.
In this way, the sense of "suitability" (*samatthana*) is also established. Since it was spoken after making the conclusion of speech for the purpose of going, it functions in that very same sense.
For they maintain that the word *handā* is used in the sense of exhortation (*codanā*) and in the sense of the commencement of speech (*vacasagga*).

Indeed, in such passages as “Come now, monks, I address you,” it is used in the sense of exhortation; and in such passages as “Come now, I shall go,” it is used in the sense of the commencement of speech.

It should be understood that what is called the commencement of speech is the issuing of speech, and that is simply the beginning of the utterance. Because of its performance of difficult tasks, it is said to have “many functions”; thus he says, “it has powerful functions.”
“*Kicca* is that which must necessarily be done; *karaṇīya* is that which is to be done [but not necessarily]. Or, *kicca* is what should be done first, while *karaṇīya* is what should be done later.
Or, *kicca* is a minor duty, while *karaṇīya* is a major one. This is stated in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā and other commentaries.
Because the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are in a constant relationship, because the time of going is known, and because no other action is being employed, [the meaning is established].
"It is you alone who knows the time," it was said. This means: "Knowing the time for departure yourself, go only after you have known it.
Or alternatively, just as in the assignment of duties to be performed one says, "Know this, give this, bring this," so too here: "You alone know the time known by you; act by way of going."
It should be understood that the phrase “you yourself know” is stated as a textual ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*) in order to show that he was directing her toward the departure.
The passage beginning with “having circumambulated three times to the right” is stated merely to indicate what has been established by the context according to customary practice.

In this regard, “to the right” (*padakkhiṇaṃ*) means that which is performed in a manner that is auspicious (*dakkhiṇaṃ*). Therefore, he said “three times. [The phrase] “resplendent with the joining of ten fingernails”...
It is blazing with the combination and unification of the ten nails produced on the two hands;
by this, it shows the bringing together of the two palms. *Añjali* means the hollow of the hands. It is called *añjali* because "by this one manifests (*añjati*) proficiency.
For those learned in grammar maintain that the root *añju* signifies proficiency and that the suffix *-ali* is added.
"Facing him" (*abhimukhova*) means being right in front of him, not turning one's back to the Blessed One; this is the meaning. The method for the five-point prostration has already been explained.
(Verse 253) "Wounded" (*khata*) by the destruction of the roots of merit he himself previously performed, which were to ripen in this very life;
"afflicted" (*upahata*) by the impairment of those same roots—by these two terms, he demonstrates that it was solely due to the fault of his own karma.

Because the two terms are synonymous, it is said, "He has become one whose foundation is broken," in order to show the state of being destroyed by the breaking of the foundation known as the roots of skillfulness (*kusalamūla*). "Foundation" (*patiṭṭhā*) and "root" (*mūla*) are identical in meaning.

For it is a "foundation" because by means of it one stands firm upon the entry into the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*); that is the perfection of the supporting conditions for skillfulness (*kusalūpanissaya*), which [is lost] through a failure in action.
"Bhinnapaṭṭho" means that by him his own foundation has been split and destroyed. Expounding upon that very point, he said "tathā" (thus), and so forth.
The construction is: "Just as his own foundation, consisting of the roots of merit, was established, so too has this king himself wounded and cut himself.
For here, the word "khatō" (wounded) is established in the sense of the object of the action, whereas in the Pāli text it should be understood in the sense of the agent.
Because it is a synonym for both feet, the word "afflicted" (*upahata*) is not mentioned here.
Based on such statements as, "Lust is dust, but it is not called grit," it is said that lust, hatred, and delusion alone are what is meant by "dust" (*rajo*) here;
thus, it says "free from the dust of lust and so forth. By the words "because of its being gone away" (*vigatattā*), he shows that the prefix *vi-* is a synonym for "gone away" (*vigata*).
By this [phrase]. "The eye regarding phenomena" (*dhammesu cakkhu*) means that which functions with respect to the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths as an eye in the sense of seeing them.
Alternatively, "regarding phenomena" (*dhammesu*) refers to the three lower path-phenomena. "The eye" (*cakkhu*) refers to the single eye known as the stream-entry path;

this is a locative compound in the sense of a container (*ādhārattha-samāsa*), taking a part for the whole (*samudāyekadesavasena*), and not a genitive determinative compound (*niddhāraṇattha-samāsa*). That...

For it is prohibited everywhere in the canonical scriptures (*sāsana-gantha*) as well as in the works of the Sakyas (*sakka-gantha*). "Consisting of the Dhamma" (*dhammamaya*) means produced by the Dhamma of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*);
by this, he states the meaning as "the eye produced by the Dhamma is the 'Dhamma-eye'.

Furthermore, "consisting of the Dhamma" refers to the very aggregates of the threefold Dhamma beginning with virtue (*sīla*), because the word *maya* functions in its own sense [of identity]; by this, he implies that "it is the Dhamma itself..."
He states the meaning as "the eye is the Dhamma-eye. Regarding the phrase "in other places," this refers to other passages in the Suttas;

by this, he shows that there is a threefold meaning according to the literal reading. However, in this context, this is a designation specifically for the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), because even when that has not yet been attained, there is simply no possibility of [the term] being applied to anything else—this is the intended meaning.
Now, showing the easily understood intention of the passage beginning with “This king, bhikkhus, has been executed,” he said, “This is what is meant,” and so forth.
Therein, “nābhavissa” means “if you had not been”; the sense is: “this being the case.
For this should be regarded as a statement of past time (kālātipatti), not of future time. This same method applies to the path of stream-entry.
The same applies here in the phrase "he will have attained. One might ask: "Is not the expression 'reaching the path' future in tense because it refers to something yet to come?
True, it would be so if unspecified; however, here it must be understood as past tense because it is specified by the words, "seated right here on this very seat.
For the Blessed One said this while the King had not even long departed after rising from his seat. [Regarding the phrase] "through association with evil friends":
[This is] due to association with Devadatta and with evil friends reckoned as Devadatta’s retinue. *Assa* means "of the stream-entry path.

With the words "Even though this is so," etc., he shows the remainder of the statement not included in the [standard] recension. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) connects with "he shall be liberated because he has gone for refuge.
The reading "And because of the greatness of my teaching" (*mama ca sāsanamahantatāya*) is appropriate; however, in some places...
The word *ca* (and) is not seen; in that case, it should be understood as being indicated by elision (*luttaniddiṭṭha*).

The intended meaning is that liberation will come about not only through having gone for refuge, but also through the place where one has faith, through manifesting that state of faith, and through the excellence of that threefold Teaching—thus the sense is intended with a cumulative conjunction (*saha samuccayena*).
“*Yathā nāmā*” and so forth is an illustration by way of simile, showing liberation from the ripening of a difficult deed through an easy means. *Koci* means a certain person.
*Kassaci* means for a certain person; here, in the word *vadhā*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*kamma*) due to its connection with the abstract noun (*bhāva*).
*Pupphamuṭṭhimattena daṇḍena* means by a monetary fine consisting of a mere handful of flowers. *Mucceyya* means he would be released.

"He would be released from the punishment of execution"—here, the instrumental case *daṇḍena* is used in the sense of an ablative (*nissakkatthe*), as in such expressions as "we are well freed from that great ascetic.
The meaning is that he would be released from a fine of money consisting of even a mere handful of flowers, and from the punishment of execution.
"In the iron cauldron" means in the hell named Lohakumbhī; for therein, for those experiencing it—
By the power of the karma of sentient beings, a great iron cauldron is produced; therefore, it is called the "Iron Cauldron.
Falling from the upper surface downward and rising from the lower surface upward, it remains in both states for sixty thousand years. And it is said:
"Sixty thousand years, in their entirety; in every respect."
"When will there be an end for those being cooked in hell?
By saying, "They will be released after reaching the bottom floor and reaching the top floor," he illuminates this meaning:
just as other sons of wealthy merchants and so forth, falling down and going upward again and again, [pass through] many...
“They are roasted there for a hundred thousand years, but this one is not like that;
rather, because of the aforementioned reason, this king will fall downward and rise upward only once, and after being roasted for sixty thousand years, he will be released.
Anticipating the question, “From where was this matter obtained? he maintains the position by saying, “This too, it is said, was indeed spoken by the Blessed One.”

He says: Here, the word *kira* has the sense of "having been heard. By this, it indicates that the fact of [the teaching] having been spoken by the Blessed One is being heard through the succession of teachers (*ācariyaparamparā*), and it demonstrates that this meaning has come down through the lineage of teachers.

Then, with the words "but it has not been included in the Canon" (*pāḷiyaṃ pana na āruḷhan*), he removes the objection that it might have been chanted in the Canon, because it is of the nature of a miscellaneous instruction (*pakiṇṇakadesanā*).

The intention is that because it is not included in the Canon (Pāḷi), it was not recited as part of the textual tradition. For it is stated in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) that the miscellaneous teachings (Pakiṇṇaka-desanā) are not included in the Canon.
If one is to be cooked in hell in the very next existence, then what benefit would there be for the King from hearing this teaching?
The phrase "laddho" (obtained) might give rise to some suspicion; therefore, in order to dispel that suspicion, the text says "But this...
and so forth, after first setting aside the objection, in order to provide a comprehensive explanation. With the words "For this...

and so on, it demonstrates by way of specific characteristics the manifold great benefits—both pertaining to the present life and to future lives—such as the attainment of sleep and others. For herein, [it is said]: "This... obtains sleep."
By this, he shows the attainment of sleep; and by way of that attainment of sleep, he shows the state of being free from bodily and mental suffering.
By the phrase “he performed... for the Three [Jewels],” he shows the performance of great honor toward the Three Jewels. By the phrase “it was not...

of the ordinary person,” he shows the acquisition of an extraordinary degree of faith belonging to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Such as these are benefits pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmika*).
By the phrase “in the future... will attain final Nibbāna,” the future benefit is shown in its highest degree;
however, in its entirety, the future benefit should be understood as being truly immeasurable throughout subsequent existences.
In that context, “sweet” means having the nature of a sweet taste; “nutritious” means being the essence even of that sweet taste.
*Ojāya ojavatiyā*: [the genitive singular of *ojas*]. *Puthujjane bhavā pothujjanikā*. One who has especially conquered the five Māras is a *vijitāvī*;
here, the state of being "especially" refers to being devoid of instruction from another. One who has awakened to enlightenment individually is a *paccekabuddha*;
the meaning is that he has awakened to full enlightenment by himself (*sāmaññeva*) without having a teacher. For it is said: "The *paccekabuddhas* [awaken] by themselves..."
They awaken, but do not cause others to awaken; they penetrate the flavor of the goal (*attharasa*) alone, but not the flavor of the Dhamma (*dhammarasa*).

For they are unable to teach by applying the supramundane Dhamma to conventional designations (*paññatti*), like a dream seen by a mute, or like the taste of a sauce savored in a city by a forest-dweller;
such is their realization of the Dhamma, including all its varieties of psychic power, meditative attainments, and analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
"...will attain [it]," so it is said in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).

Here one might ask: "If the Dhamma-eye were to arise in that very seat for the King in the absence of any obstacle to his karma, then how will he later become a Paccekabuddha and attain final Nibbāna? And if he is to become a Paccekabuddha in the future..."
Having offered the sacrifice, he will attain final Nibbāna; how then could the Dhammacakkhu arise for you on that very same seat?
Is it not the case that these two—the support for Sāvaka-bodhi and Pacceka-bodhi—have different bases, because the two types of enlightenment are not shared?
For these two are indeed distinct, respectively, by virtue of the perfection of five factors and two factors, and by way of the success of their respective resolves.
Is this not a contradiction, given that [the requisites] are fulfilled through the time of accumulating the perfections (*pāramī*) and through the act of awakening?
This is not a contradiction because from this point onward, he must indeed accumulate the requisites for *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment).

For even those beings who awaken to the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*) will, in the absence of its attainment, awaken to *paccekabodhi* at a later time, since the possibility of making such a resolution (*abhinīhāra*) exists.
Others, however, say: "This king had indeed made a resolution for *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment).

For even those who have made such a resolution, if they have not reached certainty therein because that knowledge has not yet matured, will attain *sāvakabodhi* (disciple-enlightenment) upon meeting the Teacher;
it was with this in mind that the Blessed One said, 'If, monks, this king...,' and so forth, referring specifically to those who are *mahābodhisattas*."
And he attained liberation from the immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), whereas other Bodhisattvas did not.
For Devadatta, being fixed for Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment (*paccekabodhi*), committed even weightier immediate karmic deeds due to his long-standing resentment toward the Lord of the World;
therefore, by way of this obstruction of karma, this King—whose realization of the vision of the Truth was not yet fully assembled—is now [reborn] according to the destiny of a Pratyekabuddha.
It should be understood that he will, in the future, become a Paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī and attain Parinibbāna;
one should examine which of these [two accounts] is more appropriate and accept it.
Showing the conclusion of the commentary upon the aforementioned Pāḷi itself, he said, "This he spoke," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:

For it was stated previously. Furthermore, it should be understood that even though a certain meaning has not been included in the actual text (pāḷi), he provides a conclusion with the words "This he said" and so forth, in order to summarize that meaning.
Thus ends [the section] from the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which elucidates meanings that are most subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend.

By the Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati—the great preceptor and great grammarian; one endowed with the qualities of uprightness, gentleness, heroism, faith, mindfulness, fortitude, wisdom, patience, and energy, which generate exceedingly pure and vast analytical discernment;
one who possesses unimpeded, unwavering, and confident knowledge regarding the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries;
one who has plunged into the dense thickets of his own and other systems in their many varieties; and the venerable of the Great Dhamma King, the Adhirāja.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta*, titled *Sādhuvilāsinī*, is completed.
The Commentary on the *Sāmaññaphala-sutta* is finished.
3. Commentary on the *Ambaṭṭha-sutta*.
254. Having thus explained the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, now, while explaining the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta*,
[the commentator] clarifies that it has reached its turn for explanation according to the proper sequence, as the sutta was recited immediately after the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*.
In order to reveal the nature of the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, he said: "Thus have I heard... [pe] ...among the Kosalans: the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. Such is the case with these and similar instances.

Here, the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*); however, the word *iti*, which indicates a reversal of the word-meaning, is indicated by elision, or this is a contraction of the word *ādi*, or it is an indication by way of a characteristic mark (*upalakkhaṇa*).
The commentary on words not previously mentioned is so called because they were not included below.
This is the analysis of the meaning of a word not previously explained. For it was said: "I shall clarify the meaning, having abandoned the matter of repeated recurrence.

Although in some places the reading "anupubbapadavaṇṇanā" (a word-by-word commentary in sequence) occurs, that is indeed inappropriate, because it is not cited in the *Ṭīkā* and likewise has not been commented upon there.
“The princes are named Kosalas according to their clan,” so it was said by the teacher. However, the etymologists say:
“They take (laṃ) the treasury (kosaṃ), or they inquire after what is wholesome (kusalaṃ); thus they are the Kosalas.

“The inhabitants of the country” means those who possess a country, or those who are lords over a country. Although it would have been sufficient simply to say “the princes named Kosalas,” the word “inhabitants of the country” [is added]...

Even though there are other inhabitants designated by various names living there, the statement [is made] for the purpose of showing that this is the conventional designation (*samaññā*) for the country, based on the fact that it is the dwelling place of those very people.
By the phrase "their dwelling," he demonstrates the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) [formation]: "The dwellings of the Kosalans are the Kosalans.
However, by the phrase "even a single country," he shows that this [designation] exists solely by way of linguistic convention.
The plural form is used; however, he clarifies that in meaning this is actually only one. Here, the word *api* (even/also) is used in the sense of favoring [the position];
by it, he shows favor, implying: "Granted that this country is indeed only one, nevertheless, for this reason the plural form is appropriate.
To the question, "If it is only one country, how can there be a plural number there?", he says: "By way of conventional usage (*ruḷhisadda*)," and so forth, because it is a conventional term.

"What is stated is that the plural number is appropriate. Here, "conventional usage" (*ruḷhi*) refers to the application of a plural form—either the plurality itself or the state of being plural—to the support (*nissaya*) when it is employed in relation to those things supported.
Therefore, the Teacher has stated here, as well as elsewhere in the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā* and other works:
"For grammarians desire such genders and numbers in such instances as if they were actually joined [to the supports]; this is the case here."

"Conventional usage [is the reason], just as it is said: 'He dwells elsewhere too, in the Kuru country; he dwells in Aṅga. However, some maintain that this refers to the application of the name "Kosala";
this is incorrect, because the plural form would not be applicable. For even when applying a name, the singular may be used, as in "The lion sings.
And even when that [name] qualifies the word for "country," the singular alone is used because it is a generic term (*jāti-sadda*). Therefore, he said:
“In that country of the Kosalans”: the meaning is, in that country named Kosala. For conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) is a mere designation based on what is not real;
the actual meaning must be determined from what is real.
Just as it is said: “There are sons of the Videhans; Dīghāvu is the increaser of the kingdom.”

In such passages as, "They shall exercise sovereignty over Mithilā, O Pajāpatī," the plural usage of "sons" (*puttā*) occurs by way of conventional metaphorical application (*ruḷhivasena*) to the single referent designated as "his sons.

Likewise, here too, the plural usage of "among the Kosalans" (*kosalesu*) occurs by way of conventional metaphorical application to the single referent designated as "the inhabitants thereof. Just as...

And as in such passages as “one should not kill a living being (pāṇaṃ), nor take what is not given,” where the singular number is used for a plural sense by way of genus (jāti), so too here the singular usage of “janapade” occurs for a plural sense due to the distinction of its constituent parts by way of genus.
And it was said by the Teacher in his commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya: “Even in the word ‘janapada,’ which is a term denoting a genus...”
It is indeed in the singular. Therefore he said: "In that [place] among the parts of the country.
Having thus shown the plural number as if it were used for a plurality by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhivasena*), he now says "But the ancients have said...
and so forth, showing the plural number even when a plurality of objects is to be expressed according to its actual sense. And here, the word *pana*...
It illuminates a specific meaning; thus, because its referent is manifold, this plural form expresses a distinction that will be explained as not being used in the conventional sense (*ruḷhi*).
For that region, measuring three hundred *yojanas*, is of many varieties;
however, according to this method, the meaning should be understood as "in those Kosala provinces. "Mahāpanāda" refers to the Mahāpanāda Jātaka.
[It refers to] the prince named Mahāpanāda, the son of the Videha king named Suruci, who appears in the *Surucijātaka*.
"Various theatrical performances" (*nānānāṭakāni*) means six hundred thousand kinds of theatrical performances, headed by the *Bhaṇḍukaṇḍa* and *Paṇḍukaṇḍa*.
In some places, however, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is also seen; it is not found in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, but if it were to be found there, [it would refer to the following].
By this, the inclusion of actors, acrobats, and so forth is to be understood. "Even a mere smile" means even a mere laugh.
It is said that because he had seen divine dramas in his immediately preceding existence, human dramas appeared unpleasing to him.
"Having abandoned even the ploughs" means having relinquished the ploughs by way of abandoning agricultural work; and this is merely an illustration.
Indeed, it was not only the farmers, but other people dwelling in both kingdoms as well who, having abandoned their respective duties, gathered at that auspicious place.

At that time, it is said, they performed three auspicious ceremonies together for Prince Mahāpanāda: the palace-consecration festival, the parasol-consecration festival, and the marriage festival; and so too did the inhabitants of the kingdoms of Kāsi and Videha.
Regarding the phrase "having gathered there, they enjoyed festivities for more than seven years": however, the reading "ploughs and so forth" (*naṅgalādīni*) is now seen;
this is not the ancient reading, because it is not cited in the *Ṭīkā*.
As for the gathering of the great multitude of people, some say: "We shall make the prince laugh by showing him various amusing performances."
When a great multitude had gathered together, thinking, "We shall see that performance," they displayed various amusements such as climbing the Atula pillar, entering a wooden statue, and so forth.
It is said that a celestial dancer sent by Sakka stood in the air over the royal courtyard and displayed what is called a "half-body" performance:
one hand, one foot, one eye, and one tusk danced and moved, while the other half remained still.
It quivered, while the rest remained motionless; seeing this, Mahāpanāda smiled slightly. It is with reference to this matter that it is said:
"Having displayed a celestial performance, he made them laugh. Those called *suhajjā* are trusted friends, [so called] because one thinks, "Their hearts are truly [with me].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of kinsmen, attendants, and so forth. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because of such speech.
“Taking the word ‘skilful’ (kusala) as the basis”: here, because those people spoke of what was skilful by way of the exchange of questions and answers—“Is all well?
Yes, it is well”—they first received the designation “the Skilful Ones” (Kosalā).
Because the princes were lords over those Skilful Ones, they became known as the Kosalas; and because it was their place of residence, the region itself came to be called Kosala.
The method is exactly as stated previously. Therefore, he said: “That region is called Kosala.
Thus it was stated by the Master himself in the *Majjhima Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā*. Herein, this may be the intended meaning:

because the terms for the designatum (*saññī*) and the designation (*saññā*)—namely, “that region” and “Kosala”—are stated respectively in the singular and plural numbers, here too, as in the previous method, they are used according to conventional usage (*ruḷhi*).

The plural number is used. Here, the distinction lies merely in the fact that they have received the name "princes. However, in this context, it was stated by the Teacher as "that region" (*so padeso*);
this was said by way of a commonality with the term "region," or else through a change of grammatical number, meaning "those regions" (*te padesā*).

As for the statement "it is called Kosala," this is because the skillful ones (*kusalā*) themselves are called "Kosala. In this regard, the intended meaning might be as follows: [he refers to them]...

“Regions” (*padesā*) is expressed in the plural because it is stated either by way of a generic term (*jāti-sadda*) or through a change of number (*vacana-vipallāsa*), since its referent consists of many individual things.
Here, “region” (*padesa*) acquires the designation [of “skill”] by virtue of being a specific instance (*visesa*).

For, taking the word “skillful” (*kusala*) as the basis, it is spoken according to the method of conventional names (*ruḷhi-nāma*), just as “the Kosalans” [are so called] based on the word “skillful,” similar to the expressions “miscellaneous” (*yevāpanaka*) or “the section not belonging to you” (*natumhāka-vagga*). Furthermore, it is also [understood] by way of question and answer.
They say that because they speak of what is "wholesome" (*kusala*) therein, they are called the *Kosalas*. For the application of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) is manifold.
Furthermore, "wholesome" (*kusala*) means health, as in such passages as, "Is it well with you, sir?

Is it free from illness with you, sir?"—the meaning being, "Is there health for you?"—or it means skillful, as in such passages as, "The women are skilled in dancing and singing; they are trained in the fourfold arts."
The meaning is: "Do those actors possess skill?
*Caraṇa* means walking (*cārikā*), or *caraṇa* means movement (*cāro*); that itself is *cārikā*.

To show that what is intended here is specifically traveling on a journey and not merely moving about in small increments, it is called "traveling on a road" (*addhānagamana*). This word is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*).

It means "wandering on a journey characterized as travel along a road. Or, even though there is no actual difference, it is expressed by a term implying a distinction, as in the phrase "he sat for his midday rest.
Thus, "wandering on a journey characterized as travel along a road" means "performing the act of wandering.
For the meaning of all roots ending in *kṛ* (to do) is "performing. In some places, it is also called "the path of travel."

That reading is not good, for the word *cārikā* does not denote a "path. Now, having shown that by way of analysis and specifying what is intended here, he says, "And this so-called *cārikā*," and so forth.

Since a *cārikā* can also occur for disciples by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), he distinguishes it from that by means of the word "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*). For thus it is stated in the *Madhyamāgama-aṭṭhakathā*:

Regarding the phrase "wandering on a journey" (*cārikaṃ caramāno*): although this so-called "journey" is obtained for Buddhas alone for the purpose of gathering the great masses of people, it is nevertheless said—by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhisadda*) based on the Buddha—to apply to disciples as well, just as a fan made of reeds and such materials is called a "palmyra-leaf fan.
Regarding the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even at a distance" (*dūre pi*): by means of the particle *pi*, there is an inclusion of the sense "even not too far" (*nātidūre pi*).
And because wandering is possible even there. "A person to be awakened" means a person worthy of being awakened by means of the penetration of the Four Truths.

"Going hastily" means going quickly. He shows in its own form what was already stated [in the commentary] as "the welcoming of Mahākassapa and so forth," beginning with the words "For the Blessed One. "Welcoming" means going toward him; "rising up" means...
The meaning [is as follows]. By the word “likewise” (*tathā*), the phrase “thirty *yojanas*” is drawn forward. Pakkusāti was the king of Gandhāra;
Mahākappina was the king of Kukkuṭavatī; Dhaniya was Gopa, the son of the merchant Koraṇḍa.
Having thus shown, by way of praising his reverence for the Dhamma, certain instances such as the Great Kassapa’s going out to meet him, etc., now—
Having related in detail the story of the novice Tissa who lived in the forest, the following passage beginning with “One day” was commenced in order to show his wandering.
But who was this novice named Tissa? He was born into a family that served as attendants to the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) in Sāvatthī;
being one of great merit, he had previously been known by the names “Tissa the Almsgiver” and “Tissa the Blanket-Giver,” but later became known as “Vanavāsi-Tissa.”
The novice Saṃanera Khīṇāsava was well-known. The detailed account is in the *Dhammapada*.

Desiring to go through the air together with those who travel through the air, the Blessed One said, “Announce the sixfold higher knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*) to him. “To him” refers to the novice Saṃanera Tissa.
“Him” refers to the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, putting on his robe. The connection is: “Neither an elder, nor one of merely small stature.”
The meaning is that he does not become one who is inferior in virtue.
"In his own bowl and seat" means within the limit of the seats of the bhikkhus. Having spoken a blessing connected with the gift for those village-dwellers, [the opponent] raises this objection:
"But why did the Blessed One speak thus, even though he is the teacher of the path to the world including the devas?"

The passage beginning with “The Blessed One, it seems,” was spoken in order to purify [the candidate]. “One who shows the path” means one who teaches the path to Nibbāna or the path to a happy rebirth.

“By that” refers to the perception of the forest. Although full ordination (*upasampadā*) is accomplished through a formal act of the Sangha (*saṅghakamma*), they say it is stated, “I shall give you the inheritance of the Buddha,” because it is accomplished by virtue of the Teacher’s command.
Others, however, [say this regarding] one who is less than twenty years of age...
"Granting him full ordination (*upasampadā*), the Teacher said, 'I shall give you the inheritance of a Buddha,'" they say.

Having been ordained by the General of the Dhamma as his preceptor (*upajjhāya*), he is therefore described in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) as the personal attendant (*saddhivihārika*) of the General of the Dhamma.
However, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, [it is stated that] the Elder Theras, beginning with the General of the Dhamma, were accompanied by a retinue of forty thousand bhikkhus.
The departure of each [of the elders] together with their respective retinues, as well as the departure of the Blessed One alone, is stated according to the opinion of the Khuddaka-bhāṇakas;

however, here, in the Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā, the departure is described differently, which should be understood as being according to the opinion of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas and the Majjhima-bhāṇakas. "Ayam" refers to [the journey] for the sake of Mahākassapa and the others.
Regarding "the journey": the connection is that the Blessed One’s departure while not taking [them] along is called the "non-hastening journey" (*aturitacārikā*).

This "journey," moreover, refers to the non-hastening journey. "The great circle" (*mahāmaṇḍala*) is a larger circle because it is delimited by the outer measurement included within the Middle Country.
"The middle circle" (*majjhimamaṇḍala*) [is so called] in relation to the other two.

The circle proceeding in the middle. "The inner circle" (*antomaṇḍala*) refers to the smaller circle among the others, or because it is included within the others, it is the final circle; thus, it is called the "innermost circle.
As for their measurement, he says "where," and so forth. Therein, the extent of nine hundred yojanas is due solely to its inclusion within the Middle Country.
Beyond that, it should be understood as such because he does not travel with non-urgent speed. For thereafter, the Tathāgata travels only with urgent speed, not with non-urgent speed.
It is said that "undertaking the journey after performing the *pavāraṇā* is the practice of the Buddhas," as expressed in the passage beginning, "having performed the *mahāpavāraṇā*.
"On the first day of the month" means on the first day (*pāṭipada*) immediately following the full moon of the month of Kattika.
“On all sides” means on all four sides of the place already traversed.
Because of the gathering of a great multitude of people, those who arrive first and first receive the invitation. To demonstrate that very gathering, the words beginning with “in others” were spoken.
Regarding the statement “serenity and insight are tender,” here the tenderness of serenity is by way of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).

In the case of insight (vipassanā), however, it should be understood by way of four knowledges: the knowledge of the delimitation of formations, the knowledge of the overcoming of doubt, the knowledge of comprehension, and the knowledge of what is and is not the path. For "incipient insight" is a designation for those four knowledges.
"Having granted the invitation" means having given it by way of granting permission. "On the full moon of Kattika" means on the final full moon of the month of Kattika.

The phrase “on the first day of the month of Migasira” is stated with reference to the first day of the waxing moon of the month of Migasira according to the terminology of the Middle Country; however, according to current usage,
it should be understood as the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika.

"By another reason as well" means: because the monks' tranquility (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) were still immature, and by another reason such as the ripening of the wisdom of those to be trained (*veneyya*) in the Middle Region.
"For four months" means from the full moon of Āsāḷhī until the full moon of the latter Kattika;
that is, for four months. "In the manner stated by the phrase 'a hundred leagues all around,' etc. *Vasanaṃ* (dwelling) is the rain-retreat (*vassa*), which is the act of dwelling.

"One who has spent the rains" (*vutthavassa*) means one for whom the rainy season (*vassa*) has been lived and passed; [the phrase] "beings to be converted by the Blessed One" (*bhagavato veneyyasattā*) is stated as a genitive of ownership because they are to be guided by the Tathāgata, or it is a genitive of the agent.
And "beings to be converted" (*veneyyasattā*) refers to those beings who are to be guided in accordance with their respective temperaments (*carita*).

"Waiting for the ripening of the faculties" (*indriyaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno*) means [waiting] for the state of the faculties such as faith (*saddhā*) which brings about the ripening of liberation (*vimutti*).

"Waiting for it to ripen. It should be understood that no fixed rule regarding the month is established here, since the departure may take place on the first day of any one of the months of Phussa, Māgha, Phagguṇa, or Citta. Therefore he said:

"Having stayed right there for one month, or two, three, or four months. "Right there" means precisely at the place where the rains residence was entered. "Or with seven," and so forth, [refers to] "one month..."
The phrases beginning with “or” should be applied in their respective order:
if he stays in that very place for another month, he completes his wandering tour in seven months; if for two months, in six; if for three months, in five;
if he stays in that very place for four months, he completes his wandering tour in four months. But why is it called “going on a wandering tour”?
The phrase beginning with "iti" was spoken for the purpose of removing doubt. "Exceedingly weak from old age" means very decrepit.
When will they see them? They will certainly not see them. "Out of compassion for the world" means precisely out of compassion for the world. Therefore it was said:
"not for the sake of robes and so forth."
"By way of walking about on foot" means by way of wandering about on foot, or by way of staying for a few days here and there after having wandered about on foot;
for the term "dwelling" (vihāra) applies generally to all postures.

"For the sake of bodily comfort" means for the sake of the comfort of the body whose elements have become aggravated due to residing constantly in one place alone, [to be achieved] through wandering about.
"For the purpose of desiring an occasion for the arising of a meaning" means:

for the purpose of desiring an occasion for the arising of a meaning suitable for the teaching of the Dhamma—just as in the case of the *Agniskandhopama-sūtra*, the *Maghadeva-jātaka*, and so forth—or for the purpose of desiring such an occasion for the arising of a meaning;

that is to say, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma at an occasion when a meaning has arisen. "For the purpose of laying down a training rule" refers to the training rule on drinking fermented liquor and others.

For the purpose of laying down the training rules, as in the case of the *paññāpana*. "For the purpose of awakening" means for the purpose of awakening sentient beings capable of being awakened—such as Aṅgulimāla and others—to the Four Noble Truths.
"Great" means great. A journey undertaken with reference to a certain individual or a few individuals is a "fixed journey.
Any other [journey] undertaken with reference to many people, proceeding through villages, market towns, and cities in succession, is a [non-fixed journey].
“Wandering” (*cārikā*) means wandering without a fixed destination. Therefore he said, “There,” and so forth. “That which he wanders” is a reference to the action.
To show in detail what was already stated as “this is intended here,” he said, “At that time indeed,” and so forth.

“In the ten-thousandfold world-system” is said with reference to the ten thousand *cakravāḷas* that constitute the field of birth. Why? Because it is only there that beings are capable [of attaining enlightenment].

According to possibility. For it is said that the Blessed One, having directed his Buddha-knowledge toward seeing those beings who are capable and whose faculties are mature, spreads out a net of knowledge; and this is stated with reference to devas and brahmās.
However, as for humans, those to be enlightened are found only in this very world-system, and specifically within this Jambudīpa together with its surrounding regions.
[They] exist. "Relatives to be awakened" means the relatives of the Blessed One, consisting of those beings who are to be awakened.
For just as there is a connection through lineage and so forth, those to be trained are called the "relatives" of the Blessed One by virtue of their connection through the penetration of the Truths.

With reference to their coming within the range [of his influence], it is said: "He has entered into the net of omniscient knowledge. It is said that the Blessed One, having attained the meditative absorption of great compassion...

Having entered [the attainment] and emerged from it, he resolves his mind thus: "May those beings who are capable and whose knowledge is mature appear before my knowledge," and he applies his attention.
Immediately upon his application of attention, one, two, or many of those to be trained who are ready for discipline come within the range of his knowledge;
this, in this context, is the power of the Buddha. For those who have thus come within the range...
However, he observes their decisive support (upanissaya), past conduct, past causes, and their present practice.
For when attention is directed for the purpose of discerning beings who are ready to be trained (veneyya-satta), they first appear to him by virtue of their being ready to be trained;
then, thinking "What indeed will happen?", [he perceives] some accomplishment by way of going for refuge and so forth.
While investigating, he examines his former supports and so forth. Therefore, it says, "Then the Blessed One," and so on. "He" refers to Ambaṭṭha.

"Having engaged in debate and counter-debate" means having given a reply such as, "And those shaveling ascetics, Master Gotama," etc., to my words beginning with, "Is it thus for you, Ambaṭṭha? "Asabbhivākyaṃ" means the speech of a base person.
It means that he will speak various kinds of words—utterances unfit for one of good character—by way of addressing him three times as a slave.
"Nibbisevana" means free from stinging; the meaning is that it is devoid of the agitation caused by pride and arrogance.
"Avasaritabba" means to be approached. This is merely the name of that village; what is the point of searching for further meaning here?

It is stated: "The reading ‘ijjhānaṅgalanti’ also exists. By the phrase "he went by way of that direction," he shows that the accusative case is used in the sense of the instrumental, in accordance with the instrumental designation "yena disābhāgena" (by which direction). However, in accordance with the locative designation "yasmiṃ padese" (in which place), it is said "or he went to that [place].
He explains the meaning of both these cases with the words beginning "tena disābhāgena" (by that direction).
"Gata" means "approached"; the sense is "he went. Again, "gata" means "arrived"; the sense is "he reached.
"At Icchānaṅgala" is an indication of the Blessed One's alms-resort village at that time; here the locative case is used in the sense of proximity.
"In the grove of Icchānaṅgala," however, is an indication of his dwelling place; here the locative case is used in its primary sense of location. Thus, both of these [expressions] are locatives.
Explaining the word *pada* by showing its specific meaning, he said, “In dependence on Icchānaṅgala,” and so forth.

The description of the Blessed One’s dwelling as a “camp for the aggregate of virtue” and so on is a demonstration of the Blessed One’s abiding solely out of regard for the welfare of those to be trained, according to the method already stated.
In that regard, the practice of the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, is entirely devoted to the suppression of non-Dhamma, and that [practice] occurs by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
There is the inclusion of only the triad beginning with virtue (*sīla*). The connection is as follows:
"Having established a camp of virtue"—that is, having established a camp known as virtue that resembles the wooden or stone-made camps of a universal monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*)—he dwells there.

For a *khandhāvāra* is so called because wood, heaps, and so forth (*dāru-kkhandha-ādi*) surround or enclose it on all sides; the vowel *a* is lengthened [to *ā*], and it refers to a place where kings have recently resided.

In that context, virtue (*sīla*) is also spoken of in that way because it resembles [the Blessed One] in the sense of warding off fear, by virtue of its mere connection with the Blessed One’s recent act of dwelling there.
"The tip of the arrow of concentration" (*samādhikonta*) refers to the auspicious arrow consisting of right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*).

"The word for the knowledge of omniscience" (*sabbaññutaññāṇapada*) refers to the victorious mantra-word consisting of the knowledge of omniscience. "Reciting" (*parivattayamāno*) means muttering [it]. It is also called "the essence of the knowledge of omniscience" (*sabbaññutaññāṇasara*).
"Recitation" means the thunderbolt-tip sound of omniscient knowledge revolving again and again.

"In whatever dwelling one pleases" is a statement common to all dwellings; the meaning is that one dwells by whichever dwelling among the divine dwellings (dibbavihāra) and so forth one personally prefers.
Commentary on the Pokkharasāti Sutta: 255. *Manteti*:
in the body of secret lore (*manta-śāstra*) such as the *Iruveda* and others. For the *Iruveda* and so forth are called "secrets" (*manta*) in the sense that they must be spoken with restraint.
He says "recites" (*sajjhāyati*) because the word *aṇa* means "sound. However, the worldly folk say: "The offspring of Brahmā..."
“*Brāhmaṇo*, *nāgamo*, *ṇattaṃ*, *dīghādī*. Why was this very etymological derivation (*vacanattha*) stated?

He says, “This very [one],” and so forth. Then, he removes the objection as to what the other etymological derivation is by saying, “But the Noble Ones,” and so forth. Alternatively, this was said in order to reject the worldly etymology they speak, such as “a *brāhmaṇa* is one born from Brahmā,” and so on. “This very [one],” etc.
By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he rejects that [former position].

Then, by means of the phrase "of the birth-Brahmins" (*jātibrāhmaṇānam*), showing the etymological derivation (*nirutti*) for those who are "Brahmins by purification" (*visuddhibrāhmaṇa*)—as there are two kinds of Brahmins shown by this intervening expression, namely birth-Brahmins and purification-Brahmins—he says, "But the noble ones," and so forth.
For, according to the method of etymology, they are called "noble Brahmins" (*ariya-brāhmaṇā*) because they cast out (*bahi karonti*) much evil (*bahū pāpe*).
“His body, it is said, was like a white lotus”—this alone is the demonstration of the reason for obtaining that name;

the rest, however, is merely a demonstration of the specific qualities found therein by way of association with that. Therefore he said: “Thus they knew him as ‘Pokkharasāti’ because of his resemblance to a lotus (pokkhara).
For, according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*), one whose body (*kāya*) is similar to a lotus (*pokkhara*) is a *pokkharasāti*. The word *sāti* [is derived from] *sāta*.
Or, it has a meaning similar to "lotus" (*pokkhara*); his body is as white as a lotus, thus he is *Pokkharasāti*. "White like a lotus" means having the color of a white water-lily (*setapaduma*).
