"In the city of the gods" refers to the celestial cities such as Āḷakamanda. "A silver archway erected" refers to a silver threshold-stake (*indakhīla*) that is deeply set in its foundation and rises very high.
"A streak of black clouds" refers to a line of dark clouds that appears only occasionally.
“Silver tube” (*rajatapanāḷikā*) means a vessel made of silver. “Well-rounded” (*suvaṭṭitā*) means well-circular in the places appropriate for being circular.

“Extremely pure” (*suparisuddhā*) means due to the absence of black stains, spots, and the like. By the phrase beginning with “in a kingless land,” he likewise demonstrates that it has attained a state of supreme excellence.
Now, showing another reason for its receiving that name, he says “But this,” and so forth. And therein, “in a region of the Himalayas...”

“‘He was reborn in the calyx of a lotus in a great lake’—this alone is the demonstration of the cause for his receiving that name. The remainder, however, is merely a demonstration of the manner in which he appeared in connection with that [rebirth].
Therefore he said: ‘Thus, because he lay in a *pokkhara* (lotus), they knew him as *Pokkharasāti*.
For one who lies (*sayati*) in a *pokkhara*—that is, in a lotus—is a *pokkhara-sāti*; or else, *sāta* is said to mean a beautiful shape (*samasaṇṭhāna*), [and thus] in a *pokkhara*...”
“Likewise, Pokkharasāti, it was born with a symmetrical shape, and thus it is called ‘possessing darkness’ (tamassatthi).

As for what the Teacher said—“Of what kind was this brahmin’s previous application (pubbayoga), such that the Blessed One approached that place to favor him?”—that was said referring only to a portion of the statement beginning with “But this one.
This is because of the statement beginning with “From there, he [came] to the world of men.”
Regarding the phrase "reborn in the world of the devas," it should be understood that what is stated here is rebirth in successive states.
With reference specifically to such a rebirth through karma, it was said, "having loathed dwelling in a mother’s womb," and so forth.
By the phrase "reborn within the calyx of a lotus," he shows that he was reborn having been born from moisture (*saṃsedaja*). "It does not bloom" means it does not open.
"Tenā" means by the ascetic. "Nāḷato" means from the flower-stalk. "Suvaṇṇacuṇṇapiñjaraṃ" refers to that which is tawny with gold dust—that is, golden-colored;
the meaning is that it is golden in color due to being strewn with gold dust. For it is stated in the *Sāratthadīpanī* that the word *piñjara* is a synonym for golden color.
This same method applies here as well in the phrase "tawny with lotus pollen."
"Silver image" (*rūpiyamaya-rūpaka*) refers to a figure made of silver. "I shall tend to it" means I shall support it. "The further shore" (*pāra*) is said to mean the end or the completion;
it is so called because it is like the "further shore" (*pāra*) that constitutes the terminus of rivers, oceans, and the like.

One is "wise" (*paṇḍita*) by virtue of the knowledge of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-ñāṇa*), which is termed the wisdom of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-paññā*). Thus, regarding those things to be done, or regarding the Vedas, one possesses proficiency (*veyyattiya*) characterized by confident wisdom (*visāradapaññā*).

*Byatto*: learned. *Aggabrāhmaṇo*: a preeminent brāhmaṇa, one who is foremost in his field. *Sippaṃ*: the craft of the Vedas (*vedasippa*), because it was acquired through its specific treatises (*pakaraṇa*).
*Brahmadeyyaṃ adāsī*: he gave it as a royal grant (*brahmadeyya*), having made it a grant according to the method that will be explained later.
In the phrase "he dwells" (*ajjhāvasati*), the prefixes *adhi-* and *ā-* are merely intensifiers; following them is the word "Ukkhaṭṭhaṃ."

In the compound *ajjhāpubbavasayoge*, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. Alternatively, the word *adhi* has the sense of sovereignty (*issariya*), while the word *ā* has the sense of a limit (*mariyāda*);

thus, by the phrase "in the name of Ukaṭṭha" (*ukkaṭṭhanāmaka*), it is shown that *ukkaṭṭha* is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative when joined with a direct object (*kammappavacanīya*).
To explain this very meaning, the passage beginning with "of that" (*tassā*) was stated. "Of that... [and so on].
“Having become the master of the city” is an explanation of the meaning of the word “having overcome”;
by this, it is shown that “the state of being a master is ‘overcoming. The phrase beginning with “by which boundary,” however, is an explanation of the meaning of the prefix *ā-*;
by this, it is shown that “the prefix *ā-* has the sense of a boundary (*mariyāda*), and a boundary is that within which one must dwell.”
"...independence. For the phrase "by which boundary" means by which state called independence, which is not shared with others.
The passage beginning with "by way of prefixes," however, is an explanation of the meaning of the term "in the name of *ukkaṭṭha*";

by this he illustrates that even though there is an occasion for the locative case, [the suffixes] are of two kinds—those that follow the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) and those that serve as qualifiers (*visesaka*).

“Because it is joined with a prefix (*upasagga*), only the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) is prescribed here. As for the phrase beginning with “*tassa kira*,” it is an illustration of a conventional designation (*samaññā*) that follows the actual meaning.
A “site” (*vatthu*) refers to a plot of land suitable for building a city, as in expressions such as “the site of a monastery” (*ārāmavatthu*) or “the site of a vihāra” (*vihāravatthu*).
A “torch” (*ukkā*) is a staff-mounted lamp. They “took” [it], thinking: “Today is an auspicious day; therefore, it is a favorable constellation (*sunakkhatta*); even there—”
Thinking, “May this auspicious moment not pass,” they guarded against the break of day;
having set up torches for the purpose of providing light during the night, they took up the site of the city while the torches were burning. This explains it thus:

they were at Ukkaṭṭhā because the torches (ukkā) were standing there. [The form] *mūlavibhujā* and so forth is included by way of the class of derivative forms (*ākṛtigaṇa*), or according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), [it means] while the torches were shining.
“Ukkaṭṭhā” means “situated among torches”; likewise, because it was built even while the torches were standing [there], it is also called “Ukkaṭṭhā.

However, in the *Madhyamāgama-ṭīkā*, it is stated thus: “And that city is also called ‘Ukkaṭṭhā’ because it was constructed at night while torches were standing [there], thinking, ‘This is an auspicious day, a favorable moment; let us not let a good constellation pass by. While the staff-lamps were being lit and carried [there]...”

"It has been said, 'because it was measured'"; this too should be understood as consistent with and in agreement with that [previous statement], since even the acquisition of the city-site is included within the act of measuring out the city. However, others say:
"That city is called Ukkaṭṭhā because of its possession of superior qualities due to the excellence of its location, the excellence of its equipment, and the excellence of its inhabitants."
"It receives its name. However, the worldlings say: "It is called Ukkaṭṭhā because a torch was carried [there] at the time it was founded;
it is merely a change in the phonetic form," and this designation is in the feminine gender. Therefore, its usage is seen here in such passages as:
"And just as the venerable Gotama approaches other clans of lay followers in Ukkaṭṭhā" (in the *Mūlapariyāyasutta* and others).
And: “At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a king sāla tree,” and so forth.
Let it be thus here that the accusative case occurs by virtue of the prefix; but how can this be the case in the remaining instances? In response to this inquiry, he says:
“Because of its non-accusative nature in the remaining instances. Therein, “of that” (*tassa*) refers to that which has been designated as an accusative by virtue of the prefix.
Regarding the word "ukkaṭṭha": "Because it is not employed" means because it is not employed as a qualifying attribute (*visesana*).
"In the remaining words" refers to the seven words beginning with "sattussada.
He removes the objection—"Is this linguistic usage consistent with the characteristics of words?"—with the passage: "In that case... [etc. ...should be sought."

By this [word]. "Therein" (*tattha*) means: in both types of construction mentioned—namely, that which is expressed by way of a prefix (*upasagga*) and that which is expressed by way of a non-objective case (*anupayoga*).

"Characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) refers to the characteristic of words (*saddalakkhaṇa*), which is the method or principle for grasping [the meaning], or it refers to a grammatical rule (*sutta*). "Should be sought" (*pariyesitabba*) means:
because it exists within the treatises on grammar (*saddasattha*), it should be investigated by means of knowledge; what is meant is that it should be grasped. For by this...
This demonstrates that this application of sound (*saddapayoga*) conforms to the characteristic of sound (*saddalakkhaṇa*); and those learned in sound (*saddavidū*) maintain:

"When preceded by *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, *ā*, and so forth, the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) is reached in the sense of the locative; and in the case of words to be qualified (*visesitabbapada*), there is non-application (*anupayoga*) according to the rule for qualifying words that share the same grammatical referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
In that context, when the word *adhi* and the word *ā* are merely prefixes (*upasaggamatta*), then...
Regarding the phrase “and for the third and seventh [cases],” by this rule, when used in conjunction with *vasa* preceded by *adhi*, the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) is employed. For they say:

“In the sense of the seventh case, when used in conjunction with *upa*, *anu*, *adhi*, and *ava*—referring to time and direction—and in the usage of *adhi* preceded by *pati*, *si*, *tha*, and *va*, as well as in the cases of *tappa*, *ānaca*, and *āre*, the second case is used.

Regarding time: having dressed at the time of forenoon (*pubbaṇhasamayaṃ*); ‘at one time’ (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*), the Blessed One; ‘for some time’ (*kañci kālaṃ*), by way of the condition of prior arising (*purejātapaccayena*).”
The condition: this night, the Four Great Kings. In the eastern direction is Dhatarattha. In the usage of *upa* preceded by *ādi*, [examples are]:

he dwells near the village (*upavasati*), he dwells around the village (*anuvasati*), he dwells in the village (*āvasati*), he lives in the household (*ajjhāvasati*). In the usage of *adhi* preceding *si*, *ṭhā*, and *vas*, [examples are]:

he will lie upon the earth (*adhisessati*), he stands over the village (*adhitiṭṭhati*), he dwells over the village (*ajjhāvasati*). In the sense of "sufficiency" (*tappāna*) and "wandering" (*cāra*)...
"...drinks from the river," "wanders through the village," and so forth.

However, when the word *adhi* has the sense of sovereignty (*issariya*) and the word *ā* has the sense of a limit (*mariyāda*), then, by the rule "when joined with a term that functions as an object (*kammappavacanīya*)," the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) is used due to its connection with such an object-term.
For they say: "The prefixes (*upasagga*) beginning with *anu*..."

“Terms such as *dhī* and particles (*nipāta*) are designated as *kammappavacanīya* (terms denoting the object). Those by which an action—reckoned as ‘action’ (*kiriyā*)—is to be expressed are *kammappavacanīya*.

But as for the remaining words, when they are used without a [direct] application (*anupayoga*), by what characteristic do they become the term for the application (*upayogavacana*)? By the very characteristic already stated.
If that is so, then because they also possess the state of being a locus (*ādhāra*), would there not be a lack of distinctness in their loci?
Could it be so? No, because even many words may have a single meaning by virtue of referring to a city.
For their difference consists merely in their individual meanings. However, other grammarians maintain this:
"Words in apposition (samānādhikaraṇa) possess grammatical concordance with the qualifying word through their respective connection to an action, as in: 'He makes a mat, [one that is] large.'"

Regarding the statement, "In the phrase *dassanīyaṃ*, the accusative case is used solely in the sense of the object through its connection with each respective action— as in 'he makes a mat,' 'he makes it large,' and 'he makes it beautiful' (dassanīyaṃ)—

this must be examined, because qualifying words (*visesanapada*) that share the same grammatical basis (*samānādhikaraṇa*) lack a connection with an action. For when there is a connection with an action, then [the word] is no longer a qualifier."
“Abundance” (*ussadatā*) here means “multitude,” as expressed by the term “many people. That abundance is further shown by the phrases “crowded with people” and so forth.

Those who are to be nurtured and raised in the forest and other such places are called “those to be nourished” (*posāvanīya*); by this, he shows their status as beings (*dhamma*). “Having enclosed” (*āvijjhitvā*) means having surrounded.
A lotus pond is one made by digging; a reservoir (*taḷāka*) is one made by damming. [This refers to] precisely in a place where water was previously cut off.
It is said that "water-born flowers have grown" because "they were always filled with water.

In the phrase "of water," the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) in connection with the action of filling, as in such examples as "having had large sacks made and having them filled with gold and bullion.
The term *sadhañña* ("with grain") is neuter in gender, owing to its dependence on the word *nagara* ("city").

It is stated either according to the specific wording or by means of a term expressing general application; this applies everywhere. Regarding the phrase "a vast accumulation of grain consisting of various kinds such as morning-grain and evening-grain," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) here includes vegetable soups such as those made from gourds, pumpkins, and so forth, which are distinct from those two types of grain.

By this, the following meaning is understood: here the word "grain" (*dhanna*) does not denote specific grains like rice and the like, but rather refers to anything that is merely excellent for nourishment.
Alternatively, it is employed by way of *virūpekasesa* (the single remainder of dissimilar forms) as a term denoting all kinds of food—both solid and soft—as well as soups without exception.

"By this much" means by the three aforementioned phrases. "In the royal manner" (*rājalīlāya*) means by the elegance of kings. "The perfection of success" (*samiddhisampatti*) is the excellence consisting in the state of being fully provided with the enjoyment and utilization [of requisites] by means of *Samiddhi*.
When it is said, “Enjoyed by the king” (*rājabhogga*), one must necessarily ask, “By whom was it given?”; thus he shows that it is spoken in this way with the words beginning “by whom.
Alternatively, another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā* is that it is called “enjoyed by the king” because it is to be enjoyed as if by the king himself.
Because it has been obtained from the king by way of family inheritance through the succession of sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, it is called “the king’s inheritance” (*rañño dāyabhūta*).
It has been said: "Bhikkhus, be my heirs of the Dhamma," and so forth. In such passages, the word *dāya* is a synonym for *dāyajja* (inheritance);

thus he says, "the meaning is 'heritage'. He addresses the objection—"How is it called a *brahmadeyya* (a royal gift) because it is given?"—with the words beginning "having raised the umbrella," and so on.
For [it is so called] because, after being used according to royal prerogative, the subsequent gain of its use...
"Brahmadeyyatā" (the state of being a royal grant) does not exist [in this case]; however, since this has been given in that very manner, it is therefore said to be "brahmadeyya.

"Chejjabhejja" refers to punishment consisting of various forms such as corporal punishment or fines. "In river fords, mountains, and so forth" means in river fords, at the foot of mountains, at village gates, at the entrances to forests, and so on.
By the mention of the white parasol, all other insignia of royalty are also implied.

It should be understood that this is taken as the primary meaning. When it is simply said, "it must be eaten by the king," the intended sense here is not made clear; therefore, the word *eva* (only) is employed.
For the intended sense here is that even one who has not come from the royal family is permitted to eat [the food] if he is a king.
"Dāya" means that which is to be given; by the phrase "rājadāya" (king’s gift), it is implied...
Since the fact that it was given by the king is already established, he asks: "What is the purpose of the further statement, 'given by King Pasenadi of Kosala'?

He replies: "For the purpose of indicating the donor-king," and so forth. The intention is that this was stated because the donor-king had not yet been specified by saying, "it was given by such-and-such a king.
Furthermore, in this context, within the first method of interpretation, the question arises regarding the term "rājabhogga" (the king's domain).
This has been stated; however, in the second method, the phrase “the king’s gift” (*rājadāya*) should also be noted as a distinction.
In that context, because there was no space to place [the food] before him due to his great multitude, rice, curry, condiments, and so forth were given to him even from the side (*passena*);

thus he is called *Pasenadi*, by way of a compound without elision (*aluttasamāsa*). For that king, even from a doṇa-measure of rice, would take the boiled rice along with its corresponding curry and condiments...

He eats. For at the time when he has finished his morning meal, having come into the presence of the Teacher, he rolls here and there, overcome by sleepiness, unable to sit upright; and the Blessed One [said]:
"When one is drowsy and a great eater..."
Sleeping and rolling about,
like a great boar fed on fodder,
the dull-witted one enters the womb again and again.
With this verse he exhorted his nephew, the young brahmin named Sudassana:
“For a person who is always mindful,
Who knows the proper measure regarding food obtained,..."
"Feelings arise for one whose body is worn;
he ages slowly while guarding his life.
Having learned this verse in the presence of the Blessed One, [he recited it] daily at the time of the final alms-offering while he was eating.

He had [the verse] recited; later, on another occasion, having discerned the meaning of that verse and by repeatedly consuming only the final morsel of alms-food, he became established upon a measure of a single *nāḷika* of rice, and with his body emaciated, he became strong and attained happiness.

However, in the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated thus: "He conquers enemies and the enemy army, therefore he is Pasenadi. For even those learned in grammar [recognize] the substitution of the letter *ja*.
Regarding the letter *da*, they cite this example: "He indeed conquers his own nephew, King Ajātasattu, as well as the five hundred thieves and others who were imprisoned.
Because he is the sovereign (*adhipati*) of the kingdom of Kosala, he is called "Kosalan";
therefore, the meaning should be understood as "given by the king named Pasenadi, the lord of Kosala. This refers to the state of being relinquished and abandoned.
Because it was given precisely for the purpose of not being taken back again, it is here called a *brahmadeyya* (a gift to Brahmins);
it is not, as in the previous method, given for the purpose of being enjoyed under the designation of "royal property. Thus he says, "Just as," and so forth.

Having been relinquished, or abandoned by way of the state of being relinquished, it is "relinquished and abandoned" (*nissaṭṭhapariccatta*); the meaning is that it was renounced through the exercise of liberality.
By the word “perceived” (*upalabhi*), he shows that “hearing” (*savana*) is what is perceived. And this perception is a form of knowing by way of hearing; thus it is said:

“He knew by following the sound of the speech that had reached the ear-door. For here, “hearing” refers precisely to the knowing that occurs through the cognitive process (*viññāṇa-vīthi*) following the ear-door.
By that very means, the meaning stated in the passage beginning with “The ascetic Gotama, indeed... [was understood].
Because it has been realized; however, it is not merely heard by way of the auditory process (*sotadvāravīthi*), since its meaning has not yet been realized by that means.
Because the employment of words has the function of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), every sentence contains an implicit restriction. Therefore, even without a word expressing that meaning, the sense is:
"He indeed heard," excluding other possibilities, and there was no obstacle whatsoever to his hearing. This is the meaning.
Because it is understood [in this sense], he says: "It is a particle used merely for the purpose of completing the metrical line.

Furthermore, although the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is already included within the entire sentence, the word *kho* is employed for the sake of explicit restriction from the perspective of the literal meaning (*nītattha*).

Since this specific meaning is understood through the force of the word *eva*, the first alternative was stated. What is the definitive purpose of the restriction from the perspective of the literal meaning? It is absolute certainty.
It has been stated that [the word] is "done" and "determined" by the phrase beginning with "therein" (tattha).

Now, he removes the objection—"What is the purpose of the particle *kho*, which serves merely to fill out the line?"—with the words beginning with "by way of filling out the line," meaning that its purpose is solely to provide elegance (*siliṭṭhatā*) for the sentence, which is a collection of words formed from a collection of syllables.
For the word "heard" (*assosi*), when the particle *kho* is included, it is by means of that...
That which is full-blown, adorned, and decorated is called "filled" (pūrita); by means of that, the preceding and following words become smooth through easy pronunciation.
It is not [smooth] when that [filler] is not taken up; therefore, it is said that even a mere filler of the word serves the purpose of ensuring the smoothness of the words and syllables.
And here, the word *matta* has the sense of excluding any further qualification.
By this, its quality of illustrating a non-literal meaning is shown; by the word "eva" (indeed), however, its definiteness due to the elegance of the words and syllables is indicated.

With the passage beginning "The ascetic indeed," etc., he shows that it is an illustration of the matter as it was heard, using the phrase "now," etc. Regarding the term "one who has stilled evil" (*samitapāpa*):

here, the meaning to be understood is "one who has stilled evil absolutely, without remainder, together with its latent tendencies. For it is in this way [that the meaning is distinguished] from the stilling of evil by outsiders, those free from passion, those in training (*sekha*), and those beyond training (*asekha*).
The Blessed One’s pacification of evil is distinguished according to its specific nature. Therefore it was said:
“And the Blessed One has pacified evil by means of the unsurpassed Noble Path. To establish this very meaning through the text of the *Niddesa*, he said:

“For it is said,” and so forth. “By him” (*assā*) means by this bhikkhu, or by the Blessed One. “Pacified” (*samitā*) means brought to an end, or one who has caused it to reach a state of equilibrium (*samabhāva*).
The meaning is that they exist within him who has become the recipient (sampadāna).

And it is said, "And the Blessed One," etc., because this designation conforms to the actual state of things. "By that" means by virtue of having thus stilled evil. "Yathābhūtaṃ" means that which proceeds according to reality;
that itself is the quality (guṇa), and it is attained in that manner. "Khalu" is an indeclinable particle (nepātika) used in the phrase *khalupacchābhattika*.
It is not a noun; and since particles have multiple meanings, it is intended here specifically in the sense of "hearing from another," thus he says, "a particle in the sense of hearing from another.
And here, "hearing from another" (*anussavana*) means hearing by way of tradition. "Accomplished in the brahmin caste" (*brāhmaṇajātisamudāgata*) means arrived at the brahmin caste;
what is meant is that it is established by birth. "Mere address" (*ālapanamatta*) means merely words of affectionate address, and nothing more than that.
This is an explanation of the meaning. These [terms]—“bho,” “āvuso,” or “devānaṃ piyā”—are used as forms of address for those who are dear.

He said, beginning with “And it has also been said,” in order to establish that these are modes of address arising from the brahmin caste, by means of the passage on the Brahmin in the *Dhammapada* and the passage from the *Vāseṭṭha-sutta* in the *Suttanipāta*.

In this context, the meaning is as follows: If one were "possessing something" (*sakiñcana*) due to the "possessions" (*kiñcana*) such as lust and the like, he would indeed be called a "mere addresser of 'Bho'" (*bhovādī*), because he wanders about addressing people with "O, sir!
during invitations and the like; he would not be a *brāhmaṇa*. The remainder of the verse is: "One who possesses nothing and grasps at nothing—him I call a *brāhmaṇa*.
Therein, lust and the other defilements crush living beings as if they were "something" (*kiñca*).
They are called *kiñcanāni* because they obstruct (*palibuddhanti*). It is said that when people have threshing floors trampled by oxen, they say, "Trample it, Kapila! Trample it, Kāḷaka!
Therefore, the word *kiñcana* should be understood as having the sense of "trampling. As it is said in the *Niddesa*:
"‘Nothing’ (*akiñcana*) means the ‘nothingness’ of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, the nothingness of defilements, and the nothingness of misconduct."
“He for whom these possessions have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge—he is called ‘possessing nothing’ (akiñcana).
The term “Gotama” is a designation based on his clan, which people in the world also call the “Solar Clan” (Ādiccagotta);
whereas “Son of the Sakyans” (Sakyaputta) and “Sākiyan” are synonyms for him based on his birth. For this has been said in the *Pabbajjā-sutta*:
“By clan I am named Ādicca; by birth I am named Sākiya.
I have gone forth from that family, not aspiring after sensual pleasures.
Likewise, it is said: “He describes the Blessed One as ‘Gotama’ by way of his clan,” and so forth. In this context, *gaṃ tāyati* means...
The meaning is that it protects both the lineage (*gotta*)—the designation occurring as "Gotama"—and the intellect (*buddhi*), because they share a single objective domain.
For just as the intellect does not function without an object that serves as its referent, so too the designation does not function without the thing designated;
therefore, that object termed "lineage" is said to protect them. And here, the word *go* refers to the designation.
And it occurs in the sense of intelligence (*buddhi*). For thus they say:
"It occurs in the sense of a cow, a bull, a sense-faculty, the earth, speech, the sun, a ray of light, and also in the sense of water."
“Among those meanings, ‘goṇa’ [the word for cow] refers to the bull; the others refer to the male.
In this regard, in such expressions as “He went while the cows were being milked; the bull was the fifth,” the word *go* refers to the bull (*goṇa*).

In such expressions as “pasture” (*gocara*), it refers to the sense-faculties (*indriya*). In such expressions as “cattle-herding” (*gorakkha*), it refers to the earth. For thus it is said in the commentary on the Vāseṭṭha Sutta of the Suttanipāta:
It is said: “Cattle-keeping means the protection of fields; what is meant is the work of plowing. For the earth is called ‘go’ (cow), and its various divisions are called ‘khetta’ (field).
In such statements as “A lineage (gotta) means two kinds of lineages: a low lineage and a high lineage,” it functions in the sense of intellect (*buddhi*).
In the ancient poetic composition, “I bow to Gotama of the *gogotta* [lineage],” it refers to the sun.
The meaning is: "I pay homage to Gotama, the Kinsman of the Sun, the Perfectly Enlightened One. In such expressions as "uṇhagu," it refers to a ray;
for "uṇhagu" means one whose rays (gāvo) are hot (uṇhā), namely the sun. In such expressions as "gosītacandana," it refers to water;
for it is cool like water known as "go" (cow), and that itself is the sandalwood. For in that case, [it refers to] boiled oil removed from the hearth.
When it is poured in, that oil becomes cool at that very moment. Among these meanings, when the word *go* refers to a bull, it is appropriately feminine and masculine;
however, in the remaining senses, it is exclusively masculine.
But what is this so-called *gotta* (clan)? It is that which is not shared with other family lineages, having originated from the first ancestor of that particular family.
This should be understood as a common generic form belonging to that clan. For this is indeed common to those included in that clan;
it is a generic form by virtue of being shared. Thus, even those born in that clan, such as the Great King Suddhodana and others, are called simply "Gotama.
It was for this very reason that the Blessed One addressed his father, the Great King Suddhodana, as "one who has transcended excellence."

“Indeed, Gotama, they are Tathāgatas,” said the Great King Vessavaṇa; and the Blessed One [was addressed] by the Great King Vessavaṇa as well: “We pay homage to the Buddha, Gotama, who is perfected in true knowledge and conduct.
And the Venerable Vaṅgīsa [addressed] the Venerable Ānanda:
“Please speak of Nibbāna out of compassion for us, Gotama. But here, it refers specifically to the Blessed One. Therefore he said: “The Blessed One by way of his clan...”
"...he proclaims. Therefore, one refers back to the threefold meaning as previously stated.

And here, by the term "ascetic" (*samaṇa*), the Blessed One's state of being highly esteemed by those of similar standing is shown, because of the proclamation of his having stilled evil within that specific domain;
and by the term "Gotama," his being born of a noble lineage renowned among worldly people is shown, because of the proclamation of his origin from that specific noble clan.

He is the son of the great king Suddhodana of the Sakyan clan, hence he is called "the Sakyan" (*Sakyaputta*). This, moreover, is a designation that illustrates his high birth, praising him for being born into a vast and ever-exalted kshatriya lineage.
For the royal Sakyan family is the most eminent of all kshatriyas, its line unbroken since the time of the great King Mahāsammata, the progenitor of all kshatriyas.
As it has been said:
“The Great Sage was born into the lineage of King Mahāsammata;
indeed, in the first aeon, he was the king named Mahāsammata. (The first verse in the second chapter of the *Mahāvaṃsa*).
How does this illustrate the state of having gone forth out of faith? He said, “By someone,” and so forth. *Parijiyanaṃ* means declining or falling away.
"Pārijuñña" means "wasting away" (parijirati), or one who wastes away is "parijiṇṇo"; the state of that is "pārijuñña," by which [means]. The meaning is:
having gone forth without being overcome or eclipsed by any such wasting away—such as the wasting away of relatives or the wasting away of wealth—and thus remaining unassailed by decline.
To clarify that very point through a different formulation, it is said: "having abandoned that family while it was still undecayed. "Undecayed" (aparikkhīṇaṃ) means...
"By no loss whatsoever" means not by any loss such as the loss of kinsmen, the loss of wealth, or the like.
"Gone forth out of faith" means gone forth solely out of faith; for it is in this way that the phrase "by no [other cause]" and so forth becomes appropriately explained.
But is it not the case that the statement "gone forth from the Sakyan clan" is merely an illustration of having gone forth from a noble family, since its meaning is precisely that?

Is it not because [the fact of having gone forth out of faith] is not being understood that this does not indicate the state of having gone forth out of faith, since its meaning is not being understood?

But it should not be viewed in this way, because the state of having gone forth out of faith is established in substance by his having abandoned a vast circle of kinsmen and a great mass of wealth. For such was the case at the birth of the Lord of the World.
There was no loss whatsoever for the clan; rather, there was only growth, and thus its state of supreme prosperity became manifest and renowned in the world.
Therefore, when it is merely said, "He went forth from the Sakyan clan," the fact that he went forth out of faith—having abandoned such a supremely prosperous clan—is already established.
This is the resolution [offered] by the passage beginning with "by some kind of loss."
It should be understood that he "makes it manifest. "Thereafter" refers to the passage beginning with, "While wandering on tour among the Kosalans," and so forth.
[As in: "Excellent is the king who delights in the Dhamma; excellent is the man possessed of wisdom;
excellent is one who does not betray his friends; happiness lies in not committing evil. And so on.
Just as the word *sādhu* here means "beautiful," he says, "Indeed, it is beautiful" (*sundaraṃ kho pana*). The particle *kho* is a fixed expression used for emphasis;
*pana* is used in the sense of an alternative point. Indeed, these two are included in this commentary for the purpose of making known its meaningfulness.
Furthermore, "beautiful" (*sundara*) means auspicious (*bhaddaka*), and its auspiciousness consists in its being a bringer of welfare and happiness to those who behold it.
It is said, “bringing benefit and bringing happiness. Here, “benefit” (attha) is threefold, according to the categories of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal;
and “happiness” (sukha) is likewise threefold.
Regarding the phrase “of such a kind” (tathārūpānaṃ), this is the meaning from the standpoint of the word itself. However, to show the mere sense of the matter, it says “of such a sort” (evarūpānaṃ).

It has been said. And as for those qualities with which the Blessed One is endowed—by virtue of which he is, at all times, worthy of being inspired with absolute faith and confidence by the world of the fourfold measure because of their being such as they truly are—it is with reference to his possession of such qualities that the phrase “of such Arahants” was spoken;
showing this, [the author] said “of such a kind,” and so forth. “Laddhasaddhānaṃ” means “of those who have acquired faith.”
This means "those who are gaining faith from other people. Alternatively, it means "those who have acquired fame," that is, those who have acquired a reputation (*kittisadda*).
By this, the meaning of the word *arahanta* as "those who are worthy" (*arahantānaṃ*) is shown, and the manifestation of the designation *arahant* is demonstrated;
furthermore, by the phrase "of what kind that venerable Gotama is," the indefinite sense of the word *tathārūpānaṃ* ("of such a kind") is indicated.

Having shown the meaning, in order to show it also by way of a formal definition of its specific form, it is said: "of those who have acquired the title ‘Arahant’ in the world through the attainment of qualities as they truly are. For this too is a demonstration of the meaning of the very phrase "of such persons" (*tathārūpānaṃ*);
and this alone is the method intended by the teachers here in this *ṭīkā*, because it is stated in exactly that way in the *Sāratthadīpanī*. "Of such persons... [the text continues].

He did not say, “Those venerable ones are arahants,” but rather said, “Such as that venerable Gotama is,” using the plural form “of such arahants” (*tathārūpānaṃ arahataṃ*) in order to indicate that the state [of being an arahant] was pointed out by means of a plural expression specifically out of profound respect for the Blessed One alone.
For those learned in grammar require the plural form when referring to oneself or to one’s teachers. Thus: “...as it truly is... of such arahants.”
And by this, he shows, according to the literal sense, that even those beings of small stature and coarse appearance inspire confidence in the Blessed One;
for the state of Arahantship is, as appropriate, the domain of those very beings.

However, it should be understood that by showing this, the fact that others of small physical stature and small voice also inspire confidence is likewise demonstrated, because of the inseparable connection between them.
“Serene and cool” means clear and cool; or, by way of serenity, they are cool. By this, he shows their state of being serene and limpid.
Although the word “seeing” (*dassana*) is used, because there is the possibility of further action beyond that, this sense of esteem is obtained;
thus he says, “even mere seeing is good. For otherwise, it would imply that “only seeing is good, not... [listening].”
The phrase "performing beyond that" results in an unintended meaning; here, the particle *pi* has the sense of "reverence," or the particle *api* is indicated by elision.
In the expression "he proclaims the holy life (*brahmacariya*)," the particle *iti* connects with the word "exalted" (*abbhuggato*);
therefore, this [particle]—as in the phrase "it is good"—is here [connected] to the Brahmin Pokkharasāti.
This [phrase] is to be connected with the words, “he addressed the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.
Furthermore, the phrase “having formed an aspiration” (*ajjhāsayaṃ katvā*) is a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*), because its meaning is understood from the context.

That which is understood in meaning but whose word is not explicitly employed is called a “textual supplement. Explaining this point, he said: “Even a mere sight is good; thus, having formed such an aspiration...”
"Having done so. Herein, the story of the Kosiya bird, as it appears in the commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta of the Mūlapaññāsa, should also be told.
256. Regarding the commentary on the discourse with the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha:
"A reciter"—this is, in its primary sense, a term of reproach, but in its secondary sense, a term of praise.
Having done so, they speak [of them] just as one would say "a man, a person. To demonstrate this, the passage from the Aggañña Sutta has been cited.
In that context, "these" refers to people known by the designation "meditators" (jhāyaka). "They do not meditate" means they do not apply themselves to or produce jhāna in leaf huts;
rather, the meaning is that they remain near villages and market towns, occupied only with composing Vedic texts. That...
Regarding these [three], since the third was born precisely after taking the first and second names—namely, "brāhmaṇa" and "ajjhāyaka"—it is said:
"The third syllable, 'a', was produced specifically for the ajjhāyaka. Here, "syllable" (*akkhara*) refers to etymological derivation (*nirutti*) and conventional designation (*samaññā*).
For it is called a "syllable" because, by virtue of being firmly established in that very sense, it does not wander elsewhere. Regarding the *manta*s...

"Reverses" means he recites the Veda; the meaning is that he masters it. For here, the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) of words is by way of the root *adhi-i*, whereas in the other case it is by way of the root *jhe*.
"Bears the mantras in mind" means that he places in his heart the mantras as they were studied, having rendered them free from confusion.
Because the *Āthabbana-veda* involves the harming of others and is therefore not to be used by the virtuous, it is stated: "of the *Iru-veda*, *Yaju-veda*, and *Sāma-veda*.

In this context, it is called *iru* because the gods are sought after (*iccyante*) and praised (*thomīyante*) by means of it; the letter *c* has been changed to *r* based on the verbal root *ica*, and this word is feminine.
It is called *yaju* because the gods are sacrificed to (*yajjante*) and honored (*pujjante*) by means of it; this is based on the masculine and neuter genders.
They bring about an end, or they experience and diminish evil by means of this; thus, in the *sāma* root-group, the vowel *o* is changed to *ā*.

They know the Dhamma, or they perform action by means of these, thus they are the *vedas*; they are indeed the *mantas*, because "by means of them one knows even [the way to] a happy destination, and they are heard.
Striking is the collision; that which is struck is the *pahata*. That which is produced is the *oṭṭhāna*.

Likewise, by way of its performance—that is, by moving the lips and making them proficient—it has "gone to the further shore" (pāraṅgata), meaning it has not gone [there] by way of explaining the meaning.
And the compound *pāragū* is a *kitanta*-compound because it is always dependent [on a preceding word].
By the phrase "together with the *nighaṇṭu*" and so forth, there is a demonstration of the derivation according to the case-ending of each sentence. [The phrase] "of the *nighaṇṭus*, trees," etc.,...
*Nighaṇṭu* is the name of a particular tree; the meaning is "of things beginning with that.
By this, since the remaining synonyms are shown therein, beginning with the synonym *nighaṇṭu-rukkha* (the Nighaṇṭu tree) as the primary one, that book is named *Nighaṇṭu*.
This meaning is shown by the literal expression itself, just as in the cases of "the Pārājika Chapter" (*pārājikakaṇḍo*) or "the Kusala Triplet" (*kusalattiko*).
Because it has been attained. However, the teachers say this:

"It is called *nikhaṇḍu* because it 'scratches' (*nikhaḍati*), that is, it digs out, breaks open, and shows the meaning and the word by analyzing them; and by changing the letter *kha* to *gha*, it is called *nighaṇḍu*.
This should be understood as showing a different method from the method of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For otherwise, that...
There may be a contradiction with the *Aṭṭhakathā*; this should be investigated. However, the etymologists (*akkharacintakā*) maintain this:
"Because it brings together names that have come down in various places without exception and arranges them into a collection (*rāsi*), it is called *nighaṇṭu* [with the elision of the nasal *ṇ*].
It is "that which elucidates synonyms" (*vevacanappakāsaka*), meaning it illuminates words used as alternatives; it is that which reveals many alternative expressions for each single meaning.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, this is merely an illustration, for that treatise was composed in order to demonstrate how even numerous meanings can be expressed by a single word.
But what is it? It is the *Nāmaliṅgānusāsana*, the *Ratanamālā*, the *Abhidhānappadīpikā*, and so forth.

It is called *kiriyākappa* because by means of it, action characterized by verbal expression and the like is prescribed (*kappīyati*); likewise, it is so called because it prescribes various things in that very way.
By this [term] "eti," there is the sense of *vikappa* (variation/division); and since it is both *kiriyākappa* (the mode of action) and that *vikappa*, it is called *kiriyākappavikappa*.
For it is called "*kiriyākappavikappa*" because it possesses many variations (*bahuvikappa*) due to its divisions into phonemes, words, their relations, word-meanings, and so forth;

and since it is indeed a specific type of literary composition (*ganthavisesa*), it is described as "a treatise that brings benefit to poets. This is said with reference to the four types of poets, by way of the purpose consisting in the attainment of poetic status, the attainment of aesthetic enjoyment, and so on.
The meaning is: "A book that brings about benefit. But what is it? It refers to works such as the *Kāvyabandhanavidhi*, the *Kāvyālaṅkāra*, the *Gītā*, and the *Subodhālaṅkāra*.

However, this is said with reference to the *Mūlakiriyākappa* treatise; for that indeed has a vast scope and consists of one hundred thousand verses, which they also call the "treatise on methods and conduct" (*Nayacariyādi-pakaraṇa*).
As for the etymological derivation of the word, however, it means "it makes known," "it causes to go," or "it informs."
*Keṭubha* refers to the classification of action (*kiriyā*) and so forth. It is derived from the verbal root *kiṭ* with the suffix *abha*, and the vowel *a* is changed to *u*.

Alternatively, it is *keṭubha* because it illuminates (*obheti*)—that is, fulfills—the classification of action and so forth by exhausting them without remainder, according to the verbal root *ubh* preceded by the word *kiṭ*.
Furthermore, it is *keṭubha* because by means of it, poets (*kavayo*) go (*kiṭanti*), that is, proceed, toward skill (*kosalla*) in compositions (*bandhesu*).
*Keṭubha*: the derivation of the word here is according to the same method as before.

It is called *akkharappabheda* (the analysis of syllables) because by means of it syllables are analyzed through the classification of their places of articulation (*ṭhāna*), modes of formation (*karaṇa*), and so forth, as well as through the classification of etymological explanations (*nibbacana*). Furthermore, it is stated that this consists of only two treatises included among the six Vedāṅgas:
"phonology (*sikkhā*) and etymology (*nirutti*). In that context, they train in the system of syllables by means of this [phonology].
*Śikṣā* is the science that establishes the places of articulation (*ṭhāna*), the modes of formation (*karaṇa*), and the efforts (*payatana*) for the phonemes beginning with *a*.
*Nirutti* is, by way of certainty or exhaustively, *utti*; it is characterized by the addition of phonemes (*vaṇṇāgama*), the substitution of phonemes (*vaṇṇavipariyāya*), and so forth.
And it is said: "The addition of phonemes, the substitution of phonemes..."
And two others are the modification of phonemes and elision;
the connection with the excellence of meaning of the root—
that is called the fivefold nirutti.
Furthermore, here the term *nirutti* is intended to signify the science that elucidates etymologies in manifold ways through the elision of the second member of a compound (*uttarapadalopa*).
This is because the teachers have stated that the differentiation of phonemes exists even within the analysis of etymologies;

and because, apart from that [phonetic analysis], the analysis of etymologies is included within the branch of grammar (*byākaraṇa*). For grammar (*byākaraṇa*) and etymology (*nirutti*) are indeed each a separate limb of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), as they have said:
“Grammar (kappa), etymology (byākaraṇa), the science of light (jotisattha), phonetics (sikkhā), philology (nirutti), and prosody (chandoviciti)—these they call the six limbs of the Veda.
Therefore, what is intended here is a derivation according to the method of philology (nirutti) that is indeed distinct from the limb of grammar (byākaraṇa). It is not...

It should be understood that, as in the case of the six grammatical suffixes (*byañjana*), the etymological derivation common to both [the root and the suffix] pertains to the domain of the *vedaṅgas*.
This, then, is the analysis of the method of etymology (*nirutti-naya*) as it appears in the *Mahāniddesa-ṭīkā*.

For therein, in the phrase "like the king of constellations among the stars," the addition of a letter not previously existing, such as the letter *r* in *rājā*, is called the "addition of a phoneme" (*vaṇṇāgama*).

The transposition of syllables (*vaṇṇavipariyāyo*) is the reversal of existing syllables by way of their upper and lower positions, such as when one who is to be called "a killer" (*hiṃsa*) because of the act of killing is instead called "a lion" (*sīha*).

The modification of syllables (*vaṇṇavikāro*) is the substitution of one syllable for another, such as the change of the letter *a* to the letter *e* in the phrase "now the field is being sown" (*navachannakedāni diyyati*).
[An example of a compound is: "one who has died while living" (*jīvanassa mūto jīvanamūto*).
It should be stated that "destruction of phonemes" (vaṇṇavināsa) refers to the destruction of existing syllables,
such as the disappearance of the letters *va* and *na* in the word *jīmūta*. Just as in the passage, "O youths, you speak to me with harsh words,
having assailed me," the term *pakubbamāno* is interpreted as meaning "overpowering," so too in various instances there is the interpretation of specific meanings according to the context.
The application [of the word] "Veda" is by way of a preeminence of meaning among the elements (dhātu).
This would be the fourth among the three Vedas classified as previously stated; therefore, he asks with what it becomes the fifth, and replies:
"having made the Āthabbana-veda the fourth. The so-called Āthabbana-veda is that which is prescribed by the practitioners of the Āthabbana-veda.

The mantra is harmful to others; however, it is included here merely by way of its being counted as one of the five, for the purpose of illustrating their status as the "five including the Itihāsa," and not because of its own specific form.
And this being the case, the meaning of the word "of these" (etesaṃ) must be taken as referring specifically to those three Vedas.
For that [word] is an adjective qualifying "of the three Vedas" (tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ). "Itiha asāti" means "thus indeed here."
In the world, there is also a reading in some places as “āsā,” which has the same meaning. In this context, the meaning is: “iti” means “thus,” or “this action,” or “this subject matter”;
“āsa” means “desire” or “longing. Furthermore, the distributive repetition (vicchāvacana) is used here to indicate that the scope of that composition is vast.
By this expression “itihāsā,” he shows the meaning [of the word] “Itihāsa” as being derived through the formation of a secondary derivative (taddhita).

They say that *itihāsa*—connected with such expressions as "Thus it was" (*itiha āsa*) and "Thus it has been" (*itiha āsā*)—is also shown to be a meaning according to the method of etymology (*nirutti*).
However, the grammarians (*akkharacintaka*) maintain this: "The word *itiha* is a single indeclinable particle used for traditional instruction.
*Asa* means 'it exists' (*vijjati*) when there is no [other source]. *Itihāsa* is formed by way of a compound: 'that in which there is *itiha asa*. According to their view, "thus..."
Regarding the phrase "it was thus," the meaning is that such a traditional instruction did not exist in this way.
By the expression "consisting of ancient tales," he indicates its nature as a specific literary work:

it refers to the collection of texts known as the *Bhāratapurāṇa*, *Rāmapurāṇa*, *Narasīhapurāṇa*, and so forth, which consist of ancient tales such as the account of the war between the two royal brothers named Bhārata, the story of King Rāma’s abduction of Sītā, and the account of the appearance of King Narasīha.
"Itihāsa" is what is meant by "legend. By the phrase "of those Vedas with Itihāsa as the fifth," [the author] shows its status as an adjective in accordance with the sentence "of the three Vedas.
A "pada" (word) is that by which meaning is reached; it consists of many divisions according to nouns, verbs, prefixes, particles, and so forth, and includes inflected words (*vibhattiyanta*).
It is said that "even that" is indeed included in grammar (*byākaraṇa*), hence the term "the remainder thereof" (*tadavasesa*).

The meaning is: the remainder from the perspective of words, consisting of the characteristics of linguistic forms such as roots (*pakati*), suffixes (*paccaya*), and so forth. It is called *byākaraṇa* because it explains (*byākaroti*) or expounds (*byācikkhati*) various words and their meanings by means of this [treatise].

Alternatively, it is *byākaraṇa* because therein or by means of this, the roots, suffixes, and so forth, are specifically analyzed (*ākarīyante*) or produced (*abhinipphādīyante*). It is the systematic exposition (*anvākhyāyaka*) of correct words.
The Muddhabodha-Byākaraṇa, Sārassata-Byākaraṇa, Pāṇini-Byākaraṇa, Canda-Byākaraṇa, and other such treatises existing even now are [the texts].

"Adhīyati" means he studies. "Vedeti" means he causes others to recite. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of combining two meanings, or it has the sense of an alternative because another meaning is being proposed;
for the function of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) is manifold. "Padaka" refers to those skilled in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

This was said with reference to skill in the words already arrived at; "grammar" (*veyyākaraṇa*), however, refers to skill in the rules of linguistic forms such as roots, suffixes, and so forth that remain.
To make this meaning known, the two terms are explained together.
For it is the nature of teachers to make another meaning known by whatever means possible. This is another method [of interpretation] from the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
He who recites that very Veda word by word is a *padaka*. In this context, "word by word" (*padaso*) means by means of the words of the *gajjabandha* and *pajjabandha* meters.

"Recites" (*kāyati*) means he speaks; as in the term "*jātaka*," this demonstrates his capacity as a composer of the Veda. For in this way, his distinction from those such as the mere "reciter" (*ajjhāyaka*) becomes evident.
The world known as the foolish folk does not strive or exert itself for future welfare; thus it is *lokāyata*.

For by relying on that treatise, beings do not even arouse the thought of performing meritorious deeds. Or, the world—that is, foolish people—exerts themselves (*āyatanti*) or take pleasure in its doctrine;
thus it is *lokāyata*. It stretches out (*tanoti*) things that are mutually contradictory, or that which is contrary to heaven and liberation.
"Ettha" (here) is [derived] from the root *taḍ* by means of the suffix *-ḍa* and by changing the letter *na* to *ṇa*;
thus, "vitaṇḍo" is that wherein disputants strike (*tāḷenti*) with a staff of contradictory arguments (*viruddhena vādadaṇḍena*), according to the root *taḍ*.

Furthermore, the place where the debate of the disputants proceeds is also called "vitaṇḍo" by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), even though it is not the primary meaning. Just as: [example].
“The eye is a lovely thing in the world, a pleasant thing; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.
Or alternatively, it is called *vitaṇḍa* because by means of it they strike and shake the minds of the wise;
those who speak that [doctrine] or whose doctrine is that are *vitaṇḍavādā*; their treatise is likewise. This is the treatise that elucidates characteristics (*lakkhaṇadīpaka-sattha*).

By means of the elision of the final member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*) or by way of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), he shows that it is a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) through the phrase "illuminating the characteristics" (*lakkhaṇadīpaka*), and so forth.

It is a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) because by means of it the state of Buddhahood and so on is characterized; [it refers to] such things as the trunk-like body of a banyan tree. Therefore he said, "by means of which," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "measuring twelve thousand units of text" (*dvādasasahassaganthapamāṇa*), here, as in the case of the measure of recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*) and so on, it refers specifically to a text consisting of thirty-two syllables.
This is what is intended. For it is said:
"Eight syllables make one word; a stanza has four words;
one stanza is considered a composition (gantha); a composition consists of thirty-two syllables."
The meaning is that its extent is thirty-two thousand verses multiplied by twelve. "In which" (*yattha*) refers to that treatise on characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-sattha*);
this locative case is used for the locus (*ādhāra*), as in the expression "the branch in the tree. "Sixteen thousand" (*soḷasa-sahassa*) means sixteen thousand [verses];

the meaning is that its measure consists of more than sixteen thousand stanzas (*gāthā*). For in this way, the statement regarding the container and the contained (*ādhārādheyya-vacana*) becomes well-established.
They are called "Buddha-mantras" because they reveal the characteristics of the Buddhas by way of their exertion (*padhāna*).
For the characteristics of the Paccekabuddhas and others are also revealed therein. Therefore it was said: "By means of which... and so forth.

The phrase "not deficient, fulfilling [the purpose]" is a mere indication of the meaning; however, in order to show the meaning as it is attained from the words (*saddato*), [it is explained as follows]:
It is said: “He is not one who has passed away (avayo). To address the inquiry as to what this “one who has passed away” (avaya) is, [the text] says:

“One who is called ‘avaya’,” and so forth. This is the intended meaning: he who is able to sustain those [aggregates] is called “vaya” (one who has passed away); however, he who is unable to do so is called “avaya” (one who has not passed away).
And as for him who is not one who has passed away, according to the rule that “two negations convey the original sense,” [he is established as such].

"Vayo eva": it is called *vayo* because it "carries" (*vayati*). The meaning is that, without becoming exhausted or faltering at any point—whether in the beginning, middle, or end—it carries forward and conducts those texts within the continuum [of the teaching].
This, however, is the method according to the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*: *anavayo* means "not lacking" (*anu-avayo*);
the vowel *u* is elided by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*). "Not lacking" (*anu-anu-avayo*) means "complete," i.e., one whose craft is perfected.
The term *vaya* here means "loss," as in expressions such as *āyavayo* (gain and loss). *Avaya* means that there is no *vaya*—that is, no deficiency—as found in the aforementioned texts;
thus, *anu-anu-avaya* is *anavaya*.
Furthermore, the word *anuññāto* is explained by way of the objective case (*kamma-sādhana*), while the word *paṭiññāto* is explained by way of the agentive case (*kartṛ-sādhana*).
Showing the meaning, he said, “By the teacher,” and so forth. “Assa” means “of Ambaṭṭha.
In the Pāli, the statement “What I know, you know that” shows the manner of granting permission, while “What you know, I know that” shows the manner of making a formal admission;
this is demonstrated by the passage beginning with “yaṃ ahaṃ. For [Ambaṭṭha replied], “Yes, teacher.”
The statement "acknowledging it as it was received" is spoken for the sake of the meaning. "Yaṃ" refers to the scripture of the Three Vedas (*tevijjaka-pāvacana*).

"Tassa" refers to the teacher. "A promise" (*paṭiññā*) is simply the act of giving a reply; thus, the meaning is that it is acknowledged by him himself through that [reply]. The passage beginning with "In one's own...

is a demonstration of the context of acknowledging and admitting [the teaching]. It is said, "In which [place]? and so forth, because even for what is not a place, it is treated as if it were a place by means of mere conceptualization (*kappanāmatta*).
*Sassa* means one's own, belonging to oneself. *Ācariyakaṃ* refers to that which has come down through a succession of teachers, or from teachers who exist in a lineage.
*Tevijjakaṃ* is the collection of the three types of knowledge (*tisso vijjā*), namely the Three Vedas.
*Pāvacanaṃ* is the supreme word, or the word of the eminent ones such as Aṭṭhaka and others.

257. Now, explaining the intention with which the brahmin Pokkharasāti addressed the young man Ambaṭṭha, saying, “This one, dear,” and so forth, he spoke the passage beginning with “It is said that this one.
Therein, “of the eminent” refers to the ancient people who were formerly well-known and famous. “Many people” is said with reference to Pūraṇa Kassapa and others.
"Someone" (*ekacca*) refers to a person belonging to a caste such as the Khattiya, or one esteemed by the world. "A heavy burden" (*garu*) means something weighty;
it is said that even merely releasing oneself from it and departing is difficult, let alone performing anything further.
"Disadvantage" (*anattha*) refers to censure, accusation, and attack resulting from such departure and so forth.

Regarding the word "abhuggato" (exalted), because of its connection with the prefix *abhi*, the accusative case "Gotamaṃ" is used specifically in the sense of describing a state of being (*itthambhūtakhyāna*).

He shows that even in the phrases "that venerable one" and "being exactly thus," the accusative is not employed; rather, it is used in that same sense [of description] by saying "of that venerable one," and so forth.
Therefore he says, "here too," and so on. "Being exactly thus" means in whatever manner [he exists], such as an Arhat, etc.
The sound has gone forth; the meaning is that the sound of that very Gotama, who exists and has come to be in such a manner, has indeed gone forth.

Furthermore, the statement "that venerable Gotama is thus existent" is spoken twice in connection with the same fact for the purpose of making known a specific distinction in meaning by means of conceiving of both the general and the particular.
Therefore, having separated [the phrase] by way of a general connection as “of that venerable Gotama,” it should be joined by way of a specific connection as “only for one who is thus.
Here, the word *yadi* (if) has the sense of doubt, because both meanings are subject to doubt;
and the word *vā* (or) has the sense of an alternative, because one of those two is to be chosen as an alternative. Thus say the grammarians.
However, they say this: in expressions such as “whether his word is true or false,” both the word *yadi* (if) and the word *vā* (or) have the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*).

For the word *yadi* is seen to have the sense of *vā* in passages such as, “Whatever assembly he approaches—whether it be an assembly of kṣatriyas or an assembly of brahmins. [And so on: “A short hundred years...”
And here, as in such passages as “O Āyu, it exists even now,” there is the employment of words with identical meanings.

Regarding the phrase in the Pāḷi, “whether it be so or not,” this too should be connected with “the sound has indeed arisen while [the person] was present,” and applied according to the method already stated.
To the objection that the accusative case should apply only to the word “Gotama” and not here [to the name], the text says “here too,” and so forth.
It has been stated [that the accusative case is used] because that [instrumental] is not employed, or because it must be construed by breaking the connection and establishing a specific relationship;
thus, here too, it is said that the "accusative" is so called by virtue of its function as a designation of a state of being (itthambhūtākhyāna).

That which has the designation of a state of being as its meaning is "thus"; likewise, the prefix *abhi* is such, or rather, the meaning is precisely the designation of a state of being, and that alone is the meaning. Insofar as...
For there is a connection with the word *hi* (for/indeed), and by that same principle, there is also a connection with the meaning (*attha*). 258.

The word *bho* is used to address one's own teacher. Having made the word *yathā* meaningful, the phrase beginning with "as far as possible" (*yathā sakkā*) was stated in order to connect it with the remainder of the text.
The word *so* refers to the Blessed One (*bhagavā*), because he is suitable for the word *yathā*, which indicates the sense of manner (*ākāra*) in the preceding method.
"How" is merely a question; however, because it is unsuitable here [for that], it is called an "inquiry regarding the manner" (*ākārapucchā*).
In the non-Buddhist systems, the conduct toward a teacher is that toward a preceptor (*upajjhāya*); thus he said, "Then the preceptor," meaning the teacher-brahmin who is designated as a preceptor.
Although the Veda is indeed threefold—consisting of mantra, brāhmaṇa, and kalpa—nevertheless, the *Aṭṭhakā* and so forth are mentioned because they are the primary components.
The *manta* is the root; the *brahman* is the exposition of its meaning; and the ritual procedure for sacrifice as described therein is the *kalpa*.

Since the *manta* alone is primary, and because the others arise only by depending upon it, he shows by the phrase "in the three Vedas" that the inclusion of the *brahman* and *kalpa* is already established by the mention of the *manta* alone. For the term *manta* [is used] by the Aṭṭhakas and others...

The term *isīhi* (by the seers) refers specifically to the name of the *Mūlaveda*; whereas *veda* refers to all [the Vedas]. Therefore, it should be understood that when the word "in the Vedas" (*vedesu*) is used, the inclusion of all [four] is established.
"Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇāni*) refers to the mantra-words that indicate the characteristics. Having inserted them by way of the *pajja*, *gajja*, *bandha*, and *pavesana* [metres].
"In the very guise of a Brahmin" means by means of the outward signs of a Brahmin who recites the Vedas. He recites the mantras concerning the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*).
“Beings of great power” means beings who possess great merit and are wise. The connection is: “They will know,” having kept this in mind, they teach [the texts].
“By that” means by teaching in such a manner. “In the past” means from the time it was first said, “A Tathāgata will arise,” until the time the Tathāgata was actually living.
They come to be manifest through the state of being studied and taught.
They exist. By means of one verse, two verses, and so forth, they gradually disappear.

The Teacher stated that it is not only the *lakṣaṇa-mantras* that disappear gradually due to the ignorance of the brahmins, but rather that other Vedas as well gradually disappear for that same reason.
Aspiration for Buddhahood is *paṇidhi*; the accumulation of the perfections (*pāramī*) is *samādāna*; and wisdom regarding the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatā*) and so forth is *ñāṇa*.
"The word 'great' (mahanta) should be applied to each term individually, as in the phrase ‘greatness of aspiration, greatness of undertaking,’ and so forth,” thus it was said by the Teacher.

And this being the case: compassion is the first of those qualities such as faith, virtue, and so on; these are the "compassion-and-the-rest" (karuṇādayo). These very qualities are the "qualities of compassion-and-the-rest" (karuṇādiguṇā).

Aspiration, undertaking, knowledge, and the qualities of compassion-and-the-rest—by these he is great; thus, [he is] "Great through the greatness of aspiration, undertaking, knowledge, and the qualities of compassion-and-the-rest."
The etymology must be established. For in this way, because the compound has ceased to be a *dvanda*, the word "great" (*mahanta*) is applied to each [member] individually.

Furthermore, the meaning is well-established by the following etymology: "those whose primary qualities are aspiration (*paṇidhi*), undertaking (*samādāna*), knowledge (*ñāṇa*), and compassion (*karuṇā*);
he is 'Great' (*Mahā*) by virtue of those very qualities. And his greatness of aspiration and so forth is described in the *Buddhavamsa*.

It should be understood by means of the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and other such texts. However, in the *Mahāpadānasuttavaṇṇanā*, it is stated: “‘A Great Man’ (mahāpurisa) means a great person by way of birth, clan, family lineage, and so forth. In that context, “a khattiya, a brāhmaṇa,” and so on, refers to birth (*jāti*). “Koṇḍañña, Gotama,” and so on, refers to clan (*gotta*). “The Poṇikas, the Cikkhallikas, the Sākiyas,” and so on, refers to family lineage (*kula*). “The inhabitants of the Rose-apple Island (*Jambudīpa*), the inhabitants of the Eastern Continent (*Pūrvavideha*), the inhabitants of the Western Continent (*Aparagoyāna*), the inhabitants of the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*), gods, and humans” refers to place (*padesa*). “The past, the future, and the present” refers to time (*kāla*). “The world of form (*rūpaloka*), the formless world (*arūpaloka*), and the sense-sphere world (*kāmāvacara*)” refers to realm (*dhātu*). “The world of beings (*sattaloka*), the world of containers (*okāsaloka*), and the world of phenomena (*dhammaloka*)” refers to sphere (*visaya*). “The world of the aggregates (*khandhaloka*), the world of the bases (*āyatanaloka*), and the world of the elements (*dhātuloka*)” refers to constituent (*sabhāva*). “The world of suffering (*dukkhaloka*), the world of origin (*samudayaloka*), the world of cessation (*nirodhaloka*), and the world of the path (*maggaloka*)” refers unconditioned (*tajjālitaloka*)” refers to the threefold division. “The world of the inferior (*hīnaloka*), the world of the superior (*paṇītaloka*), and the world of the equal (*sad
“Koliyas,” and so forth—this refers to specific clans; all of these should be understood as being included here by the word “etc.
For this being the case, the statement that “there are only two destinations” is justified as a common term for both.
“Niṭṭhā” means consummations or accomplishments. Now, since this word *gati* has many meanings, why is it used here specifically in the sense of “consummation”?
He said, “Granted, this...,” and so forth. “In the distinction of existence” means in the specific types of existence such as the hells and so on.

For that [existence] is a *gati* (destination) because it is to be gone to by beings by way of rebirth through deeds of good or bad conduct. It is a *gati* because one goes to or proceeds therein; it is a place of abiding.

It is a *gati* because one goes to it, meaning one knows its true nature; it is wisdom (*paññā*). Or, *gati* is the act of going, the process of pervading, the state of being manifest. That is [the meaning].

Rather, it is simply the state of being spread out here and there. "Going" (*gati*) means accomplishment, reaching, or completion; furthermore, it is taken in the sense of intention and refuge by way of illustration.

For instance, in the passage, "Monks, I do not know the coming or the going of these virtuous monks of noble character," it refers to intention; and in the passage, "Nirvana is the destination of the Arahant."
Here, the meaning is "in the refuge," "the ultimate resort," or "the support. It is called *gati* because one goes toward it or proceeds according to one's inclination;
it is the underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*). It is called *gati* because one goes into it, dwells within it, or proceeds by way of dwelling therein;
thus, it is the refuge (*paṭisaraṇa*). For the Arahant, who is dissociated from all conditioned things, Nibbāna alone is the refuge; however, in this context, it refers to the final goal (*niṭṭhā*).
It should be understood that [the term] "occurs" is used because it is not the domain of others.
Now, one might raise an objection: "Are not the characteristics, which serve as the causes for the two accomplishments, indeed dissimilar?
Then why is their similarity stated in the passage beginning with ‘endowed with which’? Having thus indicated the essence of the objection, he clarifies it: "In this regard—"

He said, "And furthermore," and so forth. To show that even though they possess the same characteristics such as those of Nigrodha and Bimba, there is indeed a certain distinction between them, it was stated: "One does not become a Buddha by those [characteristics] alone.

Furthermore, this distinction—that while the characteristics of Buddhas are very clear, well-defined, and complete, they are not so for wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavatti)—was stated by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla.
It has been explained [as follows]: It is called *jāti* (genus/class) because by means of it, undifferentiated concepts and words arise even when the objects are differentiated.

It is merely the state of being a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). For it has been said: “In the case of differentiated things such as ‘variegated’ (*sabala*) and so forth, that by which an undifferentiated cognition and word proceed—this is *jāti*; and it is like a thread running through a garland.”

Therefore, the meaning is this: because they share a common state by virtue of being mere characteristics (*lakkhaṇatāmattena*), even though they are dissimilar, those very characteristics that are the causes for the production of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) are treated as if they were similar; thus, the statement "these are the characteristics that are the causes for the production of a Buddha" is spoken.
He said [this] using the accusative case in the sense of the locative, due to the connection with the prefix *adhi* and the root *vas*.
“He dwells at home” means by way of four wonderful qualities: beauty, long life, freedom from illness, and being dear and pleasing to brahmins and householders.
These are the four supernormal powers (iddhi) consisting of a wonderful nature.
As it is said: “Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was endowed with four supernormal powers. With which four? Here, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana was handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing,” and so forth.
Even while adopting the method found in the *Cetiyajātakā*, they speak thus: "The scent of sandalwood wafts from his body;
this is the first supernormal power (*iddhi*). The scent of a blue lotus wafts from his mouth; this is the second.
Four sons of gods, with swords in hand, constantly provide protection in the four directions; this is the third. He travels through the air; this is the fourth."
In the *Anāgatavaṃsa-vaṇṇanā*, however, it is stated: “The state of being handsome is the first supernormal power;

the state of being endowed with a digestive faculty that is balanced in its maturation is the second; the state of satisfying the sight of the entire world for as long as one’s lifespan lasts is the third;
and the state of walking through the air is the fourth. Therein, “the state of being endowed with a digestive faculty that is balanced in its maturation” means:

It is due to the perfection of the fire element of karma that ripens evenly. For one whose food is digested as soon as it is eaten, or for one where it remains just as it was, like a meal placed in a closed vessel—neither of these possesses the fire element that ripens evenly.
However, he for whom the desire for food arises again at the time of the next meal is one who possesses the fire element that ripens evenly.
The meaning is: "of such a nature. "By means of the bases of sympathy" refers to these methods of winning over others: giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. As it is said:
"Giving and kind speech, And beneficial conduct here in this world..."
And impartiality toward all things, as is appropriate in each case—
these indeed are the means of integration in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
If these means of integration did not exist, a mother would not, for the sake of her child, [act with such care].
One may receive honor or worship, just as a father does for the sake of his son;
yet because the wise regard these things with equanimity through their mastery,
they attain greatness and become worthy of praise.
"From delighting" means from delighting by way of joy and gladness, not by way of lust; what is meant is that it gives rise to joy and gladness.

Furthermore, the designation "king" (rājā) in the sense of delighting by means of the four bases of sympathy is a conventional title for all kings, occurring by way of metaphorical usage (*ruḷhivasena*), just as the term "palmyra fan" is applied even to those who do not actually make them, such as to the seeds of the *vilīva* plant and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that the etymological definition (*nibbacana*) of "wonderful phenomena" (*acchariyadhammehi*) was stated as something unique.
By means of the power of linguistic convention (*saddasāmatthiya*), he shows the meaning of the word *cakkavatti* in many ways;
first, in order to show the primary meaning, he says "the wheel-treasure" (*cakkaratana*), and so forth. For this alone is the primary [meaning] of the wheel-treasure.
Because one cannot attain the state of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) without its revolving. For it is said in the Commentaries:
"In what way does one become a wheel-turning monarch? When the precious wheel, even by the measure of a single finger or two fingers, rises up into the air and revolves.
Furthermore, the wheel-turning monarch, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, with his left hand [grasps] the trunk-like stalk...

Having lifted up a golden water-vessel and sprinkled the Wheel-Treasure with water from his right hand, he caused the Wheel-Treasure to ascend into the air and set it in motion by uttering the words, “May the noble Wheel-Treasure turn! May the noble Wheel-Treasure conquer!
Therefore, with reference to such an act of setting it in motion, it is said: “He turns the Wheel-Treasure.”
It has been stated. As it is said: “Then, Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana rose from his seat... [and] sprinkled the Wheel-treasure with water, saying:
‘May the noble Wheel-treasure turn! and so forth. Furthermore, the word *cakra* (wheel) does not apply solely to the Wheel-treasure;
rather, it also applies to the wheel of prosperity (*sampatti-cakra*) and others. Therefore, by the very power of the words expressing those respective meanings—
He shows the meaning of the words with the passage beginning, “By the wheels of prosperity,” and so forth. Therein, “by the wheels of prosperity” refers to:
“A person who dwells in a suitable locality, Who makes noble friends his own, Who is endowed with right aspiration, And who has performed merit in the past;”
"Grain, wealth, fame, renown, and this happiness revolve [around him]."—by these aforementioned wheels of excellence, such as dwelling in a suitable locality and so forth.
"Revolve" (*vattati*) means it proceeds, succeeds, or one practices wholesome states higher and higher.
"By those" refers to the wheels of excellence. "The multitude" (*paraṃ*) refers to the assembly of beings, just as...
It should be understood that the word *sayam* indicates the sense of the pure agent (*suddhakattū*), and likewise the word *param* indicates the sense of the causal agent (*hetukattū*).
"He causes to proceed" means he sets in motion or accomplishes; or, he causes one to engage in wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) higher and higher. As it was said:
"King Mahāsudassana spoke thus: 'Living beings must not be killed, what is not given must not be taken, [one must not commit] misconduct in sensual pleasures...'"
"One should not engage in misconduct, one should not speak falsehoods, one should not drink intoxicants, and you should eat only what has been properly prepared.
