And furthermore, Ānanda, those rival kings in the eastern direction became followers of King Mahāsudassana, and so forth.

Regarding "the wheels of the modes of conduct": this refers to the wheels that constitute the modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*). For even a mode of conduct is called a "wheel," as in such passages as "four-wheeled, nine-gated. As it has been said:
“The term *cakra* [is used] in reference to a chariot part, a characteristic mark,
the Dhamma, the protective rim, the paths of virtue, sovereignty, the wheel-treasure, a mandala, strength,
a potter’s vessel, command, a weapon, a heap of gifts, and a peak.”

"Vatta" means turning or proceeding, which is to say arising; by this very term, it also shows the etymological derivation that he sets the wheel of the postures in motion—that is, he produces it for the welfare of others—since they are identical in meaning. Thus it is said:
"Then, Ānanda, that Wheel-Treasure proceeded toward the eastern direction, and King Mahāsudassana followed right behind it with his fourfold army.
And in whatever place, Ānanda, the Wheel-Treasure came to a halt..."
“In that place, King Mahāsudassana took up residence together with his fourfold army,” and so forth.
This is another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā*: one who turns the wheel known as unimpeded command is a *cakkavattī*. For it is said:
“Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a wheel-turning monarch turns the wheel by means of the Dhamma alone.”
"That wheel becomes irreversible by any human adversary or enemy.
By which five? Here, monks, a Wheel-turning Monarch knows what is beneficial, knows the Dhamma, knows moderation, knows the right time, and knows his assembly.
By these... [as before] ...by any human adversary or enemy," and so forth.
He is also a *cakkavattī* because he causes the circle (*cakkam*), that is, the assembly known as the circle of khattiyas and so forth, to revolve and follow under his own control.
For it is said: “And as for those rival kings in the eastern direction, Ānanda, they became followers of King Mahāsudassana,” and so on.
He is also a *cakkavattī* because the mark of the wheel (*cakka-lakkhaṇam*) revolves upon him. Thus he said: “Of this... [text truncated]”
“O King, on the soles of the Prince’s feet, wheels have appeared, with a thousand spokes, with rims, with hubs, and complete in every detail,” and so forth.
He is also called a *cakravattin* because a great wheel (*cakra*) of bodily power turns for him.
For it has been said: “O King, this Prince has seven protuberances... O King, this Prince has the forequarters of a lion,” and so forth.

By that characteristic, his state of great power is understood. One who causes the wheel—whether tenfold or twelvefold—to turn and proceed according to its nature is a *cakkavattī*. Therefore it was said:
"For you, dear son, there is no divine Wheel-treasure as an inheritance from your father; come now, dear son, conduct yourself according to the noble way of a *cakkavattī*," and so forth.
He is a *cakkavattin* because he causes a great wheel of giving to turn and proceed.
And it is said: "Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana established such a gift on the banks of those lotus ponds:
food for one desiring food, drink for one desiring drink, clothing for one desiring clothing, and a vehicle for one desiring a vehicle."
“Bed for one who needs a bed, a woman for one who needs a woman, gold for one who needs gold, and bullion for one who needs bullion,” and so forth.

“King” (*rājā*) is a general term because it is shared by others besides him; “wheel-turning monarch” (*cakkavattī*) is a specific term because it is not shared by others. The word “dhamma” (*dhamma-saddo*)...
Since the method (*ñāya*) is indeed the same as what is called the "method," he says, "by the method and by the even. The meaning is that it proceeds, arises, or is practiced.

Even though it is not explicitly stated, "it practices this," [the phrase] "one's own goal and the goal of others" is connected because a general indication establishes itself upon a particular instance, and because a specific term must be applied by one who seeks the specific.
For if there were no mention of a particular part (*padesa*), [the connection would not be established].
The fact that what is to be taken up is exhaustive is understood from such statements as, "one who has gone forth does not give.

Since a wheel-turning monarch attains sovereignty solely through the Dhamma, and not through unrighteousness such as harming others, it is said, "having obtained sovereignty through the Dhamma," and so forth;

here, "through the Dhamma" means by way of the proper method (ñāya) or by way of wholesome states (kusaladhamma). Sovereignty (rajja) is the state of being a king (rañño bhāvo), that is, lordship (issariya).
He is called *dhammika* because he performs or practices the Dhamma that serves as the means for the welfare of others.

Or, he is a *dhammarāja* because he is a king who performs or practices the Dhamma that serves as the means for his own welfare; by the phrase "or by performing the Dhamma for the welfare of others," etc., he shows this distinguished meaning.
This, however, is the method according to the *Mahāpadāna-ṭṭhakathā*: [in] the tenfold wholesome Dhamma, which is free from wrong courses...
He is called *dhammika* because he is devoted to the duties of a king (*rājadhamma*). He is a *dhammarāja* because he delights the world by means of that very same *dhamma*.
Indeed, these two terms are merely synonymous expressions. However, the Teacher has stated it thus:

"He practices the *dhamma* known as the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), or the *dhamma* known as the conduct of a wheel-turning monarch belongs to him, or it exists in him; thus he is *dhammika*. From *dhamma*..."
“Because he is not separated from it, he is Dhamma; and in the sense of delighting, he is a king (rājā); thus he is a ‘Dhamma-king’ (dhammarāja).

Because of the statement, “He becomes a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavattī),” the term “of the four quarters” (cāturanto) clarifies his sovereignty over the four continents; thus he says, “Of the four quarters,” and so forth.
That which has the four oceans as its boundaries (anta) and limits (pariyosāna) is “the four-quarters” (cāturantā), namely, the earth. For that [earth] is in the four directions...
It is called thus because it extends as far as the four oceans, beginning with the eastern ocean. Therefore it is said:

“to the ends of the four oceans. Furthermore, by the phrase “of the earth adorned with the four kinds of islands,” he shows that this is simply the earth included within a single world-system (*lokadhātu*), embellished by the four types of islands which constitute its parts. As it has been said:
“As far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance—
all these were slaves of Mandhātā, as were all living beings established upon the earth. And here,
instead of saying “adorned by the four continents,” the word *vidha* (kind/type) is included, as in “adorned by the four kinds of continents.”

It should be understood that even though there are five hundred minor islands for each [continent], they are included within the term "Great Island" (Mahādīpa) because the surplus of meaning is understood from the surplus of the word;
or alternatively, because the word *vidha*—which denotes a portion—includes those things that share a common category.

Regarding the phrase "enemies such as anger," the word "such as" (*ādi*) includes lust, delusion, conceit, arrogance, and so forth. "He conquers" (*vijeti*) is said with reference to that specific time.
This is a present tense verb; the meaning is "one who has conquered. For those learned in grammar accept the suffix *tāv* in the sense of the past.

When one says, "He conquers all kings," although there is indeed no battle for a Wheel-Turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*) with anyone, it is shown that because of the accomplishment of victory—which is to be achieved through battle—he is called "one who has won the battle" (*vijitasaṅgāmo*).
*Thāvariyaṃ* is the state (*bhāva*) of that which is stable (*thāvara*) and constant (*dhuvā*).
To demonstrate how one has attained stability in the countryside (*janapada*), it is said, "It cannot be shaken by anyone," and so forth.

By this, he shows the *tappurisa* compound in the sense of being unshakable by anyone—that one has attained stability in the countryside—and by the other [phrase], he shows that the countryside has attained stability because of the state of firm devotion.
*Etasmin ti* is a compound where the meaning is other than that of its constituent members (*aññapadatthasamāsa*). *Tamhi ti* means "in this king.
To reveal how the country attained stability under him, he said, "devoted" (*anuyutto*), and so forth. Therein, "devoted" (*anuyutto*) means constantly engaged.

"Delighting in his own work" (*sakammanirato*) means always occupied with the duties of a wheel-turning monarch. "Unshakable" (*acalo*) and "unperturbed" (*asampavedhī*) are synonyms; [this refers to] the thieves...
Or he is "unshakable" (acala) by the mere act of plundering, and "unperturbed" (asampavedhī) by the practice of banditry.
He is unshakable by thieves and unperturbed by rival kings. Or he is unshakable by being neither too mild, and unperturbed by not being too fierce.

For indeed, when a king who is excessively fierce oppresses the world with taxes, forced labor, and so forth, people abandon the central provinces and flee to mountain ranges, seashores, and other such places.

Relying on such a king, people take up residence in the border regions; however, when a king is too lenient, people oppressed by thieves, violent men, and plunderers abandon the borders and settle in the heart of the country. Thus, under such a king, the country does not attain stability.
But when he is free from both of these faults and has attained a state of balance like a golden scale—

While the queen was exercising sovereignty, the countryside became immovable, unshakable, and attained stability, like a place set upon a stone slab and surrounded by an iron fence. Regarding the phrase *seyyathidaṃ*:
it is a single particle used according to the context, as in expressions such as "which one?", "that which?", or "which [feminine]? and so forth.
It is employed according to gender, case, and number; as to what those [factors] are here, he says "of that volition" and so forth.
It moves (cacati) according to the will of the Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti), revolving through the sky and other realms, thus it is called a wheel (cakka).
Indeed, by means of the air-element arising within it, the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) [moves] immediately upon the word of the Wheel-turning Monarch.

It is stated in the *Vimānavatthu-aṭṭhakathā* that it proceeds not by means of the external wind element arising from outside, as is the case with the celestial mansions of the moon and sun, but rather in the sense of producing delight—that is, in the sense of generating joy and gladness.
For when one sees or hears it, no small measure of joy and gladness arises because of its wonderful nature. As for the etymological meaning, however, it "delights" (*rameti*).
It is called a *ratana* because it causes delight (*ratiṃ karoti*); or, "delight" (*rata*) is the act of enjoying, and it is called a *ratana* because it leads to that (*taṃ neti*).

Alternatively, according to etymologists (*neruttika*), it is a *ratana* because it generates delight (*rataṃ janeti*), with the letter *ja* being elided. "In all cases" refers to the elephant-treasure and the others.

The meaning of "treasure" for the Wheel should also be understood through its state of being esteemed and so forth; however, it is included within the single category by virtue of its meaning as the generator of delight.
It was not taken separately. If one asks why it is included in a single category, it is because the state of being "esteemed" (*cittīkata*) and so forth is also a cause for delight (*rati*).
Alternatively, it should be understood that the state of being esteemed and so forth was not included by one who wished to avoid overburdening the text.
However, in other commentaries, it is stated as follows:
“It is a treasure in the sense that it produces delight. Furthermore:
‘Admired and of great value, Incomparable and rare to behold, To be enjoyed by beings who are not inferior— Therefore it is called a treasure.’”
“From the moment the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*) is produced, there is no other divine station;
for all pay it worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and perform such acts as salutation. Thus, in the sense of being highly esteemed, it is a treasure (*ratana*).
Furthermore, there is no price that can be set for the Wheel-Treasure, saying ‘it is worth this much wealth’; thus, in the sense of being of great value, it is a treasure.”
It is a treasure (*ratana*). And because the Wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*) is unlike any other treasures existing in the world, it is a treasure in the sense of being incomparable.

Furthermore, since Universal Monarchs (*cakkavattin*) arise only in the same aeon (*kappa*) in which Buddhas arise—and Buddhas arise only once in a great while—it is also a treasure in the sense of being difficult to behold.
This [Wheel-treasure] is [distinguished] by its birth, physical form, lineage, sovereignty, and so forth.
It arises only for an extraordinary being and not for anyone else; thus, it is a "jewel" (ratana) in the sense of being the possession of an extraordinary being.
And just as with the Wheel-treasure, so it is with the remaining ones as well.
Herein, the explanation of the meaning according to the method stated in the commentary and elsewhere regarding the words beginning with "highly esteemed" (*cittīkata*) is as follows:

This is not stated by way of etymological derivation; rather, why is it so? It is stated because of the quality of being worthy of veneration in an object that is recognized in the world as a "jewel" (*ratana*).
As for its literal form, this refers to: (1) gold, silver, and so forth, which are esteemed by the common people of the world;

(2) the wheel-jewel (*cakkaratana*) and others that arise for a universal monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*); (3) individuals such as those who are grateful and mindful of benefits; and (4) [all things] by way of the most excellent limit.
And the threefold refuge beginning with the Buddha should be regarded. It is "cherished" (*cittīkata*) because it is to be held in the mind with the thought, "Oh, how captivating!

They explain that the meaning of "to be honored" (*pūjanīya*) is established by taking this cherishing to be due to its worthiness of worship. However, some say it means "made variegated" (*vicitrakata*);
that should not be accepted here, because the word *citta* in this context denotes the heart (*hadaya*).

This is as in the canonical text spoken by the Buddha himself: “Having honored it, listen to me. Likewise, they have said: “In the case of *bhū* and *kara*, there is the augment *i* according to the rule.

However, in such instances as “Behold the form made beautiful (*cittīkata*) by the jewel and the earring,” the meaning to be understood is that what was previously unadorned has now been made variegated; for in those cases, the word *citta* denotes “variegated.”

It is "of great value" (*mahaggha*) because it is worth a great deal, being vast, extensive, and immeasurable. It is "incomparable" (*atula*) because there is no scale (*tulā*) or comparison for it, or because nothing is similar to it.
It is "rare to behold" (*dullabhadassana*) because it arises only occasionally and its sight is obtained with difficulty.
It is "the enjoyment of extraordinary beings" (*anomasattaparibhoga*) because it is to be utilized only by beings possessing peerless and sublime qualities.
Now, having shown how these qualities such as being honored (*cittīkata*) and so forth are obtained specifically by the Wheel-Treasure (*cakkaratana*),
the passage beginning with “And just as the Wheel-Treasure” was commenced in order to extend those [qualities] to the others as well. In this context,

there is no other place for the gods because it is the cause for the king’s attainment of sovereignty and other perfections not shared by others, and because it is the cause for other beings to attain whatever aims they desire.
And there is no price [for it], because of its exceedingly sublime and pure jewel-nature and because of its quality of being wonderful and marvelous.
And to the same extent that it is of great value, to that same extent it is incomparable.

Just as there is a particular time—free from the stain of evil in beings due to their devotion to merit—which is worthy of the arising of a Buddha, it is precisely at such a time that a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) also comes into existence; thus he said.
“*Yasmā panā*,” etc. *Kadāci karahacī* is a synonymous expression;
or rather, *kadāci* refers to the aforementioned time, while *karahacī* refers to the region known as the Island of Jambusiri. Therefore he said:
“The time and the island, the country and likewise the mother;”
"Having made these five observations, one of great glory arises.
This was spoken by way of a simile. Furthermore, there is no absolute similarity between the simile and that which is illustrated by it;
therefore, while Buddhas arise only once in a great while, wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavattins) do not arise in such a manner, for wheel-turning monarchs may arise many times.
The meaning should be understood as "they arise in an era when a Buddha has appeared. Even so,
because fulfilling the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti) is difficult to accomplish,

it should be understood that their "rarity of appearance" is stated here by way of this common quality of being rare, even though the merit achieved through the power of the wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) is shared in common with the people in the monarch’s retinue.
Nevertheless, it is the Wheel-turning Monarch alone who deserves to be called its "owner" because he enjoys it through his sovereignty, since it arises for that very purpose;

showing this, he said, "Therefore, this... and so forth. As for the statement, "In the same way, the others too," this is because the five or six aforementioned purposes are found even in the remaining treasures.
To the objection, "For what purpose does the wheel-turning monarch enjoy these treasures?

Is it not possible for a wheel-turning monarch to exist even without any of them?", the passage beginning with "But as for these" is commenced to demonstrate that he enjoys the benefits that ought to be attained through them, thereby clarifying that he is never separated from any one of them. [The text continues: "Ajita, in the eastern direction... and so forth.
He conquers the circle of kṣatriyas because of the natural outflow of karma conducive to great power.
He traverses [the earth] at his pleasure, having mounted the elephant-treasure and the horse-treasure;
by their majestic power, he circumambulates the earth bounded by the ocean even before breakfast and returns to the capital city itself. By means of the counselor-treasure...

He guards his conquest by seeing to the performance of duties here and there. He experiences the pleasure of enjoyment proceeding from the use of the remaining jewels—the jewel of the gem, the jewel of the woman, and the jewel of the householder—since such experience is established through their being enjoyed accordingly.
For he, by means of the jewel of the gem, dispels the darkness over an area measuring a league and experiences pleasure through the sight of light and so forth.

He experiences happiness by means of the Woman-Treasure through such things as beholding forms that surpass those of human beings, and by means of the Householder-Treasure through the acquisition of whatever wealth he desires, such as gems, gold, silver, and so forth.

Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned point by way of the sword and the fruit of the sword, the passage beginning with “By the first” was spoken. For there are three kinds of swords (satti), so called because kings are able (sak-konti) or capable of accomplishing their aims by means of them. As it has been said:
“Power, majesty, and counsel—these are the three swords (sattiyo); by their mastery, indeed, [kings rule].”
“Power is the heat born of punishment, while majesty is that born of the treasury.
Counsel is both the mantra and the deliberation; it has four ears and two spheres of activity.
That which has three spheres of activity has six ears; what is secret is called ‘hidden.’”
In this context, the power of energy (*vīriyabala*) is the strength of exertion (*ussāhasatti*). Its application is fulfilled by the first treasure, the Wheel-treasure (*cakkaratana*). Why is that?
Because through that strength of exertion, the state of the unimpeded wheel of command (*appaṭihata-āṇācakkabhāva*), which is to be set in motion, is accomplished.
The power of wisdom (*paññābala*) is the strength of counsel (*mantasatti*). Its application is fulfilled by the last treasure, the Counsellor-treasure (*pariṇāyakaratana*). Why is that?
Because of his skill in all royal affairs, he possesses an unfailing application of power, like the potency of a mantra;

thus, he is "abundant in power" (*pabhūsatti*) through his mastery and wealth. Furthermore, his engagement with these [resources] is fulfilled by means of the treasures of the elephant, the horse, and the householder.
Why is this so? Because of the great majesty of the elephant and horse treasures, and because of the excellence of the treasury obtained from the householder treasure.
And because the perfection of the excellence of radiance is established through the power of radiance, as in the case of [the sun].
The connection is that the fruit resulting from the conjunction of the threefold power through the woman and the jewel is complete.

The meaning is: whatever fruit is to be obtained by means of the application of the three kinds of powers as previously described, all of that becomes complete through them. Why is that? Because the happiness of enjoyment is accomplished by those very things.
In order to further clarify the aforementioned meaning by way of two kinds of happiness, it is said: “He [possesses] women, jewels, and so forth.

“Happiness of enjoyment” (*bhoga-sukha*) refers to the happiness that arises through the act of utilizing what is placed nearby. “By the rest” means by the remaining five jewels, such as the wheel and so on.
“Happiness of sovereignty” (*issariya-sukha*) is the happiness that arises by way of being free from adversaries. Now, [the text proceeds] by way of the causes for their attainment:
In order to clarify that [the result] is indeed invariably concomitant with something, he says "specifically" (*visesato*), and so forth.

By the power of karma produced by the wholesome root known as non-hatred (*adosa*)—meaning, by the efficacy of the karma generated through such conditions as co-nascence (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and the like—the [results] succeed because they are of a nature consisting of exceedingly gentle jewels.
For, as a general rule, the fruit of karma corresponds to the nature of the karma itself.
The middle gems— the jewel, the woman, and the householder— come into being through the power of karma produced by the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*),

because they are caused by the perfection of generosity, which is the means for obtaining great wealth and the cause for the acquisition of such wealth. The final gem, the counselor (*pariṇāyaka-ratana*),

comes into being through the power of karma produced by the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*), [serving] precisely the functions of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) who possesses great wisdom.
Because it is to be carried forth, and because it is a natural outflow of karma produced by the wholesome root of non-delusion and the state of great wisdom.
"In the Saṃyutta on the Factors of Enlightenment" refers to the second Saṃyutta on the Factors of Enlightenment within the Mahāvagga.
"Of the Ratana Sutta" refers to the second Ratana Sutta recited there in the fifth vagga. What is called *Upadesa* is a method that proceeds by way of a detailed investigation of the seven treasures.
They are "brave" (sūra) because they destroy their adversaries through recourse [to courage]; the meaning is that they bring about fearlessness. Therefore he said, "of a nature not given to fear.
Because he stands having conquered the asuras, Sakka, the lord of the gods, is called "the Wise One" (dhīra); a son of the gods who is a constituent part of his army is called an "aṅga.
Those whose form is like the form of that aṅga of the Wise One are "those whose form is the aṅga of the Wise One" (dhīraṅgarūpā). By this—
It was said: “with bodies like those of the sons of gods. “Some” refers to the teachers named Sārasamāsa; not accepting that, he says: “But here, however,” and so forth.
“Sabhāva” means a meaning that constitutes its own nature. “Uttamasūra” means supreme warriors; for the word *sūra* here has the sense of a warrior.
For in this way, there is a distinction between this [term] and the previous method; thus it is also said: “the word *sūra* has the sense of ‘supreme’ (*uttama*).”
They say: for the reading “the supreme ones are called heroes (sūra)” is also seen. “Of the brave” (vīrānaṃ) means of those possessing energy (vīriya).

“Factor” (aṅga) means cause, based on the derivation: “it is known (aṅgīyati) or understood through this as a result. Since it is by means of that energy that they are called “wise” (dhīra), that very thing is named the “factor of wisdom” (dhīraṅga);
thus he said, “it is what was called ‘energy’. “Form” (rūpa) means the body. Therefore it was said:

“Like those whose bodies consist of energy” (*vīriyamaya-sarīrā viya*). Energy itself is “consisting of energy,” just as [one speaks of] “consisting of giving” (*dānamaya*); therefore, the meaning is: “like those whose bodies are designated as energy.
However, because energy is not a physical form (*rūpa*) in the literal sense, the word “like” (*viya*) was employed.

Furthermore, it is said “like those whose bodies consist of energy” in order to show the meaning that [the body] is produced from the factor of wisdom (*dhīraṅga*), namely, “the wise one’s factor” (*dhīraṅga*); thus, too, [it is derived] from energy.

By the word "as if," he shows that form (*rūpa*) does not arise as something absolute. Alternatively, it should be construed thus: "form" refers to the body, which is a constituent of wisdom; and "these have vigor as their essence.
Even so, he demonstrates that what is called "vigor" has no physical form by means of the phrase "as if they had bodies made of vigor.
Here too, the suffix *-maya* should be understood in its own primary sense (of "consisting of"); therefore, they are like vigor that possesses a physical form.
The meaning is as follows: this is what is intended—namely, that if there were such a thing as "embodied energy" (*saviggahaṃ vīriyaṃ*), then his sons would indeed be identical to it;
this alone is the meaning accepted by the Teacher. However, in the *Mahāpadāna-ṭṭhakathā*, it is stated thus:

"They have energy as their limb and form, therefore they are 'those whose limbs and forms are energy' (*dhīraṅgarūpā*); they are born of energy, of the nature of energy, made of energy, and untiring."
"Even when fighting by day, they did not grow weary"—this is what is meant. This should be understood as having been said with reference to the word *rūpa* in its sense of "nature.
Indeed, here and elsewhere in some places, the reading "dhitaṅgarūpā" is found.
For the word *dhiti* also has the meaning of "energy" (*vīriya*), as in such passages as: "Truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—he overcomes what is seen," and so forth.
It is like the word *dhiti*. However, in some places the reading is seen as “*vīraṅga*. It should be accepted according to what one prefers.
Now, one might raise the objection: "Since a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*) has no opposing army that his sons could crush, why is it said they are 'crushers of enemy armies'?
To clear this objection, he says "If... and so forth, regarding the enemy army.
Whether it be so or not, the intention [of the text] is that it was stated in that way merely as a supposition—“if, however, it were to exist”—in order to demonstrate their such power.

Even when it says “crusher of enemy armies,” the meaning to be understood is “capable of crushing an enemy army,” because another meaning is discernible from the context, just as in the case of: “Monks, by one who is training... [and so forth].

In the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*) on the passage, "A bhikkhu should know, inquire, and question," the phrase "by one desiring to train" (*sikkhitukāmena*) is taken as the intended meaning; to show this point, it is said, "capable of crushing them.
For they do not stand merely crushing the enemy army, but rather they are indeed capable of crushing it. The same applies elsewhere.
"Accordingly. Some also say that the meaning is "those capable of crushing the enemy's army," thus showing [the word] *parasenappamaddanā*.

To show the state of excellence in practice—consisting of the fulfillment of the duties of a wheel-turning monarch—which serves as the condition for the long-term ripening of the merit accumulated in the past that is now coming to fruition, [the text says]:
Regarding the phrase “by means of the Dhamma,” he explains its meaning as “by means of the Dhamma of the five precepts, such as ‘a living being must not be killed’ and so forth.
For this is the meaning [of the passage]: “Now, Ānanda, those rival kings in the eastern direction approached King Mahāsudassana and said:
‘Come, Great King! Welcome to you, Great King! This is your own realm, Great King.’”
"Give us instruction, Great King. King Mahāsudassana spoke thus: "Living beings must not be killed; what is not given must not be taken;
one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehoods; intoxicants must not be drunk;
and you must eat only as much as is appropriate. And as for those rival kings in the eastern direction, they [listened] to King Mahāsudassana...
This was said with reference to the Dhamma of counsel given to the king, which is recorded in the passage beginning, "They were followers...
For in this way, even the qualifying expression "without rod, without weapon" becomes well-established. This same meaning is stated in other works such as the *Sutta Nipāta Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, in the *Mahāpadāna Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "Without rod means those who seize even a hundred or a thousand beings who have committed an offense..."

Those who rule by means of punishment with wealth are said to exercise sovereignty through the "staff of wealth"; those who instruct through cutting and breaking are said to exercise sovereignty through the "staff of the sword.
But he, having abandoned both kinds of punishment, dwells without a staff. Regarding the phrase "without a sword":
those who harm others with a sword having a single edge and so forth are said to exercise sovereignty through the sword; but he [does not even harm] a tiny fly with a sword.

It is said: "Having conquered the earth in the manner described—having been welcomed by rival kings with the words, 'Come, Great King,' and having done so through Dhamma alone, without shedding even a drop of blood for anyone—he dwells there, having overcome it;
the meaning is that he dwells as its master. This refers to the phrase "through Dhamma" (*dhammena*) as [the merit] accumulated in the past.
This was said with reference to some meritorious deed (*puññadhamma*) that is currently ripening. For it is for this very reason that it is said:
"Having been received by rival kings in accordance with the Dhamma, he has conquered and dwells over the aforementioned earth.
And the Teacher also said: "In accordance with the Dhamma" means by his own accumulated merit (*puññadhamma*).

Thus urged, all the kings on earth go out to meet him, saying, "Welcome to you, Great King," and so forth, and they hand over their own kingdoms to the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). Therefore it is said:

"Having conquered this earth, bounded by the ocean, without punishment and without weapons, by means of the Dhamma, he dwells [therein]"; by this also, the very same meaning as previously stated is expressed.

Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning is appropriate in both ways here; for such a dwelling is not possible through the mere perfection of the means of fulfilling the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) and so forth,

without the karma previously accumulated, nor is it possible through the perfection of the means of fulfilling the duties of a wheel-turning monarch and so forth, without the karma previously accumulated.
Having thus explained the first accomplishment, in order to explain the second accomplishment, he spoke the words beginning with "If, however...
To show the meaning not yet fully expounded therein, he said: "Regarding 'an arahant... [up to] ...one whose veil is removed'...
Because the seven evil states, such as lust and the rest, arise in the world, and when they do arise, they [afflict] the continuum of sentient beings...

Having covered and enveloped them, they obstruct the arising of the wholesome; therefore, he shows by means of the phrase "lust and hatred," etc., that these are expressed here by the word *chada* (covering).
"Misconduct" refers to the three types of misconduct together with mental misconduct other than wrong view;
however, wrong view is mentioned specifically because it especially covers beings and because it is the most blameworthy.
And they have been taken separately. For it is said: “All those [wrong views] are encompassed within these very sixty-two bases;

emerging, they emerge only while remaining fixed here,” and so forth. Likewise, delusion (*moha*) is in the sense of being bewildered, and ignorance (*avijjā*) is in the sense of making things unknown;
thus, nescience itself is stated in two ways according to the distinction in its mode of occurrence. For in both cases, its meaning is that of covering.
It has been said: "Then it becomes utter darkness for the man whom delusion overcomes," and, "The world is shrouded by ignorance;
through stinginess and negligence, it does not shine. In this way, the sense of "covering" should also be stated for lust, hatred, and the rest.
In the *Mahāpadāna-ṭṭhakathā*, however, seven unwholesome states are taken according to lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and craving. Among these, in the sense of coloring...
Lobha (greed) itself is stated in two ways: as *rāga* (lust) in the sense of being a "flowing" (*taṇhāyana*), and as *taṇhā* (craving) in the sense of a differentiation in the mode of manifestation.

For in both cases, its meaning of "covering" (*chadana*) is absolute. As it is said: "When lust overcomes a man, then there is blinding darkness," and "Blinded by desire, covered by a net, shrouded by the covering of craving.
And by the inclusion of the term "defilement" (*kilesa*), those remaining [factors] not already mentioned are also included.
Doubt and the others have been mentioned.
"Concealed by seven" is a statement containing a causal implication; the meaning is that because it is concealed by the seven evil qualities, the world is in darkness due to the defilements.
"That covering" refers to the covering consisting of the seven evil qualities. "Having uncovered" means...
"Having uncovered and having caused to disappear. That very same thing is stated by another synonym as "having become possessed of light all around.
For light is simply the disappearance of the covering of defilements (*kilesa*). By this [light], that which is to be uncovered and caused to disappear is called *vivaṭṭa*.
It covers or conceals, thus it is *chada*. That by which there is an uncovering of the covering is *vivaṭṭacchadā*; or the meaning is *vivaṭṭacchado*.

[The text] shows this. For this term *vivaṭṭacchada*—like the terms *daḷhadhamma*, *paccakkhadhamma*, and so forth—is both masculine, ending in *-ā* (as *vivaṭṭacchadā*), and ends in *-o* (*vivaṭṭacchado*). Thus it is said in the *Mahāpadāna-aṭṭhakathā*:

“That by which the covering, the obscuration—consisting of the defilements of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, and craving—is uncovered, destroyed, and dispelled, is *vivaṭacchada*; [it is also called] *vivaṭṭacchadā*.”
"This is the reading; this is the very meaning. And in its *Līnatthappakāsinī* commentary it is also stated:
"The designation 'vivaṭṭacchadā' is made by changing the vowel *o* to *ā*.

However, those learned in grammar, having stated that "by the rule *ādhanvāditō*, the suffix *āp* occurs in certain instances after words such as *dhanu* when they have entered into a compound," cite the following examples of usage: *kaṇḍivadhanvā*, *paccakkhadhammā*, and *vivaṭṭacchadā*.

Anticipating the question, "Why were these three terms spoken? he provides the answer by way of the method of causal ornamentation (*hetālaṅkāranaya*), saying "In that regard" (*tattha*) and so forth.
The meaning of "in that regard" (*tattha*) is "among the three terms. He is worthy of receiving a special honor; thus, by this sense, his worthiness for honor (*pūjārahatā*) is stated.
Since he is the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddho*), therefore he is worthy of honor; this is the reason for that worthiness for honor.

It has been stated. Since the state of Buddhahood is preceded by the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*), the "uncovering of the wheel" (*vivaṭṭacchadatā*)—which is the cause of Buddhahood—is stated here.
The "wheel" (*vaṭṭa*) is threefold by way of kamma and so forth, and the "coverings" (*chada*) are sevenfold by way of passion (*rāga*) and so forth; thus they are the "wheel-coverings.

One who is free from these wheel-coverings, or one from whom the wheel-coverings have departed, is "one whose wheel-coverings have been uncovered" (*vivaṭṭacchado*). [The term *vivaṭṭacchada* is explained as follows:]... [repetition of the preceding definition]... [end of commentary].
Alternatively, in order to show that the word *vi-* should be construed with both members when it precedes a *dvanda* compound, it is said: "both *vivaṭṭo* and *vicchado*.
Even so, they say: "'*Vivaṭṭacchado*' means 'that which is both *vivaṭṭo* and *vicchado*';

this shows the meaning by means of the elision of the first member of the compound in the latter term. Regarding the phrase "an arahant by way of the absence of the round (*vaṭṭa*)," this refers to [freedom] from defilements (*kilesa*).

This was said with reference to the meaning of being "far removed" (araka) from the enemies that are the defilements, of having destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, and of there being no secrecy (raha) in the performance of evil.
For this is a demonstration of the inference of the cause by means of the fruit—just as fire is inferred from smoke, or rain above from a flood of water.
And according to this meaning, the state of being an Arahant is the cause and the absence of the round of existence is the fruit; such is the opinion of the Teacher.
“Because he is worthy of the requisites, etc., and of special honor”— this may also be shown as an inference of the effect from the cause,

just as smoke [indicates] fire, or a flood of water [indicates] rain above. However, the statement “He is a Perfectly Enlightened One because of the absence of a covering” is an inference of the effect from the cause,
since the state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One is preceded by the absence of the covering of all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*).

For by means of the path of arahantship there is the state of being stripped of defilements (*vicchadatā*), and by means of omniscient knowledge there is the state of being a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddhabhāvo*).
"Turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) and being stripped of defilements (*vicchada*)"—these two constitute the pair of causes.

Granted that, according to the teacher’s view, in demonstrating the inference of a cause from its fruit, the state of turning away is itself the fruit; nevertheless, because such knowledge [of turning away] and the knowledge of suchness (*tathāñāṇa*) serve as the cause for the demonstration of the inference of a cause.
It should be understood that "the cause itself" is what is meant by the name.

Thus, having shown the purpose of the statement of the three terms according to the method of the ornament of causes (*hetālaṅkāranaya*), he now speaks the words beginning with "by the second" in order to show it also by way of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*).
Therein, "by the second ground of self-confidence" refers to: "O monks, these four... [and so forth].
"By means of those grounds of self-confidence (vesārajjāni) with which the Tathāgata is endowed, the Tathāgata claims the place of the leader,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel"— according to this sequence spoken by the Blessed One, [the second ground is]:
"While you claim to be one whose taints are exhausted, if anyone should say to you, 'These taints are not yet exhausted,' then regarding that..."
“Monks, I do not perceive any ground on which any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could rightfully challenge me.

Since I do not perceive such a ground, monks, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained self-confidence. This is [the perfection] illustrated by this self-confidence (*vesārajja*). “The prior accomplishment” means:

The accomplishment of the meaning of the first term, “arahant,” is the accomplishment of *arahatta* (worthiness); because that meaning exists within the second intrepidity (*vesārajja*), it is said that the accomplishment of that meaning is achieved by means of that intrepidity.

For the second intrepidity—stated as “‘These taints (*āsava*) are not fully destroyed in you who claim they are destroyed,’ etc.”—is indeed what was described [earlier] as “being far removed (*āraka*) from defilements,” and so forth.

This is the meaning of the word “Arahant. From this, it is understood that “just as the first accomplishment [of the goal] is by means of the second intrepidity, so too the accomplishment of the second intrepidity is by means of the first meaning.
By establishing it thus, the demonstration of the purpose for the utterance of the three words by way of the four intrepidities becomes logical.
Otherwise, indeed, there would be no purpose whatsoever.
"This very statement would be unutterable here. This same method applies to the remaining [confidences] as well.
"By the first" means by the first [confidence], described according to the stated method, as the confidence manifested by the words:

"In regard to those things which you claim, O Fully Enlightened One, to have fully awakened to, yet say 'these things have not been fully awakened to'—in that regard... I abide [fearless]. "The second accomplishment" means:
The accomplishment of the meaning and the accomplishment of the state of being a Buddha for the second term, “Sammāsambuddho,” is due to its possessing that specific meaning.
By the third and fourth [terms], according to the method already stated—namely, by those which constitute the third and fourth [terms]:
“‘Those things which were spoken of as obstructive, if one indulges in them, they are not sufficient to be obstacles,’ and therein... [I dwell]”; and “Of whomsoever... [and so forth].

...by means of the confidences (*vesārajjāni*) thus illustrated: "But the Dhamma has been taught by me for their benefit; it leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering"—and so forth.
"The accomplishment of the third" (*tatiyasiddhi*) means the accomplishment of the meaning of the third phrase, "with the veil removed" (*vivaṭṭacchadā*);
the sense is that its meaning is made manifest by those [confidences]. "In accordance with reality" (*yāthāvato*)...
"For it was through the teaching on the obstructive and the emancipating factors that the Teacher’s state of having the veil withdrawn became manifest in the world"—thus it was said by the Master.
Since the teaching on the obstructive and emancipating factors is established precisely by virtue of his state of having the veil withdrawn, it is also appropriate to say:
"By the third [verse], the third and fourth [qualities] are established."
Having thus shown the purpose by means of the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) in the statement of the three words, he now says "And the first...
and so forth, showing it also by means of the three eyes (*cakkhu*). Therein, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of introduction.

The first word, "Arahant," establishes the Blessed One’s Dhamma-eye (*dhammacakkhu*), which consists of the knowledge of the three lower paths and fruits regarding the enemies that are the defilements (*kilesa*).

This is because it illustrates the destruction of the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra. The second term, “Sammāsambuddho” (the Perfectly Enlightened One), establishes the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakkhu*), which consists of the knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies (*āsaya-anusaya*), and the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of others (*indriya-paropariyatta-ñāṇa*); for that [eye] arises only in a Perfectly Enlightened One. Indeed, these two types of knowledge do not arise in disciples (*sāvaka*) or paccekabuddhas.
The third term, “Vivaṭṭacchadā” (one who has uncovered the veil), establishes the all-around eye (*samantacakkhu*), which is the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

It establishes [the meaning] by illustrating the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*). For after saying "He is the Fully Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddho*), the statement "whose veil is rent asunder" (*vivaṭṭacchadā*) clarifies that for the state of being a Fully Enlightened One, there must be the abandonment of all defilements along with their latent tendencies.
The statement, "But I, dear Ambaṭṭha, am the giver of the mantras," is secondary; whereas the statement, "you are the receiver of the mantras," is primary.
With reference to this very exhortation as a word of encouragement, it is said: "By saying 'Receive the mantras,' he produces in him courage regarding the mantras.
The meaning is that he produces a state of courage, which consists of lucid knowledge, in the discernment of characteristics (*lakkhaṇavibhāvana*). 259.
Regarding the phrase "So be it" (*evaṃ bho*), here the word *evaṃ* is a particle used for accepting a statement; and in this context, the acceptance of the statement is—
"In this way we shall know that venerable Gotama, you being the recipient of our counsel"—this is the acceptance of the words spoken by Pokkharasāti.
By the phrase "the meaning of which," etc., he shows that very same point.
And thus it is said: "having assented to the brahmin Pokkharasāti"; for he [assented] to that teacher.

Showing that he speaks because he perceives the Buddha’s presence through his state of being free from delusion regarding the characteristics of the exhortation (*samuttejanā*), [the author] says, “He too,” and so forth.
Regarding this, the Teacher (Ācariya) stated, “By that—that is, by that aforementioned exhortation”;
however, the reading “by that discourse of the Teacher” is now seen in the manuscripts. In terms of meaning, this is as follows:
It is indeed not contradictory. For in the *Mantas*, a discourse that arouses mindfulness is called "inspiration.
"A non-ground for vehicles" means a place that is not a ground for a vehicle, a place where it is impossible to travel by vehicle; the meaning is "having gone near the gate-tower.
He said this because even though a statement is made in a general sense, its specific meaning must be understood according to the authority of the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

“At the time of midday”: having stated the first method according to the practice of all [monks], the second method is stated according to the specific practice of those who exert themselves by day (*divāpadhānika*).
“Those who exert themselves by day” means those who devote themselves to exertion during the daytime;
it is said that they walk back and forth in this manner for the purpose of performing the duties of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*) during the day. Therefore he said, “For such as these,” and so forth.

“While coming from one cell to another, I was distracted; I shall enter only after asking permission”—thus he spoke the words beginning with “It is said that he,” explaining Ambaṭṭha’s intention for approaching him.

[The term] *abhiññātakula* means born into a well-known family; and although, according to the method about to be explained, the Ambaṭṭha family was previously unknown, [he is so called because of his present renown].
But then, because it was well-known, he said, "At that time, it is said," and so forth.

By the four castes—those possessing beauty, birth, and wealth—which serve as the grounds for designation, [meaning] by the four castes characterized by beauty, birth, and wealth, through which one designates [someone] saying, "This person is such-and-such.

To reveal the intention with which those monks thought, the passage beginning with "For whoever" was stated. Although stated without distinction, it is intended for the meaning to be understood specifically.
By the phrase "with reference to the fragrant chamber" (gandhakuṭiṃ sandhāyā), he shows that it refers to spoken words.
This applies to similar cases as well. "Without haste" (aturo) means not hurrying; there is also a reading "aturanto," which has the same meaning.

To the question, "How can one who enters be said to enter without haste? he says "slowly," and so forth. In that context, "at the place of the measure of a footstep" (padappamāṇaṭṭhāne) means between two footprints.
In a space the size of a closed fist. *Sinduvāra* is a certain flowering tree that has white blossoms;
it is also called *nigguṇḍī*. *Pamukhaṃ* means the front entrance of the inner chamber of the fragrant hut (*gandhakuṭi*).
The phrase "near the keyhole" was stated in order to justify the statement beginning with "the door, it is said."
261. By the phrase "giving gifts," he shows that the opening of the gates occurred spontaneously through the power of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Regarding the expression "they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One," the author states "just as" and so forth, demonstrating the implicit meaning (*neyyattha*) understood from the prefix *sam-*—namely, the initial joy experienced by the Blessed One upon meeting them.
For the Blessed One, too, when asking questions such as, "Is it endurable, young men?
Is it sustainable? was the very first instance of joy arising through prior conversation with those young men.
"Joy arising equally" means that the exchange of greetings proceeded in a manner identical to his own [previous] practice, by way of emulating him. To illustrate this point along with a simile:

“Like cold water,” and so forth, was said. Therein, the Blessed One’s resemblance to cold water should be understood as being due to the complete extinguishment of the distress of the defilements (*kilesa*), while the young brahmins’ resemblance to hot water is due to their lack of such extinguishment.

“Greeted with joy” (*sammodita*) means brought together. Here, the word *muda* refers specifically to meeting or coming together, not to gladness; for it is in this sense that the aforementioned simile is made consistent.
It exists. For it has been said: "oneness" (*ekībhāva*); the meaning is the state of equality or uniformity through the act of mutual greeting.

"Is it endurable? (*khamanīyaṃ*)—they ask this, wondering whether [the body], which is a machine of four wheels and nine doors, can endure its own nature which is difficult to bear due to the abundance of suffering.
"Is it sustainable? (*yāpanīyaṃ*)—referring to that whose livelihood is dependent upon conditions such as food and so forth.
May I be able to maintain myself through sustenance known as long-term continuity;
may I be free from illness by the absence of afflictions such as diseases of the head; may I be free from distress by the absence of a painful livelihood;

may I have lightness of movement through ease in undertaking various duties; may I have strength through the possession of corresponding power; and may I have comfort through the presence of the fruit of dwelling in happiness.
The meaning should be understood by connecting the word *kacci* with "there is" (*atthi*) in every instance.
Rapture that has reached its full strength is simply *pīti*. Fresh rapture is *pāmojja*. It is called *sammodanika* because it generates or produces gladness;
the same term becomes *sammodaniya* by changing the letter *ka* to *ya*. This shows the sense of "to be greeted with gladness" (*sammodanīya*) in the phrase "to greet with gladness."
This is shown by the phrase "because of its suitability. Thus it was stated by the teachers.

It should be understood that this also demonstrates the meaning: "It is worthy of being greeted, thus it is *sammodanika*; by the method already described, it is precisely that which is *sammodaniya*.

The word "to cause to remember" (*sāretun*) has the synonymous expression "to cause to proceed uninterruptedly" (*nirantaraṃ pavattetun*). "Because of its state of being remembered" means because of its state of being recollected (*anussaritabbabhāvato*).
In the sense of "worthy of being reminded," it is stated as *sāraṇīya* with a long vowel according to the specific grammatical rule (*yathāpada*).
However, in the sense of "that which is to be remembered," it should be understood that although it ought to be said *saraṇīya*, it is stated as *sāraṇīya* by lengthening the vowel.

Having thus shown the meaning from the perspective of the word (*saddato*), he now shows it from the perspective of the mere meaning (*atthamattato*) with the words "because of the pleasure of being heard," and so forth.
It has been stated. In that context, "pleasant while being heard" refers to its sweetness upon first entering the range of hearing;

"pleasant when being recollected" refers to its delightfulness when subjected to thorough investigation. "By way of purity of phrasing" refers to the eloquence of the speech in that discourse by virtue of its being natural expression;
"by way of purity of meaning" refers to the state of the meaning being free from defilement. "By many methods" means by many reasons.
"I will drive him away" means "I will cause him distress. Having fastened the cloth over both shoulders, with reference to hanging it from the neck, it is said "having hung it from the neck.
"Having grasped the corner of the cloth" means having grasped the edge of the wrapped garment with one hand. With reference to ascending the walkway, he says "having ascended the walkway."

“Balance of the elements” (*dhātusamatā*) means the state of equilibrium among the elements such as taste; the meaning is health. “For the sake of inspiring confidence” (*pāsādikatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of generating faith;

this is connected with the phrase “in every place he went. There is also a reading, “Because of his inspiring confidence” (*pāsādikattā*); its meaning is: because he brings serenity to the limbs and members of the body;
this is connected with the phrase “inspiring great respect. “Mocking talk” (*uppaṇḍanakathaṃ*) means speech that is fit to be treated with derision.

“*Anācārabhāvasāraṇīyan*” is its qualification; the meaning is that it is to be reminded of by way of improper conduct—that is, it is something to be remembered [with the thought], “Alas, this is indeed improper conduct. 262.
To show that he has undertaken a task that is difficult to perform and impossible to accomplish, [the text says]: “Desiring to seize the peak of existence...”
Thus it was said, beginning with "viyā" and so forth. For this—namely, the disparagement of the Blessed One—is impossible even for the world including the devas.
Therefore he said, "He exerts himself in an improper place.

Thinking, "Come now, I shall deliberate with him," even though this fool exerts himself in an improper place, he [only] maintains his pride, thinking: "If I say nothing to him, he does not dare to speak further with me."
"He will take it up"; however, as he speaks, when his birth and clan are revealed, there will be a suppression of his pride.
"Come, let me discuss this with him"—this is the meaning of what the Blessed One said to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha.

They are "teachers" (*ācariya*) because they instruct in proper conduct and behavior; and those who are pre-eminent among such teachers are "great teachers" (*pācariya*), just as [the term] "grandfather" (*papitāmaha*) conveys that same sense.
To show this, it was said: “by their teachers and by their teachers’ teachers.
263. Although the statement beginning with “or while lying down” should not have been made, he nevertheless formed a pair [of opposites] out of pride.
Showing that [the Buddha] says this, he said, “Granted, in three...,” and so forth. Therein, “in three postures” means in standing, walking, and sitting.
For it is only in those [three] that one may converse with a teacher;

however, not while lying down, because even for those who are to be honored, lying down in their presence is something that should not be done by those who show them respect. “Discourse and conversation” means, by way of discourse, for the purpose of engaging in mutual exchange.
"Conversing. For indeed, conversation with a teacher while both are lying down is not considered proper conduct;
likewise, here "discourse-conversation" (*kathāsallāpa*) refers to speaking by treating [the teacher] as equal to others.
As for this passage: "Indeed, Master Gotama, a Brahmin while lying down may converse with a Brahmin who is also lying down."
The Teacher, while conversing with Ambaṭṭha, demonstrated that the aforementioned dialogue was of an improper nature;
although that [demonstration] was not included in the formal recitation (saṅgīti) of the Canon, it has been handed down to the present day by an unblemished lineage of teachers.
Thus, showing its connection with the subsequent passage beginning with “But as for those, Master Gotama,” [the author] says:
He said, beginning with “*Tato kira*. [The word] *gorūpaṃ* means “cow,” because it is stated by way of its form (*rūpaka*), and because the word *rūpa* expresses that very state.

To show that if he were not contemptuous he would have said “shaven-headed recluses” (*muṇḍā samaṇā*), whereas being contemptuous, he extends the word by the syllable *ka* in the sense of reproach and says “shavelings, wretched recluses” (*muṇḍakā samaṇakā*), the passage beginning with “*Muṇḍe muṇḍā*” was stated.

“Ibbhā” and “gahapatikā” are merely synonymous in meaning; however, from the perspective of etymology (*saddato*), it is derived from the application of the word *ibha* (elephant) with the elision of the latter member of the compound.
They are called “ibbhā” because they are worthy of that elephant, with the doubling of the consonant (*dvittaṃ katvā*). What is meant?

Just as one who is reckoned an “ibha” due to his beautiful gait—being a mount for another, such as an elephant—proceeds under the control of another and not by himself, so too these [brahmins]... [of the brahmins].
Suddas are those who act under the influence of others and not according to their own will; therefore, because their conduct is like that of outcasts (ibbha), they are called "ibbhas.
Furthermore, the term "gahapatikas" indicates the essential meaning that, by virtue of being householders, they are residents of houses and masters of homes.
"Kaṇhā" means those of dark birth. His intention is that only the twice-born (dvija) are of pure birth, not others; therefore he says "the black ones.
Because they are kinsmen and relatives by virtue of being grandfathers, they are "bandhu"; therefore he says "they are called 'grandfather' (pitāmaha). "Apacca" means sons.
"Issued from the mouth" means that the ancestors of the brahmins issued from the mouth of Brahmā.
The intention is that this was their first appearance. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. However, there is this distinction here:
having said "the outcasts were black," he says "the descendants of Bandhupādāpacca" to show that, by way of lineage, these ascetics belonged to the Vessa caste;
yet, by way of their first appearance, they emerged from the back of Brahmā's foot, and not from the navel like ordinary Vessas.

Regarding the phrase "he shows": this statement, moreover, is even more of an unconsidered utterance than his previous words beginning with "issued from the mouth," because the state of being a recluse can only occur for one who is included within the four castes. "Without specifying" means without making a distinction;
the sense is that it was done by way of not naming [the person]. "He spoke relying solely on pride" means: having made pride itself his support, exalting himself and disparaging others.
He spoke the words beginning with, “shaven-headed ascetics. “I shall make known”: I shall cause [him] to understand by explaining my own lineage and status as they truly are.
“Meaning” (attha) means welfare or a desired object; however, since that is precisely the duty to be performed, it is said:
“the meaning consisting of the duty to be performed upon arrival. That which possesses this is “one who has a purpose” (atthika), just as...

Regarding the word “daṇḍiko”: since the second personal suffix *-vā* (denoting possession) exists here as well, it is understood from the first instance that this refers specifically to the consciousness that has that [staff] as its object;
thus he says, “the consciousness of that young brahmin. The term *atthikavā* means “one who possesses what is needed,” just as one is called *guṇavā* (“possessing virtues”).
He shows by means of the phrase “yeneva kho panatthena” that the expression “yāyeva kho panatthāya” was stated through a change of gender (liṅgavipallāsa).
Therefore he said: “‘Tameva atthaṃ’—this was stated specifically in the masculine gender.
For in that [previous] instance, the natural gender was shown, whereas here the non-natural gender is established. Furthermore, this is another method from the Commentary: “yāya atthāya” means...
The term *sampadāna* (the recipient) is used here in the masculine gender to refer to that purpose; it means "for the sake of that purpose," which is defined as the duty to be performed.
The word *assa* (of him) is connected with *dassetvā* (having shown), referring to Ambaṭṭha.

The phrase *aññesaṃ santikaṃ āgatānaṃ* refers to those of noble character who have approached the presence of those worthy of honor. *Vattanti* means their established custom. This is understood from the context itself.

The meaning “in the teacher’s family” is understood; and the expression “one who has not lived [the life]” (*avusitavā*) is used by way of conventional terminology to denote the state of being untrained, just as the phrase “he clothed him with the three robes” refers to the giving of robes. Therefore it is said: “one who has not lived [the life] in the teacher’s family, one who is untrained.

Precisely because he is untrained, he is “of little learning”; and the term “one who fancies he has lived [the life]” (*vusitamānī*) is used because, in relation to the word *vusita*, it expresses the state of not having completed it.

By the phrase "being of little learning" (*appassuto va samāno*), he shows that there is a textual ellipsis (*pāṭhaseso*) [to be supplied]. For indeed, much learning (*bāhusacca*) should be sought only for the purpose of attaining tranquility;
since Ambaṭṭha lacks this, it is understood that he is one who has not lived the holy life, is untrained, and is of little learning.
Thus, explaining the reason through the implication of the meaning, he said: "What else [could it be] but his failure to live the holy life? (*kimaññatra avusitattā*).

He explains this connection as well with the words, "For of him," and so forth. However, according to the literal meaning, this is a demonstration of the cause for non-appeasement through the practice of harsh speech.
Herein, the construction is as follows: "What else [could it be] but lack of training?"—this is the reason;
that is, the reason for this Ambaṭṭha’s practice of harsh speech. Also, [the phrase] "by the practice of harsh speech."
The meaning is that it is stated as the cause by way of habitual practice (*samudācāra*). They also construe it thus:
"Apart from his state of being unvirtuous (*avusita*), what other cause could there be for such harsh speech?

However, the first construction is more appropriate here, because it should be construed according to the reading of the text. This is due to the connection with the particle *aññatra* ("apart from").
“Avusitattā” (because of not having lived [the holy life]) is an ablative used in the sense of the accusative. He supports that very reason with the words beginning “in the teacher’s family.
264. “Asakamanō” means one whose mind has not come under its own control because it follows after another person characterized by anger.

“Mānanimmadanatthaṃ” means for the purpose of crushing out pride—that is, for the purpose of suppressing it, or for the purpose of not being intoxicated by it; the meaning is for the sake of being free from the intoxication of pride.
"Having vomited up the humors (*dosa*)" means having caused the wind, bile, and phlegm humors, which were moistened by the drinking of oil, to be brought up.
"By clan, clan"—that is, by means of that blameworthy ancient clan name uttered by Ambaṭṭha when questioned by the Blessed One, [he refers to] the clan name now designated as blameless.
"By family-lineage, family-lineage"—here too the same method applies. "Having raised up."
"Having risen from what is blameworthy" means having pulled oneself out of it.

Here, "clan" (*gotta*) is to be understood by way of the primordial ancestor, whereas "family lineage" (*kulāpadesa*) is to be understood by way of the well-known persons born among his descendants, just as in the expression "the Ādicca Māghava.
For the clan of the Sākiyas has its primordial ancestor in one who was the son of the divine maiden named Aditi.
They also call him "of the Gotama clan. As it is said in the Pabbajjā Sutta:
"By clan I am an Ādicca, by birth I am a Sākiya;
from that family I have gone forth, not aspiring for sensual pleasures."
Furthermore, the Māghava clan became well-known among his descendants as belonging to the people of Macalagāma.

Because the root of the lineage was censurable and because it was made known that he did not have a divine status as his foundation, it was said: "I shall cut down and fell the banner of pride at its root.
"Ghaṭṭento" means insulting on account of birth and clan. "Hīḷento" means making contemptuous reproach. "Caṇḍā bho... [O fierce ones...]
The intention is that when [the Sakyans] are accused of faults such as ferocity by saying, "Gotama is of the Sakyan clan," the ascetic Gotama will also be accused.
He shows that one in whom there is mutual arrogance and anger is called "ferocious" by the words, "possessed of anger based on pride."
Here, the state of being supported is by way of the natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) and the object (ārammaṇa), not by way of co-nascence (sahajāta) and so forth.
"Harsh" means rough with the mind and speech. "Light" means young, those whose karma has not yet matured. Therefore he said, "Even with a small amount," and so on.
"A gourd-bowl" refers to the unbroken shell of a gourd fruit. To show the method not mentioned in the Commentary, he says, "Speech..."

"Some say they are reckless, others that they are contentious"—thus it was said by the Teacher. Regarding the word "samānā," he stated, "Being those who exist (bhavamānā), the meaning is derived from the sound 'asa,'" and thus said, "'Santā' is a synonym for the preceding word.
By the phrase "not of the brahmins" and so forth, he makes known the very meaning: "they do not honor" means "they do not perform acts of honor. "Apacitikamma" means an act of prostration.

Regarding the phrase “Yadime Sakyā,” it should be understood that the indefinite pronoun *ya* in the subsequent sentence—which refers back to the action—is restricted by the pronoun *ta* in the preceding sentence, “Tayidaṃ bho Gotama. Thus he says, “Yaṃ ime Sakyā,” and so forth.
“Not in accordance” (*nānuloma*) means not suitable for one’s own birth.

265. The etymological analysis of the term *sandhāgāra* has already been stated above. Here, the phrase “the anointed Śākya kings” is said with reference to the great number of Śākya kings who were anointed at that time.
For indeed, whoever was the eldest among all [the members] of the Śākya royal family—
And only one who is capable receives the consecration.

However, some, having been consecrated, become disillusioned with kingship, thinking, "This thing called kingship involves many duties and much toil," and hand over the kingdom to their immediate successor;
sometimes that successor does the same for another. In this way, through the successive handing over of the throne, there were at that time many Sakyans who had previously received the consecration.

The phrase "there are" is the opinion of the Master (the Teacher). Furthermore, it is also appropriate to say this with reference to the great number of Śākya kings who were consecrated in various other positions as was fitting; for they too are called "kings. As it is said:

"Those called 'kings' are: universal monarchs of the earth, regional kings, provincial rulers, governors of intermediate districts, judges, high ministers, or whoever else rules by inflicting punishment and execution—these are called 'kings.'"
A couch, a throne, or a cane chair made by means of magically conjured animal forms. "Mere smiling" and "mere laughing.
"Laughing along" means they perform a loud, boisterous laugh that is directed toward me; for this is the explanatory phrase for the term "laughing along.
And the word *jaggha* occurs in the sense of a loud laugh, as in such passages as, "I shall not go among the houses with loud laughter," and so forth.
They know their ancestral lineage handed down by tradition starting from Kaṇhāyana through oral report.
For those who are proud of their clan generally describe the high and low status of others in various ways while knowing their own ancestral lineage;
so too did Ambaṭṭha, for he was later questioned by the Blessed One out of fear of Vajirapāṇi.
"He spoke of his own family lineage as it truly was. "Having hung down" means having let the garment hang down in the shape of an elephant's trunk and so forth.
"From that" means from knowing it thus, and from going [there]. "I think they are mocking me alone" means, I think, they are laughing at me alone.
The commentary on the third rebirth as a slave.
266. *Khettaleḍḍūnaṃ* means of the clods of earth raised up by the act of plowing in a field.

Because it dwells among clods of earth, this small bird is known by the name "Leḍḍukikā" (the Clod-Bird). In the commentary on the *Leḍḍukikopama-sutta* in the *Majjhima-paṇṇāsaka*, it is called the "Cātaka-bird";
however, in the *Nighaṇṭu* lexicons, they call it the "Lāpa-bird. [The following refers to] by way of anger...
*Laggituṃ* means to bring near; the meaning is "to bind up resentment.

When one says, "He makes us out to be like swans, cranes, and peacocks," this statement—"No swan, crane, or peacock comes along and restrains him by saying, 'Why do you prattle?'"—is also not included in the formal recitation (*saṅgīti*).
This shows that it was indeed spoken by the Blessed One at that time; for one who speaks at that very moment is fit to be said to act in such a way.
Ambaṭṭha thinks that the words beginning with “Is it thus for you? and the words beginning with “He has not lived the holy life,” were spoken by the ascetic Gotama out of pride;
it is with this intention that he says, “thinking that [Gotama] had now become free from pride.”

Commentary on the Discourse on the Son of a Slave Girl (Dāsiputtavādavaṇṇanā): 267. "He makes one lose self-possession" (*nimmādeti*): this is a designation formed by changing the vowel *a* to *ā*, showing that it is derived from the word *ummāda* (insanity) combined with the word *mada* (intoxication/arrogance).

By the term "he makes one lose self-possession," he shows [this meaning]. "He makes one free from pride" (*nimmāneti*): [it means] one whose pride has departed. "But if I were to ask about his lineage... (*yadi panāhaṃ gottaṃ puccheyyaṃ*)...
“Sādhu vata” means “it is indeed good. He spoke three times with a loud voice out of a desire to make it manifest.

As for the question, “Why did he speak thus?”—even though he knew the state of impurity, this is a query regarding the reason for speaking in that manner. What is intended is the name derived from the clan (*gotta*), not the clan itself as a separate entity;
thus he said, “*Mātāpettika* means ‘belonging to the mother and father. For the clan is what is received from the father.
It is derived from both the mother and the father, not from the father alone. For among the Brahmins, marriage is not desired with one who belongs to the same *gotta*;

however, the name of the *gotta* is established by birth, not artificial, nor is it a name based on qualities. And since birth pertains to both lineages, it is derived from both the mother and the father, not merely from the father.
"Name-and-*gotta*" (*nāmagotta*) refers to a name that constitutes a *gotta*, not an artificial one.
Or, because it is stated as a name with the qualifier placed last, it is like "Agyāhita.
And that very name, because it has come down through tradition, is also a clan (gotta); thus it is called "name-and-clan" (nāmagotta).

In this context, referring to that conventional designation (paṇṇatti) which is established as "Kaṇhāyana," he says: "Name by way of designation. Furthermore, this name [has been used] from the time of Kaṇha onwards.
It is said that this [gotra] has come down through the succession of families and is not merely established in this very [individual]; thus it is stated:
"Gotra by way of lineage. The explanation of the term *gotra* has already been given above.
Regarding the phrase "of one who recollects," it is intended here not merely as simple recollection, but specifically as an investigation into the purity of the family.
He said, "Of one purifying the lineage-peak," which means "of one purifying the pinnacle of the family.

Regarding the term "Ayyaputtā" (sons of masters), the word *ayya* is explained as *ayyiraka*, meaning "the sons of the lord. Among the four slave-girls, Disā was the slave-girl born within the household of King Okkāka;
therefore he said, "the son of a house-slave. And here, because Ambaṭṭha was stiff with pride on account of his birth—
Furthermore, if one's birth is not understood as it truly is, the subduing of pride cannot be accomplished;
and if pride is not subdued, one will commit offenses against the Triple Gem out of pride. However, once pride has been subdued, one will later gain confidence in the Triple Gem.
And such speech is not called harsh speech, because the mind is gentle. (From the *Majjhimapaṇṇāsaka*)
The *Abhayasutta* provides an illustration of this point. Furthermore, some people, when addressed with harsh speech, become softened—like iron and other metals when heated by fire.
Therefore, desiring to make Ambaṭṭha free from his arrogance, the Blessed One said:
"The Sakyans are noble sons; you are a slave-born son of the Sakyans."
In such passages as, “Here, a certain wicked bhikkhu, having mastered the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, burns himself,” the word *daha* has the sense of “bearing” (*dhāraṇa*).
And here, “bearing” means making known by way of one’s ancestors; thus he said, “Okkāka was our ancestor,” and so forth.
For those learned in grammar maintain that the word *daha* signifies both “reducing to ashes” and “bearing. Radiance.
"Emits" means that it issues forth having become radiant, due to such meritorious karma, because of the radiant nature of the teeth.
"Them" refers to the eldest princes. "Of the first-era beings" means those born at the beginning of the first eon (*paṭhamakappa*).
Here, by the word "it is said" (*kira*), which has the sense of tradition, he indicates any difference of opinion regarding some of the royal lineages being described.
For by the mere statement of what has been heard, the diversity of opinions among those such as the inhabitants of Uttara-vihāra—who have not themselves heard it—is refuted.

"Of Mahāsammatassa" means of him who was thus appointed (sammatassa) by the great multitude having agreed, saying "This is our king," in accordance with the method that will be explained in the Aggañña Sutta; concerning whom they say:
“Born of the Solar Clan, a mine of perfectly pure virtues,
you are a king of great majesty named Mahāsammata.
You are the eye of the world, radiant with the rays of your qualities.”
Dispelling the darkness, he shone forth like a second sun.
By him, who seeks the welfare of the world, the boundaries established in the world are fixed such that people are unable to transgress them.
“They speak of him as ‘Manu,’ the illustrious and majestic one,
the protector of the world’s boundaries, the primordial Great Hero.
And with reference to the succession of his sons and grandsons, they speak thus:
His son was Mahāteja, a lord of the earth named Roja;
his son was Vararoja, preeminent within the circle of kings.
His biological son was Kalyāṇa, possessed of auspicious virtues.
The king had a son named Varakalyāṇa.
His son was the great hero Mandhātā, the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures,
who was honored by Mahinda with half the kingdom.
His son was Mahāteja, named Varamandhātu;
his son was the highly renowned one known by the name Uposatha.
His son was Mahāteja, named Vara; his son was Mahāvara.
To her was born Upavara, a king of great power.
His son was Makhādeva, a lord of the earth equal to a god;
his lineage of sons numbered eighty-four thousand.
“The last of those kings, renowned as Okkāka, was of great fame and great majesty, no mean figure within the circle of kings.
This is the statement that does not contradict the Aṭṭhakathā. However, that which is stated in the Dīpavaṃsa—
“The first consecrated king, a protector of the earth who possessed splendor,
was a Khattiya named Mahāsammata who ruled the kingdom.
His son was named Roja, and the Khattiya Vararoja was his [son].”
Kalyāṇa, Varakalyāṇa, Uposatha, Mahissara,
Mandhātā as the seventh among them, the lord of the four continents;
Varo, Upavaro, Rājā, Cetiya, and Mahissara— so forth.
And as it is stated in the *Mahāvaṃsa* and other texts:
"The Great Sage, born of the lineage of King Mahāsammata,
was a king named Mahāsammata in the first aeon."
"Roja and Vararoja, likewise the two Kalyāṇakas;
Uposatha and Mandhātā, Varaka and the two Pavaras," and so forth.
