All of this is, for the most part, a statement that contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathā*. For in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, King Mandhātā is the sixth.
The eleventh was King Maghadeva; the last of the eighty-four thousand kings in his lineage of sons was King Okkāka.
Among those [kings], King Mandhātu is said to be the seventh;
King Maghadeva was the last of many thousands of kings, and the last of many thousands of kings in his own lineage of sons.
By means of such expressions as "King Okkāka," the *Aṭṭhakathā* refutes the various contradictory statements. Did we not say:
"And here, by the word ‘it is said’ (*kira*), which has the sense of tradition, one indicates that there was a divergence of opinion among some regarding the royal lineage being described"?
"After them" refers to those who followed in the lineage of Makhādeva, ending with Kaḷārajanaka.
"Subsequent to eighty-four thousand kṣatriyas"—this was stated by the Teacher according to what he had heard.
However, in the *Dīpavaṃsa* and other chronicles, it is stated: "The last king in the line of descendants from King Kaḷārajanaka was named Sujāta;
his son was King Okkāka. [This refers to] many thousands of kings in the lineage of Maghadeva.
In a later period there was a king named Okkāka the First; after many thousands of kings descended from him in succession, there was a king named Okkāka the Second;

and after many thousands of kings descended from him in succession as well, there was a king named Okkāka the Third. It is with reference to this that it is said: "There were three Okkāka lineages," and so forth.
It is said that on the fifth day after birth, it is the worldly custom to perform auspicious rites such as the naming ceremony; thus it is stated, "having adorned [him] on the fifth day.

"He gave a boon hastily" means that, overcome by intense joy at seeing his son, he gave a boon impulsively and without reflection, saying out of a desire to grant satisfaction, "Take whatever you wish. "She" refers to the mother of Prince Jantu. "To transfer the kingdom" [means...].
"He desires" means he wishes to divert this kingdom to me by interposing my granting of the boon.

"They will exercise sovereignty" means they will cause the great multitude, or the populace, to establish him in the state of kingship. "He would not prevail" means it would not be sufficient for his dwelling.
Because of his dark-brown complexion, the brahmin was named Kapila. "Having gone forth" means having departed from the household life and from sensual pleasures.

*Sāka* is the name for a particular type of tree made entirely of heartwood, by which palaces and such are constructed; the meaning is "in a grove consisting of a collection of those [trees]. *Bhummajāla*:

that which moves upon the earth is *bhummam*; it "kindles" (*jāleti*) or illuminates (*joteti*) its virtues and faults, or else it is called *bhummajāla* because by means of it the earth "blazes" (*jalati*), shines (*jotati*), or becomes manifest (*pākaṭa*).
Regarding the phrase "and below," the word "and" (*ca*) here includes the term "at eighty cubits."
This he brings forward. "In this place" refers to the grove of plantain trees. By way of the rows of trunks, it was curved to the south; by way of the rows of branches, it faced the east.
"By them" means by the deer and pigs, and by the frogs and mice. "They" refers to the lions, tigers, and so forth, as well as the snakes and cats.
"Therein" means in the city being thus laid out. Even a single man included among your men who has become an adversary—

The construction is: "He will not be able to overcome even another hundred men or a thousand men. By the power of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) means by way of possessing the strength of a wheel-turning monarch.

"Exceedingly superior" (*atiseyyo*) means he would become pre-eminently excellent. It is called "Kapilavatthu" because it is the dwelling place of the seer Kapila. "It would be near them" is the connection [of the sentence].
"In the union with the peerless" refers to the cause for the practice of household life with those who are peerless in birth. "With the remaining [daughters] each of their own younger sisters."
"Vaḍḍhamānānaṃ" (of those growing) is a term of address used in disregard;

the meaning is that [the thought] arose even while they were growing, despite the growth of their sons and daughters which was free from obstacles. Because of its redness, it resembles *koviḷāra* flowers.
Regarding "leprosy" (*kuṭṭharoga*), it is said that "this disease spreads," because, like the diseases of *sāsa* and *masūrī*, it is for the most part of a contagious nature. Above, with the foot...
"Having covered it" means having made it into a heap of earth. "Dancing women" (*nāṭakitthiyo*) refers to those who dance.

"Royal wives" refers to the women of the harem (*orodhā*). "Of that" refers to the hollow. "Of deer, birds, and so forth"—here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes forest-dwellers, *petas*, and others.

"While he was sitting in that delightful forest"—this is the grammatical connection. "On a slab" (*padare*) means on a wooden plank. "By declaring his Kṣatriya lineage" means making known his status as a member of the warrior caste.
*Mātikaṃ* means "derived from the mother. *Pābhataṃ* means "capital stock" or "a gift.
*Rañño* refers to the King of Bārāṇasī, who was the eldest son of King Rāma. *Tattha* means "in Bārāṇasī. *Idheva* means "right here in the Himalayan region.
*Nagaraṃ* refers to the great city that served as the royal capital. *Kolarukkho* is the name of a particular tree species used as a remedy for leprosy (*kuṭṭha*).
*Byagghapatha* means on a tiger’s path.
*Mātula* means maternal uncles (a mother’s brothers). *Kesaggahaṇa* means the binding of hair with a hair-tie. *Dussaggahaṇa* refers to the manner of wearing a cloth as a lower garment.
*Nhānatittha* refers to the bathing place in the water of the aforementioned lotus pond. Even now...
Showing the absence of any distinction in their birth, he said, "Thus for them," and so forth.

*Āvāha* is the taking of a girl; *vivāha* is the giving of a girl. "Therein" means among those Sakyas and Koliyas. Because words denoting elements (dhātu) have multiple meanings, the prefix *sam-* has the sense of "dwelling";
thus it is said, "they dwell. In the word *agge*, the locative case is used in the sense of the accusative, and the word *agga* also carries the sense of "beginning"; it refers to a specific action.
And he shows this by saying, "That was the beginning," and so forth. As for what was said here by the Blessed One:
"Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka uttered this inspired utterance: 'Truly, these princes are Sakyans; truly, these princes are supreme Sakyans.
From that time on, Ambaṭṭha, the Sakyans became known"—this is an illustration of the natural etymology both in terms of the word and its meaning.
“Because they are able and capable of protecting their family lineage without breaking the purity of birth even through cohabitation with their own sisters, they are called Sakyas”;
it is by this very distinction in linguistic formation that they are [also known as] Sākiyas.
As for that which is stated in the *Sakkata-nighaṇṭu* lexicon:
“Because they formerly made their dwelling concealed by a grove of sugarcanes (sāka), therefore, when seen among the bamboo-clans (vaṃsajāta), they became renowned on earth as ‘Sakyas.
This is merely a verbal derivation showing an unconvincing etymology: “They are Sakyas (or Sākiyas) because they dwell in a sugarcane grove at the residence of the sage Kapila.”
Because of his black color, he was called "Kaṇha" (the Black One); thus it is said, "black-colored," and so forth. "Beard" refers to hair grown on the jaw;
"mustache" refers to hair grown on both sides of the upper lip in the shape of fangs. This is stated according to the literal meaning;

however, by way of a derivative suffix (*taddhita*), just as the common designation for a *yakkha* today is "pisāca," so too was he called "Kaṇha" at that time. Therefore, [the name] was applied even at the very moment of his birth.
He is called Kaṇha because of his resemblance to a *pisāca* (ogre) due to his speech. For it is said:
"Just as, Ambaṭṭha, people nowadays perceive *pisācas* when they see them and recognize them as 'pisācas,' even so, Ambaṭṭha, at that time people perceived *pisācas* as 'Kaṇhas,'" and so forth.
In this context, "born as a *pisāca*" refers to what is now commonly known by that name.

A synonym for the first word was stated for the sake of easy understanding. In expressions such as “I shall not speak with a mouthful in my mouth,” the root *har* has the sense of making a sound through the force of a prefix;
when joined again with a second prefix, it functions in the sense of making a loud sound—thus it is said, “he made a loud noise.”

268. "For the sake of releasing oneself from reproach" means for the purpose of removing the slander that must be leveled against each of them by the Teacher and by Ambaṭṭha respectively. The word "oneself" (*attano*) here is an elided distributive expression.
"He will cause a breach" means he will effect a division by proclaiming his lack of goodwill; what is meant is that he will instigate slander.

Alternatively, according to the method of *nirukti*, speech itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*) because it is the means for making something known; thus, one who possesses beautiful speech as an instrument is "one of beautiful speech" (*kalyāṇavākkaraṇo*).

Regarding the phrase "in this statement," although it is true that by the word "this" (*tasaddena*) the theory of caste previously stated by Ambaṭṭha—"There are these four castes, O Gotama"—is being referred to, nevertheless, even this theory of caste is [to be understood] precisely according to the procedure stated in the Veda.

He should be questioned by him; therefore, in order to show that it is precisely the statement of the three Vedas—which is well-known as the cause for such questioning—that must be referred to, it was said:

"in the statement of the three Vedas learned by oneself. Now, showing that the words spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with "But, Ambaṭṭha, your ancient maternal and paternal lineage... are also to be referred to, he says: "Or in this..."
He said, "In the words 'the son of a slave woman. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "to reply" (*paṭimantetuṃ*): here, "replying" (*paṭimantanā*) means answering a question or further discourse;
therefore, it should be understood that he shows the reference by the word *ta-* to its respective object in accordance with these two meanings. 269. *Tāva*:
"At the very beginning of the deliberation," meaning even before the deliberation has been carried out. "Difficult to know" (*dujjāna*).

The intention was: "Let Ambaṭṭha release it himself, since it is difficult to discern [the truth], because he is unable to lift his head even at the very outset, because birth is difficult to discern, and because the matter is hard to establish.

By referring to the fact that he himself had brought this upon himself through the accusation of being an outcaste among the Sakyans, it is said, "a bundle tied by oneself"; the meaning is, "a knot tied by oneself."

270. "Dhamma" means a cause, as in such expressions as "analytical knowledge of the dhamma" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*). That which exists together with the dhamma is "sahadhamma"; that very thing is called "sahadhammika.
Thus he said, "it has a cause" (*sahetuka*), and so forth; this is a figurative expression.

Alternatively, the producer is the "cause" (*hetu*), while the supporter is the "condition" (*kāraṇa*). It is another statement regarding what is not the case, expressed by means of something else that is not the case.
Therefore he said, "He who," and so forth.
"From that" means after the second admonition; it is implied that he will depart even before the third admonition has arrived.
271. Because he is worthy of worship, Sakka, the king of the gods, is called a *yakkha*. He is endowed with the natural form of fire.
It is said: “‘Blazing’ means having the color of fire. *Kandala* is a specific type of flowering tree that bears white blossoms;
even its buds are white in color and shaped like fangs. “Of various forms” means having a distorted shape.
During the eighth week, while sitting at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, all Buddhas customarily maintain a state of ease and lack of concern.
Having intended this, he said, "I myself," and so forth. "While not turning" means while not practicing or while not following along.

"Therefore" means because of having made such a promise at that time. He came with the thought, "I will cause him to answer the question by intimidating him," just as in the case of the encounter with the wanderer Saccaka who appeared in the Mūlapaññāsa.
Regarding the phrase, “The Blessed One and Ambaṭṭha both see,” he says “If indeed,” etc., showing two reasons for not seeing others.
The word *hi* is a particle used in the sense of a reason. The connection is: “Because it is not difficult, and because they would speak [of it], therefore.
It is common to others as well that it is not difficult (*agaru*), meaning not burdensome. “Having summoned” (*āvāhetvā*) means summoning by the power of mantras.
"Having done so. "His" refers to Ambaṭṭha. "Inside the belly" means within the intestines, the small intestine, the large intestine, and so forth.

"In the collision of debate" means in the clashing of speech. "Thinking" (*maññamāno*) means because of conceiving; for this is a demonstration of the connection [between the preceding and following]. 272.
"Seeking refuge" means thinking, "This very ascetic Gotama alone is my protector from this danger," and thus [seeking] the Blessed One himself.
“Seeking protection (*tāṇa*): this means he approaches it. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.
“It protects (*tāyati*): it guards one from the fear that has arisen. Therefore he said, “it protects (*rakkhati*); this is an analysis based on the agent (*kattusādhana*). “He hides (*nilīyati*):
being afflicted by the very fear that has arisen, he becomes hidden; this is an analysis based on the locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*). The root *sar* means to injure, and that is precisely destruction.
“Intended” means it is said that “fear harms and destroys”; this is an instrumental derivation based on the agent (*kattusādhana*).
Commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Lineage Account 274.
“To the south of the Ganges” means in the southern direction of the river named Ganges. “Brahmin ascetics” (*brāhmaṇatāpasa*)...
The ascetics are of the Brahmin lineage. When one desires to hurl a spear or other weapons at another, through the power of the mantra, the hand does not move;
and since the hand does not move, how could the weapon move?
It is with reference to this non-moving that it is said, "the weapon does not turn. "Bhadraṃ bhoto" is an expression of acceptance.

The meaning is "it is well. By way of the method of explaining the constituent parts (*sasambhārakathānaya*), it is called "the unapproachable bow" because of the arrow shot from the bow, just as one says "he pierces with a bow" or "he sees with the eye. There are indeed beings called *ambaṭṭha*;

they are so named by way of etymology (*niruttinaya*) because they place an ointment (*abbhaṅga*) upon the bodies of living beings; such is the name of that branch of knowledge consisting of spells (*mantavijjā*).

The meaning is as follows: Since the seer Kaṇha was known as “Ambaṭṭha” because he possessed this knowledge (*vidyā*) in this [lineage], this young brahmin is also designated as “Ambaṭṭha” due to his being born into that same clan.
It is said that, loathing that lowly birth, thinking, “How indeed have I been reborn from the womb of a slave-girl of the border regions? he resolved, “Well then, by whatever means...”
“I shall purify this birth,” he thought, and so he went forth. Therefore it was said: “Now I shall fulfill my heart’s desire.

For this was his desire: from the moment he had obtained the king’s daughter after intimidating the king with the power of his magic knowledge (*vijjā*), he thought, “This birth of mine as a slave will have been purified.”
"Seṭṭhamante" means the most excellent Vedic mantras. The meaning is: "Who indeed, for what reason, being the son of a slave-girl, asks for a daughter as beautiful as Maddarūpī?
It cuts or shaves, or it drinks from a razor; thus it is a "khurappa" (razor-headed arrow).
Or, because the razor is fixed or placed at its tip, it is a "khurappa," namely an arrow. By the power of the mantra, [it caused] the king’s arm to tremble.
When that [sign] had arisen, the king—due to his paralysis of the arms—became fearful, suspicious, and terrified, thinking, "Who knows?
What will happen? And so it is said: "He stood trembling with fear.
Regarding the account of King Daṇḍaki and others mentioned in the *Sarabhaṅga Jātaka*, King Okkāka came after them; such was their history.
And because these [powers] were manifest everywhere for a long time, he said, "Of King Daṇḍaki," and so forth.
The connection is: "When King Daṇḍaki had offended, Nāḷikera and Ajjuna also offended. Even though there was rain of sand and other things, destruction occurred specifically by the rain of weapons;
thus it is said, "by the rain of weapons. Thinking, "This one also possesses such great power," they reflected in this way.
It should be understood that they spoke out of fear.
"Undriyissati" means it will be split. This "earth" is a product of karma (*kammarūpa*); it is spoken of in terms of the object and the agent, just as one says, "the grain is broken.
Therefore he said, "it will break. "A handful of husks" means a handful of straw or a handful of chaff.
Or [why is this said]? He says: “Merely due to the stiffening of the body,” and so forth.
Those who are frightened and terrified have their bodies trembling due to fear and their hair standing on end;
however, those who are not frightened or terrified, because of the absence of fear and calamity, have bodies that do not tremble and their hair does not stand on end, being secure.
They stand in safety; however, because the hair on his body has fallen away, his state of safety becomes manifest.
Thus, in order to clarify the cause by means of the result, it is shown in the Pāḷi that the term “palloma” is used, as expressed in the passage beginning with “pannalomo.

According to the method of etymological derivation (*nirutti*), the formation of the word is as found in the *Bhayabherava Sutta*: “I attained even greater confidence (*palloma*) for dwelling in the forest.”
“This is the concluding statement. The making of the promise—“If the king shows that girl to me, the prince will become safe and at ease”—is evident from the context itself.
“By him” means by Kaṇha. “In the charm” (manteti) refers to the charm known as the science for quelling the paralysis of the arms.
For such charms that cause fear and calamity are, in every respect, [to be avoided].
They are pacifying mantras, such as those of the *kusumāra* charm and others. "Parivattita" means uttered or recited.
For the sake of clearing the reproach against his own daughter, he made that slave-girl a free woman (*bhujissā*).
And for the sake of establishing her in a suitable position of authority, he placed her in a high station. "By one faction" means by the mother’s faction. Feeling compassion...
He spoke for the purpose of providing consolation, and not for the purpose of displaying his high birth. Therefore he said, “Then the Blessed One,” and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the state of being the most excellent among the kṣatriyas: 275.
“Among the brahmins” is a mere conventional expression; it refers to the seats and other things to be received from brahmins in their presence.
"May he obtain" is what is meant. Therefore it was said, "among the brahmins.

Regarding the term *saddha* (alms for the faithful), in order to show its derivation—that one should perform [the offering] solely through faith toward those who have gone to the other world, and not by aspiring for anything else—it was stated, "alms prepared specifically for the deceased. As for the phrase "at meals such as auspicious occasions," etc.:

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes meals for festivals, offerings to propitiate deities, and so forth. "Sacrificial meal" (*yaññabhatta*) refers to a meal prepared with the perception of it being sinful and so on;
for here, the fire sacrifice (*aggihoma*) is what is meant by "sacrifice," as in the phrase, "One will eat a meal with the perception of sin," etc.
"Of guests" (*pāhunakānaṃ*) means of visitors. Even for those who are not arriving [at that moment], a meal sent as a gift is called "guest-food" (*pāhuṇa*); thus he says, "in a meal that is a gift."
“Or” means: *āvaṭaṃ* is an obstruction; *anāvaṭaṃ* is non-obstruction. One who has not attained the status of a khattiya because of not possessing the state of being well-born on both sides.
Therefore he said, “impure. 276.
Regarding the phrase “or having made a woman [into] a woman”: here, “making” (*karaṇa*) refers to the general domain of action for the verbal roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *dhā*.
Because [the woman] is included within all elements (dhātu) by way of her function, he said, "having sought out.

Having sought out and taken a Brahmin girl as a wife for a Kṣatriya prince, one should apply the connection by citing the scriptural passage: "Between a Brahmin woman and a Kṣatriya woman, the Kṣatriya woman is superior;
the Brahmins are inferior. Regarding the phrase "or having made a man the agent," here too—

"The same method applies," said the teacher. For there too, having sought out and taken a man who was the counterpart of a khattiya maiden—whether by a brahmin man or otherwise—the construction is: "The khattiyas are the best; the brahmins are inferior.
Regarding the phrase "in some particular context" (*kismiñcideva pakaraṇe*), here "context" (*pakaraṇa*) means a cause (*kāraṇa*): "In this source, in this..."
As in the passage beginning with “in the treatise,” the meaning is: it is the cause in a situation that has gone astray through passion and so forth.
In substance, however, this is simply a transgression, and since that consists in doing what should not be done, he says, “in some fault,” and so on.
The word *bhasma* is a synonym for ashes. For it is called *bhasma* because it is scattered—that is, thrown away—due to its uselessness; it refers to ash. “Having struck down” (vadhitvā).
The explanation of its meaning is “having scattered. 277.

That which is to be produced by karmic defilements (*kamma-kilesa*), or that which is born from them, is “produced” (*janita*); it is itself the producer, namely the human being. For thus it has been said:
“those who rely on their clan. This term, like the word for offspring (*pajā*), refers to a plurality by way of the word for birth (*jāti*).
He says it is in the singular, adding: "The meaning is 'progeny' (pajā). In this context, the word *janeti* ("begets") is also appropriate.
"They recollect" (*paṭisaranti*) means that, depending on their clan (*gotta*), they take refuge and investigate [their identity], thinking, "I am a Gotama," "I am a Kassapa," and so forth.
The commentary on the first section of the recitation is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge and Conduct (Vijjācaraṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 278. Now, when this verse is recited, those who revere Brahmā will attain confidence;
and Ambaṭṭha, upon hearing the phrase "endowed with knowledge and conduct," will inquire about knowledge and conduct. Thus, this [verse] is an exposition of knowledge and conduct.
Seeing that the teaching would be beneficial for the great multitude, the Lord of the World recited this verse spoken by Sanankumāra;
explaining this point as well, he said, "But by means of this verse," and so forth.

For otherwise, even the Blessed One would be one who is not omniscient and would be dependent on others, and it is not fitting for the Blessed One to be dependent on others because of his state as a Perfectly Enlightened One.
Therefore he said, “I too, Ambaṭṭha, speak thus,” and so forth. “Established in the Brahminical tradition” means well-known through the tenets of the Brahmins.
It is connected with the doctrine of birth and so on, according to the method that will be explained. “Having reconciled” means having joined together;
the meaning is “having made it non-contradictory,” as stated by the Teacher. However, the reading “having rejected” is now seen in the manuscripts.
That is indeed inappropriate. Why? Because it is not that he rejects the *vijjācaraṇa* (knowledge and conduct) established in the Brahminical systems;
rather, having combined that very *vijjācaraṇa* conceived by Ambaṭṭha and rendered it non-contradictory, he teaches the unsurpassed *vijjācaraṇa*.
"Discourse" (*vāda*) means a tenet (*laddhi*), or a verbal expression. Therefore he said: "The words beginning with ‘Brahmin...’. For a tenet is also to be spoken of.

It is precisely the statement itself. The word "this" (*idam*) includes—by means of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*)—the meaning that such actions as reciting, causing others to recite, sacrificing, and officiating at sacrifices belong neither to a Vaiśya, nor to a Kṣatriya, nor to anyone else.

"In all cases" refers to both the mention of lineage (*gotta*) and the mention of pride (*māna*). For even there, the "mention of lineage" is a discussion concerning lineage, such as the statement: "This is appropriate for one of the Kassapa clan, but not for one of the Kosika clan," and so forth.
"Meaning. "The talk of conceit" (*mānavāda*) means talk based on conceit in the form of self-exaltation and disparagement of others;
the meaning is such statements as, "This is suitable only for a brahmin, not for a *sudda*," and so forth. "Bound to the talk of birth" means bound to talk dependent upon birth.
"In all cases" refers to those bound to the talk of lineage (*gotta*), and so on. For "bound to the talk of lineage" refers to talk concerning lineage.

"Bound up. "Bound up by conceit and talk" means bound up by conceit and talk; for those things which proceed by way of self-exaltation and disparagement of others, such as the Brahmin’s own study, teaching, sacrificing, and officiating at sacrifices, these are "bound up by conceit and talk. "Bound up by marriage alliances" means bound up in marriages;
for those who, by way of being bound up [in these three ways], say: "You ought to [marry] me, or you ought not..."
"Are you worthy of me?"—those who speak thus are bound by marriage alliances; it is with reference to this remaining point that "this is the method" was stated.
For, in order to clarify the state of being bound by marriage alliances, the text says: "Are you worthy of me, or are you not worthy of me?
This [statement] is [included] among the three, beginning with the doctrine of birth.
The words should be construed accordingly. For, by way of repetition (*āvutti*) and other such methods, the terms "one who speaks of birth" (*jātivāda*) and so forth indicate the meaning twice.

Thus it was said by the Master: "But those who are bound by marriage ties, it is they who, on account of their threefold relationship, engage in such talk as: 'You are worthy of me, or you are not worthy of me.'"
One might object: "Was not *vijjācaraṇa* (knowledge and conduct) already asked about previously? Why does he ask it again? To clear this objection, he says, "Then Ambaṭṭha... and so forth.
In that context, "wherein" (*yattha*) refers to that perfection of knowledge and conduct.

This is said with reference to what is established in the Brahminical tradition. "We shall cling" (*laggissāma*) means we shall become attached or included within it. "From that" (*tato*) means from that perfection of knowledge and conduct.

“*Avakkhipī*” means he spoke. For one who stands having grasped ignorance and misconduct as “knowledge and conduct” from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), is indeed said to have been removed far away when knowledge and conduct are being analyzed according to their ultimate meaning.

“*Yattha*” refers to that perfection of knowledge and conduct; this is stated with reference to unsurpassed knowledge and conduct (*anuttara-vijjācaraṇa*). [This occurs] in connection with the activity of knowing.
Action (*kamma*) also arises only from an agent when it is connected with a suitable performance. For it is said that "agents" are so called in relation to a primary action:
"It is fitting for this perfection of our knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampadā*) to be known. Such is the case in instances like these. "From its origin" means from its initial arising. 279.
Granted that it is appropriate to categorize it as "conduct" (*caraṇa*) because it is included within the category of conduct; however, for Ambaṭṭha...

In order to clarify the point that one leads [beings] to liberation by means of virtue alone while preventing them from traveling on the uneven path, it is said: "even that which is included within conduct.
According to the method explained in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*, virtue is threefold, consisting of the minor and other divisions. "By means of virtue alone" means by way of the various modes of virtue.
"Some small portion of virtue" refers to the minor rules characterized as prohibitions and observances—such as non-violence—which are established by birth among the brahmins.
"Virtue. Therefore, because it exists in that way, the intention is: "One might cling even by relying on mere virtue existing within oneself.
Regarding this, the Teacher (Ācariya) stated: "'One might cling right there and then' means one might cling to 'conduct' in mere virtue established in each respective Brahmanical system.
This is precisely what was said in the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as a statement with its specific form.
Because it has been so stated, this must be investigated; or rather, this is merely a demonstration of the underlying intention (*adhippāya*). Here, however, is the meaning:

"It should stick to each respective [instance]" means that in each respective place connected to the mere virtue existing within oneself, one should stick to the thought, "We too are endowed with good conduct.
Therefore, the connection is that [the Buddha] leads [beings] out by way of virtue alone, because there is no possibility of such an attachment occurring otherwise.
However, showing that [the path] leads out by means of the higher stages alone, he says, "But as for what... and so forth.

Since the form-sphere (rūpāvacara) fourth jhāna exposition itself results in the exposition of the formless-sphere (arūpāvacara) jhānas as well, it is stated: "The eight attainments are also presented as 'stages' (caraṇa).
For those too, by virtue of the equality of their factors, are indeed fourth jhānas. And "presented" (niyyātitā) means having extracted them without remainder.
"Seized" means "demonstrated. "But from insight-knowledge" means starting from insight-knowledge according to the method beginning:

"When his mind is thus concentrated, pure, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge and vision [of the passing away and reappearance of beings]."
Commentary on the Discourse on the Four Gateways to the Lower Realms (Catupāyamukhakathāvaṇṇanā): 280. "Failing to reach [the goal]" means being unable to accomplish it even after having begun.
"Unable to endure" means being unable to even begin it. "A khārī" is a designation for the requisites of an ascetic; and since that consists of many varieties, [the text] analyzes it as follows:
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “araṇī” was spoken. Therein, “araṇī” refers to the pair of fire-drills consisting of an upper and a lower block used for kindling fire by friction.

“Kamaṇḍalu” means a water-pot (kuṇḍikā). “Sujā” means a sacrificial ladle (homadabbī). Indeed, the word *sujā* is used for the ladle made of wood for the purpose of lifting up the sacrificial food and other offerings during a ritual;
as it is said in the *Kūṭadanta Sutta*: “Whether the first or the second [priest] is holding the *sujā*.”

For in this very place, the Teacher has stated: “*Sujāti* means a ladle (*dabbī*). It is called *sujā* because it is produced for the purpose of easily holding the sacrificial offerings, rice, and so forth.
However, some, without considering this meaning and taking only the sense of “sewing,” read it as *sūcī* (needle);
that is indeed incorrect, because the Teacher did not explain it in that way. A *camara* is one who gives skin; it is a particular kind of deer. Of that...
A *bījanī* (winnowing fan) and a *cāmara* (fly-whisk) are made from hair. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes items such as triple-staffs and water-clocks.
It is called a *kāja* because it is produced in a base or crooked form, as in the term "black salt" (*kālavaṇa*);
or alternatively, it is a *kāca* because a burden is bound there. Grammarians accept both forms of the word. "Filled with a *khārī*" means completely full of *khārīs*.

Having expanded the word by means of the prefix *vi-*, he says "But those who... and so forth, demonstrating the meaning according to a collective compound (*samuccaya-samāsa*) in the opinion of those who recite it as "khāri-vividhaṃ.
Is it not the case that for an ordained monk, anyone who is unordained—even if they belong to the Dispensation—is in fact merely an attendant?

To show the distinction in that regard when considering the question, "Is there even a novice monk whose taints are exhausted, let alone one who has gone forth among outsiders," the passage beginning with "Granted" (*kāmañca*) was stated.

"In the manner already described" (*vuttanayena*) means by the method thus described: "by way of [observing] what is allowable... and by way of performing the duties. This refers to the state of being fully ordained (*upasampanna*) by virtue of undertaking the discipline (*vinaya*) of many hundreds of thousands of restraints (*saṃvara*).
Because of his superior state, even a novice monk whose taints are destroyed is called an attendant to an ordinary bhikkhu.
"Nine thousand million, eight hundred million,
fifty thousand, and another thirty-six [thousand]."
"These restraints and disciplines were proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One;
they are pointed out by way of enumeration within the training in the restraint of the Vinaya.

Thus, "ordination" (*upasampadā*) is the excellence that stands above and is supreme through the undertaking and training in the hundreds of thousands of various kinds of restraints and disciplines mentioned in this way. And by means of that ordination, he is called an "ordained ordinary monk" (*puthujjana-bhikkhu*).
"But this" refers to the ascetic (tāpasa) possessing the characteristics already described. For ascetics are proponents of karma and proponents of action;

they are not obstacles to the Dispensation (sāsana), which is why the ordination (pabbajjā) was permitted in the Khandhaka for those who came to go forth among them, even without the probationary period required for other sectarians (titthiya-parivāsa).
They are called "ascetics" (tāpasā) because they possess austerity (tapas); the short *ta*-sound is lengthened, as in the case of words such as "lomasā."

For those learned in the language require the prefix *sa-* [in this context]. This is what is meant: Granted that even a novice whose taints are destroyed is in fact an attendant to an ordinary monk, he is an attendant merely by virtue of performing his duties, not because of inferiority.
The ascetic, however, is [an attendant] both by virtue of his qualities and by virtue of performing services, yet precisely because of his inferiority.
He is not a servant merely by performing services; thus, with reference to this distinction between them, it is said that he is a servant only to the ascetic.
With the words “For what reason,” etc., the challenger puts forward the objection. With the words “Because,” etc., the teacher provides the answer by showing the reason.
To explain the meaning already answered in brief, the passage beginning with “For in this case,” etc., was stated. [The word] “unable” means...
One who practices wrongly due to incapacity is shameless (*alajji*). "Like walking on the edge of a razor's blade" means walking by treading directly upon the very edge of razor blades.
"Honored by the many" means esteemed as the best by the great multitude. "Others" refers to other monks.
"In this world" refers to the life of a forest-dwelling ascetic. "Walking according to their own will" means those who act with personal desire, practicing according to their own whims.
This has been stated. "Training after" means training by following the example of others. There were many ascetics (*tāpasa*), but not many monks (*bhikkhu*).

The etymological explanation of *kudāla* (hoe) and *piṭaka* (basket) has already been given above. "For the purpose of deceiving many people" means for the purpose of causing wonder among many people.
"Fire-hall" means a hall for the fire-sacrifice (*aggihutta*). "With various kinds of wood" means with various types of fuel-wood such as the staffs of the *palāsa* tree and so forth.
"By way of performing a sacrifice" means by way of performing a *yañña* (offering).
Here, "by way of water" refers to a drinking-house (*pānāgāra*). Therefore he said, "having set out drinking water," and so forth.

The connection is: "either the bowl of rice or the rice and other grains. "Sour gruel" (*ambilayāgu*) means gruel mixed with sour substances such as buttermilk (*takkā*) and so on. By craving (*taṇhā*) and the rest...
"Material things" (*āmisa*) refers to robes and so forth because they are objects to be touched or handled. "For the sake of increase" means for the sake of doubling, tripling, and so on.
"He establishes a household" means he establishes wealth. He says, "But this is the entrance to his practice," because the aforementioned matter was stated in the Canon merely by way of illustration;
furthermore, this canonical statement refers to the practice of hypocrisy (*kohañña*) of this fourth type of person.
The meaning is "merely by way of appearance. Why is that? For he remains there, deceiving the world with various kinds of hypocrisy.
Therefore he said, "By this," and so forth. "In this way" means according to the method described in the passage beginning, "Having set out drinking water there," and so on.
"All the ascetic renunciations have been demonstrated" refers to what was shown by way of the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna-naya), even though it was presented by way of the Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna-naya).

To explain this, the passage beginning with “eightfold” was stated. “Gleaning” (*uñchā*) refers to gathering rice, mung beans, māsa beans, sesame seeds, and so forth, by standing near threshing floors and other such places in the vicinity of people, according to the practice of alms-gathering;

those whose way of life (*vutti*) consists of that very practice are called “those who live by gleaning” (*uñchācariyā*). Those who subsist on food obtained as alms that has been cooked over fire are called “fire-cookers” (*aggipakkikā*).
"Not cooked by fire" means not cooked with fire; it is said that their livelihood consists solely of alms of rice.

For those who practice the "gleaning way of life" (uñchācariyā) go to threshing floors and other such places and receive what is called "threshing-floor grain"—the grain given by people as they stand there—whereas those who do not cook with fire do not accept such things but accept only rice; this is the distinction between them.

"Those who do not cook for themselves" are *asāmapākā*; they subsist solely on cooked alms-food (*pakkabhikkhā*). An iron-like stone, as hard as iron and the size of a fist, is called an *ayomuṭṭhi* (iron-fist);
those who live by means of it are *ayamuṭṭhikā*. Bark stripped from a tree with the teeth is *dantavakkala*;
those who live by means of it are *dantavakkalikā*. "Falling fruit" is fruit that has been shaken down from a tree or similar source.
“They eat by means of virtue” means they subsist on fallen fruit. The term *paṇḍupalāsa* has a twofold meaning according to the method of single-remainder (*ekasesanaya*):
first, the leaf that has become pale due to decay; and second, flowers, fruits, and so forth, which resemble it because of their state of being withered and ripe.
Therefore, he will say: “They sustain themselves eating only those flowers, fruits, and withered leaves that have fallen of their own accord.”
They are called *paṇḍupalāsika* because they subsist on them; they are those who feed on leaves, flowers, and fruits that have fallen of their own accord.

Now, in order to show these eight types according to their specific characteristics, the passage beginning with “therein” (*tattha*) was spoken. The story of Keṇiya the matted-hair ascetic is to be found in the commentary on the Khandhaka.
“Having gathered together” means having brought them into one place by way of going for alms.

"Rice alms" (*taṇḍulabhikkhā*) means rice itself as alms. It is called "alms" (*bhikkhā*) because it is to be begged for or requested, or because it comes to the monks; thus the word *bhikkhā* is established in usage even for rice and other such things. Therefore it is said: "having cooked it, they consume it.
"The search for alms is suffering" means that the seeking of alms by going from one person's house to another is suffering due to its nature as a miserable way of life.

However, those who say, "For a renunciant, the handling of stones is painful," and thus eat [the fruit] after tearing it apart with their teeth alone, are called *dantavakkalikā* (those who eat with the teeth);

this is the method not found in the Aṭṭhakathā. By the phrase "flowers, fruits, and withered leaves (*paṇḍupalāsa*) and so forth," he shows that the term *paṇḍupalāsa* refers to flowers and fruits as well, by way of their similarity.

"They" refers to the *paṇḍupalāsikā*. This is merely an illustration, since a similar division occurs for others as well. "In the place of reaching" means in the place where one is able to reach out and grasp them. "From a single tree" means from the tree first approached.
To the objection, "How is it that by this much all the ascetic renunciations have been demonstrated?"—since that has not yet been fully cleared up—it says, "But these," and so forth.
"By only four" means by only the four types of ascetic renunciations mentioned in the passage beginning with "taking a load of firewood," namely:
those who subsist on fallen fruit, those who subsist on roots and fruits, those who maintain a sacred fire, and those who live as householders. *Agāram*...
“They resort to” means they approach the household as their place of residence.
By this, he shows that those [ascetics] are included within the fourth type of ascetic renunciation mentioned here, namely: “having made a four-doored house, he dwells therein,” and so forth.
In the same way, the application should be understood in reverse order for the others as well. They resort to the fire-chamber by means of tending the sacred fire.
However, it should be understood that by stating their non-inclusion in this way, the Teacher shows that these [other factors] also each possess a twofold nature accordingly.
281. "Accompanied by the teacher Pokkharasāti" means *sācariyako*; it refers to him. "Even a door to ruin" (*apāyamukham*) means even a cause of destruction.
"All the more so regarding the perfection of knowledge and conduct" (*pageva vijjācaraṇasampadāya*); the particle *pi* here expresses censure. By that...

It was said: “Now, do you, together with your teacher, manifest this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct (vijjācaraṇasampadā),” and so forth. Regarding that, here is the method not found in the commentaries:
after rejecting the manifestation by saying, “Certainly not, Master Gotama,” the passage beginning with “And who am I?
was spoken in order to clarify the manner of non-manifestation. [The question is: “Who am I, together with my teacher, and of what sort am I?”
"Having sacrificed, I shall manifest through the unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇasampadā*);

and what is this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct like, such that it manifests in me together with my teachers? Far am I... [and so on]... from being one who is together with my teachers"—this is the construction, including the ellipsis of the text. 282.
One who is intent upon the means of destruction in the states of misery (*apāya*) is "one bound for the states of misery" (*āpāyika*). He does not fulfill that state; he is unable to fulfill it.

"Not being fulfilled" means not being complete by virtue of that state. Since this statement was spoken by Pokkharasāti—who, though himself destined for a state of woe, was not yet fulfilled in that state—the word is used in the nominative case despite its connection to a sense of agency (the *katv-attha*).
Therefore, he says: "by one who is not fulfilled even while being destined for a state of woe. Furthermore, [it refers to] one who is not fulfilling himself.
Although Pokkharasāti himself was one who had not yet fulfilled [the path] and was subject to rebirth in the states of misery, he spoke these words;

thus, from the perspective of the meaning, this is stated as a nominative singular used in the sense of a characteristic (itthambhūtalakkhaṇa). For the sequence of words is one thing, and the sequence of meanings is another.
However, some say that it was stated in this way merely to show the sense of the instrumental case; but that is indeed incorrect.

Because the two words have the same meaning as the word for the agent (*kattūpada*), and because it is impossible for words that have the same meaning to stand in a reciprocal relationship of instrumentality (*karaṇabhāva*) toward one another, enough with this excessive elaboration.
283. Commentary on the Practice of the Former Seers:
It is given, thus it is a *datti*; that very thing is a *dattika*. Therefore, he said "given" (*dinna*). Having made even one who does not wish to give into one who wishes to give—
It is called *sammukhāvaṭṭanī* because one causes confusion by confronting [the other] face-to-face. Therefore he said: "He is unable to say, 'I will not give.
Again, "of him" refers to the brahmin. He said, "Why was it given to me? referring to the kings' bowl of merit (*puṇṇapatta*) which corresponds to the reason.
"Shell-white leprosy" (*saṅkhapalitakuṭṭha*) means white leprosy like a polished conch shell. From "white lotus-silver" (*setapokkhararajata*)...
One who has attained a body equal in virtue spoke thus. "He follows" means he closely pursues another.
If the king does not grant his presence to the brahmin for either of these two reasons, then why was approaching him not prohibited?
To this he said, "But because... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in the science of fields," the Teacher [explains it as] "in the treatise on political ethics (nīti)."

It has been stated. Below, in the *Brahmajāla-vaṇṇanā*, it was likewise stated: “Agriculture (*khettavijjā*) refers to the treatises on statecraft (*nīti-sattha*), such as those of Ambhiya, Māsurakkha, Rāja, and Satta.
Here, “cloth” (*dussa*) means that which serves as a screen (*tirokaraṇiya*). Therefore he said: “standing inside a fence of hemp-cloth (*sāṇipākāra*).

By the word “inside” (*anta*), when the term is extended by its own presence, it becomes “the edge of the cloth” (*dussanta*), just as in the case of “the edge of the forest” (*vananta*). “*Payātaṃ* means ‘faithful’; [it is] eternal.”
Therefore, the Teacher said, "having brought it, it was given.
Consequently, the meaning should be understood as: "they beg for what has been brought and given, either by way of a funeral meal or by way of a regular meal. The passage beginning with "But this...
is a statement regarding the attainment of the goal (*atthāpatti*). "Niṭṭhaṃ" means certainty. But why did the Blessed One speak such an unpleasant thing to the brahmin?
The phrase "he spoke the vital words" (*mammavacanaṃ avoca*) was stated beginning with "But this... in order to demonstrate the reason for the accusation and to provide a justification.
The connection is: "He revealed even the secret, even that which was concealed, as vital words.
(284) Regarding the term "royal throne" (*rājāsana*), it refers to the region of the elephant's shoulder; thus, the text says, "seated upon the neck of the elephant."

It has been said. *Rathūpatthare* means on the portion spread over the chariot. Therefore he said, "In the chariot," and so forth. *Uggatuggatehi* means by those who are exceedingly elevated among the elevated;
for a distributive compound (*vicchā-samāsa*) is not accepted by worldly grammarians. A king’s offspring is a *rājañña*;
with respect to their plurality, it is stated as "*rājaññehi*" according to the rule of single-remainder (*ekasesa-naya*). *Pākaṭamantaṃ* means...
“Counsel” (mantana) means that which is made manifest. It is this [manifest] kind that is intended here, not secret counsel, because it is desired even when being heard by the *sudda* and others.
Therefore it was said: “Now, a *sudda* or a *sudda*-slave might come,” and so forth.
“By those very like him” means by those whose appearance resembles that of the king. Just as the speech capable of accomplishing that purpose was spoken by the king...
Likewise, it should be construed as follows: "Does he also speak words that are capable of establishing that very same meaning?
Regarding the term "pavattāro," its literal meaning (saddato) is "those who speak" by virtue of being speakers of the sacred word (pāvacana).
However, since they are indeed those who set forth (pavattakā) such mantras, the word "pavattayitāro" ("those who cause to proceed") is used to show the intended meaning (adhippāyato).
It has been stated. For the word-form "vattāro" (those who speak) is established by means of the root *vad* and the suffix *tu*;
likewise, "pavattayitāro" (those who cause to proceed) is established by means of the root *vatu*. This is the opinion of both the Master [the Buddha] and the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta.
Some, however, say that he shows the formation of the word "pavattāro" by means of the root *vatu* alone, because the two words share a common grammatical basis (*tulyādhikaraṇa*).
“It is precisely counsel (manta)” is what was stated. For it is a coordinate construction [meaning]: “In the sense of being spoken in secret after excluding the servants, it is precisely counsel;

and because it is the cause for the attainment of various goals, it is a ‘footing’ (pada). Furthermore, according to the method found in the *Aṭṭhakathāmuttaka*, it is called “counsel-footing” (mantapada) because it is a means for attaining [the goal] through the act of deliberating (mantana), which is to be spoken in secrecy due to its unshared nature with those not initiated. “Chanted” (gīta):

"Chanted" means recited by way of singing; and here, even "singing" is intended specifically as the accomplishment of musical tones such as *udātta* (high-pitched) and *anudātta* (low-pitched), which is why it is said, "by way of perfection of tone.
It is called "the word of the Teacher" (*pāvacana*) because it belongs to him. It is "recited" (*vācita*) by way of causing others to speak it.
It is "well-arranged" (*samupabyūḷha*) by way of being compiled and stacked one above the other. This is by way of the *Iruveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, and so forth.
There too, they are grouped individually according to the *mantras*, the *brahmans*, and so forth, as well as according to the *adhyāyas*, *anuvākas*, and so forth;

they are established by being compiled into a collection in the very manner previously described. Regarding the phrase "they cause others to recite what has been recited by others": this means that today’s brahmins cause others to recite those *mantra*-passages which were previously caused to be recited by them when they themselves were performing the ritual duties of others.

"Of them" refers to those who possess the power of thought-reading (*manta-kattūnaṃ*). The phrase "with the divine eye" is said with reference to both the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*), which is an adjunct to the divine eye in the sense of direct perception, and the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*), which is similar to the divine eye in its mode of seeing.

Therefore, by means of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their deeds—which is an adjunct to the divine eye—and by means of [the knowledge of recollecting past lives] which is similar to the divine eye, [one perceives] the fact that beings are the owners of their own karma (*kammassakatā*) and so forth.
The meaning to be understood is: "having observed the methods for the mastery of mantras by brahmins in past aeons through the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
For it is only visible form (*rūpa*) that is the object of the divine eye in the present; therefore, [to claim otherwise] here is irrelevant.
"Having compared it with the scriptures" means that which was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa concerning the basis of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Having compared it with that [other] statement and made it non-contradictory. For the meaning of those [statements] based on the turning away from existence (vivaṭṭa) is not directly perceived.
"They composed" means they bound them in the Pāli language by way of *pajja*, *gajja*, and *bandha*.

"Others as well" means others besides Aṭṭhakā and the rest—namely, other later ones who appeared during the time of King Okkāka and so forth. [The terms] beginning with "killing living beings" (pāṇātipāta).
"Having inserted" means having inserted, here and there, words based on the defilements such as the taking of life into the very sections of the mantras bound together by the *aṭṭhaka* and others.

"They made them contradictory" means they made them into opposites by illustrating meanings pertaining to defilement, according to the method found in the *Brāhmaṇadhammika-sutta* and others in the *Suttanipāta*. "The seers" (*isī*) is merely an illustration.
“For one who is a seer, or one practicing for the state of a seer”—this indeed should have been said.

But why does he not here follow the sequence of the teaching by way of taking a formal admission (*paṭiññā*)? To this he says: “In this case, the Blessed One,” and so forth. “In this case” refers to the passage where it was said:
“I am studying these mantras; you think, ‘He is with his teacher. “Without taking a formal admission” means as was done below [in the previous section] regarding the admission.
Likewise, [the Buddha] did not here take a formal admission [from Ambaṭṭha], as when he said: "What do you think, Ambaṭṭha?
To that extent would you be a seer (isi), or one practicing for the state of a seer, together with your teacher? No indeed, Master Gotama. 286.
"Free from the stench of raw flesh" means being devoid of the foul odor of the impurities of the defilements (kilesa). "Free from the odor of women" means [free from the influence] of women.

By not tolerating even the mere scent of [sexual] desire, they were free from the scent of women. "Wearing dust and dirt" means wearing the natural dust and dirt arising from sedentary habits and so forth.
"Enclosed by walls and guarded by men" refers to the enclosure of walls and the protection provided by men.

Here, however, by the phrase "free from the scent of raw flesh" (*nirāmagandhā*), he shows that those ten brahmins had suppressed their defilements; and by "free from the scent of women, living the holy life" (*anitthigandhā, brahmacārino*), he shows the same.
And by this [phrase], their dwelling alone; by the phrase "wearing dust and dirt," the absence of adornment and decoration;
by the phrase "they dwelt in forest regions at the foot of mountains," a secluded life having abandoned the vicinity of humans;

by the phrase "they dwelt subsisting on roots and fruits from the forest," the rejection of refined food such as rice, meat, and boiled grain; and by the words beginning with "when," the rejection of vehicles and conveyances.
By the words beginning with “in all directions,” he rejects [the notion of] protection and defense.

And in demonstrating this, he shows that even the conduct of those brahmins—which belongs to the side of the wrong practice—when compared to the right practice in the Noble One’s Discipline (ariyavinaya), is indeed a wrong practice. For how could their conduct possibly be [right]?
“Engaged in the practice of self-effacement (*sallekha*). By the words “Is it so with you? and so forth, the Blessed One also makes it clear that he is rebuking and restraining Ambaṭṭha.
For this is a demonstration of the summarized meaning of the passage about to be recited.
*Dussapaṭṭikā* means a strip of cloth; *dussakalāpo* means a bundle of cloth. *Veṭhakehi* means by wrapping-cloths, that is, by strips of cloth. *Dussehi*.
It is said that this means having the sides of the head shaved and the hair on the temples left uncut. "To have it fashioned" (kappetuṃ) means to cut it with a razor.
The same principle applies here as well regarding the phrase "with the hair fashioned" (kappitavālehi).

For in such passages as "Monks, the beard must not be fashioned," the word *kappa* is used in the sense of cutting (*chedana*). "In the appropriate places" refers to the neck, the head, and the tail. "Hair" (*vālā*) refers to the hair in those locations.
They were born with hair. They are called "tail-hair" (*kuttavāla*) either because they move together [with the body] or by way of their location.
Some, however, invent the reading "because they are possessed of hair" (*vāḷayuttattā*) and explain the meaning as "because they are possessed of the form of hair";
their fault is simply that they disregard the canonical text (*pāḷi*). The text states: "with mares' chariots having tail-hair. "Around the city" means on all sides of the city.
The place where the plastering work has been done on the lower part of the rampart is called "upakārikā" because it must be constructed near the city and because it provides assistance.
Those which provide assistance to the city are "nagarūpakārikāyo"; this feminine designation is used in relation to the capital city.
Therefore he said, "But here," and so forth. "Mati" is knowledge that is non-conclusive due to the influence of doubt.
Showing the reason why the teaching was not expanded further, he said, "The Blessed One [said this]," and so forth.

In the Pāḷi, the phrase *so maṃ pañhena* means "that person would clear it up for me by way of a question. The phrase *ahampi veyyākaraṇena sodhessāmi* means "I too shall clear it up by way of an answer";
the meaning should be understood according to the context as appropriate.
Commentary on the Vision of the Two Characteristics (Dvelakkhaṇadassanavaṇṇanā):
287. In the phrase “of those who are seated,” etc., the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used either in a sense of disregard or as a qualification.

It is said that “he is not able” because when the postures (*iriyāpatha*) are contracted, the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) cannot be clearly discerned in their entirety; conversely, it is said that “he is able” because they can be clearly discerned [when the postures are relaxed].
The practice of that [search] should be understood as being solely for the sake of the pleasure of seeking.
"By that" means by both of these two reasons. "Seeking" (gavesī) means he performed the search with knowledge. "Counting" (gaṇayanto) means calculating with knowledge itself.

"He brought together" (samānayī) means he properly brought them together; he collected them. Regarding the word "kaṅkhati," its meaning is "he desires" (ākaṅkhati); thus he said, "Oh, indeed," and so forth. Even without a prefix...
For the word *hi* sometimes expresses a specific meaning as if it were accompanied by a prefix, as in the term "gotrabhū. From here and there, from various parts of the body.
"Is distressed" means he suffers. Therefore he said, "he is unable to see.
"By that" refers to the doubt mentioned in the phrase "while searching, he is distressed. "From that" means because he has not reached a definitive conclusion. Thus [it is said]: "he is in doubt."
Having shown that the word has the sense of "wishing for," he now says "or by doubt" (*kaṅkhāya vā*) and so forth, in order to show its sense of "doubt.
Therein, "by doubt" means by the doubt expressed by the word "he doubts" (*kaṅkhati*). For a verbal form primarily denotes an action. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
The very same perplexity (*vimati*), having reached various states, is what is referred to by the phrase "by three factors" (*tīhi dhammehi*); it is of three kinds.
The meaning is: "by things subject to doubt. "The state of turbidity" refers to a state of agitation that serves as the cause for lack of confidence.
"By the sheath of the organ" means by the cloth-covering (pasibbaka) produced upon the organ located in the lower part of the abdomen, below the navel.

For, as in the case of terms such as *aṇḍakosa* ("egg-sheath"), the word *kosa* here denotes a surrounding covering or sheath. It is called *vatthaguyha* because it is to be concealed by a cloth (*vatha*).
Because the Blessed One’s sheathed private organ is unique to all Buddhas, not shared by others, resembling a perfectly pure circle of gold;
because of its own beautiful shape and configuration, it possesses the supreme loveliness of the choice limbs of a noble Ājāneya scent-elephant;

it has the playful grace of the whorls of filaments in a blossoming golden lotus; and it bears the splendor of the full orb of the moon distinguished against the expanse of a forest of waters colored by the radiance of twilight.

He shines forth, having surpassed others by his own glory; for, because he is unstained by external or internal impurities, because of his long-standing commitment to the holy life (*brahmacariya*), and because of the perfection of his well-proportioned form, even though he was clad in a loincloth, he became as if unclothed.
Therefore it is said: "Of the Blessed One," and so forth. "Like a noble elephant" means like a preeminent scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*).
"Abounding in being" (*pahūtabhāva*) means "extensive being. For his doubt concerned only this;
he had no deliberation at all regarding qualities such as "slender," "soft," or "delicate.
Regarding the phrase "of such a form" (*tathārūpa*), he says "of that form" (*taṃrūpa*) because it is a compound word. "Therein" refers to how Ambaṭṭha [beheld] the sheathed [organ].
[It is used] in the sense of "showing the private parts" as well as in the sense of "performing a feat of supernormal power" (*iddhābhisaṅkhāra*).
For by this [term], there is a reference to such Pāli passages as, "He performed such a feat of supernormal power," and so forth;

therefore, the reason for showing the private parts here, along with the method of performing feats of supernormal power, is elucidated by the reading from the *Milindapañha*. However, some [read] "vatthaguyhadassane."

To misinterpret it in that way is entirely incorrect. For there is nothing in the Canon (Pāḷi) or the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) that could justify such a misinterpretation, and the method of the exercise of psychic power (iddhābhisaṅkhāranaya) remains unexplained.

What more need be said here? Since this must be accepted according to the very method stated by the Venerable Elder Nāgasena—the foremost of debaters who had attained the four analytical knowledges (catu-paṭisambhidā) and the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā)—it should be so received.
“Hirikaraṇaṃ” means that which is made shameful here; it is likewise the occasion for such shame, the object of shame.
“Uttarassa” refers to the young man Uttara who appears in the Suttanipāta. The background story for all of these should be taken from the Suttanipāta.
“Chāyā” means a reflection. To the question, “How did he show it? Of what kind was it? he says: “By means of psychic power (iddhi),” and so forth. It was merely a shadow-form.
It is merely a reflected image of the Blessed One, not his natural physical organ;
and because it is distinct from the Buddha’s own continuum, it is a mere material form, a magical likeness possessing a color, shape, and limbs identical to those of the Blessed One.
By taking it in this way, the use of the word qualified by the letter *ka* in the sense of "small" becomes appropriate. It is a mere shadow-form produced by supernormal power (*iddhi*).

The connection is: "Having fashioned it by supernormal power, he showed it. Regarding this, the teachers say: "In showing it, the Blessed One did so having made it such that his own form as a Buddha was not visible.
This view accords with and agrees with the statement made by the Venerable Thera Nāgasena concerning the mere showing of a shadow-form fashioned by supernormal power (*iddhi*).
It should be understood as being like "milk with milk" or "the waters of the Yamunā with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
For by that very statement, it follows by implication that the remaining form of the Buddha was not visible at that moment.

Furthermore, by the mention of his being clothed in the lower robe and so forth, it is shown here that even for the shadow-form—which is distinct from the Buddha’s own continuum—the lower robe and other garments are external to it.
And one should not raise the objection: "How does the Blessed One show a shadow-form that has entered within the lower garment, and how does Ambaṭṭha see it?
For the domain of psychic power (*iddhi*) is inconceivable. "Having seen the shadow" means when the shadow was seen. "This" refers to the shadow-form.
The intention is that if there were someone capable of awakening [to the truth], he would have shown even the heart-flesh as the sign of life.

“Having brought forth” (*ninnetvā*) means having led out. Or rather, this is the very reading [of the word]. “You are clever” (*kallōsī*): in the context of answering, it means you are skillful and dexterous;
or the meaning is that the path of answering as it has been stated is appropriate and fitting for you. Some read “skillful” (*kusalo*), but this is incorrect.
For in the *Milindapañha*, in every instance at the conclusion of an answer, only the word “clever” (*kallō*) is seen.
“Having bent down” means having directed [the tongue] toward the ear-canal and so forth by way of drawing it out from the mouth;
“having drawn out” is said in order to show the intended meaning. “Like a stiff needle” means having made it like a hard needle by bringing about a state of dense fineness.
“By making it thus” means by making it like a stiff needle. “Herein” refers to the abundant tongue. Its softness...

The Master has stated that length and thinness are shown [in the case of the breath] because it is impossible for one who is not soft to achieve the state of being dense and subtle. Herein, this is the intended meaning:

since only one who is soft is able to achieve the state of being dense and subtle, therefore, by means of performing that [action], the state of being soft is demonstrated, just as fire is by smoke. And since only one who is soft...
Because it becomes long by attaining a state that is both dense and subtle, its length is demonstrated by the touching of the ear canals.
Furthermore, because it becomes thin precisely by attaining a state that is both dense and subtle, its thinness is demonstrated by the touching of the nostril canals.
Because it is impossible for something that is not broad to be concealed in such a manner, [the head] is shown by the covering of the forehead.
The state of being broad has been shown.
289. It should be construed as "looking up while stretching out. 290.
A statement is a primary utterance; a reply is a conversation.
291. In passages such as "the bloated corpse" (*uddhumātaka*), the word *ka* has the sense of loathing;
thus it is said, "loathing that very thing. "That very thing" means the state of being a wise man, or alternatively, it refers to Ambaṭṭha himself.
For he spoke thus with reference to Ambaṭṭha. Indeed, it is stated in the Pāli: "Thus... [he] said this to the young brahmin Ambaṭṭha. And although it was Ambaṭṭha—
It should be understood that this was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*); however, when censuring by making no restriction based on name or clan, he speaks using a plural form.

By the words "of such a kind" (*yādiso*) and so forth, he shows that while the phrase "you yourself" (*yadeva kho tvaṃ*) is an unrestricted statement, the phrase "of such a kind" (*evarūpena*) is a restrictive statement.
In the sense of the locative case used to indicate a characteristic of one state by another state (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe*), the instrumental case is employed.
It is said: “In such a benefactor. “Not elsewhere” means not in another [state], namely, in a happy destination (*sugati*).

Here, however, it should be understood that by the phrase “by a benefactor,” he clarifies precisely the state of being a non-benefactor by way of contrast (*vyatireka*). Regarding the expression “having brought near, having brought near” (*upaneyya upaneyya*), this is a distributive form ending in *-tvā*;
thus he says, “But the brahmin... and so forth. “Having thus brought near, having brought near...”

Having repeatedly brought him to each successive fault, he said: "Having thoroughly imposed the status of a slave and so forth upon him. He caused him to fall means he caused him to fall by way of making him roll down.
And as for the place where he went—that place, characterized as his going in such a manner—he deprived him of it; this is the construction.
Commentary on the Approach to the Buddha Pokkharasāti.
"But how much [time] has passed? To this it is said: "There was not even time for a cordial conversation.
"Āgamā nu" means "has he come? "Kho" is merely a particle. "Idha" means "here," that is to say, "in your presence. "Adhivāsetu" means "may he consent";
however, since that consent here is an acceptance by mind alone and not by body or speech, he says "sampaṭicchatū" (may he accept).
The passage beginning with “yaṃ me” was spoken in order to show this matter: the merit being performed today, the present day, as well as the joy and gladness.
“Kāraṃ” means assistance or honor. “Acopetvā” means without moving or displacing.
Regarding “sahatthā,” this is an ablative expression used in the sense of an instrumental; therefore he said, “by one’s own hand. “Suhitaṃ” means...
“Satisfied” means made happy by the absence of the suffering of hunger. “As much as needed” (yāvadatthaṃ) means: as long as there is need, for that long it was done with food.
Here, the refusal (*paṭikkhepa*) and the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) are intended, not the invitation to accept more (*nimantanapavāraṇā*);
thus he said “Enough,” and so forth. “By a hand-signal” is merely an illustration; elsewhere, the refusal may be made by a facial expression or by a verbal utterance.

Because it has been so stated, and because such a negation is possible even at a single moment. "Onītapattapāṇī" (one who has removed his hand from the bowl) is a three-word external compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) with a non-co-referential scope (*bhinnādhikaraṇavisaya*), meaning "one whose hand (*pāṇi*) has been removed (*onīta*) from the bowl (*patta*).

However, by means of the *muddhajaṇa*-type and the *saññogata*-type [of elision], the word *oṇitta* is shown to be a variant; thus he says, "The reading ‘oṇittapattapāṇin’ti is also found," and so forth.
Alternatively, the word *oṇitta* has the sense of making clean. For one whose bowl and hands have been made clean (*oṇitta*) by the removal of food scraps is called *oṇittapattapāṇi*.
Therefore, he said: “having washed both hands and the bowl. In the *Sāratthadīpanī*, it is explained: “*Oṇitta* means separated or detached;
or, because the bowl has been made clean from the hand by the removal of food scraps, one is *oṇittapattapāṇī*.”
It has been stated. In this regard, the latter statement must be examined because it does not correspond with the phrase "having washed both hands and the bowl.
"Become such" means one who has become in the manner described by the words "one who has finished eating and has removed his hand from the bowl.
(298) "Graduated talk" refers to a discourse that should be delivered in successive order; therefore, he said, "talk in regular sequence."
But as for Sāti, who said, "Virtue follows immediately after giving," and so forth—the meaning understood from this is as follows:

First, the discourse on giving should be taught at the outset because it is common to all people, because it is easy to practice, and because it serves as the means for establishing oneself in virtue.
For a person whose nature is one of relinquishment, due to the state of having let go of things belonging to themselves...

One undertakes the precepts with ease and becomes well-established therein. Following the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue (sīla) is presented because virtue purifies both the donor and the recipient;

because it speaks of benefiting others while teaching the cessation of harming others; because it teaches the principle of action (kiriya-dhamma) after teaching the principle of non-action (akiriya-dhamma);

and because it teaches the cause for the attainment of existence (bhava-sampatti) after teaching the cause for the attainment of wealth (bhoga-sampatti). Thus, the discourse on virtue follows the discourse on giving.

It should be told. If that practice of giving and virtue is dependent on the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), then the discourse on heaven follows immediately after the discourse on virtue in order to show that this excellence of existence is its fruit. For by that [discourse], it is shown in this way:

"By means of these bases for meritorious action consisting of giving and virtue—which are distinguished by various degrees such as superior and more superior—these immeasurable [realms] among the Cātumahārājikas and so forth, distinguished by various degrees such as superior and more superior, [are attained]."
“Divine attainments are to be obtained. Now, this heaven is defiled by lust and the other [defilements], whereas the Noble Path is entirely undefiled by them;
it is for the purpose of showing this that the discourse on the Path follows the discourse on heaven. And when explaining the Path, one must show the means for its realization;
thus, there is the discourse on the danger, the degradation, and the corruption of sensual pleasures, and on renunciation.
And the benefit must be explained. For all sensual pleasures included within the heavenly realms are indeed fraught with many dangers, impermanent, unstable, and subject to change;
how much more so, then, are others—this is their "danger" (ādīnava). Furthermore, all sensual pleasures are base, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—this is their "meanness" (okāra).
And all states of existence are the basis for the defilements.
The defilement [itself], and Nibbāna, which is dissociated from all defilements—thus the benefit of renunciation must also be told.
This meaning too should be understood as being "awakened" (bodhita). For here, by the word *iti* in the sense of "beginning," the dangers of sensual desire (*kāma*) and so forth are also included;
thus this commentary on the meaning has been made. Therefore he said: "Namely—the talk on giving, the talk on virtue, the talk on heaven..."
“He proclaims the danger, the degradation, and the defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation. The detailed exposition should be taken from the *Sāratthadīpanī*.
Regarding the word *kasi* (plowing), he says “seized,” etc., because it means grasping by means of knowledge.

By the word *sāmaṃ* (by oneself), he shows the meaning that is to be excluded, namely, “not shared with others,” because in the attainment of supramundane states there is an absence of instruction from another, [being attained] by oneself alone.
Because he was the first in the world to awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, it is said that [these qualities] are not shared with others.

Regarding the term "dhammacakkhu," here only the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) is intended, not the three lower paths as in the *Brahmāyu Sutta*, nor the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya*) as in the *Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta*. [The phrase] "for the purpose of showing the manner of its arising" [is used].

Why was it said? In order to clear away the objection, "Is it not the case that path-knowledge has only the unconditioned dhamma as its object, and not conditioned dhammas as its object?", he said, "For that...

and so forth. "By way of function" means by way of the function of penetrating without confusion. This concludes the commentary on the discourse regarding the declaration of becoming a lay follower by the upāsaka Pokkharasāti.

299. In the text, regarding the phrases "one who has seen the Dhamma" (*diṭṭhadhammo*) and so forth, the term "seeing" (*dassana*) refers not only to knowledge (*ñāṇa*) but also to other forms of seeing such as that by the eye;

therefore, to exclude those, the term "one who has attained the Dhamma" (*pattadhammo*) is stated. Furthermore, since "attainment" (*patti*) exists in other senses besides the attainment of knowledge—such as physical movement and so on—in order to show its specific distinction, the term "one who has realized the Dhamma" (*viditadhammo*) is stated. Now, this state of having realized the Dhamma...
The phrase "one who has plunged into the Dhamma" (*pariyogāḷhadhammo*) is stated to show that he has understood the Dhamma without exception—not merely in part.
By this, it illuminates his very full awakening to the Truths (*saccābhisambodha*).

For path-knowledge (*maggañāṇa*), by accomplishing the four functions such as full understanding (*pariññā*) through a single penetration (*ekābhisamaya*), is said to have "plunged all around" into the Dhamma of the Four Truths without exception. Therefore, he says: "It has been seen..."

"The noble truth of the Dhamma is seen by this [knowledge], thus it is 'seen in this very life' (diṭṭhadhamma). One should not say: "But how can a single knowledge, performing four functions simultaneously in a single moment, proceed? For such a thing is not seen in the world, nor is there any such scriptural authority.
For just as a lamp, in one and the same moment, burns the wick and consumes the oil;
It dispels darkness and shows light; thus should this be understood as knowledge.

Herein, the following passage from the Sutta should be cited: “The knowledge of one who possesses the path is knowledge regarding suffering, it is knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, it is knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and it is knowledge regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
"Crossed over doubt": he has crossed over the doubt based on sixteen grounds and eight grounds, which is like a perilous wilderness full of fear.
"Free from perplexity": his perplexity—which occurs as "Is it thus? Is it not thus?
