regarding the process of existence and so forth—has departed and been utterly cut off. "He has attained confidence": [he has attained confidence] in those things that cause timidity...

Because evil qualities have been abandoned and because he is well-established in the opposing virtues such as morality (sīla) and so forth, he has attained and reached a state of confidence and proficiency.
To show that this attainment of fearlessness and well-establishedness was stated in response to the inquiry "Where [is it]?
he said, "Where? In the Teacher’s Dispensation. [He realized this] by his own direct experience.

The meaning is: because it has been seen and attained, there is no other condition to be recognized for it. Regarding this, he states the intended sense with the words "not of another," and so forth. "Does not proceed" means it does not function or it does not practice;

or, it is also appropriate to explain it as "not dependent on another" (aparappaccaya) in the sense that it does not rely upon or place its trust in another. Furthermore, whatever remains to be said here that has not yet been stated is as follows:
It should be understood that [this] has not been stated because it was already mentioned previously and will be mentioned later.
Thus ends the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which elucidates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend,

which generates a vast and stainless clarity of wisdom, and which was composed by one endowed with the qualities of integrity, gentleness, modesty, faith, mindfulness, fortitude, intelligence, patience, energy, and so forth.

This is the *Līnatthapakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta*, composed by the Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati— a great preceptor, a master of exposition,

whose conduct was characterized by unimpeded, unshakeable, and confident knowledge regarding the Three Pitakas together with their commentaries, who had plunged into the dense thickets of his own tradition and those of other traditions in their many varieties,
and who was the venerable teacher of the Great King of Kings— within the work titled *Sādhuvilāsini*.
The commentary on the Ambaṭṭha Sutta is finished.
4. Commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta: 300.
Having thus commented upon the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, he now, following the proper sequence, comments upon the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.
In order to clarify that it has attained the status of being subject to commentary, or to indicate that the discourse recited immediately after the Ambaṭṭha Sutta is the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, he said:
"Thus have I heard... [pe] ...in Aṅga: the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.
They are called Aṅgas because they possess limbs (aṅgāni) that are preeminent in their beauty. This is derived from the taddhita suffix used in the sense of "distinguished by excellence."

Because it occurs in the sense of "existence," and because they are the primary [inhabitants], they are called "princes" (*rājakumāra*); however, by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), they are called "the people of the country" (*janapada*).
Thus it is said, "named Aṅgas," and so forth. Here too, this is intended, not only in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta.

The passage beginning with "At that time, it is said... is a statement of the reason for that journey. By showing the danger in coming and thus refusing [the invitation], they will not allow him to come.
The intention is that they will not grant permission.

Because it is interspersed with blue *asoka*, *kaṇikāra*, *koviḷāra*, *kunda*, royal tree (*rājarukkha*), and other species, that campaka grove is adorned with flowers of five colors—blue and so forth;
they say it is not because the campaka trees themselves possess flowers of five colors such as blue. However, by means of such an element (*dhātu*)...
Indeed, even *campaka* trees blossom with flowers of five colors, such as blue and so forth. For even today they are seen in certain regions;

thus, the commentary’s statement is consistent with the literal meaning. "Fragrant with the scent of flowers" means fragrant with the scents of either mixed flowers or pure *campaka* blossoms, according to the method already stated. Speaking in this way...
This shows that it was not only at the time of the measuring that *campaka* trees were abundant in that city, but rather that they were so even at a later time.
For it was because of the abundance of *campaka* trees at the time of the measuring that the city received the name "Campā. "Sovereignty" (*issaratta*) means the state of being a ruler (*adhipati*).
"Senika" means one who has an army (*senā*); he himself is "Seniya. And here, the distinction lies in their great number.
It is said that "existence" (*atthitā*) is indicated by a *taddhita* suffix in the phrase "because of being endowed with a great army.
"Because of its resemblance to refined gold" means because of its resemblance to the finest quality of gold. However, in the commentary on the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha-sutta*, it is stated thus:
"Seniya" is his name; "Bimbī" is said to be the name for his physical form (*attabhāva*), and he was its essence, beautiful to behold.
“Because of the excellence of his majestic physical form, he is called Bimbisāra.
301–2. *Saṃhatā* means gathered together by way of assembly; it is said that they have come together.
*Ekekissāya disāya* means in each direction, that is, in each region constituting a direction. Since brahmins and householders are intended in the text...
He shows by the word "of these" (*etesaṃ*) that although "belonging to a group" (*saṅghino*) should be said, the singular form "a group-member" (*saṅghī*) is used to express plurality.
Thus it was stated by the Teacher; however, the plural form "group-members" (*saṅghī*) is also seen with a long vowel.

"Agaṇā" means those who have not formed a multitude, being unbound into a group; there is also a reading "agaṇanā," which has the same meaning, because a sense of numerical calculation is inappropriate here.
"For they have no number. This is what is meant: previously they were not a group within the city, but later, having become a group outside the city, they "became a group" (*gaṇībhūtā*).
For when the suffix *ka* (or *sa*) is used in the sense of becoming something that was not previously so, there is a substitution of the vowel *ī* for the vowel *a*, or the suffix *ī* is applied.
He is like a man who carries the staff for kings, royal ministers, and others, protecting the Kṣatriyas here and there.
He is a "minister" (*khattā*) in the sense of protection (*rakkhaṇa*), according to the method of etymology.
For wherever he is sent by them, he speaks on the matter asked of him in a fitting and appropriate manner, avoiding their faults. Therefore it is said: "capable of answering questions when asked.
He is a "high minister" (*mahāmatta*) because his measure (*mattā*) or magnitude (*pamāṇa*) is great due to his noble lineage, position, and so forth.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Qualities of Soṇadaṇḍa: 303.
The domains where a king’s commands prevail are called *rajjāni* (kingdoms). Those distinguished kingdoms are *virajjāni*; these very ones are *verajjāni*.
Likewise, there are various kinds of *verajjāni*. Regarding the phrase "born therein" and so forth, there are three types of derivative (*taddhita*) etymological explanations.
"For the application of secondary (taddhita) suffixes is indeed manifold. "For the purpose of experiencing whatever sacrifice" means for the purpose of experiencing any sacrifice whatsoever.
"They" refers to the brahmins from various kingdoms. "His" refers to the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa.
"A supreme brahmin" means a brahmin who is more exalted or eminent by virtue of his lineage, wealth, and knowledge. "The artifice of enticement" has already been explained.
Because of being oppressed by stinginess regarding gain (*lābhamacchera*), there will be no assembly.

It is called a *aṅga* because it leads to (*gameti*) its own fruit, making it known; or, it is itself led to (*aṅgīyati*), gone to (*gamīyati*), and made known (*ñāyati*), thus it is a *aṅga*, meaning a cause (*hetu*).

Therefore he said, "by the reason. By showing that other reasons were also stated through the recollection of the nature of worldly phenomena (*lokadhammatā*), he spoke the words beginning with "thus" (*evaṃ*).
“By two sides” means by the two sides of kinship: the mother’s side and the father’s side.
For if only the phrase “well-born on both sides” were stated, one might understand it as being well-born in any two parts whatsoever;

moreover, since the word *sujāta* (well-born) can also function as a synonym for excellence of physical proportions—as in “well-born and beautiful to behold”—it is here understood specifically in terms of birth (*jāti*).
In order to clarify this, it was said: “on the mother’s side and on the father’s side. Therefore he said: “The Blessed One’s mother was a brahmin woman,” and so forth.
“In this way” means by the aforementioned manner; that is to say, by a threefold circle of kinsmen on each side, both from the mother’s side and from the father’s side.
By the phrase “of pure descent through seven generations,” the very same meaning as expressed by “on the mother’s side and on the father’s side” is further clarified.
"He is capable," thus it is said: "Your wife is pure (*saṃsuddhā*)," meaning she is indeed pure, not shared with any other man.
For in the world, the designation "mother" and "father" is seen even in reference to children who are not of the body;

however, here it is intended specifically in reference to a child of the body (*orasa-putta*), and so it is stated as "one whose wife is pure. She conceives and bears the embryo, thus she is the "womb" (*gahaṇī*).
The third whorl, known as the womb-site, refers to the region within the mother’s belly; "samavepākiniyā" means that which causes even digestion.
"Ettha" refers to the *Mahāsudassana Sutta*. It is called the "gahaṇī" because it receives the food as it is eaten and digests it rather than discarding it;
it is the element of fire born of karma, which is known in the world as the "stomach-fire."
“Pitupitā” means the father’s father. “Pitāmaho” is established as a derivative (*taddhita*) by means of the suffix *-āmaha*.

Just as in the case of “catuyuga” and similar terms, because it is applied in that sense, a specific period of time is called a *yuga*. This use of the word *yuga* as a designation for the measure of a lifespan is merely a verbal expression, a mere term of worldly convention;
however, from the perspective of the intended meaning, it is simply the grandfather who is referred to by the term “grandfather-yuga.”
The intention is that [the word "father"] is stated because it is intended as the primary factor. "Beyond that" means above the grandfather.
Therefore he said, "former ancestors"; the meaning is the six preceding ancestors remaining after him.

And here, the mention of "men" (purisa) should be understood as a formal designation (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*). For in this way, the scriptural expression "from the mother's side" (*mātito*) is properly accounted for.
In this regard, here is the method not found in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā): "Mother and father" are *pitaro*; "the fathers of the fathers" are the grandfathers (*pitāmahā*);
their pair or dyad is the "grandfather-dyad" (*pitāmahayugo*). Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "as far as the seventh grandfather-dyad," that is, the seventh pair of grandfathers.

And in this way, by the mention of "grandfather" alone, the maternal grandfather is also included. Furthermore, the word "dyad" (*yuga*) here is used in the singular form [by the grammatical rule] *ekasesa*.
“‘Yuga and yuga and yuga’—therefore, in each respective circle of relatives, a pair of grandfathers is included.
Regarding the phrase “as far as the seventh generation of grandfathers,” he says “thus,” etc., because it connects with both sides, like the maxim of the crow’s eye.
The connection is: “as far as the seventh person, so far [one is] untainted and unblamed in terms of birth.”

"Accused" (*akkhitto*) means one who has not been formally charged. "Not accused" (*anavakkhitto*) means not discarded in matters such as offerings of cooked rice made out of faith. "Not reviled" (*na upakuṭṭho*) means not censured.
To show that the phrase "by way of birth" (*jātivādena*) is used in the instrumental case to express the cause, the words "for what reason" (*kena kāraṇena*) and so forth were spoken.
"In this way too" (*itipi*) means for this reason as well. And here, by the phrase "both... yokes" (*ubhato... yugā*), [the status] of the brahmin...
The absence of faults in his lineage is shown by the description of his perfectly pure descent;
by the term "uncensured" (*akkhitta*), the absence of any transgression in action is indicated, for it is through a transgression in action that beings incur censure.
By the term "unreviled" (*anupakuṭṭha*), the absence of improper association is indicated, for it is in dependence upon improper association that beings receive abuse.
“Lord” (*issara*) means one who has the nature of ruling by the power of karma that leads to sovereignty.
That lordship of his becomes manifest through the condition of the attainment of great wealth; therefore, showing it by way of the synonym for being wealthy, he said, “The wealthy is the lord.
He is “of great wealth” because he possesses vast riches both buried in the earth and stored above ground. “Of that” means of each respective quality; this very [term]...

And this reading is seen now. Thinking, "I shall show only the lack of virtue," [the author] first stated his virtue through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and then, through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), shows that the Blessed One’s reason for not approaching him was indeed a lack of virtue.
"Adhikarūpa" means having a distinguished form, an excellent body. Regarding "dassanīya" (worthy of being seen), he says "fit for seeing."
It brings about confidence, thus it is "inspiring" (*pāsādika*). Therefore he said: "because it generates confidence.
Here, the word *pokkhara* is established in the sense of "beautiful" and in the sense of "body. Regarding the phrase "of the color": this refers to the color-element (*vaṇṇadhātu*).

Because the word "color" (*vaṇṇa*) functions in the sense of the color-element by means of a clear and pure sign, its beauty (*vaṇṇatā*) is precisely that sign; and that [beauty] is dependent upon color.
It is stated by way of non-distinction as “with the most excellent, perfectly pure complexion.

The body, however, is a collection distinguished by its arrangement—namely, the hands, feet, neck, head, and so forth—and it is apprehended through the characteristic of its configuration (*saṇṭhāna*) which constitutes its parts.

Therefore, it is said that “the lotus-like quality” refers precisely to that characteristic: “by the excellence of the body’s configuration,” or alternatively, “by the supreme excellence of the body’s configuration.”
It should be applied [in this way]. For there is a change of gender and case-ending according to the sense.
Since among all colors, the golden color is the most excellent, he said: "He is endowed with the golden color, which is the best even among pure colors.
For it is indeed the Buddhas and the Wheel-turning Monarchs who possess the golden color. Furthermore, because the word *vacchasa* refers to the radiance of the body...
It occurs; therefore, *brahmavacchasī* means having the radiance of an excellent body, that is to say, the radiance of gold.

Indeed, it is with reference to this very meaning that it is said, "He was endowed with a body exactly like the body of Mahābrahmā," and not because of his being straight-limbed like Brahmā (*brahmujugattatā*).
*Okāsa* refers to the location of all the limbs and members. [This is] by way of the perfection of height and girth, and the completeness of the parts.
And the meaning is that there is no lack of opportunity for vision. Therefore he said, "all indeed," and so forth.
*Sīla* is virtue characterized by restraint and observance; because his virtue had been long practiced and increased, it is specifically called "one of increased virtue" (*vuddhasīlī*).
By "one of increased virtue" is meant one who, through constant right application, possesses mature and stable virtue. And thus...
Having formulated these three phrases, they become distinguished by their intended meaning; however, with reference merely to the literal sense of the words, it is said:

"This is a synonym for the term *vuddhasīlī* (one who has grown in virtue) alone. He says "merely the five precepts" because there is no further virtue beyond the five precepts in that context, and because [the others] do not know them.

It is said that "the state of being beautiful" refers precisely to the speech having well-rounded words and phonemes (*parimaṇḍalapadabyañjanatā*); thus it is stated: "beautiful, with well-rounded words and phonemes.
Because of the perfection of the points of articulation (*ṭhāna*) and the places of formation (*karaṇa*), and because of the perfection of training (*sikkhā*), there is no deficiency whatsoever;

thus, her words and phonemes—meaning the syllables (*akkhara*)—are well-rounded, hence she is "one whose words and phonemes are well-rounded. For it is the syllable itself, by virtue of its capacity to express this or that meaning, [that constitutes the word].
A delimited word (*pada*). Alternatively, the word itself is the "expression" (*byañjana*) because it manifests the meaning;

and through the completion of the phonemes—such as those that are soft or hard—the expression of the word becomes perfectly rounded (*parimaṇḍala*). She who possesses such a perfectly rounded expression of the word is thus [described].

Furthermore, a "word" (*pada*) is that by which the meaning is understood, namely a noun-base (*nāma*) and so forth; it is called an "expression" (*byañjana*) because it manifests the intended meaning, that is, a sentence (*vākya*).

Because of their completeness, they possess well-rounded words and phonemes. Or, because speech itself is the instrument for making the meaning known, the term "vākkaraṇa" (speech-instrument) is used to show the identity of the substratum;
thus it is called "the sound of an utterance," meaning the sound consisting of a vocal differentiation.
By means of the perfection of the qualities of that [speech] or of the meaning to be expressed by it, it is filled.
The word *porī* means "complete" in the sense of being perfected in its qualities (*guṇehi*). Again, it refers to the royal capital, the great city (*pureti rājadhānīmahānagare*).

"Because of its growth" (*bhavattā*) means because of its development. "By its delicacy" (*sukhumālattanena*) means by way of its tender nature; by this, he expresses the softness and smoothness of that speech.

"Unobstructed" (*apalibuddhāya*) means not enveloped by bile, phlegm, and so forth; this is a phrase containing a reason (*hetugabbhapada*). For it is precisely because of this that the aforementioned defects are absent.
"Staccato" (*saṇṇiddha*) refers to speaking in parts, as if biting off the words; "drawn out" (*vilambita*) refers to speaking slowly after a long delay.

There is also a reading: "staccato, drawn out, and so forth. "Speech not produced by sound" (*saddena ajanakaṃ vacanaṃ*) or the utterance of a single syllable known as *mammaka* two or three times is "staccato.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes "labored" (*dukkhalita*), "dragged out" (*anukaḍḍhita*), and others.
“With saliva dripping” (*eḷāgaḷenā*) means by the trickling of saliva. To show the two-fold meaning of what was stated as “saliva is trickling,” it is said, “or saliva is flowing,” and so forth.
For the word *eḷā* occurs in reference to both saliva and phlegm, as in such passages as “See the serpent with mucus, double-tongued. “Phlegm-sprays” (*kheḷaphusitāni*) means drops of phlegm.
In this regard, here is the method not found in the Aṭṭhakathā: *ela* refers to fault (*dosa*), as in such passages as "that speech which is *nelā* (faultless), pleasant to the ear," and so forth.
Since those of poor wisdom speak only faulty speech and cause that fault to flow out, their speech is called *elagalā*;
the meaning is "opposite to that. [The phrase] "making the beginning, middle, and end clear" means...
By this, he explains the fulfillment of the meaning of that statement. It is connected with the word *viññāpana* (making known).

"Worn out by old age" (*jarājiṇṇatāya jiṇṇo*) means having reached a state of being broken, grey-haired, and so forth. "Having reached the limit of growth" (*vuddhimariyādappatto*) means having attained the boundary or the end of growth.
"By way of being aged through birth" (*jātimahallakatāyā*) means by virtue of being advanced in years due to the fact of rebirth. Therefore, he said:
Regarding the phrase “one who has been long departed”: the word *addha* refers to a duration of time and denotes a long period.
To the question of how long that is, he says, “two or three royal successions,” meaning the sequence of the reigns of two or three kings.
Although the term “one who has gone a long way” (*addhagata*) was used, the mention of “age” (*vaya*) is intended with reference to the final stage of life; thus it is said, “the latter age.”
"has arrived. "The final third part" refers to the third and concluding portion when a hundred-year lifespan is divided into three parts.
Each of these is further subdivided into thirty-three years, as well as months and fortnights;

therefore, the final stage of life should be understood as beginning from the appropriate month, fortnight, and day within the sixty-seventh year. This was also stated by the Venerable Ācariya Sāriputta Thera:
For it was with reference to this very point that it was said: "The latter portion of life begins from sixty-seven years.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the commentary’s statement: "The latter portion of life is called the last third of a hundred years.
Having thus stated the first alternative based on birth alone, he now states the second alternative by way of a mixture of qualities.
The passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apica*) is commenced. Therein, this state of being "aged" (*jiṇṇatā*) is not merely a matter of age, but rather an antiquity by way of family lineage;

thus he says, “Aged means ancient,” and so forth. “One whose family lineage has been active for a long time” (*cirakālappavattakulanvayo*) means one whose family circle has been active for a long time;

by this, he expresses his state of being ever-increasingly exalted (*uditodita*) by way of his family. By the phrase “one who has reached old age” (*vayoanuppatto*), since the increase of his birth will be explained later, [the meaning is established].
And because he is preeminent through the growth of his virtues, it is said: “He is called ‘Buddha’ because he is endowed with the growth of virtues such as moral conduct (sīla) and behavior (ācāra).
This is indeed an exclusive definition (pārisesa-ggahaṇa) in view of what is yet to be stated.

Likewise, since his being great by birth will be mentioned by that same term, and since his greatness in terms of wealth is not excluded, it is said: “He is ‘Mahallaka’ because he is possessed of greatness in wealth.”

He said: By the words "one who has entered upon the path" (*maggapaṭipanno*), he shows the meaning as having approached by way of conduct, without deviating from the path of proper practice belonging to the brahmins.
The phrase "having reached the state of being old by birth" means that he has reached even that final age, the very last stage of life;
this is the construction with its underlying intention. For by means of this final age, he demonstrates the state of being old by birth.
304. Commentary on the Discourse on the Qualities of the Buddha:
Even to place oneself in a position of equal standing with such beings of great power is not appropriate for those like me who are of a wise nature;
how much less so to place oneself in a superior position? Showing that this was not fitting for the brahmin, [the text says]: "No..."

He then spoke the words beginning with "But as for me... and so forth. Therein, the connection is that even those qualities which are similar to his own qualities, he proclaims while regarding them as indeed superior.
And "similar" means similar in some respect; for no qualities whatsoever found in others are entirely identical in every way to the qualities of the Buddhas.
The passage beginning with "And who am I... is a demonstration of the manner in which they are superior.
"What kind of person must I become to be his equal? And what kind of qualities must I possess to be his equal?"—this is the construction with the underlying intention (*sādhippāya-yojanā*).
Some offer a new reading, but this alone is the original text, as it appears in the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta*:
"And who am I, sir Gotama, together with my teacher, and what is this unsurpassed perfection of true knowledge and conduct?"* *Note: This refers to the passage at DN 3.1.20.*
"Others"—meaning qualities unlike his own—this is to be connected with the word "manifests. "Exclusively"—that is, because there is no possibility of [others] having similar qualities.
By thus restricting [the scope], Soṇadaṇḍa illuminates this group of meanings. In the phrase "for just as," the particle *hi* (for) indicates the reason.
Therefore he said, "We alone are worthy. "In the footprint of a cow" (*gopadaka*) refers to the water standing in the place where a cow's hoof has been set.
"Virtue" (*guṇa*) applies even to similar virtues, let alone to incomparable virtues.

"Six million families" (*saṭṭhi-kula-sata-sahassa*) means one hundred thousand families plus sixty thousand. However, it should be understood that in some places, such as the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, the statement that the Blessed One [visited] eighty thousand families refers specifically to only one side [of the population].
“Lakes with floors polished with lime” means lotus ponds prepared with lime. “Of the seven gems”:

for in the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇa), the genitive case is frequently used in connection with the word *pūra* (“filling”). “The turrets and so forth of the palaces” refers to the cornices and other structures situated on the upper stories of the palaces.
“Of the seven gems” is the governing term; this is a figurative expression of distinction where there is no actual distinction. “By way of family lineage.”
[He was born] into the lineage of the great King Suddhodana, through the unbroken succession of the kṣatriya clan. "In those too" means even in those four treasures.
Whatever place is taken from them is filled with wealth once again; it remains exactly as it was, never diminished. "Auspiciously" means beautifully.
The first stage of life should be understood according to the method described for the final stage of life. [This refers to] the mother and father.

It is said that because his going forth was against his will, he showed disregard for the purpose [of renunciation] appropriate to him; thus it is stated that the genitive case is used [for the parents].
"Of these" refers to the mother and father. "Having wailed" means having lamented with such words as, "Where is my dear son?
"Immeasurable indeed" means that it is entirely unlimited, being impossible for anyone to define it by saying, "It is this much."
"Two bamboos were only as high as his waist," thus he said: "only as high as the waist above two bamboos.

To show that by the power of the perfections (pāramitā) it appeared so only to the brahmin, while the Blessed One at that time was of his ordinary size, the word "appearing" (paññāyamāno) seems to have been used; this should be understood after careful investigation. By the words "Not indeed," etc.,...
They say: "This immeasurability is shown to be by the power of the perfections (*pāramitā*) alone, and not by the power of psychic potency (*iddhi*). *Atula* means incomparable.
The reading found in some places, "He spoke a verse in the *Dhammapada*," is indeed inappropriate; for this verse is not seen in the *Dhammapada*.
However, this verse appears in the *Sudhāpiṇḍiya-thera-apadāna* and other such works, and even there it occurs in reference to a different matter altogether, not [the present one].

In this context, it should be understood that because this verse was not included in the formal recitation (*saṅgīti*) according to the canonical text (*pāḷi*), it is merely an incidental teaching (*pakiṇṇaka-desanā*).
Therein, the phrase "such as those" (*te tādisē*) is a figurative expression (*pariyāya-vacana*), as in such passages as "the lifespan is but a hundred years; such as it is found at present.

Some also read it as "of such a kind" (*etādise*), but that is not good, because it is not seen used in that way in the *Apadāna* and other texts. [It refers to] through the final extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-parinibbāna*).
The meaning is this: when one honors such a person who has attained final Nibbāna and is fearless toward anything whatsoever, this merit cannot be calculated even by someone of great power.
"Between the arms" means the space between two arms. "Twelve hundred yojanas" means twelve hundred yojanas plus twelve more.
"Between the armpits" means all around, according to the measurement of the circumference of the body. "In width" means in breadth.
"The finger-joints" refers to each individual finger-joint. "Between the eyebrows" means the space between the two eyebrows.
Since it was stated separately that the mouth is two hundred yojanas in width, [the height] is implied. "Such is the Blessed One"—this refers to the description spoken by others.
"In what way was it suitable for her?"—by this he shows that she came because she wished to see [the Blessed One] after hearing from others a description of the Blessed One's excellence.
Alternatively, "yathākatham" means "of what kind.

For this collection of particles is used in the sense of a question, as in such passages as, "But in what way, monks, did you spend the rains comfortably, being united, in harmony, and without dispute? Or it may be a single particle.
“In the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber” means in the courtyard surrounding the Fragrant Chamber; the meaning is: outside the Fragrant Chamber and within the courtyard.

“Therein” refers to the couch. “He assumed the lion’s posture” means that he performed a feat of supernormal power (*iddhi-abhisaṅkhāra*) such that Rāhu, the lord of the Asuras, was unable to grasp the dimensions of the Blessed One’s physical body—neither in length, nor in width, nor in height.
The Master’s statement, “While performing his mental formations, he assumed the lion’s posture,” is utterly contradicted by the commentary’s words:
“O Lord of Asuras, it was not with my face turned downwards that I fulfilled the perfections; rather, having directed them upwards, I gave gifts.
For this [statement] demonstrates the accomplishment of the power of the perfections, just as in the accounts of the opening of the door to the Perfumed Chamber and so forth.
They say, "Otherwise, that very same statement would have had to be spoken," but this should be accepted after careful investigation.
"With face turned downwards" is said with reference to the state of slackened energy; "only upwards" refers to the state of unslackened energy, meaning having made it reach the ultimate limit.
On that day, Rāhu announced his status as a lay follower (upāsaka); thus he says, "On that day," and so forth.

Because it is remote from defilements (*kilesa*), it is "noble" (*ariya*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*); for that very reason, its excellence and purity are stated as "supreme and pure.
It is "wholesome" (*kusala*) in the sense of being blameless (*anavajja*), not in the sense of having a pleasant ripening (*sukhavipāka*), because such a ripening is impossible for an Arahant.

"By wholesome virtue" means by virtue that is blameless and has dispelled all defilements along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*). And by taking it thus, this set of four terms [is established].
It is distinct from the intended meaning; however, with reference to the mere literal sense of the words, it is stated that "this is its synonym.
In some instances, eighty-four thousand beings are mentioned, while in others, an immeasurable number of gods and humans are meant;
with this sense in mind, he says, "In each single teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One," and so forth. This applies to such discourses as the *Mahāsamaya Sutta* and the *Maṅgala Sutta*.
For indeed, in twenty-four places, incalculable and immeasurable devas and humans drank the nectar of the path and its fruits.
Although they are truly numerous even by a measure of hundreds of thousands of millions and so forth, it was stated in this way for the sake of illustration.

Therefore, by virtue of being the unsurpassed teacher, the Blessed One is the teacher of many; and by virtue of being the teacher of those disciples who have themselves become teachers, [he is the teacher] of those disciples to be guided.
"The Teacher. For it is by abiding in the method given by the Blessed One that the disciples train those who are to be trained; therefore, the Blessed One alone is their primary teacher.
Since the intended meaning is the authority when one speaks, and not the scope of the "method of characteristics" (lakkhaṇahāra) and so forth, he said, "But as for the brahmin," and so on.
At the end of the phrase “or of this putrid body,” an abbreviated formula (*peyyāla*) is applied, and it is stated: “scratching and rubbing.
For this passage from the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga* is understood through the use of such an abbreviated formula, beginning with “the decoration of external requisites.
In that context, “or of this putrid body” means “or of this human body. For just as even one born on that very day—
A jackal is reckoned as nothing more than an "old jackal," and even a creeper reaching up to one's thighs is reckoned as nothing more than a "rotten creeper";
likewise, even a human body with the color of gold is reckoned as nothing more than a "putrid body. Its "adornment" (maṇḍanā) means this.
"Kelanā" means playing (*kīḷanā*). They also read it as "kelāyanā. "Paṭikelanā" means counter-playing (*paṭikīḷanā*). It is the state of being fickle (*capala*).

It should be understood that "restlessness" (*cāpalya*) or "fickleness" (*cāpalla*) is a designation for that state by which a person, even if they are a hundred years old, becomes like a child born on that very day; this is its synonym. Regarding the term *apāpapurekkhāra*:

it means one who has evil as their priority (*apāpe pure karoti*), or one who does not have evil as their priority (*na vā pāpaṃ pure karoti*); thus, it is a compound formed according to the rule of *yuttāyutta*.

In order to show two meanings, it is said: “The nine supramundane states that are faultless,” and so forth. They are "faultless" (*apāpa*) because they are the opposite of evil, or because they are devoid of evil.
They are "brahmic" (*brahma*) because they exist in the Blessed One, who is supreme (*seṭṭha*), since they are born through noble birth by way of his teaching of the Dhamma;
or because they are the offspring of the Blessed One, the Brahmā, through such things as being held in high esteem, and through practicing according to his instructions.
And because one knows the supreme Brahman, the Noble Path, one is called *brahmaññā*—the people known as the noble disciples.
Therefore he said, "Sāriputta and Moggallāna," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the brahmin folk" (*brāhmaṇapajāya*), it means the folk from whom evil has been removed.
By the words "and the esteem for this folk," he shows that the word "esteem" (*purekkhāra*) in the expression "one who has no regard for evil" (*apāpapurekkhāro*) is the subject under discussion.

The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction: “Not only is there precedence for one who is free from evil, but there is also precedence for the brahminical class (*brahmaññāya pajāya*) which constitutes his own kin.
The passage beginning with “For this” (*ayañhi*) is merely an illustration of the underlying intention.
The phrase “one who is free from evil” (*apāpapurekkhāro*) must be construed specifically with the words “for the brahminical class”; it does not indicate a separate, independent meaning.
Showing that the meaning of "mind" (cetas) should also be understood by way of its natural (*pakati*) Brahmin caste, he said, "Furthermore...
and so forth. This is an irregular compound (*ayuttasamāsa*). "Evil" (*pāpa*) means evil karma; the sense is "harm" or "suffering.
Because it requires a correlative, in order to show the answer to the question "Of what is there an absence of precedence by evil? he stated, "Of what... and so forth. "By oneself," etc.
This is the explanation of its meaning. "Brāhmaṇa-pajā" means the progeny of the brāhmaṇa caste.

"Raṭṭha" is so called because kings delight (*rañjanti*) in it and resort to it for their welfare; it refers to the great provinces such as Kāsī and Kosala that constitute the kingdom of a single king.
"Janapada" is so called because people (*janā*) go forth (*pajjanti*) to it and attain a happy livelihood there; it refers to each individual constituent part within the kingdom of a single king.
The minor districts such as Uttarāpatha and Dakkhiṇāpatha. "Therein" means among those who have arrived in that manner.
"By way of questioning" means by means of a question formulated by oneself. "In the reception of the answer" means in the acceptance of the answer through one's own knowledge.

Having understood the excellence of the supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), the ripening of knowledge, and the mental disposition of certain individuals, the Blessed One himself [formulated] the question.
The intended meaning is that, having generated enthusiasm, he sends forth [speech].
“In this regard, what is gentleness? and so forth is the canonical text from the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa*. “Fatigue from the journey” means the exhaustion from traveling a long road.
“His” refers to the Blessed One; it is connected with “the lotus-face. “By the mere touch of the morning sun’s rays” means by the touch of the newly risen beams of the sun.
...as it were. For instance, the sun is well known in the world as the "friend of the lotuses" (*padmabandhu*), while the moon is known as the "friend of the night-lilies" (*kumudabandhu*).

Because its splendor is equal to the splendor of the full moon, it is called "possessing the splendor of the full moon" (*puṇṇacandasassirikam*). To explain how it is like something overturned, he says, "having arrived," and so forth.
Here, by the phrase "one who says 'Come, you are welcome,'" he indicates affectionate speech preceded by a pleasant greeting.
It should be understood that by the term "gentle" (*sakhila*), he shows softness of speech; by "friendly" (*sammodaka*), skill in welcoming;
by "not frowning" (*abbhākuṭika*), a countenance that is entirely serene in all circumstances; by "open-faced" (*uttānamukha*), ease of conversation;
and by "one who speaks first" (*pubbabhāsī*), an inclination toward welfare by creating the opportunity for assistance through the Dhamma.
Regarding the phrase *yattha kira*: here the particle *kira* indicates lack of approval—as in the verse:
“Those states which, due to the brevity of their momentary basis, do not enter the avenue of consciousness, are called ‘having mental phenomena as their object’;
those [objects] of theirs are, it is said (*kira*), visible forms and so forth.”

As in the *Abhidhammāvatāra-ṭīkā* (in the sixth section on the classification of objects, §77), this shows that in the place inhabited by that Blessed One, the absence of calamities for humans was not due to the power of deities, but rather due to the power of the Buddha;
for it is through the power of the Buddha alone that they provide protection. [The phrase] "the dust-demons (*paṃsupisācaka*) and so forth" refers to...
“Paṃsunissitapisācakādayo”: by the word “etc. (ādi), there is the inclusion of spirits (bhūta), rākṣasas, and so forth.
Now, in order to demonstrate the power of the Buddha himself as something manifest, it is said: “Furthermore,” and so on.

“The Saṅgha that is to be instructed” refers to the entire assembly of people who are to be converted. “The Saṅgha that has been produced by oneself” refers to the assembly of noble persons (ariyapuggala) who have been brought into existence.

Regarding the word “*tādiso*”: since it is understood that this refers back to the alternative mentioned as “*sayaṃ vā uppādito*,” and because the subsequent [word] functions as both an affirmation and a negation, the Teacher stated, “or rather, of the preceding word itself,” thereby including another alternative.
In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows: although “*gaṇī*” is indeed a synonym for the word “*saṅghī*,” it serves merely to clarify the sense.
However, in order to show this, by referring specifically to the second alternative within the two previously mentioned alternatives, it was stated, "He has such a group.

Thus, it was said, "Or rather, this is a synonym for the first word itself," in order to include the remaining first alternative as well. They also say this: [regarding] the individual leaders of groups, such as the Elder Dhammasenāpati and others.
The phrase beginning with "such as that" (*tādiso*) is stated with reference to either a group in general or a specific group such as those versed in the Suttantas.
For even there, the entire community of monks is said to be "instructed," whereas a noble community (*ariyagaṇa*) that has been produced is said to be "self-arisen.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the term "such as that" refers back to both of these two alternatives. Thus [is explained] the specific meaning of the two words.
Having shown this, in order to demonstrate that the meaning is identical in every respect, the phrase beginning with “of the very first word” was stated.

This genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*) from among the many founders of other sects, such as Pūraṇa Makkhali and others. “Even by the mere cause of being naked, etc.
means even by the mere reason of wearing no clothes and so forth, which is characterized by the attribution of qualities such as fewness of desires and contentment.
“Navakā” means new arrivals. “Pāhunakā” means those worthy of receiving hospitality;
by this, he shows that among the two kinds of guests, these are *atithis* (guests) because they arrived earlier, not *abbhāgatas* (visitors) because they arrived at the time of the meal.
“Pariyāpuṇāmi” means I know how to delimit [the number]; however, the word “jānāmi” (I know) was used merely to indicate the basic meaning of the verbal root.

"Even for an eon (*kappa*)" means even for the duration of a lifespan; this is how it connects with "he might speak. The construction is: "An eon would be exhausted over a long time, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted even over a long interval (*dīghamantare*), that is, even over a very long period.

And although "long" (*ciraṃ*) should have been used here, the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) is for the sake of metrical brevity out of fear of losing the meter; or else, referring to an exceedingly long time, it says "over a long and very long interval" (*ciradīghamantare*).

This has been stated; it should be connected to both instances. Just as in the case of a connection with a verb (*kiriyāraha*), etc., there is no fault in a line containing an extra syllable when there is a connection between [the words].
Furthermore, this verse was taught in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) by way of a figurative construction (*abhūtaparikappana*), because there is no one actually speaking in that manner.
305. *Naṃ* refers to the teacher (*ācariya*). Here, the word *alaṃ* has the sense of "worthy" (*arahattha*), as in such passages as "it is indeed enough to become disenchanted."
He said, “It is indeed appropriate. Because it is to be carried in a bundle (*puṭa*) and then eaten—that is, consumed—it is called *puṭosa*, meaning provisions for a journey (*pātheyya*).

By the phrase “having taken that,” he shows the instrumental case used in the sense of a characteristic mark of a state (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*). In the canonical text, the connection is shown by the words “by the son of good family with the shoulder-bundle (*puṭaṃsena*)”;
thus, the expression “with that shoulder-bundle (*tena puṭaṃsenā*)” is stated. The phrase “with the shoulder (*aṃsena*), etc. is merely an indication of the underlying intention (*adhippāyamatta*).
The meaning is that it is indeed appropriate for the son of good family who is carrying [the bowl] to approach.
Commentary on Soṇadaṇḍa’s Reflections (306–7).
Here, the word *tiro* does not have the same sense as in such passages as "he might discard it, or cause it to be discarded, behind a wall or behind a fence."

He said, "as if [the object] were outside," by the words "having gone into the forest thicket. Therein, he shows that even the monastery is included within the forest thicket by the phrase "having entered inside the monastery.

By this, it follows from the sense that those who sat down after raising their hands in reverential salutation were on both sides due to wrong view, whereas the others were on one side due to right view.
The intention is that those who were previously unknown by name or clan—due to poverty, the loss of kinsmen, and so forth, as well as being aged—desiring to become known, acted in this way.
*Kerāṭikā* means crafty. *Tattha* means among the two persons. *Tato* means from trust, or from giving.
The Explanation of the Designation of the Brahmin.

309. By way of having an unbending body, his limbs were rigid, not out of pride. Therefore, the text will say, “having raised [the body] up. With reference to mental thought (*cetovitakka*), it is stated by way of the head-word *citta* that “he knew the mind.
“Vexation” (*vighāta*) means mental suffering. 311. “In their own doctrine” (*sakasamaye*) refers to the Brahminical tenets. “Being measured” (*mīyamāno*) means being about to die.
“By the very perception of their view” means by the very perception of their own tenets. “Sujā” is a sacrificial ladle; the etymology has already been stated. “While they were taking” means...

The meaning is: "among those who take [the offerings] for the purpose of offering. For it is because they perform the *homa* sacrifice by means of the *iruvijjā* that the sacrificers and priests are called "iruvijjā.
"Or the first" refers to the one who is the most preeminent among those assembled there for the performance of the *sujā* rite.
"Or the second" refers to the one immediately following him. He said this because the word "sujam" is used in the accusative case in the sense of the instrumental.
"Sujāyā" means: because sacrifice has the fire-oblation as its head, that which is given in a sacrifice is given by way of the "sujā" (the sacrificial offering).
And it is said: "The fire-oblation is the head of sacrifices; the Sāvittī is the head of meters.

Therefore, the teacher stated that the word "being given" (*diyyamāna*) is understood as a textual supplement (*pāṭhasesa*). Furthermore, by way of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the meaning is that what is given by means of the *sujā* is called "sujā."

He spoke thus in order to show this. "The ancients" refers to the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā. Furthermore, in the former statement, the first or second [type] is by way of giving (*dāna*), while in the latter statement it is by way of taking (*ādāna*);

this is their distinction. "By way of distinction" means by way of the distinction between knowledge and conduct (*vijjācaraṇa*), not merely by way of the knowledge and conduct desired by the brahmins.
"Of the supreme brahmin" is said because of his being the unsurpassed recipient of offerings (*anuttara-dakkhiṇeyya*).
[This was said] to the brahmin Ukkhaṭṭha. For it was precisely in order to provide an occasion for the statement beginning with “But what, brahmin, is that brahmin conduct?

What is that wisdom?”—which is intended to illustrate the specific excellence of knowledge and conduct—that the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “But of these five factors, brahmin. Therefore, the connection [of the text] follows the primary statement.
It should be understood that the passage beginning with “The Blessed One, however,” was spoken in order to demonstrate this.
(313) “He refutes” means he speaks by setting aside [the categories of] beauty and so forth; however, to show the mere sense, it is said “he rejects.
“This” refers to the statement beginning with “Let the venerable Soṇadaṇḍa not speak thus. “The Brahmin system” means the established doctrine of the Brahmins.
"Do not break" means do not destroy.

"Being equal, he is equal" (*samova hutvā samo*) means he is equal in every respect; for the two prefixes (*pari-* and *ā-*) indicate an intensification of meaning, as in the expressions "suffering-suffering" (*dukkhadukkha*) or "form-form" (*rūparūpa*).
However, because he is equal to them even by way of a mere fraction, such as his small stature (*aṅgaka*), he is called "equal."
In order to turn him back, he said, "Except for a mere portion," and so forth. "An indication of the family's origin" means an indication of the beginning of the lineage.
Since [he would not know] his own sister... [and so on] ...he will not know, therefore he does not speak with reference merely to his mother and father;
rather, the intention is that he speaks with reference to an indication of the family's origin. By the phrase "one who destroys welfare,"...
He speaks of that which has reached the state of a path of action (*kammappatha*). "Guṇeti" refers to the five precepts as previously described. "Atha pi siyā" means:
even if such a reflection should occur to you—that even for one whose virtue is broken, if he again stands firm in natural virtue, his caste and so forth will be perfected—such might be the case;
this is the meaning of "siyā. In the reading "sādheti," the word "vaṇṇo" (caste) is supplied by the Teacher as the agent.
And this is an illustration. For the same principle applies even to the classes of mantras. "Virtue alone" means that virtue, in its natural state, will accomplish the state of a brahmin.
If one asks why, it is said: "For in that case... [omission] ...the complexion and so forth.

Therein, "the complexion and so forth" refers to the misconception that complexion, mantras, and birth are factors for the state of a brahmin; this is merely a delusion, spoken without due reflection.
Commentary on the Discussion of Virtue and Wisdom (Sīlapaññākathāvaṇṇanā):
317. "The question asked by the brahmin" means that the question, as it was asked, has been answered exactly as it stands by way of these two factors alone, beginning with the words "He is virtuous.
"In this" refers to the meaning thus explained, namely, in the pair of factors.
"Of him" means of Soṇadaṇḍa. If he were to set aside even one factor, then he would not be able to establish [the doctrine];
but if he were not to set aside any, then he would be able. He spoke thus for the very purpose of investigating whether or not he would be able to do so;
it is not said that one particular factor must necessarily be set aside. Likewise...
And he said, "It is even so, O brahmin," and so forth. Regarding the statement "it is purified by washing," he said, "purified in virtue" (*sīlaparisuddhā*);

the meaning is that they are entirely pure and unstained by means of the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampatti*). From where [could there be] wisdom in one who is immoral? Because of his lack of concentration.
Or from where could there be virtue in one who is dull and mute, being devoid of wisdom? For virtue is the classification [of conduct] and the means for purifying virtue.
And because of not knowing. "One whose saliva (eḷa) drips from the mouth" is *eḷamūga*; by changing the letter *kha* to *ga*, it becomes *elamukha* or *elamūka*.
Thus, there are many readings, as stated in the commentary on the *Bhayabherava Sutta*.
Having taken *paññāṇa* to mean "exalted" or "superior" knowledge (*ñāṇa*), the term is used to exclude ordinary knowledge; for [it refers to] insight and other such forms of knowledge.
This is what is intended here; because it knows by way of various modes, it is called "wisdom" (paññā), thus he said, "by wisdom alone.

"Washed by the fourfold purification of virtue" means washed—that is, purified—by the fourfold purification of virtue, which has concentration as its proximate cause, through the cleansing of all defilements and stains.
Therefore he said, "But how? and so forth. In that context, "washes" means it is purified. "Sixty-eight years" means...
For sixty years or eighty years—at the time of death, let alone at any other time.
"Like the Great Sixty-Year Elder" means like a great elder of sixty years. "Even the mere discernment of feeling":

here, "discernment of feeling" means that after one has examined a feeling as it arises according to its own intrinsic nature and essence, one further examines it from the standpoint of its proximate cause, thinking, "This is feeling..."
“Dependent upon contact, [feeling] arises; and that contact is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.
Having thus applied the three characteristics, insight (vipassanā) has proceeded. For one who sees in this way, it is possible to endure that feeling with ease, thinking, “Feeling itself feels.
“Having suppressed the feeling” means having followed along with the arisen painful feeling as it occurs.
Having begun insight meditation and having dispelled that [hindrance] by means of insight that has entered its proper course.
"By one fallen into a pit of thorns" means by one lying on the ground with the chest down, like a *kumbhīla* (a type of demon).

He says "I am not," etc., making it clear that guarding virtue in such a manner is indeed difficult. For for one established in virtue, *arahantship* is as good as already in the palm of the hand. As it is said:
“Established in virtue... [etc. ...one should unravel the tangle”—this is the domain specifically of the person who gains knowledge through what is suggested (*ugghāṭitaññū*).

Therefore, he says, “by means of being one who gains knowledge through what is suggested. “Having washed virtue with wisdom” means having made virtue thoroughly purified by wisdom through bringing it to a state of being unbroken and so forth in its beginning, middle, and end.
This is the story of the minister Santati in the *Dhammapada*.
318. “Why did he say so?”—with these words, he asks for the reason behind the subsequent instruction.
“Shame” (*lajjā*) means being recognized by the assembly as one who has answered the questions posed by the ascetic Gotama by disclosing his virtue, birth, and qualities or faults;
the meaning is that this [reputation] will be destroyed because of his inability to answer in such a manner. Even though he was previously without shame, now...

"It will be shameful" is what is meant. "Supreme" (parama) means the limit or measure. The phrase "we are such as these" is used to show the grammatical coreferentiality (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) of the words;
thus it is said, "those we [are]. This is what is meant: the mere mention of "virtue and wisdom" is our supreme [measure];
having extracted the five precepts—which constitute that purpose—and wisdom, which clarifies the three Vedas, by way of their defining characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), etc., [one understands them].
There is no knowing; we consider that there is merely the limit of what has been expressed in words. Here, however, is the method not found in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*):
"The limit of this much" means the limit of excellence is this much; the sense is that the first answer to the question itself is our highest point of excellence.
Therefore he said, "The question was answered by me according to my own system. "Beyond" (*para*) means exceeding. "Of what was spoken" (*bhāsitassa*) refers to the speech, the sound.
This, however, is the distinction: it is stated in the *Sīlaniddesa* (Description of Virtue) with reference merely to the act of handing over. Therefore he said, "Virtue alone is handed over.
For in the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, although virtue was handed over, the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) were subsequently handed over as well.

Since all sublime states of consciousness (*mahaggata-citta*) are associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*), and since the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are associated with that [knowledge], [it is said] "in terms of meaning..."

“Perfection of wisdom,” it is said. For in the Exposition of Wisdom (*Paññāniddesa*), having taken the wisdom of meditative absorption (*jhānapaññā*) as the foundation, the wisdom of insight (*vipassanāpaññā*) is presented first.
Therefore he says, “by means of the wisdom of insight,” and so forth. This concludes the commentary on the account of the lay follower Soṇadaṇḍa’s declaration of his status.
321. Regarding the phrase *daharo yuvā*: here, by the word *dahara*, the state of early youth is indicated. For one who has reached the time of early youth is called "a youth" (*dahara*).
*Nattā* means a grandson (*puttassa putto*). *Nappahoti* means it does not suffice; the meaning is that even the measure of sons and grandsons is not attained.
To demonstrate the logical consequence of the statement "My rising from my seat [is for him]," he says "out of lack of respect for me," and so forth.
It has been said. "This" refers to the grasping of the hands in reverence (añjalipaggahaṇa).
For he wanders about seeking to procure gain by creating esteem for himself among the multitude in whatever way possible and by deceiving others through hypocrisy;

therefore, showing his extreme state of being a deceiver, he says, "By this, it is said," and so forth. "There is no lack of respect" is a statement regarding the absence of disrespect (agāravavacana).
It is not that he spoke the words beginning with "But as for me" out of disrespect toward the Blessed One;
rather, it is said that he spoke them solely out of fear of the loss of his own gains.
"Appropriate to that moment" means: by the elision of the middle term (*majjhepadalopa*), it means "in accordance with whatever state of intention (*ajjhāsayappavatti*) he had at that time."

The meaning [is as follows]. At that time, because such ripening of knowledge based on the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*) was absent, only the welfare based on worldly prosperity (*abbhuddaya*) was shown;
thus he said, "having demonstrated the welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life," which means having made it manifest through direct perception.
"Wholesome states" (*kusale dhamme*) refers to wholesome states belonging to the three planes; this is the sense here.

This is the meaning according to the direct method (*nippariyāyato*). However, according to the figurative method (*pariyāyato*), it is also appropriate to say "in the four planes" (*catubhūmake*), because even supramundane wholesome states (*lokuttarakusala*) are obtainable in the future.
For he will say: "for the sake of nibbāna in the future, or for that which partakes of the residual impression (*vāsanā*).
"Therein" (*tattha*) means in wholesome states as they have been undertaken. "Him" (*naṃ*) refers to the brahmin Soṇadaṇḍa. "Having encouraged" (*samuttejetvā*)...
Having reflected properly again and again, and having brought about a state of sharpness and intensity toward the performance of meritorious deeds.
As for that, in its actual meaning, it is simply the generation of enthusiasm therein; thus he said, "having made it enthusiastic.
And by that state of enthusiasm—meaning that such enthusiasm for the performance of meritorious deeds necessarily accomplishes aims pertaining to the present life and so forth—as stated above.
"And having encouraged him with encouragement" (*saussāhatāya ca sampahaṃsetvā*) is the grammatical connection.
"And with other existing qualities" means that such possession of qualities by him is exclusively productive of welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth;
thus, the meaning is: having encouraged him with other existing qualities, having properly brought about a state of joy and satisfaction.
To resolve the objection—"If the Blessed One rained down the rain of the Dhamma-jewel, why then did he not attain distinction?"—the passage beginning with "But the brahmin...
was spoken. "Because of his craftiness" means because of his deceitful nature according to the method already stated;
by this, he shows the absence of success in his application. If this is so, why did the Blessed One rain down the rain of the Dhamma-jewel for him in such a manner?
Regarding the word *vassī* (eloquent), in order to clear away any further objection, he said, "It is exclusively his," and so forth.

Therein, *kevalaṃ* means unmixed with that which pertains to penetration (*nibbedha*) or the wings of higher training (*asekkha*). *Nibbānatthāya* means for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, or for the sake of final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*).

*Vāsanābhāgiyā* means that which pertains to the habituation consisting of the cultivation of meritorious deeds—which serves as the means for attaining distinction in the future; it is called "pertaining to habituation" because it occurs as such a means.
For there is not even a single four-line stanza of the Blessed One’s teaching on the Dhamma that is without purpose. Therefore he said:
"All the discourse from beginning to end. Here, the "prior discourse" extends from the start up to the conclusion of the brahmin’s reply;
however, the Blessed One’s exposition on virtue and wisdom is the "subsequent discourse," even though it was spoken by the brahmin.
For indeed, discourses connected with the qualities of the Buddha and so forth are conducive to the impression (*vāsanā*) for the sake of Nibbāna in the future. The remainder is easy to understand.

Thus ends the elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, within the *Līnatthappakāsinī*—the "Expositor of the Hidden Meaning"—a sub-commentary to the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which illuminates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend, and which generates the clarity of perfectly pure and vast wisdom, and is named the "Graceful One" (*Sādhuvilāsini*).
The commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta is finished.
5. Commentary on the Kūṭadanta Sutta: 323.
Having thus commented upon the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta, now, following the proper sequence, while commenting upon the Kūṭadanta Sutta...
In order to clarify that the opportunity for commentary has been reached, or to indicate that the *Kūṭadanta Sutta* was recited immediately after the *Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta*, he said:
"Thus have I heard... [pe] ...in Magadha: the *Kūṭadanta Sutta*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Magadhans were princes of the realm," this refers to the description of the Kosala country in the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta*.
The method we have explained should be applied accordingly. However, there is this distinction here: they are called *Magadhā* because they run along the path (*maga*), namely the princes;
or, according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), they are called *Magadhā* because they greedily long for meats (*maṃsa*).

According to the grammarians (*neruttikā*), even though the name refers to the country where they dwell—due to conventional usage (*ruḷhi*) and the elision of suffixes—the plural form does not apply. The plural is used only for the name of the country itself.
It is stated that the word "country" (*janapada*) is not synonymous with the word "caste" (*jāti*), as it says: "in that country of Magadha.
"From here onwards" refers to the passage beginning with "while wandering on tour," which follows the word "in Magadha. "In the two preceding suttas" refers to the *Ambaṭṭha* and *Soṇadaṇḍa* suttas.

"In the same manner as stated" means that whatever has been included here that is similar to what appeared there, its method of explanation is exactly as it was stated in the commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*).
It is said that this should be understood according to the method already stated.
Because it was stated in the *Brahmajāla-sutta-vaṇṇanā* that "the young mango tree is the *ambalaṭṭhikā*," he says, "The *ambalaṭṭhikā* is similar to what is described in the *Brahmajāla*.
Having prepared a sacrificial enclosure, for the purpose of a great sacrifice, [he gathered] both animate and inanimate sacrificial requisites.
The phrase "prepared" (*upaṭṭhapitāni*) is stated in the *pāḷi* as "the great sacrifice has been set out" (*mahāyañño upakkhaṭo*) with reference to its purpose;
however, by the word "arranged" (*sajjito*), it shows that these requisites were indeed prepared for them in that manner.

"A hundred young bulls" (*vacchatarasatāni*) refers to a hundred strong, youthful bulls. For they are called "young bulls" (*vacchatara*) because they are a specific class of calves (*vaccha*). And those calves...
“They are thus [calves], not bulls, nor even oxen,” he said, using the term “vacchasatāni” (hundreds of calves). This is the opinion of the Teacher (Ācariya).
Alternatively, the word *tara* is said to be meaningless; thus it is stated as “vacchasatāni. For in this way, the entire classification of calves is included.

“These” refers to those beginning with the bull and ending with the ram. “Of many kinds” means of various species. “Of beasts and birds” refers to the *mahiṃsa*, *ruru*, *sasa*, *kuruṅga*, *gokaṇṇa* deer, and so forth.
And of birds such as peacocks, partridges, quails, and lapwings.
By way of number, their manifoldness is delimited by the mention of "seven hundred," which is expressed as "seven times seven hundred"; the meaning is seven hundred and seven hundred.
*Thūṇa* refers to the tethering post for the deer and birds used as sacrificial offerings; *yūpa* is also a name for it.
Therefore he said, "reckoned as a sacrificial post.

328. *Vidhā* means the dispelling of remorse. For that which is the defilement of merit reckoned as sacrifice—because it dispels, wards off, and suppresses that [defilement]—it is called *vidhā*, namely, the dispelling of remorse; these very things constitute the outflow of merit.
It is called "establishment" (*ṭhapanā*) because it establishes [the sacrifice] without interruption. For it is precisely from non-regret that an ever-increasing flow of merit proceeds.
And since this establishment occurs in three ways according to the beginning, middle, and end of the sacrifice—that is, throughout the three periods—it is called "thrice-establishing" (*tiṭṭhapana*).
Furthermore, the word *parikkhāra* here is a synonym for "retinue" (*parivāra*), as in the phrase "they surround the sacrifice."
Having considered that they "are performing [the sacrifice]," he therefore said, "accompanied by sixteen [attendants].
Regarding the commentary on the Discourse on the Sacrifice of King Mahāvijitī: 336.
He said, "former conduct" (*pubbacarita*), meaning that which was previously become or occurred in the past, just as one says "previously seen. [This refers to] his own...
The meaning is: "meritorious conduct" (puññacariyā) that arose in previous births and served as the equipment for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra).
For thus, the illustration by means of a stable treasure (thāvaranidhi) is appropriate for that following treasure (anugāminidhi). However, those learned in grammar say:
"'Bhūtapubbaṃ' is a derivative word (nepātika-pada) formed from the locative case of time. According to their opinion, the meaning is "in past time. "Assa" means "by him."
The connection is: "the great circle of the earth is his conquest. Alternatively, the meaning is: "he has a great conquered realm that is a circle of the earth.
For the word *vijita* (conquest/realm) occurs here in the sense of a kingdom, as in such passages as, "within his own kingdom," "in the kingdom of him who dwells in his conquest," and so forth;
by this, he indicates his status as a single king, not his status as a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*).

Because the state of being endowed with the seven treasures (*sattaratanasampannatā*) was not explicitly mentioned. In the *Pāḷi*, after saying "wealthy" (*aḍḍho*) to show that one is not considered wealthy merely by possessing some small amount of property, it says "of great wealth" (*mahaddhano*). Therefore, he said "anyone whatsoever," and so forth.

For what is called "wealthiness" (*aḍḍhatā*) consists in being endowed with prosperity (*vibhava*), and that is predicated in relation to this or that [specific possession]. Likewise, "great wealth" (*mahaddhanatā*) refers to that which has reached its full measure and attained its highest excellence.

He said "by an immeasurable number" in order to show this. He shows that, in the sense of being something to be enjoyed, sensual pleasures (kāmā) are specifically what are called "possessions" (bhogā) here, by means of the phrase "by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure.
"By way of lumps" means not by way of distinctions such as vessels, ornaments, and so forth, but solely by way of individual pieces.

A *māsaka* is that which is made by means of a measure of one month, whether by applying [the value] to physical form (*rūpa*) or not. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), items such as bowls (*thālaka*) and so forth are included.
"By a number of many tens of millions" is said with reference to a measure of hundreds of millions (*koṭi*) of *kahāpaṇas* and so on;
for at the very minimum, it is by a measure of hundreds of millions that the status of a great noble *khattiya* is attained.
*Tuṭṭhi* means gladness (*somanatā*). Here, the word *upakaraṇa* is used in the sense of a cause (*kāraṇa*). To the question "What, then, is it? he says:
"It consists of various kinds of ornaments and vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), clothing, bedding, dwellings, and the like are included.
They say that there are seven treasures: gold, silver, gems, pearls, beryl, diamonds, and coral. As it has been said:
“Gold, silver, pearls, gems, beryl, diamonds, and coral—these are the seven jewels,” so it is said.

The seven kinds of grain, beginning with *sāli* rice and *vīhi* rice, together with their corresponding varieties, are called *pubbanna*; they are designated as such because they are the first-fruits of the harvest.

By way of its opposite, mung beans and so forth are called "other grain" (*aparanna*). Grain that occurred before other grain is "earlier grain" (*pubbanna*), while grain that occurs after it is "later grain" (*aparanna*).
However, when the letter *n* is changed to *ṇ*, etymologists (*neruttika*) say it becomes *pubbaṇṇa* and *aparaṇṇa*.
As for their sequence of priority and posteriority, it is based on whether they were possible or impossible during the First Eon (*ādikappa*).

This should be understood. The previous statement, “wealthy, possessing great riches, with abundant gold and silver,” was spoken in reference to daily expenditures, the receiving of gifts, and so forth, as well as to the circulation of wealth and grain;

however, this statement, “possessing abundant wealth and grain,” refers to wealth stored in hoards and grain kept in reserve—it is with reference to this distinction that this method is shown. Even the daily use of twenty kārṣāpaṇas, cowries, and so forth...
For this is the characteristic of a great *sāla* tree.
Now, in order to show the distinction by way of its opposite, the second method beginning with "Alternatively" (*atha vā*) is commenced.

For it is precisely by means of this that the previous statement was spoken in terms of wealth stored as a hoard and in terms of grain gathered together; thus, [the meaning] is established through the sense.
This is established. In this context, "this" refers to the statement "possessing abundant wealth and grain. "His" refers to King Mahāvijita.
"Daily" (*devasikaṃ*) means that which is to be enjoyed day by day; this is a neuter abstract noun.

"The granting of wages" refers to the provision of subsistence for slaves, laborers, servants, and so forth. "The taking up and acquisition of wealth and grain" occurs by way of clearing debts and other such means.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of lending money and so forth is intended.

"By way of wealth and grain for exchange" means by way of the wealth and grain that are to be exchanged through the act of buying and selling. However, in some places a reading devoid of the conjunction (*samuccaya*) is seen.
In that case, the phrase "by way of giving and taking provisions" (*paribbayadānaggahaṇādivasena*) should be connected with the term "exchange" (*parivattana*); such being the case—
The meaning should be understood as being by way of the wealth and grain that must be turned over from here and there according to rule.
A *koṭṭha* is called a place for storing grain; that itself is likewise an *agāra*. Therefore he said: "a storehouse full of grain.
Having thus shown that the inner core is a treasury (*kosa*) and the place for storing grain is a granary (*koṭṭhāgāra*), he now [shows] otherwise than that.
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “Alternatively” was stated.

In that context, just as the equipment that protects a sword from losing its sharpness is called its “sheath,” so too, because it preserves the king’s own sharpness (power), the fourfold army is called his “treasury. Thus he says, “The treasury is fourfold,” and so on.
Furthermore, the elephants and other components here are defined by the characteristics stated in such passages as, “A chariot consists of twelve men,” and so forth.

It should be understood as follows: Since the mention of "storehouse" and "treasury" already includes every place where perishable goods (*kuppabhaṇḍa*) are kept, it is stated that "the storehouse is threefold," and so forth.

For anything other than gold and silver—such as iron, copper, wood, horn, cloth, and so on—which is not of intrinsic value (*asāradabba*) but is to be guarded, is called *kuppa* by changing the letter *ga* to *ka*. The storage of gold and silver is the "treasury of wealth" (*dhanakoṭṭhāgāra*).
"Ratanavilokanacārikā" means wandering about while looking for jewels here and there.
Granted that the king already knows this matter, he nevertheless asks thus after having consulted with the treasurer, solely for the purpose of ensuring that the assembly remains silent.
For if he were not to have it announced in this way, the assembly would make noise, saying, "Why does the king [act thus]?"—[referring to] what has been handed down through tradition.

"He destroys the family wealth. From that, there will be an agitation of the natural state; however, if he speaks in such a way, [the other] will think, "He abandons it for this reason," and thus will fall into silence. Consequently, there will be no agitation of the natural state;
therefore, it should be understood that he asks in such a manner. "The domain of death" means of death, or the object characterized as death.
337. Regarding the word "having addressed" (*āmantetvā*) in the Pāli, the phrase "having consulted with one wise man" is stated in order to clarify its meaning as "desiring to consult.

For here, the prefix follows the root-meaning, and in certain instances, a specific sense is understood from the context, such as: "Monks, by a monk who is training, it should be known and inquired about..."
"It should be asked. For thus it is said in the word-commentary (padabhājana): "By one who is training means by one who desires to train;
'to be known' means to be understood," and so forth. "He addressed" means he desired to deliberate.

The brahmin reflected for the sake of ensuring there were no calamities in the country and for the sake of the long-term performance of the sacrifice; thus he said, "This king," and so forth. "Of those bringing [the offerings]..."
The connection is with "the houses of people," or this genitive case is used in the sense of disregard.
Because they spoil the welfare and happiness of beings and bring about harm and suffering, they are like thorns;
thus, thieves themselves are called "thorns" here, as in the phrase "thorny with thorns that are thieves. Just as those who kill the village-dwellers [are called thorns].
"Village-destroyers" refers to those who cause division and those who act through intimidation, because even though they reside [in the village], they operate by means of its vicinity;

likewise, "road-robbers" are those who plunder and harass travelers on the road. One who is habitually disposed to do what is contrary to the Dhamma and improper is an "unrighteous-doer" (*adhammakārī*).
Alternatively, it is the duty of a Kṣatriya to protect his own realm, such as the countryside and so forth, from various kinds of harm.

The meaning is that he has the habit of not committing it. "Dassū" is a designation for thieves; for they "sting" (daṃsenti) and "pierce" (viddhaṃsenti), thus they are called *dassavo* through the elision of the nasal (*niggahīta*).
Because they are like stakes (*khīla*), they are called *khīla*; thus, it is a "thief-stake" (*dassukhīla*).
For just as a stake in a field obstructs the easy progress of plowing and so forth, and hinders the growth of the crop through its root-system, [so too does this thief-stake].

In this way, even one who possesses vision [of the truth] obstructs the occurrence of happiness through royal command over the kingdom, as well as the growth of the countryside through the flourishing of its roots.
To show the sacrifice of life, it is said "by killing"; to show injury, it is said "by beating. For the word *vadhā* (killing) also has the sense of injuring, as in such passages as:
"He strikes; he does not weep; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so forth.
The meaning is: by means of beating with wooden blocks (*kappara*) and so forth. *Addu* is a specific type of binding apparatus made from a block of wood;
binding with that is what is meant here. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes binding with ropes, binding with chains, binding in a house, and so on.
With the phrase "by way of loss" (*hāniyā*), he shows the derivation of the word from the verbal root *hā*; and that [loss] refers specifically to the depletion of wealth.
It is said: “Seize a hundred,” and so forth.
Shaving with the exception of the five locks is called *pañcasikhamuṇḍakaraṇa*. This is also commonly referred to as *kākapakkhakaraṇa* (making [the hair] like a crow’s wing).
Pouring dung-water on the head is *gomayasiñcana*. A *kudaṇḍaka* is four cubits long.
The short staff is deficient, which is also called a "gaddula"; binding with that is "binding with a short staff.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of shaving the head, smearing with ashes, flogging, and so forth. The word *sammā* has the sense of "knowing" (*ñāya*), thus he says "by a cause" (*hetunā*) and so on;
this is a synonymous expression. "I shall remove" (*ūhanissāmi*) means I shall pull out, I shall take away; previously, in that regard...
