They exert effort because they have become familiar with the practice. Regarding the phrase "let him bestow," the meaning is "let him bestow repeatedly";
it is with reference to this that the words "when what has been given is not sufficient" and so forth were spoken.

By the mention of "the implements and goods for ploughing"—such as the plough, the goad, the yoke, and the pole—it is shown that in the text only seed and food are mentioned by way of illustration. [This refers to] the making of witnesses, the recording on leaf-plates, and the binding [of the agreement].

When one wishes to take [the property] again, whether with or without an increase, it constitutes giving; however, in this case, neither of those two conditions exists because there is no desire to take it again.
Therefore, it is said, "without making a witness," and so forth. For that reason, he said, "by way of cutting off the root.
"A witness" refers to a person who was an eyewitness at that time. "Without recording on a leaf" means by way of writing as was customary on leaves of the *tāla* tree and other such plants.
"Without having added. The word *pābhata* is used elsewhere for a gift (*paṇṇākāra*), but here it refers specifically to the cost of goods;

thus he says, "of the cost of goods," and so forth. For the cost of goods is called *pābhata* because by means of it one brings (*ābharati*) or gathers (*saṃharati*) various kinds of merchandise for profit.
Etymologists say that *pābhata* is that which has already been brought (*ābhata*) even before the wealth from profit; however, a gift is that which is brought by those who desire its purpose.
“*Pābhataṃ*. For this prefix *pa-* indicates the sense of “intention” (*patthana*).

With the words “As it is said,” etc., he establishes that the word *pābhata* has the meaning of “original stock” (*mūlabhaṇḍa*) by means of the reading from the *Cūḷaseṭṭhi-jātaka*. In that regard, the commentary says:

“Even with a little” (*appakenapi*) means even with a small amount or a trifling amount. “The wise one” (*medhāvī*) means one possessed of wisdom (*paññavā*). “With his merchandise” (*pābhatenāti*)...
"By means of merchandise. "Discerning" (*vicakkhaṇo*) means skilled in trade.
"He raises himself up" means that by generating great wealth and fame, he establishes and settles himself therein. How is this like what?
"Like a tiny fire being fanned": just as a wise man, taking a small fire, gradually adds cow-dung powder and other materials [to increase it].
Just as one blowing with the breath of the mouth fans it up, increases it, and makes it into a great mass of fire,
even so the wise man, having obtained even a small amount of income, employs various means to increase both wealth and fame;
and having increased them, he establishes himself therein, or else by that very greatness of wealth and fame—
"It raises oneself up; the meaning is that it makes one well-known and famous.
"Daily" means what is to be given day by day. "Monthly" means what is to be given month by month. By the word "etcetera," [the text] includes the fortnightly offerings and so forth.
"Of each respective person" means according to their skill, according to their work, and according to their courage.
The word *anurūpa*, which follows the pair [of terms] and is heard [there], should be construed with each [member].
And here, "conformity to the state of being skilled" (*chekabhāvānurūpatā*) means conformity to skill (*kusalānurūpaṃ*). In some places the word *kula* is seen;

and that is indeed appropriate because it must be given in accordance with the family, just as in the case of the *Jāṇusōṇi* and other families. "High positions such as general" (*senāpaccādi-ṭhānantaraṃ*)—by this, the food and wages are merely indicated.
[The text] shows this. Because he was intent on his own work and because his wealth and grain were free from calamity, he was a hoarder—one who made a heap.
"Established in safety" means existing without misfortune. Therefore it says "fearless," the meaning of which is being devoid of fear from any quarter.
"Rejoicing with joy" means rejoicing through joy; they rejoice solely with mental gladness (*somanassa*), not merely by way of socializing—thus it is said.
It occurs [thus]. For in such phrases as “he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One,” the word *muda* also functions in the sense of meeting;
or alternatively, the meaning is: “others having become joyful (*modā*), others too dwell being joyful (*modamānā*). Therefore he said: “With minds mutually delighted.

Even in the absence of physical contact, the desire for speech itself constitutes growth; thus two readings have been stated. “The state of being suffused with success” means the state of abundant fulfillment.
Commentary on the Four Requisites (Catuparikkhāravaṇṇanā) 339.
They are called *anuyantā* because they follow and conform to this or that duty. These very things are also called *ānuyantā*, just as "power" (*anubhāva*) is the same as "great power" (*ānubhāva*).
There is also the reading *ānuyuttā*; for they are called *ānuyuttā* because they are devoted to this or that duty.
In the manner already stated. *Assa* means "of the king. *Te* refers to the subordinate kṣatriyas and others.
They will not be pleased [thinking], "He is excluding us from here. "The arrival of a large number of dependent people constitutes a village (*gāma*) or a market town (*nigama*).

A place with greatly increased revenue is a great village (*mahāgāma*)," so it was said by the Teacher. "A market town (*nigama*) is one without a surrounding wall or enclosure but with shops; a city (*nagara*) has both walls and shops; that which is the opposite of these is a town (*pura*)."
"Village" (*gāmo*)—this should be consulted in the *Kuladūsaka-sikkhāpada* of the *Saṅghādisesa-khaṇḍa* in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-abhinavaṭīkā*, as well as in the *Vinaya-ṭīkās*.

It is called a "village" (*gāmo*) because people (*ga*) go (*ganti*) and rejoice (*madanti*) there. If that very [place] is well-known, it is called a "market town" (*nigama*), being considered a village with an excess [of inhabitants].
Here, the prefix *nī-* has the sense of "intensity," and because it is a technical term (*saññā-sadda*), it is shortened according to the grammarians. Its meaning is "province" (*janapada*).

It has already been stated: "The counselor, the friend, the treasury, the fortress, the conquest, and the army"—among these seven royal constituents mentioned, there is an increase in welfare and happiness for the king through the remaining six, and the followers and so forth are but a portion of those;
thus he said, "Whatever belongs to you," and so on.
They are called *amaccā* because they exist together with (*amā*) the king in their respective duties.
Grammarians explain that, as in the word *amāvāsī*, the indeclinable particle *amā* signifies "together" through shared action, and the formation is established by the suffix *-ca*.
Furthermore, the phrase "dear companions" (*piyasahāyakā*) indicates that at the time when royal duties are concluded, they remain dear to the king and continue to act in concert with him.
Those in the king’s assembly are called "councillors" (*pārisajjā*). As for who they are, it is said:
"The rest are executors of commands," meaning those remaining besides the aforementioned kṣatriyas and others who are devoted [to him], who carry out the king’s orders.

Even if there is wealth to be given, if there is a lack of majesty and a lack of a retinue, one is unable to give such things. Furthermore, in old age, even for such kings, both of these qualities surely decline.
In order to show that [one should give] even more so when there is no gift to be given, he said, "When there is a gift to be given," and so forth.

The construction is: "When there is no gift to be given, and when one is advanced in age, it is not possible to give. "By this" means by the two aforementioned reasons. "By consent" means by granting permission.
"Partisans" means those belonging to one's own side who constitute the constituent parts of the sacrifice. "They prepare the sacrifice" means...
The requisites and the materials, because they constitute parts of that sacrifice, are like its attendants; thus he says, "they become attendants.
By the words "chariot," etc., he negates the meaning not intended here:
"A chariot with white equipment, with meditation as its axle and vigor as its wheels..."
“Equanimity is the concentration of the burden;
non-desire is the protection,” so it is said in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, Mahāvagga. Therein, “chariot” refers to the chariot of the Eightfold Path, known as the Brahma-vehicle.
“White equipment” refers to the ornament of the fourfold purification of virtue (*sīla*); there is also a reading, “equipment of virtue. “Flame of jhāna”... [text fragment]
The axle made of jhāna consists of the five jhāna factors associated with insight (*vipassanā*). The wheel of energy (*vīriya-cakka*) refers to the wheel of energy.
Equanimity as the yoke and concentration (*upekkhā-dhura-samādhi*) means that equanimity is the balance between the two yokes.
Non-craving as the fender (*anicchā-parivāraṇa*) means that non-greed (*alobha*) acts as a protective fender, just like the lion’s quality (*sīhadhamma*) and so forth.
Commentary on the Eight Requisites (Aṭṭhaparikkhāravaṇṇanā) 340.
By the words "well-born in both ways" and so forth; by "glory" (yasasā), it means by fivefold majesty. Therefore he said: "Because of the capacity for issuing commands.
To show the meaning of the word "faithful" (saddho), namely, "he experiences the fruit of giving and he has conviction," [the text continues].
“Of giving,” and so forth, was said. One who is brave in giving is a “giving-hero” (*dānasūra*); one who is freely generous, without forming even the slightest attachment to the object to be given.
That state, however, should be understood as resulting from the sharp and keen nature of the knowledge that one’s own actions are one’s own property (*kammassakatā-ñāṇa*).
Indeed, it should be seen that the term “hero of giving” was stated after saying “sound” in order to clarify its sharp and keen nature. Therefore he said, “not by mere faith,” and so forth.

For one to whom the fact that one is the owner of one’s own kamma stands as if before one’s very eyes, it is said thus. "Whatever gift he gives" means whatever object of giving he bestows upon another.
"Being its master" means he gives while thoroughly overcoming greed regarding that object, acting as its sovereign;
for this is a figurative expression based on the cause. The same method applies to the subsequent phrases as well, according to their respective objects.
Because he cannot be drawn away by greed, he is neither a slave nor a companion.

Showing this very point by way of both contrast (*vyatireka*) and agreement (*anvaya*), he says, "For whoever... and so forth. Here, there is a demonstration by way of contrast with the two types [of persons], the slave and so on, which are not intended.
This is because, among solid foods (*khādanīya*), soft foods (*bhojanīya*), and the like, only that which is sweet is considered excellent.
"‘She eats sweetly’—this is said as a mere illustration; it means she enjoys what is refined.
She gives while being a slave because she has entered into slavery through craving. She gives while being a friend because she does not relinquish her state of affection for him.
She gives while being a master because, having freed herself from the slavery of craving therein and having overcome it, she acts with mastery. That which...
As for this statement by the Teacher, “similar to the enjoyment of an owner,” it was said with reference to the commonality of having transcended the state of being a slave to craving.

For it is not tenable that the enjoyment of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is like the enjoyment of an owner, nor does the sense that “the gift belongs only to the one whose taints are destroyed” hold as the meaning of the phrase “owner of the gift.
Alternatively, this may have been written later by mistake. “Such” refers to the nature of the material object of the gift.
The *samitapāpa* ascetics and *bāhitapāpa* brahmins are mentioned here by way of the highest standard;

alternatively, it should be understood that those who are merely ordained as ascetics or merely born into the caste of brahmins are included under the mention of the "wretched" and so forth. "Destitute" (*duggata*) means those who have entered upon a difficult livelihood, whose mode of existence is arduous;
hence he said, "poor people. "Travelers" (*pathāvino*) means those going on a journey. "Beggars" (*vaṇibbaka*) refers to them by way of praising the virtues of the donors.

And in order to show the meaning—that beggars are like those who practice naked asceticism and so forth by way of describing the fruits of kamma—it was said, "Those who have given what is desired," and so on. For it is through both of these [the giver and the recipient] that the praise of giving arises.
It should be construed thus: "Those who wander about are called 'mendicants' (vaṇibbaka). "A mere *pasata*" refers to a measure of rice grains and the like.

It is said, "the measure of a bowl" (*sarāvamattaṃ*) by way of rice gruel, food, and so forth. A "drinking place" (*opānaṃ*) is called a ford (*titthaṃ*) common to all, such as rivers, lakes, and the like, because one must descend into it to drink;
that which has become like a drinking place is "become a drinking place" (*opānabhūto*). Therefore he said, "become a well" (*udapānabhūto*), and so on.

"Having been" (*hutvā*) refers to its state of being. He states that the word *jāta* expresses no difference in meaning from *suta* in the phrase "what was heard is itself 'heard-born'" (*sutameva sutajātaṃ*), just as in the expression "born of a sheath" (*kosajātaṃ*).
The capacity for contemplating the meaning of the past and so forth should be understood as belonging to that king by way of inference and by way of what ought to be done;
it is not, however, through direct perception of those matters as possessed by the Buddhas. To show this, the words beginning with "in the past" were spoken.
And here, the contemplation of the results of merit and demerit should be understood according to what has been established in this treatise. Of merit...
Regarding "of the sacrifice and merit": "the mind of the donor" means either the minds of the donors, or the mind that is the donor;

what is meant is "even the mind desiring to give. Now, among these eight factors, let the five beginning with wealth be the requisites for the sacrifice first, since it cannot be accomplished without them. But how are being well-born and having handsome limbs a requisite for the sacrifice?
In response to the objection that it might be accomplished even without both of these, he says, "For it is said that these...
and so forth, demonstrating through both positive (anvaya) and negative (vyatireka) concomitance that all eight factors constitute the requisites. And here, some say this:

"Just as the five qualities beginning with 'wealth' (*aḍḍhatā*) are factors of sacrifice (*yañña*) by way of absolute necessity, such is not the case with being well-born (*sujātatā*) and having a beautiful form (*surūpatā*)."
"However, the particle *kira*—which indicates disapproval—was employed to show that both of those [views] are non-conclusive (*anekaṃsika*) regarding the factors [of sacrifice].
For they speak thus, thinking that the statement 'this one is ill-born,' and so forth, is non-conclusive;
but this is without substance. For this demonstration of the sacrificial factor through contrast (*vyatireka*) is made in a way that is common to all."
In this regard, it might occur to some that such a reflection [could arise];

however, [the word *kira*] is used here for the purpose of showing that there is no occasion for even that [reflection], and because the state of being a factor [of the path] is not shown to be non-exclusive to both of those [types of persons].
Furthermore, the word *kira* here should be understood as indicating the manner in which the brahmin was thinking at that time. Having reflected thus, he [thought]: "These too..."
The eight factors are said to be the requisites for that very sacrifice; by the word *kira*, his state of thought is indicated.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*evamādīni*), here the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes: "How much will this deformed man [offer]...?
He is poor, of little influence, faithless, unlearned, not one who knows the goal, and not wise; how much will he [offer]...? and so on.
The inclusion of these [terms] should be understood as:

“he will cut off. Regarding the commentary on the four requisites and so forth, in the phrase “for those raising the sacrificial ladle,” there are two alternatives stated in the commentary on the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta.
In order to refute the second alternative, he said, "The great sacrifice," and so forth.
By this, and by the indication that the chaplain himself took up the ladle, he shows that one should desire to be thus personally engaged and intent upon giving with due respect.

Regarding the phrase "of one ill-born" (*dujjātassa*), one should not take it merely as showing that being well-born is not an absolute factor (*anaṅgabhāva*) [for success], but rather in accordance with the method explained below.
The meaning should be understood solely by way of what is common to all. For by the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the following should be seen:
"To what extent will a gift given through the provision for one who does not study... [and so on]... for one who is immoral... [and so on]... for one who is witless continue?
Therefore, it is "from both those causes."
Commentary on the Threefold [Purity] 342.
“Of the three points” means of the three stages (bhūmi) consisting of the beginning, middle, and end of giving;
the sense is “of the states” (avatthāna). “They waver” means they shake; they do not remain in their former mode. “In the sense of the instrument” (karaṇatthe).
In the sense of the third case ending (*tatiyāvibhatti*). For, in relation to the word *karaṇīya*, this genitive (*sāmivacana*) refers only to the agent (*kattar*), not to the instrument (*karaṇa*).

Since the meaning of an expression indicating an instrument is generally understood through its function, it is intended here as the "instrumental sense" (*karaṇattha*) precisely because it is not explicitly stated.
To show the means for avoiding subsequent regret, it is said: "The former... should be established. In that regard:
“Unshakable” means firm and unassailable by anyone. “Should be well-established” means it should be made to rest securely.
Showing the means for establishing it in such a way, he said, “For thus,” and so forth.

For by establishing it in that manner, just as that gift succeeds in its intended purpose at present, so too in the future it becomes of great fruit through its abundance of results, because it remains untainted by remorse.
"In two places" means in the two places of the sacrificer and the recipient. "Regret...
should not be made"—it is with reference to this meaning that it is said, "The same method applies. "Intention of relinquishing" (*muñcacetanā*) is the intention of giving;

its "steadfastness" refers to its excellence due to prior volitional formation (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*). "Subsequent recollective intention" (*pacchāsamanussaraṇacetanā*) is the subsequent intention. Of that...
However, the state of being unwavering is to be understood as the careful reflection upon the gift, thinking, "Oh, a gift has been given by me; it is well and excellent.
To show, by way of contrast, the means for making both those volitions unwavering, it is said:
"In that way... it becomes. In that context, "for one who does not act in that way" refers to the volition of releasing [the object] and the subsequent volition of recollection.
This means "to one who makes [the mind] unshakable" and "to one who arouses remorse.

Furthermore, the statement, "Nor does the mind incline toward magnificent wealth," is a demonstration of the means for making [the mind] unshakable by way of contrast (*byatireka*) through the volition of subsequent recollection (*pacchāsamanussaraṇacetanā*).
For in this way, the illustration as it was pointed out becomes logically consistent. In that context, "toward magnificent wealth" refers to a particular field (*khettavisese*).
Because he has performed an act of relinquishment, even when excellent wealth is obtained, his mind does not incline toward it due to being defiled by subsequent regret.

To explain how this is so, he says: "In the Mahāroruva [Jātaka]," and so forth. The story of that merchant householder is found in the *Kosalasaṃyutta* and the *Mayhakajātakaya*. For it is said there:
“In the past, Great King, that householder merchant provided almsfood to the Paccekasambuddha named Tagarasikhī.
Having said, ‘Give almsfood to the ascetic,’ he rose from his seat and departed.
But after giving it, he later felt remorse, thinking, ‘It would have been better if these slaves or laborers had eaten this almsfood,’ and so forth.”
It is said that on other days he would see that Paccekabuddha, yet the thought to give did not arise in him;
however, on that day, this third son of Queen Padumavatī, the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī,
having spent the time on Mount Gandhamādana in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), emerged at the time of forenoon from Lake Anotatta.
Having washed his face, put on his lower garment upon a surface of emerald, fastened his waist-belt, and taken up his bowl and robe,
he entered into a jhāna that serves as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). Rising into the air by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*),
he descended at the city gate, donned his upper robe, and taking his bowl, stood at the doors of the houses of the city-dwellers, placing a thousand coins (*bhaṇḍika*) there.
Approaching gradually with graceful movements such as walking and so forth, he arrived at the gate of the merchant’s house.
On that day, the merchant had risen early, eaten a choice meal, and was sitting at the porch of his house door on a prepared seat, cleaning the spaces between his teeth.
Seeing the Paccekabuddha, [he thought: "On this very day, having eaten early..."

Because he was seated there, he conceived a mind for giving; having summoned his wife and said, "Give alms-food to this ascetic," he departed for the purpose of attending upon the king. The merchant’s wife, being of a reflective nature, thought:
"In all this time, I have never before heard the word 'give' from him; and even now, as he causes [me] to give, it is not for anyone else."

Or she causes it to be given to him; or she causes it to be given to a Paccekabuddha who is free from lust, hatred, and delusion, who has vomited out the defilements, and who has laid down the burden.

Thinking, “Without giving this or that, I shall give excellent almsfood,” she goes out from her house, pays homage to the Paccekabuddha with the fivefold prostration, takes his bowl, and having seated him on a seat prepared within her residence, [she serves him] with very pure...
Having prepared a meal with polished rice, and having prepared corresponding hard foods,
condiments, and soups, he filled a bowl, adorned it externally with perfumes, placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha,
and paid homage. The Paccekabuddha, thinking, "I shall provide for other Paccekabuddhas as well," did not consume it.
Having expressed his appreciation, he departed. The merchant, too, while returning from attending upon the king, saw the Paccekabuddha and asked, "We gave you almsfood;
did you receive it? "Yes, merchant, I received it. "Let us see," he said, and lifting up his neck, he looked. Then the fragrance of the almsfood—
Having risen, he struck his nostril. Being unable to restrain his mind, he later felt remorse;
the manner in which that remorse arose is stated in the Pāḷi itself with the words, "It would have been better," and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of this gift of alms-food, he was reborn seven times in a happy destination, in the heavenly world, and for seven times more in Sāvatthī.

He was reborn in a merchant family; this is his seventh existence. However, due to his subsequent remorse, his mind no longer inclines toward magnificent wealth. For it is said in the *Saṃyuttanikāya-varalañchaka*:
"That householder merchant, O Great King, having given [the gift], later felt remorse, thinking: 'It would have been better if this alms-food had been..."
‘May slaves or laborers eat,’ as a result of that karma, his mind does not incline toward the enjoyment of abundant food,
nor toward the enjoyment of abundant clothing, nor toward the enjoyment of vehicles, nor does his mind incline toward the enjoyment of the five kinds of excellent sensual pleasures.”
In the Mahākajaṭaka as well, it is said:

“Thus, Great King, the visiting merchant obtained great wealth by means of the requisites given to the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī; yet, because he was unable to produce further refined volition after having given, he was unable to enjoy refined luxuries.
Furthermore, this [man] took the life of his brother’s only son for the sake of the inheritance; by that kamma, many...
He was boiled in hell for many years, and seven times he was born without a son; even now, by that very same kamma, he has been reborn in Mahāroruva.
Therefore it is said, "as if for a merchant householder reborn in Mahāroruva.
Here, the meaning should be understood according to the priority of the preceding and succeeding volitions (*cetanā*); for one single volition does not produce two rebirth-linkings (*paṭisandhi*).
343. Explanation of the Ten Aspects (Dasa-ākāravaṇṇanā): It is called an *ākāra* because it produces a fruit by establishing a proper limit (*pariccheda*) according to its own suitability;
thus, it is said to be a "cause" (*kāraṇa*), as in the phrase "by ten causes. Here, the prefix *ā-* has the sense of a limit (*mariyādā*). It does not refer only to those who are immoral.
Then, indeed, he will produce remorse even toward those who are virtuous.
The word *api* (even/also), or the particle *pi*, is used here to indicate that both [types of remorse] should not be produced.
The statement "it arises from the recipient alone" is said with reference to a stronger remorse; however, weak remorse arises from the gift itself, and also from the retinue of people.
It indeed arises. "Worthy to arise" means fit to arise. The connection is: "you even dispel remorse.
"Of those very ones" refers specifically to those who have committed the taking of life. Here, by "sacrifice" (yajana), only giving is intended, not the offering of fire;
thus he says, "May you give. "Let it be relinquished" means let it be abandoned through the practice of open-handed generosity. "Internal" means within oneself, in one's own mental continuum.
Commentary on the Sixteen Aspects (Soḷasākāravaṇṇanā) 344.
The items beginning with the consent (anumati) were previously described as the "sixteen requisites" by being established as the basis for the sacrifice;
however, here, because the expression of thanks (anumodanā) is undertaken by way of pointing out [the merit] and so forth, it is stated: "by sixteen aspects."
"Having shown" means having shown the fruit as if it were directly before one's eyes through the power of his own teaching;

because he showed it many times, the expression "having shown and shown" (*dassetvā dassetvā*) is a distributive term, which the Master [the Commentator] describes as an intensive repetition (*āmeḍita-vacana*) in the sense of repeated manifestation.
The same method applies to expressions such as "having encouraged and encouraged" (*samādapetvā samādapetvā*). "That matter" refers to the fruit of giving.
The meaning is the connection between action and its fruit. "Having encouraged" means:

not merely having him hear it, but having caused him to take it up with care—just as the king correctly adopts that matter, making it his own in mind and grasping it well—and thus having made him adopt it thoroughly.
The phrase "by dispelling remorse" is merely an illustration; [it includes] greed, hatred, delusion, envy, stinginess, pride, and so forth as well.
For these are the defilements of the mind intent on giving; by their removal, that [mind] is called "cleansed" and "encouraged," because it attains a state of sharpness and clarity.
However, the removal of remorse is specifically mentioned because of its proximity, for remorse can arise once the act of giving has been performed.
It is the production of a state of being "joyful and exceedingly joyful" through qualities that truly exist.

He said, "It is 'consoling' (sampahaṃsana)," beginning with the words "it is beautiful" (sundaraṃ). "According to the Dhamma" (dhammato) means according to truth. To demonstrate that very meaning, it is stated:

"by means of the Dhamma, by means of the equitable, by means of the reason. For truth is called "Dhamma" because it does not depart from the Dhamma; it is called "equitable" (samaṃ) because of its state of peaceful conduct; and it is called "reason" (kāraṇaṃ) because of its state of being appropriate.
345. In that sacrifice, there was not even the cutting of trees or grass, let alone the killing of living beings.
To reinforce the absence of the taking of life and to demonstrate that it was entirely untainted by erroneous views, the text states "not even cows were slaughtered" and so forth;
yet, showing that even this was followed by the statement "no trees were cut down" and so on, he says: "Those [trees] called sacrificial posts," etc.
"Barihisatthāyā" means for the purpose of delimitation. "By way of a forest-garland" means by way of garlands scented with forest flowers;

this is what was stated by the Teacher, meaning in the form of a forest row. "Or spreading upon the ground" means they spread here and there, encircling the altar-ground (*vedibhūmi*). For it is by means of mantras and so forth that the ground is consecrated.
Having made it [the tree] the recipient of gain and honor, it is called "vedī. The connection is that both those trees and those materials are the object and the agent;
or rather, this is a case of the expressed object (*abhihitakamma*). For according to one's desire, the factors of action (*kāraka*) function according to their capacity.

And this is for the purpose of strengthening the absence of killing living beings in the manner already stated, and for the purpose of showing that [the practice] is not defiled by a mistaken apprehension.
[The text] shows this with the words beginning “But what...? A house-slave born within the home is one born inside the house.
By the word “etcetera,” there is an inclusion of those who are slaves purchased for money, those captured in war, those inherited, and those who have entered slavery of their own accord.

“Even beforehand” means prior to performing labor for wages. “Having taken payment” means having taken it day by day according to the work performed. “Food and wages” refers to both the daily meal and the monthly or other periodic maintenance allowance. This meaning has already been stated.
"Tajjitā" means terrified. "Parikammāni" refers to all types of preliminary tasks; the meaning is "various kinds of work.
"By means of affectionate conduct alone" means by means of agreeable speech alone. "According to their respective names alone" means in accordance with their well-known names.
In the phrase "with ghee, oil, fresh butter, curd, honey, and molasses," the word "ca" (and) has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*avuttasamuccaya*); therefore—

The gathering of various kinds of excellent foods and drinks—both solid and soft—as well as clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and so forth, is what should be understood here.
Therefore, he said: "with excellent things mixed with ghee, oil, and so on," and so forth.
The connection is: "with gruel... pe ... and drinks suitable for each respective time. "Of ghee, etc. means by means of ghee and the rest.
346. Wealth (*dhana*) is called *saṃ* because it is to be gathered together (*paṭisāmetabba*) and because it belongs to one's own self (*attano attano santaka*).

One who possesses that is a *sapati*; [the *t* becomes *p*] by the elision of the *niggahīta*. Because it brings about welfare (*hita*) both in this present life and in future lives, it is "welfare" (*hita*);
thus it is *sāpateyya*, which is simply wealth. Therefore he said: "abundant wealth. It is indeed of an inexhaustible nature.

It is precisely of an indestructible nature. "By means of a portion of the village" means either by way of mentioning it as a village, or by means of a portion of what is to be taken from the village;
thus it was stated by the Teacher. Alternatively, the meaning is "by means of a portion of a village that is similar [to the donor's own]. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well. 347.

"Sacrificial enclosure" (*yaññāvāṭa*) is a designation for a dug-in enclosure, a place for performing sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (*assamedha*); it is spoken of by way of that conventional usage.

However, by the phrase "to the east of the city gate" and so forth, he shows that the meaning here is specifically within the gift-hall itself, and because that hall was built at the eastern gate of the city, it is in the eastern part [of the city].
Furthermore, he says "just as" and so forth to show that this place was not very far from the king’s gift-hall.
Since, having eaten breakfast there, they were not at all weary...
In the evening, they arrive at the king’s hall of offerings (*dānasālā*). The same method applies to such passages as “to the south of the sacrificial enclosure” (*dakkhiṇena yaññāvāṭassa*).
By saying “having drunk the rice-gruel” (*yāguṃ pivitvā*), he refers by way of the term “rice-gruel” to the entire meal of the morning. 348.

“Sweet” (*madhura*) means having a pleasant taste. The meaning of what is to be said further on is expressed by the passage beginning with “Moreover, sir, this occurs to me” (*apica me bho evaṃ hotī*).

Regarding the meaning being stated: "By way of avoidance" means by avoiding disrespect toward the Blessed One—that is, by removing straightforwardness—or by setting aside upright conduct and asking about the intended matter through crooked conduct;
this is what is meant. Therefore he said: "One who asks in a straightforward manner appears as if lacking respect."
349. Commentary on the Praise of Constant Giving and Family Sacrifices:
“Having risen” refers to the energy of exertion in giving; “having fully risen” refers to the practice of constancy therein.

The intention is that if one does not perform such works as agriculture and trade, one will perish by falling into misfortune such as poverty. Furthermore, it is [a sacrifice] requiring fewer materials...
“Yet it is of even greater fruit” is stated thus in brief in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, in the *Pāḷi*, the reading is: “It is of less trouble, of less exertion, of greater fruit, and of greater benefit.
Therein, “of less equipment” means having extremely meager requirements, requiring no effort to assemble the requisites. “Of less trouble,” moreover, means having extremely few duties.
In this context, *attha* means "function"; by changing the letter *ttha* to *ṭṭha*, there is also the reading “*appaṭṭhataro*.
That by which a sacrifice is properly undertaken (*samārabhīyati*) is a *samārambha*; it refers to the oppression of beings occurring through the gathering of requisites.
One for whom such undertaking is slight is thus described; furthermore, one who is even more so is *appasamārambhataro*. [This refers to] that which is designated as the result (*vipāka*).
"Great fruit" means that its fruit is great and equal [to its cause]; "even greater fruit" means it is even more excellent than that.
"Great benefit" means that its outflow and other fruits are great and designated as arising; "even greater benefit" means it is even more excellent than that.
"Fixed gifts" refers to gifts that should be given by making them constant, stable, and uninterrupted. Regarding "regular meals": here—
The taking of the four requisites was by Bhattasīsa. "Anukulayaññānī" means gifts that are to be given according to the family lineage (*anukula*).
Therefore he said, "ours," and so forth. It should be construed that those which are to be performed are called "anukulayaññāni.
"Nibaddhadānānī" means gifts that have been established and fixed, being carried out by way of tradition.
“Dent-sticks made of ivory” refers to tooth-sticks fashioned from elephant tusks upon which the names of donors are engraved;

by this, he shows that the *niccabhatta* (regular meal) was given by way of such dent-stick offerings. “That family” refers to the family of Anāthapiṇḍika. “By poverty” means by the state of being destitute.
By the phrase “he was unable to give more than one dent-stick,” it is shown that because he could not afford to give even a single dent-stick, he was unable to interrupt his regular giving.
He spoke of protection. "Of the king" means of King Setavāhana.
Regarding the phrase "having said such things," here the word "etc. includes the words of urgency regarding the equal distribution [of alms], such as:
"Why did you spring upon me and seize me like a hawk seizing a piece of meat? "Galaggāhā" means seizing by the throat. "By way of interrupting the work" means...
By this, he shows that even the giving of an opportunity for one’s own karma is indeed an affliction (*pīḷā*).

He says, “the undertaking (*samārambha*) is reckoned as an affliction,” because the word *samārambha* here has the sense of afflicting. There are three factors on the part of the giver, consisting in the attainment of prior volition, volition at the moment of release, and subsequent volition;
and there are three on the part of the recipient, consisting in the practice of being free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion.
Thus the offering is endowed with six factors; the *Nandamātā-sutta* in the *Chaḷaṅguttara* is the proof for this meaning.
By way of volition arising again and again, like a great river or a mighty flood, it flows and surges hither and thither;
thus, merit itself is the "overflowing of merit" (*puññābhisanda*). "Of such a kind" refers to its measure.
He said it is difficult to perform. Because of the greatness of the cause, the greatness of the fruit should also be understood, like the great flood resulting from rain falling upstream;
thus he said, "Therefore," and so forth. 350.
"Ever new" means always fresh, because the donor's activity occurs day after day, there is no end to the task.
"It does not exist" is stated by the phrase "by one," and so forth. Because the dwelling that has been begun must be completed after some time, there is a conclusion of the task;

thus he said, "a leaf-hut," and so forth. To show the means by which the conclusion of the task exists even in a great monastery (mahāvihāra), it was said, "having made a single act of relinquishing wealth.
"By way of the Suttanta" means according to the method of the *Sabbāsavasutta* and other such discourses.

The "nine benefits" refers to the nine advantages—beginning with the warding off of cold and ending with delight in seclusion—that are enumerated according to their respective reflections; these are stated by way of heedfulness.
For when one gives a dwelling, it is as if all requisites have been given. As it is said in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the excellent seal of the scriptures:
“And he is a giver of all who gives a dwelling,” for this is a means for the constant increase of merit.
Indeed, it is said in that very same place: “For those who give a dwelling, their merit constantly increases by day and by night.
For even one who has wandered through two or three villages for alms and returned with nothing at all [finds comfort] in a place endowed with shade and water.
Having entered the monastery grove, bathed, and lain down for a short while in the dwelling, when he rises and sits up, strength is brought back to his body as if it had been restored.
Furthermore, while wandering outside, the element of beauty (*vaṇṇadhātu*) in his body is exhausted by the wind and heat;
but having entered the dwelling, closed the door, and lain down for a short while, there arises a dissimilar continuity (*visabhāga-santati*).
It subsides; the continuity of similar states becomes established, as if a particle of color had been brought and placed therein.
For one wandering outside, a thorn pierces the foot, a stump strikes him, and dangers such as reptiles as well as the fear of thieves arise;
but for one who has entered a shelter, closed the door, and lies down, all those dangers [cease].

They do not occur; rather, for one who recites the texts, the joy and happiness of the Dhamma arises, and for one who attends to the meditation subject, the happiness of tranquility arises due to the absence of external distraction.
For one who wanders outside, sweat breaks out on the body and the eyes twitch;
at the moment of entering the lodging, the bed, chair, and other items are no longer perceived; and after lying down for a short while, [the mind remains unsettled].
Furthermore, it is as if the eye-socket has been filled and inserted; doors, windows, beds, chairs, and so forth become visible.
Seeing one dwelling in such a residence, people respectfully attend to them with the four requisites.
Therefore it is said: “By one giving a residence… [and so on]… it becomes,” and “This is always a means for increasing merit. Consequently:
All these aforementioned benefits are to be understood.
"By way of the Khandhakas" means by the method of the Vinaya Piṭaka as it appears in the Senāsanakkhandhaka. For therein it is said:
"It wards off cold and heat, and likewise from wild beasts..."
From snakes and mosquitoes, from cold and also from rains,
and then from the terrible wind and heat that have arisen,
he is shielded; for the sake of shelter, for the sake of comfort, and to meditate and to practice insight.
The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised as the foremost by the Buddha.
Therefore, a wise person, clearly perceiving their own welfare,
should have delightful monasteries built and cause those learned in the Dhamma to dwell therein.
To those who have become upright, one should give food and drink, as well as clothing and lodging,
with a mind full of serene confidence. They, in turn,
teach him the Dhamma that dispels all suffering.

“Having understood this Dhamma here, he attains final Nibbāna, free from taints.”—These verses of thanksgiving for the gift of monasteries by the merchant of Rājagaha and others are presented by way of a formulaic series (*peyyāla*). In that context, “cold and heat” is stated by way of the discordance of the seasons.
Regarding the phrase “and rain even in the cold season,” here “cold season” (*sisira*) refers to the misty wind.
It is said. "Showers" refers specifically to showers from upright clouds. All these [terms] should be connected with the word "paṭihanti" (warding off).

"Paṭihaññati" means it is warded off by the dwelling (vihāra). "For the sake of a shelter" means for the sake of concealment. "For the sake of happiness" means for the sake of dwelling in happiness through the absence of dangers such as cold and so forth.
The two phrases "to meditate and to gain insight" are also included within this very phrase "and for the sake of happiness."
It should be connected with the preceding word. For this is what is meant: the gift of a monastery is for the sake of happiness;
for what kind of happiness? For the sake of that happiness which consists in meditating and practicing insight. Alternatively, it may also be connected with the following word:
the gift of a monastery is for the sake of meditating and practicing insight—the gift of a monastery given by one thinking, "He will meditate here, he will practice insight here," for the Saṅgha.
The foremost has been praised by the Buddha. For this was said: "He is a giver of all who gives a dwelling.
And because it is praised as the foremost, there is the verse beginning, "Therefore, a wise man...

One should cause those who are learned to dwell here—in this monastery—both those who are learned in the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and those who are learned through realization (*paṭivedha*). And their food... whatever for them...
"Suitable food and drink, robes, and lodgings such as beds and chairs—all that he should bestow upon those who are upright and whose minds are not crooked.
'He should bestow' means he should offer it. And this should be done with a serene mind, not by violating the clarity of his heart.
For when one's mind is thus serene, they teach him the Dhamma... [and so on].
"He attains final nibbāna, free from taints"—this is the method according to the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary).
However, this is the method according to the *Ṭīkā* (Sub-commentary) as elaborated by both the Venerable Ācariya Dhammapāla and the Venerable Ācariya Sāriputta:
"Cold" refers to the coldness that arises either through the disturbance of the internal elements or through the change of the external seasons.
"Hot" refers to the heat of fire; its occurrence should be understood as arising from forest fires and the like. "Repels" means he wards it off;
that is, he acts in such a way that no affliction of body or mind occurs due to those two.

For when the body is afflicted by cold and heat, a monk whose mind is distracted is unable to apply himself with wise effort. "Wild beasts" refers to fierce animals such as lions, tigers, and so forth.
For indeed, even when entering a forest dwelling (*āraññaka-*) and sitting with the door closed, no dangers (*parissaya*) exist for you.
"Reptiles" (*sarīsapā*) refers to any long-bodied creatures that crawl or move, such as snakes and the like. "Gnats" (*makasa*) is merely an illustration;
by this term, gadflies and the like should also be understood to be included. "In the cold" (*sisire*) refers either to the cold season or to periods such as a week-long rainstorm.
"And when the contact of cold arises. "Showers" is to be construed as: whenever showers of rain arise, they ward them off.
"Fierce wind and heat": fierce wind—whether characterized by dust or free from dust—which occurs by way of uprooting and breaking trees, shrubs, and so forth;
and fierce solar heat, which arises during the seasons of summer and the burning sun—both are warded off and repelled.

"For the sake of a shelter" means for the purpose of delighting in seclusion by turning the mind away from various objects. "For the sake of comfort" means for the purpose of living at ease through the absence of the aforementioned dangers.
"To meditate" means to contemplate after fixing the mind upon any one among the thirty-eight meditation subjects.
"To practice insight" means to comprehend mental formations as impermanent and so forth.
*Vihāra* means a dwelling place. *Kāraye* means he should have it built. *Ramma* means delightful, a pleasant place for living.
*Vāsayettha bahussute* means that after having it built, he should cause those who are learned (*bahussuta*), virtuous (*sīlavanta*), and of noble character (*kalyāṇadhamma*) to dwell there.
Furthermore, while causing them to dwell, he should provide food and so forth in such a way that those learned ones do not suffer from a lack of requisites.

One should give drinks, robes, and lodgings to those who have become upright and are endowed with noble aspiration, with a mind serene through faith in the results of actions and the qualities of the Triple Gem.
Now, in order to show the mutual assistance between householders and those who have gone forth, he spoke the verse beginning with "te tassā. Therein:
"Thus they are very learned. "Of him" means of the lay follower (*upāsaka*). "Teaching the Dhamma" means they teach the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*), which dispels the entire suffering of saṃsāra.

"Having understood that Dhamma here" means that the lay follower, having understood the True Dhamma in this Dispensation through right practice, becomes free from taints (*anāsava*) by attaining the highest path and attains final Nibbāna.
"By the extinguishing of the eleven fires, one becomes cool.

Thus, thirteen benefits beginning with the warding off of cold and ending with insight (vipassanā) are mentioned; furthermore, the acquisition of food and so forth, hearing the Dhamma, understanding the Dhamma, and final Nibbāna—these seventeen benefits are stated here.
The fruit of giving a monastery by donors should also be understood as corresponding to the fruits that arise for those who receive it, according to their dwelling therein.

For it is generally the case that beings receive results corresponding to their actions; thus he said, "Therefore," and so forth. By the phrase "because it was relinquished to the Saṅgha," he speaks primarily of a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha.

A "monastery belonging to the Saṅgha" (saṅghika-vihāra) is one built for the sake of the Saṅgha of the four quarters; with reference to this, it is stated in the Word-Commentary (Padabhājaniya): "Belonging to the Saṅgha..."
“Indeed, this monastery has been given and dedicated to the Saṅgha.

For wherever a shrine is established and the hearing of the Dhamma is performed, monks coming from the four directions—even without being asked—wash their feet, open the door with the key, attend to the lodgings, and then depart as they please; such a place, at the very least...
Even a leaf-hut with four posts is called a monastery built for the Saṅgha of the four quarters.
The phrase "for even a single bhikkhu," and so forth, is a practice customary among lay followers when making such a commitment;
it is stated here to demonstrate that their undertaking is even more firm, though the taking of refuge is [the primary requirement] for them.
They say that even what is undertaken by oneself is indeed undertaken [as a formal act]. The construction is: "in the presence of the Saṅgha or the Gaṇa.
"Therein" means in the refuge as it was taken; there is also the reading "tassā," which means "of that refuge as it was taken.
It is said with reference to those of intelligent nature that there is no need to perform it again and again; for it is only for those of intelligent nature that—
Just as lion’s fat remains in a golden vessel, the going for refuge stands unshakable due to one’s skill in the meaning of the refuges and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “merit consisting in the sacrifice of life”:
even if someone were to deprive one of life with a sharp blade, saying, “If you do not break the refuge as it was taken, I shall kill you,” nevertheless, “I would never—”
This was said with reference to one who has firmly grasped the refuge by saying, "The Buddha is not the Buddha," "The Dhamma is not the Dhamma," and "The Saṅgha is not the Saṅgha.
The statement "It bestows the attainment of heaven" is merely an illustration;
however, its fruits and benefits have already been explained in the commentary on going for refuge.
352. According to the method that will be explained, the term *vera* refers to unwholesome states such as killing (*pāṇātipāta*), because they are the cause of enmity.
It is called *veramaṇī* because it restrains—that is, it wards off—those [unwholesome states] as if threatening them, saying: "How can you come here while I am standing here?

Alternatively, it is called *viramaṇī* (though it should be *viramaṇī*) because one desists from those unwholesome states by means of it; in this case, the letter *i* is changed to *e* according to the rules of phonology (*niruttinaya*).
Having done so, it is stated as “veramaṇī” (abstinence). However, in the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā*, it says: “They perform the recitation in two ways:

‘veramaṇi-sikkhāpada’ and ‘viramaṇi-sikkhāpada. Here, what is intended is abstinence associated with wholesome consciousness (*kusala-citta*), not that associated with the fruit (*phala*), because of its connection with sacrifice (*yañña*).
[It is defined] by way of the attainment of one who has not undertaken the precept, and by way of the object to be transgressed as it has been established.
Abstention through attainment is *sampattavirati*. Abstention arisen by way of undertaking is *samādānavirati*.

The "bridge" (*setu*) refers to the Noble Path; abstention that functions as the destruction of evil states by means of their total eradication while being included within that [Path] is *setughātavirati*.
It is also called "abstention through eradication. Now, to show these according to their specific characteristics:

The passage beginning with “Therein,” etc., has been stated. “Birth, etc. refers to the birth, clan, family, and so forth that should be pointed out. By the word “etc.,” there is the inclusion of age, learning, and so on.
“He avoids” means he shuns them by way of non-transgression; this should be understood as the abstinence from what is encountered, like that of the lay follower Cakkana in the Island of Siṃhala.
In such expressions as “I shall not kill a living being,” the inclusion of individual meanings—

such as “I do not take what is not given,” “I abstain from taking what is not given,” and “I undertake the restraint”— should be understood through the word *iti* used in the sense of ‘beginning’ (ādi),
or through the word *vā* used in the sense of ‘option. And because this is the case, it is stated as “training rules” (*sikkhāpadāni*) rather than simply “the training rule” (*sikkhāpada*).
The connection is with the phrase "abstaining from the destruction of life. "I undertake" means I correctly undertake it;

that is to say, I take it up with the intention of non-transgression, ensuring it is unbroken, flawless, unspotted, and untarnished. This should be understood as a restraint consisting of formal undertaking, like that of the lay follower who dwelt on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna.

“Associated with the path” means associated with the path beginning with right view. Now, regarding the various analyses—by way of dhamma, by way of constituent parts, by way of object, by way of feeling, by way of root, by way of grasping, by way of classification, and so forth—concerning those [factors] that have arisen here and there, the words beginning with “therein” are stated in order to show the analysis by way of object in brief.
“The first two” refers to the abstinences consisting in both natural and undertaken restraint.

Regarding the phrase "the bases for the life-faculty, etc.," in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), it refers to a living being (*pāṇa*); however, from the perspective of conventional designation (*paññatti*), it should be called "the bases for beings, etc.
For in this way, it accords with and agrees with the statement in the *Khuddakāgama-ṭīkā*: "It is precisely with reference to beings that one abstains from taking life and from unchastity.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*) here, the basis of what has not been taken by way of the category of beings (*satta-saṅkhāra*) is included, as well as the basis of tangible objects (*phoṭṭhabba*).
The inclusion of the basis for false speech and the basis for fermented and distilled liquors should be understood as occurring through the very same mode of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

"Arising by taking that as their object" means they proceed by taking as their objective support the aforementioned basis for transgression, proceeding by way of abstaining from the basis to be avoided—which is termed the volition of transgression.

"The latter" refers to the abstinence consisting in the destruction of the bridge (*setughāta-virati*). Although it has Nibbāna as its object, it is nevertheless so called because of the accomplishment of its specific function.
However, it should be understood that among the three teachers' doctrines presented right there, two were refuted and only one was authorized.

Some say: "Both natural abstinence (*sampattavirati*) and abstinence through undertaking (*samādānavirati*) proceed by taking as their object precisely that unwholesome act, such as killing, which one is abandoning.
Others say: "Abstinence through undertaking takes as its object either that from which one abstains, whether it be one's own [action] or that of others..."
Others say: "Or [abstinence] occurs by taking precisely unwholesome states such as killing living beings as its object.
However, abstinence from what has been attained occurs by taking as its objective support precisely those objects of killing living beings and so forth from which one abstains. And yet others say:

"Both of these take as their object-cause precisely that thing to be transgressed, which serves as the objective support for those unwholesome states such as killing living beings, from which one abstains."

Others say: "Having made the preceding meaning of the words its object and basis for transgression, one desists from the subsequent meaning of the words—that is, from the basis for desisting. However, the first statement here is indeed untenable. Why?
Because that unwholesome state, such as the destruction of life, does not exist in the present for itself, and because it does not exist externally. [As stated] in the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*:
For it has been stated that the five training rules (sikkhāpada) have present objects and external objects. Likewise, the second position is also untenable.

Why? Because it is a mixture with the first position, because it treats the state of being an object for the unwholesome acts of others—such as killing—as manifold, and because it speaks of two different classifications of objects. However, the third position is tenable and is accepted by all reciters (bhāṇaka).

Therefore, it should be understood that he authorizes only that [one position]. Thus it was said: “Among the three teachers’ doctrines, one should understand that two are rejected and only one is authorized.
Here it is asked: If these two types of abstinence take as their object precisely those things, such as the life-faculty, which are to be transgressed—
"If it were to proceed [in that way], then while thinking of one thing, one would be doing another;
and as for what one abandons, one would not know it"—does this unintended consequence follow? It is said:
No, for one who proceeds by way of accomplishing a task is not said to be "thinking of one thing while doing another," nor is he said to be "not knowing what he abandons."

Just as the Noble Path abandons defilements by having Nibbāna alone as its object, so too these two types of abstinence abandon the immoralities such as killing living beings by having the bases of the life-faculty and so forth as their objects. Therefore, the ancients said:
"Having set out for the Deathless, abandoning all evils..."
“And herein, the person who stands on the path is the one to be illustrated.
Now, in order to show the exposition by way of summary or analysis, it is said: “In this regard,” and so forth.
One undertakes [the precepts] all at once and together, saying: “I undertake the virtue endowed with five factors,” and so on. For even in this way...
Their fivefold nature is understood by way of their functions. Although all [the precepts] are distinct, they are undertaken together as one;
for at that time, the state of being "five-limbed" (pañcaṅgika) does not apply to the virtue.

One is bound by karma only through that which is transgressed. One undertakes each one separately, as in: "I undertake the training rule of abstaining from the destruction of life," and so forth. Thus, it is called a "training rule of abstention" (veramaṇi-sikkhāpada).

And this was stated in the *Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā* by way of summary; however, in the palm-leaf manuscripts of the Pāli Canon, it appears in its expanded form as "veramaṇī" with the final nasal (niggahita). Furthermore, this was stated with reference to householders;
for novices, however, whether they undertake the precepts in whatever manner, if even one is broken, all are broken due to the offense of a defeat (pārājika).
Thus, the distinction regarding undertaking [the precepts] both collectively and individually has been stated here; however, in the *Khuddakāgama-ṭīkā*, it says:
"When one undertakes them collectively, there is only one abstinence (*virati*) and only one volition (*cetanā*); yet, their fivefold nature is understood by way of their functions.
But when one undertakes them individually, there are five abstentions and five volitions. This is [the explanation].

The distinction has been stated. Even regarding the schism: "In whatever way they may undertake [the precepts], when one among the novices (sāmaṇera) has broken [a rule], all of them have broken it as well;
for those rules constitute for them the grounds for a defeat (pārājika). However, by whichever [rule] he has transgressed, he alone is bound by that kamma.
But for householders (gahaṭṭha), when one has broken [a rule], only that one person has broken it; because for them, [the offense occurs] only through the undertaking of that [specific rule]."
Furthermore, it is said: "The fivefold nature of virtue is thus accomplished. Although this was stated, the doctrine of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas is designated as the "other doctrine" (apare-vāda) therein.

However, there is no distinction in the case of the abstinence consisting in the destruction of the bridge (setughāta-virati), because its nature is unshakable due to the complete eradication of its opposites.
To demonstrate this very point, it was said: "Even in another existence," and so forth.

"Yadattha" means "for the sake of whom"; although there is no actual difference [in the referent], this is an expression of distinction where there is no distinction.
Or for the sake of that which serves as their qualification. "Tet" refers to the noble fruit-states (*ariyaphaladhamma*). There is also a recent reading, "taṃ. For these are what must be realized;
and here the "dhammas to be realized" are mentioned in the passage: "There are, Mahāli, other dhammas... for the purpose of realizing which bhikkhus lead the holy life under me."
Commentary on the Four Noble Fruits (Catuariyaphalavaṇṇanā) 373.
"They bind" means they fetter. "Therefore" means because, by way of binding, they bind beings there to the fear of the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāra*);
therefore. In some places the reading is "in the chariot of the fear of the suffering of the round," but that is not the ancient version.

Because he was disparaged by the teacher. He has "entered the stream of the Path" (maggasota), not the stream of faith and so forth; for it is said: "Monks, 'stream' is a designation for the Noble Path.
And regarding the word "entered" (āpanna), the meaning is "one who has reached from the beginning," because the prefix *ā-* functions in the sense of an initial action;
however, this is stated by way of the state of fruition (phalaṭṭha). For this is a term referring to past time, [since it is used] at the moment of the Path.
But it is said that one "enters the stream of the Path. For this very reason, it is said in the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga*: "One gives a gift to a stream-enterer;

one gives a gift to one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. "Of a nature not to fall" means having the characteristic of not being reborn [in the lower realms]. "By the fixed order of the Dhamma" means by the fixed order of the higher paths.
Alternatively, according to a method not mentioned in the Commentaries, he is "fixed" because of the quality of not being subject to rebirth beyond the seventh existence at the very least.
The meaning is: "one for whom the supreme course (paraṃ ayanaṃ) or the supreme goal (parāgati) exists. The phrase "by this" (*anena*) is a further statement regarding a third compound;
here, the word *vā* is indicated as being elided (*luttaniddiṭṭha*).
"Tenuity" (*tanuttaṃ*) means slowness in occurrence and sparseness; thus it is said, "by tenuity," and so forth. "Only occasionally" (*karahaci*).

It is either a mere particle or a synonym. Just as in such passages as, "If less than a month remains of the summer, one should seek a rainy-season robe," the word *ora* does not mean "excessive"; thus he says, "of those belonging to the lower portion.
The meaning is: "beneficial because they serve as conditions for the lower portion, which is the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*). "In the Pure Abode plane" indicates their place of rebirth.

"Opapātika" means one who is spontaneously born (*upapātiko*), one who is accomplished in spontaneous birth (*upapātane sādhukārī*). Therefore it is said: "This is a term for the exclusion of the remaining modes of birth.
"Possessing the nature of final Nibbāna" (*parinibbānadhammo*) means having the characteristic of attaining final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

"Liberation" (*vimutti*) means that which liberates; thus, "mind itself is liberation" is called "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*), as stated in the passage beginning with "purity of mind. This is expressed by way of the head-term "mind" (*citta-sīsena*).
And here, concentration (*samādhi*) is included, as in such passages as: "A wise man, established in virtue, develops the mind and wisdom.
The same principle applies here to the term "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*). Therefore he said: "Liberation by wisdom is indeed the wisdom of the fruit of arahantship.

"By himself" (*sāma*) means by one's own self, that is, without depending on another. By the word "having directly known" (*abhijānitvā*), the grammatical function of the suffix *-tvā* and so forth [is indicated].

The elision of the letter *ya* has been shown. By the word “having directly known” (*abhiññāya*), it should be understood that this refers to a grammatical operation (*vacanakāriya*) involving the letter *n*.

*Sacchi* is a non-Pāli derivative (*nepātika*) used in the sense of “directly. Direct realization (*paccakkhakaraṇa*) means making an object the focus of experience in its own form, setting aside hearsay, verbal expression, reflection, and so forth.
Commentary on the Noble Eightfold Path (Ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga): 374–5.
"Having arisen" means having flown through the path of the air. A noble disciple enters upon it toward Nibbāna;

and because one proceeds (*paṭipajjati*) by means of this, it is called the "way of progress" (*paṭipadā*). Since that [Nibbāna] is its prior stage, the Noble Path is designated by the name "prior-stage way of progress."

This is what is stated here. [The path] is fivefold by way of being spread out (*ātata*) and stretched out (*vitata*), and so forth; it is eightfold by way of the locations situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions. He said, "It consists merely of eight factors," and so on, because there is no other so-called "eightfold path" apart from those eight factors.
For there is no such thing as a whole that exists independently of its parts. Therefore, [the term *aṭṭhaṅgika*] is a *bahubbīhi* compound meaning "that which has eight factors."

The Master has stated: "Without forming a compound, one should establish the word-form by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) containing a compound, as follows: 'Eight parts' (*aṭṭha aṅgāni*), and 'that which possesses these' is 'eightfold' (*aṭṭhaṅgiko*). However, the underlying intention here must be considered.

For if a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (possessive compound) were formed, it would not be possible to determine the distinction between "eight parts" and "eightfold" even by reversing their mutual relationship.

In a *abyāsa* (analytic) compound, because the meaning is arrived at through the predominance of both constituent meanings (*padattha*) together with the delimitation of number, their distinction can be established by reversing them from one another.
However, when a *taddhita* suffix is applied to a *samāsa-gabbha* (compound-nested) formation, it is indeed possible to restrict their distinction by reversing them;

for in a *samāsa*, the meaning is arrived at even without the predominance of the subsequent member’s meaning, due to the delimitation of number. This is characterized by the state of having a single referent (*ekatthibhāva*).
This is indeed a compound. However, in the *Dhammadāyādasuttanta-ṭīkā*, the Master himself has stated thus:

"Because the designation 'path' applies to the collection of path-factors, and because a collection is possessed of its constituent parts, it is called 'eightfold' (aṭṭhaṅgika) in the sense that it possesses eight factors which are its own constituents.
Furthermore, in this first method, the state of being eightfold belongs to the factor by means of the possessor of the factor.
In the second method, however, it is said that "the whole [is defined] by its parts"; this is the distinction between them.
Now, demonstrating the analysis of the Eightfold Path according to its characteristics, functions, moments, and objects, he says "Therein," and so forth.
"Characterized by right seeing" means [seeing] the four Noble Truths non-erroneously, exactly as they are.
It has the nature of seeing by way of direct perception. It has the characteristic of right directing, which means its nature is the non-erroneous directing of the mind toward the object of Nibbāna.

It has the characteristic of right embracing; because speech endowed with four factors embraces people, right speech—by virtue of its nature as abstention from their opposites—[functions] through the abandoning of divisive and false speech.
O people, it possesses the function of grasping both the person and the associated mental states; thus, its intrinsic nature is that of grasping without error.

"The characteristic of correctly originating" means that just as a work such as the making of a robe originates one thing to be done, or the work consisting of volition—which produces various actions—originates an action such as the moving of hands and feet.
Thus, by abandoning wrong action (*micchākammanta*) which gives rise to blameworthy deeds, right action (*sammākammanta*) has the function of giving rise to blameless deeds;
and since it proceeds only while giving rise to its associated states, its intrinsic nature is the non-perverted act of giving rise [to the blameless].

It has the characteristic of perfect purification because, through the abandoning of wrong livelihood (*micchājīva*), which is a defilement of body, speech, and the continuity of the aggregates (*khandhasantāna*), [it purifies them].

Its nature is non-perverted purification. Its characteristic is right exertion: its nature is to exert correctly, not allowing the associated states of consciousness to fall into the side of defilement. Its characteristic is right establishment:
its nature is to establish itself therein non-perversely by means of the characteristic of the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*). Its characteristic is right concentration...
Its intrinsic nature is the non-perverted concentration of the mind through the destruction of distraction.
Because they are abandoned together with it, ignorance and the rest—other defilements opposed to itself—are called "wrong views" distinct from [the specific] wrong view.
"Sees" means it manifests; it penetrates by means of the penetration of its function. Therefore he said: "By the penetration of that... because of non-delusion."
This indeed is the demonstration of the mode of seeing for her. For it is by means of that very factor termed right view that reflective contemplation occurs therein.
Since the first two functions are common to all [the factors], he says, "Right intention and the rest as well," and so forth.
By the phrase "in the same way," he brings forward the expression, "together with their own opposing defilements."

"In the prior stage" means at the moment of access concentration (*upacāra*). Because it occurs many times by way of access development (*upacāra-bhāvanā*), it consists of various moments (*nānakkhaṇa*).

Because its objects are the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, it has various objects (*nānārammaṇa*). Because the Path (*magga*) lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, it is of one moment (*ekakkhaṇa*).

Because its object is Nibbāna, it has a single object (*ekārammaṇa*). "By way of function": here, by that which is to be performed through the knowledges of suffering and so forth in the prior stage...
It receives its name from the pre-eminent function it performs upon arising, or from the function of this very knowledge in revealing suffering and so forth.

It receives four names when the functions to be performed regarding the Four Truths have been accomplished; it receives three names when the abandoning of sensual thoughts and so forth has been accomplished.
In the *Sikkhāpadavibhaṅga*, it is said: "The volition of abstinence and all associated mental states are the training rules (*sikkhāpada*)."
In that context, however, it is said that "there are both abstinences and volitions" by way of the volitions of striving and the volitions of abstinence.

Alternatively, this should be construed as follows: at the time of refraining from false speech and so forth, there are abstinences; at the time of uttering well-spoken words and so forth, there are volitions.
Because volitions are not factors of the path, he said, "but at the moment of the path, there are only abstinences. This refers to a single instance of knowledge.

It should also be understood that this is stated because, just as there is the knowledge of suffering and so forth, and just as a single *virati* (abstinence) possesses the nature of abstaining from false speech and so on, it is impossible for a single volition (*cetanā*) to accomplish the three functions of right speech and so forth; thus, the status of [right speech] and the rest cannot be established.

Furthermore, if those were established, the state of being the three factors (*aṅga*) would not be established. By this, he shows their twofold nature and their non-differentiation. "By way of the right efforts and the foundations of mindfulness..."
By way of the cultivation of the four right efforts and the four foundations of mindfulness.

Although right concentration is analyzed by way of the four jhānas— consisting of applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and equanimity, which are directed toward, closely placed upon, delighted in,
and developed as aids to concentration— nevertheless, just like effort, it possesses the fourfold function of effort, such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states.

Just as in the case of mindfulness, a single concentration does not fulfill both the task of abandoning the perception of beauty and so forth regarding the body and other aggregates—which are actually impure, painful, impermanent, and non-self—and the task of the fourfold jhāna-concentration.

Therefore, even in the preliminary stage, first-jhāna concentration is simply first-jhāna concentration. Likewise, at the moment of the path, second-jhāna concentration in the preliminary stage is simply second-jhāna concentration.
In the same way, at the moment of the path as well as in the prior stage, third-jhāna concentration is simply third-jhāna concentration.
Likewise, at the moment of the path as well as in the prior stage, fourth-jhāna concentration is simply fourth-jhāna concentration.
Thus, he said: "At the prior stage as well as at the moment of the path, it is simply right concentration."
Therefore, one should apply the following as appropriate: because it is the lamp of wisdom (*paññā-pajjota*), it dispels the darkness of ignorance;
and because it is the sword of wisdom (*paññā-sattha*), it slays the thieves of the defilements (*kilesa*).

Furthermore, since in this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) this practitioner has never before eradicated the mass of defilements, and the Noble Path (*ariya-magga*) is that which eradicates them—and herein, right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) functions by way of the full comprehension of realization (*pariññā-abhisamaya*) and so forth.

It is the forerunner of the process and is of great service; therefore [it is so called]. To show that very quality of being of great service by way of its causal nature, it is said: "because it is of great service to the practitioner.
"Of that" means of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*). Having stated that it is "of great service," he illustrates that state of being of great service by means of a simile:

He says, “Just as,” and so forth. This is a counterfeit made of copper, bronze, or other such materials. One who is skilled [in detecting it] is so because of his ability to avoid it due to its lack of great value.

Just as, for example, in the case of a money-changer, when discerning the distinctions between coins after seeing them with the eye, the hand is of great assistance as the most effective instrument for performing that action;
even so, for the yogi, when discerning the distinctions between phenomena after having observed them with wisdom (*paññā*).
Because of its prior activity, another factor is of great assistance—namely, *vitakka* (applied thought)—since it is only after one has applied thought that wisdom (*paññā*) realizes that object.
Therefore, the intention is that right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) is of great assistance to right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).
In the second simile, "thus" means just as a carpenter, having had the building materials turned over and over again by another, carves them with an adze.
Just as one applies [materials] to the work of building a house and so forth, so too the yogi, having applied initial application (vitakka) by way of its characteristics and so on,
and having delimited the phenomena thus given according to their true nature, applies them to the work of the clear comprehension of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya),

and so forth— this is the construction [of the meaning]. Initial application, which assists verbal expression, also assists right speech (sammāvācā), which effects the cessation and engagement of blameworthy and blameless types of speech.

He says, “‘One’s own,’ and so forth. With the words “As it was said,” etc., he shows by way of proof the passage from the *Cūḷavedalla-sutta* spoken by the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā to the householder named Visākha. “It breaks” means it emits.
Or rather, speech which determines the breaking of words is an auxiliary to the action of the body which determines the course of karma; such is the meaning of that [passage].
The phrase beginning with “But because... was stated in order to make [the meaning] clear to the world. Both types of good conduct refer to bodily good conduct and verbal good conduct.

What is called the virtue consisting of the eight factors of right livelihood is the virtue pertaining to the fundamental practice of the holy life (*ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla*), which is described by making right livelihood the eighth factor together with the fourfold verbal good conduct and the threefold bodily good conduct. It is with reference to this that [the Buddha said]:
It is said: "But previously, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood were already perfectly pure.

"Immediately after those two" means immediately after right speech and right action—the pair that serves as the cause for fulfilling the two types of good conduct by abandoning the two types of misconduct.
