"By means of a loose thread and through negligence" means by means of a loose [thread] and by being negligent. "This energy" is fourfold.

The energy of right effort. "In the body, etc. means in the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dhamma*). Factors such as the balance of the faculties (*indriya-samatā*) are conducive to concentration;
factors contrary to them are not conducive. "Modes" (*gatiyo*) refers to accomplishments, or to the intrinsic nature of functions and so forth.
"Having investigated" (*samanvesitvā*) means having examined; here the suffix *-tvā* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
Commentary on the Two Instances of Going Forth (376–7).
Having asked for the reason for the connection—“Why was it begun?”—the passage beginning with “It is said that this... is stated in order to answer it;
by this, he shows that the subsequent teaching proceeds by way of a connection based on the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*). “By him” means because he held such a view.
"Assa" means of King Licchavi. "In the teaching" means in the teaching as it was taught—subtle, delicate, and connected with emptiness (*suññatā*).
"He does not resolve" means he does not have faith or confidence.

"When they speak of the 'mere thread of the Dhamma'" means that for those for whose sake the Dhamma is spoken, even though there is no penetration of the Path (*magga*) therein, [the teaching] is merely the lineage within the Dispensation.
Or, by making the Dhamma of the discourses (*tantidhamma*) his own through study and then teaching it, he thereby shows that at that time they lacked penetration of the Path.
"Of such a one" refers to the Teacher, who, because he is a Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), possesses a body of Dhamma (*dhammakāya*) so manifest due to his unerring teaching.
"Of him" refers to a clansman whose mind is concentrated through the attainment of the first jhāna and the others. This...

He asks whether it is appropriate to grasp at views such as annihilationism by means of the passage beginning with “that living being,” etc.; however, since those [views] have not yet been refuted merely by the attainment of jhāna due to the persistence of their underlying tenets, they reply, “This is appropriate for him.
[The Buddha] then rejects that grasping—which is indeed inappropriate even for one who has attained jhāna—by means of the passage beginning with “I, indeed...
do not say,” etc., thereby rejecting both the doctrine of annihilationism and the doctrine of eternalism.
This is the meaning with its underlying intention (*sādhippāyattha*). "This" refers to the first jhāna and so forth.

"In this way" means according to the method already stated. Furthermore, the phrase "and yet" (*atha ca pana*) is used to show that although the vision of the practitioner of insight (*vipassaka*) and others is indeed included in the text, the teaching is brought to its conclusion by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship;
thus it is said, "having shown one whose taints are utterly destroyed. For those two...
The renunciants, beginning from the point of insight (vipassanā), said, "It is not fitting for him to say such a thing. "Of this one" refers to the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava).
Although it is not stated in the Canon that "they were satisfied," their satisfaction should be understood precisely through the words of the reply, beginning with "it is not fitting";
thus he said, "They [said] to me," and so forth. In that context, because the one whose taints are destroyed is free from delusion (vigata-sammoha):
"Having crossed over doubt"—therefore, because it was improper for him to speak in such a manner, they became "glad at heart" upon hearing my words due to the certainty that had arisen in them;
this is the meaning. That Licchavi king also, like them, became glad at heart because he had likewise developed such a conviction.
Hence he said: "When this was said, he too became glad at heart. As for whatever is not analyzed here in terms of its meaning, that is indeed easy to understand.
Thus ends the elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Mahālisutta, from the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.

This work illuminates the extremely subtle, profound, and difficult-to-comprehend meanings; it generates a pure and vast clarity of wisdom; and it is called the *Sādhuvilāsinī* (the Delight of the Virtuous) as a clarification of the hidden meaning.
The commentary on the Mahālisutta is finished.
7. Commentary on the Jāliya Sutta:
Explanation of the Two Instances of Renunciation. 378.
Having thus commented upon the Mahāli Sutta, he now comments upon the Jāliya Sutta, according to the sequence of the occasion for the commentary.
In order to reveal its status as a *patta* (a distinct discourse), or to show that the discourse recited immediately after the *Mahālisutta* is the *Jāliyasutta*, he said:
"Thus have I heard... at Kosambī: the Jāliyasutta. By the phrase "by Ghosita," etc., he demonstrates a compound with the middle term elided (*majjhelopasamāsa*);
it could also be called "the monastery of Ghosita. For in this way, [it is like] "Anāthapiṇḍika’s... [monastery].

In passages such as "in the ārāma," there is a glorification of the donor; however, it is stated elsewhere that by thus praising him, the Venerable Ānanda encourages others to follow his example. Regarding that, in response to the questions:
"Who was this merchant Ghosita? How was the ārāma built by him? And how did the Blessed One dwell there? all of that [is explained].
Presenting the answer in brief, beginning from its full accomplishment, he said, “In former times indeed...,” and so forth.
“The kingdom of Allakappa” is seen in many manuscripts; however, in some places it is written as “the kingdom of Addila” and in others as “the kingdom of Damila.
“From there” means from the kingdom of Allakappa. “He went... to his son,” etc.—this too [is included] under the phrase “this was his deed.”
It is said [in the text] in order to make this known. "Then" means on the day they had entered the village. "Abundant thick gruel" means a large quantity of heavy porridge.
"To digest" means to cause it to be cooked by a digestive fire that is properly balanced. "When not present" means when he has gone elsewhere from his home.
"Barks" means he howls; the meaning is that he makes the sound of a dog, "bhubhu. This too is one of his functions.
However, while the Paccekabuddha had gone elsewhere for the purpose of making robes, the dog’s heart burst open.
These animals are upright by nature and not crooked; humans, on the other hand, think one thing with their hearts and say another with their mouths.
For this very reason it was said: "This, venerable sir, is a thicket as regards human beings; this, venerable sir, is clear as regards animals."
Thus, because of his affection for that paccekabuddha, through his upright view and lack of crookedness, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
With reference to him, it is said: “He... [and] was reborn. Furthermore, when he speaks into the ear of another, his voice pervades an area of sixteen yojanas;
however, the sound of ordinary conversation pervades the entire city of the gods, which is ten thousand yojanas in extent.
Thus, because of his perfection of voice, he came to be known by the name “Ghosaka-devaputta.

This was the result of his crying out out of affection for the Paccekabuddha. “Falling away” means falling away due to the exhaustion of his food. For from the world of the gods, devaputtas fall away due to four causes:
the exhaustion of their lifespan, the exhaustion of their merit, the exhaustion of their food, and through anger. Of these—
However, while he was indulging in the strands of sensual pleasure, his mindfulness lapsed and he passed away due to the exhaustion of his food.
He took rebirth in the womb of the courtesan Nagarasobhinī in Kosambī. It is said that the courtesans rear daughters but not sons;
for daughters maintain their lineage, whereas sons do not. Therefore, she had him abandoned on a heap of refuse.
This was the result of his former deed of abandoning his son. Indeed, one should not underestimate such evil karma, thinking it to be "insignificant.
A certain man, seeing him surrounded by crows and dogs, thought, "I have found my son," and took him home;
however, the Kosambī merchant paid a thousand kahāpaṇas from his own hand and took him back. It is with reference to this matter that [the Buddha said]:
It was said: “He was reborn in a certain family’s house in Kosambī,” and so forth.

Even the employment of means for the purpose of having him killed seven times was merely the consequence of the act of abandoning his own son. “The merchant’s daughter” refers to the daughter of the guild-president of the countryside.
“With discernment” means with the discernment of wisdom (*paññā-veyyattiya*). For she [recognized] the letter sent by her father to have him put to death...
Having split open the marriage contract and bound it [there], he secured his life. By that very excellence of his essence, he became known as the merchant Ghosita.
"For the purpose of refreshing the body" means for the sake of fattening a body exhausted by subsisting on roots and fruits in the Himālaya through the consumption of salt and sour liquids.
"Thirsty" means parched with thirst. "Exhausted" means with bodies worn out. "The vaṭa tree" refers to the great banyan tree.
Having reached that place, they sat down at its foot. Then, the eldest ascetic, seeing the splendor and perfection of the banyan tree, thought:

"I suppose a deity of great power dwells here. It would be well indeed if this deity would dispel the fatigue of the journey by giving the company of seers water and other refreshments. The deity, perceiving his thoughts, [acted accordingly].
He gave water, bathing facilities, and food to the group of seers. Therefore he said, “There,” and so forth.
However, having applied the elder ascetic’s way of thinking universally to all cases, it is said, “seeking favor.
By the phrase “stretching out his hand,” he shows that by the mere act of stretching out his hand, whatever she desired was accomplished.
The deity said: although she was unable to speak because of her shame due to the meagerness of her own merit, being repeatedly pressed, she spoke thus.
"He" refers to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika. "Of the laborers" means of the slaves, servants, and workmen who perform services for wages.
"Only the ordinary food and wages" means only that food and wages which are to be given as usual.
The meaning is that because it was the Uposatha day, even those who did not perform the work were to be given the food and wages due on the day of labor,
and nothing less than that. In the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, according to the opinion of the Khuddaka-bhāṇakas, it is said,
"He came for the sake of the evening meal," whereas here, according to the opinion of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas, it is said, "He came at midday for the sake of the morning meal."
The connection is either "even a small amount of wages" (*kañci pi bhatakan*) or "even a small amount of wage-earning work" (*kiñci pi bhatakakammaṃ*).
Because it was the time of midday, he said, "half the day has passed. By this, he shows that because it was undertaken for only half a day, people refer to it as "half a *uposatha*.
In the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, "half a *uposatha*" is stated by way of a portion of the night.
But here, it refers to either the portion of the day starting from midday, or the remaining portion of the day and night.
For the term "half" (upaḍḍha) is used even for an unequal division. "On that very same day" is said with reference to the time of sunrise.
"Even the sound 'Buddha' is rare in the world"—thus he spoke, having conceived joy and gladness. "On that very same day" [refers to] Kosambī.
On the very second day from the day they arrived. "Turitātthā" means those who have urgent business; the meaning is, "be swift in your journey.

The word "having gone forth" (pabbajitvā) is said with reference to the "Come, monk" (ehibhikkhu) ordination. "Arahatta" refers to the state of an Arahant, adorned with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
Having established those three merchants in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti), and having given gifts for about half a month, [he departed].
Having relied upon [the king], they had three monasteries built. The Blessed One, however, dwelt in each monastery for one day at a time.
And in whichever monastery he stayed, he would go for alms in that very house; on this occasion, he was dwelling in the Ghosita monastery.
Therefore it is said: "He dwells at Kosambī in the Ghosita ārāma."
He is a preceptor merely by external convention, not by the characteristic of a preceptor as found in the Dispensation.
*Upārambha* means approaching another with speech that is offensive or injurious; the meaning is a provocation by way of perceiving faults. Therefore he said, "desiring to bring forward a dispute.
For it is called a *vāda* (dispute) because they speak (*vadanti*)—that is, they speak by way of censure—through it; thus it is fault.
The meaning is: "desiring to mount it," that is, desiring to place it upon [the body]. To explain how they desire to mount it, he says:
"Thus, indeed... and so forth. "That is the soul, that is the body" means: whatever entity is designated as the soul, that very same thing is designated as the body.
For these people speak by adopting the doctrine stated thus: "One regards form as the self. [They regard] both form and the self...
By means of viewing them as non-dual and unified, they speak of a "being" (satta) with reference to the self (attā) imagined by outsiders.
For it has been said: "Right here the being perishes. "Of him" (assa) means of the ascetic Gotama.
"Perishes" (bhijjati) means it is destroyed by way of cessation and dissolution. Because of that, he admits there is no difference between the life-principle and the body.

And because the disintegration of the body is perceived. For here, it cannot be argued that—just as the disintegration of the soul is not stated [by the opponent] despite being unperceived, on the grounds that it is non-different from the body which possesses perceived disintegration—likewise the body must also be non-disintegrating, on the grounds that it is non-different from the soul which possesses unperceived disintegration;
for that disintegration of the body is established by direct perception, and because a body distinct from the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) does not exist.
With this intention, namely, that it is because of non-existence, he said, "It becomes an annihilationist doctrine.
[The view that] "the soul is one thing and the body another" means that the basis designated as the soul is indeed one thing, and that designated as the body is another.
For they speak by taking up the doctrine that proceeds according to the method beginning with, "One regards the self as possessing form," and so forth. It is precisely of the various types of form...

Because [the self] is seen, and because that [self] is absent within the self, the meaning "the self is eternal" follows; it is with this intention that he says, "a being would be established as eternal.
(379–380) This is like imagining the height or shortness of the son of a barren woman; therefore, this...
This question is to be set aside. For it is not based on the goal (attha), nor is it based on the Dhamma;

it does not pertain to the fundamental practice of the holy life (ādibrahmacariyaka), nor does it lead to disenchantment and the other [stages] of the goal. The *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta* serves as an illustration here.

Having closed the session for the sake of the king, the Teacher began his teaching of the Dhamma to them with the words, "Therefore, friends, listen," and so forth; thus he said, "Then the Blessed One," and so on.
The two extremes are the views of eternalism and annihilationism. The Noble Path is the Middle Way.
"Of that very way" means of the wrong way itself.
"Of one who has gone forth out of faith" means of one who has gone forth through faith [thinking], "In this way I shall escape from this suffering of the round of existence."

For one who has gone forth into homelessness, having fulfilled the corresponding virtue and whose mind is concentrated through the first jhāna—this refers to the defilement of views expressed in statements such as "the soul is the same as the body," which illustrate the growth of the cycle of defilements.
"He is not free from doubt" means he is not one who has crossed over doubt regarding phenomena; the meaning is that he continues to move back and forth, wavering and fluctuating, in various matters.
“I know this thus”: by means of that first jhāna which that bhikkhu enters and dwells in, I know this associated state as “lofty consciousness.
For it is said: “He established the perception: ‘This is lofty consciousness.
But I do not speak thus, [in the way] that those who hold wrong views [speak], regarding that class of phenomena together with its support as an undifferentiated whole.

Those who grasp [the view] that "the soul is the same as the body," or those who grasp both of these as distinct, declaring "the soul is one thing and the body another," proclaim their own false grasping;
I do not speak thus because of my thorough and complete understanding of that teaching.
Therefore he said, "But rather," and so forth. It is stated that outsiders for the most part produce only the meditative absorptions (jhāna) based on the kasiṇas.

"Of one developing the preliminary work of the kasiṇas. Because the attainment of jhāna occurs through the power of meditation (bhāvanā), and because that meditation takes place by way of perceiving the earth-kasiṇa and so forth, it is described by way of its characteristic of perception (saññā); therefore, he said, "arisen by the power of perception.
Thus it was stated: "One perceives the earth-kasiṇa," and so on. Furthermore, because [it was taught] by the Blessed One...

In various instances, it is stated, "And yet I do not say so. Therefore, taking the Blessed One’s word as the authoritative instruction (upadesa), they said, "It is not right for him," with the underlying intention that this [statement] should not have been made by a Kevalin, a Supreme Person.
To show that this was not spoken out of their own independent insight, it is said, "They speak while thinking [otherwise]. The rest is as in the immediately following sutta.
Because it has been explained according to the method already stated and because it is evident,

this is indeed easy to understand. Thus ends the elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Jāliya Sutta, titled *Līnatthapakāsanī*, which is a clarification of the meanings in the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*—

the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya* that illuminates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend, and which generates the clarity of vast and stainless wisdom— and which is called the *Sādhuvilāsinī*.
The commentary on the Jāliya Sutta is finished.
8. Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta:
The account of Acela Kassapa.
381. Having thus commented upon the Jāliya Sutta, now, while commenting upon the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, [the author] explains that it has reached its turn in the sequence of the commentary;
or, he reveals that the sutta recited immediately after the Jāliya Sutta is the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, beginning with:
“Thus have I heard... [pe] ...while staying at Uruññā: this is the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.”
He said: "The very name of that country where that city is located, and likewise the very name of that city where the Blessed One stayed, is 'Uruññā.

Therefore, the meaning should be understood through the method of ellipsis (*āvutti*) and so forth as: 'In Uruññā' means in the district named Uruññā, in the city named Uruññā. By this, he shows this point: not...
In all cases, words denoting a country are exclusively masculine plural;

however, in some instances they are also indefinite masculine plurals, as in the phrase "he dwells at Āḷavī," where some say this refers to the country itself. To exclude that interpretation, the words "the Blessed One" and so forth were stated.
It is called "delightful" because of its charming terrain, its excellence of shade and water, and its seclusion from people.
And it is delightful. Because deer are granted safety (*abhaya*) there, it is called a *migadāya* (deer park). Therefore he said, "He," and so forth. *Cela* means clothing;
because he has no such thing, he is *acela*, as stated: "a naked wanderer. *Nāma* refers to a clan name (*gottanāma*).
*Tapa* is burning, scorching, or the exhaustion of the body; one who possesses that is a *tapassī*. Since he is of such a nature, [he practices] austerity...
It is dependent; since that austerity is dependent upon it, he therefore says "dependent on austerity" (*tapanissitaka*). Regarding the phrase "loose conduct, etc.," the word "etc.

includes hand-clapping and so forth as they appear later in the text. One who lives or conducts oneself with what is coarse and harsh, because it is devoid of the conduct esteemed by the virtuous and is offensive, is called "one who lives coarsely" (*lūkhājīvī*);
this is the method not mentioned in the Aṭṭhakathā. "He ridicules" means by way of mocking.
"He reviles. "He censures" means he speaks in dispraise preceded by contempt; hence it is said, "he despises and ridicules.

In passages such as "knowledge of the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*), the word *dhamma* is used in the sense of a cause; thus he says, "the secondary cause of the cause.
This is because the meaning of the word as previously stated is here the state of being a cause for the word "cause. By way of purpose.

For the application of sound is dependent [on something else]. And that very meaning of the sound, when spoken by others, is an imitation—either corresponding to it, resembling it, or occurring after it—because it functions as a cause stated subsequently.
"By others" means by those others, you, to whom this was said. "By the stated cause" means: if what was spoken by them is not likewise spoken by you, then in this way...

If, by reason of those [arguments] stated by them, your own doctrine were to become possessed of a cause, then neither your doctrine nor any subsequent criticism of it would ever reach even the slightest point that is censurable by the wise; how then could it fail to reach such a state?
This is the construction. With the words “This is what is meant,” etc., he shows that very same meaning in brief.

382. Now, having briefly stated with reference to the doctrine of analysis (vibhajjavāda), "These are not speakers of what has been said," the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "Here, Kassapa, I...
in order to demonstrate that very doctrine by way of analysis; showing it through such analysis, he said, "In this case, someone...
For the Blessed One [rejects] useless physical exhaustion that does not lead to tranquility (upasama).
“Devotion to self-mortification is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial,” and so forth.
He censures [this], but he praises bodily exertion that is purposeful and conducive to tranquility, such as by saying, “He is a forest-dweller; he is a wearer of rag-robes,” and so forth.
“Due to a lack of merit” means due to demerit. And here the word *appa* (little/lack) refers to the practice of using only two or three coverings in a place with little vegetation.
In passages such as "it should be resolved by one who is established," the meaning is that of non-existence. With regard to the statement "having fulfilled the three types of misconduct":

this refers to the fulfillment of misconduct in various ways for the sake of maintaining one's livelihood, preceded by wrong view—such as "there is no gift," etc.—by one who denies the fruit of action because of the presence of wrong view.
“*Bhiyyosomattāya*” means exceeding the proper measure. For this word *bhiyyoso* is a derivative (*nepātika*) having the same meaning as the word *bhiyyo*.

“*Anesanavasenā*” means by way of improper search—that is, by way of wrong livelihood consisting of searching for what should not be sought by performing various kinds of asceticism out of a desire to gain credit for non-existent qualities while remaining in hypocrisy.
It is for the sake of maintaining one’s livelihood according to the method already described.
"Having fulfilled the three types of misconduct. "These two" refers to the two types of persons who commit misconduct when it is said, "one of little merit" and "one possessed of merit.
In the second method, "these two" refers to the two types of persons who practice good conduct when it is said, "one of little merit" and "one possessed of merit.
The meaning in the third and fourth methods should be understood in the same sequence as that stated in the first and second methods.

In this context, it should be understood that those who hold the first and third methods are proponents of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) and non-action (*akiriyavāda*), whereas those who hold the second and fourth methods are proponents of action (*kammavāda*).
"Living with little suffering" means living with only a small amount of suffering.

"Engaged in the conduct of outsiders" means being engaged in the conduct of non-Buddhist sectarians (*titthiya*) rather than the conduct prescribed by the Teaching (*sāsana*). "Having comforted oneself" means [comforting oneself] by means of requisites obtained through unrighteousness and wrong search (*an-esanā*).
Having comforted oneself with happiness and made oneself happy, the current reading is “having established oneself in happiness.
By means of the three conceivings (maññanā)—namely, craving, pride, and views—expressed in the passage beginning “Now there is no one equal to me,” he speaks of the fulfillment of misconduct.
Or, while producing gain and honor, he fulfills the three types of misconduct.
The connection [is as follows]. "By way of wrong view" means by way of the wrong view occurring in such a manner as, "There is no fault in sensual pleasures.
"Of a female wanderer" refers to a young woman of the ascetic class who has entered into an external renunciant life, as well as to a concealed female wanderer (*channaparibbājikā*).
For here too, in the phrase "another," the subject is either "an ascetic" or "a concealed male wanderer. "Young" means youthful.
“Mudukāya” means delicate. “Lomasāya” means having fine, thin body hair; that is, possessing sparse hair.

Grammarians maintain that the word is formed by adding the suffix *-sa* even when the feminine gender marker is present. “In sensual pleasures” (*kāmesu*) refers to objective sensual pleasures (*vatthu-kāma*).
“To be tasted” (*pātabbaṃ*) means to be enjoyed. Here, the prefix *pā-* has the sense of enjoyment, while the root *tabba-* signifies necessity.
And it is a noun formed by means of the suffix -ana (bhāvasādhana). Furthermore, the word *tā* is used in its own sense (*sakatthe*), as in the term "deity" (*devatā*);

or else it signifies the state of being fit to be consumed (*pātabba-ta*), that is, the state of being enjoyed. And here, the word *tabba* is a noun formed by means of the suffix -tabba (*kattusādhana*), as in the *Pañcattaya Sutta* of the *Upari-paṇṇāsa*:
"For whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, [claim] the attainment of this base (*āyatana*) merely by means of the conditioned phenomena consisting of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized..."
"...they describe it. For thus it is said in the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) on that passage: "It is 'to be cognized' (*viññātabba*) because one cognizes;
by means of the mere state of having seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, and by the mere occurrence of five-door perception—this is the meaning here. And in the sub-commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on that:
"Just as the word *niyyānika* (leading out) is a term denoting the agent (*kattusādhana*) because it is frequently used in the sense of 'those who lead out,' so too here is the word *viññātabba*."

He said: "That which is cognized is called 'the cognizable' (*viññātabba*)," where the suffix *-tā* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). When standing on the side of that which is being relished, even *kilesakāma* (defilement-desire) is included within *vatthukāma* (object-desire);
therefore, the meaning is: "one enjoys them according to one's liking.

"This" refers to the analysis of the distinctions in meaning as stated by way of the fourfold method (*nayacatukka*). [The passage] "as it appears in the commentary by way of the heretics" (*titthiyavasena*)...
"It is analyzed in that same way," so it was stated by the Teacher; however, it should be understood that it is analyzed in exactly that same way in the Pāḷi as well.
"In this Dispensation" means in this very Dispensation.
To the question "How is it obtained?", he said: "For a certain person," and so forth. Because one does not obtain it, [the text says] "having practiced wrong search," and so on.
It should be applied as follows: either by claiming, according to the literal expression, that one possesses within oneself the state of Arahantship which one does not actually possess;

or by resorting to the three bases for hypocrisy—namely, hinting, accepting conditions [for gifts], and dependence on modes of deportment—or by being one who lives austerely through the undertaking of ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). The phrase "by way of wrong search" is merely an illustration; for it should also be stated: "by claiming to be an Arahant," and so forth.

The intention is: "I shall experience difficult happiness through rebirth in the miserable states (*duggati*). Regarding the word "asakkonto" (being unable): here the term *anta* functions as an indicator of a state (*bhāvalakkhaṇe*), meaning "when one is unable.
383. "From such-and-such a place" means from such-and-such an existence (*bhava*). "Come" means come here by way of rebirth.
"And the place to be gone to now" refers to the existence to be reached in the future by way of rebirth. "From there" means from the past existence. "Again, rebirth" [is explained as follows].
"Rebirth again in a future immediate existence, and from that immediate existence, rebirth once more in an immediate existence"—this refers to repeated arising.

"For what reason would I reproach?"—here, one who does not know things as they truly are might reproach anything at all under the influence of desire and aversion; but I am not like that. Rather, knowing everything as it truly is, for what reason...
Showing the intention that "there is no reason whatsoever to censure this asceticism," he said, "It is indeed to be censured," and so forth.
"Bhaṇḍika" means a small bundle or packet. In the case of the simile, it is "washed" because of its purity, and likewise "unwashed.
However, in the case of the subject of the simile (the asceticism), it is "washed" and pure because of its praiseworthy qualities.
Likewise, the meaning is "and unlearned. "That matter" refers both to the censuring of what is to be censured and the praising of what is to be praised.
(384) Because its activity consists in accomplishing welfare pertaining to the present life and the future life, it is of great importance;
therefore, no one says that it is not good. "Fivefold enmity" refers to the fivefold enmity beginning with the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*). For that—
It is called "enmity" (*vera*) because it stands as the opposite of the fivefold virtue and because it is a cause of hostility among beings;

for that very reason, no one says of it, "This is good," since it does not accomplish any welfare pertaining to the present life and so forth, and because it corrupts the goodness of sentient beings. "It should not be suppressed" means it should not be prevented from being apprehended as a form.
For their intention is that "the acquisition of the eye has the purpose of seeing what is worth seeing. This same principle applies to the ear and the other [senses] as well.
The intention is that to the extent that non-restraint is good for them in the five doors, to that same extent restraint is not good there;
thus he said, "Again... non-restraint."
Herein, this is another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā*: those whom some say "it is good" are called "certain recluses and brahmins," namely the sectarians (*titthiya*).
That which they say is "good"—such as the pursuit of self-mortification and so forth—that we do not call "good. But that which they [say is] "not good"...
[and so on]... however, that which they [practice], such as the use of blameless requisites and the right practice of being well-clad and well-robed, we do not call "not good."
“They say ‘it is not good,’ and we say ‘it is good.

Thus, in order to indicate that the tetrad shown based on the opponent’s position is the very same tetrad shown again based on one’s own position, the words beginning with “even so” (evaṃ) were spoken.
For whatever is common to anyone, by that [commonality] too—
It is exactly the same. Whatever is dissimilar to anything else, by that too it is indeed dissimilar; thus he said, "the state of being similar and dissimilar" (*samānāsamānata*).

And here, "similarity" (*samānata*) refers merely to the quality of being similar. For the abandonment of all phenomena to be abandoned and the attainment of all phenomena to be attained are seen only in our own doctrine, not in the doctrines of others. Therefore it was said: "Having approached them..."

“I speak thus,” and so forth. The meaning should be understood according to the method already stated, in accordance with one’s own doctrine and the doctrines of others, by way of the five precepts and so on.
385. Regarding the commentary on the discussion for eliciting an inquiry:
*antaṃ* is a fifth-case personal pronoun used in the sense of an injunction. “Asking about the tenet” means: “What [is the position] of the ascetic Gotama?”
"Does he proceed having abandoned all things subject to defilement without exception, or do other teachers of schools [proceed thus]? First, state your own doctrine in this matter.
Thus he asks regarding the established tenet that has been accepted. "Asking for the reason" means:
when it is stated, "The ascetic Gotama proceeds having abandoned all things subject to defilement without exception," one asks, "By what reason is this matter [established]?"

"Make him understand"—thus he asks for the reason. "He asks for both" means that after stating the reason—"this indeed is the cause here"—and when the matter asserted is being established, he asks for two types of examples, distinguished as similar and dissimilar, in order to corroborate the reason through both positive (anvaya) and negative (vyatireka) concomitance.
Furthermore, by way of the reason and the example, [he establishes] the possession of the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa).
When the matter has been properly established exactly as promised, one who speaks subsequently and brings the case to a conclusion is also said to "cross-examine" (*samanubhāsati*);

this should be understood. The word "having brought together" (*upasaṃharitvā*) is an ellipsis [to be supplied]. The phrase beginning with "What to you? (*kiṃ te*) and so forth is a demonstration of the manner of bringing them together.
"In the second phrase as well" refers to the phrase "by the Saṅgha or to the Saṅgha. This is stated with reference to the ellipsis and the manner of bringing them together.
“The same method applies” is what was stated.

“That meaning” refers to the meaning consisting in practicing after having abandoned, without remainder, those states that are to be abandoned, and practicing after having undertaken, without remainder, those states that are to be undertaken.
“Having joined” means having joined it with the terms beginning with “unwholesome.”
Because they arise from heedlessness and so forth, they are both unwholesome (*akusala*) and are designated as "unwholesome" (*akusalā*);
here, the term *saṅkhāta* has the sense of "known" (*ñāta*) and also fits the sense of "division" (*koṭṭhāsa*). Thus he said: "They are known, or they are established by being divided into parts.
Here, by the former phrase he refers to those that are exclusively unwholesome, and by the latter, to those associated with them and their opposites.

Thus, by means of this division into sections, the establishment [of the categories] becomes logical. For "division into sections" (koṭṭhāsakaraṇa) is the defining [of factors] by way of their belonging to the unwholesome side.
The word *avajja* has the sense of "fault," because it is a synonym for what is censurable (*gārayha*), and because the prefix *a-* functions in the sense of the absence of that [fault].
Therefore, he said, "they are with fault" (*sadosā*). Noble ones (*ariya*) are indeed faultless. But these unwholesome states are not faultless in any way whatsoever.
They are incapable, meaning they are unable, to become noble ones in the sense of being faultless.
(386–392) By the phrase "by which" (*yenā*), he shows that the word "which" (*yaṃ*) here is used in the nominative case to indicate a cause.

Furthermore, "or whatever" (*yaṃ vā pana*) is an expression of impossibility; its meaning is "or whatever little [there may be]. And the phrase "they proceed having abandoned" is used according to the requirements of the context.
"Transformation of the plural number" refers to what was said: "they proceed having abandoned this or that trifling thing. Here, the teachers of the groups are Pūraṇa, Makkhali, and so forth.
Because the Saṅgha originates from the Teacher, the excellence of the Teacher is also made manifest through the excellence of the Saṅgha;
thus he said, "from the perfection of the Saṅgha... by way of its accomplishment. Furthermore, since that praise is caused by confidence, it is presented by way of confidence.

To demonstrate this, it is said: “Even those who are gaining confidence,” and so forth. Therein, by means of the particle *pi* (even/also) in the sense of inclusion (*sampiṇḍana*), it is included that even those who are not gaining confidence do not gain confidence in this very same way.

For just as, through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), confidence in the disciples is gathered from the excellence of the Teacher, and confidence in the Teacher is gathered from the excellence of the disciples;

likewise, through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), [lack of confidence in the disciples is gathered] from the deficiency of the Teacher, and [lack of confidence in the Teacher] from the deficiency of the disciples.

And it should be understood as "lack of confidence in the Teacher. The phrase beginning with "For thus" (*tathā hi*) is its explanation. "Perfection of the body" (*sarīrasampattiṃ*) means perfection of form;
the meaning is the complete fulfillment of the physical body (*rūpakāya*). This was said with reference to beings who are limited by their physical form;

however, the phrase "or having heard the teaching of the Dhamma" refers to those limited by sound and those limited by the Dhamma. And [the passage] beginning with "the conduct and resort of the bhikkhus" refers to...
However, there are those who take form as their standard (*rūpappamāṇa*), those who take sound as their standard (*ghosappamāṇa*), and those who take the Dhamma as their standard (*dhammappamāṇa*).

Through conduct, sphere of activity, and so forth, the Dhamma becomes "coarse" (*lūkha*) when it is practiced correctly. Therefore, regarding the phrase "there are those who speak," in the first clause one should apply [the standards] of form, sound, and the Dhamma;
in the second clause, only those who take the Dhamma as their standard should be applied. "Of what kind? means of what sort or of what nature. That which belongs to the Saṅgha...
"Praise" (pasaṃsā) is connected [to the preceding context],
or this very reading [is the one intended]. Therein, having extracted that which is manifested as the state of praise belonging to the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha alone,
and the absence of that in others— by way of the teaching on abstinence, abandoning, and restraint— he said, "This is the underlying intention," and so forth.

In this context, regarding the abstinence consisting in the destruction of the bridge (*setughāta-virati*), it is said that "it does not exist in any way whatsoever" because it is associated with the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

As for the other types of abandonment, they should be applied according to what is obtained: mere suppression (*vikkhambhana*) by means of the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and mere partial abandonment (*tadaṅga*) by means of insight (*vipassanā*) alone.
And by the phrase "by means of insight alone," it refers to contemplating [the object] in various ways as "impermanent" (*anicca*) or as "suffering" (*dukkha*).

This is by way of mere seeing, and not by way of the comprehension of formations after having first undertaken the discernment of name-and-form and the grasping of conditions, and then superimposing the three characteristics. For outsiders lack both the delimitation of name-and-form and the contemplation of non-self.
As for the other three—the abandoning through cutting off, subsiding, and escape—they do not exist at all in any way whatsoever.
Because of the nature of the path, its fruits, and Nibbāna: (1) every form of restraint of virtue other than the five mundane precepts;
(2) the perfectly pure restraint of patience, described by such passages as "he is patient with cold and heat";

(3) the restraint of knowledge, consisting of the knowledge of the path that utterly eradicates the defilements, described by such passages as "by wisdom these are shut off"; and [the restraint] of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth...

The perfectly pure restraint of the faculties that proceeds by way of guarding; and the restraint of energy, termed "right exertion," which is described as "for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states," and so forth—
it is with reference to this pentad of restraints that it was said, "the rest does not exist in any way whatsoever."

The phrase beginning with “There are, moreover, these five recitations of the Pātimokkha” is a restatement of the aforementioned virtue in order to show the great extent of virtue within the Dispensation, and to demonstrate that others are established in only a portion of it. The reading now is “the recitation of the Uposatha.
It is “manifested” (paññāyati) in the sense that it becomes evident through its state of being firmly established; therefore, [it is said]: “Indeed, by me... there is none.”
It should be applied as follows: "Lion’s roar" means the best roar, the roar of one who is fearless, a discourse that cannot be countered by anyone. As for what they say:
"In the subsequent [list of] words—tiger, bull, ox, elephant, lion, leopard, nāga, and so forth—the masculine [terms] have the sense of excellence and are the domain [of such qualities]."
This should be understood by way of the majority of cases.
393. Commentary on the Noble Eightfold Path:
"Furthermore, this doctrine of mine as it has been stated is indeed non-erroneous; its state of being non-erroneous is due to this path..."
“Having practiced it, it is to be known by one’s own authority, not dependent on another”—thus [it is said] for the purpose of awakening to the state of non-perversion.

Regarding the passage in the Pāḷi beginning with “There is, Kassapa,” this is the construction: the path that one has entered, one will know and see for oneself through direct personal experience, thinking:
“The ascetic Gotama, when speaking at the appropriate time, speaks what is real because of its being such as it is.”
“Because it brings benefit unilaterally, he calls it ‘the goal’ (attha); because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, he calls it ‘the Dhamma’;

and because of its connection with discipline and its disciplining of others, he calls it ‘the Vinaya. This path, O Kassapa, which is the means of escape from the entire suffering of saṃsāra, has been proclaimed by me after having realized it for myself through direct knowledge;
and also the preliminary practice which serves as the means for attaining that [path]. Therefore, ‘ascetic’...”

This shows that the proclamation, proceeding according to the method beginning with, “Gotama conducts himself having abandoned these states without remainder,” is an unshakable lion’s roar as it truly is.
Furthermore, the word *dakkhati* (he sees) is established here by means of the verbal root *ssati*,
as in such passages as, “Indeed, where a disciple will thus know, or see, or bear witness.”
In passages from the Suttas such as, “One sees this thus as it really is with correct wisdom,” he shows the Path and the Way together as one.

The restrictive expression “this very one” (ayameva) is for the purpose of negating any multiplicity in the Path, for the purpose of showing its commonality to all Noble Ones, and for the purpose of showing its well-known status within the Dispensation. Therefore he said: “The one-way path.”
“Monks, this is the path for the purification of beings. “This indeed is the path, there is no other, for the purification of vision,” said the one who sees the end of birth:
“The single way, for the one who sees the destruction of birth.”
The one who is compassionate for their welfare understands the path;
by this very path, those of old have crossed over, and those yet to come will cross, as well as those currently crossing the flood.
In all the passages of the Suttas and the passages of the Abhidhamma, this is the one way that is manifest.

Regarding the commentary on the discussion of the undertaking of asceticism (tapopakkama): because it is to be undertaken and initiated, it is called "the undertaking of asceticism" (tapopakkama); thus he says "from the undertaking of asceticism" (tapārambhā), and here "undertaking" (ārambhaṇa) refers to—

By the phrase "austerities" (*tapokammāni*), he shows that these are indeed the instruments of austerity. "Designated as the work of recluses" (*samaṇakammasaṅkhātā*) means recognized as the work to be performed by recluses.
The same principle applies here to the phrase "designated as the work of brahmins" (*brāhmaṇakammasaṅkhātā*).

"Naked" (*niccolo*) means one who has cast off clothing; one who has entirely rejected all clothing. "Cloth" (*cela*) and "garment" (*cola*) are synonymous terms. This applies even to someone wearing tattered rags of torn and broken cloth.
To exclude the possibility that one might be called "unclothed" (*niccola*) simply because of the absence of a garment with fringes, the word "naked" (*nagga*) is used;

the meaning is that he is naked in every respect due to his undertaking of the vow of nakedness. By the phrase "in the acts of defecation, etc.," it is shown that "laxity of conduct" refers precisely to being devoid of the conduct of worldly sons of noble family.
To the question "How is he devoid [of such conduct]? he says: "Standing [in the open]," and so forth.
And this is merely an illustration, for even such practices as rinsing the mouth after vomiting have been abandoned by him.
"He scrapes" means he rubs it with water because he does not wash it off. It is said that he designates a stick as a "living being";
therefore, in order to fulfill that practice, he acts in this way, as expressed in the passage beginning with "excrement or... In this context, "he scrapes" means he removes [the excrement].
When it is said, “Come, venerable sir” (*ehi bhaddanta*), the procedure consisting of approaching is called *ehibhaddanta*; one who practices that is an *ehibhaddantika*.
Here, the formation of the derivative term is achieved through conventional usage (*ruḷhisadda*), as in the case of “*ehipassiko*” (come and see). By way of contrast, there is the *naehibhaddantika*.
He shows this same meaning with the words “for the purpose of receiving alms,” and so forth. “He does not go” means he does not come. Thus, [the term] *natiṭṭhabhaddantika* [is explained].

In this case as well: with the intention that one who is called a *samaṇa* must indeed act according to his own word and not according to the word of another, he does neither of those two... [etc. ... "Earlier" means prior to his own approaching of that place;
for it is said that he does not take [alms] with the intention, "A monk may take almsfood exactly as he pleases."

However, he does not accept food prepared specifically for him with the underlying intention: "Because of me as the cause, many small living beings have been brought together [and killed] for this robe.
He does not consent to an invitation with the underlying intention: "In this way, their word will have been fulfilled.
A *kumbhī* is a pot into which cooked alms-food has been placed. An *ukkhalī* is a pot for cooking alms-food. A *pacchī* is...

“Alms-food placed in a basket”: from that [basket] as well—meaning even from a pot or a bowl. Because he perceives those [beings] as living beings even within the pots and such, it says “one who takes from a pot or a bowl,” and so forth.
The same method applies to the phrases “this is me,” and so on. “In between” means the space between the two.
“An obstacle to a mouthful” means an obstacle to a morsel of food. Here too, he perceives them as living beings. “One who has gone into the presence of a man” means one who has gone near a man.
“An obstacle to delight” (*ratyantarāya*) means an obstacle to the delight of sensual pleasure. It is called *saṅkitti* because they gather together and praise it;
thus, a collection of rice and so forth brought together in that way, and the meal prepared from it, is what is intended here—hence the phrase “in meals prepared by gathering.
However, in the commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, the Master himself [explains] as follows:

It is said: "They call it together by means of this, thus it is *saṃkitti*; it is an action performed collectively by village-dwellers. But here, the 'calling together for alms' (*bhattasaṃkitti*) is intended;

therefore he says, 'having called together those who have prepared their meals. Furthermore, by the words "exalted" (*ukkaṭṭho*) and so forth, he shows that this is his superior practice (*ukkaṭṭhapatipadā*).
And just as it is here, so it is also in the case of [the terms] "one who does not say 'Come, venerable sir'" (*naehibhaddantiko*) and the rest.
The demonstration of the superior practice (ukkaṭṭha-paṭipadā) should be understood. The word *sā* is a synonym for a dog. *Tassa* means "of the dog. *Tattha* means "in that place.
*Samūhasamūhacārinī* means "moving in groups and groups" [or "moving in a multitude of multitudes"]. *Manussā* refers to people who perform services. *Sovīrakaṃ* means sour gruel (*kañjika*).
Some say it is "salted sour gruel" (*loṇasovīraka*), but that is quite incorrect; [it is made] from all the ingredients of the harvest...
Because it is stated [in the text] as "it is said. For *loṇasovīraka* (salted sour gruel) is prepared with all kinds of ingredients such as fish, meat, flowers, and fruits.

"Only the drinking of *surā*" means the drinking of that which has attained the characteristic of *surā* (fermented liquor). Here, *meraya* (distilled liquor) is also included either by way of its shared characteristic or by the principle of mentioning one representative member (*ekasesa-naya*).
"In all" refers to even those among the sour gruel, *surā*, and so forth, that are both blameworthy and blameless. "He enters only a single house for the purpose of wandering for alms."
“Visiting a single house”: he returns; that is to say, if there is an alms-offering, he does not go further than that.

He subsists on a single mouthful alone, thus he is “one who lives on a single mouthful. It is given by means of this, thus it is a “datti”—a small bowl for distributing alms-food, used for taking only two or three mouthfuls.
Therefore he says, “a small bowl. “The first alms-food” means alms-food that has not yet been touched.
Or it is the "highest alms-food" (uttamabhikkhaṃ) because it is specially prepared. It is called *ekāhika* because one [period] consists of this [fasting] by way of not eating;
the meaning is that one consumes that food. In terms of its actual sense, it is said to be "skipping one day," as in the phrase "with an interval of one day.
This same method applies to the terms "*dvāhika*" and so forth. Furthermore, it is the act of eating for one day after having fasted for one day; thus, it is a "one-day cycle."
Or it is *ekāhika* (once-daily). Eating on every second day after having fasted for two days is *dvāhika* (every-other-day eating), or it is the practice of the two-day interval.
This same method applies to the remaining two [terms] as well. For one who eats by turns (*pariyāyabhattabhojanika*) in the highest degree, having fasted for two days, eats for only one day;
likewise for the remaining two. However, in the *Majjhimāgama-ṭīkā*, it says: "It is *ekāhika* because it has a single day occurring within its interval."

"The same method applies to the remaining phrases," it is said. In such passages as "The elder bhikkhus exhort the bhikkhunīs in turn," the word *pariyāya* has the sense of "turn" (*vāra*). "By a one-day turn" means by a turn lasting one day.

It should be understood that the phrase "in this manner" and so forth was stated in the Canon in order to show that the procedure described by the words "lasting one day" and so on occurs in successive order.
395. *Sāmāka* is a type of wheat. "Self-grown rice varieties" refers to uncultivated rice varieties; that which people call simply "rice. "Having plowed" means having tilled.
"Resin" (*silesa*) refers even to the resin of trees such as the *kaṇikāra*. "Grain-powder" (*kuṇḍaka*) is the finer portion of the rice grain;
the meaning is "fragments of rice. "Rice-gruel" (*odanakañjiya*) is gruel made from boiled rice. "With scented sesame paste" (*piññāka*).
In passages such as "one should bathe," the word *piññāka* is a synonym for sesame flour (*tilapiṭṭha*). As it has been said: "What is called *piññāka*? It is said to be sesame flour.
Some say that "the young trunk of a plantain tree is itself *piññāka*"; this should not be accepted, because it is nowhere stated in that way.
396. *Sāṇa* garments are those produced from *saṇa* hemp; *masāṇa* garments are those made of *saṇa* mixed with other materials.

According to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), these are not rags included among the six types of robes. However, some, having imagined that "moss-cloth" (*masāṇa*) refers to a particular kind of cotton cloth, read it as "moss-cotton cloths" (*massakacoḷāni*); this is indeed incorrect, because it was not stated so by the ancients.

Regarding the phrase "eraka-grass and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes *akkama*, *kaci*, *kadali*, *vāka*, and others; for garments made from eraka-grass and such are indeed wretched and inferior.
They deserve to be called "rags" (*dussāni*). Here, the word *chava* is a term for something inferior; however, in the previous interpretation, it refers to a dead body.

"Discarded rags" (*chaḍḍitanantakāni*) means discarded pieces of cloth. "A deer-skin" (*ajinassedaṃ*) means a deer-skin; that is, the natural hide of a deer, or specifically, that very same skin when split down the middle.
"Half-split deer-skin" (*ajinakkhipaṃ*) means a deer-skin that has been split into two halves. It is also called "with the hooves."
Regarding the statement, "They say," it is stated in the *Papañcasūdanī* that if two or three [skins] are combined, their intended meaning is "a cloak of antelope skin" (*ajinakkhipa*).
However, in the commentaries on the Vinaya, it is stated that "the word 'ajinakkhipa' refers to the antelope skin itself without distinction.
"Having wailed" means having wailed repeatedly and alternately. There is also a reading, "having knotted" (*ganthetvā*), which means having wound and bound it together.
In this way, the illustration of the bark garment is appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "which was said with reference to that," it was stated in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* with reference to the hair-blanket (*kesakambala*) in order to show a simile for the fact that the doctrine of Ajita is even more base.
"Woven" (*tantāvutāni*) means woven after stretching out the warp-threads. "Base" (*paṭikiṭṭha*) means inferior. As to why, it is said: "the hair-blanket," and so forth.
In the Pāḷi, the meaning of "ubbhaṭṭhako" is stated in the *Mahāsīhanādasutta-vaṇṇanā* of the *Majjhima Nikāya-aṭṭhakathā* as "standing upright" (*uddhaṃ ṭhitako*).
For the word *ubbha* is an indeclinable (*nepātiko*) used in the sense of "above," just as in the expression "ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalaṃ" (with knees raised).
Indeed, there are many particles (*nipātā*) that possess multiple meanings and multiple measures.
He said, "devoted to the energy of squatting," because the practice of squatting is undertaken specifically through the influence of wrong speech. One does not merely squat while sitting;
rather, one also squats while walking... [and so on] ...one walks. "Iron thorn" means a thorn made of iron.
"Natural thorn" means a wooden splinter thorn. The term *thaṇḍila* refers to a high ground, as stated in the phrase "on a high place."
This is another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Thaṇḍila" refers to natural ground that has been leveled, as in such passages as "he appeared on level ground (*patthaṇḍile*).
For it is stated in the *Nighaṇṭu* treatise within the *Amarakośa*: "A *vedi* is a prepared ground;
*thaṇḍila* and *cātu* are even ground" (verse 18 in the seventeenth chapter). Therefore, on *thaṇḍila*, meaning on natural ground that is not excavated—
The meaning is that he makes it his bed. With reference to this, it is said in the *Nighaṇṭu* treatise itself:
“He who dwells in a vow upon the bare ground, he is one who sleeps on the bare ground” (*Sattarasama-vagga*, verse 44). Dust itself is *jalla*; when it is soiled, it is *rajojalla*.
Therefore, it is said: “the body,” and so forth. “A seat obtained” means a seat as it was obtained for the purpose of sitting.
"Without disturbing" means not approaching elsewhere; thus it is said: "one whose habit is to sit right there.
For one who sits in this manner is indeed one who does not disturb it. Among the four great *vikaṭas*, excrement is intended here; thus it is said: "excrement is called...
For that is called "*vikaṭa*" because it is foul (*virūpa*) due to its state as a receptacle (*āsaya*). This is the third.

The third period, known as the evening time. "Assa" means of the practice of descending into water. Just as the word "pāta" (morning) is used, the word "sāyaṃ" (evening) is used here as a conventional designation.
However, by eliding the following vowel, the reading "sāyatatiyakaṃ" is also seen.
And herein, the ascetic practices beginning with "he is naked" and ending with "he drinks rice-gruel water" constitute one set.
Furthermore, the various sections beginning with “he is one who lives in a single house,” etc., belong to different periods.

Likewise, [the sections] beginning with “he eats only vegetables,” etc., and “he wears hempen garments, he also wears garments made of bark,” etc. Thus, here the particle *vā* (or) and the particle *pi* (also/even) have been employed.
Here too, the particle *pi* should be understood as having the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*). However, in the preceding [sections],...
In the case of the [relevant] passages, neither of these two [interpretations] has been adopted;

and by adopting this [latter view], there is established no contradiction between the statement “he is naked” and the subsequent statement “he wears hempen garments,” nor between the statement “he wears dust and dirt” and the statement “he dwells devoted to the practice of frequenting water.
Alternatively, what is the point of considering non-contradiction here? It is like the offense of a madman.

For this is the doctrine of the sectarians. Furthermore, it should be understood that after beginning with the words "he is naked," the ascetic Kassapa, in the course of discussing his austerities, spoke such things as "he wears hempen garments" and so forth, thereby demonstrating that all other mutually contradictory forms of self-mortification are likewise [futile].
This concludes the commentary on the pointlessness of undertaking such austerities.

397. Regarding "by means of the perfection of virtue and so forth": this refers to the supramundane perfections consisting of the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*), the perfection of concentration (*samādhisampadā*), and the perfection of wisdom (*paññāsampadā*).
*Vinā* means "devoid of" or "without"; for without these, neither the state of a recluse (*sāmañña*) nor the state of a brahmin (*brahmañña*) ever comes to be.
Thus, the construction is to be understood with an elliptical supplement (*sapāṭhasesa-yojanā*), showing that those ascetic practices are useless.
“Free from enmity consisting of hatred” means free from that which is reckoned as hatred (*dosa*). This is stated because hatred is the direct opposite of loving-kindness (*mettā*).
As for what was said by the Master: “By the mention of ‘hatred,’ all defiled states (*saṃkilesadhamma*) that are opposites to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) are included;
by the mention of ‘enmity’ (*vera*), sentient beings who act as adversaries are included. For to the extent that it is free from hatred, to that same extent...”

Regarding the phrase “free from enmity” (*verarahita*): since the word *vera* (enmity) itself exists in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), and since the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) uses the word *dosa* (fault/defilement) specifically to demonstrate that same meaning, this point must be investigated.
398. “Merely this much” refers to mere practices such as nakedness and so forth.
It is called *pakati* because it makes manifest (*pākaṭabhāvena kāyati*) and leads to the understanding of the meaning.
This is a conventional worldly expression; therefore, he said, "This is a discussion concerning the nature of things.

Just as in such passages as "a small amount of the sacrifice of happiness," the word *matta* is taken to mean "measure" by including within it that which has not yet been reached; thus he said, "By this," and so forth.
By that measure, the very method of practice to be abandoned is brought into the context of the treatise. Or rather, it is understood through this other term, "by means of this ascetic exertion."
He shows this by means of the phrase "by way of the sequence of practice. "Therefore" (tato) means:

for that reason, because the state of being extremely difficult [to achieve] arises through a sequence of practice that is merely trifling for one who is a recluse or a brahmin. With reference to this causal connection, it is said:
"together with the connection of the words. "In all instances" (sabbattha) means: in all sections.

399. "In another way" means: if asceticism (*sāmañña*) or brahminhood (*brahmañña*) were to exist by means of such things as the state of being naked (*acelaka*), then it would be easy to recognize a recluse (*samaṇa*) and easy to recognize a brahmin.

But since you describe asceticism as one thing and brahminhood as quite another than this [true nature], therefore it is difficult to recognize a recluse and difficult to recognize a brahmin; this is the meaning. Thus he said: "This..."
"Having spoken with intentional meaning. This means that having rejected that doctrine of "naturalness"— namely, that which was previously held in the heart by Acelaka Kassapa when he said,

"It is difficult, very difficult," and by the Blessed One when he spoke the words beginning with "This is indeed the nature [of things]" with reference to that very same thing— it refers here specifically to the domain of ordinary recluseship and brahminhood.

How [does he] withdraw [the previous statement]? Revealing that the state of being difficult to know belongs to the ascetic and the brahmin by their very nature and in the ultimate sense (paramattha), he spoke again, beginning with “Indeed, the nature...”.

Therein too—that is, even within the discourse on ascetics and brahmins—he explains the connection of the words, namely the syntactical connection between the preceding and following sentences together with the causal term.
Commentary on the Perfection of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom (Sīla-samādhi-paññā-sampadā): 400–1.
"A wise man" (*paṇḍita*) means one endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*) accomplished through the perfection of its causes.

"How did he learn it?"—because his knowledge was fully matured, by means of the clarity of wisdom (*paññā-veyyattiya*) shining within him like a lamp inside a jar, [he learned] here and there from the Blessed One...
Grasping the meaning taught, he reflected upon that teaching. Because he had mastered it, therefore... [the connection is] "having understood. And "of him" means:
of one who is naked, even to the extent of dwelling devoted to the practice of bathing in water;
or alternatively, the word-division is *tassa ca* (and of him), with the construction being "and [for him] these are uncultivated and unrealized. These are the attainments.

"I ask" means "go," with the intention that one becomes both a *śramaṇa* and a *brāhmaṇa*. "For the purpose of knowing the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampadā*) and so forth" means for the sake of the cause of knowing the perfection of virtue and so forth.
For it was asked: "Why does he ask? Here, the word *atha* (then/for) signifies a reason, as it does in similar instances.
In the phrase "of the perfection of virtue," the word *iti* has the sense of "and so forth" (*ādi*), or this is an elliptical expression (*upalakkhaṇaniddesa*); by this [it is meant that...]
The two phrases “perfection of mind” (*cittasampadā*) and “perfection of wisdom” (*paññāsampadā*) are included [here]. Therefore, he says: “other than the perfections of virtue, mind, and wisdom.

And since these include the three aggregates beginning with the virtue of one beyond training (*asekha*), it is stated: “namely, the fruit of arahantship itself. He shows the reason for this with the words:
“culminating in the fruit of arahantship,” and so forth. For this statement, like the gaze of a crow, refers to both [the cause and the result].
Commentary on the Discourse on the Lion’s Roar (Sīhanādakathāvaṇṇanā):
402. "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) means unsurpassed because it is not shared by others and because its object is a meaning not shared by others.
"The Great Lion’s Roar" (*mahāsīhanāda*) refers to the great lion’s roar of a Buddha. It is supremely pure because of its extreme and ultimate purity.
"Supreme" (*parama*) means "excellent" (*ukkaṭṭha*). Therefore, the Teacher said, "It is the highest" (*uttama*); his intention was that the word *parama* possesses the sense of excellence.
"Virtue alone" (*sīlameva*) refers to the commonality of virtue because it consists merely of mundane virtue.
Just as the supramundane virtue of the Blessed One is unique, inasmuch as it destroys opposing states along with their latent tendencies, so too is mundane virtue.
It is indeed not shared by others because it occurs in a manner appropriate to that [state]. For in this way, the scriptural statement, “I am not therein,” becomes logical.
The passage, “As far as, Kassapa, there is noble, supreme virtue,” is an illustration of the manner [of speaking] in the phrase, “speaking praise of virtue.
However, the phrase, “namely, the higher virtue,” is an indefinite expression regarding the two terms beginning with “therein.”
The phrase “that which is called higher virtue” (adhisīla) is stated by combining both types of the Buddha’s virtue—both mundane and supramundane—into one;
therefore, it is shown that the word “therein” (tatra) refers to both by saying, “therein, in virtue as well as in supreme virtue,” and so forth.
To explain the meaning of “equal with the equal” (samasama) as being “equal with the virtue that serves as the qualifier,” he says, “by virtue equal to my own.”
"By virtue equal to mine" is what was said; that is, regarding both kinds of virtue (*sīla*). "Thus this" means thus this subject of virtue (*sīlavisaya*).
"The first" means it is the first because it occurs first in the order of its arising.
"It heats" means it scorches the defilements (*kilesa*); the meaning is that it dispels them. By the word "that very same," he indicates a compound with a common substratum (*tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa*).
"It loathes" means it despises; it sets [the defilements] aside as base. They are "noble ones" (ariya) because they have placed themselves far away from the defilements due to being faultless.
"By way of the bases for exertion" means by way of the eight bases for exertion. "Designated as the energy of insight" means designated as the energy associated with insight.
Because it is merely mundane, it is "austerity and loathing"; however, that which is designated as the energy associated with the paths and fruits is "austerity and loathing."
The connection is by way of the governing category (*adhikāra*). It is called "supreme" (*paramā*) because it is the most excellent of all states.

Just as the state of one who is young is "youth" (*yobbana*), so too the state of one who is disgusted is "disgust" (*jeguccha*). That which is "with regard to disgust" (*adhijeguccha*) refers to both types of Buddha-disgust—the mundane and the supramundane—just as in the case of virtue (*sīla*).
"Therein" (*tattha*) means both in the context of disgust and in the context of that which is with regard to disgust. "Wisdom regarding the ownership of kamma" (*kammassakatā-paññā*)...
It is the knowledge that proceeds according to the method beginning with, “There is what is given; there is what is sacrificed,” and so forth. As it is said in the *Vibhaṅga*:
“In this context, what is the knowledge of one’s own karma? There is what is given; there is what is sacrificed; there is what is offered;
there is the fruit and result of deeds well done and ill done… [and so on] … excluding the knowledge conforming to the truths, all [this constitutes it].”
“Wholesome wisdom accompanied by taints is the knowledge of self-agency.
For indeed, whatever is unwholesome—whether it belongs to oneself or to another—is not called “one’s own. Why? Because it destroys one’s welfare and produces harm.
Likewise, all that is wholesome is called “one’s own. Why? Because it destroys what is harmful.

And because it produces meaning (*atthajananato*). Thus, wisdom that functions regarding the state of being the owner of one’s own kamma is called "wisdom of being the owner of one’s own kamma" (*kammassakatā-paññā*). As for "insight-wisdom" (*vipassanā-paññā*):
because it conforms to the truth of the path and to the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*), insight-wisdom is designated as "conformity-to-truth" (*saccānulomika*);
it is simply wisdom from the perspective of being mundane (*lokiya-matta*). Here, the change of the feminine gender into the neuter gender is a "reversal of gender" (*liṅga-vipallāsa*).
This which is called "higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā*)—like virtue (*sīla*), it is twofold according to the mundane and supramundane, and is the wisdom of the Buddha.
"Therein" means both in wisdom and in higher wisdom. According to its suitability, whether as limited (*paritta*) or sublime (*mahaggata*), it is simply called "liberation" (*vimutti*).
Through the paths and fruits, the severing and the subsiding of defilements are the "liberations by severance" (*samucchedavimutti*) and "liberations by subsidence" (*paṭippassaddhivimutti*). Now...
Because right speech and so forth are included by the inclusion of higher virtue (*adhisīla*), right effort by the inclusion of higher disgust (*adhijeguccha*),
and right view by the inclusion of higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), those not [explicitly] mentioned— namely right intention, mindfulness,

and concentration as they pertain to the paths and fruits, and the deliverances consisting in eradication and subsiding— are to be understood here. This is the deliverance of escape (*nissaraṇavimutti*).
But it is indeed Nibbāna. This "higher liberation" (*adhivimutti*) is twofold, according to the method explained regarding virtue (*sīla*).
"Therein" (*tattha*) means both in liberation (*vimutti*) and in higher liberation (*adhivimutti*). 403. Any secluded place from people is intended here as an "empty hut. Without crying out there...
The phrase beginning with "only one" was spoken to show that there is no other person [who can do so]. "In the eight assemblies" refers to these eight assemblies:

the assembly of kshatriyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmas.
To establish this meaning, he spoke the passage beginning with "four kinds of conceit," citing a line from the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta in the excellent Majjhima Nikāya.
In this context, "fearlessnesses" (*vesārajjāni*) means states of being confident (*visāradabhāva*).

The meaning is: states of fearlessness arising from the absence of any hesitation whatsoever regarding the knowledge of the [four] grounds, the abandonments, the obstacles, and the teaching of the factors leading to deliverance.

Indeed, "fearlessness" (*vesārajja*) is the name for the knowledge consisting of joy that arises in one who reviews the absence of timidity (*sārajjābhāva*) in these four points. However, by others...

To show their uniqueness, it is said: "the Tathāgata’s grounds of self-confidence of a Tathāgata. Alternatively, because the second word *tathāgata* functions as a coordinate term (tulyādhikaraṇa), it is stated thus:
"grounds of self-confidence that have come [to him] in the same way that the grounds of self-confidence of previous Buddhas came [to them] through the attainment of a store of merit (*puññussaya*).
This is the method of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*). However, the etymologists (*Neruttika*)...

They say: "Since the compound is already established, it is stated thus because of its general nature and because it is a technical term (*saññā-sadda*). "The bull-like state" (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*) means the best state, the supreme state.
Alternatively, they are called "bulls" (*āsabhā*) because they go forward toward omniscience by way of professing it, or because they approach the eightfold assembly;
thus the meaning is "the state of those [Buddhas]."
Furthermore, there are three types of leaders: the bull (*usabha*), who is the leader of a hundred cows;

the great bull (*vasabha*), who is the leader of a thousand cows—or the bull who is the leader of a hundred buffalo, or the great bull who is the leader of a thousand buffalo. Or, the bull is the leader in a single village district, while the great bull is the leader in two village districts;
but the one who is the best of all cattle, the leader everywhere, the conqueror of all dangers, white and handsome—[he is the supreme].
“Nisabha” means one who bears a great burden and cannot be shaken even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts.
Here, it is “usabha” that is intended by the term “nisabha,” for this is also a synonym for it. That which belongs to an *usabha* is *āsabha*;
furthermore, that which is like an *āsabha* is also called *āsabha*. For just as the bull known as *nisabha* is endowed with the strength of an *usabha*, [so too is this].
Just as a mountain peak, having pressed down upon the earth with its feet, stands in an immovable position, so too the Tathāgata,
endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, having pressed down upon the earth of the eight assemblies with the four feet of self-confidence,
stands in an immovable position, unshakable by any adversary or enemy in the world with its devas. While standing thus, he—
He penetrates the bull-like state (*āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ*), approaches it, does not reject it, and takes it upon himself. Therefore it is said:
"He claims the bull-like state. He roars the lion's roar means:
"He roars the best roar, the fearless roar"—this is the meaning already stated. Alternatively, it is like the lion's roar.
He roars his roar. This meaning should be illustrated by the Sīhanāda Sutta found in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, Khandha-vagga.

Or, just as the lion, the king of beasts, is called "sīha" because he endures dangers and because he slays bulls, buffaloes, elephants, and so forth, even so the Tathāgata, the king of sages, is [called "sīha"] because he endures the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*) and the doctrines of others.
And because he slays, he is called a "lion. He roars the roar of the lion as thus described.
In this regard, just as the lion among beasts, endowed with the strength of a lion, fearless in every respect and free from horripilation, roars his lion’s roar;
even so the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, is fearless in the eight assemblies and free from horripilation.
“Thus, ‘form,’ etc.”—by means of such methods, he roars the lion’s roar, endowed with the manifold elegance of teaching. Therefore it is said:
“He roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies.
“Having formulated a question” means having formulated the matter desired to be known in accordance with the power of his own knowledge.
"At that very moment" means he answers with spontaneous eloquence at the very instant of being questioned.
Because he answers in accordance with their inclinations and in accordance with the meaning and the Dhamma, he truly satisfies the mind. "Of him" means of the ascetic Gotama.
"They think it worth hearing" means that because it is obtainable through the ninth opportunity—avoiding the eight inopportune moments—they [think], "What our Teacher..."
"She is instructing; we shall listen to her," thinking thus, they conceive with great enthusiasm that what is to be heard must be received with a sense of reverence.
"With a ready mind, with a pliant mind" means that through the increase of serene confidence (*pasāda*) and the removal of defilements (*upakkilesa*), their minds become ready and pliant.
"With hollow confidence" means having a confidence that is empty or useless. This is the manner of such confidence.
The honor that should be performed by those who have faith is twofold, according to the distinction between the worship of the Dhamma and the worship of material gifts (*āmisa-pūjā*).

In this context, showing the worship of material gifts, he says, "exquisite [foods]," and so forth. However, the worship of the Dhamma is shown in the text itself by the phrase, "practicing for suchness" (*tathattāya paṭipajjanti*).
"For the sake of becoming such" (*tathābhāvāya*) means for the sake of becoming that which is such—that is, for the purpose of escaping the suffering of saṃsāra.
The Dhamma has been taught for the sake of becoming such [as it truly is]. To demonstrate that very point, it is said:

"for the purpose of fulfilling the practice in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipattipūraṇatthāya*). For the practice in accordance with the Dhamma culminates in the escape from the suffering of saṃsāra;

and that practice in accordance with the Dhamma is to be undertaken by means of a specific gradual sequence, and for those undertaking it, when there is a convergence of internal factors, it becomes certain.
