Regarding "its fulfillment," he spoke the passage beginning with "some in the refuges" while showing that sequence.
To show how it is fulfilled in such a way that one is indeed able to fulfill it, it was said: "but they fulfill it in every aspect.
In this context, "in this place" refers to the scriptural passage establishing the fulfillment of the function of the lion’s roar: "and those who have entered the path are successful."

"Should be combined" means they should be totaled. "I see some ascetic... and so forth—this is one of the Blessed One’s lion-roars, which is unique, unassailable by others, the best of roars, and a roar of fearlessness;
this same method applies to the remaining [roars] as well. "Another ascetic" is the subject of reference.
Regarding the "ten previous ones," it refers back to the lion-roar stated as: "I see some ascetic reborn in hell."
From the beginning up to the lion’s roar stated as, “There is no one equal to me in liberation,” there are ten preceding lion’s roars;
here the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Therefore he said, “Of each one.
The ten lion’s roars beginning with “And he roars amidst the assemblies” and ending with “Those who have entered the path please me” are the surrounding retinue. “A certain... [text truncated]”
“I see Tapassī reborn in hell”—thus the Blessed One roars his lion’s roar among the assemblies;
he roars having become confident. There they pose questions to him, and he answers those questions;
by his answering, he satisfies the minds of others. Having heard him, they think it worth hearing; and having heard it, they gain confidence in the Blessed One. Being thus confident—
They manifest an attitude of confidence; they practice according to the way of practice he teaches;
and having practiced, they please him—thus, by surrounding [him] in this manner, the application of the meaning is possible. This same method applies to the remaining nine as well.
By the words "In this way" and so forth, there is a presentation that summarizes the aforementioned lion's roars. "Those ten" refers to [the assemblies].
"And he roars," and so forth, are the ten lion-roars. "Of the former ten" refers to the ten preceding lion-roars mentioned above which serve as the root.
"By way of retinue" means that when each of these is joined with its own respective retinue, taking the root as the basis, there are one hundred lion-roars.
"And the former ten" refers to those not being joined by way of retinue, but rather taken as the roots of the roots.
"And the ten former ones"—thus there are one hundred and ten lion-roars.

However, in another sutta, such as the *Cūḷasīhanāda-sutta* of the *Majjhima Āgama*, it is called "Mahāsīhanāda" because of its great number [of roars], not because it is based on the *Cūḷasīhanāda-sutta* like the *Mahāsīhanāda-sutta* in the *Majjhimanikāya*; this is the intended meaning.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Probation for Heretics (Titthiyaparivāsakathāvaṇṇanā) 404.
"Having refuted" means having rejected by demonstrating the existence and non-existence of such states.

In the Udumbarika-sutta of the Pāṭhika-vagga, the Blessed One [taught] the classification of defilements and the classification of purity, beginning with the words: "Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic... and so forth.
To show that he roars the lion’s roar before Nigrodha the wanderer and his assembly, the passage beginning with “Now” was spoken.
“Roared previously” means it was previously roared by [the Buddha] in the presence of Nigrodha the wanderer according to the method set forth in the Udumbarika Sutta.

“A practitioner of austerity” (*tapabrahmacārī*) means one who practices supreme austerity, or one who lives the holy life (*brahmacārī*) through austerity or vigor. “This” refers to: “In Rājagaha... [etc.]”
The words "he asked a question" are found in the canonical text (*pāḷi*). However, the Teacher has here restated precisely the words from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) as previously cited.

Furthermore, although it was not at that time when Nigrodha asked the question and the Blessed One gave the answer that the Blessed One was dwelling on Mount Gijjhakūṭa; rather, he was in the vicinity of Rājagaha, at the residence of Queen Udumbarikā.
He dwelt in the park because he was questioned and answered there; nevertheless,
the Blessed One’s residence on Vulture Peak Mountain had not yet ceased, which is why the words "there, me" and so forth appear in the Canon (Pāḷi), and the words "to me,
dwelling there at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain" and so forth are stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
It should be understood that this very point is made known by the passage beginning with, "That which the Blessed One...
The phrase "on Vulture Peak Mountain" is shown to refer to the monastery established there by the words "in the Great Monastery on Vulture Peak.
"Of Udumbarikā" means of the one who bears that name. "In the park" refers to the hermitage for wanderers (paribbājakārāma) built there.
Nigrodha was a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka) who lived in disguise. Sandhāna was an upāsaka who had attained the stage of non-returner (anāgāmi), accompanied by a retinue of five hundred upāsakas.
"Discourse" (*kathāsallāpa*) refers to a conversation such as, "Come now, householder, you should know with whom the ascetic Gotama converses," and so forth.
*Para* is a particle used in the sense of excellence; *viya* is used merely for metrical completion, as in the expression "atisiya" (exceedingly).
"Andhabāla" means a foolish person who is blind to the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). "Yoge" means in the method; the meaning is:

in the means for escaping suffering. "Anena" refers to the Blessed One. Regarding "in the Khandhaka," the construction is: "that which one undergoes as a probationary period (*parivāsa*) in the Pabbajjā-khandhaka within the Mahāvagga.
As for the statement, "One who was previously a follower of another sect is called 'formerly of another sect' (*aññatitthiyapubba*)," this was said by the Elder Ācariya Sāriputta.
It has been stated. He said, "standing on the level of a sāmaṇera," meaning that one dwells having first taken the going-forth (pabbajjā).

"That" refers to the probation (parivāsa) mentioned in two ways. "Going-forth" refers to the taking of the going-forth mentioned here in the passage: "He desires the going-forth; he desires the full ordination (upasampadā).
"He might share a sleeping place for more than two or three nights" [is the further context].
Here, the mention of "two nights" is stated merely for the sake of the smoothness of expression.

However, since one must dwell while remaining in the status of a novice (sāmaṇera) and not as a layperson (gihī), one receives the going-forth (pabbajjā) without having completed the probationary period.
Regarding the phrase "not entering villages, etc.," the word "etc. includes [the prohibitions against] frequenting new female slaves, widows, grown-up maidens, eunuchs, and the domain of bhikkhunīs.
Skill and lack of indolence in what is to be done for one’s fellow practitioners; intense desire for the recitation of the scriptures, inquiry, and so forth;
delight when speaking of the dispraise of that person from another sectarian school from whom one has come here; displeasure when speaking of the dispraise of the Buddha and the others;
and displeasure when speaking of the praise of that person from another sectarian school from whom one has come here, [but] delight when speaking of the praise of the Buddha and the others.
The inclusion of these seven observances (*vatta*) should be understood as "joyful praise.
"One who fulfills [them] should undergo probation" means that when one is undergoing probation, one must do so while fulfilling them.

"By the fulfillment of the eight observances" means by the fulfillment of the eight observances already mentioned. "In this case" refers to either probation (*parivāsa*) or full ordination (*upasampadā*). "Having rubbed and pounded" means...
Having tested and refined him like gold by way of examining his underlying disposition (*ajjhāsaya*). The phrase "for the going-forth" (*pabbajjā*) is merely an illustration;
for by it, full ordination (*upasampadā*) is also included.
"Sitting in the midst of the assembly" means that the senior of the Saṅgha sits in the midst of those monks who are sufficient in number to constitute the formal act of full ordination.

The teacher said, "having sat down for the sake of favoring him," yet now, in many manuscripts, the reading "having had him sit down" is seen in the sense of causing [him] to act. "Acirūpasampanno" means one who has been ordained not long ago;
however, to show the mere meaning, he said, "having become ordained, not long after. [This refers to] seclusion of body and mind alone.
Here, because the context concerns the practice for the sake of seclusion from the substrata (*upadhiviveka*), it is said: "both by body and by mind.

"Withdrawn" (*vūpakaṭṭha*) means secluded. Since diligence in purifying virtue is established even without being explicitly stated for such a person, he demonstrates diligence specifically regarding the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"One whose mind is directed" means one whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna; that is, one who is inclined toward it, prone toward it, and leaning toward it.

It has been said; and in order to reveal the intended meaning that one who is thus constituted is called "one who has relinquished the body through lack of concern," it was stated: "one whose personal existence has been cast off.
And here, "self" (*atta*) refers to the mind, because the physical body is not its object.
"Of whom" refers to the fruit of Arhatship. Even sons of good family who are endowed with virtuous conduct have a longing for the going-forth in order to attain Arhatship.
Thinking that those sons of noble birth are included within the same category as those sons of noble birth who possess right conduct, he said, “sons of noble birth possessed of right conduct.

For by this, even those sons of noble birth who are endowed with right conduct are included. Furthermore, the fact that only those endowed with right conduct are intended is understood through the inclusion of the word “properly” (*sammadeva*).
Indeed, it is preceded by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), according to the method beginning with, “I am immersed in birth,” and so forth.
It is said, “in the right way,” with reference to the going-forth as instructed. Therefore he says, “by means of the cause itself, by means of the reason itself.

In this context, “by means of the cause” (*hetunā*) refers to the method or the means. “By means of the reason itself” (*kāraṇeneva*) is a word that explains that same point. “That” (*taṃ*) refers to the fruit of arahantship.
For it alone is worthy of being called “the unsurpassed consummation of the holy life” (*anuttaraṃ brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ*), because others do not possess it in such a manner.
By the method of words (*saddanaya*), he shows that meaning through the phrase “tassa hi” and so forth, [explaining] that “those sounds are always connected.
The intention is as follows: for the sake of that fruit of arahantship—which was previously mentioned in the passage “for the sake of which...
they go forth”—sons of good family go forth; therefore, it should be understood that the fruit of arahantship is what is intended here. There is no other.
"One for whom people are the condition for realization" is *aparappaccaya*; that [is what is meant]. Just as the prefix *upa-* follows the verbal root, the prefix *sam-* also follows the verbal root;
thus it is said "having reached," meaning having attained or arrived at. Alternatively, the prefix *upa-* follows the verbal root while the prefix *sam-* specifies the particular sense of the root;
hence it is said "having accomplished," namely, the virtues, concentration, and wisdom of one beyond training (*asekha*).
"Having brought to completion" means having fulfilled.
"To bring to a conclusion" means to finish by way of a conclusion. For it is by this very statement—"He dwelt having reached the culmination of the holy life...
[etc.]"—that the teaching is concluded with the pinnacle of Arahantship; yet, in order to conclude that, [it says] "A certain one... [etc.]"
"Was there?"—thus it was said by the compilers of the Dhamma. Here, "one" (aññataro) refers to someone who is not well-known by name, clan, and so forth.
The genitive case in "arahantānaṃ" is used in the sense of selection (*ubbāhana*). And because they were selected in that manner, the intended meaning is that he was among them;
showing this intention, [the author] says "of the Blessed One," and so forth. However, some speak as follows:
The genitive case here, "arahantānaṃ," must be construed with [the word "sāvakānaṃ" from the previous phrase];

therefore, the words "of the Blessed One" (*bhagavato*) and so forth were spoken in order to show the intended meaning by supplying the missing portion of the text. As for that which has not been analyzed here according to its meaning, it is indeed easy to understand.
Thus ends the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which elucidates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning, a commentary on the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta*, composed by the one named Sādhuvilāsini, who brings forth clarity in vast and stainless wisdom.
The commentary on the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta* is concluded.
9. Commentary on the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*.
Commentary on the Background Story of the Wanderer Poṭṭhapāda:

406. Having thus commented upon the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta, and now commenting upon the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, [the author] explains that it has reached its turn for commentary in the proper sequence, as it was recited immediately after the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.
In order to reveal that this sutta is the *Poṭṭhapādasutta*, he said: "Thus have I heard... [pe] ...at Sāvatthī: the *Poṭṭhapādasutta*.
To show that "at Sāvatthī" is used in the locative case in the sense of proximity (*samīpatthe*), it is stated:
"in dependence upon Sāvatthī" (*sāvatthim upanissāya*). The meaning is: "having made it a support because of being dependent on requisites such as robes. There was a prince named Jeta.
Because it was planted, nurtured, and protected by him, the meaning of "Jetavana" (Jeta’s Grove) is explained as "the grove of Prince Jeta.
The householder named Sudatta was called Anāthapiṇḍika because he gave alms-food to the destitute.
Having purchased that [grove] from the hands of Jeta by covering it with eighteen crores of gold, [he built the monastery] for eighteen crores of gold.

Having had lodgings constructed and having completed the monastery itself at a cost of eighteen crores of gold, he dedicated that park to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha by means of a gift of fifty-four crores of gold.
Therefore it was said: "The park was caused to be built by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.
[It is called a 'park' (ārāma)] either because of its perfection in qualities such as flowers, fruits, and foliage, or because of its suitability for the comfortable dwelling of living beings.
*Ārāma*: Specifically, it is called an *ārāma* because those who have gone forth come from here and there and delight [therein], dwelling there without weariness.

Alternatively, even when one has gone to various places, one brings back and delights in one's own inner self through the attainment of the aforementioned qualities; thus, it is an *ārāma*. *Poṭṭhapāda*:
He is called *Poṭṭhapāda* because a *poṭṭha* was born at his feet. For *poṭṭha* and *poṭṭha* are synonyms. There are two kinds of wanderers (*paribbājaka*).
There are two types of wanderers: the covered wanderer and the uncovered wanderer. Among them, the uncovered wanderer is also twofold:
the naked ascetic (*acelaka*) and the Ājīvika. Of these, the naked ascetic is entirely naked in every respect;

however, the Ājīvika wears a single garment by tucking it between his armpits and carrying it about, while remaining naked below. Since this [latter type] does not exist here, it is said, "the covered wanderer."
The meaning is that he has entered the reckoning of the "covered wanderers" (channa-paribbājaka) because he has gone forth [into homelessness] with the covering of robes.
"A brahmin mahāsāla" refers to a brahmin who has attained great worth through his vast wealth. "Teacher of a group" (gaṇācariya) is a compound used in a sense of mutual dependence.
"Samaṇas" is a general designation, or it is a singular-inclusive (ekasesa) expression; the meaning is "those various samaṇas. "They proclaim" (pavadanti) is from the root *pavada*.
They speak; the meaning is that they speak according to whatever convention has been adopted by each individual.

*Tārukkha* is his name. By the word "and so forth" (*pabhuti*), he includes Todeyya, Jāṇussoni, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and others; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), he includes Channa the wanderer and others.
A *tinduka* is a tree with a black trunk. *Cīra* means a row. *Tindukā*...
"Tindukacīra" means "there is *cīra* (bark) here. Similarly, "ekasālaka" means "there is one hall (*sālā*) here.
He spoke the passage beginning with "because" (*yasmā*) to explain that matter in detail by way of its past history. "Thus having done so" (*iti katvā*) refers to this reason.
The passage beginning with "in that" (*tasmiṃ*) is a demonstration of the case endings according to the text.

Because it distinguishes the objects of knowledge in their manifold and exhaustive aspects, and because it arises again and again, the Blessed One’s knowledge is said to be "spread out" (pattharitvā) over the world;
hence, it is called a "net of knowledge" (ñāṇajāla). That those to be converted are included within that net has already been stated above.
When the mental application (samannāhāra) is made for the purpose of grasping the beings who are to be converted—
First, their appearance occurs simply by virtue of their being fit to be converted; then, the accomplishment of the task is examined by way of their going for refuge and so forth.
Thus he said: "Examining, [he thought], 'What indeed will happen? "Cessation" means the cessation of perception.
"Emergence from cessation" means the emergence from that cessation, the arising of perception. By the knowledge of all Buddhas...
"Having reconciled" means having reconciled by way of their explanation, just as they have explained, are explaining, and will explain both cessation and emergence from cessation.
"After a few days" means after two or three days; for the text itself will state this matter.
"He will go for refuge" means he will go [saying] "refuge. "Hatthisāriputta"—so it is said.
“Citta, the son of Hatthisārin,” was what the teacher said. However, the reading currently seen is “Citta Hatthisāriputta,” which means Citta, the son of the elephant trainer (hatthācariya).
“A well-dyed double-layered cloth” means having put on an inner robe (antaravāsaka) that has been properly dyed with color and is of two layers by way of folding it over.
“Having encircled Mount Yugandhara”—this is a hypothetical expression meaning “if there were such [a mountain], as if it were that.
“Cloud-colored” means the color of a red cloud; the sense is that it resembles a cloud suffused with the radiance of twilight.
Here, by the first [epithet] he shows perfection of shape, and by the second, perfection of color. “With its top facing one direction”...
"Having draped the robe over one shoulder. For it is said in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, in the commentary on the *Vaṅgīsa-sutta*:
"'Over one shoulder' is a designation for one who stands having draped [the robe] over the left shoulder. Therefore, its meaning should be understood as:
'having arranged the robe in such a way that it remains draped over the left shoulder. [Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, Nigrodhakappa-sutta]
[Commentary on the Vaṅgīsasutta]: Therein, "this" refers to the statement, "having arranged his robe over one shoulder.
"From which" is to be understood as follows: because the aforementioned statement is a designation for one who stands having already put it on, such is its meaning; this is the connection.
"Paccaggha" means that when it is not yet formally resolved (*adhiṭṭhita*) by being made into a single whole, each part is individually of great value; or else, *paccaggha* means new or fresh.
The meaning is that they arise at that very moment. In this context, some do not accept the first alternative interpretation.
For it was stated by the Master himself in the Udāna-aṭṭhakathā: "‘Paccaggha’ means ‘new.
Some say it means ‘of individual high value,’ but that is not correct. For the Blessed Buddhas do not accept anything of great value."
Regarding the phrase "and they partake [of it]," here too, only the latter alternative meaning is intended.
It is called "priceless" (*paccaggha*) because of its novelty—having been designated by that term from the very beginning—and because it has not been used by anyone else;
or rather, through the Teacher’s resolve, that bowl is always called "priceless. "Made of stone" means made of green-bean-colored stone.
The bowl given by the Four Great Kings. For this very bowl was used daily by the Blessed One, as it is stated likewise in the commentary on the *Samacitta Sutta* and other texts.
(407) “According to his own preference and inclination, not urged by others”—this is the intended meaning.
And the phrase “seeing that it was already too early” is a statement of fact, intended to show that the time for wandering for alms had not yet arrived.

For at that time, the Blessed One had already emerged from his dwelling early in the morning with the thought, "I shall favor Poṭṭhapāda with a teaching on the Dhamma pertaining to the residual impressions (vāsanā).

In the text, regarding the phrase *atippago kho*, the word *pago* here is established according to the opinion of Kaccāyana through the addition of the vowel *o* and the letter *k* after the prefix *pa-*;
the word *pa-* itself expresses the meaning of "morning. However, for other grammarians...

According to this opinion, *nepātika* is like the word *pāta* (morning). For that very reason, it is stated in various places in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that "it is too early" means "excessively early.
Furthermore, the etymology is shown by this: it goes first, or proceeds by way of the day, thus it is *paga*.
Indeed, just as the word *khalu* is twofold, the word *paga* is threefold, according to its classification as a noun, a particle (*nipāta*), or a prefix (*upasagga*).
For it is in this way that the statement here, “having seen precisely the state of being too early,” is appropriate.
As for the particle *yaṃ nūna*: elsewhere it indicates doubt, but here it indicates something that resembles doubt.
Why was it said, “it indicates doubt”? Is it not the case that Buddhas have no doubt? To this he says: “And of the Buddhas,” and so forth.
There is no doubt [regarding this], because it has been eradicated right at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
"The preliminary stage of reflection" refers to the reflection that occurs prior to the intended task.
This mental disposition—such as "we shall do it" or "we shall not do it"—is found and possible for all Buddhas, because it proceeds by way of investigation alone; it is not...
But [it is] by way of doubt. "Therefore he said" means: because this [attainment] is obtainable for all Buddhas, the Blessed One spoke thus;
thus he makes this very canonical text (pāḷi) the proof for this meaning. This is another method from the commentary:
*yaṃnūna* is a particle used in the sense of supposition (*parikappana*). For the meaning being expressed by the verbal form *upasaṅkameyya* is indeed indicated by this [particle].
It shines. Therefore, the construction is: "What if I were now to approach him? It would indeed be good.
Regarding the phrase "yadi pana" (if, however), it is said that this has the same meaning as that [term "assu"], thus: "the meaning is 'yadi panāhaṃ' (if, however, I).
408. "Assā" refers to the assembly of wanderers. "By way of ascending upwards" means by way of rising higher and higher due to its great loftiness.
"By way of spreading. "By way of extending through the quarters" means by way of expanding in all directions through a vastness consisting of a continuous succession of beings.
And here, just as the word *unnāda* (uproar) is used for a sound that rises upward (*unnata-pāya*), so too what proceeds higher and higher by way of vastness is also called an *unnāda*;
thus, taking both together, it is said: "of the one that is uproarious (*unnādiniyā*)."
Furthermore, having divided those two [terms] themselves, it says, “with loud noise and great clamor.
Therefore, it should be understood that he explains the meaning in exact accordance with the method of the Pāḷi.

Now, showing the reason for the loud noise and great clamor of the assembly of wanderers, as well as the manner of its occurrence, he said, “For of them...,” and so forth. “In the morning sun” means in the heat of the newly risen sun.

“Delight in sensual pleasures” (*kāmassāda*) means the delight in the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). “Delight in existence” (*bhavassāda*) means the delight in states of existence accompanied by sensual lust and so forth.

The statement “they have become like fireflies” is said with reference to their being devoid of luster, like a firefly when the sun rises. The meaning “our gain and honor have not diminished” is to be illustrated by the *Bāveru Jātaka*. “Faults of the assembly” (*parisādo*) refers to faults occurring within the assembly. 409. “He established” (*saṇṭhapesi*) means he properly settled them through the means of restraint.
And here, “establishing” refers to [restraining] them from frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).
“‘He trained him’ and so forth means that he taught him proper conduct by way of causing him to abandon mutual disrespect, and he concealed the aforementioned fault.
‘The assembly’ (naṃ) refers to the gathering. ‘Quiet’ (appasaddaṃ) means noiseless, due to the absence of loud or great clamor.
‘He sat alone,’ etc., is a demonstration of what is implied by the sense. ‘Prosperity’ (vuddhiṃ) refers to the increase of gains and virtues. ‘Aspiring’ (patthayamāno) means...”
*Patthayana-hetu*: for those learned in grammar accept *māna* in the sense of a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) and in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
Now, in order to elaborate upon that meaning, the passage beginning with “Paribbājakā kira” has been commenced. *Aparaddhaṃ* means having offended.
*Nappamajjanti* means they do not fall into negligence; it is said that they do not show disrespect.
410. "There is joy (*ānanda*) at his arrival": when our Blessed One has arrived, there is joy and rapture.

Regarding the statement, "It has been a long time, Bhante, since the Blessed One made this occasion," he raises an objection—namely, that because [the Buddha] had previously come there before, it is as if the words were already spoken—and while resolving it, he says, "Why did he say...?
and so forth. "Affectionate greetings" means endearing speech.

Therefore, because such affectionate conduct was thus maintained, it is said, beginning with "For the Blessed One," in order to establish that purpose through a generalization applicable to others as well—that not only this person, but for the most part other renunciants too were performing honor toward the Blessed One.
Regarding that, he states the reason: "Because of his high birth," [referring] from King Mahāsammata...
The meaning is: "from the time [he was born] into an unadulterated khattiya lineage. For it was said by Soṇadaṇḍa:
"Indeed, sir, the ascetic Gotama has gone forth from a high lineage, from an unadulterated khattiya lineage.
Thus, even those who lack confidence in the Teaching show respect toward the Blessed One out of reverence for his family. "In the meantime, what kind of talk? means within the aforementioned limits.
What kind of talk? "Interrupted" means having been commenced but left unfinished. However, one who says, "What talk was interrupted?
effectively promises to bring that very talk to its conclusion by way of its meaning. Furthermore, the question "What talk? is an inquiry without specification;
therefore, a promise to conclude *any* talk whatsoever is thereby made, and that is the promise.
Those who know only a portion do not venture [to debate], as it was said: “As far as... [and so on]... he invited the omniscient one to a formal invitation.
*Esā* refers to the talk concerning kings and so forth, spoken by the assembly of wanderers. *Nissārā* means devoid of essence due to being purposeless.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse on the cessation of perception.
411. To demonstrate the meaning already established by the phrase "tiṭṭhat’esā" (she stands), he says "sace" (if) and so forth.

"Sukāraṇaṃ" means a beautiful cause that brings about welfare and benefit. "Yattha" means in a certain hall. They are called "nānātitthiyā" because they are devoted to various tenets known as "nānātittha";
this is expressed by the word "niyutta" with the suffix "ṇika," or alternatively, by changing the letter *ka* to *ya*.
Just as in the case of the word “antiyo. Because there is curiosity (*kutūhala*) and clamor (*kolāhala*) here, thinking, “What is this one saying?

What is that one saying?”, it is called *kotūhala*; that very hall is thus a *kotūhalasālā*. He said, “from the place where curiosity arises,” because the prefix merely follows the meaning of the verbal root.
This teaching is given by way of the technical designation (*saññā*); therefore, all phenomena associated with that designation are included.
They are grasped; however, it is stated that "in the cessation of consciousness" because consciousness is the primary factor therein.
But since their intention was not directed toward absolute cessation by way of abandoning, and because [absolute cessation] is not their object, he said "in momentary cessation.
Granted, that too is not their object; nevertheless, when a discussion of cessation is being spoken of in terms of its meaning, it remains precisely there. Therefore—
It should be understood that this was said with reference merely to the occurrence of the circumstance.
"Of that" refers to the discourse on the cessation of perception. "'Kittighoso' means the sound of praise: 'Oh, the power of the Buddha!

He shows even a cause concealed by another existence as if it were a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, directly before the eyes, and establishes disciples in such a commitment to self-restraint.'"

"It spreads as far as the peak of existence," so it was said by the Teacher. However, the reading now seen is: "The sound of the fame of the Blessed One’s speech spreads throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
"A corresponding action" means an application that has become a counterpart due to the influence of the *paḷāsa* (a type of plant or affliction).
"At the time of another existence" refers to some imagined time of emergence in various places.

They speak by establishing their own system as the basis for transgression. They prescribe some minor training rule (*sikkhāpada*)—such as "it must be based on a single root" or "one must sit in one and the same place for such a length of time"—having made such a reason a category of training.
The "discourse on cessation" (*nirodhakathā*) is the discourse on the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"In them" means among the various ascetics and brahmins of different sects who had assembled in the Hall of Wonders. "Some" means certain individuals. "The former" refers to the proponent who stated:
"Perceptions arise and cease for a person without cause and without condition," and so forth.
"In this regard" refers to among these four proponents. The connection is: "he who here [says] 'it arises. "Attainment" means that which brings about the state of non-perception.
He attains either the preliminary work for the air-kasiṇa, the preliminary work for the space-kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna absorption of the fine-material sphere, or the fifth jhāna absorption.
He brings about the cessation of perception in the manner explained below regarding the cessation of perception.

"Not seeing a cause" means that he does not see the cause by which there would be the cessation of perception and its total non-arising in the non-percipient realm, nor the cause by which one who has passed away from there [would be reborn] here.
In the five-aggregate existence there is the arising of perception; not seeing either of these two as having the cause for its object, [he spoke].
"The second" refers to the one who spoke thus: "For perception, sir, is a person's self," and so forth. "Him" refers to the first speaker.
"Having refuted" means having rejected it by saying, "But this will not be so, sir. [This was said] regarding the ascetic Migasiṅga.
Of the ascetic named thus. It is said that two tufts of hair grew on his head in the shape of deer horns;
thus he was also called "Isisiṅga" (Deer-Horn). "The state of being unconscious" refers to the absence of perception due to the occurrence of a swoon or fainting.
For it will say later, "having become unconscious. This is the story of the ascetic Migasiṅga, according to the method found in the *Cattālīsanipāta*.
To show this in brief, it was said: “The ascetic Migasiṅga, it is said,” and so forth.

He was one who tormented himself (attantapo) because he scorched away the defilements by means of suppression. He was one of fierce asceticism (ghoratapo) and intense asceticism (tibbatapo) due to his performance of difficult austerities.

He possessed supremely developed faculties (paramadhitindriyo) because, through the removal of all habitual indulgence, his sharp faculties such as sight were completely withered [of worldly attachment]. “Sakkavimāna” refers to the stone seat of the yellow blanket (paṇḍukambalasilāsana).
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). For that [body] can, due to such conditions, sometimes be warm, sometimes stiff, and sometimes moving.
Having thought improperly (*ayoniso*), he sent [the messenger], saying, “Sakka... pe... prays. *Bhagga* means one whose inclination toward skillfulness has been broken;
however, they now write the reading as *lagga*. “By that divine touch” means by the mere divine touch of taking the hand.
"Thus he spoke regarding the attainment of perception. "He spoke thus" means he spoke of the cessation of perception in such a manner as: "For perception, sir, is the self of a person," and so forth.
By this same method, the application [of the commentary] should be understood by citing the Pāḷi for the two subsequent instances as well.

"The third" refers to the one who spoke the words beginning with: "For there are, sir, certain recluses and brahmins... "The practice of *āthabbaṇa*" means that which is prescribed in the *Āthabbaṇa* Veda.
The practice for inducing unconsciousness among those who employ *āthabbaṇa* (sorcery). *Upakaḍḍhanaṃ* means bringing near; *apakaḍḍhanaṃ* means carrying away.

"Having employed *āthabbaṇa*" means having employed the mantra-words found in the *Āthabbaṇa-Veda*, preceded by the offering of fire, which brings about the cessation of consciousness by showing [visions] such as the head being cut off.
"Of him" (*tassa*) means of that person to whom the cutting off of the head and so forth was shown.
“Fourth” refers to the speaker who said, “For there are, sir, deities of great psychic power,” and so forth. “Yakkha-wives” means goddesses;
they are also called “yogavatiyo,” and are well known as *yoginīs*. “Sleep induced by intoxication” is sleep caused by the influence of liquor.
“Offerings to deities” is worship of deities through dancing, singing, and so on. “Drinking liquor” means drinking it to satiety.
*Suraṃ*: *Divā* means "beyond the day," that is, "too late"; the meaning is "having overslept. *Taṃ* refers to the act of waking up after having slept in such a manner.
The intended meaning is that [the meditator] thinks: "At the time of sleep, I entered cessation by way of being drawn out of perception by the deities;
at the time of waking, I emerged from cessation by way of being drawn back into perception."
"Like the talk of the blind" means that the talk of these who pride themselves on being wise is similar to the talk of blind children.
"The four cessations" refers to the four cessations which are mutually incompatible. "It must be one" means it must exist as a single nature (*ekasabhāva*).
"Not many" means it must not exist as many different natures (*nānāsabhāva*) that are mutually contradictory. For that reason also...
"By one" means by that cessation which possesses a single nature. "By another indeed" means it must exist in a manner different from the modes described by them.
"It" refers to the cessation that possesses a single nature. "Except for the Omniscient One" means setting aside the Buddha, the All-Knowing One.
"Here" means in the Hall of Wonders. "This is cessation, this is cessation"—this is a statement expressing a desire for explanation made twice.
This was done to show that the Teacher, through the elegance of his own teaching, would manifest cessation in its manifold aspects and forms.
Regarding the phrase "Aho nūna": here, *aho* is a particle expressing wonder, and *nūna* expresses recollection.

Therefore, in the expression "Aho nūna Bhagavā," because the Blessed One possesses a teaching not shared by others, one should think: "The Blessed One, having made even cessation a source of wonder, would bring [the listener] to fulfillment."
The intended meaning is "he conceives. The same method applies here to the phrase "O, surely he is a Sugata!

Furthermore, the repetition of the word occurs twice precisely for the sake of manifesting its wonder. For this particle *aho* also possesses the sense of wonder, and it was grasped by Poṭṭhapāda specifically through the medium of recollection.
Therefore, it is said: "the two particles have the sense of recollection. By that [phrase], it is by way of the medium of the sense of recollection.
“Because of its occurrence. The construction is: “With the words ‘Oh... Sugata,’ this thought occurred [to him].

To show the construction along with its underlying intention—that the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are always connected—he said, “Of these,” and so forth. Because these phenomena subject to cessation possess many divisions according to distinctions of time, place, person, and so on, the genitive case is used for their plurality;
furthermore, in connection with the word *kusala*, this should be understood as having the sense of the locative case.
"Skilled," "proficient," and "clever" are synonyms. "Oh, would that he might speak! expresses a sense of wonder, meaning "I think he might speak.
"He is a Sugata" is the connection. "Because of mastery in practice" means because of having attained mastery in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"He knows the true nature" means he knows the true nature of cessation as it really is.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Arising and Cessation of Rootless Perception (Ahetukasaññuppādanirodhakathāvaṇṇanā) 412.

“They stumbled right in the middle of the house”: the meaning is that just as men wishing to go out from a house might stumble on the level, open courtyard within the house itself, without even descending onto the path, so too is this case.
The distinction such as "the uncommon cause" (*asādhāraṇo hetu*) and "the common condition" (*sādhāraṇo paccayo*) has been stated elsewhere;
however, there is no need for that distinction here, because the objection is directed toward the refutation of the notion that perception is without a cause. Therefore, it is said:
"It is indeed called a cause. Furthermore, as it is stated in the Pāli: "For, Poṭṭhapāda, with a cause and with a condition, a person..."

“Perceptions arise and also cease. In this context, the statement “they also cease” is for the purpose of showing that they arise with causes and conditions, but once arisen, they simply cease and do not remain;
it is not, however, for the purpose of showing that cessation itself has causes and conditions. For arising alone is with cause, not cessation. If...
For even cessation would then have a cause, and there would have to be a further cessation of that [cessation], just as there is a further sprout for a sprout and so forth;
yet there is no further cessation of it. Therefore, the meaning of the text should be understood according to the method already stated.
And this method has been explained by way of momentary cessation (*khaṇanirodha*). However, that which [ceases] by way of the time-limits as they have been defined...
Non-arising and cessation are to be understood as "having a cause," because they do not exist without such a form of practice.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Through training, one perception arises; through training, another perception ceases.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) as well: "In order to illustrate the arising and cessation of perception as having a cause. For this is the word of the Canon (*Pāḷi*).
It should be understood that the statement in the *Aṭṭhakathā* was spoken with reference to non-arising and cessation (*anuppādanirodha*).

The word *sikkhā* is in the nominative case used in the sense of a cause (*hetvatthe*), or else it is a contraction of the *ya*-suffix, as in expressions such as "even a number [of people] must depart from that forest.
Its status as a cause will be made clear below. Furthermore, the word *eka* is a synonym for "other" (*añña*), not a term denoting numerical unity.
“In such cases as ‘of a certain existing being,’ etc.,” he says, “a certain perception arises regarding the training. The same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. 413.

“Desiring to explain in detail” means by way of the desire to explain in detail. “By way of a question” means either by way of a question arising from the desire to speak, or by way of a question arising from the desire to explain in detail;
this is the compound. [This is said] because of the apprehension that “this question belongs only to Poṭṭhapāda.”
“The Blessed One said,” so it is stated in the Pāḷi. It should be construed as: “in order to show them, he explained [the training] by way of perception...
and so forth. “Therein” refers to that teaching which will be spoken of above. “The third” is connected with the phrase “the training in higher wisdom has come down. Regarding the statement, “This...
was taught,” it should be understood here as having come down by way of right view and right intention. Why? Because they are included [within that training].
The intention is that they are included because they are subsumed within the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) according to their respective natures and functions.
For it is said in the *Cūḷavedalla Sutta*: “Friend Visākha, whatever is right view and whatever is right intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom.
Certainly, by the method stated here, all three trainings (*sikkhā*) are also brought forth.
Nevertheless, the cessation of perception (*abhisaññānirodha*) is shown specifically through the training in higher consciousness (*adhicittasikkhā*).
However, the meaning that the other [trainings] are brought in as its requisites (*sambhāra*) should be understood from the Pāḷi text itself.

"Lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇika-rāga*) is the lust that arises with reference to the five categories of sensual objects. "Non-arisen sensual conduct" (*asamuppanna-kāmacāra*)...

By way of being presently arisen, "not yet arisen" refers to any kind of arbitrary conduct (*kāmacāra*) or any arising of greed (*lobha*). However, the reading "not yet arisen sensual lust" (*asamuppanna-kāmarāga*) is inappropriate, because it is contradictory in meaning.
Furthermore, in this context, sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) should be understood as greed having the strands of sense pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) as its object, since it is delimited by way of its object;
whereas arbitrary conduct (*kāmacāra*) is divided into various types, such as attachment to meditative absorption (*jhānanikanti*) and lust for existence (*bhavarāga*), and so forth.

The entire range of greed (*lobha*). It is "conduct regarding sensual pleasures" (*kāmacāra*) in the sense of being a desire and in the sense of occurring with respect to sensual pleasures. For all phenomena belonging to the three planes are "sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) in the sense of being desirable.

Since both [types of conduct] possess the state of being a perception of sensual pleasure (*kāmasaññā*) by way of association, it should be understood that after extracting the term "perception of sensual pleasure," both of these are indicated. "Therein," etc.

This is either a demonstration of the distinction between lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure and unarisen sensual conduct, or a demonstration that it is precisely unarisen sensual conduct that is intended here.
Granted, lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is indeed eradicated by the non-returner path even when it is unarisen;
however, even when that has been eradicated, not all lust reaches eradication. This is because...

Because it has been eradicated by the supreme path (aggamagga). Therefore, since the inclusion of the other [types of lust] does not occur merely by mentioning lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure (pañcakāmaguṇika-rāga), the term "perception of sensual desire" (kāmasaññā) is employed in the Canon by way of a figurative expression (pariyāya) common to both, thereby encompassing both.
Consequently, having shown both of them according to their literal form and their specific distinctions, [the text proceeds] because of its all-inclusive nature.
"But one who has not yet given rise to sensual perception is suitable for this stage," it is said. Therefore, the construction is as follows:
since only one for whom sensual perception has not arisen is suitable here, this meaning should be understood. "Of him" refers to the person possessing the first jhāna.

"By way of similarity" means by way of being identical in terms of the presence of sensual perception and so forth; by this, the term "preceding" in the Pāḷi is used in the sense of establishing a similarity.
This indicates that it is "stated. For here, future states are stated as "cease" because non-arising is intended.
Therefore, in order to show only the future, it is said: "not having arisen, it does not arise.
"Designated by the joy and pleasure born of seclusion" means designated together with the joy and pleasure born of seclusion; it does not mean the joy and pleasure born of seclusion themselves.
It is explained [thus]: for here it is perception associated with that [first jhāna] which is intended, not the joy and happiness born of seclusion (*vivekaja-pīti-sukha*).

Alternatively, the meaning is "consisting of the factors of joy and happiness born of seclusion. Here, the word *saṅkhāta* has the sense of a "factor" (*koṭṭhāsa*), as in such passages as "one might take what is not given, which is reckoned as theft" (*adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyeyya*).
By way of abandoning the gross factors such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth, [it is distinguished] from the perception of diversity and the perception of aversion.
They are subtle because of their proficiency; they are true because of their reality. He shows that very meaning by the word "bhūtā" (true). The meaning is:

they possess an unerring intrinsic nature both by way of subtlety and by way of ultimate reality. Having thus shown the meaning according to the text by way of analysis (*vyāsa*), he says "Or else" (*atha vā*) and so forth, showing it again according to the text by way of synthesis (*samāsa*). [This concludes] by way of analysis and synthesis.

For indeed, two readings are seen. By the phrase “by way of abandoning the gross factors such as sensual desire,” it is shown that the subtle and refined nature of perception—which is established through the power of the cultivation of associated states—is understood by way of the suppression of the hindrances.
“By its reality” means by way of its subtle state, its ultimate state, its non-erroneousness, and its actual existence.

"Born of seclusion" (*vivekaja*) means born from the seclusion of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Now, in order to show the meaning of the second phrase stated by way of one possessing the jhāna, it is said:
"That [jhāna] would be," and so forth. "In all instances" means in all sections.
Just as entering the attainment (*samāpajjana*), emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) is also included within the jhāna, just as it is with phenomena (*dhamma*).
The moment of dissolution among phenomena, as well as the moments of adverting and reviewing, are not included within the jhānas;
therefore, taking only that which is included within the jhānas as mastery, it is said: "One trains while entering, resolving, and emerging.
"That" refers to the first jhāna. By means of that... [etc. ...by means of the jhāna—this too is called "training."
This is the word for its commentary. The term *tena* (by that) is used in the instrumental case to express a cause;

the meaning is "by means of the first jhāna as a cause. Furthermore, the causal nature of the jhāna here consists in its being a co-nascent and other such conditions for the arising of the subtle and true perception of rapture and pleasure born of seclusion (*vivekaja-pīti-sukha-sukhuma-sacca-saññā*).

As for the cessation of the perception of sensual desire (*kāma-saññā*), it is simply by way of being a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), and this is according to the method of the Suttanta.

And just as it was explained below by the method, "because [the first jhāna] does not exist without such practice," this refers to the method stated here in the passage, "One perception arises through training;
one perception ceases through training," by way of the perceptions that are the opposites of the first jhāna. "In all instances" means in all sections.
414. Now, explaining the reason for showing perception as having the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) as its limit, he says, "But because...
and so forth. The connection is: "Because this... [etc. ...is extracted. To the question, "Of what is this 'comprehension by factors' (*aṅgasammasana*) said?

he replies, "Of the eight attainments," and so on. "By way of factors" means by way of the factors of jhāna. For this [comprehension] belongs to insight into phenomena according to their sequence (*anupadadhammavipassanā*).

This is a statement of its characteristic. For one who practices insight into phenomena according to their sequence (anupada-dhamma-vipassanā) attains absorption and then performs a comprehension of the factors themselves;
yet perception (*saññā*) is not actually a factor of that absorption. Nevertheless, it is said:
"And this 'perception, perception'—thus the comprehension of the factors has been extracted. Therefore, this is a statement of its characteristic. [The phrase] "as a factor" (*aṅgato*).
The meaning is "by way of a factor" (*avayava*); it is what is meant by "by way of successive phenomena" (*anupadadhamma*). "By way of a cluster" (*kalāpa*) means by way of a collection.

However, since here—in the context of describing the arising and ceasing of various perceptions by way of attainment—that [cessation] is stated by way of the factors (*aṅga*), it should be understood that the contemplation (*sammasana*) is shown precisely by way of the factors through the passage beginning with "And this... Therefore, it is by way of perception alone...

Because it has been extracted from the contemplation of the factors (*aṅga*). "That very same" refers to the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) itself, and not the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*), because perception is not sharp there.

Regarding what should have been said as "which" (*yo*), it is stated as "from which" (*yato*); thus he says "which by name" (*yo nāmā*), just as when one should say "in the beginning" (*ādimhi*), one says "from the beginning" (*ādito*).
It is said that when the meaning is grasped, the suffix *-to* is obtained through its appropriate grammatical analysis.
Here, the word *nāma* serves merely for the elegance of expression, just like the word *kho*. Regarding the phrase *sakasaññī*: *sakaṃ* means "one's own," referring to the jhāna attained by oneself;
*saññā* means "perception" regarding that [jhāna]; and since one possesses that, one is called *sakasaññī*. Thus it is stated: "by means of one's own perception of the first jhāna..."

“Possessing perception” (*saññavā*): here, the vowel *ī* should be understood as indicating the presence of a particularly distinguished perception of jhāna that serves as the basis for the cessation to be described below.
For this very reason, it is said: “He touches the peak of perception in successive order,” and so forth.
Therefore, it should be understood that by mentioning his own specific perception in each instance, the state of complete mastery (*vasībhāva*) well-practiced in each respective jhāna is illustrated.

“Of the mundane” (*lokiyānaṃ*) is a genitive used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*), or it is used in the sense of possession (*sāmi-atthe*). For in whatever respect that [supramundane attainment] is the best among them, in that same respect it is also the best for them.
Alternatively, the genitive is used in the sense of a limit (*vibhattāvadhi-atthe*).

Here, however, the qualification “of the mundane” is made because it is not the best among those [mundane states] when compared with supramundane attainments (*lokuttara-samāpatti*). The remainder [of the compound] is “of the functions, the factors, and the attainments” (*kicca-kāraka-samāpattīnaṃ*).
However, this qualification should be understood as referring to its lack of excellence compared to the attainment that performs its function.
Its state of performing no function is shown by the passage, "For just as perception is there, so too are contact and the rest," and by the fact that, at that stage,
the phenomena remain in a form that cannot be comprehended by those who practice natural insight, because they have reached the state of being mere residual formations (*saṅkhārāvasesabhāva*).

It is understood from the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) that, for that very reason, they are not capable of performing their functions with proficiency, just like the states of the lower attainments, because it is stated there that they lack the function of clear perception (*paṭusaññākicca*).
This matter has been explained in detail by the Master (*ācariya*) in the discussion on the formless attainments (*āruppakathā*) in the *Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā* named *Paramatthamañjūsā*;
therefore, it should be understood according to the method set forth therein. Some...
However, as for the claim that "just as each lower attainment fulfills the function of a basis for each higher attainment,
the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception does not fulfill the function of a basis for anything;

therefore, it is one that performs no function, whereas the others perform functions," that is incorrect, because even that [attainment] serves as a basis for such things as insight and the taming of the mind.
Because it accomplishes the function of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), the former meaning alone is appropriate.

As to why this is their "peak," he says: "of the attainment of the base of nothingness," and so forth. Having said "thus," its meaning is stated as "because they are the peak among worldly [states]...";
or else, "because they are the peak" is itself the illustration for that.
*Pakappeti* means he prepares (*saṃvidahati*). For one entering a jhāna indeed prepares the bliss of jhāna within himself.
*Abhisaṅkharoti* means he exerts and compiles; for the meaning of "compiling" is the meaning of "assembling.

Since the function of volition reaches its peak through the influence of attachment (*nikanti*), [the author], showing the cause by way of a metaphorical designation of the effect, says: "attachment... etc."
It is said: "These are the perceptions of the base of nothingness. These are the perceptions of the base of nothingness currently being obtained.
They would cease because the volitional formation (*cetanābhisaṅkhāra*) for the sake of the higher jhāna becomes possible only through the transcendence of them.
"Other" means other than the perceptions of the base of nothingness. "Gross" means coarser than those. But what are they? He says: "the life-continuum perceptions (*bhavaṅgasaññā*)."
For indeed, after emerging from the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), there would be volitional formations (*cetanābhisaṅkhāra*) for the sake of the higher jhāna;
and thus the perceptions of the base of nothingness would cease. Furthermore, emergence occurs by way of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*);
thereafter, until the attainment of the higher jhāna, perceptions of the life-continuum would arise intermittently, and these [perceptions]—compared to the perceptions of the base of nothingness—...
The intended meaning is "gross.
"While intending" means while still applying oneself to the attainment of the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception even for one or two mental cycles.

"Does not intend" means that he does not apply himself in that way, either because, as in the case of the lower jhānas, there is no prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*), or because [the state] is beyond such intention.
[This is] the name. For here, one who intends by means of prior application (*pubbābhoga*) is said to "will" (*ceteti*).
"While forming" (*abhisaṅkharonto*) means precisely while exerting effort (*āyūhanto*) there due to the presence of unabandoned attachment (*nikanti*).

"He does not form" (*nābhisaṅkharoti*) means that, as in the case of the lower jhānas, he does not exert effort because of the absence of prior application. [The thought is: "I shall produce this jhāna; I shall attain it."
For such volitional formation as "I shall attain [it]" occurs only for one who has attachment (*sālaya*) toward that state, not for one who is without attachment (*anālaya*).

Therefore, even when one is practicing jhāna for only one or two mind-moments, because of the fact that craving (*nikanti*) has not been abandoned toward it, one is said to be "volitionally forming" it. However, since there is no prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*) toward it in that way—as there is in the case of the lower jhānas—[the distinction is made].
Therefore, it is said: “he does not volitionally construct. The passage beginning with “of this bhikkhu” is an exposition of the very same meaning already stated.
In that context, the intention is that because this [bhikkhu] possesses such qualities... [as previously described], therefore it is said: “he does not intend, he does not volitionally construct.

“Exertion and mental application” (*ābhoga-samannāhāra*) means that which is characterized as exertion, or by way of exertion, the turning of the mind toward the object, or [the turning] of the object...
Or it is a subsequent addition directed toward the mind. With the words “This very matter,” etc., he demonstrates that same meaning by means of a simile.
“By way of announcing the son’s house” means by the method of reporting the son’s house.
The connection is: “having gone and returned with [something] taken. “In the rear part” means standing in the western direction of the assembly hall.
At the rear of the father’s house. “From there” means from the son’s house. “Only the house where he received alms” refers to that very house, the son’s home, from which he obtained the alms.

It is like the assembly hall because one must approach the attainment of the base of nothingness as being analogous to the father’s house and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of cessation as being analogous to the son’s house.
The attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is like the father’s house, because it is not to be brought to mind and because it stands in the middle.
Cessation-attainment is like the son’s house, because it is to be brought to mind and because it stands at the limit.

"Without bringing the father’s house to mind" means that even though one has entered and transcended the father’s house, one does not bring that house to mind; rather, [one brings] only the son’s house to mind.
Just as in the case of explaining, even though one must enter the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception for one or two thought-moments,
it should be understood that one does not attend to it, but rather attends solely to the subsequent attainment of cessation. Thus,

the relationship between the simile and the subject illustrated is stated both by way of the commonality of non-attention and the commonality of attention, since even "explaining" is a manifestation of attention itself.
For without attention (*manasikāra*), description is not possible.
"Those perceptions of jhāna" refers to the perceptions of the jhāna of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) that occur for one or two mental moments.
For in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the wholesome or functional javanas of the fourth immaterial sphere proceed only twice, and not beyond that.
“They cease” means they cease by their own inherent nature; however, there is no further arising due to the power of prior volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*).

And just as it is with the perceptions of the jhānas, so it is with the other perceptions; thus he said, “and another,” and so forth. The intention is that they do not arise for the duration of time previously delimited.
“That bhikkhu who has practiced in this way” means he has practiced by being established at the aforementioned summit of perceptions (*saññagga*).
The meaning is this: that bhikkhu—whether a non-returner or an arahant—is endowed with two fruits; he has entered upon the practice of establishing cessation by way of these:
the subsiding of three formations, the sixteenfold course of knowledge, and the ninefold course of concentration.
It is precisely the non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors by way of successive cessation that is referred to under the heading of "perception and feeling."
It is called "the cessation of perception and feeling. Regarding the word "touches" (*phusati*), it shows that "touching" means finding or obtaining, by means of the phrase "finds and obtains.

In terms of its actual meaning, however, according to the method already stated, it is simply the absolute non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors for the duration of time as previously delimited.
Because it is meaningless, it is merely a prefix; therefore, the meaning is simply "perception" (*saññā*).

Having placed the word *sampajāna* between those two—since the word for attainment (*samāpatti*) ought to follow immediately after the word for cessation (*nirodha*)—he said, "stated with the word for cessation intervening.
By this he meant: "anu... [etc. ...the meaning"; thus, this is an improper compound, as the reading is according to the literal sound.

It shows [this]. Regarding the phrase "there too" (*tatrāpi*), the construction is: even in that aforementioned sequential arrangement according to the order of the terms, this is the specific meaning.

"Of one who is fully aware" (*sampajānantassa*) refers to a person who, having entered and emerged from each respective attainment, understands through the method of contemplating the conditioned formations (*saṅkhārā*) in each instance.
"At the end" (*ante*) means at the conclusion of the practice of proceeding toward cessation as previously described.
In the second alternative, "of one who is fully aware" (*sampajānantassa*) means "one who acts with full awareness.

By this, the wisdom that accomplishes the purpose—along with the wisdom of all the miraculous feats—is shown from the very beginning for the monk who enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Therefore, he says, "of the wise monk. The difference between the two alternatives lies in whether they require or do not require a supplementary word (*vacana-sesa*).
The discussion on the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) should be explained because the opportunity for its detailed commentary has now arisen.

"In every respect" means by way of all its modes, such as the specific nature of the attainment of cessation itself, the person who attains it, the place where it is attained, the cause for attaining it, and the manner of attaining it.
"Therein" means from the very place where it was already explained, namely in the *Visuddhimagga*.
The meaning is "from the twenty-third chapter"; the intention is that we do not state it here because of the fault of redundancy and because of the resulting bulkiness of the text.
In the passage "Thus indeed was it," the word *evaṃ* (thus) has the sense of "manner," since it shows the manner in which [the teaching] was grasped.
However, in the passage "Thus, Poṭṭhapāda," it has the sense of "acceptance," since it signifies assent in that very way. Therefore he said:
“‘You have reached the pinnacle of existence’—thus he grants permission. 415.
That in which perception (*saññā*) is supreme is the “pinnacle of perception” (*saññagga*), namely the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).

Although the pinnacle of perception exists in the remaining meditative attainments as well, here the state of being the pinnacle of perception is called “the pinnacle of perception”; it is a coordinate compound (*tulyādhikaraṇa-samāsa*) meaning that perception itself is the pinnacle.
Or: “*Puthū* (many)”—this is a reversal of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), or it is said that the suffix *nika* has been elided, hence “*bahūni* (many [objects]”).

By the word “*yathā* (as/how),” he shows that a specific mode consisting of the manner of the instrument is intended, not the generality of the mode; this is indicated by the passage beginning with “*pathavīkasiṇādīsū* (in the earth-kasiṇa, etc.).

The phrase beginning with “*idaṃ vuttaṃ hotī* (this is what is meant)” is its explanation. First, the state of being an instrument is appropriate for the jhānas in relation to the touching of the cessation of perception.
But how is it that [the kasiṇas] possess the state of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*)? That [state] applies to them as well.

For to the same extent that the jhānas possess the state of being the most effective means for touching cessation (*nirodha*), to that same extent the kasiṇas do too, because they are inseparable from them. Furthermore, an action can indeed have multiple instruments, as in the expression:
"He goes by way of another path, by vehicle, and by torchlight."

"Once" means a single time. "Cessation of prior perception" refers to the cessation of sensual perception (*kāmasaññā*), but not to the cessation of perception known as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
"One peak of perception" means one summit that is itself perception, or the state of being a single peak of perception because it is superior to the preceding perception.
For it is "perception and it is a peak" that constitutes the "peak of perception" (*saññagga*); it does not mean "the peak among perceptions."
Just as the "summit of perception" (*saññagga*) is the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*) because the summit of perception is at its peak, so too are the remaining jhānas.

And as for the sign by which a jhāna is called the "summit of perception," that very sign—termed "perception"—is what is intended here either by the elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvalopa*) or by emphasizing the state itself (*bhāvappadhāna*).
"Twice" means two times. "A hundred thousand summits of perception" means...

The Description of the Tracing of the Footprint of a Bird. Regarding the phrase "in the remaining kasiṇas," only the kasiṇas themselves are intended because of their relevance to the discussion on cessation (*nirodha*).
For that very reason, it should be understood that here, by the mention of "jhāna," only the kasiṇa-jhānas are meant.

Just as it was stated [previously] using the expression "by means of the earth-kasiṇa acting as the instrument" without referring to the jhāna that has that [earth] as its object, so too [is it here] with the phrase "by the first jhāna."
By saying "by means of that which has become the instrument," he speaks without touching upon its object. With the words "Thus," etc., he concludes by summarizing that very same meaning.
"All" means even the perception of jhāna entered into once. "Having summarized" means having made a summary because it does not transcend its own nature through the characteristic of perceiving;
this is done both by way of entering [into absorption] and by the characteristic of perceiving.
"Singlefold" is what is meant. "Successively" means again and again. There are many types of perception-peak (*saññaggāni*).

In the first method, the knowledges of perception (*saññā*) and knowledge (*ñāṇa*) are shown by way of the individual who is developing insight (*vipassanā*) with the jhāna as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*).
In the second method, however, because one who has intensified insight and joins it with the path possesses the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*), [that is shown].
Because [insight] arises, the perceptions and knowledges are shown by way of the path of insight.

And in the third method, since the first method is coarse and the second method is mixed, both of these being disregarded, the perceptions and knowledges are shown by way of the path and fruition solely to demonstrate the supramundane that has been produced, which is extremely subtle and profound. These three...
These have been shown by way of clarifying the path through various methods.
To clarify that "this, however, is the essence here," the opinion of the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva has been cited.

For thus, in the subsequent commentary on the meaning, it is explained in full accordance with the Elder’s view, beginning with the words, "from the arising of the perception of the fruit of arahantship. "These bhikkhus" refers to those who hold the former opinion.

"Bhikkhus. At that time, while the monks were reciting the Dīghanikāya, having reached this passage and explaining the three methods according to the aforementioned sequence, the Elder spoke thus with reference to those bhikkhus.

Having asked about cessation (*nirodha*) and it having been explained, he next asks about the arising of the knowledge of perception (*saññā-ñāṇa*), which in meaning is equivalent to asking about emergence from cessation (*nirodhā vuṭṭhāna*).
[This is] the name. And emergence from cessation may occur either through the arising of the fruit of Arahantship or the arising of the fruit of Non-returning;
in that case, perception is predominant, and immediately following it is the knowledge of reviewing.
Distinguishing between these two, the Elder said, "Poṭṭhapāda, below... and so forth. Therein, "Bhagavā" is a term of address.

Just as when the knowledge of the path and its fruits arise within the cognitive process of the path, there necessarily follow the knowledges of reviewing the path and its fruits, so too in the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition, there arises the knowledge of reviewing the fruit. This is what is meant by the phrase "subsequent reviewing knowledge.
It is a demonstration of the mode of arising of the reviewing knowledge that thinks, "This is the fruit of Arahantship. This alone is the condition.
The term *idappaccaya* is formed by changing the letter *ma* to *da*. Some etymologists maintain that the word *pakati* (nature) also contains the letter *da*.

However, in the Theravāda tradition, this is not recognized as being synonymous with *phalasamādhi* (fruition-concentration); thus he says, "conditioned by the perception known as fruition-concentration," the meaning of which is: conditioned by the perception associated with the fruition-concentration of Arahantship.
The particle *kira* is a grammatical indeclinable used in the sense of recollection; for reflective review (*paccavekkhaṇā*) belongs to the class of recollecting the Dhamma as it has been attained.
And here, by way of its synonym, the entire fruit of Arhatship is included according to the principle of concomitance;
for in its absence, reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*) would be impossible—thus it is said in the Pāḷi: "with this as condition" (*idappaccayā*).

In this way, according to the opinion of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas, the absolute certainty of the reflective contemplation of the fruit is demonstrated. [This is stated] in the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasutta-ṭīkā*.
However, it has been stated thus: "But that [reviewing knowledge] is not complete for everyone. For one reviews only the defilements already abandoned;
another, only the remaining defilements; another, only the path; another, only the fruit; and another, only Nibbāna.
Among these five kinds of reviewing, it is not permissible not to obtain at least one or two. This refers to the reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya.
This was stated according to that opinion. However, the Abhidhammikas say:
"The wise one reviews the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna;

he may or may not review the defilements abandoned and those remaining" (*Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha-ṭīkā*, in the section on the analysis of meditation subjects within the classification of purification).

Commentary on the Discourse on the Self as Perception (Saññāattakathāvaṇṇanā): 417. By the phrase "village pig," he excludes the wild forest pig. For in this way, the statement of the simile becomes well-founded.
Through the smoothness of the teaching, which cleanses away the impurities of agitation, malice, and attachment, knowledge consisting of what has been heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa) is bathed.
It is as if anointed with a subtle essence, and due to being struck by the three characteristics, it is as if adorned with ornaments such as earrings.

Because of the state of the knowledge that enters into it, and because of the attainment of that same state by the person possessing it, the announcement regarding the discourse on cessation is like entering the royal bedchamber; thus he said: "Subtle and delicate... [etc.]..."

"Even though it has been explained. "Therein" means in this discourse on cessation (*nirodha*). "Not finding pleasure" means not experiencing, not obtaining, or not understanding [it] due to dullness of intellect.
"Like a place of excrement" because it is defiled by impurities. "One's own doctrine" means one's own view (*attadiṭṭhi*).
"Having obtained consent" means having received permission, having caused [the teacher] to authorize [the claim], "My self is such," regarding one's own doctrine.
"Having established" is what is meant.
In the Pāḷi, "But which? means: among the three kinds of self-theories—namely, the gross, the mind-made, and the formless—which self did he reply was his?
By the phrase "skilled in teaching," [it is implied]: "Surely for me..."
"‘The Blessed One will shatter his tenet’—this shows his state of mind. ‘Avoiding’ means removing it by shattering it;
the intention is that he is concealing his own tenet, namely, ‘the self is formless. In the Pāḷi passage beginning with ‘Coarse indeed...
in the words of the wanderer, this is the intention: because [the wanderer] has grasped the continuity of the fourfold stream of materiality as a unity..."
Because of its material nature, the proponent of self (attavādī) believes, "The self is gross";

and by imagining the presence of food and drink in it, he conceives of it as "eternal. Furthermore, because of its material nature, the distinctness of this [self] from consciousness is indeed established by reason—precisely that which the proponents of the Vedas describe in two ways as "consisting of food" and "consisting of drink.
Therefore, the wanderer [identifies] that view of the proponent of self as his own self.
Having intended this, he spoke the words beginning with, “Coarse indeed...”.
Furthermore, the intention behind the Blessed One’s statement, “If, Poṭṭhapāda, your self were coarse,” and so forth, is as follows:
if the self were material (rūpī), then in that case, form would be the self; yet it is not percipient because of its lack of form (arūpabhāvato).

And because material phenomena (rūpadhammā) have the nature of being non-cognizant. Furthermore, if according to your view that which possesses form (rūpī) is permanent, then consciousness (saññā)—because it arises successively and thus breaks up here and there due to its state of disintegration—is impermanent.
In this way, since "consciousness is one thing and the self is another," the self would be devoid of consciousness due to the absence of consciousness; therefore, this self is not [permanent].

The Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with "and coarse" in order to point out this fault: that it would follow [from your position] that one is the doer of the action but not the experiencer of the fruit.

In that context—"in the doctrine that the self possesses form"—the accusative case is used in the sense of the object because it depends on the remaining verb; and "paccāgacchato" means "of one who returns," "of one who knows," or "depending on."
Or the meaning is: "by way of discourse. Why was it said, "One perception arises and another perception ceases"?
To resolve the objection that cessation must precede arising, and that there is no such thing as what has arisen not being subject to cessation, it was said, "of the four aggregates," and so forth.
This was stated even though they possess a single object and a single basis.

Because the context concerns arising and cessation, only the state of simultaneous arising and cessation is mentioned. "Successively" (*aparāparaṃ*) means one after another, like the flight of an arrow.
(418–420) In the text, "mind-made" (*manomaya*) refers to being mind-made by way of the mind of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).

For that which does not depend on external conditions is produced by the mind alone; thus it is "mind-made. He speaks with reference to the body produced in the realm of form (*rūpaloka*). As for those who proclaim the Vedas...
They describe it in two ways as "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) and "consisting of consciousness" (*viññāṇamaya*).

In that case too—that is, even in the doctrine that "the self consists of mind" (*manomaya attā*)—when the fault was pointed out by saying, "there will be another perception," and so forth, he spoke the words beginning with "it is indeed formless" (*arūpiṃ kho*), while still asserting his own position;
this is the connection. Here too, according to the method stated in the previous discussion, if the self consists of mind...
"Should he have all limbs and members and unimpaired faculties, in that case form would be the self;

yet one would not be percipient through perception because of the absence of form"—all such [statements] should be understood as the demonstration of faults. Indeed, showing this meaning, the Blessed One said:
