"And for you, Poṭṭhapāda, it is mind-made," and so forth. But why did this wanderer first [assert] a gross self?
Having asserted that doctrine and then abandoned it, does he again assert a mind-made self? And having abandoned even that, does he again assert a formless self?
Although the reason for this has already been stated below—"Even though he was one who held such a view as 'therefore the self is formless'...
[etc.]... they began [the discussion] again"—nevertheless, these sectarians are indeed of unsettled minds.
To show another reason for its instability—likening it to a stake driven into a heap of chaff—it is said, "Just as if," and so forth.
"Perception does not become established" means that perception does not become established by way of perceiving an object; what is meant is that one does not form a perception of the object.
This same method applies here to the phrase "at the time when perception becomes established."
"In that case too" means even in the doctrine that "the self is formless. "Of perception" refers to ordinary perception;
this is how the Venerable Dhammapāla Thera has stated it. For the connection is with "the arising and ceasing" in another sectarian school.
By this, he shows that according to the opinion of the Vedins, one desires the arising and ceasing of a perception that arises at different moments and has various objects. Some...
However, they read "with the perception of a teacher" (*ācariyasaññāya*); that is incorrect because it contradicts the meaning and was not cited by the Elder.
By seeing the arising and passing away of a perception that occurs in succession, one desires [the cessation of] arising and ceasing.
Nevertheless, grasping the conventional designation (*samaññā*) that occurs as "perception, perception" and imagining its non-interruption as "self," one [clings to] eternalism (*sassata*).
He conceives [it]. Therefore he says, “But he conceives the self as eternal.

For this reason—because of conceiving eternity based on the mere name of perception as it occurs in succession—he shows the fault by grasping at a view of eternity that goes beyond the mere arising and ceasing of perception;
such is the intended meaning. “In the same way” means just as [one conceives] “the self is material,” “the self is mind-made,” and so forth.

And in both of these two positions, one’s own lack of restraint [is evident]; thus, the undesirable consequence of such faults as "insentience" (acetanatā) and so forth is difficult to avoid, and the meaning is that it is exactly the same in this position as well.
By "wrong view" (micchādassana), it means by the wrong adherence known as the view of self (attadiṭṭhi).
By "being overcome" (abhibhūtatta), it means because of being overwhelmed by a state cultivated since beginningless time; it is said to mean that the range of knowledge has been obstructed.

There is [this]. The "resolution of the mass" (ghanavinibbhoga) is the knowledge of things as they truly are, having analyzed that "mass of continuity" (santatighana) and "mass of collection" (samūhaghana) by which the fool—deceived by them—clings through wrong grasp to the collection of phenomena occurring in a continuous sequence, and expresses it as "self" and "permanent.
This refers to the resolution of the mass known as unity and the mass of collection.
And that [knowledge] does not exist at all among the followers of other sects.
Therefore, because this wanderer lacked such ripening of knowledge, he did not understand the diversity even though it was being explained; thus it is said, "not knowing that diversity.
This perception arises with various objects at various moments and passes away—this is the doctrine of the Vedins. [He did not know] the arising and ceasing of perception.

Even one who is passing by, having imagined a self consisting of perception (*saññāmaya*) and made of perception (*saññābhūta*), conceives through the conceiving of views (*diṭṭhimaññanā*), taking it to be permanent because of the absence of the aforementioned resolution of the compact mass. And for one who has become thus, the subtle, delicate, supreme, and profound nature of phenomena (*dhammatā*) is simply not known.
Showing that this is the reason why the Blessed One said, "It is indeed difficult to know," and so forth, [the commentator] observes:
Then the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “athassa bhagavā.
Regarding view and the rest: the adherence to the view that “this is exactly so” is *diṭṭhi* (view).

The acceptance of that very [view] through the mode of reflection, thinking “this is exactly so,” which constitutes its preliminary stage, is *khanti* (acceptance). Likewise, the finding of pleasure in it is *ruci* (liking). “In quite another way,” and so forth...

The analytical exposition of those views and so forth. In that context, "in quite another way" means that it is in a manner entirely different from how there is a vision in the Noble Discipline by way of the Middle Way, without falling into the two extremes.

"Quite another thing" refers to that which exists in the ultimate sense, such as the aggregates, bases, and so on, as well as their impermanence and other characteristics; it is quite another thing than that [mere conceptualization] in the ultimate sense.
The meaning is: "You tolerate and you find pleasure in such things as the eternal existence of a self, which do not actually exist.

*Āyoga* is the application of thorough effort (*ābhūso yuñjanaṃ*). Therefore it is said: "the state of being engaged and devotedly applied" (*yuttapayuttatā*). "By way of practice" (*paṭipattiyā*) means by way of the practice of a wanderer (*paribbājaka*), such as the contemplation of the supreme self (*paramattacintanā*) and so forth.
The state of a teacher is *ācariyaka*; it is the instruction and admonition (*ovādānusāsana*) in whatever manner [is appropriate]. One who possesses that is called *ācariyaka*.
Just as he said, "One who has faith," [he said] "in another place" and so forth. The construction is: "In another sectarian order (titthāyatana), you possess the status of a teacher.
The passage beginning with "Therefore" and so forth shows the meaning according to the sentence together with its construction.

"This is the ultimate truth (paramattha), this is conventional truth (sammuti)"—because this distinction is difficult to distinguish, this diversity is hard to understand. "Let this which is hard to understand remain for now."
Having thought, "But I shall ask the Blessed One for another purpose," he spoke the words beginning with "Then the wanderer" in order to show that he had acted accordingly.
"Or another perception" means: let the self (attā) be of a nature other than the nature of perception;
this is the meaning. However, the reading "or another perception" (aññā vā saññā) is seen now. "Of it" (assa) means of the self.
It is called *loka* because merit and demerit, as well as their result, are seen (*lokīyati*) or established (*patiṭṭhahati*) therein; thus, it refers to the self (*attā*).

For that [self] is intended by him to be both the doer and the experiencer. "A speculative view" (*diṭṭhigata*) refers to a position of wrong view proceeding according to such methods as "the self and the world are eternal.
Indeed, this adherence to a view is not based on matters pertaining to the present life and so forth, because it does not lead to those ends.
For that which leads to something may be said to "depend on it," just as the equipment of merit and knowledge [depends on its cause].
By this same method, dependence on the Dhamma should also be described. The beginning of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) is the "beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariya*);

that itself is "pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyaka*), just as "the discipline itself is the disciplinarian" (*venayika*). Therefore he said: "of that which is comprised of the three trainings," and so forth.
Every statement contains an implicit restriction, as its fruit is that very restriction; thus it is said, "only the beginning.
Here, however, it refers specifically to the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).

For this is the beginning of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) comprised within the three trainings, unlike other instances where the "beginning of the holy life" refers to the eightfold livelihood and so forth; this is what he shows by saying, "only the training in higher virtue."

By this [phrase]. "For the sake of disenchantedness" means for the state of being weary of it. They say: "'For the sake of higher knowledge' means for the sake of knowing by way of full understanding through knowledge (*ñāta-pariññā*);
'for the sake of awakening' means for the sake of awakening by way of full understanding through investigation and abandonment (*tīraṇa-pahāna-pariññā*).

Furthermore, "'For the sake of higher knowledge' means for the sake of knowing by way of the wisdom of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-paññā*); that, moreover, is simply the making manifest of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*)."
He said, "By way of direct action. "For the purpose of full awakening" means for the purpose of penetration by means of the clear realization of thorough knowledge (*pariññābhisamaya*).

The fact that adherence to views does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and peace within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) should be understood as being because it is included within the round and because it binds one to the round.
Likewise, it should be seen as not leading to direct knowledge, full awakening, and Nibbāna.
Granted that craving (taṇhā) is indeed of the nature of suffering (dukkha), it is stated as "setting aside craving" because it is grasped separately by virtue of its being the origin (samudaya).
"From production" means from arising. Although craving produces suffering, it does so only when accompanied by other conditions such as ignorance (avijjā);
it does not do so alone. Therefore, he says "with conditions" (sappaccayā). "Non-occurrence" means the cause for non-occurrence. Not...
The origin of suffering proceeds here, or rather, it has ceased in this; thus, there is non-proceeding.
It goes toward the cessation of suffering, which is Nibbāna, and one must practice for that purpose; thus, it is the "practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
The manifestation of the path is the arising of the path. The realization of the fruit is the making manifest by way of the attainment of the fruit. That is its mode.
As if announcing the sign of departure by means of that state known as silence, he does not, however, announce it directly.
(421) *Sannitodakaṃ* is the prodding or piercing by way of restraining from all sides.

Because the qualifiers such as "mind" (*mano*) and so forth are indicated by a neuter gender, it is said, "by the prodding of speech" (*vācāya sannitodakena*). Therefore, he says, "by the goad of words."
Alternatively, in the phrase “by speech,” this should be understood as an instrumental expression in relation to “with the goad.

For the meaning of “with the goad of words” is “with words as a goad”; or, when construed with “speech,” it is a genitive expression. It should be connected thus: “they were filled with the act of goading by means of speech.
Regarding the term “sajjhabbharitaṃ,” it is [to be analyzed as] “saṃ adhi abhi aribhaṃ.”
The word division is *samantato bhusam ari* (pierced thoroughly and intensely);
the meaning is that it was pierced by various discourses of wandering mendicants, like being struck by hundreds of spears. Thus it is said, "They pierced from above.
"Existing by its own nature" means being apprehended as an ultimate reality (*paramattha-sabhāva*), not being unapprehendable like primordial matter (*pakati*) and so forth.
They speak the truth. "Tatha" means unerring. These three terms are synonyms in meaning. "In the nine supramundane states" is a locative used in the sense of an object;
having made those states the object. "Of stable nature" means of a fixed nature; the meaning is that which produces them.
"Fixed by the certainty of the supramundane states" means determined by the certainty of attaining the supramundane states. Now...
However, the reading “the fixed order of supramundane phenomena” (*lokuttaradhammaniyāmatā*) is not ancient, because it was not cited by the Master (Buddhaghosa).

Why, then, does he say “for [it is] of the Buddhas,” etc., regarding why this practice is the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*) and the fixed order of phenomena (*dhammaniyāmatā*)? “That” refers to the practice.
“Of such a kind” means of the type described by the passage beginning with “the stability of phenomena,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Accounts of Citta, Hatthaka, Sāriputta, and Poṭṭhapāda. 422.

"One who trains and tames an elephant" (*hatthisārī*) means an elephant trainer, a master of elephants. "In subtle matters" (*sukhumesu atthantaresu*) refers to those phenomena such as the aggregates (*khandha*) and bases (*āyatana*), which are the domain of subtle knowledge.
It is said that he was an expert in the *Abhidhamma*. "Virtuous" (*kusala*) means that even previously, in the teaching of the Buddha...
"Skilled because of his practiced familiarity. "In such a state of mind" means in a mind characterized by the household life.
The other, however, did not leave the order upon hearing that; rather, the intention is that he took delight in the very going-forth (pabbajjā).

"Because it was spoken as a discourse on the benefits of the household life"—here, since the monk who possesses virtue was thus exhorted to leave the order by that discourse, now [the author] himself...
The intended meaning is that even while being virtuous, he disrobed six times. For the fruit of an action must correspond to the nature of the action.

"While they were speaking" is a genitive used in a sense of disregard. "Spoken by a Great Disciple" means it was spoken by the Elder Mahākoṭṭhita while acting as a Great Disciple, in the manner of one who disparages;
[the subject] was unable to find a basis for the purpose of that speech.
The meaning is as follows: “Having disrobed, he became a householder”—this is stated as if it were the seventh time.
However, in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and in the *Kudālapaṇḍita-jātaka*, the account of his disrobing is given as occurring only six times.

“A householder companion” means a companion during the period of being a householder. “Even though he has retreated” (*apasakkantopi nāma*)—the word *nāma* here is a term of reproach; [it implies] even though he has retreated [from the path]. “To go forth” (*pabbajituṃ*).
"It is fitting" means that going forth (pabbajjā) is fitting.
"Due to the absence of the eye of wisdom" means due to the lack of the eye of wisdom capable of discerning well-spoken and ill-spoken words, as well as the even and the uneven.
To show what kind of eye he is called "possessed of vision" (cakkhumā), [the text] says "well-spoken," and so forth.
It has been stated. This is another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "One-sided" (*ekaṃsikā*) means categorical;
it is said to be determined by its nature of leading to Nibbāna. "Laid down" (*paññattā*) means defined. "Not one-sided" (*na ekaṃsikā*) means not categorical;

the intention is that it is not determined by its nature of leading to Nibbāna because it is included within the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*). For this meaning [is explained] in the passage: "And why, Poṭṭhapāda, have these been declared by me..."

It accords with and conforms to such sūtra passages as: “These categorical teachings have been taught and proclaimed; these, Poṭṭhapāda, are beneficial... [and so on] ... they lead to Nibbāna. This concludes the commentary on the categorical teachings (*ekaṃsika-dhamma*).
425. Having asked the reason with the words, “For what purpose was it begun?”, the purpose is answered with the words, “In order to show its lack of leading to liberation.
For when the fruit is established, the cause is also established; this is the teacher’s opinion. Others, however, say:

“In such instances, the word *attha* refers to the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the nominative case is used in the sense of the causal ablative (*hetvatthe*); therefore, [the meaning is] ‘in order to show its lack of leading to liberation.’”
"In this context, they maintain that the meaning is 'for the purpose of showing the state of not leading to liberation' (aniyyānikabhāva). Regarding the phrase *paññāpitaniṭṭhāya*:

it refers to the path to deliverance (*vimuttimagga*) that has been proclaimed. For it is said that *niṭṭhā* is deliverance (*vimutti*), because the word *ṭhā* occurs in the sense of 'going' (*gati*), as in the passage from the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta:
'The cattle have gone to their respective stalls' (*goṭṭhā paṭṭhitagāvo*). And here, the path to deliverance (*niṭṭhāmaga*) is [meant]."

By the elision of the latter member of the compound, it is intended as "niṭṭhā" (the goal). For it is the state of being conducive to liberation (*niyyānika*) and the state of not being conducive to liberation that is spoken of here, not the goal itself.
It is called *niyyānikā* because it leads forth (*niyyāti*), with the letter *y* changed to *k*. Indeed, the suffix *-aniya* frequently expresses the sense of the agent;
thus, "not leading forth" is *aniyyānikā*, and its abstract state is likewise [expressed]. Alternatively, *niyyāna* means going forth or departure.

"Escape" (nissaraṇa) means the subsiding of the suffering of saṃsāra; "leading out" (niyyāna) is that which leads out (niyyānika), while that which does not lead out is "not leading out" (aniyyānika).
The state of being such is its "own-nature" (sabhāva), namely the state of not leading out (aniyyānikabhāva); this should be construed as "for the purpose of showing that.
The passage beginning with "All indeed... is an exposition of that meaning. The connection is: "He proclaims how the deathless Nibbāna is the ultimate goal."
"They define the ultimate by way of the 'World-Pinnacle' (lokathūpikā) and so forth" means that they define it in such a manner by grasping merely the common verbal designation "nibbāna, nibbāna.
The "World-Pinnacle" is said to be the plane of Brahmā, by way of imagining it to be like a pinnacle for the world.
However, some say that the "World-Pinnacle" is the plane of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana); that is incorrect, as [stated] in the commentaries.
Likewise, [liberation is] from non-speaking. And here, by the word "etc.," liberation is understood as the realization that "the person is one thing and the nature is another";
liberation is the abiding of the self in its own stateless condition, being devoid of qualities such as intelligence;
liberation is the non-occurrence of the cycle of births and bonds through the departure from bodily failure; and liberation is the separation from another person.
One should see that this includes such statements as "liberation is in his proximity" and "liberation is union with him.
For at each respective time, there is no one who does not designate a final goal. For the Brahmins, the first jhāna and the Brahma-world is the final goal;
for they have a persistent adherence to permanence therein, just as Baka the Brahmā did, while for the Vekhanasa ascetics and others, the Ābhassara realm is so.
For the wanderers such as the Sañcayikas, it is the Subhakiṇha realm; for the Ājīvakas, it is the state of non-perception (asaññībhava) conceived as "the infinite mind.
But in this teaching, the final goal is Arahantship. All these [others], by way of their views, designate the Brahma-world and so forth;
and through the conceit of Arahantship, they take up the mere commonality of the term "Nibbāna, Nibbāna" and describe it accordingly, but not in the ultimate sense.
He said, "And that is not leading," and so forth, because it is impossible for them to establish [the path to] Nibbāna at such a time.
"As it was established" means in whatever manner it was established; the sense is: having become of the very mode in which it was established. "It does not lead" means:
it does not lead in the manner by which the goal is to be reached as proclaimed by them, because that [goal] cannot be attained through that manner. By the wise...
"Rejection" means that this "finality" is rejected by the Buddha and other wise ones because it does not transcend the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
"It turns back" is a statement regarding the reason for that rejection;
for the finality and the practice prescribed by them do not lead out or proceed forward, but rather cause the person possessing them to wander only within *saṃsāra*.
It turns back; therefore, the meaning is that it is rejected by the wise. "That" refers to the state of not leading to liberation (*aniyyānikabhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "knowing and seeing," he says this because of the reversal of the plural number [in the original rule];
for in cases such as, "Whatever nun, knowing that a monastery has monks, should enter without asking permission," the words beginning with "going" (*gacchantādi*) are used according to the gender.

The opposite [meaning] is "knowing," which is the sense intended. In such phrases as "one who does not grant a request is unloved," the meaning is "to one who is requesting," by way of grammatical case (vibhatti).
But here, it should be understood as being by way of the plural number (puthuvacana).
What is called "primary knowing" is knowing through direct perception, because of its status as the preeminent factor; seeing is secondary, because it is accompanied by doubt. This is the sequence.
It was said: "Knowing, see. Herein, by means of knowing, seeing is distinguished.
For in this way, the single intended meaning—that the bodily forms and so forth of humans in that world have indeed been seen before—is well-established. This is the intended meaning here:
"What [proof] do you have for the direct knowledge and vision of a world of absolute happiness?"
"It exists. Or rather, they know that this world is an object of inference (*anumāna*), and they see it as an object of direct perception (*paccakkha*).
This is what is meant: "Is the world known to you through direct perception, or is it known through inference?

Since an object that has become directly perceived in the world is manifest by virtue of being within the range of the sense faculties (*indriya-gocara*), therefore, by means of that which is manifest...
In order to show the intended meaning through its purpose, the phrase beginning with "previously seen" was stated.

Alternatively, it should be understood that this was said in order to clarify the intended meaning through both the term "seen"—which includes the act of seeing as well as the knowledge concomitant with it—and by means of both together.
For "previously seen" means things previously grasped by means of seeing and the knowledge concomitant with it.
This is the meaning. By doing so, the statement “the shape of the body and so forth” is established as being within its proper limits.

Regarding the expression “appāṭihīrakataṃ,” this is a grammatical indication of the elision of a nasal vowel (*anunāsikalopa*); thus he says, “that [statement] becomes *appāṭihīrakaṃ*. The connection is:
“that statement becomes non-authoritative (*appāṭihīrakaṃ*). Some maintain that in the word *appāṭihīra*, there is an elision of the nasal vowel, and that “*kataṃ*” constitutes a single word.

That is incorrect, because it would entail the formation of a compound and because the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) cannot be stated [in this case]. Thus they explain it here: it is called *paṭihāriya* because it removes opposing views;
that very thing is the *pāṭihāriya*. It is a term devoid of anything superior to itself.
Here, the word *pāṭihīraka* is used for the *pāṭihāriya* itself because it possesses a superior when contrasted with what is being asserted by others. It is not...
“Pāṭihīraka” means “appāṭihīraka. Here, the negative particle *a-* has the sense of “devoid of. Thus he said, “devoid of refutation (*paṭiharaṇa-virahita*”).
For a statement that has a superior [to it] is refuted—that is, overturned—by that superior statement;

therefore, a superior statement is called “refutation” (*paṭiharaṇa*), and the meaning is “devoid of that. Precisely for that reason, [it is devoid of] the refutation of the path leading to deliverance.
Because of its non-existence, it receives the designation "not leading out" (*aniyyānika*). Therefore it is said: "not leading out. 426.

*Vilāsa* is feminine coquetry, which is also called "action born of the sentiment of love" (*siṅgārabhāvajā kiriyā*). *Ākappa* is a particular mode of appearance, such as the way of binding the hair or wearing clothes, or the arrangement of one's dress.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *hāva* and so forth is intended. For *hāva* refers to cleverness or artfulness.
**Commentary on the Attainment of the Three Selfhoods (Tayo-attapaṭilābhavaṇṇanā)** 428.
That wherein the conceit "I am" (ahaṃmāna) is established is the self (attā); thus, he says "the attainment of selfhood" (attabhāvapaṭilābho).

How does he demonstrate this? He states, "by the attainment of a gross selfhood," and so forth. This demonstrates the existence of the sense-sphere realm (kāmabhava) by way of its selfhood, as distinguished from the selfhood of the other two realms of existence.
Because of its grossness. It shows the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), since it is perceived as having a material form once it has been produced by this jhāna.

It shows the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), since it is perceived as being immaterial. The so-called defiled states (*saṃkilesikā dhammā*) are the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness, because in their absence no defilement whatsoever can occur.
The so-called purifying states (*vodāniyā dhammā*) are serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Because the complete purification of the mind is accomplished by means of those [factors]. 429.
When opposing states have not been eradicated, neither the fulfillment nor the abundance of blameless states can ever occur;
however, when they have been eradicated, these do occur. Therefore, only the wisdom of the path and the fruit is mentioned here.
It should be seen that these [factors], even when once fulfilled, remain truly fulfilled because they are not subject to decline.
"Taruṇapīti" (nascent rapture) is weak rapture that has merely arisen and has not yet been cultivated through repetition.

"Balavatutthi" (strong satisfaction) is firmer rapture that has been cultivated through repeated arising and serves as a condition for attaining further distinctions. Now, showing the summarized meaning in brief:
He said, “What is meant [by this]? and so forth. Therein, the connection is: “We have spoken of that monastery which he himself...

will dwell in. This is what is meant: that monastery which is the culmination of the abandoning and increase of defiled and purifying states, which has become the fullness and abundance of the perfection of wisdom, and which is directly perceived in this very existence by knowledge independent of others.
“We shall dwell having accomplished [it],” we said. “Therein” means in that monastery.
“Of him” refers to the monk who follows the instruction. “Dwelling thus” means for the sake of dwelling in the manner described, or while dwelling [therein].
Joy (*pāmojja*) arises on account of that; rapture (*pīti*) has joy as its source; the two kinds of tranquility (*passaddhi*) have that as their condition; likewise, well-established...
When it exists, because it has reached its peak, it is "supreme knowledge. The construction is: "And there will be a pleasant abiding.

For tranquility of body and mind is what is called "tranquility," or this very reading [“passaddhi”] alone may be used. Some also read “nāmakāyapassaddhi,” but that is indeed incorrect, because the two types of tranquility are inseparable.
Why, then, is this a pleasant abiding? To this he says: “In all abidings,” and so forth.
Because it is peaceful and sublime in all postures and dwellings, and because it is bliss itself, it is said that this alone deserves to be called "a blissful dwelling.
How is it called "bliss"? It is stated: "It is tranquil and supremely sweet.
In the first jhāna, when it has merely been attained, rapture is weak and belongs to the side of gladness due to its inferior state; [but] when well-developed...
But when that [first jhāna] has become familiar, that rapture (pīti) is called "gladness" (pāmojja) because it is superior, powerful, and its function is fully perfected; thus it is said:

"In the first jhāna, all six factors beginning with gladness are found. "Gladness ceases" means that gladness, which is characterized as weak rapture, ceases—that is, diminishes—among those six factors.
For [this occurs] by means of that which is free from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra), as analyzed according to the fourfold method.
It is said that in the second jhāna, rapture (*pīti*) is always powerful, and unlike in the first jhāna, it is never weak at times.
Rapture ceases precisely through its abandonment, because the third jhāna is attained by means of that very relinquishing.

By the phrase "pleasant abiding" (*sukho vihāro*), concentration (*samādhi*) is included; thus he says, "likewise in the fourth. However, as for those who [interpret] "pleasant abiding" as pleasure (*sukha*)...

They say, "It has been grasped. According to their opinion, because it exists in a state of tranquility (*santavutti*), equanimity (*upekkhā*) is also spoken of as "happiness" (*sukha*) in the fourth jhāna;
thus it should be understood that it was stated in that way. Having cited the various methods of teaching found in this very *Dīghanikāya*, the passage beginning with "In these...
is stated here in order to determine the method of teaching presented in this context. *Suddha...* etc.
"Explained" means that without explaining the higher paths, only the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā) was explained.
"By four... explained" means that after explaining the jhānas by way of their being the basis for insight, the four paths preceded by insight were subsequently explained.
"The attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) consisting of the fourth jhāna was explained" refers to the attainments of fruition consisting of the first jhāna and so forth.
Without mentioning [the other jhānas], only the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) belonging to the fourth jhāna was spoken of. Regarding the phrase "having made *pīti* a synonym for [joy]":

since the two types of *pīti* do not arise within a single moment of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), it is said that "gladness" (*pāmojja*) is made a synonym for *pīti*, meaning that both are treated as non-distinct.
Because joy and bliss have not been abandoned, it is called "a blissful abiding" (*sukho vihāro*), and because it is preeminent—
Because a pleasant abiding has been grasped, it is said: "The attainment of fruition belonging to the second jhāna is what is meant.
Granted that joy and happiness are also found in the first jhāna, they are not peaceful and sublime there due to the agitation caused by applied and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra);
however, here only those that are peaceful and sublime are intended. Therefore, the attainment of fruition belongs specifically to the second jhāna.
It should be understood that [these] have been included, but they do not belong to the first jhāna.
432–437. "The sense of manifestation" (vibhāvanattha) means the sense of making clear, the sense of defining by way of its own nature, as in such passages as:
"The ascetic Gotama does not pay homage to aged brahmins... nor does he rise for them, nor does he invite them to a seat," and so forth. Therefore, he said:
“This is that,” and so forth. Having thus clarified and revealed it by its specific characteristics, saying, “This acquisition of a self (*attapaṭilābha*) is that very one”:

for here, the Blessed One refers to the acquisition of a self previously mentioned with the word “this” (*ayam*), because it is present before his eyes; whereas he refers to it with the word “that” (*so*), because it was being asked about by others as something not present before them.

Regarding the phrase “I do not speak of it thus,” the word “it” (*taṃ*)— *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Pali commentary (likely the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*). The translation reflects the technical exegetical style.*

The acquisition of a gross self. Regarding "possessing a foundation" (*sappāṭihīraka*): here the meaning should be understood according to the method explained previously. For this is the distinction:
that which provides a rebuttal to the words of others who challenge it, being speech that has something superior to it, is "possessing a foundation.
"Empty" (*tuccha*) means false and unreal. "That" (*so*) refers to the mind-made or formless acquisition of a self. "That very same" (*seva*) refers to that very gross [acquisition].
"Acquisition of self. At that time it is real means that at that present time it exists.
"He concludes with the very term 'acquisition of self'" means he finishes with that same expression;
he does not, however, extract the designation from its own form and show it by saying, "It goes by the name 'acquisition of self.'"
The intention [is as follows]. Here, "dhammas" refers to form and so forth; thus, in this world, only form, feeling, and the rest are dhammas possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"This is a mere designation of name" means that, based upon the five aggregates beginning with form, this "acquisition of a self" is a mere conceptual designation (*paññatti*) consisting of a name.

"Expressions such as these" refers to conventional expressions such as "the gross acquisition of a self. "By way of a designation consisting of a name" means by way of a mere designation that has become a name.
“It is reckoned as ‘the acquisition of a self’”— this is for the purpose of handing over [the teaching].
And having spoken thus— meaning, having stated the point that this "acquisition of a self" is a mere designation based upon form and so forth by means of the passage beginning with “At whatever time,
O Citta,” etc.— he asked a counter-question in the manner that others might ask.
Having asked about the methods according to the divisions of time: "for the purpose of training" means for the sake of training by way of making known the meaning as it was asked.
"Those phenomena which were past" refers to the phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which served as the basis for the acquisition of pastness during the past period;
they do not exist now because they have ceased. For that very reason, they have come to be reckoned as "they were."
Therefore, because clinging is obtained only at a past time, "that too" refers to my acquisition of a self characterized by that clinging.
"At that very time" means at the past time itself. "It was real" means it existed as if it were present and actual.

"Of future and present [phenomena]" refers to those phenomena such as form, which serve as the basis for clinging, in both the future and the present. "Because of its non-existence then" means at that [future] time...

In the past time, they were non-existent because they did not exist. The acquisition of a self (*attapaṭilābha*)—whether future or present—which would have been based upon them, was in that past time vain, empty, false, and non-existent; this is the meaning.

"In its sense" means in its sense as a designation (*paññatti*). "Merely a name" means merely a conventional appellation (*samaññā*). Because it is not found in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), one asserts the acquisition of a self.

“‘The same method applies’ means: those future phenomena that do not exist at present, but are reckoned as ‘will come to be,’ for that reason my acquisition of self (attapaṭilābha) will also be real at that very time.
However, because past and present phenomena are non-existent at that time, in that moment it is said: ‘The past is vain; the present is vain. Thus [it is said].

In actual fact, it claims to be the acquisition of a self merely by name. Those phenomena which exist now have attained the designation "they exist" at this present time; therefore, this acquisition of a self of mine is now real.
However, because past and future phenomena do not exist at this moment, [the claim] "the past is vain, the future is vain" is thus [denied] in actual fact.
"He claims the acquisition of a self is a mere name"—this is what he indicates by way of extension. 439–443.
*Saṃsandituṃ* means to bring together. *Gavā* means from the cow. *Tattha* refers to the five products of the cow, such as milk and so forth.
"At the time when there is milk" means at whatever time, depending upon a particular kind of clinging designated as the primary elements and the derived matter (*bhūta-upādāya*).

It is a designation for milk. It does not [arise] from that... because when the primary and derived matter (bhūtupādāyarūpa) which is the basis for the designation "milk" ceases, there is no taking up of the designation "curd" and so forth;
for these worldly conventions have fixed bases. Therefore he said, “depending on those phenomena,” and so on.
It is called a *saṅkhā* because by means of it one calculates (*saṅkhāyati*) or speaks; having extracted the self (*atta*), they are uttered.
They say it is *nirutti* because beings come (*eti*) by means of it. It is called *nāma* because beings incline toward that meaning by means of it;

likewise, it is called *vohāra* because they express themselves by means of it—it is simply a designation (*paññatti*). With the words "At whatever time," etc., he extends the method stated regarding milk to curd and so forth, indicating that "this same method applies everywhere."

"Merely by way of approval" means that, just as one approves of the conventional designations handed down through tradition in the world regarding such specific derived and primary material forms— as in "this is milk," "this is curd," and so on— so too,

by depending upon the aggregate of the form-aggregate and the others as distinguished by their specific conditions, one speaks of "the gross acquisition of a self" and "the mind-made acquisition of a self."
And it is said that [terms] such as "formless acquisition of self" are merely ways of assenting in various ways;
there is nothing else existing in the ultimate sense apart from clinging that is distinct from them. "Merely linguistic" means they are merely the means for grasping verbal expression.

For, after the initial grasping of the sound—such as in the phrase "a being, contact," and so on—it is precisely by way of grasping the designation (paññatti) permeated by that sound that [the meaning is understood].
This is the comprehension of its meaning. And so it has been said:
"First, the sound is heard by the ear; then, it is grasped by the second consciousness;
the name is apprehended by the third mind; and the meaning is understood by the fourth consciousness" (as stated in the *Paccayasaṅgahavibhāga* section of the *Maṇisāramañjusā-ṭīkā*).

“Merely paths of speech” is a synonym for that very same term. For etymological derivation (*niruttī*) itself is the path of speech in the sense of being the cause for others who follow along with one's views.
“Merely conventional designations” means merely various kinds of conventional usage. “Merely nominal concepts” is another way of saying the same thing;
the meaning is: merely the designation by this or that name. “All this” refers to what is called “the acquisition of a self.”

Whether it be called a "being" (*satta*) or a "person" (*puggala*), all of this is merely conventional designation (*vohāramattaka*). Why? Because it is not to be found in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*);
thus he said "because" and so forth to demonstrate this. "Empty" (*suñña*) means secluded from the ultimate sense.
Anticipating the objection, "If that is so, why is this spoken of even by the Buddhas? he said "But for the Buddhas... and so forth.
Discourse on conventional designation is the speaking of conventional usage (*sammuti-vohāra*).

Discourse on the ultimate truth is the speaking of phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-dhamma*) as the ultimate truth (*paramattha*). Because it is discourse based upon the ultimate truth, discourse concerning impermanence and so forth is also called "discourse on the ultimate truth.
For it is only a phenomenon of the ultimate truth that is described as "impermanent" and "suffering," not a phenomenon of conventional designation.
“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self;
and Nibbāna and designations (paññatti) are non-self’—according to this statement, it is called ‘non-self.
However, the designation of the aggregates and so forth is based on ultimate reality, just like a designation that corresponds to its object.”

Furthermore, it is more proximate and not remote like the *Puggalapaññatti* and other such works; therefore, even the discourse on the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth is called "discourse on the ultimate" (*paramatthakathā*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that by means of the aggregates and so forth, only those phenomena whose intrinsic nature consists of the appropriation of those [aggregates] are actually included.

But is it not the case that even phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) enter into the teaching only through the door of conventional designation (*sammuti*), and not through the door of the ultimate? Therefore, all [of them]...
Could it be that the teaching (desanā) is merely conventional discourse (sammutikathā)?

No, this should not be said, because the distinction of discourse is intended here by way of the distinction of the phenomena (dhamma), and a word does not manifest its meaning without some basis for its occurrence (pavattinimitta).
Why, then, does the discourse of the Buddhas proceed in these two ways? To answer this inquiry, he proceeds to explain the underlying cause.

“Regarding that, ‘he who’ and so forth was said. He is able to understand the meaning, to penetrate the Four Truths, to emerge from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and to seize the victory known as Arahatship.

Since the penetration of the Truths occurs only through discourse on the ultimate sense (*paramattha-kathā*), and since discourse on the Noble Truths is the culmination of the teaching, therefore, with reference to the individuals to be trained, [the Buddha] first [gave] discourse on conventional designation (*sammuti-kathā*).
Even when speaking, the Blessed One speaks only of the ultimate meaning (paramattha) from beginning to end; thus he says, “Of that,” and so forth.
For by saying, “From the very beginning he speaks of conventional discourse (sammutikathā),” he indicates that he also speaks of ultimate discourse thereafter;

however, since he does not say “he speaks from the very beginning” in the other case, it applies to all instances. By the words “In that way,” etc., [the text] refers to the presentation of the two types of discourse.
He clarifies another method. "Having awakened" means having made known the matter to be taught in such and such a way according to the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

By this, however, he shows this point: in some cases there is a discourse on the ultimate truth (*paramattha*) preceded by a discourse on conventional truth (*sammuti*), depending on the inclination of the person;
in other cases, there is a discourse on conventional truth preceded by a discourse on the ultimate truth. Thus [it is] for one who is skilled in training those to be disciplined.
The teaching proceeds in such and such a way according to the disposition of those to be trained by the Teacher.

In all instances, however, the Blessed One follows conventional designation (*sammuti*) without ever abandoning the nature of reality (*dhammatā*), and he elucidates the nature of reality without relinquishing conventional designation;
therein lie neither dogmatic adherence nor excessive mental proliferation. For this was said by the Blessed One: "The local dialect..."
"One should not adhere [to them], nor should one overstep conventional designation.
Now, the first discussion on conventional designations is generally the custom of the Buddhas for the sake of those to be trained;
showing this along with its reason, he said, "But by nature," and so forth. "Rough modes" refers to the way those to be trained do not fully comprehend [the teaching].

[They are] like the coarse. But surely, since what is called "conventional" (*sammuti*) does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), it is non-existent; how then do the Buddhas speak of it? To this it was said:

“Even when speaking conventional discourse,” and so forth. “It is indeed true” means it is exactly as it is. “It is indeed its own nature” means that by way of its conventional state, it has that very nature.
Therefore he said: “It is not false. However, regarding the status of being true and so forth in the case of ultimate reality:
There is simply nothing more to be said.

But what is the distinction between these conventional and ultimate phenomena? That which, when broken or when its parts are analytically separated by the intellect, no longer evokes that same designation—such as the various types of jars, cloths, and so forth—is conventional; the opposite of that is the ultimate. Not...
For this method is applicable to things whose intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) consists of hard contact and so forth.
Even so, because conventional designation (*sammuti*) and the true intrinsic nature are both real according to the stated method, he said: "He proclaimed two truths," and so on.

In that context, "he proclaimed two truths" means that, like a teacher skilled in various regions, languages, and the exegesis of the meaning of the three Vedas, [the Buddha] was skilled in the various kinds of conventional and ultimate truth.
The meaning is that the Blessed One taught only two truths, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
He demonstrates these by their nature and by their number with the words: "The conventional (*sammuti*) and the ultimate (*paramattha*); a third is not found.

"The best among speakers" means the most excellent of all who speak. Conventional truth (*sammuti*) is established merely through worldly convention. Ultimate truth (*paramattha*) is supreme, highest, and non-erroneous.
The ultimate reality (*paramattha*) is the nature of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtasabhāva*).
Now, in order to demonstrate their true nature along with its cause, the verse beginning with “conventional speech” (*saṅketavacana*) was spoken.
Because it is the cause for worldly convention, conventional speech is true; and because it is the actual characteristic of phenomena (*dhamma*), [the ultimate is true].
Therefore, the construction is: "The word for the ultimate meaning (paramattha) is truth.

For the phrase "the cause of worldly convention" is a demonstration of the reason why conventional language possesses the status of truth; the meaning is that worldly-established convention is the cause for the non-deceptiveness of conventional language.
Thus it is said that conventional language is truth because of its lack of deception. [And] "the actual characteristic of phenomena (dhammānaṃ bhūtalakkhaṇaṃ)."
And this is the demonstration of the reason for the ultimate reality (*paramattha*) of the word "truth" (*sacca*).
The meaning is that it is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), the ground (*aṅgana*), and the means of making known (*ñāpana*) of the true, non-erroneous intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.

The intention is that the word "ultimate" (*paramattha*) is "truth" because it functions by way of being non-deceptive according to reality. However, in the commentary on the *Anaṅgaṇa-sutta*, the Master himself [uses] an ablative expression...
Having indicated the word *pada*, it is said: “Because they proceed by depending on worldly convention (*lokasamañña*), they are ‘causes of worldly designation’ (*lokasammutikāraṇa*).

‘Of phenomena’ (*dhammānaṃ*) means of phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*). Because they proceed by depending on the actual intrinsic nature as it truly is, they are ‘causes of reality’ (*bhūtakāraṇa*).
However, elsewhere—
“Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, who is skilled in conventional usage, no false speech arises when he employs conventional designations.
This verse is also seen as one that elucidates his qualities. In this context, “therefore” refers to the twofold nature of truth, [namely] the truth of conventional designation...

Or [it is] from the perspective of conventional reality (*saccabhāvato*). "For one who employs conventional designation" means that for one who speaks the common worldly usage such as "person," "being," and so forth, no false speech (*musāvāda*) arises;
this is the meaning. Furthermore, "for eight reasons the Blessed One speaks of the person:

to illustrate moral shame (*hirotappa*) and dread of blame; to illustrate that one is the owner of one’s own karma (*kammassakatā*); to illustrate individual personal effort (*paccattapurisakāra*); to illustrate the immediate retribution of deeds (*ānantariya*)."

One should also state here, bringing forward the reasons given in various places such as: "for the purpose of illuminating the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), for the purpose of illuminating past lives (pubbenivāsa), for the purpose of illuminating the purification of offerings (dakkhiṇāvisuddhi), and for the purpose of not abandoning worldly convention (lokasammuti).
Even if the Tathāgata remains having perfectly awakened to the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca), [he does not abandon worldly convention]...
He speaks only by taking conventional truth (sammutisacca) as his basis; thus, if one asks, "In what way does he differ from the ordinary people of the world?

it is said, "Go," and so forth—this is the connection in the Pāḷi. This is what is meant: the ordinary people of the world, because they have not abandoned their misconceptions (parāmāsa), speak while grasping [things] with the thought, "This is mine," and so on.
The Tathāgata, however, because he has completely abandoned all misconceptions, speaks without grasping at all.
Because a worldly matter cannot be easily understood by the world without the conventional designations of the world, he expresses it through them.
And by expressing it in this way, through the excellence of his teaching, he establishes the beings to be trained in the ultimate truth.
"Having turned back from the teaching" refers to the discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*) associated with the aforementioned adherence to views.
"Having turned back and having separated [them]. "He brought it to completion by means of the pinnacle of Arahantship":

by this phrase, through the description of the abandonment of the misapprehensions of craving and conceit, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle known as Arahantship, which abandons those [misapprehensions].
As for that which has not been analyzed here in terms of meaning, it is indeed easy to understand.
Thus ends the Elucidation of the Obscure Points in the Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, from the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*.

This work illuminates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend; it generates a pure and vast clarity of wisdom; and it is named the *Sādhuvilāsinī* (the Delight of the Virtuous) because it reveals the hidden meaning.
The Commentary on the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta is finished.
10. Commentary on the Subha Sutta:
Commentary on the Story of the Young Brahmin Subha 444.
Having thus explained the Poṭṭhapāda Sutta, now, in explaining the Subha Sutta in due order:

In order to clarify that the occasion for the commentary has been reached, or to show that the discourse recited immediately after the *Poṭṭhapāda-sutta* is indeed the *Subha-sutta*, he said: "Thus have I heard... at Sāvatthī: the Subha-sutta.
By the phrase "not long after his final Nibbāna" (*aciraṃ parinibbute*), he shows that [the word] was stated with the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika-lopa*) as "acira-parinibbute."
As it is said in the *Poṭṭhapāda Sutta*: "That speech turns out to be without foundation.
Or, [the term] *aciraparinibbuto* means "one who has recently attained final Nibbāna," just as one says "recently departed" or "one month old.
However, this was stated merely to indicate the sense. And by the phrase *aciraparinibbute*, there is a negation of the long duration of the Teacher’s state of having attained final Nibbāna.
The proximity [of the time] has been shown, but the specific limit of the duration was not; therefore, in order to show that, he said, "from the Parinibbāna," and so forth.
The phrase "within a month" refers to the period from the full moon of Visākha up to the full moon of Jeṭṭha.
By the word *matte* (within), he indicates that this duration is not quite complete. His residence was the village known as Tudigāma.
“Of him” refers to Todeyya. Since he, like Soṇadaṇḍa, presided over Campā, and like Kūṭadanta, over Khāṇumata, it is said:
“on account of his lordship,” meaning because of his status as a master.
For he too was the brahmin chaplain to King Pasenadi of Kosala. “He spoke even to his son” means that he spoke while instructing the young brahmin Subha.
"Eye-ointments" (*añjanāni*) refers to ointments ground for the purpose of applying them to the eyes.

"Ant-hills" (*vammikānaṃ*) is connected with "having seen a heap," meaning a collection of ant-hills brought together by insects. "Honey" (*madhūnaṃ*) refers to honey from bees. "Gathering" (*samāhāraṃ*) means a store of nectar.
A wise person lives at home because even when wealth is being consumed little by little, it eventually exhausts; even when [consumed] little by little...

And as it is being accumulated, it increases; therefore, having seen with wisdom this aforementioned threefold analogy, a person of discernment, without doing anything else, should live the household life and attend to domestic affairs while generating only income. Thus he points out the practice taught by greed.
Having been trained only in non-giving, and because of being overcome by greed due to that very training, he became a dog in that same house.
He was reborn. For one who is a slave to greed, a miserable destination is to be expected;

the meaning here should be understood according to the method stated in the passage: “He was reborn as a yakkha named Janavasabha. Because of his previous familiarity, he felt great affection [for him].
For it is said: “On account of former association,” and so forth. When he had gone out means when he had gone outside on some business. [He saw] the young man Subha.
Desiring to show favor, the Blessed One entered for alms all alone. "Bhukkāra" refers to the making of the sound "bhu-bhū" by a dog.
[The phrase] "Bho bho" was used as a form of address to insult him, on account of that insult. For it is said: "He is called a 'bhovādin' (one who says 'bho') if he possesses anything.
But was it not stated earlier that, having been taught only non-giving, he became a dog?
He said, "I have been reborn. But why does he say here, "In the past as well, having been insulted with 'Ho! Ho!', I was born as a dog"?

It is because that particular rebirth is a fruit common to both [types of karma]. For it should be understood that a fruit of merit (ānisamsa-phala) arises even from a common action, unlike a fruit of karmic maturation (vipāka-phala), which arises from a single specific action alone.
"You will go to Avīci, for you have made room [for yourself]."
Because it was impossible to ward off the result of that kamma. [The brahmin] became remorseful, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama knows me.
"Between the hearths" means between the cooking stoves. "Him" refers to the dog.
"That occurrence" refers to the reason already stated by the Blessed One. This was said with reference to not abandoning his status as a brahmin.
Likewise, praising his father, he said, "He was reborn in the Brahma-world. "Spoken from the mouth" means that which has arisen spontaneously from one's own eloquence.
"He asked about that occurrence" means he asked, "Master Gotama, I have heard it said that my father was reborn as a dog;
is this true or not? He spoke exactly in that manner.
Having spoken exactly as was previously said regarding the dog, [he did so] for the sake of non-deception—that is, for the sake of making it true;
what is meant is that it was for the purpose of demonstrating his own reliability by means of the non-deception of the statement, “The Brahmin Todeyya was reborn as a dog.
“With little water” means prepared with a small amount of water. “Honeyed milk-rice” means sweet-tasting, mixed with honey.
Or [he gave] milk-rice. He acted accordingly, just as spoken by the Blessed One. Regarding the statement, "He showed everything":
through the power of the Buddha, that dog led him [to the place] and showed it all; it was not through the power of remembering past births (*jātissara*).

However, his barking upon seeing the Blessed One was due to the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) established in a previous birth—thus it was stated by the Teacher. Furthermore, in the *Cūḷakammavibhaṅgasutta-ṭīkā* within the *Uparipaṇṇāsa*:

“The dog, thinking ‘I am known by him,’ wept, then making the sound ‘hum hum,’ went to the place where the treasure was hidden, dug at the earth with its paw, and gave a sign”—this describes the manner of one who remembers past births; it should be accepted after investigation.
“Such a thing as this—namely, the intermediate rebirth-linking as a dog concealed by existence—is made manifest to the ascetic Gotama.”
“Surely he is omniscient,” thinking thus with a mind full of confidence toward the Blessed One. It is said that this man was a student of the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavijjā*).
Therefore, it occurred to him: “Having prepared this gift of the Dhamma, I shall ask the ascetic Gotama a question.
Then, having formulated fourteen questions, he asked the Blessed One. For this reason it is said: “having asked fourteen questions.”
In that regard, he asks fourteen questions: “For, Master Gotama, we see humans who are short-lived and those who are long-lived;
we see those with many ailments and those with few ailments; the ugly and the beautiful; those of little influence and those of great influence;
those of little wealth and those of great wealth; those born into low families and those born into high families; we see those who are witless and those who are wise. Who indeed...?”
“Sir Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why among those who are human beings, being born as humans, differences in inferiority and superiority are seen?
These are the fourteen questions contained in the Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta.
At the conclusion of the answer—both in brief and in detail—beginning with, “Young man, beings are owners of their karma, heirs to their karma,” [the interlocutor addressed] the Blessed One.
He had gone for refuge. His name was Subha because of his physical beauty. He is called a "young man" (māṇava), even at an advanced age, by way of conventional usage.
He was staying there for the time being after coming from his own village of Tudigāma;
for that very reason, it is said in the text, "on some business."
445. By the phrase, “I have one doubt,” he shows that the question about to be asked below had already been prepared by him.
He says “young man” (*māṇavaka*) to indicate a youth, since the word *ka-* occurs in the sense of "small" in such expressions as “only one son” (*ekaputtaka*) or “beloved son” (*piyaputtaka*).
“Dissimilar feeling” (*visabhāgavedanā*) refers to painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*), for it is...
It is called "dissimilar feeling" (*visabhāgavedanā*) because it is the opposite of the pleasant feeling that arises in a personal existence produced by wholesome karma;
and it is called "affliction" (*ābādha*) because it oppresses and torments the body with intensity. As to what kind of feeling it is, he says:
"That which, in one part," and so forth. "Having arisen in one part" means that although it has manifested in a single part of the body, it acts in such a way as to prevent recovery.
"He grasps it as if binding it with an iron band" shows that a powerful disease is called an *ābādha*.
"One who makes life difficult" brings about an unhappy existence; this shows that a weak, minor disease is called an *ātaṅka*.
"Rising" (*uṭṭhāna*) refers to rising from lying down or sitting; by this, he means the turning of the body here and there in whatever manner necessary.
He speaks. "Heavy" means burdensome and incapable of accomplishing what needs to be done. The connection is that there is no strength in the body of one who is ill.

And here, by the term "lightness," the absence of illness is inquired after. Although the absence of an uncomfortable dwelling was already inquired after with the four preceding terms, he now asks again about the state of a comfortable dwelling; therefore, the comfortable dwelling here is distinguished as being superior.

It is understood that [the Buddha] asked. For even when there is no word expressing the sense of intensity (*atisaya*), the sense of intensity is indeed obtained through the implication of the meaning, just as in the expression, "A maiden should be given to one who is handsome.

Therefore, he said, "from the place of going," and so forth. He shows the distinction between these two by saying, "Then to her," etc., indicating that the former is the statement of the command, whereas this [latter] is the demonstration of the manner in which she was to be questioned.
447. "Time" (kāla) means the appropriate and opportune moment for approaching; "occasion" (samaya) means the convergence of the necessary conditions for that very act.
In terms of its actual meaning, however, this consists of both the physical strength of the body suited for it and the absence of obstacles related to those conditions.
"Grasping" (upādāna) refers to the apprehension and discernment of these by means of knowledge; thus he said, "by wisdom," and so forth. [He thought: "Tomorrow will be the time for going."
By this [phrase], he shows the time; and by the words beginning with “in the body,” he shows the occasion in its specific form. “He will pervade” means he will remain by way of pervading. 448.
“In the country of Cetī” (Cetiyaraṭṭhe) means in the country of Cetī. For the word was spoken thus by extending it with the letter *ya*. Some also say:
“It is a separate, distinct country altogether from the country of Cetī. Because death, for such as the Ten-Powered Ones, is...

"It occurs solely by the power of disease; therefore, there is a question regarding the nature of that disease by which it was born, a question regarding its cause, a question regarding the mental anguish caused by death, the universality of that anguish throughout the world, and likewise the inevitability of death.
In this way, he spoke a friendly discourse connected with death.
It should be understood that the passage beginning with “O Ānanda” was spoken in order to demonstrate this. Specifically, by the words “What is his name? and so forth, he asks about the disease;

by “Has the Blessed One eaten? he asks about the cause; by “Moreover,” and so forth, he expresses his mental anguish; by “The Teacher indeed,” and so forth, he shows that the Teacher is common to all the world;
and by “Now there is but one,” and so forth, he demonstrates the irremediability of death.

"Mahājānī" means a great loss. "Yattha" (where/in which) should be construed with such phrases as: "By what cause has he attained final Nibbāna? Who else now shall be released from death? and so forth.
The word "idāni" (now) is used merely as a conventional expression referring to one's own mental attention.
"Lajjissati" means it will be like a sense of shame; the meaning is that it will be evident. "Food and sustenance appropriate to the medicine drunk."
“It was practiced by the ancients,” he said, adding “having drunk... having given.
The word “having been” (*hutvā*) is a grammatical supplement (*pāṭhaseso*), used as a qualification for the state of being one who dwells in proximity.
He was not like Māra the Evil One, seeking a vulnerability, nor like Uttara the student, whose intention was to test [him]; rather, indeed, he was an attendant who dwelt in his presence.
For it qualifies [the subject]. "Not seeking faults" means not seeking flaws. "In those states" refers to the means of liberation, the states leading to deliverance (*niyyānika-dhamma*).
"They endure" means they currently exist; the sense is that they are active. 449.
In terms of meaning, because of the application of words, the three Piṭakas—characterized by the arrangement of words—are [defined] by their meanings which constitute the essence of those [states].
It is said that they are "comprised within the three aggregates of the Dhamma" by virtue of the three aggregates beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
Regarding the phrase "spoken in brief," it was spoken in summary both in terms of enumeration—as "of the three aggregates, young man"—and in terms of their general nature.
The question, "Of which three? is indeed a question intended to reveal what has not yet been seen.
This is not a question out of a desire to speak; for this question belongs to the young man alone, not to the Elder. Thus he said, "The young man," and so forth.
In other places, however, in such instances, only a question out of a desire to speak is seen, not a question intended to reveal what has not been seen.
But here in the commentary it is stated thus; this should be understood according to the authority of the commentary. At that time...

Indeed, having made the currently existing [text] their direct authority, they also included the Aṭṭhakathā in the compilation. However, in the absence of a formal inquiry out of a desire to speak, it would be considered the word of the Elder himself.
[End of] the Commentary on the Aggregate of Virtue (Sīlakkhandha).
Regarding the phrase *sīlakkhandhassāti*: here, the word *iti*—which normally functions as a particle indicating a change in the meaning of the preceding term—is elided.

Just as there is a description of the meaning (*atthaniddesa*), there is likewise a description of the sound (*saddaniddesa*). Furthermore, the word *iti*, according to its literal pronunciation, has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or "manner" (*pakāra*).
Therefore, it should be understood that by this [use of *iti*], the reading "of the noble aggregate of concentration... [etc. ...he established" is included. Hence it was said: [the aforementioned].

“In those being shown”: the meaning is, “in those three aggregates being shown by way of enumeration. “In the very manner spoken by the Blessed One” means in the very manner taught in the *Sāmaññaphala* and other discourses; by this it should be understood that he demonstrates the fact that this sutta was spoken by the Buddha.
“In the Dispensation, it is not merely virtue that is the essence” means that in the Blessed One’s Dispensation, which has the Noble Path as its essence, [virtue is] as it has been shown.
Virtue alone is not the core, because it serves as the outer bark for a great tree that possesses a core.
For the particle *eva* is used in an inappropriate sense here and should not be construed with its proper place [in the phrase "virtue alone"]. If this is so, why is it included here? He says:
"merely," and so forth. It is merely a basis for one desiring to attain the higher human states such as jhāna, etc., but not for one who is not established therein.
Because these [other qualities] are impossible for them. For it is said: "A wise man, established in virtue," and so forth.

Alternatively, it is not as if virtue alone is the essence in the Dispensation; indeed, while supramundane virtue—comprising the virtues of the path and its fruits—is certainly an essence in this Dispensation, nevertheless, it is not only the aggregate of virtue that is the essence, but also the aggregate of concentration and the aggregate of wisdom.
"It is the essence indeed" (*sāro eva*): here, the meaning should be understood according to the word *eva* as it is employed; however, the former meaning alone is more appropriate.
For it has been stated: "Beyond this," and so forth. "Another [aggregate] should also be performed": this refers to the remaining two aggregates.
This concludes the commentary on the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).
454. Why, then, did the Elder, although questioned here regarding the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*), answer concerning the restraint of the faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) and so forth?

To show that such an objection as—"In that case, is he not answering one thing when asked another, like one who, being asked about a mango tree, answers about a breadfruit tree?"—has no place here, he said: "And how... [etc.]... he began. By this, it is shown here that...
This shows that even the restraint of the faculties and so forth are taught as belonging to the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*) by virtue of their being supportive to concentration.
The connection is: "those [factors] which are the restraint of the faculties and so forth.

Having considered that the occasion for the teaching on the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) follows immediately after the teaching on the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), only the fine-material jhānas have been presented here, and not the immaterial jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*). These [jhānas] are the foundation for the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere.

Indeed, even the superknowledges (abhiññā) together with their adjuncts [are included]. However, since worldly superknowledges do not succeed unless they are accomplished through the fourteenfold taming of the mind within the eight attainments (samāpatti), therefore, when the superknowledges are being taught, the formless jhānas are also necessarily taught because they are not separate from them.
Thus he said: "But they should be illustrated by bringing [the jhānas] in," according to the method already stated.
The meaning is that after they have been taught, they must be explained by the commentators.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the phrase "by means of the fourth jhāna," and so forth, was stated in order to show that the formless (arūpa) jhānas are also included by the very expression "he dwells having attained the fourth jhāna.
For it is precisely the fourth jhāna, when it proceeds by way of the cultivation of dispassion toward the fine-material (rūpa), that is called "formless jhāna."

471–480. Regarding the phrase "not by mere one-pointedness of mind" (*na cittekaggatāmattakena eva*), the meaning of the word *eva* should be understood here in accordance with the method explained below;
it signifies that [one-pointedness] is not the sole factor. However, because mundane concentration (*lokiya-samādhi*) is intended here, it is stated:
"There is no... [omission] ...there is. In the expression "the noble aggregate of concentration" (*ariyo samādhikkhandho*), the term *ariya* is used merely as a synonym for "pure" (*suddha*).
This is not a supramundane exposition. And just as it is here, so it is also in the passage beginning with "the noble aggregate of virtue.

The word "from this" means from the aggregate of wisdom; and since that [wisdom] is, in its highest sense, included within the fruit of Arahantship, he says "culminating in Arahantship," and so forth.

For even without the mundane higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), once Arahantship is attained, it can be said that "there is nothing further to be done"—which is the purpose for which [these qualities were taught] by the Blessed One.
The holy life is lived for the sake of its accomplishment. Here, moreover, even the mundane higher knowledges (*lokīyābhiññā*) are included. The rest here is easy to understand.

Thus ends the elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Subha Sutta, within the *Līnatthappakāsinī*—the Elucidator of the Hidden Meaning—of the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya*, which illuminates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend, and which generates the clarity of vast and stainless wisdom, and is named the *Sādhuvilāsinī*.
The commentary on the Subha Sutta is finished.
11. Commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta:
The narrative concerning the householder’s son Kevaṭṭa.
481. Having thus commented upon the Subha-sutta, he now, while commenting upon the Kevaṭṭa-sutta, says: “Thus have I heard...

at Nāḷandā: the Kevaṭṭa-sutta,” in order to clarify that it has reached its proper place in the sequence of the commentary, or to show that the sutta recited immediately after the Subha-sutta is indeed the Kevaṭṭa-sutta. [The word] “pāvārikassa” means...
Of the merchant named so-and-so. "In the mango grove" means in a nearby park abounding in mango trees.

It is said that after that merchant had prepared for the Blessed One a fragrant hut (*gandhakuṭi*) suitable for him, as well as night-quarters, day-quarters, huts, pavilions, and so forth for the community of monks, he enclosed it with a wall and provided it with gate-towers, and [dedicated it] to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha.
He handed it over; however, by its former designation, this monastery is called "Pāvārika-ambavana.
"Kevaṭṭa" is merely a name. Some say it was so called because it was well-guarded by fishermen (kevaṭṭa), or because he attained full enlightenment in their presence.
Regarding the phrase "of the householder’s son": although at that time he stood in the position of a householder, because his father had recently passed away...
By his former designation, he was addressed simply as “the son of a householder. Therefore, it says “a wealthy householder” (*gahapati-mahāsāla*);

the meaning is that he is a householder who possesses great substance (*mahāsāra*) due to his great wealth. However, by changing the letter *ra* to *la*, it is called “mahāsāla,” just as in the word “*palibuddho*,” which means one who is confident and trusting, being endowed with faith in the Three Jewels by way of the faith of a common person.
"Devoted to the Triple Gem for that very reason": either he is faithful through conviction in karma and its fruit, or he is devoted due to an abundance of serene confidence in the Triple Gem.
"Precisely because of his preponderance of faith" is a statement of the cause for such a thought; for one who has an excess of faith becomes like one who has gone mad.
"Prosperous" means truly successful, having reached fullness through the attainment of wealth and status, complete, and crowded with many [possessions].
With reference to the meaning "humans are here," it was said, "with the shoulder-peak," and so forth.

"Come, monk, every half-month, every month, or every year, perform a miracle of psychic power for the sake of inspiring confidence in humans"—this very command to a single monk is what is meant by "injunction";
and that is called "placing him in that position. Therefore he said, "in another place..."

"Let them set it aside. "Of those superior to human beings" (*uttarimanussānaṃ*) means of the supreme persons who are higher than ordinary humans—the Buddhas and others, the meditators, and the Noble Ones (*ariya*).

"According to the nature of things" (*dhammatoti*) means according to the nature of attainment; the meaning is "according to the nature of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the paths (*magga*), and the fruits (*phala*).
This is an ablative expression used for selection (*niddhāraṇa*), for it selects the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) from among those [attainments]. Thus...
Having joined the word *uttari* with the word *manussasaddena* into a single compound, and now making it a separate word to be connected with the word *pāṭihāriya*, he said:
“Or, from what is reckoned as the ten wholesome [paths of action],” and so forth. *Manussadhammatoti*: from the natural human condition (*pakati-manussadhamma*).
*Pajjalitapadīpoti*: a burning lamp. *Telasnehan’ti*: the pouring of oil. *Rājagahaseṭṭhivatthusminti*: in the case of the merchant of Rājagaha.
Regarding the occasion of the merchant of Rājagaha’s gift of sandalwood leaves:
he laid down this training rule, saying, "Monks, a superhuman state or a miracle of psychic power must not be displayed to laypeople. Whoever should display one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Thus he laid down this training rule prohibiting the miracle of transformation.
482. By the phrase "not by the destruction of qualities," he shows that this was said with reference to not falling away from the perfection of qualities.
Therefore he says, "the breaking of virtue," and so forth. "There is no one who dares" means there is no one who ventures [to transgress] in a place where it has been forbidden.
Furthermore, in order to show that "this person, however, dares" for this other reason, he says, "But this," and so forth.
It has been said. Since he is trustworthy, the construction is: "therefore, having increased his trust.
And "having increased" means having expanded, that is, having made it manifest and clear.
This concludes the commentary on the miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*).
483–4. "Dangers" means faults (*ādīnava*). To explain how it was performed by him and where it arose, he says, "It is said that there...
and so forth. "By one" refers specifically to the seer named Gandhāra; for it is in this way that what precedes and follows cohere. This *vijjā* (knowledge) called Gandhārī is twofold:
the Lesser Gandhārī (*cūḷagandhārī*) and the Greater Gandhārī (*mahāgandhārī*). Among these, the Lesser Gandhārī [is practiced] from three years...
Now, the knowledge that knows the place of rebirth for deceased beings is *vijjā*. In this regard, the story of Vaṅgīsa is the supporting evidence.
The knowledge of his [rebirth] as "Mahāgandhārī" is also [a form of *vijjā*], as is the knowledge that accomplishes the task of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*).
For this [knowledge] generally accomplishes the function of the supernormal powers. It is said that the person who accomplishes that *vijjā* [must be] in such a location...
And having recited a mantra at the proper time, he displays himself in many ways; he displays himself as an elephant and so forth, or becomes invisible;
he creates pillars of fire and pillars of water, and displays himself even in the sky—all this should be regarded as being like a magician’s trick (*indajāla*).
*Aṭṭo* means one who is pained and afflicted; therefore he said, "oppressed" (*pīḷito*).
Commentary on the Miracle of Declaration (Ādesanāpāṭihāriya) 485.
Granted, the term "mental factor" (*cetasika*) is a general designation for those things connected with the mind and associated with consciousness;
yet, when the general is grasped, a specific state of consciousness is thereby indicated. For a general description comes to rest upon a particular instance.
