Therefore, showing the intended meaning of the term "mental factor" (*cetasika*), he said: "Joy and grief are intended.
Here, by the mention of joy (*somanassa*), states such as greed (*rāga*) and so forth, as well as faith (*saddhā*) and so forth, which are associated with it, are shown;

by the mention of grief (*domanassa*), hatred (*dosa*) and so forth are shown. However, applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are shown in their own form. As for the word *pi*...

The purpose of summarizing what is to be said is for easy comprehension; thus he says, "In this way your mind [is]," meaning that your mind functions in this manner. To the question "In what manner?", he says, "Whether joyful," and so forth.
"Your mind is thus" is a mere indication of the state of being joyful and so on, but it does not specify the particular cause by which one is joyful or dejected.
“Seeing” (*dassana*) refers to that consciousness; it is stated in the Pāḷi as “thus indeed, O mind” (*itipi te cittaṃ*) in order to show it.
Here, the word *iti* has the sense of illustration (*nidassanattha*), as in such passages as “‘It exists,’ Kaccāna, this is one extreme. Therefore he said: “this and that meaning.
The particle *pi* here also has the sense of including what has been mentioned. [The term *cittamanta*] means that by means of this, one thinks—that is, knows—the thought of another.
By changing the *na*-sound of *cintāmaṇi* into a *ṇa*-sound, that very same word becomes *maṇikā* through the intervention of the preceding word.
Since what is called "thought" (*cintā*) does not exist without the mind (*citta*), he says: "She knows the minds of others.

It is said that the person who practices this spell (*vijjā*), having recited the mantra at a suitable place and time, [knows the mind] by way of perceiving the specific details—seen, heard, and so forth—of the one whose mind they wish to know.
"Some say he speaks by inferring the movement of the mind; others say he speaks by means of observing the syllables after causing the speech to issue forth.
That science, however, should be illustrated by the *Padakusalajāta*ka.
This concludes the commentary on the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*).
"Causing to proceed" means being those who cause [the thoughts] to proceed; what is meant is that one should apply thought by way of causing them to proceed.
"Thus" refers to the manner of occurrence according to the method of the instruction as it was taught, both by way of affirmation and by way of negation.
And that instruction is for the purpose of showing the manner of occurrence of right thoughts and wrong thoughts therein.
It proceeds for the purpose of discerning both the benefit and the danger. It is the perception of impermanence itself, not the perception of permanence;

for the inclusion of the word "only" (*eva*) is for the purpose of excluding its opposite. Here too, the meaning and the purpose of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
The same method applies to the inclusion of the word "this" (*idaṃ*). The phrase "the craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure" is merely an illustration.

This is because there is a desire for the abandoning of that specific lust as well as for hatred and the other [defilements], and because the abandoning of those [defilements] serves as the means for the removal of that specific lust and so forth—just as the removal of corrupted blood requires the removal of the previously corrupted flesh.

The restriction "only supramundane states" (lokuttaradhamma) should be understood as intended to exclude blameworthy states (sāvajjadhamma), since they are its opposites; [this applies] to those [supramundane states] which constitute the means and the benefits for its attainment.

This is because other blameless qualities do not possess such immediate succession. He shows that the "wonder of psychic power" (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) is simply psychic power itself by treating it as a wonder;
the same method applies to the other two terms as well.

As for the etymological meaning of the word *pāṭihāriya*, it is explained as: "It is a wonder (*pāṭihāriya*) because it removes opposing factors, that is, because it eliminates the defilements such as lust."
They say that the Blessed One has no opposing factors such as lust and the like which would need to be removed.

Even in the case of ordinary persons, when the mind is free from defilements, endowed with the eight qualities, and its opposites have been destroyed, the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) function;
therefore, it cannot be called a "miracle" here based on the conventional usage found in those other cases. However, if [one were to consider] the Greatly Compassionate One...
The defilements present in those to be trained by the Blessed One are the adversaries; because he removes them, it is called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*).
This being so, this [etymology] is appropriate. Alternatively, the adversaries of both the Blessed One and his teaching are the non-Buddhist sectarians (*titthiya*);
because he removes them, it is a miracle. For they are [removed] by way of removing their views, since [the Buddha] is incapable of manifesting their views.
And [the defilements] are carried away and removed by means of psychic power, direct instruction, and exhortation.
Alternatively, this word *paṭi* conveys the meaning of "afterwards," as in the passage from the *Pārāyana Sutta*: "When he had entered therein, another brahmin arrived.
Therefore, once the mind has been concentrated, freed from defilements, and its task accomplished, it must afterwards be carried away—that is, set in motion [toward liberation].
A miracle (*paṭihāriya*): either the subsequent removal of one’s own defilements after they have been removed by means of the fourth jhāna and the Path;
or the performance of miracles, mind-reading, and instruction by one who is free from defilements and has accomplished his task, for the sake of the welfare of beings;
and the removal of the defilements of other beings once one’s own defilements have been removed.

They are called *paṭihāriyāni* because they are things that oppose [defilements]; *pāṭihāriyaṃ* is simply *paṭihāriya*. Alternatively, each individual member of the collection consisting of psychic power (*iddhi*), direct manifestation (*ādesanā*), and instruction (*anusāsanī*) is called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*).
Or, the fourth jhāna and the Path are "opposing" (*paṭihāriya*) because they remove opposing factors;
that which is born therein, or that which has that as its sign, or that which comes from that, is a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*)—namely, by means of psychic power, direct manifestation, and instruction.

Or, it is called a "miracle" (*pāṭihāriya*) because, according to the method already stated, it removes the defilement that is the opposite of faith and so forth within the mental continuum of another.
"Constant teaching of the Dhamma" means the teaching of the Dhamma that ought to be taught at all times.

In the phrase "by the miracle of psychic power" (*iddhipāṭihāriyena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*saha-ādi-yoge*); the meaning is that [the teaching] was practiced together with that [power]. This also applies to the other cases.
This is the method. It should be construed as: "It was the custom of the General of the Dhamma.
Demonstrating that point by means of the narrative from the Khandhaka, he said, "Regarding Devadatta," and so forth. "At Gayāsīsa" means:

not far from the village of Gayā, there is a flat rock named Gayāsīsa, resembling the frontal globe of an elephant, where there is space even for a thousand monks; it is on that flat rock. "The movement of the mind..."
By the phrase "having known," he shows the miracle of mind-reading (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*); by the phrase "he taught the Dhamma," he shows the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*);

and by the phrase "having displayed his supernormal transformations," he shows the miracle of psychic power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*). "Great Nāgas" refers to the Arahants who have destroyed the great outflows (*khīṇāsava*).
For "Nāga" is a designation for an Arahant, based on the fact that "there is no *āgu* (sin) in him. As it is said in the Sabhiya Sutta: [text follows]
“He does nothing in the world that leads to rebirth;
having cast off all fetters and bonds,
he is liberated and clings to nothing anywhere.”
“Such a one is called a Nāga because of his being thus.

In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) on this, however, it is said: “Upon hearing the Dhamma teaching of the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), five hundred bhikkhus were established in the fruit of stream-entry;
upon hearing the Dhamma teaching of Mahāmoggallāna, they were established in the fruit of arahantship. In the *Saṅghabhedakakkhandhaka* of the Canon (*Pāḷi*), [it is stated as follows].

But then, as those bhikkhus were being exhorted and instructed by the Venerable Sāriputta through the miracle of direct declaration and by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna through the miracle of psychic power,
the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose in them: "Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation."
By means of the Dhamma-teaching of both elders, the acquisition of the Dhamma-eye by those [monks] is shown;
this discrepancy in wording should be understood as being due to a difference in the opinions of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas and the Khandhaka-bhāṇakas.
For this text was spoken by the compilers (saṅgāhakas), and the commentary was compiled by them as well; moreover, in the Pāḷi...
It should be understood that even including the fruits of the higher paths, it is said, "the eye of Dhamma arose," as in the *Brahmāyu Sutta* and the *Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta*.
However, it is stated with special emphasis that "the miracle of instruction is the constant teaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas."
They are "subject to reproach" because they can be criticized by means of the counterfeit [teachings] as previously described.

They are "with fault" because they are not a proper method for cutting off the faults attributed to others. Precisely because they are with fault, they do not endure; that is, they are not long-lasting.

From the fact that they do not endure over time, it is inferred from the result that they do not lead [to liberation]. For it is due to their lack of leading [to liberation] that they are not enduring.
The miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*) is without reproach because it originates from purity and is based on purity.
For that very reason, it is faultless; for there is no possibility of faults such as contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Precisely because it is faultless, it stands firm for a long duration, since it cannot be struck down by the winds of rival doctrines nor by the winds of the defilements (*kilesa*). Because it stands firm for a long duration...
"Leads out" (*niyyātīti*): here too, there is an inference of the cause from the fruit. For it is because of its quality of leading out that it is "far-reaching" (*addhaniya*).

"Therefore" (*tasmā*): for the reasons already stated; and by that [word], he refers back to both "objection and so forth" and "non-objection and so forth," respectively, as being the causes for the states of being censurable and praiseworthy in both cases.
Commentary on the Basis for the Cessation of the Elements (Bhūtanirodhesakavatthuvaṇṇanā) 487.

"For the purpose of showing that [the world] does not lead to liberation": because even a monk seeking the great elements—who, though proficient in the first two wonders and well-skilled—[failed to see] the cessation of the great elements known as their complete and total extinction...

He did not realize Nibbāna; therefore, because both of those lack the quality of bringing about deliverance, they are "not leading out" (aniyyānika). This is for the purpose of showing their state of being non-leading-out.
As for "for the purpose of showing the state of being leading-out": the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya) leads the practitioner unconditionally to deliverance;
thus, it is for the purpose of showing its state of being leading-out.
Having thus shown the primary purpose of this teaching, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) is commenced in order to show its incidental purpose.
For the primary purpose of this teaching is indeed deliverance (*niyyāna*), since that is its actual objective.
However, the greatness of the Buddhas is an incidental purpose, as it is to be understood through the force of what is implied (*atthāpatti*). Of what kind [is this greatness]?
"He said, 'This monk... [referring to] "who [perceives] the great elements," and so forth.
"Seeking" means seeking the great elements by way of their cessation through non-seeking; what is meant is that he is investigating their cessation without remainder.
"Having wandered about" means having moved about, being impelled by the nature of things (*dhammatā*). This is indeed established by the nature of things, namely, for that monk—
"Moving in such a way" refers to the great earthquake and other phenomena occurring at the time of his birth.
"Vissajjokāsaṃ" means the place of answering; there is also the reading "vissajjakaraṃ," which has the same meaning.

"Therefore" means because he had no doubts after questioning the Buddha himself, and because the Buddha alone was capable of answering—this is what is intended. "For the purpose of manifesting his greatness" means in the world including the devas...
This is for the purpose of illustrating the great majesty and great power of the Buddhas’ greatness, which is not shared by anyone else in the world.
And this is the reason: it is also for the reason that "in the dispensation of all Buddhas, there is one such bhikkhu who manifests their power.

Regarding the word "where" (*kattha*), it is the locative case used in the sense of a sign; it is used to show the meaning "by depending on what place acting as the cause," hence [the question] "having approached what? (*kiṃ āgamma*).

It has been stated: what is the meaning of "having attained what object as a condition"? The sense is: having attained what as a cause for attainment. Therefore he said, "of one who has attained what. The construction is:
"for a person who has attained what object do [the aggregates] cease? This is a qualification containing the reason. "Those" refers to the great elements (*mahābhūtā*).

"By way of non-occurrence" means by way of their not arising again. "In every aspect" refers to the analysis of the meaning of the words, their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), functions (*rasa*), manifestations (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*), origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), groups (*kalāpa*), atoms (*cuṇṇa*), and their diversity and unity.
In every respect: by way of the analysis of the conditions consisting of the distinction between homogeneous and heterogeneous, internal and external, and the inclusion and application of conditions;
and by way of the modes of analysis of the concise and detailed characteristics, including both the components and their divisions.
488. Herein, those endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure sport, play, and shine forth.
And the gods, and the divine worlds. They go to or approach by means of these, thus they are "divine paths" (*devayāniyo*).
Just as in the word "leading out" (*niyyānikā*), where the suffix *-anīya* has the sense of the object (*kamma*), so here it should be understood as having the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
For it is said: "For by that... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "exerting mastery": here, "exerting mastery" (*vasavattana*) means going to whatever place one desires. That...
The knowledge of the various kinds of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*). The Cātumahārājikās are those for whom the four Great Kings are lords.
But why did he approach the gods who were far away instead of asking the Blessed One—who was standing nearby as the light of the world including the devas—for this matter?
This objection is removed by the passage beginning with "standing nearby. "Those gods who have attained the paths and fruits—they too [know] that matter..."
Thinking, "They might know it by a partial aspect, but this question asked concerns the domain of a Buddha," they said, "We do not know.
Therefore he said, "In the domain of a Buddha," and so forth. "It cannot be obtained" means it is not possible;

"overwhelming" (ajjhottharaṇa) here refers to the pressure of the questioning, which is why it is said, "he asks again and again. "We shall release him from our hands" is said in a conventional sense.
It has been said; well then, let us take it far away—this is what is meant.
Regarding the word *abhikkantatarā*, the prefix *abhi-* here has the sense of the prefix *ati-*, hence he says "surpassing" (*atikkantatarā*).

The meaning is: having overcome us by means of their physical beauty as well as qualities such as wisdom and eloquence, they are more desirable to others. *Paṇītatarā* means more excellent. Therefore it is said: "more supreme" (*uttamatarā*).
491–493. But as for Sakka, the thousand-eyed one—who has fully realized the truth, attained the fruit, and understood the teaching—why did he direct that bhikkhu through such a stratagem?

To remove this objection, [the author] introduces the passage beginning with "But this is the distinction. *Khajjopanaka* refers to a small glow-worm that shines at night. *Dhamanto viya* means as if blowing air from his mouth.
*Atthi ce vā* means that such a person, a seeker of the great elements, would indeed exist; by me...
The intention is that he will know [the truth] later, precisely because he has yearned for it. "Thereafter" means after such reflection.
Because only the knowledge of the modes of psychic power (*iddhividhañāṇa*) is intended here, it is similar to the "deva-pathway.

This is stated in the Pāḷi and in the commentaries in various places according to the conventional names used there: "Whether it is called the 'deva-pathway'... or 'direct-knowledge' (*abhiññāñāṇa*), all this is merely a name for the knowledge of the modes of psychic power."

It has been said. For in all superknowledges (*abhiññā*), there appropriately occurs what is called absorption (*appanā*) lasting for a single moment of consciousness, such as the path leading to the world of the gods (*devayāniya-magga*) and so forth.
494. "The sign prior to the arrival" (*āgamanapubbabhāge nimittaṃ*): this refers to the sign that arises prior to Brahmā’s arrival.

It is to be connected with the phrase "prior to its arising" (*udayato pubbabhāge*). "These" (*ime*) refers to those belonging to the retinue of Brahmā (*brahmakāyikā*). "By way of explanation" (*veyyākaraṇena*) means by way of exposition (*byākaraṇena*).
“Anāraddhacitto” means one whose mind is not won over, whose mind is dissatisfied. “Vādaṃ” means fault. “Vikkhepaṃ” means a various diversion by means of speech. 495.

“Kuhakattā” means, according to the method already stated, because of the desire to deceive others with what is unreal. Some, reading it as “guhakattā,” also explain the meaning as being because of the desire to conceal [one’s faults].
The commentary on the simile of the shore-viewing bird.

497. "In part" (*padesena*) means by way of a portion; the meaning is: by that which is clung-to (*upādinnaka*) and included within the continuum of a sentient being (*sattasantāna*). "Even in the case of what is not clung-to" (*anupādinnakepi*) means even in the case of those things not bound to the sense-faculties (*anindriyabaddha*).
"Without remainder" (*nippadesato*) means exhaustively. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) refers to the fact that [the question] was asked in such a manner; the intention is that the question was inappropriate.
"Of one confused by the question" (*pucchāmūḷhassa*) means of one who is bewildered regarding the question because of not knowing how to ask it.
For one who asks falsely is called "confused in his question," just as one is called "lost on the path.

"Having shown the fault in the question" means having made manifest the defect in the manner of the question posed by him. "The answering of the question" is the response to a question that has been correctly formulated according to the training;
for an answer is indeed that which conforms to the question and shares the same nature as the question.
Because [the answer] must be given, and because the Tathāgatas do not fail to answer in accordance with the question asked— nor do they answer by failing [to understand it]—
and because questioners become confused when they do not comprehend the meaning of the answer due to its similarity to other meanings,
it should be understood that it is the custom of the Buddhas to first instruct on how to ask the question and then to provide the answer to that unerring inquiry.
Therefore he says, "For what reason," and so forth. "Difficult to convince" means one who is hard to persuade for the reasons already stated.
"Does not stand firm" means it does not persist by taking a condition as its basis. Regarding the word "where," he says "by resorting to what?
because this is a locative case used in the sense of a cause or motive (*nimitta*). "Does not stand" means without a condition; the meaning is that the cause has been entirely and completely severed.
"Only what is clung-to" (upādinnaṃyeva) means only that which is bound to the sense faculties.

Because the perception of "long" occurs in a series of material phenomena (rūpappabandha) that are arranged in many ways facing a single direction, and based on that, the perception of "short" occurs in what is arranged to a lesser degree than that—and since both of these are grasped specifically by way of the apprehension of matter—therefore it is said, "by way of shape," and so forth. [This applies] when the dimension is small.
In a composite form, there is the perception of atoms; based on that, there is the perception of something large and gross.
Since these two are specifically grasped by way of the apprehension of form, he says, "By this too," and so forth. Furthermore, by the word "also" (*pi*), he includes the following point:
"In the phrase 'derived form is stated by way of shape,' here too it is merely color that is being spoken of."
They say this. Here, the word *vaṇṇa* is a synonym for the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). *Subha* means beautiful; the meaning is "desirable.
*Asubha* means unattractive; the meaning is "undesirable. Therefore he said: "Thus it is described as having desirable and undesirable objects.
In the three instances—long, short, fine, coarse, beautiful, and ugly—it is only derived form (*upādārūpa*) that is intended by way of the sense-sphere of visible form.
The inclusion of the primary elements (bhūtarūpa) should be understood as their being grasped separately. For in the verse, “Where do water, earth, fire, and air find no footing?
the primary elements are indeed grasped separately. “Name” (nāma) refers to the four aggregates beginning with feeling.
It is called “name” because it bends toward the object (namana) and because it performs naming (nāmakaraṇa). Previously, by means of [the categories] such as “long,” “short,” and so forth...
By the phrase "divided into long and so forth," he shows that what was already stated here is included under the perception of form (rūpasaññā) in the sense of being "formed" (ruppana).

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of water and the other [elements] is intended. Alternatively, since designations such as "long" and so on do not have only the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) as their foundation, but rather have the primary material elements (bhūtarūpa) as their foundation—since shape (saṇṭhāna) is also apprehended by way of contact—therefore, by the inclusion of "long, short, and so forth," [all forms are encompassed].
To convey the meaning that even "actual form" (bhūtarūpa) is indeed included, it is stated simply as "form divided into long and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having reached what" (kiṃ āgamma), this means having attained what, or by reason of attaining what.
The statement "it ceases" (uparujjhati) is said with reference to non-arising cessation (anuppādanirodha), not momentary cessation; thus he says, "this [form] does not proceed without remainder."

499. Regarding the phrase "therein there is an exposition" (*veyyākaraṇaṃ bhavati*): this is merely a statement of connection. Having stated the prose recitation (*cuṇṇiyapāṭha*), the intention is that he then utters the verse beginning with "consciousness" (*viññāṇaṃ*), which constitutes the actual exposition.
"To be known" (*viññātabba*) means it is to be known by distinguished knowledge;
the meaning is that it is to be directly realized through the noble path-knowledge, the supreme among all knowledges. Therefore he said: "This is of Nibbāna..."

"Name" [is the term]. "Illustration" (*nidassana*) means that which is illustrated; they explain the meaning as "that which is not an illustration" (*anidassana*), meaning it is not cognizable by the eye.
Alternatively, an "illustration" is a simile; since this [Nibbāna] has none, it is "without illustration.
For indeed, no similar illustration can be found anywhere for Nibbāna, which is eternal, unitary, and of an absolutely sublime nature.
That which, having not been, comes to be, and having been, passes away, is conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and possesses the limits of arising and passing away.
However, for the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) Nibbāna, which is eternal, neither of those two limits exists;

for that very reason, it also lacks aging, which is defined as the departure from a new state. Thus it is said: "the limit of arising," and so forth. In this context, "the limit of arising" refers to the state of arising.
“Vayantī” (they are passing away) refers to the state of dissolution (*bhaṅgāvatthā*). “The alteration of that which stands” (*ṭhitassa aññathattaṃ*) refers to aging (*jaratā*).

By the inclusion of the term “the rest,” the state of persistence (*ṭhitāvatthā*) is permitted. “Titthassa” means of a drinking ford (*pānatittha*). He shows the derivation there with the words beginning with “For that” (*tañhi*).
“Papanti” means they drink thoroughly (*pakārena pivanti*); for thus it was stated by the Teacher: “They drink here, thus they are called ‘papanti.’”
For here, by way of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*), the letter *pa* becomes *bha* in the sense that "they go down to it" (*pappanti*) as a drinking-place;

or, according to the characteristic of the literal sound, the letter *pa* is changed to *bha*. "From all" means from the perspective of every meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore he said: "By whichever door among the thirty-eight meditation subjects.
This is another method from the Commentary: *Pabhā* is speaking, illuminating, or shining forth in a particular manner (*pakārena*).
"Sabbatopabhaṃ" means "radiant on all sides"; the meaning is that it is pure and luminous on every side because it is undefiled by anything.
Here, in the phrase "having arrived at this Nibbāna," the locative case is used to indicate the sign (nimitta).
That by which Nibbāna has been attained is itself the non-arising and cessation of those things included within the continuity [of existence] in this context.
"Intended" means it is stated that "the class of phenomena that has been appropriated ceases and becomes non-occurrence.
"Therein" refers to that phrase which was spoken as "by the cessation of consciousness. He extracts "consciousness" because it is that which must be analyzed.
"Final consciousness" refers to the mind of final Nibbāna, known as the death-consciousness of an Arahant.
“Volitional consciousness” (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) refers to the mind that performs volitional formations such as merit and so forth.
“It ceases right here” means that this name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) ceases in this Nibbāna within the element of Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesā nibbānadhātu*). Therefore he said:

“It goes to the state of being like a lamp’s flame extinguished,” etc. “Like a lamp’s flame extinguished” means like the flame of a lamp that has gone out. By the passage beginning with “Of the volitional consciousness as well,” etc., [he explains].

By means of the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining, he speaks of the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining, because the complete cessation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is what is intended.
Therefore it is said: “It ceases by way of non-arising. In the phrase “by the knowledge of the path of stream-entry,” the instrumental case is used either for the agent or for the instrument;
however, in the word “by cessation,” it is used in the sense of cause. “Therein” refers to Nibbāna. The rest...
In all instances, the meaning is indeed clear.

Thus ends the elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta, within the *Līnatthappakāsinī*—the "Expositor of the Hidden Meaning"—a sub-commentary to the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīgha Nikāya*.

This work illuminates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend, and it generates a vast and stainless clarity of wisdom, serving as a graceful ornament for the virtuous.
The commentary on the Kevaṭṭa Sutta is finished.
12. Commentary on the Lohicca Sutta:
Explanation of the Background Story of the Brahmin Lohicca.
501. Having thus commented upon the Kevaṭṭa Sutta, he now, while commenting on the Lohicca Sutta, says: "Thus have I heard...

in the Kosala country: the Lohicca Sutta. This is said either to clarify that the occasion for the commentary has been reached in its proper sequence, or to show that the Lohicca Sutta is the discourse recited immediately after the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.
"Sālavatikā" is the name of that village based on its feminine gender, even in the absence of a specific reason; some say it is due to its status as a "village of headmen" (*gāmaṇikā*).
"Vatiyā" means by means of a fence made of thorny branches and the like. "Lohita" was a distinguished ancestor in his family;
the name "Lohicca"—meaning a descendant of Lohita—is the clan name (*gotta*) derived from that Brahmin lineage.
502. “What indeed can one person do for another?”—this is base because it is devoid of compassion for others. But it does not refer to either annihilationism or eternalism;
thus he says, “but not...,” and so forth. For by “a speculative view” (diṭṭhigata), merely a particular opinion is intended;
otherwise, since there is no such thing as a speculative grasp apart from the grasping at annihilation or eternalism, it would necessarily be one of those two.

By the words “‘It has arisen’—this shows that it is a term common to both what has arisen in the mind and what has arisen in speech,” [the author] indicates this with the phrase “and not only... and so forth.
“He, it is said... speaks indeed” expresses the public renown of that particular tenet in the world.
However, because another (para) exists as distinct from oneself (attā), therefore, just as there is one who instructs and another who is to be instructed, [so too does the other exist].
In order to show that he is an instructor even by way of being one who is thus instructed, the words beginning with "another" (paro) were spoken.
Furthermore, the expression of future time, "he will do" (karissati), is used here in relation to the word "what" (kiṃ);

or else, it is for the purpose of showing that there is nothing to be done by him even in the future. "Wholesome state" (kusalaṃ dhammaṃ) means a blameless state, a state free from defilements, a state of liberation.
The meaning is as follows: What is the purpose of wandering about having surrounded oneself with others, thinking, "I shall preach the Dhamma to others"?
Even for one whose intentions have increased, that [preaching] does not occur without them; therefore, he says that one should dwell by oneself...
and so forth. Thus he said: "In this same way, I speak of this evil state of greed."
504. By the phrase "by way of the feminine gender," he shows that even for a meaning belonging to the masculine gender, there is a conventional designation (saññā) in the feminine gender.
"He" refers to the brahmin Lohicca. "A burden" means heavy and difficult to bear because of the great size of the Blessed One’s assembly and because of his own many duties and responsibilities.
508. "For the sake of conversational ease" means for the sake of the pleasure of conversation; the sense is that it is easy both to speak and to hear the discourse.
“This is a lay follower,” he said to the barber and the bath-attendant. In the phrase “perhaps it might be so,” the repetition (*āmeḍita*) should be understood as being due to joy;
for that is called the “Buddha’s thunder. Indeed, in such instances, the Blessed One especially experiences joy and gladness;
therefore, out of joy, he thunders first and thunders again in response. What is the distinction between the thundering and the responsive thundering?
It is said: "This," and so forth. Speaking at the beginning is *allāpa*; when followed by a consonant (*saññoga*), it is short. Speaking together after that is *sallāpa*.
Commentary on the Inquiry of the Brahmin Lohicca (509):
"Arising of a collection" means the arising of life; thus he says, "the arising of wealth. "From there" means from Sālavatikā. "Causing an obstacle to gain."

It creates an obstacle to the acquisition of wealth and grain. The prefix *anu-* indicates the sense of desiring; this is shown by the word "he desires" (*icchati*). Here is another method from the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
one who is compassionate and supportive through preeminent welfare is called "one who has compassion for welfare" (*hitānukampī*).
"It succeeds" (*sampajjati*) means it is accomplished through the attainment of repeated practice; the meaning is that it becomes powerful and firm.
Therefore it was said: "It is certain. 510–511.
Regarding the second proof: the second proof, instance, and logical justification stated by means of the passage beginning with, "Was not King Pasenadi of Kosala...?
For the Blessed One demonstrates the reason through the medium of a simile; and by this proof, you—
By including "both these and others," the sense of urgency (*saṃvejana*) is established. The construction is: "And those sons of good family who bring the divine wombs (*dibba-gabbha*) to maturity.
Being unable [to do so] due to the absence of the perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya-sampatti*) or the maturation of knowledge (*ñāṇa-paripāka*).

Because the word "kamma" lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*atulyādhikaraṇa*), it is used in the sense of the object (*upayoga-attha*) through a transposition of case endings (*vibhatti-vipallāsa*) with respect to the action of bringing to maturity.

This is the nominative case. As for those who read it as *paripaccanti* using the passive form (*kammarūpa*), in their view there is no need for a change in case-ending (*vibhattivipallāsa*) because of its status as both object and agent;
however, its meaning should be understood as a specific kind of merit such as giving, according to the method explained in the second alternative.
Furthermore, its quality of compassion for the unfortunate arises by virtue of the beings associated with it. They are called "divine" (*dibba*) because they exist in heaven (*divi*).

They are called *gabbhā* because they contain (*gabbhenti*) and bind within themselves by way of ripening; thus, they are the divine worlds (*devaloka*). The phrase "of the six divine worlds" is an illustrative statement.
For even the Brahma-world possesses the nature of a divine womb (*dibbagabbha*), since it is caused by divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*).
By taking this into account, the statement "cultivating meditation" (*bhāvanaṃ bhāvayamānā*) is also justified. [It leads] to the divine world.
Having said, "Fulfilling the path," in order to show that path in its specific form, it was stated: "Giving gifts," and so forth.

Herein, "existences" (*bhava*) are celestial mansions (*vimāna*), because beings are endowed with happiness therein according to their desire. They are "divine" (*dibba*) because they bring about the state of a deva.
By the method already described, they are "wombs" (*gabbha*). Giving and the other [perfections] are specific types of merit conducive to the world of the devas. Thus, they are "divine existences."

Here, the states of existence by birth included within the world of the gods (devaloka) are intended. Since the kamma-existence that brings about those [birth-states] was already taken up previously, he said:
"the resultant aggregates in the world of the gods.
This concludes the commentary on the three [types of] persons worthy of exhortation.
513. *Aniyāmiteneva* means "unspecified," that is, without specific designation such as, "You hold such a view; you are one who acts thus for the harm of beings.
Because it arises from a conviction that pervades the entire world, it is "risen up as high as the peak of existence" (*bhavagga*).
*Māna* refers to the pride of the wise (*paṇḍitamāna*) that occurs in the form of thinking, "I know this; I see this."
"Bhinditvā" means having dispelled; the sense is "having caused to abandon. Regarding "the three kinds of teachers":

these are the three teachers—the disciple who has not accomplished his own welfare and does not offer advice, the disciple who has not accomplished his own welfare but offers advice, and the disciple who has accomplished his own welfare but does not offer advice.
However, the fourth, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), is not one who ought to be reproved; therefore, when he was questioned by him...
Thinking, “I shall speak thus,” the Teacher first shows those three teachers who are worthy of censure, and afterwards the fourth teacher.
Granted that here the fourth teacher is alone, without a second, and not shared by others;

nevertheless, although he is a collection of those superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma) by virtue of which he is called “the body made of Dhamma,” those qualities—which constitute his parts—are themselves representative of the Teacher.
Having done so, the Blessed One spoke thus, pointing it out: “This teacher, Lohicca, is also [one who teaches]...
The expression *aññā* is a grammatical indication involving the elision of the letter *ya*, as in the case of *sayaṃ abhiññā* and similar phrases;

he shows that this is a dative construction used in that sense by saying “for the sake of knowledge (*aññāya*)” and so forth. Because they remain having professed discipleship, they carry out his teaching in part.

He said: “Without having carried out his instruction continuously. The expression “repeatedly stepping aside” is a distributive phrase referring to the fact that at times she acted in such a way and at times she did not; the intention is that she was doing whatever she desired.
“While she was retreating” means while she was withdrawing due to lack of interest and lack of respect. Therefore it is said: “while she was unwilling,” and so forth.

"One woman comes alone" means she comes without a second woman; "union" refers to the union of sexual intercourse. "One man should desire" is to be connected by supplying the words "should desire union," meaning a man without a second.

This demonstration of the relationship between men and women by way of their separation and so forth is for the purpose of showing the practice among the disciples of that Teacher, with reference to both those bound to the household life and those not bound to the household life. Because of his state of extreme dispassion...
"Even a woman standing with her back turned, whom he does not wish to see"—by "greed" (lobha) is meant the greed for gain and honor arising from dependence on one's retinue.
"Such a one" refers to a Teacher of such a nature. "By which"—by which state of greed.
"Establish him therein"—having established him in that dharma of practice, establish him; make him straight by means of the removal of crookedness of body and so forth.
514. "Grass that has the form of crops" means grasses such as *nīvāra* and so forth that resemble crops.
515. "Deserves correction in this way" means that he deserves correction by way of directing his disciples toward a state of little concern, according to the method already stated;
it is not like the first [case], where one says, "Such is your state of greed," nor like the second.
...as in the passage beginning, "First, strive for your own self-perfection therein. Why? Because the third [discourse] concerns one who has already achieved his own welfare.
516. Regarding the phrase "not deserving of admonition":
here, what is called "deserving of admonition" refers to either a transgression by the Teacher or a transgression by the disciples.
Whether it arises from a failure in one or both [of these], none of this exists in this Teacher; therefore, the words beginning with "For this one...
were spoken to show that he is not subject to censure. "Obedient" (assavā) means compliant (paṭissavā).
"By the view held by me": in one who is entirely blameless, faultless, and practicing rightly, and for others as well...
By means of a wicked view leading to hell—one which was wrongly grasped through the imputation of non-existent faults upon the Teacher who was demonstrating the right practice exactly as it is.
"Into the precipice of hell" (*narakapapātam*) refers to the great precipice known as hell;

for it is called a "precipice" (*papāta*) because beings fall into it. "With the hand of the teaching of the Dhamma" means with the hand consisting of the teaching of the Dhamma. "At the threshold of the path to heaven."

On the dry land of meritorious states, which constitutes the path leading to heaven; or on the dry land known as the stream-entry path and so forth, pertaining to the heavens of the Four Great Kings and the rest.
The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
Thus ends [the section from] the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which elucidates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend.

This concludes the *Līnatthapakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning), the commentary on the *Lohicca Sutta*, composed by the lady named Sādhuvilāsini, who brings forth the clarity of vast and perfectly pure wisdom.
The commentary on the *Lohicca Sutta* is finished.
13. Commentary on the *Tevijja Sutta*.
518. Having thus commented upon the Lohicca Sutta, he now comments upon the Tevijja Sutta.
In order to clarify that it has reached its proper place in the sequence of commentaries, or to show that the sutta recited immediately after the Lohicca Sutta is indeed the Tevijja Sutta, he says:
"Thus have I heard... [pe] ...among the Kosalans: the Tevijja Sutta."
"Name" means merely a name. When the word *ena* is employed following a term denoting direction (*disāvācī*), it is intended in the sense of "not far" (*adūra*).

Furthermore, by its usage, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamī*). Therefore, in order to show that the phrase "to the north" (*uttarena*) indicates the sense of "not far" and employs the genitive in the sense of the ablative, it is said: "on the northern side, not far from Manasākaṭa. [This is] because it follows a term denoting direction.
Some say that this was stated with the word *ena* in order to show the sense of proximity (*adūrattha*), because the ablative case (*pañcamīvacana*) indicates proximity;

furthermore, this third case ending (*tatiyāvacana*) is used in the sense of the locative (*sattamīyattha*), as in examples such as "the village is delightful from the east" (*pubbena gāmaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ*).

However, the grammarians (*akkharacintaka*) maintain that when the word *ena* is employed, the accusative case (*upayogavacana*) is required for the word expressing the limit (*avadhivācini pada*), while the actual meaning [of the relationship] functions solely by way of the genitive (*sāmivasena*).

This is the teacher’s opinion: "Because it is intended [in that sense], it is expressed here by means of the genitive case alone. Regarding the phrase "in a grove of young mango trees" (*taruṇa-amba-rukkha-saṇḍe*):
it refers to a multitude of young mango trees; for the conventional designation "forest" (*vana*) applies to a collection of trees.
Regarding the phrase "by reason of the perfection of family, conduct, and so forth": here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes such perfections as mastery of the mantras and physical beauty.
“In this and that place” means in various locations or families. He said “in this and that” (*tattha*) and so forth, specifying them by way of their dwelling places.
“For the purpose of reciting mantras” means for the purpose of reciting the *āthabbaṇa* (Atharvan) mantras; thus it was said:
“having prevented the entry of many others. “On the riverbank” means on the bank of the Aciravatī River.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Path and Non-Path (Maggāmaggakathāvaṇṇanā) 520. "Wandering on foot" (*jaṅghacāra*) means moving here and there by means of walking meditation (*caṅkama*).

For that [practice] is called "wandering on the legs" (*jaṅghavihāra*) or "wandering on foot" (*jaṅghacāra*) because one moves about for the purpose of dispelling fatigue in the legs. Therefore, it is said in the Canon: "While walking back and forth... (*anucaṅkamantānaṃ*).

"Of those who are walking to and fro. "Bathing requisites" refers to powdered clay and so forth. It is stated thus because both "walking to and fro" (*anucaṅkamana*) and "walking about" (*anuvicāraṇa*) are applicable [to that place].
Here, the "path" (*magga*) is the straight path consisting of the practice that serves as the means for going to the Brahma-world.

For it is called a "path" because by it one "paths toward" (*maggati*)—that is, approaches—the desired destination; anything other than that is a "non-path" (*amagga*), the prefix *a-* [denoting negation].
Or rather, the meaning of "vā" (or) should be understood as "and. For it is by means of the passage beginning with "What indeed... that he shows the path itself.
"The way of practice" (*paṭipadā*) refers to the preliminary practice leading to the world of Brahmā.

"The direct course" (*añjasāyana*) is a synonym for the straight path; this is because the two alternative terms indicate an additional sense, just as in the case of the term "proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhāna*).
In the second interpretation, the word *añjasa* is a synonym for "straight.

*Niyyāti* means "it leads out," and by the phrase "leading out" (*niyyāyanto*), he shows that it is itself "leading out" (*niyyānika*). When it is said that "the leading-out path leads out," this refers to an absolute leading out;
the meaning is that it goes while being in the state of going. Why is the path said to "lead out"? Is it not the case that this [path] is devoid of activity (*abyāpāra*) regarding the act of going?

It is true. However, because the state of leading out (niyyāna) is obtained by way of the person who goes forth, the path that leads out—by way of the person going forth practicing with wise attention—is said to "lead out" (niyyāti). It "makes" (karoti) means it causes [the fruit] to arise within one's own continuum;
for it is precisely while causing it to arise in that manner that one is said to "practice" (paṭipajjati) it. It is called "companionship" (sahabya) because it proceeds or exists together.

“Sahavattanaka” means one who lives together; its state is called “sahabyatā,” as expressed by the phrase “for the sake of coexistence” (*sahabhāvāya*). And “coexistence” (*sahabhāva*) should be understood as sharing the same world (*salokatā*) or proximity.
Thus it is said: “for the sake of manifestation in the same place. “One’s own” (*sakam eva*) means exactly what was spoken by one’s own teacher, Pokkharasāti.
“Having praised” (*thometvā*) means having commended [him] with such words as, “This alone is the straight path; this is the direct way.”
"Having thus taken up [the position]" means that Bhāradvāja also, having praised and taken up his own teacher’s doctrine as it was spoken by his teacher Tārukkha, wanders about;
such is the construction. "Stated by him" means stated in the Pāḷi by way of being adhered to, whether in this manner or that.

521–522. “Non-conducive to liberation” (*aniyyānika*) means non-authoritative (*appaṭihārika*); that is to say, they are devoid of further proof because each side points out faults in the other’s doctrine while failing to demonstrate the unerring meaning. “Weighing” (*tula*) refers to a scale for measuring. “Dispute” (*viggaha*) is the initial grasping of a contradiction between two opposing doctrines;
that same [contradiction], arising repeatedly through the process of contention, is called “quarrel” (*vivāda*). Thus he says, “originating first,” and so forth.
“Duvidhopi eso” is the analysis [of the compound]; even though this conflict is stated as being twofold, it is called *vivāda*.

It is “the doctrine of various teachers” because it consists of the doctrines of teachers of diverse inclinations. Having understood it as “various doctrines” (*nānāvādo*) meaning “a doctrine of many kinds,” the reading now is, however, “the doctrine of various teachers is ‘nānāvādo’.”
523. "Of even one" means of even one among you two. "In one" means in either of the two positions, namely, the proponent's own view or the opponent's view.
"There is no doubt" means there is no perplexity such as "Is this the path or not the path? However, there is doubt regarding whether it is straight or crooked.
Therefore it was said, "It is reported that... and so forth. "This being so" means if they perceive it as the path in all cases; this being so, in what...
“Is this your dispute?”—thus the Blessed One asks. Here, by the word *iti* in the sense of “beginning with,” both *vivāda* (contention) and *nānāvāda* (disagreement) are included.
524. “That by which one seeks out (*magga*) and approaches (*upagacchati*) the desired place straight is a path (*magga*); thus it is a ‘straight path’ (*ujumagga*).

Anything other than that is a ‘non-path’ (*amagga*), or the negative prefix *a-* should be understood in the sense of ‘increase’ (*vuddhi*); this meaning has been stated previously. Thus ends [the section on] “on the non-straight path” (*anujumagge*).

Here too, the prefix *a-* is appropriate in the sense of "increase. "That very basis" refers to the basis consisting of the path-nature of the path for all brahmins, and the straight-path nature of their own path.
"All those" refers to all those paths taught by various teachers, which are mentioned in the Canon as "the Addhariya brahmins," and so forth. This is the meaning here.

The meaning of the text (*pāḷiattha*) is as follows: A *addhara* is a particular kind of sacrifice; because they are employed for that purpose, the sacrificial formulas (*yajūni*) are called *addhariya*.
Those who recite them are *addhariya*, namely, those belonging to the *Yajurveda*. The mantras composed by the sage named Tittiri are called *tittira*;
those who recite them are *tittiriya*, likewise those belonging to the *Yajurveda*. For this is a branch of the *Yajurveda*, namely, the *Tittiri*.
*Chanda* specifically refers to the Sāmaveda; those who chant it with melody (*sarena*) are called *chandokā*, that is, followers of the Sāmaveda.
They are also read as *chandogā* with the third vowel, which has the same meaning. *Bahvṛca* means that there is much recitation (*iriyā*) and praise (*thomanā*) therein;
it refers to the Ṛgveda, and those who study it are called *bahvṛcchā*.
Regarding the word "many" (*bahūni*), here is the application of the simile: just as those various roads lead exclusively to the entry of that village or town,
so too the various paths proclaimed by the brahmins lead exclusively to the attainment of the Brahmā-world and to companionship with Brahmā.

525. "Having confessed, but later denying while being pressed" means: having previously admitted it while perceiving it to be faultless, one later denies it—saying "This was not my word"—while being pressed on account of its faulty nature;
the meaning is that one does not confess [at that later time].
527–529. *Te tevijjā* means those brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge (*tevijjakā*). By the word *eva*, it is indicated that there is no meaning [of "only"] here;
thus the letter *va* is taken, and this shows that it has no meaning [on its own], as expressed by the phrase "merely a phonetic junction" (*āgamasandhimattam*).
The meaning is that by the addition of a phoneme (*vaṇṇāgama*), a mere junction with another word has been made. *Andhapaveṇī* means a line of blind men. "Fifty or sixty blind men"—so it is said.
This demonstrates the suitability of that blind procession for wandering around the great thicket of trees.
For in this way, they perceive, "We have been traveling along the path for a very long time.
By the expression "clinging to one another in succession," their lack of a staff-bearer is shown; thus it is said, "by a staff-bearer," and so forth. By showing that illustration:
The passage beginning with “*Eko kira*” is commenced. “Having gone around” means having walked gradually all around for some time.

“*Kacchaṃ*”: this refers to the corner of the cloth used for binding the waist. For the word *kaccha* is a synonym for a particular type of lower garment, as seen in such expressions as “*kacchaṃ bandhantī*.
Furthermore, *kaccha* refers to the armpit region. “*Sambādho nāma ubho*... [the two sides...]
For the word *kaccha* denotes a part of the body, as in such expressions as "the armpits" (*upakacchakā*) or "the urinary organ" (*muttakaraṇa*).
"One with eyes" refers to one who holds a staff. The phrase "the former," and so forth, should be understood according to the sequence already stated.

"Merely a name" means it is a mere name because of the absence of an actual object; furthermore, although that which was spoken by them is perceived as having substance, it is truly inferior because, being a mere name, it lacks substantiality.
The phrase "only base" indicates the mere sense [of the word].
(530) *Ya* refers to the Brahma-world. *Yato* is an ablative used in the sense of a locative.
Because a general indication must be restricted to a specific instance, it is said "at which time. By the words "at the time of rising," etc., he states what is understood from the context.
“They entreat” means they pray for the rising [of the sun]. Why? Because of its great service to the world; the same applies to the praises and so forth.
“Gentle” means cool. It is said that this is the conviction of the brahmins: “In the past, through the entreaties of the brahmins, the moon and sun came and brought light to the world.”
532. But what can be said here? Regarding this instruction on the path to companionship with Brahmā—which is not directly perceived—what can be said of the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas?

The intention is: they are unable to point out the path even to companionship with the moon and sun, which *are* directly perceived. By the word "there" (*yattha*), the meaning already expressed by "here" (*idha*) is referred back to.
Commentary on the Simile of the River Aciravatī (542):
“Filled to the brim” means completely full; for that very reason, it is “drinkable by crows. “The further shore” refers to the opposite bank;
the word “friend” (*ambho*) is used to indicate a form of address. “The near shore” refers to this side. “Come! means “come hither. “Certainly” (*vata*) means “without fail.”
If you will go, then the construction is: "In that case, come. The phrase beginning with "These are" (*atthime*) states the reason for the invitation.
(Verse 544) ...the five precepts... should be understood as such because the duties of a brahmin, such as the restraints and observances (*yama-niyama*), are included therein.

Their opposites are those contrary to the five precepts and so forth, namely the five enmities (*pañca-vera*) and the like. "Inda" refers to the son of a deity named Inda, or Sakka. [Regarding the river] Aciravatī...
By the phrase "seated on the bank," he brings forward that very simile as an illustration for one who is seated on its bank;

this shows that the King of Dhamma has thoroughly penetrated the element of Dhamma (*dhammadhātu*). By saying "Furthermore," the expression "Another [simile]" is intended to include the other river simile as well.
546. "In the sense of being desirable" means by way of the state of being something to be desired.
"In the sense of bondage" means by way of the state of binding the minds of beings because they desire it.

Although this word *guṇa* (quality) is seen to be used in other senses, since those are impossible here, this summary of meanings is given to show that, by the method of elimination (*pārisesañāya*), only the sense of "bondage" is appropriate.
"Āraddho" means undertaken. "Ahatānaṃ" means unwashed or brand new. "Ettha" refers to the word *paṭala* in the text of the Khandhaka-pāḷi;
it is either the meaning of the word *paṭala*, or the meaning designated as *paṭala*.

"Guṇaṭṭho" is the meaning of the word *guṇa*. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. "Accenti" means they proceed by passing over. "Ettha" refers to the word *somanassajātakapāḷi*. "Dakkhiṇā" means...

The volition of giving toward an animal. "In this" refers to the words of the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta*; "garland-wreath" means a string of garlands. "In these" refers to the passages in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* and the *Dhammapada* commentaries;

and this is merely by way of illustration, as it also occurs in the sections on the divisions [of virtue], the excellence of the fundamental precepts (*āpadhānasīla*), the attainments of purity (*sukkādi*), and the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). And there is a verse on this point:

“‘Quality’ (guṇa) [is used] in the sense of a layer, a benefit, a constituent part, a bond, virtue, the bases of purification (sukkhādi), striving (padhāna), accomplishment, and a bowstring. “Is that very same” means it is precisely in the sense of a bond.
For when the state of being desirable is predicated of form and so forth, the sense of a layer is not appropriate.

This is because they are not intended as objects of desire. The same principle applies to the meanings of "heap" (*rāsa*) and so forth. However, from the perspective of elimination (*pārisesato*), only the meaning of "bondage" (*bandhana*) is appropriate;
for to the extent that these are objects of desire, to that same extent they constitute a state of bondage.

Furthermore, the meaning of "constituent part" (*koṭṭhāsa*) is also appropriate here, because they are objects of desire by virtue of being constituent parts cognizable by eye-consciousness and so forth. Moreover, the word for "quality" (*guṇa*) is seen used in the sense of a "part," as in expressions such as "the double portion must be increased."
“Incalculable are the names of the Great Sage according to his qualities; even from a thousand names, one name may be selected by way of a quality.
In such passages as these, the word *guṇa* (quality) has the sense of accomplishment (*sampadā*); however, that sense is not applicable here, and thus it is not mentioned.

He says "should be seen" because here it is seeing itself that constitutes understanding. He extends the application by saying "by this means," referring to the sense that [objects] are "to be heard by ear-consciousness," and so forth.
Although things sought after are also called "desirable," he says "whether they have been sought or not" to show that those are not intended here.
For only what is actually desired is "desirable" in this context; therefore, he says "having become desirable objects."
The meaning is: "having become an object of pleasure. "Desirable" means fit to be desired. They are called "agreeable" (*manāpā*) because they incline and increase the mind by way of being desirable.
"Of a pleasant nature" means having a pleasant intrinsic character. "Making it an object" means making oneself the object.
Since lust arises when there is an object that has become the basis for action, he said, "becoming the cause for the arising of lust," pointing to that [object] as the instrumental cause.
“Greedily” means by way of lust (*lobha*). The construction is: “having become overcome, they enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure.
“In a state of infatuation” means in a state of delusion (*moha*). “Adhering closely” means having seized upon and being attached to; therefore it is said, “plunged. “The edge” means the limit.
“Reached the conclusion” means having swallowed [the object], they have arrived at the conclusion by way of its completion.

Not seeing the danger in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, both in the present and in the future, they do not escape—that is, they do not depart from—the defilement caused by the signs of enjoyment such as food, clothing, and so forth;
thus, it is "the means of escape" (*nissaraṇa*). Wisdom regarding their enjoyment through wise reflection is that;
because of its absence, it is "wisdom lacking the means of escape. Showing this meaning, he said, "In this case, this... and so forth. [They are] "devoid of enjoyment accompanied by reflection."
They are devoid of enjoyment by means of the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) as previously described.
548–9. "Obstructing" (āvaranti) means they prevent the arising of wholesome states from the very beginning. "Blocking" (nivārenti) means they prevent them entirely.

"Enveloping" (onandhanti) means they cover them as if plunging over them. "Completely enveloping" (pariyonandhanti) means they cover them in every way. [This refers to] the obstructing factors and so forth.

"By way of" means by way of the meanings already stated, such as "obstruction" and so forth. For these [factors], through the power of repeated practice (*āsevana*), each subsequent one reaches a state of being more firm, most firm, and so on, than each preceding one.
Commentary on the Discussion of Correlation (*Saṃsandanakathāvaṇṇanā*)
550. When there is the possession of a woman, a man’s possession of the five strands of sensual pleasure is indeed complete; thus it is said, “by the possession of a woman he is possessed.

And the phrase “by the possession of a woman he is not possessed” is a demonstration that among those Brahmins learned in the three Vedas, the possession they exhibit is the most depraved form of non-possession.
Of such beings as these, the Brahmins learned in the three Vedas...
What is the communion of the brahmins with Brahmā? But Brahmā is entirely without possessions (*aparigraha*).

The intention is: he is free from enmity through a mind free from enmity; how could there be any application of enmity for him? "By what is reckoned as a mental ailment" means by that which is designated as a mental affliction (*cittuppāda-gelañña*);
by this, his state of being free from physical ailment (*rūpakāya-gelañña*) is expressed. "By distress" means by suffering. "By restlessness, remorse, and so forth..."
Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those defiled states associated with it are included.
For this very reason, the statement here—"due to the absence of restlessness and remorse"—is justified as a mention of the mere absence of both of them.

When doubt, which is the cause of non-practice, exists, the mind never remains under the control of the person; but when that [doubt] has been abandoned, the mind may indeed be under the person's control.
He said "of doubt," and so forth, meaning "subject to the round of existence" (vattana). "Gone to the state of mind" means being under the power of the mind. Therefore it was said:

"they act under the sway of the mind. "Not like that" means he is not under the power of the mind as the brahmins are; rather, because of his mastery over meditative absorption and direct knowledge (jhāna-abhiññā), he brings the mind under his own control, thus he is a "master of his will" (vasavattī).
552. "The path to the Brahma-world" means: when the path leading to the Brahma-world is to be entered upon or explained, they explain it;
this is the intended meaning. "Having approached" means: having drawn near by way of wrong practice, or having claimed [to have attained].

"Level ground" means: through the perception [of it as such]; that is, because it is dry for a finger’s breadth or half a finger’s breadth at its surface, there arises the perception that it is level ground.
"Like those who have entered a mire" means as if they had entered a great mire many fathoms deep.
"Entering" means they plunge into the path to the states of loss (apāya), perceiving it as the path to the Brahma-world; for that very reason, having become despondent, they fall into despair.

"In this way" refers to the manner described by the passage beginning with "level ground. "Having become despondent" means having sunk down. "By the mirage" means by the deer-thirst (migataṇhikā) acting as the agent. "Having deceived."
Having deceived them by explaining [the path] as being like a river. "Vāyamānā" means "striving," or this very reading [is acceptable].
"Maññe taranti sukkhataraṇaṃ" means they think they are crossing the crossing of a dry river; this is a statement of division regarding that which is undivided.

Therefore—because those possessing the threefold knowledge (tevijjā) sink away after having approached what is not a path thinking it is "the path"—therefore. "Yathā te" refers to those [who think], "It is level ground."
Beings who have sunk into the mire of perception suffer the breaking and crushing of their hands, feet, and so forth, just as [in the simile].

"In this very life" means in this present personal existence (*attabhāva*). "They do not obtain happiness or pleasure" means they do not obtain the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhānasukha*) or the gratification of insight (*vipassanāsāta*);
what need is there to mention the bliss of the Path (*maggasukha*) or the gratification of Nibbāna? This is the intended meaning.
“Lamp of the Path”: this is precisely what they intended by the term “lamp of the path. “Possessing the Three Vedas” means that which makes known the meaning of the three Vedas.

“Sacred Word” (pāvacana) refers to a recitation accepted as excellent speech. “Of the Brahmins possessing the Three Vedas” is the genitive case used in relation to the connection [between them and the word].
“Iriṇa” is a designation for wildernesses; thus he said, “a great forest without a village. “By trees not fit for enjoyment” means...
What is the use of trees such as *migaruru* and others that are unfit for enjoyment, like those with rotten and other defects? "In which" means in which forest.
They are unable even to turn around because of the dense thickets of great thorny shrubs. The ruin or destruction of kinsmen is "kinsman-ruin" (*ñātibyasana*).
The same applies to the ruin of wealth and the ruin of virtue. Disease itself afflicts or oppresses, thus it is "disease-ruin" (*rogabyasana*).
The same applies to the calamity of wrong view.
To dispel the objection that this meaning is already established by the word *jāta* alone, he says "For he who... and so forth.

The Teacher has stated that one who, having been born, has grown up is "born and grown up" (*jātasaṃvaḍḍha*); alternatively, "he is both born and he is grown up" is "born and grown up" (*jātasaṃvaḍḍha*).
However, it is appropriate [to take it as a compound] because of the posteriority of the qualifier (*visesanaparanipāta*). They are not entirely abandoned because of the absence of complete mastery.
"Long gone" (*ciranikkhanta*) means having gone for a long time. For "one who has long gone" (*ciranikkhanta*) is one who has gone and for whom a long period of time has passed.

Because the meaning is not fully complete with the two words "born and raised" (*jātasaṃvaḍḍha*), the object-case word (*kammapada*) "him" (*tamena*) is connected with "at that very moment he fell away" (*tāvadeva avasaṭa*).
It is further specified as follows: "Sluggishness" (*dandhāyitatta*) refers to dullness or slow functioning in the process of answering;
however, since that involves a delay due to doubt, he says, "delayed state by way of doubt" (*kaṅkhāvasena cirāyitatta*). "Distressed state" (*vitthāyitatta*) means being agitated or embarrassed.
In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is stated with the intention that "distressed state" means stiffness or paralysis.
"Grasping at the state of rigidity" is what was said. This shows the state of being unopposed, because that [knowledge] itself is non-obstructive knowledge.

One might suspect that even this could be obstructed by impediments; therefore, he dispels that doubt with the words "For of that," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by way of the turning of Māra and the like," this includes such things as the delusion of the eye, intoxication, and the time of death.
It is not possible for anyone to create an impediment for it in the four [directions].
Because it is included among the factors that do not constitute an obstacle (anantarāyika-dhamma). 555.
It is stated, "let him extract," because when joined with the prefix *ui*, the word *lumpa* or the word *lupi* has the sense of extraction (*uddharaṇa*).
For verbal roots acquire specific meanings through particular prefixes, just as in the case of the word "taking" (*ādāna*). The word *pajā*.
Because it was understood through the treatises (*pakaraṇa*), he said "the brahmin boy" to indicate that it is within the scope of children.
[Commentary on the Teaching of the Path to the Brahma-world, §§556–7]:
By the word "unprecedented" (*apubba*), he illuminates the reason why it must be praised. One who possesses exceptional power...
"Powerful" means "endowed with strength. One who blows a conch is a "conch-blower," one who causes sound to proceed from it by blowing the conch.
To the question, "What is the purpose of the qualifying terms such as 'powerful'? he says, "For if [the person] were weak," and so forth. The connection is:
"But for one who is powerful, the sound of the conch [is effective]. Only absorption (appanā) is suitable; because it is the direct opposite, it is truly the mind's [antidote].
The intention is that it is stated thus because of its nature as liberation.
"Kamma measured by a limit" refers to sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) kamma, because it does not suppress the defiled states that act as limits.
For such [kamma], being a preliminary stage to the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), transcends a limited measure by way of pervading specific, non-specific, or all directions.
It cannot be increased. Conversely, however, action pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres that has been made immeasurable is what is called "immeasurable.

Therefore he said, "For that," and so forth. In that context, in the immaterial sphere, pervasion by way of specifying or not specifying [an object] is not obtained, nor is pervasion by way of the directions.
Some, however, say, "That is obtained by way of its arrival [in the mind]," but that is incorrect.

For the formless attainments (*ārūppa*) are not the outflow of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), but rather the outflow of the kasiṇas; therefore, that formless attainment which has been well-developed and brought to mastery should be regarded as "immeasurable.

Or else, it is that which is produced by a mental continuum conditioned by an especially intense cultivation of the divine abodes, and that which has been entered upon after emerging from the attainment of the divine abodes.
Others say: "The immaterial-sphere jhāna is made immeasurable by this method, by way of its measure of pervasion.
This should be accepted after investigation.

Regarding "when there is kamma of the fine-material sphere and kamma of the immaterial sphere": when both kamma of the fine-material sphere and kamma of the immaterial sphere exist, [it] does not lag behind.

“It does not remain” means that even karma accumulated in the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), having been overcome and warded off by the sublime meditative absorption (*mahaggata-jjhāna*) attained without loss, remains behind and does not persist in its capacity to grant rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
For the explanatory gloss of “it will not remain” (*na avasissati*) is “it does not linger” (*na ohīyati*); thus, this [phrase]... “not...”
"Remains" is a term for its specific distinction or a synonym for it. Therefore he said, "What is meant [by this]? and so forth.
"To be latched on to" means to be obstructed or hindered. "To stand" means to be established by being capable [of doing so].
"Having pervaded" means having reacted against. "Having exhausted" means having depleted its power. "Having taken up space" means having occupied the opportunity for the giving of its result.
It should be understood that by saying "having taken [it]," he is merely elaborating upon the expression "to cling to or to stand upon.

The phrase "Then indeed" (*atha kho*) and so forth demonstrates the logical implication (*atthāpatti*). Regarding the "exhaustion of the karma" (*kammassa pariyādiyana*), it means that having prevented the arising of its own result, the karma brings about its own result;
thus he says "of that" (*tassā*) and so forth. "Of that" refers to the sensual-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) karma, having warded off its [original] result.

"Only itself" means only kamma pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. The intention is that it leads one to companionship with Brahmā in the absence of such a specific mental aspiration (*cetopaṇidhivisesa*).

For it should be understood that, as in the case of Tissa Brahmā and others, for those of great merit, a sublime kamma accompanied by a specific mental aspiration does not allow limited kamma to obstruct its own result.
Now, how does a limited, light kamma create an opportunity for its own result by warding off the result of a sublime, heavy kamma?
Regarding this, it is said in all three *Vinayagaṇṭhi* sections:
"Jhāna falls away through the power of craving alone; because jhāna has fallen away from that state, the limited kamma gains an opportunity. However, some say:
They say: "The loss of jhāna due to an inclination toward a state free from hindrances should be understood after careful investigation.

This is the more appropriate reason here: even when there is a limited (paritta) kamma capable of obstructing the ripening of a sublime (mahaggata) kamma, [jhāna arises] because of the statement, "Bhikkhus, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of the purity of his virtue," in the realm of sense-desire (kāmabhava).
The mental aspiration (cetopaṇidhi) obstructs the ripening of a sublime kamma and creates an opportunity for the ripening of a limited kamma.

Thus, "one who dwells in loving-kindness and so forth" means one who dwells by way of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra), such as loving-kindness and the rest, which have reached absorption (appanā) according to the method already stated.
559. Regarding the statement, "Having first compared it with the second, what is this that is being compared?", it says "the very first," and so forth.
The connection [of the sentence] is established by supplying the words "recited in the Majjhimapaṇṇāsaka. Taking refuge again and again makes it more firm and brings greater fruit;
therefore, it should be understood that he took the second going for refuge as well.
"After a few days" means after two or three days had passed. "Having gone forth" means having received the novice ordination (*sāmaṇera-pabbajjā*). The *Aggaññasutta* is also this very same one.
It was spoken concerning Vāseṭṭha and no one else; this is indicated by the words “in the Aggañña Sutta,” and so forth.

The meaning is that, according to the method set forth therein, they both received and attained full ordination (*upasampadā*) and Arahantship. Whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning is indeed easy to understand.
Thus [ends] the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, which elucidates meanings that are exceedingly subtle, profound, and difficult to comprehend;

which generates the clarity of vast and stainless wisdom; and which was composed by one endowed with the qualities of integrity, gentleness, fortitude, faith, mindfulness, steadfastness, intelligence, patience, and energy;

who possesses unimpeded, unshakeable, and confident knowledge regarding the three Pitakas together with their commentaries; and who has plunged into the depths of the manifold varieties of his own and other systems.
The elucidation of the hidden meaning of the *Tevijja-sutta* commentary, titled *Sādhuvilāsini*,
composed by the Great Elder named Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati— a great leader of the assembly, a great expounder, and the venerable preceptor of the Great King of Dharma—
is hereby concluded. The sub-commentary on the *Tevijja-sutta* is finished.
In this regard, here is what constitutes the excellence of the *Sādhuvilāsini* commentary upon the *Sādhuvilāsinī*:
"The phrasing and the meaning, as well as the exposition in every respect—
since these are stated by one who is a master [of the subject], there is nothing lacking therein."
Because she brings various delights to the virtuous who are wise and discerning,
thereby gladdening their hearts, she is called "the virtuous courtesan" (sādhuvilāsinī).
— The Concluding Statement.
And to this extent,
this commentary on the Sīlakkhandha has been undertaken for the sake of proficiency in the True Dhamma and for the growth of the Dispensation.
The section named *Sādhuvilāsinī* is entirely completed;
it measures slightly more than fifty recitation units (*bhāṇavāra*).
It concerns the one who broke many embankments and possessed infinite strength and vehicles.
The king named Sirīpavarādī, lord of various realms,
built in the delightful land of Jambudīpa, within the province of Maramma,
a city called Amarapura in the district of Tambadīpa.
Neighboring Mount Maṇḍala, situated on the Erāvatī River,
a dwelling place for various people adorned with golden palaces— there he,
having attained consecration, ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma.
He built the Great Stupa of Rājagāra with serene devotion.
Abandoning what was contrary to the Dhamma and contrary to the Vinaya,
he purified the teaching of the Conqueror according to reality, always with a firm mind.
In that very delightful place, provided with shade and water,
enclosed by a double wall, and worthy of those who delight in meditation—
there, the designation "Great Sage" was bestowed upon him in the presence of the Fully Awakened One.
From that palace, facing straight toward the south and nearby,
in the Asokārāma monastery, within a great five-storied hall called Ratanabhūmikitti,
adorned with the Dhamma-palace— there stands the image.
Likewise, for the Southern Queen, [a monastery] was built near the city,
named Jayabhūmi and Kittābhidhāna in the northeast; and similarly,
for the Northern Queen, one was built within the city.
Near the Soṇṇaguha Thūpa, in the place named Parimāṇaka;
likewise, in the western part of the city built by the viceroy,
near the Mahāguha Thūpa, in the place named Maṅgalāvāsa.
Thus, by turn, he resided in many monasteries made of gold;
honored by all kings, he received their official seals three times.
He was widely renowned as Ñāṇābhivaṃsa Dhammasenāpati.
Having mastered the *Dvevibhaṅga* and other texts, he attained the status of preceptor and teacher.
He was the reciter of the Dhamma for the monks who had come from the island of Laṅkā as well as those residing in foreign lands, and he was their guide in practice.
This monarch, by whom the Dispensation was purified,
has composed this commentary, perfect in both meaning and phrasing.
Forty-five years after the Parinibbāna of the Perfectly Enlightened One—
When two thousand three hundred years had passed,
this beautiful commentary on the *Netti*, known as the *Peṭakālaṅkāra*, was successfully completed.
Whatever merit has been generated by me while compiling this work— may it [be for the welfare of all].
By this merit, having attained supreme enlightenment,
may I deliver many beings and liberate them from the bonds of existence.
May kings always protect these people through the Dhamma alone.
Devoted to meritorious deeds, may they illuminate the teaching of the Conqueror.
And may all these living beings, at all times free from affliction and always possessed of noble intentions, attain the state of the Deathless.
Thus ends the new commentary named *Sādhuvilāsinī*, being the exposition of the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* of the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*.
The new commentary on the *Sīlakkhandhavagga* is completed.
